units.la: AVET in tuam (Vir Honoratissime) fidem & clientelam se conferre hoc quicquid est opusculi, ut sub tui[?] nominis præsidio prodeat in vulgus. Ad te igitur ipsum affero, iubens merito: Ad te, inquam, hominem, ut ex aliis audio, (& est perraro mendax in melius fama,) cùm natalium[?] splendore illustrem; tum generosæ mentis indole, amore literarum, humanitate, pietate, & omnium virtutum genere multò etiam illustriorem: mihi tamen (delitescenti nimirum in parvâ casulâ suaviter, nec quid rerum foris geratur, præsertim ut nunc sunt tempora, multùm solicito) de facie nunquam, ante paucos menses, nec de nomine quidem, adeóque ne nunc tandem, nisi sola munificentiæ notum. Est tamen, quod sperem habituram aliquam apud te gratiam tenue hoc munusculum: ex eo scilicet, quod me, jamdiu rude donatum (proposito per virum insigniter doctum Thomam Barloum[?], armarii Bodleiani in alma Oxoniensi Academia Protobibliothecarium, honesto salario) conatus es, iterum antiquo includere ludo; & tum sponte meâ ad aliquid scribendum quod domo exeat pigrum satis, tum factum jam, ut in senectâ ætate par est, multò etiam pigriorem, in eandem arenam denuò pellicere. Bonum factum: quod in hoc tam luctuoso Civilium pariter & & Ecclesiasticarum rerum statu, (nisi sit nefas statum dicere, quæ mera ἀκαταστασία[?] sit, & perturbatissima rerum omnium confusio,) unus aliquis fortè melioris luti, & alter repertus fuerit, qui tristes Musas Musarumque quocunque in genere alumnos, maximè qui veræ & Christianæ Philosophiæ professores, spretos ubique & velut mundi retrimenta abjectos, curet alloquio aliquo, aut levamine solari. Si quid igitur (Deo Opt. Max. donante) posthac mihi in hoc genere scriptionis, hoc est, quod ad Moralem Theologiam pertineat, tentatum editúmque fuerit, sive id Latino idiomate fiat, sive (quod sentio effe plerisque nostratium aliquanto optatius) vernaculo, quod aut in publicum utile, aut privato cuivis homini, ad vitam rectè instituendam, moresque ex Divinæ Legis & Evangelii præscripto efformandos, usui esse poterit: id tibi plurima ex parte acceptum ferri debere, & agnosco lubens, & libere profiteor; qui mihi & ut auderem author fuisti, & ut alacrius pergerem adjutor. Perge & tu, Vir dignissime, benefacere: hoc est, quod satisfacere; literas ornare, literatos fovere, pietatem colere, fidos tibi ex infidi Mammonæ impendio amicos comparare; ut ex ubere bonorum operum in hoc sæculo semente, ingens tibi surgat æternæ beatitatis messis in sæculo futuro, Amen.
units.tr: This little work of mine, whatever it is, wishes (Most Honourable Sir) to place itself under your trust and protection, so that under the shelter of your name it may come forth to the public. So it is to you that I bring it, and rightly so. To you, I say, a man who, as I hear from others (and rarely is report about someone better), is distinguished by the splendour of your birth, and far more distinguished by the nobility of your mind, your love of letters, your humanity, your piety and every kind of virtue. Yet to me, who lie hidden in my small cottage, living quietly and not greatly troubled about what goes on abroad, especially in these times, you were until a few months ago known by sight never, and not even by name, and so, until now, known only by your generosity. Still, there is something that makes me hope this slight little gift will win some favour with you. You have tried, with the help of a man of notable learning, Thomas Barlow, the honest salary and the post of chief librarian of the Bodleian library in the nourishing Academy of Oxford, to put me, long since a retired gladiator, back into the old game, and to coax me back into the same arena, both to write something for publication, which I was lazy enough about of my own accord, and now, having grown much lazier, as is fitting at my age. Well done: in this so lamentable state of civil and ecclesiastical affairs (unless it is wrong to call a state what is pure disorder [ἀκαταστασία] and the most utter confusion of all things), it has perhaps been found that some one man of better clay, and another, have taken care to address the sad Muses, and the followers of the Muses in whatever field, most of all those who are professors of true and Christian philosophy, who are everywhere scorned and cast off like the rubbish of the world, with some word of comfort or solace. If therefore, with God the Best and Greatest granting it, anything shall hereafter be attempted and published by me in this kind of writing, that is, what pertains to moral theology, whether it be done in the Latin tongue or (which I think is much more desirable to most of our countrymen) in the vernacular, and it can be of use either to the public or to any private person in ordering his life aright and forming his manners according to the prescription of the Divine Law and the Gospel, I gladly acknowledge and freely declare that this must be credited to you in very large part, since you were both the one who encouraged me to dare and the one who helped me to proceed more eagerly. Go on, most worthy Sir, in doing good: that is, in giving satisfaction, adorning letters, cherishing learned men, cultivating piety, and winning for yourself faithful friends out of the expense of faithless Mammon; so that from the rich seed of good works sown in this age, a great harvest of eternal blessedness may rise up for you in the age to come. Amen.

units.la: IN primo statim Limine mihi conveniendus es, quisquis es, amice Lector, orandúsque, ut partiare te paucis ante doceri, quàm in ipsas ædes intuleris pedem, quæ nos causa, ad isthæc quæ nunc damus evulganda, potissimùm impulerit. Equidem, si per alios licuisset, inedita malui. Cui rei vel hoc unum satis magno argumento esse posset; quod Prælectiones, aliquot ante annos mihi commentatæ, uno plus decennio ne pluteum quidem servaverint; sed sparsim in angulis inter rejectitias & nihili chartas neglectæ jacuerint: nisi mihi aliud suppeteret gravioris momenti argumentum, & quod suo indicio prodit, Operis ipsius imperfectio. Scriptorem enim oportet, qui sapit, dignitatique suæ & existimationi consultum cupit, inceptum opus ad umbilicum perducere; nec prius de emittendo cogitare, quàm fuerit (ut Cicerone loquar) aptum undique, perfectum, expletúmque omnibus suis partibus & numeris. Siquidem frùstra inde laudem speres, unde pulchrè tecum actum putes, si pro laude veniam mereare.
units.tr: On the very first threshold, I must meet you, whoever you are, kind reader, and I must beg you to be told a few things before you set foot inside the house itself, which led me to publish these things that I now give out. Indeed, if it had been possible through others, I would have preferred to leave them unpublished. One thing alone could serve as a sufficiently strong argument for this, namely that the Lectures, which I prepared some years ago, have not kept even a shelf for more than ten years, but have lain neglected, scattered in corners among discarded and worthless papers; unless another argument of greater weight were available to me, one which reveals itself by its own evidence: the imperfection of the work itself. For a writer who is wise, and who wishes to protect his dignity and reputation, ought to bring a begun work to completion, and should not think of releasing it until it is (to use Cicero's words) fitted in every way, perfect, and complete in all its parts and measures. For you will vainly hope for praise from that quarter where you think you have been treated handsomely, if instead of praise you deserve pardon.

units.tr: PREFACE.

units.la: Quid ergo ? Amicine in causa ? Qui solent ultrò currentem in hæc fata fortiùs impellere, cunctanti stimulos subjicere ? Ne hoc quidem dederim. Commune enim illud ple-rorumque scripturientium confugium, (amicorum dico hortatus & vota,) ut concedam habere posse nonnunquam honestæ excusationis locum, sic mihi nunquam habere visum est justæ & idoneæ causæ instar. Sed nec defuere tamen (sic enim fieri amat,) [illegible, ~8 letters], qui rogarent, & (ut Fabii verbis utar) quotidiano convitio efflagitarent, ut quæ ipsorum auribus inter prælegendum haud ingra-ta fuissent, omnium oculis legenda subjicerem. Ergo contra, non ignarus quanto effet acrius oculorum quàm aurium judicium, id me facturum constanter pernego. Instare illi vehementius, & urgere porrò; leniter etiam, ut fit, succensere: Ego, cui decretum erat esse pertinaci, non muto. Quicquid enim illi intentarent, aderat mihi semper in promptu quod opponerem; non esse emittendum opus inchoatum, necdum dimidiá[?], forte an vix tertia sui parte, absolutum. Sed nec illis minus in promptu quod regerent: Quid ergo cessas, inquiunt ? Quin accingis te operi, & quam occœpisti telam pertexis ocyus.
units.tr: What then? Was it friends who pressed me in this matter? Those who are wont to drive headlong one who is already running eagerly toward these fates, and to add goads to one who hesitates? I would not even grant that. For that common refuge of most authors who are itching to write (I mean the urging and wishes of friends) may, I concede, sometimes furnish a respectable excuse, but it has never seemed to me to amount to a just and adequate reason. Yet they were not lacking (for that is how it tends to happen) [illegible] who asked, and (to use Fabius' words) demanded with daily clamour that I place before the eyes of all what had not been unwelcome to their ears while I read it aloud. Therefore, on the contrary, not unaware of how much sharper the judgement of the eyes is than that of the ears, I firmly refused that I would do this. They pressed more vehemently and urged further, and gently too, as happens, they grew angry. I, who had resolved to be stubborn, did not give way. For whatever they threatened, I always had at hand something to oppose: that an unfinished work, not yet half complete, perhaps scarcely a third of it finished, ought not to be sent out. But they had no less at hand to reply: Why then do you delay? Why not gird yourself to the work and weave the web you have begun more quickly?

units.tr: ...is truer, unless some necessity compels it, which at that time, as a former professor, I had none; it cannot be done. Doubtless, like a lazy soldier whom only desperation makes brave, he is at last fiercely driven into battle when no place of escape is left: such is my nature. Give me leisure, room, time! Nothing gets done. Pens are vexed in vain. The mind scatters, wanders, runs off, grows numb. Force me into a tight corner! It halts, is roused, and gathers its strength; and whatever strength it has, since effort is needed, it puts forth entirely: and in a word, what must be done, it does. As the rays of the sun, spread over the broad and open sky, warm so gently that one hardly feels them, yet the same rays gathered into the hollow of a concave mirror, as into a focus, burn fiercely. units.la: Quod ignavæ mentis vitium, etsi nonnullis fortasse videri possit habere modestiæ speciem aliquam, mihi tamen unâ hac idoneâ excusatione defendi posse videtur, quod sit certis quibusdam hominibus, (& ego in hac cen- su.) ἐμφυὲς γὰρ συγγενὲς ἦθος, ita congenitum insitumque ab ipsis cunabulis, ut frustra sit, quisquis ex illo numero id ullâ speret à se posse, vel arte corrigi, vel industriâ superari.
units.tr: This failing of a lazy mind, though to some perhaps it may seem to have some appearance of modesty, nevertheless seems to me to be defensible by this one fitting excuse: that it belongs to certain people (and I am among them) (ἐμφυὲς γὰρ συγγενὲς ἦθος) [a natural, innate disposition], so congenital and implanted from the very cradle that whoever from that number hopes to correct it by any art, or overcome it by industry, hopes in vain.

Non aliunde sanè, inquam, quàm ex ipsa hac, de qua proximè, sermo fuit, quaeque in rebus humanis longè lateque dominatur, Necessitate.
units.tr: You will perhaps press me, for so far I have said nothing certain and we keep coming back to the same point. If, as you say, you are so naturally idle and so stubborn toward your friends, then where on earth did this edition come from? Not from anywhere else, I say, than from that very thing we discussed a moment ago, which holds sway far and wide over human affairs: Necessity.

units.tr: To spare you any further delay, I will lay out the whole matter briefly. J. A., a London bookseller, broke all that obstinacy you speak of, as if with a single blow. He wrote to me in a letter that two copies of these Lectures had been brought to him, that they were then in his hands and kept at his house, and that those who had brought them had also urged him to see to it, or at least arrange, that they be committed to print; and he said he would not do so unless I consented. Yet he warned that, since other copies also existed elsewhere, it could hardly be guaranteed, if I myself were negligent, that they would not be published by someone else without my knowledge. I praised, indeed I loved, in a man until then wholly unknown to me, his candour of mind, and that kind of regard for fairness which, in most men of his trade, is hardly anything but a pursuit of gain. I therefore wrote back that he should simply send me one of the two copies, namely…

Ἐλικτὰ πάν-τα [illegible, ~6 letters] ὑμῖν[?]. Præter eas enim quæ ab exscriptore mendas passim innumeras, eorum etiam quæ à meipso primâ illâ meditatione, dum festinaret calamus, scripta fuerunt, non pauca, incudi denuò reddenda videbantur. Hinc mihi duram sensi obortam molestiam, quæ tamen perferenda erat; totius operis de novo describendi tædium. Pertuli, descripsi, perfeci; ut potui, & (si ultra vires nemo debitor est) ut debui: Si non ut volui. hanc unam rem à te, ut æquam peto; imò ut (facienti quod in se est) debitam postulo, Veniam.
units.tr: That is, it seemed to him more elegantly and correctly copied, while I in the meantime would consider what use I might make of it. What more? It came; I read it, I weighed it. Ἐλικτὰ πάντα [illegible] ὑμῖν[?] For apart from the countless blunders here and there made by the copyist, a number of things written by myself in that first draft, when the pen was hurrying, also seemed to need to be reworked at the anvil. Hence I felt a troublesome annoyance arise, which nonetheless had to be endured: the tedium of copying out the whole work afresh. I endured it, I copied it out, I completed it; as well as I could, and (since no one is bound beyond his strength) as I ought: if not as I wished. This one thing I ask of you, as fair-minded; indeed, I demand it as due (since he does what lies in him), Pardon.

units.tr: Question: Do human laws bind the conscience? (7, etc.) First conclusion: unjust laws do not bind the conscience. This is explained (9) and confirmed (10). Second conclusion: a human law can superadd a new obligation to a prior obligation (12, etc.). Third conclusion: a law enacted by one who does not have lawful power does not bind (15, etc.). What becomes the duty of a subject, where one who no longer holds power commands in fact, is discussed at length (22). Fourth conclusion: human laws bind per se in general (23), and in particular also by consequence (24, etc.), which is confirmed in various ways (31, etc.). An objection is met, drawn from the liberty of the Christian man (36), and likewise the one drawn from the single Lawgiver, God and Christ (37), as also the remaining arguments that are disputed against this opinion.

units.la: PRÆLECTIO PRIMA. IN Qua proponitur & explicatur Con- scientiæ Definitio.
units.tr: LECTURE I. In which the definition of conscience is set forth and explained.

units.la: I COR. II. 11.
Quis hominum novit quæ sunt hominis, nisi Spiritus hominis qui est in ipso?
units.tr: Who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him?

units.la: PErmagnam esse {*} vim Conscientiæ in utramque (fiduciæ metúsque) partem & prudentes viri olim docuerunt, & satis attestatur proprius cujusque sensus & experientia. Quò magis dolendum est, plerosque mortalium, dum rerum mediocriter utilium Scientiam anxiè venantur, in tam crassa interim conscientiæ suæ ignorationc versari. Quâ tamen non est alius quisquam, aut monitor fidelior, aut accusator diligentior, aut testis gravior, aut judex incorruptior, aut solator jucundior, aut hostis importunior. Ut itaque decantatum illud jam olim γνῶθι σεαυτόν[?] studiosorum auribus & mentibus instillarem, ipsóque ab inanis scientiæ nimiâ cupiditate modicè diverterem, & ad majorem Conscientiæ curam cultúmque sensim invitarem; existimavi operæ me facturum pretium, si in Conscientiæ
units.tr: It has long been taught by wise men that conscience has great power, both to encourage and to terrify, and each person's own feeling and experience bear sufficient witness to this. It is all the more regrettable that most mortals, while eagerly hunting after knowledge of moderately useful things, remain in such gross ignorance of their conscience. Yet there is no one more faithful a monitor, more diligent an accuser, more weighty a witness, more incorruptible a judge, more pleasant a comforter, or more troublesome an enemy. Therefore, in order to instil into the ears and minds of students that long-repeated saying, "know thyself" [γνῶθι σεαυτόν], and to draw them gently away from an excessive desire for empty learning, and to invite them little by little to a greater care and cultivation of conscience, I judged that I would be doing a worthwhile task if I inquired a little more carefully into the nature and use of conscience, and shared with you, my hearers, from this place, in keeping with my office, the things that occurred to me in meditating on the matter and were worth knowing.

units.la: Naturam & Usum paulò diligentiùs inquirerem, & quæ mihi in eam rem scitu digna meditanti occurriffent, vobis auditoribus pro officii mei ratione, ex hoc loco communicarem. Statui igitur hac prælectione Conscientiæ Naturam definiendo explicare: expositurus futuris lectionibus (si Deus concesserit[?]) Conscientiæ, maximè quà facienda spectat, Usum & Officia, idque per duplicem respectum; priorem sc. ad normam legis cui subesse debet, posteriorem ad actus humanos quibus nata est præesse.
units.tr: I have therefore resolved in this lecture to explain the nature of conscience by defining it, and in the lectures to come (God willing) to set out the use and duties of conscience, especially as they concern what is to be done, and to do so under a twofold respect: the first, namely, in relation to the rule of law to which it ought to be subject; the second, in relation to the human acts over which it was born to preside.

units.la: II. Sed quum sit duplex methodus definitiva, altera συνθετικὴ & ad Compositionis modum, quæ præmissa singularum partium expensione, integram tandem colligit definitionem; altera ἀναλυτικὴ & per modum Resolutionis, quæ propositam ab initio integram definitionem postea membratim aperit & explicat: etsi prior illa videri forsitan[?] possit ordini naturæ convenientior, delegi tamen[?] potiùs posteriorem, quæ visa est mihi ad docendum aliquanto commodior. Sic ergo breviter definio Conscientiam: Conscientia est facultas, sive habitus intellectus practici, quo mens hominis per discursum rationis applicat lumen quod sibi adest, ad particulares suos actus morales. Ubi considerandi veniunt suo ordine; Primò Definiti nomen, nimirum ipsa Conscientiæ vox: deinde singula definitionis membra; illa videlicet omnia, quæ in definiendis primæ vel secundæ speciei Qualitatibus adhiberi solent, Genus, Subjectum, Objectum, & Actus Proprius.
units.tr: II. But since there are two methods of definition, one synthetic [συνθετικὴ] and by way of composition, which, after a prior examination of the individual parts, at last gathers together the whole definition; and the other analytic [ἀναλυτικὴ] and by way of resolution, which, having set out the whole definition at the start, afterwards opens it up and explains it part by part: although the former may perhaps seem more in keeping with the order of nature, I have nonetheless chosen the latter, which seems to me somewhat more convenient for teaching. So I define conscience briefly thus: Conscience is a faculty, or habit, of the practical intellect, by which the mind of man, through the discourse of reason, applies the light that is present to it to its own particular moral acts. In this definition the following come to be considered in their proper order: first, the name of the thing defined, namely the very word conscientia; then the several members of the definition, that is, all those things which are usually employed in defining qualities of the first or second kind: genus, subject, object, and proper act.

units.la: III. Definiti nomen quod attinet, observârunt viri docti non reperiri in Veteri Instrumento vocem Hebræam, quæ Conscientiam peculiariter & præcisè significet: sed ex usu loquendi Hebræorum, quoties de Conscientiâ sermo est, ad eam denotandam assumi fere duarum dictionum alterutram ידע[?] sive רוח[?], quarum illam proprié Cor, hanc Spiritum. ritum significare sciunt omnes. Illud Salomonis Prov. 4. Supra omnem custodiam custodi cor tuum, perinde est ac si dixisset, Conscientiæ suæ cuique præcipua cura esto. Itidem Eccles. 7. pro eo quod habet vetus interpres Latinus, Scit conscientia tua, quia & tu crebro maledixisti aliis; & Tremellii versio, Conscius est animus tuus; in textu Hebraico est ידע לבך [?] i. e. Novit cor tuum. Quin & in Novo Testamento, (præsertim apud Johannem Apostolum, in cujus Scriptis multi sunt passim Hebraismi) συνείδησις [?] aliquoties pro Conscientia ponitur, ut 1 Joh. 3. Si cor nostrum non condemnet nos. Cor nostrum, i. e. Conscientia nostra: cujus utique proprium munus est stantem pro tribunali reum condemnare vel non condemnare. Unde illa trita satis Bernardi & aliorum allusio, Conscientia quasi cordis scientia. Spiritus etiam nomine in sacris scriptoribus, Hebræis pariter & Græcis, frequenter appellatur Conscientia. Afferam duo tantum loca; quid enim opus est pluribus, cum isthæc sint apertissima? Ex veteri Testamento, Salomonis dictum Prov. 18. 14. Spiritus viri sustentabit infirmitatem ipsius: Spiritum autem confractum quis sustinebit? quasi dicat, Qui integra est conscientia quæcunque tandem ipsi contigerint mala, forti ea animo perferre poterit; sed est fracta & afflicta conscientia onus importabile. Ex novo Testamento pariter, illud Pauli (præsentis diatribæ Thema & fundamentum) 1. Cor. 2. 11. Quis novit quæ sunt hominis, nisi spiritus hominis qui est in eo? i. e. Nisi propria cujusque Conscientia.
units.tr: III. As regards the name of the thing defined, learned men have observed that there is no Hebrew word in the Old Testament which signifies conscience in a peculiar and exact sense; but from the usage of the Hebrews, whenever there is talk of conscience, one of two words is commonly taken to denote it, yada [ידע] or ruach [רוח], of which the former properly means heart, the latter spirit; all know this. That saying of Solomon, Prov. 4: Keep your heart above all keeping, is just as if he had said, "Let each man's chief care be for his own conscience." Likewise Eccles. 7: where the old Latin translator has, Your conscience knows, for you too have often cursed others, and Tremellius's version, Your mind is conscious; in the Hebrew text it is yada levavcha [ידע לבך], that is, your heart knows. Indeed, even in the New Testament (especially in the Apostle John, in whose writings there are many Hebraisms here and there), syneidesis [συνείδησις] is sometimes put for conscience, as in 1 John 3: If our heart does not condemn us: "our heart," that is, our conscience, whose proper office surely is to condemn or not to condemn the guilty man who stands before its tribunal. Hence that somewhat hackneyed allusion of Bernard and others, conscience as it were the knowledge of the heart. In the sacred writers, both Hebrew and Greek, conscience is frequently also called by the name spirit. I will cite only two passages; for why need there be more, when these are most plain? From the Old Testament, the saying of Solomon, Prov. 18:14: The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a broken spirit who can bear? As if he said, "One whose conscience is whole may bear with a brave heart whatever evils may befall him; but a broken and afflicted conscience is an intolerable burden." From the New Testament, likewise, that saying of Paul (the theme and foundation of the present discourse), 1 Cor. 2:11: Who knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him? That is, "except each man's own conscience."

units.la: IV. Latinorum autem Conscientia, & quæ ei per omnia respondet Græcorum Συνείδησις [?], à Scientia aperte utraque nomen accepit. Sed simplici Scientia adjecta utrobique in compositione Præpositio, amplius aliquid indicat in his vocibus & ulterius, quàm in ipso Scientiæ vocabulo, contineri: quod quid fit ab authoribus varie explicatur. Misfis duabus illis rationibus, quæ à nonnullis afferuntur, (quæ si naturam rei ipsius spestemus retineri fortassis possunt, ut allusiones haud omnino incommodæ ; ad limam verò & ἀνεξέτασις[?] legitimæ notationis revocatæ, ineptè protinus reperiuntur nec dignæ quibus immoremur : ) Conscientia quasi cordis Scientia ; & Conscientia quasi concludens Scientia : illud imprimis certum est, duo hæc vocabula Συνείδησιν[?] & Conscientiam, ultra nudam Scientiæ notionem, dicere etiam ordinem quendam & relationem istius Scientiæ ad aliud. Quippe ea vis est particularum Σύν & Con, ut in compositione significent rerum plurium conjunctionem quandam & associationem : ut sit Conscientia, quasi conjunctio multorum Scientiæ. Quod & ipsum dupliciter contingit intelligi. Potest enim dici Multorum scientia, vel ut subjectorum, quasi dicas Multorum Scientium Scientia : nempe cum multæ personæ eandem rem pariter sciunt : Vel ut Objectorum, quasi dicas Multorum Scitorum Scientia, nempe cum eadem persona multas res pariter scit. Sive hoc, sive illo modo accipiatur vox Conscientiæ; reddi potest ratio nominis, (sive rem ipsam spectemus, sive usum loquendi apud probatos authores) nec aliena multum, nec incongrua.
units.tr: IV. The Latin conscientia, and the Greek syneidesis [Συνείδησις], which corresponds to it in every respect, plainly both took their name from scientia (knowledge). But when the simple scientia is joined in composition with a preposition in both languages, these words indicate something more, and that something more is contained in them beyond the bare word scientia; what this is is explained variously by authors. Setting aside those two explanations which some offer (which, if we consider the nature of the thing itself, may perhaps be retained as not wholly unsuitable allusions, but when brought to the file and to the strict test of proper derivation [ἀνεξέτασις] they are at once found to be absurd and not worth dwelling upon), namely conscience as it were the knowledge of the heart and conscience as it were a concluding knowledge: this is above all certain, that the two words syneidesis [Συνείδησιν] and conscientia, beyond the mere notion of knowledge, also express a certain order and relation of that knowledge to something else. For indeed the force of the particles syn and con in composition is to signify a certain joining and association of several things; so that conscientia is as it were the joining together of the knowledge of many. This too can be understood in two ways. For it may be called the knowledge of many, either of subjects, as if you said the knowledge of many knowers; namely when several persons know the same thing together; or of objects, as if you said the knowledge of many things known, namely when one and the same person knows many things together. Whichever way the word conscience is taken, the reason for the name can be given (whether we look to the thing itself or to the usage of approved authors), and it is neither much foreign nor incongruous.

units.la: V. Primò enim, cum multi idem sciunt, & Conscire dici possunt, & Conscii dici solent : Sic conscii conjurationis Catilinariæ dicti sunt, quos ille in sceleris societatem delegit, & consilii sui participavit. Et conscius arcanorum Regis dicitur, cui cognita sunt & concredita occulta ipsius consilii. — Ascitus in conscientiam facinoris, in Annalibus Taciti. — ¹ O si conscius esset hic Avitus, in Epigrammatis Martialis. ²Conscia Matri Virgo fuit, in Satyris Juvenalis. Eorum omnium consiliorum periculorumque testis conscius & adjutor, in orationi-bus [?]bus Ciceronis. Infinitum esset omnia colligere, quæ in hanc rem inter legendum optimæ notæ Scriptores passim occurrent. Sed isthæc satis: nisi forte à me exigitis, ut aliquid saltem quod huc facit à Grammaticorum lacunis depromam. Fiet: non quod tanti valere debeat apud nos ístorum hominum authoritas, sed quod hisce in rebus Dictaturam sibi, quasi jure quodam suo, arrogare solent. In hoc differunt Scius & Conscius (Nonium auditis) Scius secum, Conscius cum alio scius est. Ex hac vocis originatione, qui Conscientiam dictam putant, quasi cum alio scientiam, non aliam assignare poterunt sententiæ suæ rationem idoneam, quàm quòd non homo solus novit quæ sunt à se facta, sed & Deum, qui scrutatur corda & renes, habeat omnium operum suorum, imò & abditissimarum cogitationum, conscium testem & inspectorem. Res omnino certissima, quicquid de voce fiat. Ecce in cœlis testis meus est, & conscius meus ([?]) in excelsis. Job 16. 19. Beatus etiam Paulus, Rom. 9. 1. cum Christum advocasset testem veritatis eorum quæ mox dicturus erat, subnectit continuò συμμαρτυρούσης μοι τῆς συνειδήσεως, testimonium simul perhibente mihi conscientia. Ac si dixisset οἶδν ὁ Χριστὸς, σύνοιδα κἀγώ. Scit Christus, ego etiam conscio: μαρτυρεῖ ὁ Χριστὸς, συμμαρτυρεῖ ἡ συνείδησις. Testatur Christus, contestatur & conscientia. Esto igitur hæc prima vocis ratio: Conscientiam ex eo dici, quòd facta hominis sint ipsi cognita simul, & Deo.
units.tr: V. First, then, since many men know the same thing, they can be said conscire, to be privy, and are commonly called conscii, privy. Thus those were called conscii of the Catilinarian conspiracy whom he chose for the fellowship of his crime and made sharers in his plan. And one is called conscius of the king's secrets to whom the hidden counsels of the king are known and entrusted. — Admitted to the knowledge of the crime, in the Annals of Tacitus. — Oh, if Avitus were here, privy to it, in the Epigrams of Martial. The virgin was privy to her mother's plan, in the Satires of Juvenal. A witness privy to and helper in all those plans and dangers, in the orations of Cicero. It would be endless to gather together everything that occurs in this matter, passim, in the writers of the best repute as one reads them. But these are enough, unless perhaps you demand of me that I bring forward at least something which bears on this from the quibbles of the grammarians. I will do so: not because the authority of such men ought to count for much with us, but because in such matters they are wont to arrogate to themselves a kind of dictatorship, as if by some right of their own. Scius and conscius differ in this (as you hear from Nonius): scius is one who knows for himself; conscius is one who knows along with another. From this derivation of the word, those who think conscientia is so called as if it were knowledge with another will be able to assign no other suitable reason for their opinion than that not only does a man alone know what things have been done by himself, but God too, who searches the heart and the reins, has as witness and observer of all his works, and even of his most hidden thoughts, a conscius. This is wholly certain, whatever is made of the word itself. Behold, my witness is in heaven, and my conscius is on high (Job 16:19). The blessed Paul too, Rom. 9:1, when he had called Christ to witness the truth of what he was about to say, immediately adds synmartyrousēs moi tēs syneidēseōs [συμμαρτυρούσης μοι τῆς συνειδήσεως], conscience bearing witness together with me. As if he had said, Christ knows, and I too am conscious: Christ bears witness, conscience bears witness with him. Let this, therefore, be the first reason for the word: that conscience is so called because the deeds of a man are known at the same time both to himself and to God.

units.la: VI. Altero modo dicitur conjuncta plurium Scientia, velut Objectorum, sive Scitorum: cum scilicet unusquisque plura simul scit, vel (quod eodem recidit) plures notitias, distinctas licet, conjungit tamen & invicem applicat. Unde oritur secunda vocis ratio, quæ placuit Thomæ & plerisque Scholasticorum; &, quod ad eruendam Conscientiæ naturam & vim facem præferat haud inutilem, al-teri illi jam dictæ merito præferendā videtur: nempe Conscientiam propterea dici, quia scientiæ scientiæ conjungit ; scientiam sc. Universalem, sive Juris, scientiæ Particularis, sive Facti, applicando hanc ad illam. Uno & altero adducto exemplo rem illustrabo, 1 Sam. 24. 6. Davidem, dicitur, cor ipsius cecidisse, postquam alam vestimenti Saulis abscidisset in spelunca : hoc est, pupugit eum conscientia sua. Putemus nimirum Davidem apud animum suum ita locutum ; Scio non debere vim afferri sacræ personæ Regiæ, Scio etiam id nuperrimè à me factum quod à vi inferendâ perparum abesse videtur: vereor itaque ne fecerim quod fote non debuerim, & gratias ago Deo meo qui menum meam abstinuit ne facerem quod certè non debueram. Sic Judæ proditori objecit conscientia sua: Nosti dominum non fuisse prodendum, & idem nosti te eum turpiter prodidisse. Accedente hunc in modum universali illi Juris notitiæ quæ est in mente, Facti etiam particularis (admissi scilicet, vel admittendi) notitiâ, eique conjunctâ & applicatâ, & cum eâ collatâ, exsurgit totum illud quod dicimus Conscientiam. Firmant hanc nominis rationem id genus locutiones, quæ per modum reciprocationis efferuntur, & sunt in hoc genere frequentissimæ: Cujusmodi sunt Isocraticum illud {1}'ἀ[?] τῶν ἄλλων λόγης[?], σαυτῷ συνειδήσεις, Ut alios late-re possis, tute tibi conscius eris. Horatianum itidem illud, {2}——— Hic murus aheneus esto, Nil conscire[?] sibi, ——& Virgilianum, {3}——Mens quæ sibi conscia recti. Paulinum illud denique (ne sit opus plura, & aliunde, congerere,) οὐδὲν ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα, Nihil mihi conscius sum, 1. Cor. 4. 4.
units.tr: VI. In a second sense, the term means a combined knowledge of several things, as of objects or known matters: when someone knows several things at once, or (which comes to the same) joins together and mutually applies several cognitions, though they remain distinct. From this arises the second explanation of the word, which pleased Thomas and most of the Scholastics. It seems to me rightly to be preferred to the first, and it offers a not useless torch for uncovering the nature and force of conscience. Conscience is so called because it joins knowledge to knowledge, namely universal knowledge, that is, of law, and particular knowledge, that is, of fact, applying the one to the other. I will illustrate the matter with one or two examples. In 1 Samuel 24:6 it is said that David's heart struck him after he had cut off the skirt of Saul's garment in the cave; that is, his conscience pricked him. Let us suppose that David spoke thus within his own mind: I know that violence ought not to be done to the sacred person of the king; I know too that I have just now done something which seems very little short of inflicting violence. I fear therefore that I have done what I certainly ought not to have done, and I give thanks to my God who restrained my hand from doing what I surely ought not to have done. So too his conscience objected to Judas the traitor: You know that the Lord ought not to have been betrayed, and likewise you know that you have shamefully betrayed him. When that universal knowledge of law which is in the mind is joined in this way with the particular knowledge of fact (of what has been done, or is about to be done), and is combined and applied to it and compared with it, there arises the whole thing we call conscience. Expressions of the kind which are used by way of reciprocation, and which are very frequent in this class, confirm this explanation of the name. Such is that saying of Isocrates, [ἐὰν τῶν ἄλλων λάθῃς, σαυτῷ συνειδήσῃ], If you can escape the notice of others, you will be conscious to yourself. Likewise Horace's line, Let this be a wall of bronze, to be conscious of nothing to oneself, and Virgil's, a mind conscious of what is right. Last of all there is Paul's saying (so that I need not gather more, and from elsewhere): [οὐδὲν ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα], I am conscious of nothing against myself, 1 Cor. 4:4.

units.la: VII. Satis jam constare puto nominis rationem, seu quis illam prætulerit, seu magis hanc, sive utramque pari loco habeat. Nam quas adducunt
units.tr: VII. I think the explanation of the name is now sufficiently established, whether someone prefers that one, or this one more, or holds both to have equal weight. For the arguments which they adduce

units.la: Præleεtio Prima.
units.tr: Prelection One.

units.la: [?]alias rationes pro ingenio quisque suo è plebe Scho[?]lastici, dilutiores ferè sunt quàm ut debeant currentum nostrum (quibus multa dicenda supersunt) morari. Pergo itaque ad vocis ὁμωνυμίαν[?] aperiendam, unde orta mira illa apud authores in definiendâ Conscientiâ discrepantia, usque adeo ut de termino definitionis termino (quodnam sc. sit ipsius rei) magna sit & difficilis admodum controver-
units.tr: The other explanations which each Schoolman from the common herd has offered in his own fashion are mostly too weak to delay our course, since much remains to be said. I therefore proceed to explain the ambiguity of the word [ὁμωνυμία], whence arises that remarkable disagreement among authors in defining Conscience, so that concerning the terminus of the definition (that is, what the thing itself is) there is great and very difficult controversy.

units.la: Ut itaque tollatur è medio illa ambiguitas; illud imprimis observandum est, tantum esse virium mentis (nempe Potentiarum, Habituum, & aliorum) inter se naturæ cognationem, tamque artium, quoad usum & exercitium, conjunctionem sive connexionem; ut non solùm vocabulorum, appella[?]tiones, sed & reales singulorum proprietates & officia, reliquis promiscuè & indiscriminatim attribui solent; idque non in exotericis tantum Poetarum, Oratorum, aliorumque humanioris literaturæ authorum, (quibus licentius loqui permissum est) sed & in dogmaticis Philosophorum & Scholasticorum scriptis, quibus non licet esse tam distertis. Quantumvis igitur arduum semper habitum est & difficile, res naturâ usuque conjunctas, suis quasi certis finitibus definire & distinguere; ad Conscientiae tamen vocem quod attinet, quæ & Scientia quædam est, & ab eâ dicta, non parum nobis adjumento fuerit vocis Scientiae ὁμωνυμία paulo diligentius aperuisse; ut ex simplicis vocabuli multiplici usu, impositi nominis ambiguitas rectius & penitius in-telligatur.
units.tr: So that this ambiguity may be removed, it must above all be observed that the powers of the mind (namely the Powers, the Habits, and the rest) have such a natural kinship with one another, and such a close conjunction or connection in their use and exercise, that their names and their real properties and functions are commonly attributed to one another indiscriminately. This happens not only in the popular writings of poets, orators and other authors of polite literature, who are allowed to speak more freely, but also in the dogmatic writings of philosophers and Schoolmen, who may not be so loose in their language. However hard it has always been, and however difficult, to define and distinguish things that are joined by nature and use within their own fixed limits, yet as far as the word Conscience is concerned, which is both a kind of Knowledge and named from it, it will be no small help to us to explain more carefully the ambiguity of the word Knowledge [Scientia]. Thus from the many uses of the simple word, the ambiguity of the imposed name may be understood more correctly and more thoroughly.

units.la: VIII. Primò ergo (ut habituum nomina familiariter transfeunt in sua objecta :) Scientia dupliciter dicitur; formaliter & objectivè. Quemadmodum enim de Fide distinguere solent Theologi, aliam esse Fidem qua credimus, quæ est habitus fidei in mente exsistens; aliam quam credimus, quæ est res fide credita, velut objectum prioris, & ei exex-trinsecum. trinsecum quid; quarum illa dici potest fides formaliter sumpta, hæc objectivè: pari omninò ratione de Scientiâ distinguere licet, & consequenter de Conscientiâ. Utramque scilicet sumi vel proprie & formaliter, pro ipso mentis habitu quorem [?] aliquam scimus vel conscimus; vel improprie & objectivè, pro re illâ quam scimus vel conscimus. Quo posteriore & improprio sensu, Lex illa quæ cordi-bus inscripta est, velut rectè vivendi regula dici potest Conscientia. Et in hoc sensu intelligendum est illud Damasceni in Scholis pervulgatissimum, Conscientiam esse legem mentis; quum tamen Lex mentis non sit proprie & formaliter Conscientia, sed potius Conscientiæ Objectum, aut adæquatum, aut partiale.
units.tr: VIII. First, then (as the names of habits pass familiarly into their objects), Science is said in two ways: formally and objectively. For just as theologians customarily distinguish about Faith, that there is one faith by which we believe, which is the habit of faith existing in the mind, and another that which we believe, which is the thing believed by faith, as the object of the former and something external to it; of these the former may be called faith taken formally, the latter objectively. In exactly the same way it is allowed to distinguish about Science, and consequently about Conscience. Each may be taken either properly and formally, for the habit of the mind itself by which we know or are conscious of something; or improperly and objectively, for that thing which we know or are conscious of. In this latter, improper sense, that Law which is written on hearts may be called Conscience, as the rule of right living. And in this sense must be understood that saying of Damascene, most commonly repeated in the Schools, that Conscience is the law of the mind; although the law of the mind is not properly and formally Conscience, but rather the object of Conscience, either adequate or partial.

units.la: IX. Secundò, cum ad animam pertineant tria hæc distincta illa quidem, sed tamen invicem ordinata, Potentia, Habitus & Actus; Potentia scilicet, ut virtutes ipsius animæ naturales; Habitus ut formæ perficientes ipsas Potentias, & habilitantes eas ad actus suos facilius & jucundiùs exercendos; & Actus velut exercitia, tum Potentiarum tum Habituum: Scientiæ nomen, itemque Conscientiæ, ad ista omnia aliquo modo extenditur. Sicut enim faber secare dicitur; primò, securi velut instrumento; secundò, acumine securis velut formali instrumenti dispositione: tertiò, ipsâ sectione velut instrumenti usu & actione: sic dicitur mens hominis scire, primo potentiâ cognitivâ velut instrumento; secundò, ipso habitu sciendi, velut dispositione persectivâ ipsius potentiæ; tertiò, actuali consideratione, velut usu & operatione utriusque potentiæ nimirum & habitus. Sumitur ergo Scientia tripliciter, Subjectivè, Formaliter, & Effectivè. Primo, subjectivè, pro potentiâ cui inèst, & quam est apta nata perficere, sicut omnis forma aliquo modo perficit suum subjectum: ut cum dicimus myste[ia]? fidei superare scientiam nostram, i. e. excedere mensuram potentiæ nostræ cognitivæ. Secundò, formaliter, (quæ est usitatissima hujus vocis significatio,) pro habitu cognitionis innatæ vel acquisitæ: quomodo dicimur scire principia per fe nota, & conclusiones legitimo discursu ex eis deductas, & universim omnia de quibus adminiculo sensuum aut rationis habemus aliquam certitudinem. Tertiò, effectivè, pro actuali consideratione rei prius cognitæ; quo sensu (ut illud obiter moneam) verba Pauli Apostoli, Act. 23. 5. in quibus explicandis mirè fe torquent interpretes, videntur omninò esse intelligenda [Non noveram, inquit, fratres, Pontificem esse maximum] οὐκ ᾔδειν[?], i. e. Non cogitavi, non satis attentè consideravi. Quasi diceret, Parcite, quæso, fratres, justæ meæ indignationi, fi æstuantis animi impetu abreptus, liberiùs aliquid elocutus fuerim quàm oportuit, immemor illius & personæ, & officii mei. Agnosco errorem: non debui maledicere Pontifici, quantumvis fecerit non digna suo honore; sed impediit animi ardor, ne ista, ut par erat, attentiùs cogitarem. Sensu facillimo, & commodissimo.
units.tr: IX. Secondly, since three things belong to the soul, distinct indeed but nonetheless ordered among themselves, namely Power, Habit and Act, the Power being the natural faculties of the soul itself, the Habit being the forms which perfect the Powers and enable them to exercise their acts more easily and pleasantly, and the Act being the exercise both of the Powers and of the Habits, the name Science, and likewise Conscience, extends in some way to all of these. For just as a carpenter is said to cut: first, by the axe as the instrument; second, by the sharpness of the axe as the formal disposition of the instrument; third, by the cutting itself as the use and action of the instrument: so the mind of man is said to know: first, by the cognitive power as the instrument; second, by the very habit of knowing, as the disposition perfecting the power; third, by actual consideration, as the use and operation of both the power and the habit. Science is therefore taken in three ways: subjectively, formally, and effectively. First, subjectively, for the power in which it inheres and which it is fitted by nature to perfect, just as every form in some way perfects its subject: as when we say that the mysteries of faith surpass our science, that is, exceed the measure of our cognitive power. Second, formally (which is the most usual meaning of this word), for the habit of knowledge, innate or acquired: as when we are said to know the principles known through themselves, and the conclusions deduced from them by lawful reasoning, and in general all those things of which we have some certainty by the help of the senses or reason. Third, effectively, for the actual consideration of a thing previously known. In this sense (let me note this in passing) the words of the Apostle Paul, Acts 23.5, over which the interpreters torment themselves in explaining them, seem to be wholly understood thus: [I did not know, brethren, that he was the high priest] [οὐκ ᾔδειν], that is, I did not think about it, I did not consider it sufficiently attentively. As if he were saying: Forgive me, I beg you, brethren, for my just indignation, if, carried away by the impulse of a raging mind, I spoke more freely than was fitting, forgetting both that person and my own office. I acknowledge the error: I ought not to have cursed the High Priest, however unworthy of his honour he had been; but the heat of my spirit prevented me from thinking about these things as attentively as I should have. This is a very easy and convenient sense.

units.la: X. Sed pergo: Ut Scientia, sic & Conscientia [?]nbus eisdem modis similiter accipitur. Primò, subjectivè; pro potentiâ intellectivâ practicâ: ut cum dicimus legem naturalem scriptam esse in corde vel conscientiâ. Secundò, formaliter; pro habitu pertinente ad illam potentiam, eamque informante: ut cum de homine infigniter improbo dicimus eum hominem esse nullius conscientiæ, abjecisse eum vel amisse omnem conscientiam. Tertiò, efsectivè; pro actuali aliquo motu, exercitio aut operatione illius habitus: ut cum quis dicit habere fe de hoc vel illo facto conscientiam. Quo sensu videtur à Petro accipi, 1 Pet. 2. 19. Si quis propter conscientiam Dei suffert molestias.
units.tr: X. But to continue: Conscience is taken in the same ways as Science. First, subjectively, for the practical intellectual power: as when we say that the natural law is written in the heart or conscience. Second, formally, for the habit belonging to that power and informing it: as when of a man notoriously wicked we say that he is of no conscience, that he has cast off or lost all conscience. Third, effectively, for some actual motion, exercise or operation of that habit: as when someone says that he has conscience of this or that deed. In this sense it seems to be understood by Peter, 1 Pet. 2.19: If someone for conscience toward God endures grief.

units.la: XI. Porrò, cum Scientia proprie fit ἀποδεικτικὴ[?], sive cognitio syllogistica, adeóque omnes qui de Conscientia tractant naturam ejus rationemque non posse putent aptiùs & apertiùs illustriri, quàm per syllogismum practicum: Observandum est Scientiæ nomen hoc etiam respectu quatuor modis accipi. Primò & propriissimè, pro scientiâ conclusionis præcisè: quo modo ferè accipitur ab Aristotele in Analyticis, & alibi passim. Secundò, pro cognitione Principiorum, ex quibus demonstrantur conclusiones: ut si quis dicat se scire, Omne totum esse majus qualibet sua parte. Tertio, pro cognitione totius Syllogismi: nam qui novit præmissas & conclusionem, novit totam argumentationem. Quarto, pro aggregatâ notitiâ multarum conclusionum, sive demonstrationum ad unum aliquod subjectum pertinentium: quo modo dicimus scire Physicam, Geometriam, Medicinam, &c. Idipsum & de Conscientiæ nomine dicendum; cujus discursum, unico Syllogismo practico, authores plerique comprehendunt. Sed cum sit Conscientia, ut dictum est, conjuncta scientia; ut totum illud quod sub hoc nomine venit plenius, & quasi uno intuitu perspiciatur, (universum negotium ut mihi saltem videtur) commodius expedietur, si discursum illum concipiamus, velut ex duplici syllogismo ita constantem, ut conclusio prioris sit major propositio posterioris; in hunc modum. Omne injustum est fugiendum. Omne furtum est injustum. Ergo Omne furtum est fugiendum.
units.tr: XI. Furthermore, since Science is properly demonstrative [ἀποδεικτική], that is, syllogistic knowledge, and therefore those who treat of Conscience think that its nature and reasoning cannot be more fitly and clearly illustrated than through the practical syllogism, it must be observed that the name Science is taken in four ways in this respect. First, and most properly, for the science of the conclusion alone: in which sense it is commonly taken by Aristotle in the Analytics, and everywhere else. Second, for the knowledge of the principles from which the conclusions are demonstrated: as when someone says he knows that every whole is greater than any of its parts. Third, for the knowledge of the whole syllogism: for whoever knows the premises and the conclusion knows the whole argument. Fourth, for the combined knowledge of many conclusions, or demonstrations, pertaining to one subject: in which sense we say that we know Physics, Geometry, Medicine, and so on. The same must be said of the name Conscience, whose reasoning most authors comprehend in a single practical syllogism. But since Conscience is, as has been said, a conjoined science, so that the whole matter which comes under this name may be seen more fully and as it were at one glance, the whole business (as it seems to me at least) will be more conveniently handled if we conceive that reasoning as consisting of a double syllogism, in such a way that the conclusion of the first is the major premise of the second; in this manner: Every unjust act is to be avoided. Every theft is unjust. Therefore every theft is to be avoided.

units.la: Esto hic prior syllogismus: cujus Prima propositio est per se nota lumine naturæ, Ratio assumit minorem, Conscientia infert Conclusionem. Quam conclusionem mox arripit, ut principium posterioris syllogismi : & applicando eam ad aliquod particulare factum voluntatis arbitrio propositum, arguit ad hunc modum : Omne furtum est fugiendum. Hoc quod mihi faciendum proponitur est furtum, Ergo est fugiendum.
units.tr: Let this be the first syllogism: its first proposition is known through itself by the light of nature; Reason takes up the minor, and Conscience draws the conclusion. This conclusion it straightway seizes upon as the principle of the second syllogism, and applying it to some particular deed proposed to the will's choice, it argues in this way: Every theft is to be avoided. What is now proposed to me to be done is theft. Therefore it is to be avoided.

units.la: Ad quem etiam modum procedit (mutatis mutandis) quoties de facto particulari praeterito judicandum est.
units.tr: In the same manner (with the necessary changes) it proceeds whenever a particular past deed is to be judged.

units.la: XII. His ita positis, dico Conscientiam, pariter ut Scientiam, quatuor modis accipi. Primò & propriissimè, pro ultima conclusione totius discursus utriusque syllogismi ; utpote in quâ continetur ultimum judicium intellectus practici: ut si quis dicat, Conscientia mea mihi dictat hoc furtum non esse faciendum, vel Conscientia mea clamat hoc furtum non debuisse fieri. Et notitia hujus Conclusionis est proprie συνείδησις, prout συνείδησις contradistinguitur συντηρήσις. Secundò, sumitur pro notitia primi illius principii universalis, lumine naturæ vel revelationis cogniti, ex quo pendet totius discursus filum; ut si quis dicat, Conscientia mea dictat, Nullum injustum esse faciendum. Et est hic usus vocabuli non infrequens quidem, sed tamen improprius: siquidem in istiusmodi locutionibus, Conscientia nihil aliud est quam ipsa Synteresis: tamen inter Conscientiam proprie dictam & Synteresin, discrimen sit non exiguum. Habet enim se Synteresis ad Conscientiam proprie dictam, sicut se habet habitus Intellectus ad Scientiam proprie dictam : qui duo sunt habitus mentis specificè distincti; ut ex quinto Ethicorum Aristotelis olim didicimus. Sicut ergo in Speculativis, Intelligentia est habitus primorum principiorum circa Verum & Falsum, unde deducuntur conclusiones, de quibus est Scientia : Sic in Practicis, Synteresis est habitus primorum principiorum circa Bonum & Malum, unde deducuntur conclusiones, de quibus est Conscientia. Tertiò, sumitur Conscientia latiùs, pro toto illo discursu mentis practico, à primo principio ad ultimam usque conclusionem, qui in duobus ejusmodi Syllogismis, quales jam propositi, continetur : ita ut ambitu suo & συντήρησιν[?] & εἰδήσιν proprie di&am complectatur. Facile enim suggerit sua cuique conscientia hæc omnia licet ; & nihil injustum fieri oportere, & Furtum in rebus injustis merito censeri, & hoc particulare factum, quod à me jam admissum est, vel quod ut admittam solicitat opportunitas, furti crimen habere. Quartò, sumitur Conscientia pro notitiâ aggregatâ pluritum actuum particularium, ex quibus conficitur universa vitæ, & conversationis ratio. Quo sensu videntur illa Apostolorum verba intelligenda ; Viri fratres, ego omni bonâ conscientiâ πολιτευόμενος τῷ Θεῷ[?], conversatus sum coram Deo ad hunc usque diem. Act. 23. 1. Confidimus quod bonam conscientiam habemus, in omnibus cupientes bene conversari. Heb. 13. 18. Quin & 1 Pet. 3. 16 quod initio versus, (ut observavit vir pius & doctus) συνείδησις ἀγαθὴ dicitur. id ipsum in fine ejusdem versus ἀγαθὴ ἀναστροφὴ appellatur. Quocies[?] etiam quempiam laudamus aut vituperamus ut integræ Conscientiæ virum aut corruptæ, ex intuitu morum & quotidianæ conversationis, finis respectu habito ad aliquod ipsius factum particulare ; vox Conscientiæ liquidò in hanc partem sumitur.
units.tr: XII. Having laid these things down, I say that Conscience, just as Science, is taken in four ways. First, and most properly, it means the ultimate conclusion of the whole discourse of each syllogism, since in it is contained the final judgment of the practical intellect: as when someone says, "My conscience dictates that this theft is not to be committed," or "My conscience cries out that this theft ought not to have been done." The knowledge of this conclusion is properly συνείδησις [suneidesis], insofar as it is distinguished from συντήρησις [synteresis]. Second, it is taken for the knowledge of that first universal principle, known by the light of nature or of revelation, on which the thread of the whole discourse depends: as when someone says, "My conscience dictates that nothing unjust is to be done." This use of the word is not uncommon, but it is still improper. In such expressions conscience is nothing other than synteresis itself, yet there is no small difference between conscience properly so called and synteresis. For synteresis relates to conscience properly so called as the habit of the intellect relates to science properly so called. These are two habits of the mind specifically distinct, as we learned long ago from the fifth book of Aristotle's Ethics. So just as in speculative matters understanding is the habit of first principles concerning true and false, from which conclusions are deduced, and about which there is science, so in practical matters synteresis is the habit of first principles concerning good and evil, from which conclusions are deduced, and about which there is conscience. Third, conscience is taken more broadly, for the whole practical discourse of the mind, from the first principle to the last conclusion, which is contained in two such syllogisms as those just proposed, so that in its compass it embraces both synteresis and conscience properly so called. For each person's conscience readily suggests all these things: that everything is permitted, that nothing unjust ought to be done, that theft is rightly counted among unjust things, and that this particular deed, which I have already admitted or which opportunity urges me to admit, has the character of theft. Fourth, conscience is taken for the knowledge gathered from many particular acts, out of which the whole rule of life and conduct is made up. In this sense the words of the Apostles seem to be understood: "Men and brethren, I have lived before God in all good conscience until this day" (Act. 23. 1). "We trust that we have a good conscience, desiring in all things to live honestly" (Heb. 13. 18). Indeed, in 1 Pet. 3. 16, what at the beginning of the verse is called a good conscience, συνείδησις ἀγαθή [suneidesis agathē], as a pious and learned man has observed, is at the end of the same verse called good conduct, ἀγαθὴ ἀναστροφή [agathē anastrophē]. Whenever we praise or blame someone as a man of upright or corrupt conscience, judging from his morals and daily conduct, with some particular deed of his in view, the word conscience is clearly taken in this sense.

units.la: XIII. Exposui ista fateor multò prolixius quàm initio instituieram ; fortassis etiam quàm pro vestrâ (Auditores) expectatione debueram. Verumtamen æquiores vos futuros confido, si consi[?] terit hanc in explicando Definito prolixitatem in compendium fore reliquæ tractationis, quæ in explicatione ipsius Definitionis per singula membra insumetur: quam nunc proximè aggredior. Unum hoc duntaxat præmoneo, quod est tamen ex ipsâ re manifestum, datam à me jam antè definitionem ad Conscientiam proprie dictam adæquatè pertinere; nimirum prout accipitur pro notitia ultimæ conclusionis Syllogismi practici: posse tamen cum debita aliquot vocum permutatione & ad reliquas ejus dictionis significationes explicandas adhiberi; ut in plerisque vocibus [illegible, ~3 letters] ἀναλογίαι æquivocis amat fieri. Fuit autem data definitio, quam propter tam multa interposita repetere libet, hæc; Conscientia est facultas vel habitus intellectus practici; quo mens hominis per discursum rationis applicat lumen quod sibi inest ad particulares suos actus morales. In quâ definitione quatuor ista continentur singulatim explicanda; Genus, Subjectum, Objectum & Actus.
units.tr: XIII. I confess that I have set these things out at much greater length than I had intended at the start, and perhaps longer than your expectation, gentlemen, required. Yet I trust you will be more indulgent if you consider that this length in explaining the definition will be made up for by brevity in the rest of the treatment, which will be spent on explaining the definition itself, member by member, and which I now proceed to take up. I give only this one preliminary warning, which is nonetheless plain from the matter itself: the definition I gave earlier applies fully to conscience properly so called, that is, as it is taken for the knowledge of the last conclusion of a practical syllogism. With a suitable change of some words, however, it can also be used to explain its other meanings, as often happens with words that are equivocal by analogy. The definition given was, since so many things have intervened it is worth repeating, this: "Conscience is a faculty or habit of the practical intellect, by which the mind of man, through the discourse of reason, applies the light that is within it to its particular moral acts." In this definition four things are contained, each to be explained separately: Genus, Subject, Object and Act.

units.la: XIV. De Genere magna est inter Scholasticos & acris controversia. Imprimis omnes consentiunt Conscientiam ad {1}Mentem hominis pertinere: sed utrum, ut Potentiam ejus, an ut Habitum, an ut Actum, mira est dissensio. Thomas, qui in Scholis magnam familiam ducit, statuit esse {*}Actum. Quam sententiam plerique amplexi sunt; non Scholastici tantum Scriptores, tanti viri authoritate magis (ut ego quidem arbitror) adducti, quàm momentis rationum; sed & reformatarum Ecclesiarum Theologi, qui ex fastidio rixosæ gentis, mallunt hisce in rebus receptas quasque opiniones (ab omni impietatis aut superstitionis opinione saltem liberas) sequi, quàm spinosas istorum hominum subtilitates nimis anxiè rimari. At mihi, ut quod enfeo liberè dicam, improbanda omninò videtur communissima hæc opinio: cui evertendæ (ne pluribus sit opus) sufficiet unicum hoc argumentum ; Conscientiæ sc. plurimos esse actus. Dicit[?] enim, impellit, terret, taxatur, accusat, excusat, s[?]-latur, remordet, torquet, &c. Actuum autem nulli sunt actus ; sed aut Formarum, aut Potentiarum, aut Habituum. Erit ergo Conscientia aut Forma, aut Potentia, aut Habitus : Non autem Actus. Adiumentum autem Thomistarum. Conscientiam esse applicationem Scientiæ vel luminis quod est in syn-teresi[?], & applicationem esse Actum ; Respondeo, Conscientiæ vocem, ut ex antedictis patet, sumi quandoque Effective, pro aliquo actu suo, sicut & Scientiæ vox pro actuali consideratione, impropriè tamen. Sed propriè loquendo Applicatio Scientiæ non est ipsa Conscientia, sed ejus Actus, sicut Consideratio non est ipsa Scientia, sed ejus actus. Non est ergo Conscientia Actus.
units.tr: XIV. Concerning the Genus there is great and sharp controversy among the Scholastics. First, all agree that conscience pertains to the mind of man, but whether as its power, or as its habit, or as its act, there is remarkable disagreement. Thomas, who leads a large following in the schools, holds that it is an act. Most have embraced this opinion, not only the Scholastic writers, who were swayed more by the authority of so great a man (as I at least think) than by the weight of reasons, but also the theologians of the reformed Churches, who, out of weariness with a quarrelsome tribe, prefer to follow opinions received in these matters (at least those free from any suspicion of impiety or superstition) rather than anxiously to probe the thorny subtleties of those men. But to me, to speak my mind freely, this most common opinion seems wholly to be rejected. To overturn it, lest more be needed, one argument will suffice: namely, that conscience has very many acts. For it "dictates, impels, terrifies, censures, accuses, excuses, soothes, gnaws, torments," and so on. But none of these are acts; they are either forms, or powers, or habits. Conscience will therefore be either a form, or a power, or a habit, and not an act. As for the support of the Thomists, that conscience is the application of knowledge, or of the light which is in synteresis, and that application is an act, I answer that the word conscience, as appears from what was said above, is sometimes taken effectively, for some act of its own, just as the word science is sometimes taken for actual consideration, though improperly. But properly speaking, the application of knowledge is not conscience itself but its act, just as consideration is not science itself but its act. Therefore conscience is not an act.

units.la: XV. Relinquitur ergo quòd aut Potentia sit, aut Habitus : nam quòd non sit Forma, (nempe Anima ipsa, sed aliquid ejus,) apud omnes in confesso est. Neotericorum non pauci Potentiam esse contendunt, negant esse Habitum, Quòd sit Potentia, probant : Primò, quia est quædam quasi Memoria ; quum ad Conscientiam respiciat intellectus cogitans de Agibilibus, sicut respicit ad Memoriam, cogitans de Speculabilibus ; Et Memoria est Potentia non Habitus. Secundò, quia Potentia est illud per quod agens est primò potens ad agendum : per Conscientiam autem homo est potens discere quid sibi sit faciendum, & approbare vel improbare quod est à se factum ; idque primò, quia posità conscientiâ potest ista omnia facere, sublatâ non potest. Tertiò, quia contradistinguitur potentiæ, Tit. 1. 15. Ubi νοῦς & συνείδησις, Mens & Conscientia, aperte ponuntur ut oppositæ speciei : proinde necesse est (ea enim Lex est contrariarum specierum) ut idem sit utriusque genus ; νοῦς autem potentia est, ergo & συνείδησις. Probant etiam ex abundanti, quòd Conscientia non fit Habitus : tum quia videtur esse tam Naturale homini, quàm voluntas & affectus ; tum quia reperitur in omnibus, etiam puerulis & infantibus, naturæ quodam instinctu, qui tamen non videntur esse capaces habi-tuum.
units.tr: XV. It remains, then, that conscience is either a power or a habit; for that it is not a form (namely the soul itself, or some part of it) is agreed by all. Not a few of the moderns contend that it is a power, and deny that it is a habit. They prove that it is a power: first, because it is a kind of memory, since the intellect thinking about things to be done relates to conscience as it relates to memory when thinking about things to be contemplated; and memory is a power, not a habit. Second, because a power is that by which an agent is first able to act; but through conscience a man is able to learn what is to be done, and to approve or disapprove what has been done by himself; and this first, because given conscience he can do all these things, while without it he cannot. Third, because it is distinguished from the powers: in Tit. 1. 15, mind and conscience, νοῦς and συνείδησις, are plainly set down as opposed species. It must therefore be (for that is the law of contrary species) that they have the same genus; but the mind is a power, so conscience also is. They prove, moreover, in addition, that conscience is not a habit: both because it seems to be as natural to man as the will and the affections are, and because it is found in all, even little children and infants, by a kind of instinct of nature, who yet do not seem capable of habits.

units.la: XVI. Diversam tamen sententiam tuentur Scotus, Durandus, & alii nonnulli è subtilioribus Scholasticis, quòd sc. Conscientia sit Habitus ; & nititur sanè eorum sententia rationibus non contemnendis. Prima, quia Conscientia est Scientia quædam : unde ei attribuuntur iidem ipsi actus, Scire, Nescire, &c. Ut Eccles. 7. 23. Scit conscientia tua. Et Gen. 43. 22. Nescimus, quis reposuerit pecuniam nostram in saccis nostris ; Ubi vulgatus habet, Non est in conscientia nostra. Nihil mihi conscius sum, inquit Paulus, 1 Cor. 4. 4. id est, non scio me aliquâ ex parte defuisse officio meo. Atqui Scientia est Habitus ; proinde & Conscientia. Altera, quia ex recta institutione, & nova informatione vel illuminatione Conscientiæ, homo fit habilis ad aliquid agendum, ad quod non fuit ante habilis : sed accedente ejusmodi institutione vel informatione, certum est non ingenerari animæ novam Potentiam, sed novum potius Habitum : Unde sequitur Conscientiam Habitum potius dicendam esse quàm Potentiam. Tertiâ, quia à meris Potentiis nemo denominatur moraliter bonus aut malus, sed abs Habitibus ; nec propter eas laudatur quis vel vituperatur, sed propter hos: at dicuntur homines boni aut mali laudanturque & vituperantur ; pro qualitate Conscientiarum : ergo Conscientia est Habitus. Quartâ, quòd Potentiarum non est, sed Habituum acquiri, affumi, deponi, animam : sed homines dicuntur acquirere & amittere, affumere & deponere Conscientiam : Conscientia igitur, non est Potentia, sed Habitus.
units.tr: XVI. Scotus, Durandus and some other more subtle Scholastics hold the contrary opinion, namely that conscience is a habit, and their view indeed rests on reasons not to be despised. The first is this: conscience is a certain knowledge, and so the same acts are attributed to it, to know, not to know, and so on. As in Eccl. 7. 23, "Your conscience knows." And in Gen. 43. 22, "We do not know who has put our money in our sacks," where the Vulgate has "It is not in our conscience." "I am conscious of nothing against myself," says Paul, 1 Cor. 4. 4, that is, I know that I have in no respect fallen short of my duty. But knowledge is a habit; therefore conscience is too. The second is this: by right instruction and new formation or illumination of conscience a man becomes able to do something which before he was not able to do; but with such instruction or formation it is certain that no new power is generated in the soul, but rather a new habit. Whence it follows that conscience should be called a habit rather than a power. Third: no one is named morally good or bad from mere powers, but from habits; nor is anyone praised or blamed on account of powers, but on account of habits. Yet men are called good or bad, and are praised and blamed, according to the quality of their consciences. Therefore conscience is a habit. Fourth: it belongs to habits, not powers, to be acquired, assumed and laid aside by the soul; but men are said to acquire and lose, assume and lay aside conscience. Therefore conscience is not a power but a habit.

units.la: XVII. Statuo itaque Conscientiam proprie, formaliter & prædicatione recta esse Habitum: dici nihilominus posse eandem & Potentiam, idque duplici ratione. Tum Materialiter, quia inest Potentiæ, ut Subjectum ἐν ᾧ tum per approximationem; quia est Habitus innatus; & Habitus innatus, in quantum medio quodam modo se habet inter Habitum acquisitum & puram potentiam, utriusque libet nomen induere potest, ut solent Media participare de utroque Extremo. Hinc est quod Conscientia reperiatur in parvulis, qui non sunt capaces habitum acquisitorum. Neque necesse est ut νοῦς [?] καὶ συνείδησιν [?] Tit. 1. contradistinguantur ut nudæ Potentiæ: imo aptius videtur sumi ibi utramque vocem Synecdochicè, νοῦν [?] scilicet pro Intellectu speculativo cum omnibus suis pertinentiis (ut loquuntur,) & συνείδησιν pro Intellectu practico cum omnibus suis pertinentiis; i. e. cum omnibus facultatibus, habitibus, actibus, & quæ ad eorum alterutrum pertinent respectivè.
units.tr: XVII. I therefore hold that conscience is, properly, formally and by correct predication, a habit. Nevertheless the same thing can also be called a power, and for a twofold reason. First, materially, because it inheres in a power as its subject (ἐν ᾧ), and second, by approximation, because it is an innate habit. An innate habit, insofar as it stands in a certain middle position between an acquired habit and pure power, may take on the name of either, just as middle things usually partake of both extremes. Hence conscience is found in little children, who are not capable of acquired habits. Nor is it necessary that νοῦς and συνείδησις in Tit. 1 be distinguished as bare powers. It seems more fitting that both words be taken there synecdochically: νοῦς [νοῦς] for the speculative intellect with all its belongings, as they say, and συνείδησις [συνείδησις] for the practical intellect with all its belongings; that is, with all the faculties, habits and acts, and whatever pertains to either of them relatively.

units.la: XVIII. Apposui itaque in Conscientiæ definitione, & Facultatis vocabulum; quod mihi videtur aliquo modo commune esse Potentiis & Habitibus, & est ad significandum Habitus innatos valde accommodum. Dicetis fortasse, omnem habitum esse crebris actibus acquisitum; adeoque hæc ita pertinere ad essentiam habitus, ut eo maxime velut specifica sua differentia, dignoscendi sint Habitus à Potentiis; nimirum, quod illi Acquisiti sint, hæ Naturales; proinde, nisi quis velit secum pugnantia proloqui, & admittere meram contradictionem in adjecto, non debere Conscientiam dici Habitum innatum. Respondeo, omnino fatendum esse omnes quoscunque Habitus, & esse & dici debere acquisitos, etiam eos qui videntur esse maxime naturales; eos saltem quod sensuum admiculo, & multis actionibus sensibilibus præviis indigeant, ad hoc ut Species rerum Jensibilium (quarum respectu anima ex, se est instar tabulæ rasæ) deferantur ad phantasiam, & tandem fiant intelligibiles. Hoc tamen non obstante, posse quosdam Habitus dici, idque optimâ ratione, Innatos; in quantum ex innato sibi lumine mens statim præbet assensum rei propositæ sine ullâ formidine oppositi, suppositâ duntaxat apprehensione terminorum, nec indiget ad eliciendum ejusmodi assensum adminiculo aut interni studii, aut externæ institutionis. Exempli gratiâ, Habitus intellectivus hujus Principii, [Omne totum est majus qualibet sui parte,] est Habitus Innatus; quatenus vi luminis naturalis ex solâ apprehensione terminorum veritas ipsius ultrò occurrit menti, nullo licèt adhibito vel studio, vel doctore. Est tamen idem Habitus Acquisitus, in quantum opus est adminiculo sensuum, ad hoc, ut quis ex crebris actionibus circa res sensibiles perveniat ad notitiam terminorum: hoc est, ad percipiendum τὸ[?] quid nominis Totius & Partis.
units.tr: XVIII. I have therefore included in the definition of conscience the word faculty, which seems in some way common to powers and habits, and is very suitable for signifying innate habits. You will perhaps say that every habit is acquired by frequent acts, and so these belong so closely to the essence of habit that they serve as its specific difference, by which habits are distinguished from powers: namely, that the former are acquired and the latter natural. Therefore, unless one wishes to utter contradictory things and admit a mere contradiction in the adjunct, conscience ought not to be called an innate habit. I reply that it must be wholly conceded that all habits whatever are, and ought to be called, acquired, even those that seem most natural; at least because they need the aid of the senses and many prior sensible actions, so that the species of sensible things (with respect to which the soul of itself is like a blank tablet) are conveyed to the imagination and at last become intelligible. Nevertheless, notwithstanding this, some habits can rightly be called innate, insofar as the mind, from its innate light, at once gives assent to a proposed thing, without any fear of the opposite, the apprehension of the terms alone being presupposed; and to elicit such assent it needs no aid either of inner study or of external instruction. For example, the intellectual habit of this principle, [The whole is greater than any of its parts], is an innate habit, inasmuch as by the power of the natural light its truth presents itself to the mind of its own accord, from the apprehension of the terms alone, though neither study nor teacher is applied. It is nevertheless the same habit acquired, insofar as the aid of the senses is needed so that someone, through frequent actions about sensible things, comes to a knowledge of the terms: that is, to perceiving the quid nominis of whole and part.

units.la: XIX. Si adhuc dicatur, Conscientiam Habitum Innatum esse non posse; quia quæ Innata sunt non sunt capacia erroris, nec possunt esse vitiosa, sunt quæ eadem in omnibus quibus insunt: Conscientia autem & errare potest, & esse mala, nec est in omnibus eadem. Respondeo, ex his sequi quidem Conscientiam non esse Habitum Simpliciter Innatum, (quod nemo sanus dixerit, repugnat enim naturæ Habitus, ut sit merè naturalis & innatus;) sed ut partim (eo quo jam dictum est sensu) Innatum, sic partim etiam Acquisitum. Nimirùm sic se res habet; Apportat secum anima hominis quædam quasi semina cognitionis boni & mali, quæ studio & institutione adolescunt & perficiuntur: sicut naturalis agilitas completur exercitatione, & naturalis Logica artificiali. Conscientia ergo, refpestu moralium Agibilium, quæ sunt de primo diEamine naturæ, (ut Scholastici fere loquuntur) & sunt ejus Objecta Primaria, est Habitus naturalis, sive innatus, & proinde omnibus pariter inest, & semper rectus est sine aliquo aut errore aut vitio: sed respectu eorum quæ postea addiscuntur, & primis illis principiis αὐτοπισμοῖς[?] accedunt, sive ex propria meditatione, sive ex alienâ institutione, est Habitus Acquisitus, & potest errore alióve defectu aut vitio laborare.
units.tr: XIX. If it is still said that conscience cannot be an innate habit, because things that are innate are not capable of error, nor can they be vicious, and they are the same in all in whom they inhere, whereas conscience both can err and can be bad, and is not the same in all: I reply that from these points it indeed follows that conscience is not an innate habit simply (which no sane person would say, for it is contrary to the nature of a habit to be purely natural and innate); but that it is partly innate (in the sense already stated) and so partly also acquired. The matter stands thus. The human soul brings with it certain seeds, as it were, of the knowledge of good and evil, which grow and are perfected by study and instruction, just as natural agility is completed by exercise, and natural logic by artificial logic. Conscience, therefore, with respect to moral agibilia, which are "of the first dictate of nature" (as the Scholastics commonly put it), and which are its primary objects, is a natural or innate habit; and so it is equally present in all, and is always right without any error or vice. But with respect to those things which are learned afterwards and attach to those first principles [αὐτοπισμοῖς], whether from one's own meditation or from another's instruction, it is an acquired habit, and it can labour under error or other defect or vice.

units.la: XX. Sed de Genere plus satis: reliqua percurram breviùs. Secundum definitionis membrum est Subjectum: idque duplex, Subjectum sc. §[?] & Subjectum ἐν ᾧ. Subjectum ᾧ est Homo; seu potiùs Creatura rationalis, si quidem accurate loqui velimus. Nam & Angelis inesse Conscientiam defectionis suæ, & pœnarum quas eo nomine sunt daturi, indicio est, quòd se {1}sciunt torquendos, & quòd credentes revelationi divinæ {2}contremiscunt tamen; item quòd {3}judicandi sunt in adventu Domini, & rationem reddituri rerum omnium à se factarum.
units.tr: XX. But enough has been said about the genus; I shall run through the rest more briefly. The second member of the definition is the subject, and this is twofold: the subject of which (ᾧ) and the subject in which (ἐν ᾧ). The subject of which is man; or rather, to speak accurately, a rational creature. For that angels too have a conscience of their defection, and of the punishments they are to suffer for it, is shown by the fact that they know they are to be tormented, and that, though they believe the divine revelation, they nevertheless tremble; likewise that they are to be judged at the coming of the Lord and to render account of all the things made by them.
