units.la: Sed quoniam nec nostra multum interest nosse naturam mentium Angelicarum, & Deo sapientissimo visum est eam parcissimè in Scripturis revelare: de solo Homine proprerea[?] definitionem instituit. In Brutis enim animalibus etsi appareat Conscientia quædam velut umbra, sicut & Rationis, cum faciant nonnulla, quæ habere videntur speciem quandam æquitatis & prudentiæ, (ut sunt sanè admiranda quæ de Elephantorum, Apum, Canum, aliorumque quorundam animalium Solertiâ narrantur:) sunt tamen illa omnia Phantasiæ opera, non Rationis; & ab instinctu naturali proficiscuntur, non à Conscientiâ. Est ergo Homo proprium Conscientiæ Subjectum, ut & Rationis: isque omnis non exclusis aut Ethnicis, aut Impiis, aut ipsis etiam infantibus. De Ethnicis apertè pronunciat Paulus,
units.tr: But since it is not greatly in our interest to know the nature of the angelic minds, and God in his supreme wisdom has seen fit to reveal it very sparingly in the Scriptures, I have therefore framed the definition with man alone in view. For in brute animals, although a certain conscience appears as a shadow, as reason does too, since they do some things which seem to have a certain semblance of equity and prudence (as indeed the wonderful things are which are told of the cleverness of elephants, bees, dogs and certain other animals), yet all those things are works of the imagination, not of reason, and proceed from natural instinct, not from conscience. Man, therefore, is the proper subject of conscience, as also of reason; and that means every man, not excluding heathens, impious men, or even infants. Concerning the heathen, Paul pronounces plainly:

units.la: Rom. 2. 15. Ostendere eos opus legis scriptum in cordibus, testimonium etiam perhibente ipsorum Confcientia. Quin & impuriffimis quibusque Conscientiam inesse, etsi impuram, testatur idem Paulus, Tit. 1. 15. Lapsu enim amissa est Conscientiae rectitudo & integritas; non Natura. Et cum renascimur, non infunditur de novo, quæ defuit antè Conscientia, sed quæ prius inerat, foeda peccatis atque impura, respersa jam sanguine Christi, fide purificatur, ita ut placeat Deo. Etiam in infantibus admodum parvulis, ut in lactentibus magnificetur Dei nomen, emicat cum primis è veteris incendii ruderibus, & quamvis admodum debiliter, spargit tamen utcunque igniculos suos rationis hæc scintillula; prodente se præmature in iis conscientiæ ut[?], qui siquid commiserint inhonesti, latere quærunt & commissum celare.
units.tr: Rom. 2. 15. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness. Moreover, that even the most impure have conscience within them, though it is impure, the same Paul testifies, Tit. 1. 15. For by the fall the rectitude and integrity of conscience was lost, not its nature. And when we are born again, there is not infused anew what conscience lacked before; rather what was there before, foul with sins and impure, already sprinkled with the blood of Christ, is purified by faith, so that it is pleasing to God. Even in very small infants, "that the name of God may be magnified in sucklings," this little spark shines forth from the ruins of the ancient fire, and although very weakly, it nonetheless somehow scatters its tiny sparks of reason; it reveals itself prematurely in them as conscience, so that if they have done anything dishonourable they seek to hide it and conceal what they have done.

units.la: XXI. Subjectum ἐν ᾧ[?], i. e. potentia animæ, in quâ sedem suam habet Conscientia, est intellectus Practicus: Intellectus, inquam, non Voluntas; isque non Speculativus, sed Practicus. Agitatur & hæc controversia inter Scholasticos, pertineatne Conscientia ad Intellectum, an ad Voluntatem, an ad Utramque. Nolo me huic liti[?] immiscere. Satis hactenus superque habuistis spinosarum subtilitatum. Paucis itaque quod instituto meo expediat, expediam. Partis intellectivæ tres distinctas potentias enumerat Aristot. lib. de Anima tertio: duas sc. Cognitivas, Intellectum Speculativum & Intellectum Practicum; & tertiam Appetitivam, Voluntatem. Harum trium extremæ sunt Intellectus Speculativus, qui speculatur Verum quatenus Verum, & in eo acquiescit, præcisè, sine aliquo ordine aut respectu ad Opus: & Voluntas, quæ præcisè tendit ad operationem, nec omninò speculatur quicquam. Inter utramque hanc potentiam velut in medio situs est Intellectus Practicus, qui pro more rerum mediarum, cum utraque extrema ex aliquâ parte concordat, ex aliquâ ab eâ discrepat. Concordat Intellectus practicus cum Speculativo in hoc, quòd speculatur Veritatem; cum Voluntate in hoc, quòd tendit in Operationem. Quod ad Conscientiam attinet, illud imprimis certum est, non pertinere eam ad Intellectum Speculativum, quia scientiam suam omnino dirigit ad praxin. Nec proprie pertinet ad Voluntatem: quia si hoc esset, vel per modum Potentiæ ei inesset, & sic esset idem quod Liberum Arbitrium; vel per modum Habitus, & sic esset aliqua Virtutum Moralium; quorum neutram à quoquam vel Theologo vel Philosopho assertum unquam aut admissum fuisse animadverti. Pertinet ergo omninò ad potentiam cognitivam practicam, hoc est, ad Intellectum practicum. Quemadmodum Aristoteles, postquam virtutes morales statuisset in Potentia Appetitiva; habitus tamen Artis & Prudentiæ, etsi ordinentur ad praxin, collocavit nihilominus in Potentia Cognitiva, libro Ethicorum quinto. Firmant hanc sententiam & ista; quòd Conscientia fit quædam Scientia, & Scientia omnis est in Intellectu: quòd capax fit erroris, & error est morbus Intellectus: quòd ex communi usu loquendi, qui intelligit tantum arcana Regis, sive ea approbet sive non, rectè tamen dicitur conscius secretorum ejus. Ergo Conscientia propria sedes & Subjectum in animâ humanâ est Potentia cognitiva practica i. e. Intellectus Practicus.
units.tr: XXI. The subject in which (ἐν ᾧ), that is, the power of the soul in which conscience has its seat, is the practical intellect: the intellect, I say, not the will; and the practical, not the speculative, intellect. This question too is debated among the Scholastics: whether conscience belongs to the intellect, or to the will, or to both. I do not wish to mix myself into this dispute. You have had enough, and more than enough, of thorny subtleties already. So I shall briefly set out what serves my purpose. Aristotle, in the third book of De Anima, enumerates three distinct powers of the intellectual part: two cognitive, the speculative intellect and the practical intellect; and a third, appetitive, the will. Of these three, the extremes are the speculative intellect, which contemplates the true as true and rests in it, precisely, without any order or respect to work; and the will, which tends precisely toward operation and contemplates nothing at all. Between these two powers, as if in the middle, lies the practical intellect, which, in the manner of middle things, agrees with each extreme in some respect and differs from it in another. The practical intellect agrees with the speculative in this, that it contemplates truth; with the will in this, that it tends toward operation. As far as conscience is concerned, this above all is certain: it does not belong to the speculative intellect, because it directs all its knowledge wholly to practice. Nor does it properly belong to the will: for if it did, it would be in the will either by way of a power, and so would be the same as free choice, or by way of a habit, and so would be one of the moral virtues*; and we have noticed that neither of these has ever been asserted or admitted by any theologian or philosopher. It belongs, therefore, wholly to the practical cognitive power, that is, to the practical intellect. Just as Aristotle, after he had placed the moral virtues in the appetitive power, nevertheless placed the habits of art and prudence, though directed to practice, in the cognitive power, in the fifth book of the Ethics. These views are also confirmed by the following: that conscience is a kind of knowledge, and all knowledge is in the intellect; that it is capable of error, and error is a disease of the intellect; and that by common usage of speech, one who merely understands the king's secrets, whether he approves of them or not, is rightly called conscious of his secrets. Therefore the proper seat and subject of conscience in the human soul is the practical cognitive power, that is, the practical intellect.

units.la: XXII. Vidimus Genus & Subjectum: Sequitur Objectum, id sc. circa quod versatur Conscientia. Et hi sunt Actus morales particulares proprii. Dico primò Actus; i. e. aliquod ab homine operabile quâ homo est, sive creatura rationalis: sive id spectetur ut futurum & ab ipso faciendum, sive ut præteritum & jam factum, sive ut præsens & in ipso fieri. Conscientia undique oculata est, omnia rima tui[?]. Prospicit futura ; si quid turpe facturus es, monet ne facias : Aspicit præsentia ; & in ipso peccandi actu obmurmurat, vellit, mordet, pungit, tumdit, ut desistas porrò : Respicit præterita ; & ubi peccaveris, arguit, objicit, accusat, damnat, torquet. Contra, ut benè facias hortatur : dum facis ; mulceat, excitat, erigit : ubi feceris ; laudat, defendit, gaudio & pace perfundit pectus. Dico Secundò, Actus Particulares. Non limitando Subjectum, quasi essent aliqui actus non particulares ; sed oppositè ad scientiam illam quam Conscientia supponit & applicat ; quæ scientia, cùm sit universalis, applicatur tamen ad actus particulares. Dico Tertiò, Actus particulares proprii : ut hinc excludatur illa Conscientia significatio, quâ latius acceptâ, & ad alienas actiones extenditur ; ut cum dicitur Conscius arcanorum Regis, conscius conjurationis Catilinæ, & similia : Quæ non sunt nostri instituti, qui de Conscientia proprie dicta loquimur, quæ est circa agibilia, quatenus à se facta vel facienda. Dico quarto, Actus Morales. Ubi observandum quædam evenire ex Necessitate, quædam Contingenter. Ex Necessitate ; ut ortum & occasum solis, eclipsim Luna, &c. De quibus est quidem Scientia, ob eorum certitudinem : cæterum non omnino pertinent aut ad Conscientiam, aut ad Liberum Arbitrium. Quæ contingenter eveniunt, ea aut sunt ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν, i. e. in nostra potestate, aut non sunt. Quæ non sunt in nostra potestate, ut avium volatus, coorta subito tempestas, &c. nec sub scientiam cadunt propter incertitudinem ; nec quia extra potestatem nostram posita sunt, ad curam nostram pertinent, ut de eis quicquam aut Conscientia statuat, aut Arbitrium eligat. Rursus ἐφ᾽ ἡμῶν, eorum, quæ in nostra potestate sunt, quædam sunt moraliter neutra & ἀδιάφορα[?], hoc est, quæ neque de genere suo, neque ratione alicujus permanentis circumstantiæ continent se aliquam bonitatem aut malitiam moralem, ut Ire in forum, Scribere Epistolam, &c. Et ista quidem pertinere possunt ad Liberum Arbitrium, si saltem digna sint de quibus deliberetur, quia cadere possunt sub reflexione: sed non pertinent per se ad Conscientiam. Dico per se: quia fieri potest per accidens, ratione scandali aut alterius alicujus circumstantiae, ut de his etiam cognoscat Conscientia.
units.tr: XXII. We have seen the genus and subject. There follows the object, that is, what conscience is concerned with. These are particular moral acts that are one's own. I say, first, acts: that is, something a human being can do insofar as he is human, that is, as a rational creature. This may be regarded as future and to be done by him, or as past and already done, or as present and being done in him. Conscience is watchful on every side and searches out every crevice of you. It looks ahead to the future: if you are about to do something shameful, it warns you not to do it. It looks at the present: and in the very act of sinning it mutters, plucks at, bites, stings and swells up, so that you desist from going on. It looks back at the past: and when you have sinned, it reproves, confronts, accuses, condemns and tortures. On the other hand, to make you do good, it exhorts; while you are doing it, it soothes, rouses and raises up; when you have done it, it praises, defends, and floods the breast with joy and peace. I say, second, particular acts: not limiting the subject as though there were some non-particular acts, but in contrast to that science which conscience presupposes and applies. That science, although universal, is nonetheless applied to particular acts. I say, third, particular acts that are one's own, so that the wider sense of "conscience", in which it is extended to the actions of others, is excluded. Such is the case when one says "conscious of the secrets of the king" or "conscious of Catiline's conspiracy", and the like. These are not within our purpose, since we are speaking of conscience properly so called, which concerns things to be done, insofar as they are done or to be done by oneself. I say, fourth, moral acts. Here it must be observed that some things happen of necessity and others contingently. Of necessity happen such things as the rising and setting of the sun, an eclipse of the moon, and so on. Of these there is indeed science, on account of their certainty; but they do not wholly pertain either to conscience or to free choice. Those things which happen contingently are either within our power [ἐφ᾽ ἡμῖν], or they are not. Those which are not within our power, such as the flight of birds or a storm suddenly arising, fall under neither science, because of their uncertainty, nor, since they lie outside our power, do they belong to our concern, so that conscience should pronounce anything about them or the will choose anything regarding them. Again, of those things which are within our power, some are morally neutral and indifferent [ἀδιάφορα], that is, they contain in their own kind, and by reason of no permanent circumstance, any moral goodness or wickedness, such as going into the forum or writing a letter. These can indeed pertain to free choice, if at least they are worth deliberating about, since they can fall under reflection; but they do not pertain per se to conscience. I say per se, because it can happen per accidens, by reason of scandal or some other circumstance, so that conscience takes cognizance of these too.

units.la: Alia vero sunt moraliter bona vel mala: ut Deum colere, parentes honorare, depositum reddere; pauperem opprimere, aliena rapere, fidem fallere vel servare, & cætera omnia quæ Philosophi ἐπαινετὰ[?] vel ψεκτά[?] laude aut vituperio digna, Scholastici meritoria & demeritoria solent appellare. Et circa hæc proprie versatur Conscientia.
units.tr: Others, however, are morally good or evil: such as worshipping God, honouring parents, returning a deposit; oppressing the poor, seizing another's goods, breaking faith or keeping it, and all the other things which the philosophers call worthy of praise [ἐπαινετά] or blame [ψεκτά], and which the Schoolmen are accustomed to call meritorious and demeritorious. It is about these that conscience is properly concerned.

units.la: XXIII. Objectum ergo Conscientiæ humanæ est Operabile Morale, factum vel faciendum, omissum vel omittendum. Advertendum tamen est, hominibus Christianis qua talibus, Objectum Conscientiæ aliquanto ulterius extendi: ut non solum obligetur in conscientia ad agenda quæ sui sunt officii, quatenus homo est: sed & ad credenda mysteria fidei in verbo Dei revelata, quatenus homo Christianus est. Nam & Infidelitas impuram reddit conscientiam, Tit. 1. 15. quam purificat & emendat fides, Act. 15. 9. Et remordet Conscientia tam eum, qui contemnit quæ in Baptismo vovit se crediturum; quam eum qui mandata Dei violat, quæ promisit se servaturum. Etsi fortassis haud incommodè dici posset, Fidem etiam ipsam Evangelicam inter operabilia Moralia censendam esse. Ita enim ipse Servator Christus disertissimis verbis. Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in Filium, &c. Joh. 6. 29. Et Johannes Apostolus similiter: Hoc est mandatum ejus, ut credamus in nomine Filii sui Jesu Christi, & diligamus invicem, sicut ipse mandavit nobis, 1 Joh. 3. 23.
units.tr: XXIII. The object of human conscience is therefore the moral operable, what has been done or is to be done, what has been omitted or is to be omitted. It must be noted, however, that for Christian men, as such, the object of conscience is extended somewhat further. Thus one is bound in conscience not only to do those things which belong to one's duty as a human being, but also to believe the mysteries of faith revealed in the word of God, insofar as one is a Christian. For unbelief also makes the conscience impure, Titus 1.15, which faith purifies and amends, Acts 15.9. Conscience gnaws as much at the one who scorns what he vowed in Baptism that he would believe, as at the one who violates the commands of God which he promised to keep. Although perhaps it could fairly be said that the Evangelical faith itself is also to be reckoned among the moral operables. For so the Saviour Christ himself says in the plainest words: This is the work of God, that you believe in the Son, etc., John 6.29. And the Apostle John similarly: This is his commandment, that we should believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another, as he commanded us, 1 John 3.23.

units.la: XXIV. Restat ultimum definitionis membrum; proprius sc. Conscientiæ Actus: Applicatio nempe luminis quod est in mente per discursum rationis ad actus particulares.
units.tr: XXIV. There remains the last member of the definition, namely the proper act of conscience: the application, to wit, of the light which is in the mind, through the discourse of reason, to particular acts.

units.la: Dico primò, Actum Conscientiæ proprium & primarium esse applicationem. Tritum est in Scholis Axioma, Unius habitus unium tantum esse actum; primarium sc. & palmarium, & ad quem reliqui omnes actus eò pertinentes reduci possunt. Ut ex antecedentibus satis constat, multi sunt Actus Conscientiæ in specie: sed quisnam sit ille actus communissimus qui reliquos omnes infra ambitum suum complectatur, id potissimum inquirendum est; quia non debet ingredi definitionem Habitus, nisi unicus ille primarius Actus, qui est Habitui adæquatus, & ad quem cæteri ejus Actus universi reducantur. Hunc nonnulli, cum viderent plerosque illorum actuum, quos exercet Conscientia, ad actum judicandi aliquo modo referri posse, (judicat enim Conscientia de factis præsentibus, præteritis & futuris) censuerunt esse Actum Judicandi. Sed enim sunt aliqui Conscientiae Actus, qui non nisi durè admodùm & coactè eò referri posse videntur; ut exempli gratiâ, actus ille quo Conscientia rei factae vel omissae testimonium praestat: non est enim, aut Judicis de facto testari, aut Testis de crimine judicare. Quid quòd iste judicandi actus applicandi actum necessariò suppomit, ut se anteriorem: applicet enim priùs necesse est Conscientia factum de quo judicatum it lumini mentis, quam possit de ipso judicium facere. Et est applicandi actus, ei quam jam diximus vocis notationi valdè consentaneus, Conscientiam sc. ideò dictam, quòd sit scientiae ad scientiam applicatio.
units.tr: I say, first, that the proper and primary act of conscience is application. It is a commonplace axiom in the Schools that one habit has only one act: the primary act, that is, and the chief one, to which all the other acts that belong to it can be reduced. As is sufficiently clear from what has gone before, there are many acts of conscience in kind. But which is that most common act which embraces all the rest within its compass is the thing chiefly to be inquired, because only that single primary act, which is commensurate with the habit and to which all its other acts are reduced, ought to enter the definition of the habit. Some, seeing that most of the acts which conscience exercises can in some way be referred to the act of judging (for conscience judges of present, past and future deeds), have thought that this is the act. But there are some acts of conscience which seem to be referred to judging only very harshly and forcedly. For example, the act by which conscience bears witness to a thing done or omitted: for it is neither the act of a judge to testify about a deed, nor of a witness to judge a crime. Moreover, this act of judging necessarily presupposes the act of applying, as being prior. For it is necessary first that conscience apply the deed about which judgment is to be made to the light of the mind, before it can make a judgment about it. And the act of applying agrees very well with the meaning of the word already mentioned: conscience is so called because it is the application of knowledge to knowledge.

units.la: XXV. Dico secundò; Hanc applicationem esse Luminis quod est in mente; hoc est, Luminis, pro eo tempore quo fit applicatio, menti praesentis.
units.tr: XXV. I say, second, that this application is of the light which is in the mind; that is, of the light, present to the mind at the time when the application is made.

units.la: Sive fit illud Lumen naturæ; communes sc. Notiones & ipsius Naturæ dictamine cordibus humanis inscriptæ, & in Synteresi conservatæ, velut titio ereptus e communi incendio, & reliquiæ imaginis Dei post lapsum: sive Lumen divinæ revelationis, extraordinariæ, per visiones, somnia, prophetias, &c, vel ordinaria, quicquid sc. Deus humano generi patefecit in libris Sacris Veteris & Novi Testamenti: sive denique Lumen Rationis; quicquid nimirum ex utriusque generis principiis, lege sc. Naturæ, & revelatione divinâ, sic immediatè & evidenter deducitur, ut nemini fas sit, qui illa saltem concesserit, de his dubitare.
units.tr: Whether that light is the light of nature, namely the common notions and the dictates of Nature itself, inscribed on human hearts and preserved in synteresis, like a brand snatched from the common fire, and the remnants of the image of God after the fall; or the light of divine revelation, whether extraordinary, through visions, dreams, prophecies and the like, or ordinary, namely whatever God has disclosed to the human race in the sacred books of the Old and New Testaments; or finally the light of reason, namely whatever is deduced from the principles of both kinds, that is, from the law of Nature and divine revelation, so immediately and evidently that it is not lawful for anyone who has at least granted those principles to doubt it.

units.la: XXVI. Dico Tertio, applicari hoc lumen per discursum rationis. Lumen enim illud quod applicandum est, cùm sit Universale quid, & id ad quod applicandum est, actus particulares five singulares; non potest fieri talis applicatio, nisi ejusmodi mediante discursu, qui universalia singularibus connectere valeat. Et hoc est opus rationis, per ejusmodi syllogismum aut syllogismos practicos, quales jam ante exhibuimus. Porrò, quia (ut dici solet, & docet id ipsum experientia) {1}descendendo fere contingit errare: facillimè potest in hoc discursu invenire alicubi Error. Unde fit, ut licèt non facilè erretur circa {2}prima & Universalia principia, quæ majorem habent evidentiam; in illis tamen principiis applicandis, & deducendis inde conclusionibus sæpissimè erretur. Quò majore opus est attentione & cautelâ, (ne ipsi nosmet decipiamus,) ut in hoc discursu omnia diligentissimè expendantur, ut legitimè procedatur, ut debitè concludatur.
units.tr: XXVI. I say, third, that this light is applied through the discourse of reason. For the light which is to be applied is something universal, and that to which it is to be applied consists of particular, or singular, acts. Such an application cannot be made except through a discourse of this kind, which is able to connect universals with singulars. This is the work of reason, through such a syllogism or practical syllogisms as we have already set out above. Moreover, since (as is commonly said, and experience itself teaches) one very nearly always errs in descending, one can very easily find an error somewhere in this discourse. Hence it comes about that, although one is not easily mistaken about the first and universal principles, which have the greater evidence, yet in applying those principles and in drawing conclusions from them one very often errs. The greater the attention and caution needed, lest we deceive ourselves, so that in this discourse everything is most diligently weighed, so that one proceeds legitimately, and so that one concludes duly.

units.la: XXVII. Dico Quarto, Applicationem hanc fieri oportere ad actus particulares. Id quod tribus omnino modis fieri contingit. Applicat enim Conscientia Lumen mentis quod sibi adest, vel ad facta, vel ad facienda. Ad facta, dupliciter: Pri-
units.tr: XXVII. I say, fourthly, that this application must be made to particular acts. This can happen in three ways. Conscience applies the light of the mind that is present to it either to things done or to things still to be done. To things done it applies itself in two ways: First,

units.la: {1} Ὁ τὰ ... [illegible, ~20 letters]
units.tr: {1} Ὁ τὰ ... [Greek fragment, illegible: about twenty letters]

units.la: {2} Arist. 1. Ethic. ... P. st. 17. ... Arist. 2. Metaph. [?] mò, ferendo testimonium hoc à nobis factum esse vel non factum esse: quales sunt istæ Rhetorum formulæ, in quaestione Facti, Occidistine matrem, Orcstes? Conscientia respondet, Occidi. Secundò, ferendo judicium, quod factum est vel omissum, bene sit an male factum, rectène sit an perperam omissum; ut in quaestione Juris apud Rhetores, ubi de facto constat Occidistine Clodium Milo? Occidi. Fateris ergo te sontem? Jure occidi. In Prima applicatione procedit Conscientia per modum Testis: in Secunda, per modum Judicis. Officia autem & actus ejus sunt, in primo processu testimonium perhibere: in secundo processu arguere, accusare, excusare, defendere, condemnare, absolvere. Unde oriuntur porro in anima varii effectus: à redarguente, accusante, condemnante conscientia summa animi tristitia & inquietudo, remorsus, terrores, tormenta; è contra ab excusante, defendente & absolvente, summa animi lætitia & tranquillitas, gaudium & solatium ineffabile, quies[?] arrecta, fiducia intrepida, & inconcussa mentis constantia. Tertiæ Conscientiæ applicatio respicit futura facienda; in qua procedit Conscientia per modum Legislatoris, Præceptoris, Monitoris, aut Conciliarii. Et in isto processu, ejus actus & officia sunt dictare, obligare, instigare, retrahere. Hi sunt præcipui Conscientiæ Actus: cujus vocem recta monentis qui audierit, nec Testem ipsam multum reformidabit, nec Judicem.
units.tr: {2} Arist. 1. Ethic. ... P. st. 17. ... Arist. 2. Metaph. [?] first, by bearing witness that this has been done by us or has not been done: such as the formulas of the rhetoricians in a question of fact, Did you kill your mother, Orestes? Conscience answers, I killed her. Second, by passing judgment on whether what has been done or left undone was done well or badly, rightly or wrongly left undone; as in a question of law among the rhetoricians, where the fact is agreed: Did you kill Clodius, Milo? I killed him. Do you admit then that you are guilty? I killed him by right. In the first application Conscience proceeds in the manner of a witness; in the second, in the manner of a judge. Its offices and acts are, in the first process, to bear witness; in the second process, to argue, accuse, excuse, defend, condemn and acquit. From these there further arise various effects in the soul: from a conscience that rebukes, accuses and condemns come the deepest sadness and disquiet of mind, remorse, terrors and torments; on the contrary, from a conscience that excuses, defends and acquits come the greatest joy and tranquillity of mind, an ineffable gladness and comfort, a settled quiet, an unshaken confidence and a constancy of mind that cannot be overthrown. The third application of Conscience looks to things still to be done; in it Conscience proceeds in the manner of a lawgiver, teacher, adviser, or counsellor. In this process its acts and offices are to dictate, to oblige, to urge and to restrain. These are the chief acts of Conscience; whoever has listened to the voice of it giving right counsel will fear neither the witness itself very much, nor the judge.

units.la: XXVIII. Absolvi tandem, quæ de Conscientiæ Naturâ videbantur mihi dictu necessaria. Prolixius vereor, certè obscuriùs, quàm aut voluissem, aut debuissem, si res aliter tulisset[?]; aut quàm facturum me spero, in futuris (si Deus voluerit) de Conscientiæ usu Praelectionibus. Sed profectò intricata est & perplexa omnis (quod viri gravissimi jam olim conquesti sunt) de animæ intellectivæ potentiis & facultatibus disquisitio: tum quia res ipsæ sunt à materia & motu sensibili paulo remotiores, & notiores sunt nobis quæ sensui (unde plurima nostra cognitio oritur) propinquiores ; tum etiam ob mutuam inter se connexionem cognationemque. At rem manifestam, & vulgò notam, quæ est in quotidiano usu & in omnium ore, cujúsque vim & motus nemo est qui non sentiat, definiendo non tam illustrasti, inquietis, quàm obscurâsti. Equidem nihil hinc aliud fidere possum : nimirum, sic sunt inanes nostræ hominum cogitationes omnes & universi conatus. Quæ sunt ante pedes & oculos, quæ in sensus & animos incurrunt, quæ sunt lippis & tonsoribus haud ignota, quæ capere se putant, & quidem suo modo capiunt illiteratissimi quique homunciones; hæc ipsa non capiunt acutissimi Philosophi : In his vel subtilissimis ingeniis aqua hæret. Tempus, Locus, Motus, id genus plurima, quid sibi velint, & quid sint, quotusquisque est hominum nostrorum, qui non existimet se perfectissimè intelligere? in quorum naturâ indagandâ, eruendâ, explicandâ, Doctores profundi subtiles, Angelici, Seraphici, per multa retrò secula velut in palestrâ se exercuerunt, exercentque etiamnum, nec potuerunt hactenus post tantum sudoris & pulveris optatam metam contingere. In tempore sum, & de tempore loquor, & tamen nescio quid sit tempus, inquit, Augustinus initio libri de Tempore. Quâ in re nequeo satis admirari Dei Opt. Max. infinitam sapientiam, retundentis hoc pacto humanam superbiam, & repræsentantis mortalibus velut in speculo inanem illam ἀδυναμοφίαν [?] quâ sibi videtur aliquid esse, cum nihil sint, miserè decipientes cor suum. Ut scilicet discant homunciones metiri se modulo ac pede suo, nec sapere ultrà quàm par est, sed sapere ad sobrietatem agnoscentes insipientiam suam, ut Deo integra constet sapientiæ suæ gloria.
units.tr: XXVIII. Finally, I have dealt with those matters concerning the nature of Conscience that seemed to me necessary to say. I fear I have been more lengthy, and certainly more obscure, than I wished or ought to have been, had the subject allowed otherwise; or than I hope to be in future Lectures on the use of Conscience, God willing. But truly the whole inquiry into the powers and faculties of the intellectual soul is intricate and perplexed (as very grave men have long complained): partly because the things themselves are somewhat remote from matter and sensible motion, and what is nearer to the senses (from which most of our knowledge arises) is better known to us; and partly because of their mutual connection and kinship. Yet when it comes to a plain matter, commonly known, which is in daily use and on everyone's lips, whose force and movement no one fails to feel, you have not so much illuminated it by your definitions, my friends, as obscured it. Indeed I can trust nothing else from this: truly, so empty are all human thoughts and all their endeavours. Things that lie before our feet and eyes, that come into our senses and minds, that are not unknown to the bleary-eyed and to barbers, that the most unlettered little men think they grasp, and in their own way do grasp: these very things the most acute philosophers do not grasp; even the most subtle wits are stuck fast like water here. Time, place, motion, and most things of that kind: what they mean and what they are, how few of our people are there who do not think they understand perfectly? In investigating, drawing out and explaining their nature, the deep, subtle, Angelic, Seraphic Teachers have exercised themselves for many ages past, as if in a wrestling-ground, and still exercise themselves, and hitherto they have not been able to reach the desired goal after so much sweat and dust. I am in time, and I speak of time, and yet I do not know what time is, says Augustine at the beginning of his book On Time. In this matter I cannot sufficiently wonder at the infinite wisdom of God, Best and Greatest, who in this way breaks down human pride and sets before mortals, as in a mirror, that empty self-regard [ἀδυναμοφίαν] by which a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, wretchedly deceiving his own heart. So that little men may learn to measure themselves by their own measure and foot, and not to be wise beyond what is fitting, but to be wise unto sobriety, acknowledging their folly, so that the glory of his wisdom may stand whole for God.

units.tr: In which it is shown that the Good Intention of conscience offers no sufficient safeguard on which anyone may rest securely.

units.la: Et non sicut blasphemamur, & sicut quidam aiunt nos dicere, Faciamus mala, ut eveniant bona : quorum damnatio justa est.
units.tr: And not as we are slandered, and as some affirm that we say, Let us do evil, that good may come: whose damnation is just.

units.la: Mentem humanam aliquid in se Divini continere magno consensu fassi sunt veterum Sapientes: qui eam Divinae particulam aurae ² Διὸς [?] ἀπαύγασμα [?] ἢ ἀπόσπασμα [?], decerptósque ab Diis immortalibus animos nostros & quasi delibatos, Dixerunt. Quin & altius ipsorum nonnulli surgentes, & audacius prolocuti, Mentem Deum ipsum dicere, eique velut Deo ³ templa exigere, non sunt veriti. ⁴ ʻO νοῦς γὰρ ἡμῶν ὁ θεὸς [?], inquit, apud Plutarchum, Menander: & Ovidius ⁵Mens quoque numen habet: & Seneca, ⁶ Quid aliud mens [?] animum, quàm Deum in humano corpore
units.tr: The wise men of old have with great agreement confessed that the human mind contains something of the divine. They called it a "portion of the divine breath," an "emanation or fragment" [ἀπαύγασμα ἢ ἀπόσπασμα], and said that our souls were plucked, as it were tasted, from the immortal gods. Some of them rose higher and spoke more boldly, and were not afraid to say that the mind is God himself, and to demand temples for it as for God. "For our mind is God" [ὁ νοῦς γὰρ ἡμῶν ὁ θεὸς], says Menander, as quoted by Plutarch. Ovid says, "Mind too has a divinity," and Seneca, "What else is the mind, or the soul, than God lodged in a human body?" [Epist. 13.] "The soul of each man is his guardian spirit" [ψυχὴ ἑκάστου δαίμων], from Xenophon, as quoted by Aristotle, Book 2, p. 6.

units.la: Epist. 13. ψυχὴ ἑκάστου δαίμων [?]. Xenoph. apud Aristot. 2. T.p. 6. hospitantem ? Quorum ut illi animae magis [?] & substantiam, quae cum sit expers materiae & mollis, immunis à corruptione & morte intelligentiaque & arbitrii libertate praedita, ad Deorum immortalium proprius quàm corporearum veram naturam visa est accedere : ) sic illi, ejusdem vim illam & Συνείδησιν ἐπεργνητικὸν[?], quam {1} Conscientiam dicimus, spe-ràsse potissimum videntur. Hinc illud ejusdem Menandri, [illegible, ~20 letters] Mortalibus sua cuique Conscientia Deus est. Quo nimirum sensu dixit Dominus, se constituisse Mosen * Deum Pharaoni; quod sc. is Pharaoni voluntatem Dei subinde in-culcaret, ad eam faciendam Pharaonem inflígeret, non obsequentem continentibus plagis infestaretur: eodem fere sensu dici poterit, eundem quoque constituisse in Deum unicuique hominum (singularium propriam Conscientiam. Quae sc. ipsius vice, velut praeco legis aeternae, quae essent ipsi facienda fugiendave diceret; ad ea quae oportet praestanda sedulò impelleret; rectè aut secus factorum rationem exposceret; extorqueret à sceleratissimis quibusque justitiae divinae agnitionem; praemia singulis poenaque prout commeriti fuerint, ut judex aequissimus & decerneret & tribueret. Is enim est status naturalis Conscientiae, ut medio quodam inter utrumque loco sit posita; infra Deum quidem, at supra hominem: Deo subdita, ut ministra; homini praepositâ ut Domina.
units.tr: Of these writers, just as they thought the soul itself and its substance (which, being free from matter and pliable, immune from corruption and death, and endowed with understanding and freedom of choice, seemed to come nearer to the true nature of the immortal gods than bodies do), so they seem chiefly to have had in view that power of the soul which we call Conscience [Συνείδησις], the faculty of knowing and judging. Hence that saying of the same Menander: Each mortal's own conscience is his God. In this sense the Lord said that he had made Moses "a god to Pharaoh," that is, Moses would continually impress the will of God upon Pharaoh, to make him act on it, and would harass him with repeated plagues if he did not obey.{1} In much the same sense it may be said that God has likewise set up in the place of himself, for each single person, that person's own Conscience. It acts in God's stead, like the herald of the eternal law, telling a man what he must do and what he must avoid; it diligently urges him to do what is right; it demands an account of right or wrong conduct; it wrings from even the most wicked the acknowledgment of divine justice; and as the most equitable judge it both assigns and bestows rewards on each and punishments according as each has deserved. For this is the natural state of Conscience, that it is placed in a middle position between the two: below God, indeed, but above man; subject to God as his servant, and set over man as his mistress.

units.la: II. Unde exurgit Conscientia duplex respectus; perinde ut in aliis rebus omnibus contingit, quae sunt in aliquo ordine depositae secundum Sub & Supra : in quibus quae medium occupant locum, minimum habent respectum; alterum ad Superiora, quibus subsunt, ad Inferiora quae sub ipsis ponit sunt alterum. Ut Centurio & Tribuno paret, & gregario militi imperat : ( Ego sum homo sub potestate [?]onstitutus, habens sub me milites, Mat. 8. 9.) Et in serie prædicamentali, quæ inter genus summum, & speciem infimam interjecta sunt, sunt eadem & genera specierum, de quibus prædicantur, & species generum quibus subjiciuntur. Recipit utique & Conscientia, prout ad diversa referetur, diversam conditionem. Habet enim rationem & Regulati & Regulantis: respectu Dei & divinæ legis, rationem Regulati; respectu Hominis & humanarum actionum, rationem Regulantis. Cum itaque nobis propositum sit, Conscientia, (quam nuperrimè definivimus,) usum, præsertim quod ad res agendas attinet, estque ad vitæ morumque institutionem accommodum, explicare; instituti nostri ratio postulat, ut de utraque Conscientiæ obligatione, quæ nobis usui esse poterunt, dicamus: Passiva scilicet illa, quâ obligatur conformare se Voluntati divinæ, cui ut Normæ subest; & Activa, quâ obligat ad sui conformitatem omnes actus humanos, quibus ut Norma præest. Sunt ergo institutæ tractationis partes duæ: Prior, de Conscientiæ potestate, sive Obligatione passivâ; Posterior, De Conscientiæ potestate, sive Obligatione activâ.
units.tr: II. From this arises the twofold respect of conscience, just as happens in all other things which are arranged in some order according to below and above. In such things, those that occupy the middle place have the least respect: one part looks up to the superiors to whom they are subject, the other down to the inferiors placed beneath them. Thus a centurion obeys the tribune and commands the common soldier: I am a man set under authority, having soldiers under me (Matt. 8. 9). And in a series of predicaments, those that lie between the highest genus and the lowest species are both the genera of the species of which they are predicated and the species of the genera to which they are subordinated. Conscience, too, in so far as it is referred to different things, takes on a different condition. For it has the character both of the regulated and of the regulating: in respect of God and the divine law it has the character of the regulated; in respect of man and human actions it has the character of the regulating. Since, then, it is our purpose to explain the use of conscience (which we defined a little while ago), especially as regards the doing of things, and as it is suited to the ordering of life and morals, the plan of our undertaking requires that we speak of both obligations of conscience which may be of use to us. One is the passive obligation, by which it is bound to conform itself to the will of God, to which it is subject as to its rule. The other is the active obligation, by which it binds all human acts to its own conformity, over which it presides as their rule. So the treatment of our subject has two parts: the first, on the power of conscience, or its passive obligation; the second, on the power of conscience, or its active obligation.

units.la: III. De quarum priore ut legitima instituatur disputatio
units.tr: III. On the first of these, that a lawful disputation may be set up

units.la: III. De quarum priore ut legitima instituatur disputatio, illud imprimis præmittendum est, cùm Rectitudo cujus rei consistat in conformitate sua ad regulam suam proximam & immediatam, atque ita deinceps usque ad summam & primam Regulam; cùmque immediata Conscientiæ regula sive lex sit recta Ratio, legi tamen superiori quam Deus ei præstituit subdita: Conscientiam tum demum dici Rectam, cum conformis est rectæ rationi juxta eam legem quam Deus supremus Legislator ei præstituit. Pro conditione illius actus sive operis, quodcunque tandem illud fuerit, circa quod pro tempore versatur. Ultima proinde resolutio Conscientiæ est in legem aliquam rationali creaturæ à Deo impositam: ut qui solus est Conscientiæ Dominus & supremus Legiflator; qui eam homini indidit; qui ejus solus cognitor est & judex; qui solus potestatem habet animam, prout legem ipsius servaverit aut violaverit, fervandi & perdendi, juxta illud, Jac. 4, 12.
units.tr: III. Before we set up a lawful disputation on the first of these, this must be laid down above all: since rectitude, in whatever thing it consists, lies in conformity to its proximate and immediate rule, and so on up to the highest and first Rule; and since the immediate rule or law of Conscience is right reason, yet subject to the higher law which God has laid down for it, then conscience is called right only when it conforms to right reason according to that law which God, the supreme Lawgiver, has laid down for it, whatever the condition of that act or work may be with which it is at the time concerned. The final resolution, therefore, of conscience is into some law imposed by God on the rational creature, since he alone is the Lord of conscience and its supreme Lawgiver; he who implanted it in man; he who alone knows it and judges it; he who alone has the power to save and to destroy the soul, according as it has kept or broken his law, according to that word of James 4:12: There is one Lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy.

units.la: 12. Unus est Legislator qui potest fervare & perdere.
units.tr: 12. There is one Lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy.

units.la: Id quod apud omnes, quotquot uspiam sunt hominum, adeò in confesso est, ut non facilè reperiatur, qui id ipsum in thesi non ultrò largiatur esse verissimum. Ast in hypothesi, ubi quid agendum est, nescio quâ cordis humani pravitate fieri solet, ut plerique mortalium (etiam eorum, qui nec sibi videntur, nec aliis, omnem prorsus conscientiæ curam abjecisse,) tàm pronis affectibus ad ea fe rantur quæ facta cupiunt, ut ea non ad unicam supremam regulam fideliter exigenda adducant, (quæ tamen sola potest securam præstare confcientiam ;) sed fatis esse ducant ad Conscientiæ suæ securitatem, si aut bonæ intentionis prætextu, aut javeti viri exemplo, aut alicujus magni nominis Theologi authoritate se factâque sua quoquo modo tueri potuerint. Quæ cordis humani deceptio, quum & omnibus seculis nimium invaluerit, & novissimis hisce temporibus vel maximè; rem utiliffimam me facturam judicavi, & his quibus nunc vivitur moribus pernecessariam, si tres istas vulgatiffimas ἀγνωσίας, à quibus tot conscientiis periculosissimè illuditur, de medio sublatum irem. Est ergo an ostendendum, quàm ad indagandam veram propriam Conscientiæ regulam descendatur, non e in re aliquâ faciendâ ad Conscientiæ securitatem tis prasfidii, si id quod fit aut bonâ intentione si aut viri alicujus nitatur vel pii exemplo, vel de judicio. De reliquis duabus (si Deus concesser posthac videbitur: de eâ quæ primo loco occurrit Bonâ sc. Intentione nunc agendum.
units.tr: This is so generally admitted by all who are anywhere men that it is hard to find anyone who would not readily grant in theory that it is most true. But in the practical case, where something has to be done, it happens, through I know not what perversity of the human heart, that most mortals (even those who seem to themselves and to others to have cast off all care of conscience) are carried with such strong passions towards the things they desire to have done, that they do not bring them to be faithfully measured by the one supreme rule (which alone can give a secure conscience), but think it enough for the security of their conscience if they can in some way defend themselves and their deeds, either under the pretext of a good intention, or by the example of a holy man, or by the authority of some theologian of great name. Since this deceit of the human heart has grown too strong in every age, and most of all in these latest times, I judged that I would be doing a very useful thing, and one most necessary for the morals of the present day, if I removed from the middle these three most common ignorances [ἀγνωσίαι], by which so many consciences are most dangerously deceived. It must therefore be shown how far a man may descend, in seeking out the true and proper rule of conscience, to a thing done for the security of conscience, if what is done rests either on a good intention, or on the example of some man, pious or otherwise, or on the judgment of others. Of the other two (if God shall then see fit to grant it), we shall speak hereafter. For now we must treat of the first to present itself, namely the Good Intention.

units.la: IV. Ubi pono hanc conclusionem. Ad bonitatem actûs non sufficit bonitas intentionis. Hoc est, Intentio bona non potest sola & per se efficere, ut Actus aliquis humanus sit moraliter bonus: vel quod idem est, & sunt ipsissima Apostoli verba: Non sunt facienda mala, ut eveniant bona. Actum cum dico, intelligo tùm interiorem Actum qui est in Voluntate, tùm exteriores omnes inde profluentes qui sunt in facultatibus executivis: ut sit sensus, ex sola bonâ intentione non sequi, aut voluntatem ipsam, quæ est primum principium agendi, aut opus aliquod externum inde dimanans, dicenda esse bona. Intentio autem cùm dupliciter sumatur, primò proprié & Formaliter pro Actu intendendi, i. e. pro motu voluntatis tendentis in finem per aliqua media; secundò Materialiter & Objectivè, pro re ipsa intenta, i. e. pro fine in quem sic tendit voluntas: utramque intelligo in Conclusione. Actus enim intendendi, & finis intentus, pariter se habent ad bonitatem & malitiam Actûs; saltem quod ad quantitatem ipsius actûs pertinet: nam quantitatem bonitatis aut malitiæ si spectemus, non est per omnia eadem utriusque ratio. Posito enim quòd aliquis Actus sit de specie suâ & ratione Objecti bonus, & quòd fiat etiam in bonum finem; vel è contrà, posito quòd sit malus, & fiat etiam in malum finem: quanto fortius movetur voluntas dum ad illum finem tendit, tantò erit ille Actus (respectivè) vel melior vel deterior. Ut siquis Sacræ cænæ participaret, eo fine[?] ut mortis Christi recordaretur; quò fortius mortis Christi memoriam intenderet, eò melius Actum illum Eucharisticum præstaret: Et siquis proximo calumniam faceret, intendens ipsius perniciem; quò fortius hanc intenderet, eò pejor esset calumniandi Actus. Correspondet ergo & comensuratur quantitas boni vel mali Actus quantitati finis[?] vel malæ intentionis; si attendatur Intentio quantum ad actum intendendi: non autem si attendatur quantum ad rem intentam. Neutro tamen modo sumpta Intentio sufficit ad hoc, ut actus aliquis aliunde malus fiat bonus.
units.tr: IV. Here I lay down this conclusion: Goodness of intention is not sufficient for the goodness of an act. That is, a good intention cannot by itself and of its own power make any human act morally good; or, which is the same thing, and are the very words of the Apostle: Evil things are not to be done, that good may come. When I say act, I understand both the inner act, which is in the will, and all the outward acts flowing from it, which are in the executive faculties. So the sense is that from a good intention alone it does not follow that either the will itself, which is the first principle of acting, or any external work proceeding from it, is to be called good. Now intention is taken in two ways: first, properly and formally, for the act of intending, that is, the motion of the will tending towards an end by some means; second, materially and objectively, for the thing itself intended, that is, the end towards which the will so tends. I understand both in the conclusion. For the act of intending and the end intended stand in like relation to the goodness and badness of the act, at least as far as the quantity of the act itself is concerned; for if we consider the quantity of goodness or badness, the account of the two is not in every respect the same. For supposing that some act is good in its kind and in the nature of its object, and is also done for a good end; or, on the contrary, supposing it is bad, and is also done for a bad end: the more strongly the will is moved while it tends to that end, the more (in proportion) that act will be either better or worse. For example, if someone took part in the Holy Supper in order to remember the death of Christ, the more strongly he intended the memory of Christ's death, the better he would perform that Eucharistic act; and if someone brought a false accusation against his neighbour, intending his ruin, the more strongly he intended this, the worse would be the act of slandering. So the quantity of good or evil in an act corresponds to and is measured by the quantity of the end or of the evil intention, if the intention is taken as regards the act of intending; but not if it is taken as regards the thing intended. Yet intention, taken in neither way, is not sufficient to make an act which is otherwise evil into a good one.

units.la: V. Probatur autem hæc Conclusio multis & firmissimis argumentis. Primò ex verbis sacri Textus, Rom. 3. in quibus Apostolus non fine aliquâ indignationis specie rejicit iniquam illam calumniam, quâ docuisse dicebatur facienda esse mala, ut eveniant bona. Cujus locus scopus, vis & ratio melius intelligatur, animadvertendum est inter Apostolos Dominum Paulum vel maximè copiosum esse in asserendâ passim gratuitâ Dei misericordiâ, ineuntis cum hominibus peccatoribus gratiæ fœdus, & promissiones Evangelicas fideliter adimplentis, non obstante illâ, quæ intus, in corde latet, & in vitâ quotidianâ palam & abundè se prodit, humanâ injustitiâ & incredulitate. Quas tamen tantum abesse profitetur, ut irritas faciant gratuitas Dei promissiones, ut è contra longè potiùs illustriorem reddiderint gratiæ & veritatis ipsius gloriam: siquidem {1}ubi abundavit delictum, ibi contùlit superabundasse & gratiam. Arripuere hinc calumniandi ansam, ex una parte, ut Apostoli authoritatem imminuerent, Sophistæ & Impostores; ex alia, quò viverent licentiùs & excusatiùs peccarent, profani pestoris[?] hypocritæ. Nimirum, si vera essent quæ Paulo dicerentur, cedere peccata hominum in majorem Dei gloriam; Non esse cur Deus aut peccata puniat, aut peccantibus irascatur; Non esse cur quis à peccando abstineat: imò verò peccandum esse uberius, ut uberiorem Deus adipiscatur gloriam, & omninò facienda mala, ut eveniant bona. Reliquas cavillationes diluit Apostolus justis responsionibus; ast ultimam hanc [Faciamus mala ut eveniant bona] ne dignatur quidem responsione, clamat †[?] intùm manifestam esse calumniam & blas-phemiâ. phemiæ affinem, justúmque Dei judicium interminatur (ni resipiscant) tam importunis calumniatoribus. Quasi esset hoc sophisma ex eo genere argumentorum, quibus non tàm λύσιν quàm κόλασιν deberi censuit Aristoteles. Unde manifestum est, quod & omnes interpretes agnoscunt, Apostolum constantissimè negare, malum aliquod quantàvis bonâ intentione fieri debere. “Interest quidem plurimum, inquit Augustinus, qua causa, quo fine, qua intentione quid fiat: sed ea quæ constat esse peccata, nullo bonæ causæ obtentu, nullo quasi bono fine, nullâ veluti bonâ intentione facienda sunt. Esto hoc primum Argumentum.
units.tr: V. This conclusion is proved by many very strong arguments. First, from the words of the sacred text, Rom. 3, where the Apostle, not without some show of indignation, rejects that unjust calumny by which he was said to have taught that evils are to be done, so that good may come. To understand the aim, force and reasoning of that passage better, it should be noted that the Apostle Paul, above all the Apostles, is very full everywhere in asserting the free mercy of God, the covenant of grace he makes with sinful men, and his faithful fulfilment of the Gospel promises, despite the human unrighteousness and unbelief which lies hidden within the heart and shows itself plainly and abundantly in daily life. Yet he declares that these do so little to make God's free promises void that, on the contrary, they have rather made the glory of his grace and truth far more conspicuous: for where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. From this, on the one side, the Sophists and Impostors seized an occasion for slander, so that they might diminish the Apostle's authority; on the other, the hypocrites, a profane and pestilent sort, seized it so that they might live more licentiously and sin with a clear conscience. Namely, if what was being said to Paul were true, that men's sins redound to the greater glory of God, then there would be no reason for God to punish sins or be angry with sinners, no reason for anyone to refrain from sinning; indeed one ought to sin all the more, so that God might obtain a fuller glory, and in short evils are to be done, so that good may come. The Apostle refutes the other cavils with just replies; but this last one, Let us do evil that good may come, he does not even deign to answer, but cries out that it is a plain calumny and akin to blasphemy, and threatens (unless they repent) the just judgment of God upon such shameless slanderers. As if this sophism belonged to that class of arguments to which Aristotle judged that a punishment, not a solution (λύσιν [λύσιν] but κόλασιν [κόλασιν]), was owed. Hence it is clear, as all the interpreters also acknowledge, that the Apostle most steadfastly denies that any evil ought to be done with whatever good intention. "It makes a very great difference," says Augustine, "from what cause, to what end, with what intention a thing is done; but those things which are known to be sins are not to be done on the pretext of any good cause, under the guise of any good end, or with any so-called good intention." Let this be the first argument.

units.la: VI. Secundum sumitur à Natura Mali sive Peccati; quod ex sui natura nec est, 1. Eligibile, nec 2. Ordinabile ad bonum finem. 3. Nec aptum natura ex se bonum aliquod producere. Eligibile primò non est ex sui natura, & qua tale: quum nihil sit eligibile; quod non sit idem expetibile: & omne quod appetitur, sub ratione boni appetitur.
units.tr: VI. The second is drawn from the nature of Evil, or Sin, which by its own nature is neither (1) eligible, nor (2) ordainable to a good end, nor (3) fitted by its nature to produce anything good. First, it is not eligible in its own nature, and as such: since nothing is eligible that is not also desirable, and everything that is desired is desired under the aspect of good.

units.la: VII. Nec est Malum ex sui naturâ ordinabile ad bonum finem. Quod si esset, esset etiam expetendum: siquidem appetitus non solùm fertur in finem ab agente propositum, sed & in ea quæ ad finem illum consequendum conducere videntur. Si dicas, Deum ordinare mala nostra in bonum finem suum, proinde non esse contra naturam mali, ut ordinetur in finem bonum. Respondeo primò, non esse eandem rationem omnipotentis Dei, qui naturæ Dominus est, & potest pro beneplacito suo ex malo producere bonum; & nostri, quibus nec idem jus est, nec potestas eadem: sed nec nostrum esse de Dei Providentia circa malum vel curiosiùs inquirere, vel magistraliter pronunciare. Respondeo secundò, Deum quidem abuti posse & solere peccatis nostris ut inserviant gloriæ, gratiæ, & providentiæ suæ ; quin & nobis pariter licere ipsius exemplo, pro data nobis opportunitate, alienis peccatis abuti in commodum nostrum Temporale vel Spirituale : Sed tamen quemadmodum Deus, etsi utatur malo alieno in bonum, nunquam ipse facit malum, ut inde eliciat bonum ; ita nec nobis licere malum facere, ut inde proveniat bonum. Aliud est alieno malo uti in bonum, aliud facere malum cum intentione boni. Respondeo tertiò, posse aliquid dici ordinari in finem dupliciter ; vel improprie & communiter, quo modo ordinari dicitur quicquid quoquo modo ab agente adhibetur dum tendit {*}suum finem, & postquam ab alio suapte sponte factum est, per potentiam & sapientiam ipsius agentis (præter voluntatem & intentionem ejus qui fecit,) ad illum finem assequendum disponitur : vel restrictius & proprie, & sic illud solum dicitur ordinari ad finem, quod ab agente antecedenter eligitur, ut medium ex fui natura conveniens & conducibile ad talem finem. Priori sensu intelligatur oportet, siquando dicimus Deum ordinare mala in bonum finem ; id est, Deum pro infinita suâ sapientiâ & potentiâ uti malo in bonum, vel ex malo elicere bonum : sed omninò cavendum ne ejusmodi locutiones posteriore & proprio sensu intelligantur, ac fi Deus malum aliquod antecedenter vellet, approbaret, aut eligeret, velut medium ex fui naturæ conveniens ad alicujus boni finis consecutionem.
units.tr: VII. Nor is Evil by its own nature ordainable to a good end. For if it were, it would also be desirable: since appetite is directed not only to the end proposed by the agent, but also to those things which seem to conduce to attaining that end. If you say that God orders our evils to his good end, and therefore it is not contrary to the nature of evil that it be ordered to a good end: I answer, first, that the case of almighty God, who is the Lord of nature and can at his good pleasure bring good out of evil, is not the same as ours, to whom neither the same right nor the same power belongs; nor is it for us to inquire too curiously, or to pronounce authoritatively, on the providence of God with regard to evil. I answer, secondly, that God can and does indeed make use of our sins so that they serve his glory, grace and providence; and indeed, following his example, it is equally lawful for us, when the opportunity is given, to make use of the sins of others for our advantage, temporal or spiritual. Yet just as God, though he uses the evil of another for good, never himself does evil in order to draw good from it, so it is not lawful for us to do evil so that good may come of it. It is one thing to use another's evil for good, quite another to do evil with the intention of good. I answer, thirdly, that something may be said to be ordered to an end in two ways: either improperly and commonly, in which sense anything whatever that an agent employs in whatever way while pursuing his end, and which after being done by another of its own accord is disposed, by the power and wisdom of the agent himself (apart from the will and intention of the one who did it), to attain that end, is said to be ordered to the end; or more strictly and properly, and in this sense only that is said to be ordered to an end which the agent antecedently chooses as a means naturally suited and conducive to such an end. In the former sense it must be understood whenever we say that God orders evils to a good end; that is, that God, by his infinite wisdom and power, uses evil for good, or draws good out of evil. But we must be wholly on our guard lest such expressions be taken in the latter and proper sense, as if God antecedently willed, approved or chose some evil as a means naturally suited to the attainment of some good end.

units.la: VIII. Est etiam prorsus alienum à peccati natura, ut ex fe bonum effectum producat : Sicut nec potest {*}mala arbor ex fe bonum fructum proferre, nec tenebræ ex fe lucem. Sed idem ille Deus Opt. Max. qui pro sua omnipotentia {z}eduxit e tenebris lucem, potest etiam ex peccatis nostris occasionem fumere illustrandæ summæ suæ Sapientiæ, justitiæ, & bonitatis. Verùm hi sunt effectus potentiæ divinæ, ut causæ per se & proprie efficientis, ad quorum productionem nihil adjumenti conferunt aut virium peccata nostra quæ habent se quantum ad ejusmodi effectus meré contingenter & per accidens. Ergo illa Davidis verba quæ versu 4. istius capitis adducit Paulus è Psal. LI. [Contra te peccavi, ὅπως ἂν δικαιωθῇς, ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis] non ita sunt intelligenda, quasi aut eo fine David adulterium & homicidium perpetrasset, aut eo fine alterutrum ipsi perpetrare licuisset, ut sic tandem justificaretur Deus in sermonibus suis. Sed est ibi intelligendum illud ὅπως, ut & aliæ particulæ ejusdem potestatis ἵνα, ὥστε, &c. in plurimis Scripturæ locis, non αἰτιακῶς sed ἐκβατικῶς[?], ut sæpe distinguendum docet Chrysostomus: hoc est, ita ut eventum notet duntaxat, non veram rei causam. Quemadmodum enim potest qui serio philosophatur, ex jam concessis ab alio falsis præmissis veram inferre conclusionem; ridiculum tamen se præberet interim, si ad firmandam veram conclusionem ipse falsi aliquid ultro assumeret, quia verum non indiget falsi patrocinio: sic potest Deus, (quod & nobis etiam aliquatenus licet,) aliorum male factis uti in bonum; sed nec justitiæ divinæ bonitatique congruit, nec nobis ullatenus licitum est, velle malum facere, ut inde proveniat bonum.
units.tr: VIII. It is also altogether foreign to the nature of sin that it should of itself produce a good effect: just as a bad tree cannot of itself bring forth good fruit, nor darkness light. But that same God, Best and Greatest, who by his omnipotence brought light out of darkness, can also take from our sins an occasion of setting forth the glory of his Wisdom, justice and goodness. But these are effects of divine power, as of a cause that is efficient through itself and properly; and our sins, which contribute nothing of help or strength to their production, stand in relation to such effects merely contingently and by accident. Therefore those words of David which Paul quotes from Psalm 51 in verse 4 of this chapter, [Against thee have I sinned, ὅπως ἂν δικαιωθῇς, that thou mightest be justified in thy sayings], are not to be understood as if David had committed adultery and murder for this end, or as if it had been lawful for him to commit either of them for this end, so that God might thus at last be justified in his sayings. Rather, that ὅπως there must be understood, as the other particles of the same kind, ἵνα, ὥστε, etc., in very many places of Scripture, not causally [αἰτιακῶς] but by way of outcome [ἐκβατικῶς], as Chrysostom often teaches us to distinguish: that is, in such a way that it notes only the outcome, not the true cause of the thing. For just as a man who philosophises seriously may, from premises already conceded and false, draw a true conclusion from another; yet he would make himself ridiculous if, in order to confirm a true conclusion, he himself voluntarily assumed something false, because truth does not need the support of falsehood: so God can (and this too is in some measure lawful for us) make use of the wrongdoing of others for good; but it is neither consonant with the justice and goodness of God, nor at all lawful for us, to wish to do evil so that good may come of it.

units.la: IX Argumentum Tertium sumitur à naturâ Boni actus: ad cujus complementum omnium requisitorum conditionum concursus ita est necessarius, ut si è tàm multis una aliqua abfuerit, cæteris licet præsentibus, actus ille non censendus sit moraliter bonus. Celebre est illud axioma, Bonum ex causâ integrâ, Malum ex quolibet defectu: & constat in omni genere rerum plura ad construendum requiri, quàm ad destruendum. Sufficit quidem defectus bonæ intentionis ad hoc ut aliqua actio sit mala, (cujus enim finis malus est, & ipsum est malum ; sed non sufficit aut finis bonus, aut bona intentio, ad hoc ut actio fit bona, nisi adsint & caeterae conditiones requisitae. Requiruntur autem ad hoc ut actio aliqua, five interior voluntatis, five exterioris operis fit bona, tres distinctae bonitates : bonitas scilicet Objecti, bonitas Finis, & bonitas Circumstantiarum. Qualitas cujuflibet Actus primò & principaliter pendet ex qualitate Objecti five Materiae circa quam versatur : ita ut inde denominetur Actus quilibet indefinitè & quoad totam suam speciem Bonus vel Malus. Sic dicimus esse Furtum & Adulterium de totâ suâ specie Mala : Eleemosynam & Precationem de specie suâ Bona. Hoc tamen observato discrimine, quòd quae mala sunt simpliciter mala sunt, nec possunt ratione cujuscunque finis quantumlibet boni, aut quarumcunque vel commodiffimarum εὐσχημόνων [?], fieri bona : at quae naturâ suâ bona sunt, possunt tamen à fine aut indebitis circumstantiis ita vitiari, ut desinant esse bona & fiant mala. Suppositâ ergo pravitate Objecti, abstinendum est protinus ab actu, ut simpliciter malo, veluti à Furto, ab Adulterio, &c. nec opus est ulteriori examine. At suppositâ bonitate Objecti, non statim cuiquam tutum est ad agendum fe comparare aut quod actum fuerit comprobare; nisi expensis prius diligenter & Fine ad quem digitur, & singulis quibus quasi vestitur Circumstantiis. Illa ergo quae dici solent, Bonitatem actuum pendere à fine, & Finem discriminare actiones, eatenus quidem vera sunt, fi actus ratione Objecti five Materiae sint boni, vel saltem medii & indifferentes; non autem fi mali. Objecti enim bonitas supposita, Actus bonitatem suam & malitiam praecipuè sumit à Fine. Exempli gratiâ, Actus erogandi in pauperem eleemosynam, qui est actus ti-nus respectu materiae five objecti, fi fiat ob inanem gloriam, [illegible, ~2 letters]iam, fit moraliter malus, eò quòd non ordina-tur ad rectum finem. Idem Actus, si fiat ad subvandam[?] proximi indigentiam, est quidem hactenus bonus, quòd & sit de materia licita, & fiat intentione recta, adeoque habeat utramque illam de quibus jam diximus bonitatem, Objecti sc. & Finis: non tamen adhuc dici potest simpliciter bonus, nisi [illegible, ~4 letters]erit insuper debitè (ut loquuntur) circumstantiatus. Requiritur enim ad complementum boni [?]eris, ultra bonitatem illam quæ est ex parte Objecti, & illam quæ est ex parte Finis, tertia etiam bonitas ex parte Circumstantiarum. Unde dici solet bonitatem actus pendere ex circumstantiis: non primario & principaliter; sed ultimatè & completivè; suppositis nimirum bonitate Objecti, & bonitate Finis. Cum ergo ad bonitatem cujuslibet actus moralis tria hæc requirantur, idque conjunctim, Materia licita, Intentio recta, & debitæ Circumstantiæ; manifestum est rectam intentionem per se solam non sufficere: & ex consequenti non posse bonâ conscientiâ fieri quidquam, quacunque eandem intentione fiat, quod aut ex se ratione Objecti illicitum est, aut redditur ex Circumstantiis vi-sum[?].
units.tr: IX. The third argument is drawn from the nature of a good action: for its completeness the concurrence of all the required conditions is so necessary that if even one of so many were lacking, the others being present, that action is not to be judged morally good. The saying is well known, Good arises from a complete cause, evil from any single defect; and it is evident in every kind of thing that more is required for building up than for tearing down. Indeed a defect of good intention is sufficient for an action to be evil (for if its end is evil, the action itself is evil); but neither a good end nor a good intention is sufficient for an action to be good, unless the other requisite conditions are also present. Now for any action, whether of the inner will or of the outward deed, to be good, three distinct goodnesses are required: the goodness of the Object, the goodness of the End, and the goodness of the Circumstances. The quality of any Act depends first and principally on the quality of the Object or Matter with which it is concerned; so that from this any act is named, in general and as to its whole species, good or evil. Thus we say that theft and adultery are evil in their whole species, almsgiving and prayer good in their species. Yet with this distinction observed, that things which are evil are simply evil, and cannot, on account of any end however good, or of any most becoming [εὐσχημόνων] and advantageous purposes whatever, be made good; whereas things which are good in their nature can nevertheless be so vitiated by the end or by unsuitable circumstances that they cease to be good and become evil. Therefore, once the wickedness of the Object is granted, one must at once abstain from the act, as simply evil, as from theft, from adultery, and so on, and no further examination is needed. But once the goodness of the Object is granted, it is not at once safe for anyone to set himself to act, or to approve what has been done, unless he first carefully weighs both the End to which it is directed and each of the Circumstances with which it is, as it were, clothed. Those sayings, therefore, which are commonly repeated, that the goodness of actions depends on the end, and that the end distinguishes actions, are true only so far as the actions are good, or at least indifferent and neutral, by reason of their Object or Matter; not if they are evil. For once the goodness of the Object is granted, the Act takes its goodness and its malice chiefly from the End. For example, the act of giving alms to a poor man, which is good in itself with respect to its matter or object, if it is done for empty glory, [illegible] it becomes morally evil, because it is not ordered to a right end. The same act, if done to relieve the need of a neighbour, is indeed good so far, because both its matter is lawful and it is done with right intention, and so it has both those goodnesses of which we have just spoken, of the Object and of the End; yet it cannot yet be called simply good unless [illegible] it is moreover duly (as they say) circumstanced. For to complete the goodness of the action there is required, beyond that goodness which lies on the side of the Object and that which lies on the side of the End, a third goodness on the side of the Circumstances. Hence it is commonly said that the goodness of an act depends on its circumstances: not primarily and principally, but ultimately and completively, the goodness of the Object and the goodness of the End being presupposed. Since, then, all three are required for the goodness of any moral act, and that conjunctly, lawful matter, right intention, and due circumstances, it is evident that right intention alone does not suffice; and consequently nothing can be done with a good conscience, whatever the intention with which it is done, if it is in itself unlawful by reason of its Object, or is rendered [illegible] by its Circumstances.

units.la: X. Ast huic rationi opponet fortasse quispiam verba illa Christi, Matth. 6. 22. Si oculus tuus sit simplex, & totum corpus tuum lucidum erit: si autem oculus tuus sit pravus, erit totum corpus tuum tenebrosum. Ubi si per Oculum intelligatur Intentio, (quæ mens est omnium fere interpretum;) videtur ex bonitate intentionis omnino pendere bonitas totius Actus, idque adæquatè: ita ut quas vires habet mala intentio ad vitiandum actum, etsi aliàs malum, easdem vires habeat bona intentio ad probum efficiendum actum, etsi aliàs malum. Tam enim efficax est oculus simplex ad inferendum toti corpori lumen, quàm est oculus malus ad inducendas tenebras. In quam sententiam multa afferri possent dicta Patrum & aliorum Theologorum: quale est illud Glossae, Quantum bonum intendis, tantum facis; & ille nescio cujus e trivio versiculus, Quicquid agunt homines intentio judicat illos; & istis similia plurima.
units.tr: X. But someone may perhaps set against this reasoning those words of Christ, "If thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light: but if thine eye be evil, thy whole body shall be full of darkness" (Matth. 6. 22). If by the eye is understood the intention, which is the meaning of almost all the interpreters, then the goodness of the whole act seems to depend entirely, and wholly, on the goodness of the intention. So whatever power an evil intention has to vitiate an act, though the act is otherwise evil, a good intention has the same power to make the act upright, though the act is otherwise evil. For a single eye is as effective in filling the whole body with light as an evil eye is in bringing on darkness. Many sayings of the Fathers and other theologians could be cited to this effect, such as that gloss, "As much good as you intend, so much you do," and that verse of I know not what street poet, "Whatever men do, their intention judges them," and very many like these.

units.la: XI. Ad locum Matth. 6. quod attinet, Imprimis non sum nescius ex illis Christi verbis posterioris ævi viros doctos alium sensum eruisse, ab illo veterum longè diversum, nec ei quæ de re nunc agitur affinem. Dato tamen, ob debitam nobis priscis illis Doctoribus reverentiam, dictum illud Servatoris, hominum intentiones præcipuè respicere; Respondeo intentionem, cum sit motus voluntatis tendentis ad aliquem finem per quædam media, duplicitèr posse considerari. Vel prout dicit intuitum illius boni, in quod voluntas sinaliter fertur, præcisè, abstrahendo sc. ab omni consideratione mediorum: ut si quis dicat se intendere gloriam Dei, vel utilitatem aut voluptatem propriam. Vel prout dicit integram ordinationem totius processus ab initio operis ad finem, includendo etiam & Media: ut si quis dicat se intendere gloriam Dei extruendo templum, vel occidendo idololatram; aut intendere utilitatem propriam comparando sibi divitias honesto labore, vel furto & rapinâ. Quemadmodum dici potest iter intendere Romam, & is qui de eundo Romam tantum cogitat, nec dum statuit qua via sit eò profecturus; & is etiam qui simul & quo sibi eundum cogitat, & quâ de Intentione primo modo sumptâ nos in tota hac quæstione loquimur, sc. ut finem solùm respicit, non item media: ut ita fere sumitur in communi usu loquendi.
units.tr: XI. As for the passage in Matthew 6, I am not unaware that learned men of a later age have drawn from those words of Christ a sense far different from that of the ancients, and one not related to the matter now under discussion. Yet, granting, out of the reverence we owe those early Doctors, that the Saviour's saying chiefly concerns men's intentions, I answer that intention, since it is a movement of the will tending to some end by certain means, can be considered in two ways. It may be taken as the bare view of that good toward which the will finally moves, abstracting entirely from any consideration of means: as when someone says he intends the glory of God, or his own profit or pleasure. Or it may be taken as the whole ordering of the process from the beginning of the work to its end, including the means as well: as when someone says he intends the glory of God by building a temple or by killing an idolater, or intends his own profit by gaining riches through honest labour, or through theft and robbery. In the same way one may say that he intends to go to Rome, both of a man who thinks only of going to Rome and has not yet decided by what road he will set out, and of a man who thinks both where he must go and by what way. In the first sense, which is the sense in which we speak of intention throughout this whole question, intention regards the end only and not the means; and this is how the word is usually taken in common speech.

units.la: Ast dicta illa Patrum & aliorum Theologorum, quæ videntur ex sola intentione meriti bonitatem & malitiam humanorum actuum, & in illis Christi verbis de oculo simplici & pravo fundatur, Intentionem accipiunt in posteriore significatione, prout unà cum Fine includit & Media. Scitum est illud Bernardi. Ut oculus, inquit, sit simplex, duo sunt necessaria: scilicet ut veritas sit in electione, & charitas in intentione. Hoc est, ut intentio nostra sit absolutè recta, utrumque requiritur: ut nec proponamus nobis finem, qui amori Dei & proximi adversetur; nec media eligamus quæ non sint cum justitia & honestate conjuncta. In omni igitur opere, non id solum spectandum est, ut sit nobis bonus propositus finis; sed & opera insuper adhibenda, ut idoneis, legitimis ac honestis mediis ad scopum sic propositum contendamus. Cum enim electio mediorum ex intentione finis oriatur, & sic cum eâ ita necessariò connexa, ut habeat respectu ejus rationem accidentis cujusdam inseparabilis, vel necessariæ circumstantiæ: Scholastici ferè concludunt{1} electionem malam vitiare intentionem alias bonam, reddendo eam ex bonâ malam, eodem omnino modo, quo malæ circumstantiæ vitiant actiones quarum sunt appendices.
units.tr: But those sayings of the Fathers and other theologians, which seem to ground the goodness and badness of human acts on intention alone, and which rest on Christ's words about the single and the evil eye, take intention in the second sense, as it includes the means together with the end. Bernard's saying is apt: "For the eye to be single," he says, "two things are necessary: namely, that there be truth in the choice, and charity in the intention." That is, for our intention to be wholly right, both are required: that we set before ourselves no end opposed to the love of God and of our neighbour, and that we choose no means not joined with justice and honesty. In every work, therefore, we must consider not only that we have a good end proposed, but we must also apply our works to strive toward that aim by means that are fit, lawful and honest. For since the choice of means arises from the intention of the end, and is so necessarily connected with it that, in relation to it, it has the character of some inseparable accident or necessary circumstance, the Schoolmen mostly conclude that an evil choice vitiates an intention which is otherwise good, turning it from good into evil, in exactly the same way that evil circumstances vitiate the actions of which they are attendants.

units.la: XII. Argumentum quartum sumitur à Legis Divinæ perfectione & obligatione. Propositâ nimirum est hominibus à Deo Lex; Lex perfectissima, quæ facienda præcipit, vetat non facienda. [Indicavit tibi, O homo, quid sit bonum, & quid requirat à te Dominus, Mic. 6. 8.] Huic Legi, siquidem satisfacere velimus officio nostro, parebimus oportet. Hac lege jubemur, quod & passim in Scripturis inculcatur, bonum agere, malum fugere. Quòd si nos è contrà, ubi nobis ipsis visum fuerit, agenda, fugiendáque fuscque deque habitâ Lege Dei, ex nostro commodo metiamur; & vel ea quæ Deus fieri præcipit bona metu insecuturi inde alicujus mali omittamus, vel ea quæ fieri vetat mala intuitu proventuri inde alicujus boni admittamus; quid hoc aliud est, quàm omnipotentis Dei expressæ voluntati nostra homuncionum consilia ant-ferre, & prudentiæ carnis postpònere sapientissimi spiritus authoritatem ? Longe aliter vir sanctus D[?]. vid. A mandatis tuis intellexi, propterea odivi omnem viam iniquam, Psal. 1[?]9. 104. qu. d.
