Edostus è lege tuâ, (quæ mihi de die, de nocte, in corde est, in ore, in manibus,) quæ mihi agenda sunt plane intelligo, quæque fugienda : quapropter omnem viam quæ legi tuæ consentanea non est, quocumque me tandem perducere videatur, non dicto solùm, sed & odi. Cum itaque vetitum sit Legi Dei omne malum, nec continet ea lex ullam exceptionem intentionis aut eventus boni, nec sit distinguendum ubi lex non distinguit, aut excipiendum ubi lex non excipit : omninò constat peccare eum contra Legem Dei, quisquis quâcunque de causa, quacunque intentione, sciens facit quod malum est.
units.tr: XII. The fourth argument is drawn from the perfection and the obligation of the Divine Law. God has set before men a Law, a most perfect Law, which commands what is to be done and forbids what is not to be done: "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the Lord require of thee?" (Mic. 6. 8). If we wish to satisfy our duty, we must obey this Law. By this law we are bidden, as is everywhere pressed in the Scriptures, to do good and to flee evil. But if, on the contrary, whenever it seems good to us, we weigh what is to be done and what avoided by our own convenience, holding the Law of God in little regard, and either omit what God commands as good, for fear of some evil that may follow from it, or admit what He forbids as evil, in view of some good that may come of it, what is this but to set the counsels of our puny selves above the express will of almighty God, and to prefer the prudence of the flesh before the authority of the most wise Spirit? The holy man spoke very differently: "Through thy precepts I get understanding: therefore I hate every false way" (Psal. 119. 104). That is, as if he said: Taught by Thy law, which is before me day and night, in my heart, in my mouth, in my hands, I clearly understand what I must do and what I must shun; therefore every way which is not agreeable to Thy law, by whatever road it seems to lead me, I not only reject but hate. Since therefore every evil is forbidden by the Law of God, and that law makes no exception for intention or for the good outcome, and since one must not distinguish where the law does not distinguish, nor make exceptions where the law makes none, it is wholly plain that whoever, for whatever cause and with whatever intention, knowingly does what is evil, sins against the Law of God.

units.la: XIII. Sequitur argumentum Quintum, ab exemplis eorum, qui boni finis obtentu, expresso Dei præcepto ausi contravenire, irata Deo iustas dederunt temeritatis suæ pœnas. Saulî Hebræorum Regi, qui Amalekitarum pecori, quod Deus universum deleri mandaverat, pepercit, eo fine (ut saltem præ se tulit) ut inde optimam Deo victimam immolaret, missus à Deo Samuel propheta, & peccati gravitatem ob oculos posuit, & in tantæ inobedientiæ pœnam, futuram regni amissionem prædixit. Si cui hoc exemplum firmandæ rei propositæ parùm idoneum eò videbitur, quòd non constet Saulem bona intentione id fecisse quod fecerit, nec eum finem, quem postea tamen obtendit, sibi in animo fixum & propositum tum habuisse cum id faceret ; quin potiùs verò similius sit eum non aliud adhuc quàm temporale commodum suum spestasse ; postquam autem ei obje&tum esset à propheta & criminî datum quod Dei mandato non obaudivisset, tum demum (quod hypocrisi solenne olenne est) istam excogitasse inobedientiæ suæ satisfactionem & quasi [illegible, ~12 letters] ne quid nobis molestiæ creet hæc exceptiuncula, observandum t[?], ubi accedit inobedientiæ hypocrisis, non tàm auri crimen quàm duplicari. Fuisse quidem Saulm duplicis culpæ reum nullius dubito; Inobedienia & Simulationis: ut interim taceam tertiam ilam utriusque radicem, Mandatum[?] affectum. Distincta utique sunt duo ista peccata; & nec natura, nec tempore conjuncta. Non naturâ; quia poest esse alterutrum sine altero: non tempore; præsit enim aliquandiu inobedientia, accessit postea nova occasione simulatio. Id quod ex ipsis [?]amuelis verbis non obscurè colligi potest: qui dissimulata prorsus Regis simulatione, unam ejus obedientiam severè admodum & acriter reprehenit. 'Potior est, inquit, obedientia sacrificio. Qua[?]diceret, Quid mihi sacrificia narras; quæ, seu ona fide ante intenderis, seu nunc demum excuindæ inobedientiæ tuæ obtendas, perinde est ad bsequii rationem. Mos erat gerendus præcipienti Domino, & quod abs illo in mandatis acceperas rompte & sine disceptatione adimplendum. Sed nim utcunque se habeat res Saulina, illud inte[?]im certum est, Uzzam (cujus historia, 2. Sam. 6. scripta legitur) non simulatè, sed bonâ fide & ia admodum intentione sacro vasi manum admoisse ; ne scilicet excuteretur in terram Arca fœdeis, (quod erat tunc temporis & sub œconomiâ eteris Testamenti tremendum divinæ præsentiæ ymbolum) cum succusso vehementius quo vehebatur plaustro velut mox ruitura nutaret. Leviculà hæc (ut quibusdam visò) sed importuna temeritate, etsi nulla subesset mala mens, commeruit tamen, ut magnâ spectante populi coronâ immissæ divinitus mortis præsenti supplicio afficereur. Edixerat nimirum jamdiu Dominus Jehova
units.tr: XIII. There follows the fifth argument, from the examples of those who, under pretext of a good end, have dared to contravene an express command of God, and who, with God angered, have paid just penalties for their rashness. Saul, king of the Hebrews, spared the flock of the Amalekites, which God had commanded to be utterly destroyed, with the end (as he at least professed) of sacrificing the finest of it as a victim to God. The prophet Samuel, sent by God, set before him the gravity of his sin and, as the punishment of so great a disobedience, foretold the loss of his kingdom. If anyone thinks this example not very suitable for establishing the point proposed, because it is not certain that Saul did what he did with a good intention, nor that he had in mind, at the time he did it, the end he later put forward, but it is rather more likely that he then aimed at nothing but his own temporal advantage; and that only after the prophet confronted him and charged him with not having obeyed God's command did he, as is customary with hypocrites, devise this satisfaction for his disobedience, then let it be observed that this small exception need cause us no trouble: where hypocrisy is added to disobedience, the crime is not so much increased as doubled. I do not doubt that Saul was guilty of a double fault, of disobedience and of dissimulation; to say nothing for the present of a third thing, the evil affection which is the root of both. The two sins are indeed distinct, and are joined neither in nature nor in time. Not in nature, since either can exist without the other; not in time, since disobedience came first for some while, and afterwards dissimulation was added on a new occasion. This can be gathered not obscurely from Samuel's own words, who, passing over the king's pretence altogether, reproved his obedience very severely and sharply: "Obedience," he says, "is better than sacrifice." As if to say: Why do you tell me of sacrifices? Whether you intended them in good faith beforehand, or now at last put them forward as a pretext for your disobedience, it makes no difference to the matter of obedience. The Lord's command had to be followed, and what you had received from Him in His commands had to be carried out promptly and without dispute. But however the affair of Saul stands, this at least is certain: Uzzah (whose story is written in 2 Sam. 6) laid his hand on the holy vessel not in pretence but in good faith and with a very good intention, namely lest the Ark of the covenant should be thrown to the ground (which at that time, and under the economy of the Old Testament, was a dreadful symbol of the divine presence), when it was shaken violently and, as the cart in which it was carried swayed, seemed about to fall. Though this rashness was a slight one, as it seemed to some, and an untimely one, yet even if no evil mind lay beneath it, it deserved, with a great crowd of people looking on, to be punished by a present death sent from God. For the Lord Jehovah had long before ordained

units.la: {1}Arcam humeris sacerdotum gestandam esse, non plaustro imponendam; nec ulli fas esse extra ordinem sacerdotalem, idque gentis tantum Kohathitarum, Arcae deportandae operam dare, aut {2}rem sacram attingere; qui secus faxit, mala morte periturum. Hac igitur in primum ejus legis violatorem severâ animadversione voluit Deus Legi suae reverentiam conciliare, ejusque authoritatem conservare; ne quis audacter temerario contra id quod ipse sanciverat agere aliquid aggredive quocunque praetextu praesumeret. Accensus enim ira percussit eum ibi Deus propter imprudens hoc factum, ita ut morereturibi prope arcam Dei, 2. Sam. 6. 7.
units.tr: {1}The ark was to be carried on the shoulders of the priests, not placed on a cart, and no one outside the priestly order, and of the Kohathite clan alone, was permitted to take part in carrying the ark or to touch the holy thing. Whoever did otherwise would die a wretched death. God therefore wished to make an example of the first violator of this law with severe punishment, both to secure reverence for his Law and to preserve its authority, so that no one would presume to undertake or attempt anything boldly, under whatever pretext, contrary to what he had sanctioned. For the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and God smote him there for his error, so that he died there by the ark of God, 2 Sam. 6. 7.

units.la: XIV. Argumentum ultimum, ab incommodis contrariae sententiae.
units.tr: XIV. The last argument, from the inconveniences of the opposing opinion.

units.la: Multa sunt illa: sed ego ne multus sim, unicum illum urgebo, quod instar multorum est, & ab Augustino saepe urgetur. Nempe, refixis Legum repagulis, omnia diffluere, & in incertum ferri, velut ruptis obicibus undae maris, ubi semel ripas excesserint, non se patiuntur certis limitibus contineri, sed per omnia vicini loca longe lateque vagantur. Qui semel limites modestiae transilierit, gnaviter hunc impudentem esse oportet, inquit ille. Sed D. Augustinum potius audiamus.
units.tr: There are many such inconveniences, but I will not be long-winded; I will press only that one, which is worth many and is often pressed by Augustine. Namely, once the bars of the Laws are broken, everything flows apart and is carried into uncertainty, like the waves of the sea when the barriers are burst: once they have overflowed their banks, they do not allow themselves to be kept within fixed limits, but wander far and wide through all the neighbouring places. Whoever has once leapt over the limits of moderation must be a shameless man, he says. But let us rather hear Augustine himself.

units.la: 3 “Quod sceleratissimum facinus, quod turpissimum flagitium, quod impiissimum sacrilegium (hem! annon suspicamini eum de nostro hoc saeculo, nostrisque rebus vaticinatum?) non dicatur fieri posse recte atque juste, si semel concesserimus in omnibus malis operibus hominum, ideo non quid fiat sed quare fiat quaerendum, ut quaecunque propter bonas causas facta reperiuntur, nec ipsa mala esse judicentur? Atque iterum, Cum concesseris admittendum esse aliquod malum, ne aliquid gravius admittatur; non ex regula veritatis sed ex suâ quisque cupiditate aut consuetudine metietur malum, & id putabit gravius, quod ipse amplius exhorruit, non quod amplius revera fugiendum est. Vis argumenti huc [?]edit. Si facienda sint mala ut eveniant bona ; quum certum sit non esse omnia mala facienda, nec propter quaevis bona ; aut utrique huic dubitationi certus statuendus est modus, [primo Quaenam mala [?]unt facienda, ut eveniant bona, & quae non ! secundo, propter quaenam bona aliqua mala sunt facienda, & propter quae non ! ] aut uniuscujusque hominis judicio permittendum est, arbitrari prout ei tulerit, & ipsi visum fuerit, quid faciendum & quid non, & propter quid. Quorum utrumvis concedatur, nihil inter homines tutum erit, nihil [?]instum, nihil ab injuriis, perjuriis, fraudibus, [?]pinis, caedibus, perduellionibus immune : exuent necesse est è terra, sine quibus conservari non [?]offunt Respublicae & hominum societates, Religio, Iustitia, Aequitas, Fides, Pax.
units.tr: 3 “What wickedness so monstrous, what shame so base, what sacrilege so impious (ah! do you not suspect that he prophesied of this our age and our affairs?) cannot be said to be done rightly and justly, once we have granted that in all the evil works of men we must ask not what is done but why it is done, so that whatever is found to be done for good reasons is not itself judged to be evil? And again: When you have granted that some evil must be committed, lest something worse be committed; each person will measure evil not by the rule of truth but by his own desire or habit, and will think that worse which he himself has shrunk from more, not that which truly must be shunned more. The force of the argument goes thus: If evils are to be done that good may come; since it is certain that not all evils are to be done, nor for any good whatever, either a fixed limit must be set for this doubt [first, which evils are to be done that good may come, and which not; second, for which goods some evils are to be done, and for which not], or it must be left to the judgement of each man to decide, as seems good to him and as it appears to him, what is to be done and what not, and for what reason. If either of these is granted, nothing among men will be safe, nothing just, nothing free from injuries, perjuries, frauds, plunders, murders, treasons: they must necessarily cast out of the earth those things without which commonwealths and human societies cannot be preserved: Religion, Justice, Equity, Faith, Peace.

units.la: XV. Satis jam ut opinor confirmata quam propandam suscepi Conclusione : non abs re alienum [?]erit, nec vobis uti [?]pero ingratum, certè non [?]nutile, Corollaria inde nonnulla deduxisse, quae vobis omnibus ex usu sint ad vitae & morum institutionem. Ex antedictis ergo illud imprimis sequitur, Cavendum esse piis omnibus, ne zelo gloriae Dei abrepti, ad illicita perpetranda ferantur. Esse Dei gloriam omnium operationum nostrarum finem supremum & ultimum, nemo rite Christianus negaret. Sive edamus, sive bibamus, sive quid aliud faciamus, omnia ad Dei gloriam referantur oportet, Cor. Ic. 31. [?]. Aut praepropero & praepostero gloriae Divinae zelo permoti, quantas contumelias, quas [?]ages ediderint olim in populo Judaico ejus factionis homines, cui Zelotarum peculiare cognomen adhaesit ; & inter Christianos patrum memoria in Germania & alibi Anabaptistae, a viris fide dignis & [?]rum suis temporibus gestarum gnaris prolixè perscriptum est. In quorum monimentis tam horrenda facta, & ab omni humanitate aliena narn[illegible, ~3 letters] eur ; ut vix ullam apud nos esset habitura fide[illegible, ~3 letters] nisi eandem fabulam quotidie videremus ab infel[illegible, ~3 letters] ipsorum sobole, translata tantùm in Britannias nostras Scenà, strenuè actitari.
units.tr: XV. I think the Conclusion I undertook to prove has now been sufficiently confirmed. It will not be out of place, nor, I trust, unwelcome to you, and certainly not useless, to have drawn from it some corollaries which will be of use to all of you for the guidance of life and conduct. From what has been said, the first thing that follows is that all the godly must beware lest, carried away by zeal for the glory of God, they are driven to commit unlawful acts. No one who is rightly a Christian would deny that the glory of God is the supreme and ultimate end of all our actions. Whether you eat or drink, or do anything else, all things must be done to the glory of God, 1 Cor. 10. 31. But men moved by a rash and perverted zeal for the glory of God have in the past, among the Jewish people, in that faction to which the peculiar name Zealots clung, committed how many outrages and deeds; and among Christians, in memory of our fathers, the Anabaptists in Germany and elsewhere, as has been fully written down by men worthy of trust and familiar with the events of their own times. In their records such horrible deeds, so alien to all humanity, are related that there would hardly be any credence among us, unless we saw the same tale acted out daily by their own offspring, the stage merely transferred to our Britains.

units.la: XVI. Nequis igitur vestrûm hoc tàm splendido artificio aut alios decipiat, aut ab aliis decipi se patiatur ; Cogitate primò, Omnes sedustores, Satanæ ministros, à summo sedustore Satanâ qui se 'transformare solitus est in Angelum lucis, edostos, non aliis artibus plus profecisse, aut imposturas suas plerisque Christianæ obtrusisse, aut pacem Ecclesiarum et Rerumpublicarum perturbasse efficaciùs, quàm ad summum gloriæ Dei, Reformandæ Religionis, propagandi Evangelii, extirpandæ superstitioni, exaltandi Regni Domini nostri Jesu Christi. Conquesti sunt graviter hac de re passim in suis scriptis Protestantium Theologorum proximi retrò seculi nominatissimi, Calvinus, Bucerus, Zuinglius, rcliqui, his vir eruditione, modestia, pietate paucis secundus Hieronymus Zanchius, Ego non intelligo, inquit, istam Reformatorum mundi Theologiam. Utinam earum rerum quæ nunc apud nos geruntur expectatio non confirmaret nimis esse verum illud quod vulgo dicitur, In nomine Domini incipit omne malum.
units.tr: XVI. Therefore let none of you be deceived by this most splendid artifice, nor allow himself to be deceived by others. Consider first: all seducers, ministers of Satan, seduced by the chief seducer Satan, who is wont to transform himself into an angel of light, have made no greater progress by any other arts, nor have they more effectively forced their impostures upon most of the Christian world, or more effectively disturbed the peace of the Churches and commonwealths, than under the pretext of the highest glory of God, reforming religion, propagating the Gospel, extirpating superstition, exalting the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ. The most renowned Protestant theologians of the recent past complained bitterly about this everywhere in their writings: Calvin, Bucer, Zwingli, and the rest; and among them, second to few in learning, modesty and piety, Jerome Zanchius, who said, I do not understand, he says, that theology of the reformers of the world. Would that the outcome of the things now going on among us did not confirm too well that saying which is commonly repeated, In the name of the Lord every evil begins.

units.la: Cogitate secundò, quanta cum perversitate gloriæ Dei bellis, tumultibus rixosis, contentionibus & disputationibus inutilibus prætexitur : cujus [?]ti Domini Apostoli vix unquam in suis Epistolis meminerunt (meminerunt autem frequenter) in ordine ad pacem, & fraternam dilectionem, suavem illam (quæ maximè Christianos ornat) in rebus adiaphoris συγκατάθεσιν[?] ne quis libertate Christi beneficio fruimur ita abutatur, ut sit alii offendiculo vel gravamini. Cogitate tertiò, debere eum qui sibi Dei gloriam proponit ut finem, Legem etiam Dei sibi proponere ut regulam omnino actionum nunc[illegible, ~3 letters] num suarum, Ad legem, & ad Testimonium, Psal. 8. Esto, ut par est, gloriæ Dei intuitus, agendi finalis causa: ut norma agendi & quasi ratio formalis, non est gloria Dei, sed voluntas ejus revelata. Illa ergo in toto vitæ decursu spectanda est, ut meta quam currendum; sed & hæc consulenda, ut [?]estam insistamus viam quâ ad metam perveniatur: ne illud in nos merito jaciatur quòd dici solet, Bene curritis, sed extra viam. Cogitate deique[?], Gloriam Dei respectu actionum singularium habere rationem finis transcendentalis. Transcen[?]ti autem, palam est nullum individuum immediatè subjici: velut Entis ut Ens est, non immediatè subjicitur aliquod Entium singularium, sive substantiale, sive accidentale. Sicut ergo Ens transcendentale verificatur de omni Ente, sive id universale sit, sive singulare, quod est in aliquo decem prædicamentorum: sic Gloriæ[?] Dei est finis omnium officiorum quæ in aliquo Decalogi præcepto expressè ut virtualiter continentur, omniúmque actuum ad pertinentium. Colendus est Deus, Parentes honorandi, diligendi proximi, fides servanda, justitia, veracitas, castitas colenda, cæteráque pietatis & charitatis munia præstanda, in honorem & Gloriam Dei. Cæterum sicut nihil habet verè rationem entis, quod non aptè reducatur ad aliquam speciem entis in aliqua decem classium Prædicamentalium: nulla particularis actio, quicquid homines in[?]enti in rem suam vociferentur, verè & propriè ad gloriam Dei tanquam finem referrtur; quæ non reducibilis ad aliquod Officium pietatis & charitatis, in aliquo decem præceptorum legis divinæ fundatum. Ludit ergo, quisquis Gloriam Dei obtrepere crepat; nec tamen dicere valet, quæ se facere profitetur propter Gloriam Dei, quo legis divinæ præcepto ea tueatur.
units.tr: Consider secondly, with what perversity the glory of God is pretended as a pretext for wars, tumults, quarrels, contentions and useless disputations; of which the Lord's Apostles hardly ever make mention in their Epistles (though they often mention it) in connection with peace and brotherly love, that sweet quality (which chiefly adorns Christians) of agreement [συγκατάθεσιν] in things indifferent, so that no one who enjoys the benefit of Christian liberty abuses it so as to become a stumbling-block or burden to another. Consider thirdly, that he who proposes to himself the glory of God as his end must also propose to himself the Law of God as the rule of all his actions: To the law and to the testimony, Psal. 8. Let the regard for the glory of God be, as it should be, the final cause of acting; but the rule of acting, and as it were the formal reason, is not the glory of God but his revealed will. The former is therefore to be looked to throughout the whole course of life, as the goal to be run towards; but the latter is also to be consulted, so that we keep to the right path by which the goal is reached, lest that saying which is commonly used be justly thrown at us: You run well, but outside the course. Consider also this: that the glory of God, with respect to individual actions, has the character of a transcendental end. It is plain that no individual is immediately subject to a transcendental: just as being as being is not immediately subject to any single beings, whether substantial or accidental. Therefore, just as transcendental being is predicated of every being, whether it be universal or singular and belonging to one of the ten categories, so the glory of God is the end of all the duties which are contained, expressly or virtually, in some precept of the Decalogue, and of all the acts pertaining to them. God is to be worshipped, parents honoured, neighbours loved, faith kept, justice, truthfulness and chastity cultivated, and the other duties of piety and charity performed, to the honour and glory of God. Moreover, just as nothing truly has the character of being unless it can be fittingly reduced to some species of being in one of the ten predicamental classes, so no particular action, however loudly men cry out for it as their own, is truly and properly referred to the glory of God as its end, if it cannot be reduced to some duty of piety and charity founded in one of the ten precepts of the divine Law. Therefore whoever keeps crying out that the glory of God is being abused is merely playing; nor can he say, when he professes that he does a thing for the glory of God, by which precept of the divine Law he defends it.

units.la: XVII. Ex prædictâ Conclusione sequitur secundi[?]: Errare eos vehementer qui sibi licere putant, pec-catum aliquod minus facere, ut vitetur aliud peccatum majus. In quam partem multa afferri solent: Imprimis pervulgatum illud omnium in ore, {1}malis minimum eligendum; cujus dicti hanc etiam afferunt ex Aristotele rationem, quòd scilicet {2}minus malum, si cum majore comparetur, habet rationem boni. Addunt & ex Gregorio Magno, Dum mens inter minora & maxima peccata constituitur, si nullus omninò sine peccato evadendi aditus pateat, minora semper eligantur. Nec desunt piorum virorum exempla; in quibus eximium est illud Lothi factum, & præ cæteris illustre: quem impuris Sodomæ incolis, ad nefandas libidines vitandas, stuprum filiarum suarum suasisse legimus, Gen. 19. Longum esset omnia persequi: ut plurima in pauca contraham, Dico primò, dictum illud è malis minimum, intelligendum proprie & primario de Malis (ut vocant) Pœnæ, non Culpæ; hoc est, non de peccatis, sed de externis incommodis hujus vitæ inter se collatis. Quo modo David proposita sibi trium malorum optione, Belli, Famis, Pestis, pestem {3} eligit ut e tribus malis minimum.
units.tr: XVII. From the foregoing Conclusion follows a second point: they are greatly mistaken who think it lawful to commit some lesser sin so that another, greater sin may be avoided. Many arguments are usually offered for this. First and foremost is the saying on everyone's lips, the lesser of evils is to be chosen. For this saying they also give the reason from Aristotle, namely that a lesser evil, when compared with a greater, has the character of a good. They add also a passage from Gregory the Great: When the mind is placed between lesser and greater sins, if there is no way of escape at all without sin, the lesser are always to be chosen. Nor are there lacking examples of pious men, among which the deed of Lot is outstanding and more famous than the rest: we read that to restrain the impure inhabitants of Sodom from unspeakable lusts he offered them the violation of his daughters, Gen. 19. It would be long to pursue everything, so I will reduce many points to a few. I say first, that the saying the lesser of evils must be understood properly and primarily of the evils (as they are called) of punishment, not of guilt; that is, not of sins, but of the external hardships of this life compared with one another. In this way David, having been offered the choice of three evils, war, famine, pestilence, chose pestilence as the least of the three.

units.la: Dico secundò, obtinere ad dictum ulterius etiam hoc sensu: Propositis duobus malis, altero pœnæ, altero culpæ; si utrumque vitari non potest, sed alterutrum eligi necesse est, eligendum est malum pœnæ potius quam malum culpæ: quia è duobus minus est malum, pati malum quam facere. Ergo eligenda potius est amissio bonorum quam abnegatio fidei: & exulare eligendum est potius quam peccare. Hinc illud animi robur prisCIS Martyribus spoliari, torqueri, mactari paratioribus, quàm thurificare idolis, aut aliquid in se admittere quod esset inhonestum, aut Christiano nomine indignum.
units.tr: I say second that the saying holds further in this sense as well: when two evils are put before us, one of punishment, the other of guilt, and both cannot be avoided but one of them must be chosen, the evil of punishment is to be chosen rather than the evil of guilt, because of two evils the lesser is to suffer evil rather than to do it. Therefore the loss of goods is to be chosen rather than the denial of the faith, and exile is to be chosen rather than sin. Hence that strength of mind in the early Martyrs, who were readier to be stripped, tortured and slain than to offer incense to idols, or to commit anything dishonourable or unworthy of the Christian name.

units.la: Dico tertiò, Si proponantur alicui duo pecta facienda, quorum utrumque constat esse peccatum, neutrum esse eligendum, sed utrumque vitandum. Atqui, supposito utrumque vitari non posse, sed alterutrum necessario esse faciendum, quod Gregorii verba illa manifeste supponunt; quid hisce in angustiis posito suadendum esse putes? inquietis. Respondeo, id supponi non posse. Cum enim omne peccatum tam sit voluntarium, ut si non esset voluntarium non esset peccatum, ut recte Augustinus, fieri non poterit ut aliquis in eas angustias redigatur, ut ei necessario sit peccandum. Adeo ipse sibi contradicat, si quis dixerit se mera necessitate coactum peccasse: Non enim peccatum nisi voluntate, & voluntas ita libera est ut cogi non possit. Nec alia Gregorii mens fuit: etsi verba illa praesertim [si nullus sine peccato evadenda aditus pateat] jam dictis repugnare prima fronte videantur. Non enim loquitur de duobus oppositis, quorum utrumque certo constet esse peccatum, quā de re nunc agitur: sed de duabus rebus, quarum cum alteram liquidò constet esse peccatum, alterum agens aut ex aliquo conscientiae errore, also opinatur esse peccatum cum non sit, aut ex aliquo injecto scrupulo vel læva suspicione veretur ne forte sit peccatum; qui casus alienus est à præsenti instituto.
units.tr: I say third that if two sins are set before someone to be committed, each of which is known to be a sin, neither is to be chosen, but both are to be avoided. But, supposing that both cannot be avoided but one must necessarily be done, which Gregory's words plainly presuppose, what do you think ought to be advised to a person in such straits? you will ask. I answer that this cannot be supposed. For since every sin is so voluntary that if it were not voluntary it would not be a sin, as Augustine rightly says, it cannot happen that anyone should be driven into such straits that he must necessarily sin. So much does he contradict himself who says that he sinned compelled by sheer necessity: for there is no sin except by will, and the will is so free that it cannot be forced. Nor was Gregory's meaning otherwise, although those words, if there is no way of escape without sin, may at first sight seem to contradict what has been said. For he does not speak of two opposed things, each of which is known for certain to be a sin, which is the matter now under discussion; but of two things, of which, when one is clearly known to be a sin, the agent either, through some error of conscience, judges the other to be a sin when it is not, or, through some injected scruple or faint suspicion, fears lest it perhaps be a sin. That case is foreign to our present purpose.

units.la: XVIII. Si quæras, Liceátne Caio minus peccaum in se admittere, ut majus peccatum, quod Titius alias facturus sit, impediat? puta liceátne leve [?]vitium facere, ne is homicidium perpetraret? Dico [?]arto, cum Augustino, non licere. “Si quaeratur, inquit ille, quid duorum potius debuit evitare, qui utrumque non potuit, sed alterutrum potuit: respondeo suum peccatum potius quam alienum; & levius potius quod suum, quam gravius quod alienum. Ratio in promptu est: quia nimirum in [?]sua potestate est ne ipse peccem; ne alius peccet non est in mea potestate. Sic enim, pergit ille, “ Ego utrumque malum fieri nollem ; sed id tantum “ cavere potui ne fieret, quod erat in mea potestate. At gravius est homicidium, quàm furtum. Fatetur id Augustinus, & respondet, “ Pejus est tamen “ facere furtum, quam pati homicidium. Et in eandem sententiam alibi, “ “ Quantumlibet distet inter tuum & alienum, hoc tamen erit tuum, illud “ alienum. Res clara, nec cui sit necesse ulterius insistere.
units.tr: XVIII. If you ask whether it is lawful for Caius to commit a lesser sin in order to prevent a greater sin which Titius is otherwise about to commit; for instance, whether it is lawful to commit a slight wrong so that he may not perpetrate a murder? I say, with Augustine, that it is not lawful. "If it is asked," he says, "which of two evils one ought rather to avoid, when one cannot avoid both but can avoid one of them, I answer: one's own sin rather than another's, and the lighter sin rather than the graver, if it is one's own." The reason is ready to hand: namely, that it is in one's own power not to sin oneself; that another does not sin is not in my power. For thus, he goes on, "I would not have either evil done, but I could only take care that that did not happen which was in my power." But murder is graver than theft. Augustine admits this, and replies: "Yet it is worse to commit theft than to suffer murder." And to the same effect elsewhere: "However far apart what is yours and what is another's may be, the one will still be yours, the other another's." The matter is clear, and there is no need to dwell on it further.

units.la: XIX. Quintò, si adhuc quaeratur, liceatne saltem alteri parato majus malum facere, suadere innocuus[?] ? ut parato occidere inimicum, suadere ut mutilet tantùm ? quo pertinet Lothi ad concives suos oratio. De Lothi facto non idem sentiunt omnes. Excusare id factum nil miror Chrysostomum ; furtim facit ; sic enim solet omnes Patriarcharum lap-sus[?]. Excusat etiam Ambrosius ; excusant & alii, veteres maximè. Augustinus peccasse eum censet, cujus judicium secuti sunt eorum qui secuti sunt plerique. Et sane videtur vir sanctus, ex pio ergo hospites affectu, dum valde solicitus esset ne quis eis injuria aut vis inferretur, animo perturbatiore nonnulla & dixisse & fecisse, quae non possunt facile excusari. Omisso itaque Lothi facto, ut ab hypothesi ad quaestionem in thesi transeam, liceat[?] censeo alteri, ne graviori facinore se polluat, levius peccatum suadere. Si dicas, qui alteri suadet peccatum, etsi levius, suadere tamen peccatum ; adeoque eum ad peccandum inducere : quod qui facit, ipso reum se facit peccati alieni. Respondeo, aliud esse suadere alteri peccatum absolute, quod quisquis fecerit, indubiè peccarit ; aliud suadere alteri peccatum conditionaliter, & ex ea suppositione, quòd non possit aliter gravius peccatum evitari. Quo supposito, non tam censendus est, eo consilio alterum induxisse ad peccatum illud levius, quàm [illegible, ~9 letters]
units.tr: XIX. Fifthly, if it is still asked whether at least it is lawful for one to advise another, who is ready to do a greater evil, to do a lesser one, as for instance to advise one who is ready to kill an enemy to only maim him: to this belongs Lot's speech to his fellow citizens. Not all agree about Lot's deed. I am not surprised that Chrysostom excuses it; he says it was done secretly, for so he is wont to excuse all the lapses of the Patriarchs. Ambrose also excuses it, and others too, especially the older writers. Augustine thinks he sinned, and the judgment of those who followed him is followed by most. And indeed the holy man seems, out of a pious affection for his guests, while he was very anxious lest any injury or violence be done to them, to have said and done some things in a more agitated state of mind, which cannot easily be excused. Setting aside, therefore, Lot's deed, so that I may pass from the hypothesis to the question in thesis, I hold that it is lawful for one to advise another to a lesser sin, so that he may not defile himself with a graver crime. If you say that one who advises another to a sin, even a lesser one, advises sin, and so induces him to sin; and whoever does this makes himself guilty of another's sin: I answer that it is one thing to advise another to sin absolutely, which whoever does sins beyond doubt; and another to advise another to sin conditionally, and on the supposition that a graver sin cannot otherwise be avoided. On that supposition, one is not so much to be judged to have led the other into that lighter sin with this aim, as to have prevented a greater and more atrocious sin.

units.la: † peccato[?] majore & atrociore. Non enim suadet eum ad peccatum, quà peccatum est, sed quà minus pec-catum est, & majoris impeditivum. Si porrò urgeas, Si mihi liceat suadere alteri electionem minoris peccati, cur non & illi liceat, etiam me non suadente, sponte suâ id ipsum peccatum eligere? imò cur non & mihi ipsi liceat id tutò facere quod rectè suadeam alteri? id est, è duobus propositis peccatis eligere id quod minus est? Aut cur licere putandum est è tribus primum, neutrum autem reliquorum: quum videatur esse omnium trium par omninò ratio? Eandem esse trium rationem, id verò constanter pernego: quum sit manifestissima inter hæc & illud discriminis ratio. Quòd nec illi liceat sponte suâ, nec mihi sponte meâ, ad majus peccatum vitandum eligere minus; id propterea sit, quia cum sit in potestate utriusque nostrûm (respective) utrumque vitare, tenemur uterque neutrum eligere: Cæterum quòd mihi liceat alteri suadere minus peccatum, ut evitetur majus, ex eo contingit, quod non sit in mea suadentis potestate (id enim jam supponimus) impedire utrumque. Danda certè mihi est opera, quantum in me est, ut impediatur utrumque: Sed cum videam me id efficere non posse quod maximè vellem & cupio, facio saltem quod possum & debeo, suadendo minus peccatum ut impediam majus.
units.tr: For he does not advise him to sin as sin, but as a lesser sin, and as a hindrance to a greater. If, moreover, you press: if it is lawful for me to advise another to choose the lesser sin, why should it not also be lawful for him to choose that same sin of his own accord, even without my advice? Or indeed why should it not be lawful for me myself to do safely what I rightly advise another to do, that is, of two proposed sins to choose the one that is less? Or why should it be thought lawful to choose the first of three, but neither of the others, since the reason for all three seems entirely the same? That the reason for the three is the same I flatly deny, since there is a most manifest difference between these and that. That it is not lawful for him of his own accord, nor for me of my own accord, to choose the lesser sin in order to avoid the greater, is so because, since it is in the power of each of us (respectively) to avoid both, each of us is bound to choose neither. But that it is lawful for me to advise another to the lesser sin, so that the greater may be avoided, arises from this: that it is not in the power of me as adviser (for we have already supposed this) to prevent both. Certainly I must make every effort, so far as lies in me, that both be prevented; but since I see that I cannot bring about what I most wish and desire, I do at least what I can and ought, by advising the lesser sin in order to prevent the greater.

units.la: XX. Ex iis quæ hactenus disputata sunt facilè intelligitur, quæ sit mens illius dicti è malis minimum, & quis ejus usus in omni deliberatione humana; ad quæcunque tandem mala applicetur, five Culpæ, sive Pænæ. Tenet enim, idque universaliter & in utroque malorum genere, quoties eò res devenerunt (ut rectè explicat starum[?] quæstionis Augustinus) ut è duobus malis sit in nostra potestate alterutrum evitare, non sit in nostra potestate vitare utrumque. Omne enim malum, quatenus malum, viro pro & prudenti vitandum est, quantum in ipso est: ergo duobus cujuscunque generis malis propositis; utrumque si vitare potest, debet; si non potest, eligendum est ei quod minus est. Non tamen sequitur eligendum esse de duobus peccatis id quod minus est, quia utrumque vitari posse jam ante demonstratum est. Et haec de Corollario secundo.
units.tr: XX. From what has been argued so far, it is easy to see what the meaning of the saying the lesser of evils is, and what its use is in every human deliberation, whichever evils it is applied to, whether Fault or Punishment. It holds, and holds universally and for both kinds of evil, whenever matters have come to the point (as Augustine rightly explains the state of the question) where, of two evils, it is in our power to avoid either one, but not in our power to avoid both. For every evil, as evil, is to be avoided by a wise and good man so far as lies in him. So when two evils of any kind are set before him: if he can avoid both, he ought to; if he cannot, he must choose the one that is less. Yet it does not follow that of two sins one must choose the less, since it has already been shown that both can be avoided. And this is the Second Corollary.

units.la: XXI. Sequitur ex principali Conclusione, Tertia, Nihil minus errare eos, fortasse & gravius, qui ut clavum clavo, sic malum malo pellendum existimant: ut verbi gratia, Superstitionem Sacrilegio, Tyrannidem Seditione, &c. Qui fere error est eorum hominum, qui sibi tum demum vel maxime sapere videntur, cum, ut hortulani solent plantas hac nimium inclinantes ut erectiores insurgant, illac inflectere, ab altero extremorum non se satis cavisse arbitrantur, nisi in alterum improvide ruerint. Sic Stulti dum vitant vitia in contraria currunt, & dum vitant Charybdim, in Scyllam incidunt. Sed ut aliquem locum habeat in medendis corporum affectibus aphorismus ille, (quem tamen non usque quaque comprobant medicorum filii,) Contraria contrariis curari, extrema extremis: in moribus tamen corrigendis, & in reformandis Ecclesiarum & Rerumpublicarum corruptelis, affert plerumque pro remedio certam perniciem. Grave est illud Sophoclis apud 2Stobæum, Ἐντὸς δὲ μὴ τοῦ πάντα τ' ἀνθρώπων νοεῖν [?] κακοῖς ὅταν θέλωσιν ἰᾶσθαι κακά [?]. Hinc pessum eunt mortalium res indies, Rebus medendi quod velint malis mala. Et ejusdem in Ajace aliud:
units.tr: XXI. It follows from the principal Conclusion, the Third, that those err no less, and perhaps more gravely, who think that, as a nail is driven out by a nail, so one evil is to be driven out by another: for example, Superstition by Sacrilege, Tyranny by Sedition, and so on. This is nearly the error of those men who seem to themselves to be wisest when, as gardeners are wont to bend plants that lean too far one way so that they stand more upright, they bend them the other way; they think they have not been careful enough about one extreme unless they have rashly rushed into the other. Thus fools, while they avoid vices, run into their opposites, and while they avoid Charybdis they fall into Scylla. But although that aphorism (which, however, the sons of physicians do not everywhere approve) has some place in curing bodily ailments, contraries are cured by contraries, extremes by extremes, in correcting morals and in reforming the corruptions of Churches and commonwealths it usually brings certain destruction as its remedy. There is that weighty line of Sophocles in Stobaeus, [Ἐντὸς δὲ μὴ τοῦ πάντα τ' ἀνθρώπων νοεῖν ... κακοῖς ὅταν θέλωσιν ἰᾶσθαι κακά], that is, not to understand within all human affairs... when men wish to heal evils with evils. Hence the affairs of mortals go to ruin day by day, since they wish to cure evils with evils. And another line of the same author in the Ajax:

units.la: —Μὴ κακὸν κακῷ ἰᾶσθαι [?]
units.tr: Not to cure evil with evil [Μὴ κακὸν κακῷ ἰᾶσθαι].

units.la: {2} Ἄκος, πλέον τὸ σῶμα τῆς ἄτης τίθει [?] hoc est.——addens pharmacum malum malo, Ne contrahas tibi majus infortunium.
units.tr: {2} Make not the remedy worse than the ruin [Ἄκος, πλέον τὸ σῶμα τῆς ἄτης τίθει]; that is, adding a bad remedy to a bad thing, lest you bring on yourself a greater misfortune.

units.la: XXII. At si aliàs publicis malis remedium afferri non possit, nisi aliquæ pia fraudes adhibeantur, legesque, & jura violentur, annon præstiterit aliquantisper ista fieri, quàm permittere Remp. ἀνίατα νοσεῖν[?] ; Lego quidem in sacrâ historiâ ita olim sensisse Pontificem Hierosolymitanum Caiaphām, qui in Senatu suæ gentis, posthabitâ justitiæ ratione, Jesum quamvis nullius criminis reum morte tamen afficiendum censuit, quòd sic fieri expediret.
units.tr: XXII. But if otherwise a remedy for public evils cannot be supplied unless some pious frauds are employed and laws and rights are violated, would it not be better to allow these things to be done for a while than to let the commonwealth suffer incurable diseases [ἀνίατα νοσεῖν]? I read indeed in sacred history that Caiaphas, the high priest of Jerusalem, once thought in this way: in the Council of his nation, setting aside the reckoning of justice, he judged that Jesus, though guilty of no crime, should nevertheless be put to death, because it was expedient that this be done.

units.la: Memini me alicubi olim legisse, Romanorum Pontificem nescio quem, in Cardinalium conclavi de præsentibus negotiis disceptantem, quum submonuisset quidam è purpuratis, id quod propositum esset consilium parùm sibi justum videri, respondisse, Licet non posset fieri per viam justitiæ, oportet tamen fieri per viam expedientiæ. Nimirum isthoc est sapere! hæc est eorum hominum quos Politicos vocant, ex Jesuitarum ni fallor officinis, depromta Theologia : Omnia metiri ex commodo Sanctæ matris Ecclesiæ ; Sacrosancta Dei eloquia quà lubet inflectere, nasi ad instar cerei torquere, distorquere, invita cogere in rem suam ; Et ut Lacon ille honestum esse dixit quicquid Spartæ esset utile, nil turpe ducere, aut refugiendum, quod Spartæ illi quam nasti sunt ornandæ quoquo modo inservire posse arbitrentur. Verùm apage procul è Scholis, è Suggestis, è Pestoribus nostris hanc insanam Theologiam. Longè nos aliter instituerunt Sancti Christi Apostoli, qui illi quæstioni (Expediat, necne ?) non ante locum concesserunt, quàm de altera quæstione (Liceat, necne) constaret. Quin & aliter senserunt saniores Ethnici, qui quoties pugnare videtur cum utilitate honestas, sic litem semper dirimunt, ut pronuncient utile non esse quod non sit idem honestum.
units.tr: I remember reading somewhere that a certain Roman Pontiff, disputing in the conclave of Cardinals about the affairs of the day, when one of the purple-clad men had warned him that the plan proposed seemed to him not very just, replied: Although it cannot be done by the way of justice, it must nevertheless be done by the way of expediency. Surely this is wisdom indeed! This is the theology of those men called Politicians, drawn, unless I am mistaken, from the workshops of the Jesuits: to measure all things by the advantage of Holy Mother Church; to bend the most sacred oracles of God wherever one pleases, to twist them like a wax nose, to distort them and force them unwillingly to serve one's own purpose. And as that Spartan said that whatever was useful to Sparta was honourable, so they count nothing shameful or to be shunned that they think can serve in any way to adorn those Spartans whom they have been born to be. But away, far away from our schools, our pulpits, and our plagues, with this mad theology! The holy apostles of Christ taught us very differently: they did not yield a place to that question (Is it expedient or not?) until the other question (Is it lawful or not?) had been settled. Indeed, even the wiser heathens thought otherwise: whenever honesty seems to clash with advantage, they always settle the dispute by pronouncing that what is not the same as honest is not useful.

units.la: XXIII. Ne longè abeam, Paulus hoc ipso commate omninò negat facienda esse mala, ut eveniant bona: quibus verbis quid dici potuit ad firmandam nostram Conclusionem aut apertius, aut efficacius? Audivi tamen hisce auribus qui cum istis ipsis Apostoli verbis premerentur, nec aliter quae defensa cuperent tueri possent, adhibita distinctione dicerent, nulli quidem privato viro fas esse pro suo arbitrio malum facere ut inde proveniat bonum, & hoc solum voluisse Paulum his verbis prohibere; licere tamen, hoc non obstante, ex communi gentis consilio abs his quorum interest quid Respublica detrimenti capiat id fieri, si sic postulet publica necessitas & populi Salus. Saluti populi quantum sit deferendum, dabitur fortassis posthac (si Deus voluerit) examinandi locus. Animadvertendum est interim, Primo, gratis haec omnia dici, nec occurrere quicquam in tota hac disputatione Paulina, quo nitatur illa distinctio: Deinde si scopum & vim argumentationis Paulinae hoc in loco attendamus, excludi prorsus omnes iustiusmodi limitationes & commenta hominum nugatorum. Occurrit enim Apostolus objectioni, de promovenda peccatis hominum Gloria Dei: Negat vel eo etiam fine facienda mala, ut illustretur reddatur Dei Gloria. Sequitur ergo a fortiori, non esse facienda mala, ob aliquem finem qui sit inferior Gloria Dei. Cum igitur cuilibet bono humano, privato vel publico, infinitiis[?] praeponenda sit Dei Gloria; nec liceat tamen vel ejus gloriae intuitu[?] malum facere: certè non licebit cuiquam aut hominisingulari[?] aut toti Communitati, in remedium cujuscunque mali publici vel privati, aut ipsi malum facere, aut alteri faciendum commendare.
units.tr: XXIII. Not to wander far, Paul in this very verse absolutely denies that evils are to be done so that good things may come. What could be said in words more plainly or more effectively to confirm our Conclusion? Yet I have heard men with my own ears who, when pressed with these very words of the Apostle, and unable to defend what they wished to defend in any other way, made this distinction: that indeed it is not lawful for any private man, at his own discretion, to do evil so that good may come of it, and that Paul wished only this to be forbidden by these words; but that nevertheless it is permissible, by the common counsel of the nation, for those whose interest it is, when the commonwealth would suffer loss, to do this if public necessity and the safety of the people so require. How far the safety of the people is to be preferred may perhaps be examined another time, if God wills. Meanwhile, it must be noted: first, that all this is said without warrant, and that nothing in the whole of this Pauline discussion appears on which that distinction could rest; second, that if we attend to the aim and force of Paul's argument in this place, all such limitations and inventions of trifling men are utterly excluded. For the Apostle meets the objection about promoting the glory of God by the sins of men: he denies that evils are to be done even for this end, that the glory of God may be illustrated. It follows, therefore, a fortiori, that evils are not to be done for any end that is inferior to the glory of God. Since, then, the glory of God is to be placed before any human good, private or public, and it is not lawful even with a view to that glory to do evil, certainly it will not be lawful for anyone, whether a single man or a whole community, either to do evil himself or to commend it to another to be done, as a remedy for any public or private evil.

units.la: XXIV. Recogitemus obsecro, Auditores, ista [?]quod[?] nos, idque feriò, & quò pejores dies sunt, [?]quò[?] plures tentationum laquei, & impetus fortio-res, eò ἀχεξέστεγν[?] ambulemus & majore circum[?]ectione caveamus gressibus nostris. Ne à recto [?]llo & angusto tramite mandatorum Dei patiamur [?]ullis Satanæ machinationibus, aut mundi car[?]nive illecebris ad dextram sinistramve vel tantil[?]um abduci. Memores, quæ scientes prudentes [?]ecerimus mala, nullum vel apud Deum judicem [?]vel apud testem Conscientiam, habitura esse in illo [?]ie excusationem. Et de bonæ intentionis prætextu [?]ftenus. Quæ de hominum Exemplis & placitis [?]quod ad regimen Conscientiæ attinet.) supersunt [?]icenda, pergam (Deo volente) exequi proximâ [?]tura Prælectione[?].
units.tr: XXIV. Let us consider, I beseech you, Hearers, that we must walk the more carefully and guard our steps with the greater watchfulness, the more evil the days are, the more numerous the snares of temptations and the stronger their assaults, so that we are not drawn by any machinations of Satan, or the allurements of the world and the flesh, even by a little, to the right or left from the straight and narrow path of God's commandments. Let us remember that for whatever evils we have knowingly and deliberately done, we shall have no excuse, either before God the Judge or before Conscience the witness. And so much concerning the pretext of a good intention. What remains to be said concerning the examples and opinions of men, so far as they bear on the governance of conscience, I shall, God willing, proceed to treat in the next Lecture.

units.la: PRÆLECTIO TERTIA.
units.tr: PRÆLECTIO TERTIA.

units.la: In quâ ostenditur, non esse ad con- scientiæ securitatem satis præsidi- i in virorum
units.tr: In which it is shown that the protection afforded by the examples of men or the judgement of the learned is not enough to secure the conscience.

units.la: Aut Piorum Exemplis. Peritorum Judicio.
units.tr: Either by the examples of the pious or by the judgement of the learned.

units.la: GAL. II. 13.
units.tr: GAL. II. 13.

units.la: καὶ συνυπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ[?]—— Ac simulabant una cum eo reliqui etiam Judai, adeo ut Barnabas simul abduceretur eorum simulatione.
units.tr: [καὶ συνυπεκρίθησαν αὐτῷ] — And the rest of the Jews also dissembled with him, so that Barnabas too was carried away by their dissimulation.

units.la: I. CUM mihi propositum esset propriam & adæquatam Conscientiæ Regulam, quæ nobis certa esset & tuta vivendi lex, investigare: pernecessarium duxi ante ostendere, quàm gravi & periculoso in errore versentur ii, qui in rebus agendis Conscientiæ suæ securitati satis prospectum putant, si aut boni finis intentione, aut Sancti alicujus exemplo, aut viri eruditione pietatéq; insignis judicio & authoritate, se factaque sua quoquo modo tueri poterunt. Et quidem ad Conscientiæ fructum, fiduciamque boni operis, cætera ni pariter adfuerint in nudâ bonâ intentione quàm parum fit præsidii, arbitror esse à me superiore prælectione satis demonstratum evictúmque multis rationibus, non esse facienda mala ut eveniant bona. Superest hodie ut itidem offendam non debere esse cujusquam hominis vel exemplum vel judicium tantæ apud nos authoritatis, ut in eorum alterutro securè acquiescat Conscientia : neque ex eo solo debitè concludi posse, aut de præterito omne id rectè factum esse, aut de futuro omne id simpliciter fieri licere, quod alius quisquam quantâvis doctrinâ vel sanctitate præditus, aut ipse fecerit, aut licitè fieri posse judicaverit.
units.tr: I. WHEN I had set myself to investigate a proper and adequate rule of conscience, one that would be for us a certain and safe law of living, I judged it most necessary first to show how grievous and dangerous is the error of those who think that enough provision has been made for the security of their conscience in their actions if they can defend themselves and their deeds in any way at all, either by the intention of a good end, or by the example of some saint, or by the judgement and authority of a man distinguished for learning and piety. And indeed, that a bare good intention yields little protection for the conscience, or any confidence in a good work, unless other things are present as well, I think I have sufficiently demonstrated in my previous lecture, and proved by many arguments, that evil must not be done that good may come. It remains today to show likewise that neither the example nor the judgement of any man should carry such authority among us that the conscience may rest securely on either of them; and that it cannot be rightly concluded from that alone, either that everything done rightly in the past was right, or that everything in the future is simply lawful, which someone else, however endowed with learning or holiness, has either done himself or judged could lawfully be done.

units.la: II. Porrò quàm non fit tutum ad aliorum exemplar vitam nostram actionésque instituere, nec sufficiat ad Conscientiæ securitatem, si quod facimus aut facturi sumus, id ipsum à viro aliquo pio antè nos factum defendamus; è textus propositi verbis luculentissimo argumento confirmari potest: maximè si dicti occasionem ex rei gestæ historiâ paulò altius repetamus.
units.tr: II. Moreover, how unsafe it is to shape our life and actions on the pattern of others, and how it is not sufficient for the security of conscience if we defend what we do, or are about to do, by pointing out that some godly man has done the very same before us, can be most clearly confirmed from the words of the text before us, especially if we trace the occasion of the saying a little further back, from the history of the event.

units.la: Petrus Apostolus, inter Gentiles ad Christi fidem conversos, qui Legis Mosaicæ conscientiâ non tenebantur, Antiochiæ degens, egit cum eis libera convivia, & appositos quoscunque cibos, non minùs prohibitos populo Judaico quàm concessos, pro eâ quam in Christo habuit libertate, indiscriminatim comedit. Ast, ubi Hierosolymâ Antiochiam venissent de gente Hebræa quidam Christiani, sive erant ii ficti illi fratres [ψευδαδέλφοι][?] quorum versu quarto istius capitis meminit, qui velut à Jacobo missi, sed revera clam subingressi fuerant ad explorandam Pauli aliorumque Christianorum libertatem, (ut nonnullis visum; sive potius (ut alii existimant, & fortasse rectius) infirmi fratres, à Jacobo quidem missi, sed de legalium rituum cessatione nondum fatis plenè edocti: Petrus ut apud eos gratiam iniret, vel saltem ipsorum offensionem reveritus, abstinuit protinus à Gentilium mensis & societate, & à cibis Mosaica Lege prohibitis. Cujus induc-ti exemplo, Judæi etiam Antiocheni, qui Pauli & sociorum concionibus docti erant Christianam libertatem aliquanto melius quàm Hierosolymitani illi, & de abolita Lege Ceremoniarum rectius senserant, imbecilles tamen adhuc & ipsi, & ritibus quibus diu assueverant addictiores, facilè se passi sunt à communione fratrum suorum fidelium Gentilium segregari, non sine aliqua (ut verisimile est) levi saltem suspicione, Petrum, sc. Apostolorum Coryphæum, de his rebus rectius sentire, & se fortean à Paulo gratia[?] sed inani libertatis specie la&atos hastenus fuisse & deceptos. Quin & ipse etiam Barnabas, quod magis mirere, (infirmiores enim ad lapidem offendiculi impingere, non est aut novum aut insolens) qui Pauli assiduus in itinere comes & collega fuerat, qui Christianæ libertatis doctrinam adversus Judæos constanter asseruerat, tanti Apostoli authoritate permotus, in eandem simulationis societatem concessit, non sine magno fidelium qui ex Gentibus erant scandalo.
units.tr: Peter the Apostle, while living at Antioch among the Gentiles who had been converted to the faith of Christ, and who were not bound in conscience by the Law of Moses, ate with them freely at table and, in the liberty he had in Christ, ate indiscriminately whatever foods were set before him, those forbidden to the Jewish people no less than those permitted. But when certain Christians of Hebrew stock came to Antioch from Jerusalem (whether they were those false brethren [ψευδαδέλφοι], mentioned in verse four of this chapter, who, as if sent by James, but in truth had secretly crept in to spy out the liberty of Paul and the other Christians (as some have thought); or rather (as others think, and perhaps more correctly) weak brethren, indeed sent by James but not yet fully taught about the cessation of the legal rites), Peter, wishing to win their favour, or at least out of reverence for their offence, at once withdrew from the table and company of the Gentiles, and from foods forbidden by the Mosaic Law. Led by his example, the Jews of Antioch too, who had been taught Christian liberty by the preaching of Paul and his companions somewhat better than those Jerusalemites, and had judged more rightly about the abolished Law of Ceremonies, yet being themselves still weak and more inclined to the rites to which they had long been accustomed, easily allowed themselves to be separated from the fellowship of their faithful Gentile brethren, not without some slight suspicion (as is likely) that Peter, the chief of the Apostles, judged these matters more rightly, and that they had perhaps been pleased and deceived until then by Paul with a vain show of liberty. Indeed Barnabas himself, which is more surprising (for it is neither new nor unusual for the weaker to stumble on a stone of offence), who had been Paul's constant companion and colleague on the journey, who had steadily defended the doctrine of Christian liberty against the Jews, moved by the authority of so great an Apostle, went along with the same fellowship in dissimulation, not without great scandal to the faithful who were from the Gentiles.

units.la: III. Reprehensum à se hoc nomine Petrum, idque graviter & palàm & merito, narrat hic Paulus. Non solùm, quòd ipse cum tot fratrum scandalo, ex nimio sive placendi studio sive offensionis metu, Judaismo faventiorem se quàm par erat simularet: sed quòd & alios suo exemplo in ejusdem hypocriseos participium pellexerat, eodemque exemplo pergeret credentes etiam è Gentibus ad Judaizandum, reluctante Conscientiâ & quasi invitos cogere. Non sum nescius {1}Hieronymum, post alios quos ille citat sententiæ suæ authores, longè diversam asserre ab ea quam nunc attuli Paulinæ reprehensionis interpretationem : scilicet, non ferió & uti videbatur, sed [illegible, ~6 letters] & ex composito inter duos summos Apostolos, Ecclesiae utilitate sic postulante, rem omnem gestam. Nimirum hoc voluit, simulationem Petri ad retinendos Judaeorum animos fuisse necessariam : quae tamen ne vergeret nimis in Gentium periculum, necessariam item fuisse & simulatoriam ejusdem à Paulo reprehensionem ; quâ & Judaeorum error de validâ adhuc legis rituum obligatione sic corrigeretur, & eadem interim operâ, ne quod inde crearetur Gentilibus Christianis scandali periculum, caveretur. Ex amborum utique conjunctâ simulatione id agis, ut tam Judaei quàm Gentes in Christi fide, quam non ita pridem amplexi essent, hac quasi pia fraude facilius retinerentur. Illud itaque, [illegible, ~12 letters] sic interpretatur, accommodè in illam quàm tuetur sententiam (ut solet is præ reliquis Patribus, [illegible, ~8 letters] ut [illegible, ~6 letters] ibi non palam & in faciem, i. e. coram populo & aperte significet, sed speciê tenus & secundum externam apparentiam, quo significatu [illegible, ~5 letters] alibi etiam usurpari constat, ut 1 Cor. 10. 7.
units.tr: III. That Peter was rebuked for this by him, and that gravely, openly and deservedly, Paul here relates. Not only because he himself, to the scandal of so many brethren, from an excessive zeal either to please or from fear of offence, pretended to be more favourable to Judaism than was right; but also because by his example he had drawn others into sharing the same hypocrisy, and by that same example he would go on compelling even believers from the Gentiles to Judaize, though their conscience resisted, and as if against their will. I am not unaware that {1}Jerome, following the others whom he cites as authors of his view, asserts a quite different interpretation of this Pauline rebuke from the one I have now given: namely, that the thing was not done openly and as it seemed, but [...] and by agreement between the two chief Apostles, the whole matter being so arranged for the sake of the Church's good. Clearly he meant this: that Peter's dissimulation was necessary to keep the minds of the Jews; but that, lest it should tend too far to the danger of the Gentiles, the rebuke of the same by Paul was equally necessary and a pretence; by which the error of the Jews about the continuing binding force of the legal rites was corrected, and at the same time, lest a danger of scandal should arise from it for the Gentile Christians, that was guarded against. Surely by their joint dissimulation they were aiming at this: that both Jews and Gentiles might be more easily retained in the faith of Christ, which they had embraced not long before, by this kind of pious fraud. That passage, therefore, [...] he interprets, suitably to the view he defends (as he is wont to do more than the other Fathers, [...] there it signifies not openly and to the face, that is, before the people and plainly, but in appearance and according to outward show, a meaning which is known to be used elsewhere as well, as in 1 Cor. 10. 7.

units.la: IV. Non placuit Hieronymi sententia Augustino, qui negat ex compacto quicquam hic actum fuisse, sed Paulum sincerè & ex animo intempestivæ huic [illegible, ~10 letters] semet opposuisse. Quare Hieronymum ejus erroris {1}per Epistolam amicè admonendum censuit : unde quum ille paulo commodiotior in eâdem sententia perstaret, agitari coepta est quæstio inter ipsos missis ultrò citróque Epistolis, magnô utrinque (ut par erat in tantorum ingeniorum concertatione) acumine & rationum momentis. Stetit tandem plerorumque judicio ab Augustino victoria, quod erat adductorum ab eo argumentorum pondus : ita ut ex illo tempore paucissimis pedibus itum sit in alteram sententiam. In quibus tamen mirarer si non effet{2}Baronius. Qui (cautus nequid detrimenti caperent res Romanæ, ne labesceret Jovis Ju[?]i Capitolini aut infallibilitas, si in Petrum cudi posset ulla erroris vel temerarii judicii fabecula; aut Oecumenica potestas, siquis mortalium ausus esset Petrum utcunque commeritum reprehendere, vel hiscere contrà, dicendo, Domine, cur ita facis?) nullum non movet lapidem, ut rejectam passim Hieronymi sententiam, & toto pene orbe exulantem, postliminio quasi revocatam civitate donaret. Sed profecto is est Baronius, ut se passim prodat uni partium studio debitum; quem palàm est in spissò illo & immensæ diligentiæ Annalium opere, id sibi negoti solum dari credidisse, Pontifici ut gratificaretur suo, & omnium monimentorum fidem & authoritatem, omnium opinionum & testimoniorum momenta, ex unius Romanæ sedis dignitate & utilitate metiretur.
units.tr: IV. The opinion of Jerome did not please Augustine, who denies that anything was done here by agreement, but holds that Paul sincerely and from his heart opposed himself to this untimely [...]. Wherefore he judged that Jerome should be kindly admonished of this error by letter; and since the former kept to his opinion rather stubbornly, a question began to be debated between them, with letters sent back and forth on both sides, with great keenness and weight of argument on each side (as was fitting in a contest of such great minds). In the end, by the judgement of most, the victory went to Augustine, because of the weight of the arguments he brought; so that from that time very few have gone over to the other opinion. Among these, however, I would be surprised if there were not {2}Baronius. He, careful lest the Roman interests should suffer harm, lest the infallibility of the Capitoline Jupiter should be tarnished, if any little fable of error or rash judgement could be struck upon Peter; or the ecumenical power, if any mortal should dare to rebuke Peter, however deserving, or to open his mouth against him by saying, Lord, why do you do so?, leaves no stone unturned in order to restore Jerome's rejected opinion, which has been banished almost everywhere throughout the world, as though granting it a return to citizenship by right of postliminy. But Baronius is clearly of such a kind that he everywhere betrays himself as owing everything to the zeal of one party; and it is plain that in that dense work of immense diligence, the Annals, he believed himself charged with this task alone: to gratify his Pontiff, and to measure the trustworthiness and authority of all records, and the weight of all opinions and testimonies, by the dignity and advantage of the one Roman see.

units.la: Atqui Paulus, (ut illuc unde paulùm recessi redeam) Coapostolum suum Petrum [illegible, ~12 letters] i. e. præsens præsentem, (ut ea locutio, Act. 25. 16. & alibi accipitur) audacter & palam [illegible, ~20 letters] Importunæ simulationis jure optimo redarguit: idque eo maximè nomine, quòd fasti[?] fui exemplo Barnabam & ex Antiochia Judæos in errorem induxisset, & Gentibus fidem Christianam recens amplexis, in Evangelicæ libertatis discrimen, grave scandalum præbuisset.
units.tr: But Paul, to return to the point from which I have digressed a little, rebuked his fellow apostle Peter to his face, present to present (as that expression is used at Acts 25:16 and elsewhere), boldly and openly, for unseemly dissimulation, and with the best of reason. He did so especially because Peter, by his example, had led Barnabas and the Jews of Antioch into error, and had given grave scandal to the Gentiles who had only recently embraced the Christian faith, putting evangelical liberty in danger.

units.la: V. Hæc à me pluribus eò libentius commemorata sunt: cùm ut loco aliquantum obscuro & jam olim controversò facem aliquam præferrem; tum etiam ut evidentior esset ejus argumenti vis, quod ad thesin nostram confirmandam ex hac Apostoli diatriba deducitur. Siquidem Paulus non Petrum solùm qui exemplo suo præiverat, sed & Barnabam etiam cæterosque qui Petri exemplum secuti in eandem simulationem consenserant, notandos cenfuit ὡς [illegible, ~10 letters], quod minus recte pede, nec ut Christianæ veritati & simplicitati congruebat, incederent. Omninò ut constet, apud Paulum judicem parum profuturum fuisse Barnabæ vacillanti, & inter Judaismum & Christianismum quasi claudicanti, in simulationis suæ patrocinium, Petri, summi quantumvis inter Apostolos nominis, exemplum advocasse. Esto, dignior sit acri reprehensione Petrus, quòd suo exemplo alteri nocuerit: at nihilo propterea excusatior Barnabas, quòd alieno exemplo peccaverit. Hæc de primo nostro argumento ex textu hoc Paulino.
units.tr: V. I have related these things at greater length than necessary, partly to shed some light on a passage that is somewhat obscure and has long been disputed, and partly so that the force of the argument drawn from this dispute of the Apostle, in support of our thesis, may be clearer. For Paul judged that not only Peter, who had gone before with his own example, but also Barnabas and the others who had followed Peter's example and joined in the same dissimulation, were to be marked out, because they did not walk uprightly, that they walked not uprightly, and did not walk in step with the truth and simplicity of the Christian faith. So it is plain that it would have done little good before Paul, as judge, for Barnabas, wavering and, as it were, limping between Judaism and Christianity, to appeal in defence of his dissimulation to the example of Peter, however great a name Peter had among the apostles. Granted that Peter deserved the sharper rebuke, because he had harmed another by his own example; yet Barnabas is none the more excused for having sinned by another's example. This is what I have to say about our first argument, drawn from this Pauline text.

units.la: VI. Secundum Argumentum sumitur à difficultate judicandi. quum non sint omnia piorum facta imitanda, quænam ex iis sint in exemplum trahenda, & quæ non: idque ob duplicem quæ est in eis incertitudinem. Utrumque enim fieri potest: ut quod à viro pio factum est, non fuerit recte factum; aut quod est ab eo recte factum, non tamen sit nobis imitandum. Imprimis illud utrumque certum est, & quæ constat esse perperam facta non esse imitanda; & suos fuisse viris vel sanctissimis nævos & lapsus. Quos & sapientissimus Deus permisit aliquoties in gravissima peccata labi, adulteria, homicidia, idololatriam, fidei abnegationem, &c. ut se homines esse cogitarent; discerent ex sensu suo alienis infirmitatibus compati & ignoscere: adversus tentationes non suis viribus siderent, sed ab ipsius auxilio toti penderent; sicubi validos tentationum impulsus sustinuissent invicti, inconcussi, illæsi, id omne ipsius providentia & gratia acceptum ferrent: ita eorum lapsus aliquot fœdiores in ipsis Sacrorum voluminum tabulis Sapientissimo consilio perscribi voluit, ut extarent in omne ævum ex unâ parte humanæ fragilitatis & inconstantiæ, ex alterâ divinæ bonitatis & clementiæ illustria nec peritura monumenta.
units.tr: VI. The second argument is drawn from the difficulty of judging. Since not all the deeds of the godly are to be imitated, the question is which of them are to be taken as examples and which are not; and this is because of a twofold uncertainty. For it can happen that what a godly man has done was not done rightly, or that what he did rightly is nevertheless not for us to imitate. Of these two things the first is certain beyond doubt: deeds that are known to have been done wrongly are not to be imitated; and even the most holy men had their own blemishes and lapses. The most wise God allowed some of them to fall into very grave sins, adultery, murder, idolatry, denial of the faith, and so on, so that they would reflect that they were men; that from their own experience they would learn to sympathise with and forgive the weaknesses of others; that they would not rely on their own strength against temptations, but would depend wholly on his help; and that, wherever they had withstood the violent assaults of temptations unconquered, unshaken and unharmed, they would ascribe all of it to his providence and grace. Thus, by his most wise counsel, he willed that some of their more shameful lapses should be recorded in the very pages of the sacred books, so that there might remain for all time, on the one hand, monuments of human frailty and inconstancy, and on the other, monuments of divine goodness and mercy, bright and imperishable.

units.la: VII. Dices fortasse non esse ea Sanctorum exempla sequenda, quæ ipse Dei Spiritus in sacris literis, velut virgula censoria, ut perperam facta notavit. Quis enim sane mentis sibi aut Davidis adulterium aut Petri abnegationem, imitanda proponeret? Videri tamen tuto posse ab ejusmodi factis exempla sumi, quæ in Scripturis ita narrantur, ut nullam adjectam habeant vituperationem, vel criminis aut culpæ notam. Respondeo, nec hoc esse concedendum. Multa enim hominum facta in Scripturis, ut in aliis passim historiis, nude tantum & historice narrantur prout gesta sunt, quæ a narrantibus nec difertim laudantur nec vituperantur: quorum tamen nonnulla indubie constat injusta fuisse, aut inhonesta, & a viri boni officio aliena; & de multis aliis non immerito dubitari poterit utrum fuerintne recte facta vel secus, de quibus disputare solent probabiliter & libere in utramque partem interpretes. Qualia sunt illa {1}Lothi, impuris civibus filiarum suarum stuprum offerentis; {2}Josephi per vitam Pharaonis (ut putatur) jurantis; {3}Jacobi Esavo fratri paternam benedictionem altu præripientis; aliaque id genus complura. Quæ siqui eorum exemplo sibi etiam licere putent hoc solo nomine, quod ea a viris piis facta legant, damnata non legant; næ illi, dum incertissimæ legi conscientias suas subjiciunt, sese interim certissimo errandi peccandique periculo objiciunt.
units.tr: VII. You may perhaps say that those examples of the saints which the Spirit of God himself has marked as wrongly done in the holy letters, as with a censor's rod, are not to be followed. For who in his right mind would propose for imitation David's adultery or Peter's denial? It may seem, however, that examples may safely be taken from such deeds as are narrated in Scripture without any added censure or any mark of crime or fault. I reply that this too must not be conceded. For many deeds of men in Scripture, as in other histories everywhere, are related plainly and merely as history, just as they were done, and are neither expressly praised nor blamed by the narrators. Yet it is certain that some of these were undoubtedly unjust or dishonourable, and foreign to the duty of a good man; and of many others it may fairly be doubted whether they were done rightly or otherwise, and commentators customarily dispute these questions probably and freely on both sides. Such are the deeds of {1}Lot, offering his daughters to the lustful citizens; of {2}Joseph, swearing (as is thought) by the life of Pharaoh; of {3}Jacob, snatching from his brother Esau the paternal blessing by deceit; and many others of that kind. If any of them think they are allowed to follow these examples for the sole reason that they read these deeds praised by godly men and do not read them condemned, then indeed, while they subject their consciences to a most uncertain law, they expose themselves in the meantime to the most certain danger of erring and sinning.

units.la: VIII. Atqui ea saltem Exempla nobis, quæ in sacris literis diserte laudantur, securè sequi licebit, inquies. Imo ne id quidem simpliciter concederim. Sed quod ad hanc rem attinet. Dico primo, Quæcunque hominum facta in sacris literis aperte damnantur ut vitiosa, ea simpliciter esse fugienda: Potior enim est vis & usus exemplorum malorum, ut ab illis negative arguatur, quàm bonorum ar-
units.tr: VIII. But surely, you will say, we may safely follow at least those examples that are expressly praised in the holy letters. Not even this would I simply concede. But as regards this matter, I say, first, that whatever deeds of men are openly condemned in the holy letters as faulty must simply be avoided. For the force and use of bad examples is greater when one argues from them negatively than that of good examples when one argues from them affirmatively.

units.la: {1} Gen. 19.8. guendo ab illis affirmativè. Quo arguendi genere utitur Apostolus noster, 1. Cor. 10. 6. &c. Ubi propositis ex veteris instrumenti historiâ peccatorum diversi generis exemplis, ut & judiciorum Dei in legis suæ prævaricatores, monet ut ea omnes intueamur velut typos & exemplaria, non quæ imitemur, sed quæ {1}vitemus, εἰς τὸ μὴ εἶναι ἡμᾶς ἐπιθυμητὰς κακῶν. Ne scil. concupiscamus mala, sicut quidam ex illis concupiverunt, neque idola colamus, neque fornicemur, neque Christum tentemus, neque murmuremus in adversis, quemadmodum illos fecisse legimus.
units.tr: {1} Gen. 19.8. This is the kind of argument our Apostle uses, 1 Cor. 10:6 &c., where, having set before us from the history of the Old Testament examples of sins of various kinds, and also of the judgements of God upon the transgressors of his law, he warns us to look upon all of them as types and patterns, not to be imitated, but to be avoided, [eis to mē einai hēmas epithymētas kakōn], that is, that we should not be lusters after evil things. Namely, that we should not lust after evil things, as some of them lusted, nor worship idols, nor commit fornication, nor tempt Christ, nor murmur in adversity, as we read that they did.

units.la: —hoc quidem non belle : nunquid ego illi Imprudens olim faciam simile? Hor. ibid.
units.tr: —This was not handsome of me: shall I, unwitting, one day do the same to him? Hor. ibid.

units.la: IX. Dico Secundo, quæ in Scripturis facta aperte laudantur, atque ita laudantur ut nobis quasi imitanda proponi videantur, non esse tamen omnia mox rapienda in exemplum, ita ut totum aggregatum sive integram actionem prout ab archetypo gesta est, nobis commendatam arbitremur. Sed delectu opus est & cauto; ut quæ laudantur, ea tantum ex parte imitemur, ex quâ laudantur: Cujus cautelæ hæc ratio est, quia solet Deus interdum, pro immensâ suâ bonitate, in Actione mixtâ, id solùm quod in eâ bonum est, intueri & comprobare; id quod vitiosum est, quasi dissimulando præterire. Ut in parabola, Luc. 16. 8. Laudavit Dominus villicum iniquitatis, quòd prudenter egisset, etsi fide parum integra. Imitanda ergo nobis proponitur villici illius prudentia, non injustitia. Et in obstetricum Ægyptiarum laudato exemplo, recens editos Israelitidum partus servantium, regiique mandati contemptum mendacio excusantium, non sunt confundenda, cum humanitate & pietate mendacium, sed cautè separanda: quorum hoc in vitio fuit, nec imitandum : illis solis data laus est Deo, & à nobis debita imitatio.
units.tr: IX. I say, secondly, that the deeds in Scripture which are openly praised, and praised in such a way that they seem to be set before us as things to be imitated, are nevertheless not all to be seized upon at once as an example, so that we should think the whole composite or entire action, as it was done by its archetype, is commended to us. Rather, discernment is needed, and caution; so that we imitate what is praised only in that respect in which it is praised. The reason for this caution is that God sometimes, in his immense goodness, in a mixed action, looks upon and approves only what is good in it, and passes over what is faulty as if overlooking it. So in the parable, Luke 16:8: The Lord praised the unjust steward, because he had acted prudently, though his fidelity was not whole. The prudence of that steward is therefore set before us for imitation, not his injustice.
