And in the praised example of the Egyptian midwives, who saved the newborn sons of the Israelite women and excused their contempt of the king's command with a lie, humanity and piety are not to be confused with the lie, but carefully separated from it. Of these, the lie was the fault, and is not to be imitated; praise was given to God alone, and imitation is owed by us.

units.la: X. Dico Tertiò, in Scripturis laudari etiam a[illegible, ~4 letters] heroum extraordinariorum, quos illi peculiari motu afflatu Spiritus Sancti excitati, quasi ex peculiari mandato ediderunt, praeter legem communem : qui tamen non sunt ab aliis imitandi. Ejus generis erat celebre illud factum Phinehezi, quo à Deo Opt. Max. & laudem meruit & praemium : qui cum esset vir privatus, nulla legitima authoritate publica praeditus, impudicum tamen scortantium [illegible, ~9 letters] deprehensum spiculo transfixit, Num. 25. 8. Ut & alterum illud Eliae prophetae, qui, devocato cœlitùs igne, missos se accersitum militum absumpsit, 4 Reg. 1. 1c.[?] &c. Quod ejus factum discipuli Christi Jacobus & Johannes imitari cupientes, cum praeceptorem suum ea de re consuluissent; temerarium ipsorum consilium ita non comprobavit, ut objurgantis speciem induceret, ruditque eorum impetus acri castigatione. Nescitis, inquit, cujus spiritus estis. Quasi diceret, Quin compescite ferocientis animi fervidiores impetus, & intra vocationis vestrae limites vosmet continete. Non siquid olim severius fecerit Elias, id ipsum vobis item faciendum existimate. Quod ab eo factum est, dictante & suggerente intus Spiritu Dei extraordinario factum est ; cujus dictamen fuit ei peculiaris illius mandati instar, quod Abrahae datum est de mactando filio Isauco. At non est vestrum, quos nondum Dei Spiritus ad tale facinus perpetrandum extra ordinem vocavit, simile aliquid attentare.
units.tr: X. I say thirdly, that in Scripture there are also praised the deeds of extraordinary heroes, who, roused by a peculiar motion and inspiration of the Holy Spirit, acted as if by a special commission, beyond the common law; yet these are not to be imitated by others. Of this kind was the famous deed of Phinehas, for which he earned both praise and reward from God Most Good and Great. Though he was a private man, endowed with no lawful public authority, he nevertheless ran through with a spear a shameless man whom he caught in fornication, Num. 25:8. So too is that other deed of the prophet Elijah, who, fire having been called down from heaven, consumed the soldiers sent to summon him, 4 Kings 1:10 &c. When the disciples of Christ, James and John, wishing to imitate this deed, consulted their master about it, he did not so approve their rash plan as to take on the appearance of a rebuke; he checked their impulse with a sharp reproof. You do not know, he said, what spirit you are of. As if he were saying: Check the more fervent impulses of a fierce mind, and keep yourselves within the limits of your calling. Do not think that if Elijah once acted more severely, you too should do the same. What he did, he did under the inward dictation and suggestion of the extraordinary Spirit of God; and that dictation was in the place of a peculiar commandment, like that given to Abraham to slay his son Isaac. But it is not for you, whom the Spirit of God has not yet called outside the ordinary order to perpetrate such a deed, to attempt anything similar.

units.la: XI. Quum itaque non semper certum sit, id quod à viro pio factum legitur, laudari debere, nec si quid laudatum fuerit, id continuò imitandum esse: ad Conscientiarum nostrarum securitatem multò conducibilius est, actus nostros ad Legis regulam quæ certa est, quàm ad incerta hominum exempla exigere & conformare. Rectè “Augustinus, Hæc quæ in Scripturis Sanctis legimus, non ideò quia facta credimus, etiam facienda credamus: ne violemus præcepta, dum passim jectamur exempla, lib. contra mendacium, cap. 9. Ubi post alia quædam eodem pertinentia, ita tandem concludit. “Unde constat quod non omnia quæ à Sanctis & justis viris legimus facta, transferre debemus ad mores.”
units.tr: XI. Since it is not always certain that what we read a godly man did ought to be praised, nor that, even if something was praised, it must at once be imitated, it is far more useful for the security of our consciences to bring our actions under the rule of the Law, which is certain, than to measure and shape them by the uncertain examples of men. Rightly Augustine says in his book against lying, chapter 9: "What we read in Holy Scripture, we should not therefore believe we must also do, merely because we believe it was done, lest in running about after examples we violate the precepts." Where, after some other remarks bearing on this, he concludes at last: "Hence it is clear that we ought not to transfer into our manners everything that we read was done by holy and righteous men."

units.la: Atque hactenus[?] de secundo nostro argumento, à difficultate judicandi de piorum exemplis, propter incertitudinem quæ in ipsis est.
units.tr: And so much for our second argument, drawn from the difficulty of judging the examples of the godly, on account of the uncertainty that lies in them.

units.la: XII. Sequitur tertium, à difficultate rité appliandi aliorum exempla ad res & actiones nostras, propter incertitudinem circumstantiarum. Quæ cùm infinitæ varietatis, infinities etiam variant humanarum actionum qualitates. Quod est in thesi, i.e. de suo genere licitum & liberum, atque etiam manet in hypothesi (manentibus sc. iisdem circumstantiis) licitum & liberum, (licitum autem dicitur quod sine peccato fieri; liberum, quod sine peccato omitti, potest;) idipsum additâ, demptâ, aut quovis modo immutatâ vel unâ qualitate circumstantia; reddi potest è licito illicitum, aut è libero necessarium. Ut quotidie usuvenire nimus in foro contentioso, cum inter partes litigantes causæ aguntur. Ubi ab unius partis advocato citantur è libris in causæ suæ subsidium judicatarum præcedentia (ut vocant) exempla: responderi solet ab alterius partis advocato, non esse eandem in utraque causa juris rationem, variare circumstantiis, inde immutari casum, quæ olim judicata citantur ad præsentem litem pertinere. Quod si fuerit rité demonstratum; concidit extemplo tota illa hoc fundamentanixa defensionis fabrica, nec urit apud Judices illius momenti probatio à rebus judicatis sumpta. Hinc fit ut inter argumentationis species apud Dialecticos, Exemplum in postremis habeatur; velut illustranda rei quàm demonstranda, aptius instrumentum. Et profectò, si fit verum illud Fabii, {1} Tot Seculis nullam repertam esse causam, quæ fit tu[?] Alteri similis : omnino verisimile est posse eum facilè errare, qui ex unius causâ conditione de alteri similí : non expensis ante cum omni diligentia u-triusque circumstantiis, præpropere statuit.
units.tr: XII. There follows a third argument, drawn from the difficulty of rightly applying the examples of others to our own affairs and actions, on account of the uncertainty of circumstances. Since circumstances are of infinite variety, they vary the qualities of human actions in countless ways. An action which is, in its own kind (in thesi), lawful and free, and which remains lawful and free in the particular case (in hypothesi), provided the same circumstances persist (lawful meaning what may be done without sin, free meaning what may be left undone without sin), can be made unlawful, or from free made necessary, by adding, removing, or changing in any way a single circumstance. This happens every day in the courts, when cases are argued between litigating parties. There, when the advocate of one side cites from the books the so-called precedents of earlier judgments in support of his cause, the advocate of the other side usually replies that the legal reasoning is not the same in both cases, that the circumstances differ, and that therefore the case has been altered, so that the earlier decisions cited do not bear on the present suit. If this has been rightly shown, that whole structure of defence, built on this foundation, collapses at once, and proof drawn from adjudged cases carries no weight with the judges. Hence among the kinds of argument recognised by the dialecticians, the example is ranked last, as a tool more suited to illustrating a matter than to proving it. And indeed, if that saying of Fabius is true, that in so many ages no case has been found like another, it is entirely likely that he errs easily who, from the case of one, rashly judges the condition of another similar case without first weighing with all diligence the circumstances of each.

units.la: XIII. Quo in genere, eò sumus in errorem procliviores, quòd plerique hominum ita comparati sumus, ut in exemplis aliorum applicandis ista tantùm ipsa intueamur, eáque avidè arripiamus, & in rem nostram trahamus, si saltem effectibus & desideriis cordis nostri adblandiri videantur; casu interim factorum, & finis, & modi, & circumstantiarum, earum præsertim quæ cupiditatibus nostris adversari videntur, aut nullam aut perexiguam rationem habeamus. Sugillat quosdam temporis propheta, Amos cap. 6. 5. qui in mediis publicis calamitatibus securi otio, luxu, & omne genus voluptatis genium suum oblectabant; dicebantque inter alia, se Davidis instar excogitasse sibi instrumenta musica. Quasi dicerent, Cur id nobis vitio vertatur, quod Davidi laudi fuit & honori? Musica instrumenta & modulationes exercuit vir ille sanctus; idem & nos facimus: dissimulantes interim, quod fuerat in illo exemplo præcipuè imitandum, id à Davide factum in honorem Dei, & publici cultus solennitatem; non ad conviviorum luxum, & in fomentum mollitiei & lasciviæ.
units.tr: XIII. In this matter we are the more prone to error because most of us are so constituted that, in applying the examples of others, we look only at the bare facts, and eagerly seize on them and drag them to our own purpose, if they at least seem to flatter our desires and the wishes of our hearts; meanwhile we pay little or no heed to the circumstances of the deed, to its end and manner, and especially to those circumstances which seem to oppose our passions. The prophet Amos rebukes some men of his time, Amos 6. 5, who, secure in their leisure, amid public calamities, pleasured their spirits with luxury and every kind of indulgence; and among other things they said that they had devised for themselves musical instruments after the manner of David. As if they meant: why should it be held against us that what brought praise and honour to David? That holy man practised musical instruments and melodies; we do the same. Meanwhile they overlooked that what in that example was above all to be imitated was that David did it to the honour of God and for the solemnity of public worship, not for the luxury of feasts or to feed softness and wantonness.

units.la: XIV. De Imitatione Oratoriâ multa præcipiunt Rhetores: nimirum futuro oratori utile esse, ut virum aliquem egregium, & in dicendi facultate præstantem sibi proponat, quem studeat imitari. Quod idem ad vitæ institutionem, ut salubre præceptum accommodant Philosophi. Hortatur Seneca ut ad alicujus eximii præstantísque viri exemplum vitam morésque componamus: Longum enim iter esse per præcepta, breve & efficax per exempla. Et habet Exemplum conjunctam cum suadelâ & utilitate oblectationem quandam: ut in puerulis videre est; qui aliorum jussis cûm ægrè obtemperent, facta tamen magna cum voluptate imitantur. Sed monent tamen qui ista præcipiunt, ad bene rectéque imitandum acri judicio opus esse, ut prudenter delectum faciamus, cum eorum hominum quos imitari velimus, tum earum rerum in quibus ipsos imitemur. Ridet Fabius elumbes quosdam (ut ipse vocat) oratores, qui affectata quadam eloquentia & inani verborum circuitu dum Ciceronicircum- tatibus perexi- am fui n me- xu, & abant; ogitasse Cur id & ho- exer- diffi- emplo in ho- ion ad iei & ipiunt ut vi- ulcate nitari. e præ- ptum, anum[?] dicendi genus æmulantur, magnum se quid & eximium consecutos existimabant, si in clausulis posuissent Esse posse videatur. Notat & ipse Cicero perversam quorundam hac in re diligentiam, qui propositis sibi ad imitandum summis oratoribus, nil illorum (ut ille loquitur) nisi vitium sequuntur. Qualis erat Fufius quidam, C. Fimbriæ boni oratoris imitator non bonus: de quo ita Cicero, nervos C. Fimbriæ in dicendo non assequitur, oris pravitatem imitatur. Basilium Cæsareæ Episcopum, ob eximiam erudiitionem & pietatem cognomento Magnum, in tantâ fuisse apud omnes existimatione scribit Nazianzenus, ut non pauci tanti viri ἐν τῷ σωματικῷ ἐλαττώματα[?], pallorem oris, incessum, tardam pronunciationem, aliáque corporis vitia, studiosè affectarent & æmularentur. Quemadmodum non defuisse testantur alii, qui Demosthenis magni Oratoris Rhotacismum, & summi Philosophi Aristotelis τραυλότητα[?] studiosè effingerent.
units.tr: XIV. The rhetoricians teach much about oratorical imitation: namely, that it is useful for the future orator to set before himself some outstanding man, excelling in the art of speaking, whom he should strive to imitate. The philosophers apply the same as a wholesome precept to the shaping of life. Seneca urges us to form our life and manners on the example of some outstanding and eminent man: "For the way by precepts is long, but short and effective by examples." An example also has a certain pleasure joined with its persuasiveness and usefulness, as can be seen in little children, who, though they obey the orders of others with reluctance, imitate deeds with great delight. Yet those who teach these things warn that to imitate well and rightly a keen judgment is needed, so that we make a prudent choice both of the men we wish to imitate and of the things in which we imitate them. Fabius mocks certain feeble orators (as he calls them) who, by a studied eloquence and empty circling of words, imitate the style of Cicero, and thought they had achieved something great and remarkable if they had placed "It may seem that it can be" at the ends of their clauses. Cicero himself notes the perverse diligence of some in this matter, who, having set before themselves the greatest orators to imitate, follow, as he puts it, "nothing of them but their faults." Such was a certain Fufius, a poor imitator of the good orator C. Fimbria, of whom Cicero says: "He does not attain the sinews of C. Fimbria in speaking, but imitates his crooked mouth." Gregory Nazianzen writes that Basil, Bishop of Caesarea, surnamed the Great for his remarkable learning and piety, was held in such esteem by all that not a few of so great a man's admirers eagerly affected and copied his bodily defects [ἐν τῷ σωματικῷ ἐλαττώματα]: the pallor of his face, his gait, his slow delivery, and other faults of body. Others likewise bear witness that there were not wanting men who carefully reproduced the rhotacism of the great orator Demosthenes and the lisp [τραυλότης] of the great philosopher Aristotle.

units.la: 'O Imitatores, servum pecus!
units.tr: "O imitators, a servile herd!"

units.la: Iocum moverent ista fateor, quæque apud probos authores occurrunt sexcenta istis similia perversæ imitationis exempla, magis quàm bilem; si in sermone tantùm & externo corporis habitu gestúque ea perversitas, non autem in vitâ & moribus obtineret. Sed & in his quoque, nihilo fa[?] tasse[?] rarius, certè longè perniciosius, decipit exemplar vitiis imitabile: dum pravis cupiditatibus abrepti, propriisque affectibus nimis indulgentes, è magno exemplorum cumulo ea ferè deligimus libentius, & in ipsis eas circumstantias vehementius urgemus, quæ commodissimè videntur in eam partem flecti posse quà inclinant jam animi, ut sic affectibus & cupiditatibus nostris inserviatur. Id quod facillimè deprehendet ab egregie factum, qui εὐταξίαι ex Ecclesia, è Rep. pacem exturbare moliuntur, quisquis libellos nuper ab Anabaptistis, Brownistis, aliisque ejusdem furfuris Sectariis, vel superioribus aliquot annis ab eorum verâ propagine Reformatoribus Puritanis editos, attentiùs inspexerit. Cujus perversitatis in hoc hominum genere ut vobis specimen aliquod exhibeam, (quod sine justa cujusquam cordati viri offensione factúrum me spero,) date mihi quaeso veniam, unicum ipsorum argumentorum à Christi & Apostolorum ejus exemplo duētum, brevi examine subjicere: quod quùm sit ab ipsis prolixè satis, addo & satis animosè, tractatum; quàm solidè, quàm sincerè in eo argumento se gesserint, vestrum est judicare.
units.tr: I confess that such things would move one to laughter rather than to anger, and that the many other examples of perverse imitation found in approved authors, like these, would do so, if this perversity held only in speech and outward bodily bearing and gesture, and not in life and manners. But in these matters too, no less rare but certainly far more harmful, "an example imitable in its vices deceives": since men carried away by wicked desires, and too indulgent to their own feelings, from the great heap of examples gladly choose those that are most suitable, and press upon them most vehemently those circumstances which seem most easily bent in the direction toward which their minds already incline, so that they may serve their passions and desires. This is most easily seen by anyone who looks attentively at the books published lately by the Anabaptists, the Brownists, and other sectaries of the same chaff, or in the preceding few years by the Puritan Reformers, their true offspring, who strive to overthrow the good order of the Church and the Commonwealth. To give you some sample of this perversity in this sort of men, which I hope I may do without just offence to any sensible person, I ask your indulgence to set out briefly for examination one of their arguments, drawn from the example of Christ and his Apostles. Since it has been treated by them at considerable length and with much confidence, I leave it to you to judge how solidly and how sincerely they have handled this argument.

units.la: XVI. Prodiit quadraginta circiter retrò annis, adversus ritum ingeniculationis in sacrâ synaxi, editus à quibusdam Exoniensis diœceseos ministris (justis sc. operis) libellus. Inter alia quæ undique conquisita argumenta congesserunt, in hoc uno quod à Christi exemplo petitum est præ cæteris videntur quasi triumphare. Argumenti vis & summa hæc est. Non licere homini Christiano in actione aliqua religiosa ad cultum Dei pertinente Christi & Apostolorum exemplo, quod quidem fit imitabile, ullatenus recedere, quum sit omnis Christi actio imitabilis, & quam alii sunt recte imitati, ab omnibus Christianis imitanda: Christum autem & Apostolos alio corporis situ & non genibus subnixos, sacra signa percepisse: proinde & nobis Christianis pariter faciendum. Hoc tamen diluto, pæne dixeram putido, sophismate cum impositum sit non indoctæ modò plebi, sed & aliis, qui si magis saperent melius cum Ecclesiis Christi ageretur: operæ pretium erit nonnulla vobis quæ vanitatem totius argumentationis abundè demonstrent, observanda proponere.
units.tr: XVI. About forty years ago there appeared a booklet, published against the custom of kneeling at the Lord's Supper, written by certain ministers of the diocese of Exeter (the just ones, namely, of the work). Among the other arguments gathered from every quarter, they seem to exult above all in the one taken from the example of Christ. The force and sum of the argument is this: that a Christian man may not in any religious action pertaining to the worship of God depart in any way from the example of Christ and the Apostles, which is indeed to be imitated, since every action of Christ is imitable, and whatever others have rightly imitated is to be imitated by all Christians. But Christ and the Apostles received the sacred signs not kneeling, but in another posture of the body; therefore we Christians too ought to do likewise. Yet since this sophism, which I almost called rotten, has been imposed not only on the untutored common people but also on others who, if they were wiser, would have dealt better with the Churches of Christ, it will be worth while to set before you some points to observe, which will amply demonstrate the vanity of the whole argument.

units.la: XVII. Observate itaque primò μιμητὸν[?] h'c fieri εἰς ἄλλο [illegible, ~5 letters] fœdo & vix pueris condonando errore. Cum enim de Gestu tota lis sit, difputant illi importunè admodum de Actionibus. Esto omnem Christi actionem imitandam esse: at gestum quis dixerit actionem? Quæ duo adeò latè invicem disparata sunt, ut nec in aliquo communi genere conveniant, sed ad distincta Prædicamenta pertinent: Gestus ad situm esse, Actio ad proprium & sui nominis prædicamentum.
units.tr: XVII. First, observe that this is done in another [εἰς ἄλλο] sense, through a foul error that can scarcely be forgiven even in boys. Since the whole dispute concerns the posture, these men argue very tiresomely about actions. Grant that every action of Christ is to be imitated: but who would call a posture an action? The two are so widely separated that they share no common genus; they belong to distinct categories, since posture belongs to the category of position, and action to its own category, named after itself.

units.la: XVIII. Observate secundò, quatuor illa ultima & minorum gentium prædicamenta, Ubi, Quando, Situm & Habitum, ejusdem esseferè rationis & momenti, respectu illarum actionum quibus velut comites adjunguntur, quandoquidem nihil aliud sunt quam relationes quædam inferioris notæ, & circumstantiæ actionibus ipsis prorsus extrinsecæ. Non videri proinde rationi consentaneum, ut ut vi[?] exempli Christi & Apostolorum obligemur ad eorum imitationem in Situ tantum; in reliquis autem tribus, Ubi, Quando, & Habitu, vel istorum ipsorum judicio qui hoc exemplum urgent, non obligemur. Neque enim ipsi existimant esse necessarium, aut quoad Ubi, ut sacra Eucharistia in privatis ædibus & in cænaculo domus superiore (ὑπερῴῳ[?]) celebretur, aut quoad Quando, ut primâ nocte & post cænam; aut quoad Habitum, ut à ministro tunicâ inconsutili induto. Quæ tamen omnia fuisse in primâ cænâ observata, ex sacrâ historiâ constet, nec est ab illis negatum. Cùm ergo eam libertatem & ipsi sumant & aliis concedant, ut liceat à Christi & Apostolorum praxi in hisce omnibus illæsâ conscientiâ discedere, libenter à novis his magistris edoceri velim, quid sit in illo Situs prædicamento adeò singulare, ut tam multò, sive infra sive supra, consortium suorum sensum haberi meretur, nec liceat sine grandi sacrilegio à primitivo illo exemplo ex hac tantum parte discedere. Æqua sanè res est, ut aut pari passu ambulent quatuor ista Ubi, Quando, Situs, Habitus; aut justa aliqua discriminis ratio cur id ne fiat assignetur: quod non est ab iis hactenus (quod sciam) factum nedum tentatum.
units.tr: XVIII. Second, observe that those last four categories, the where, the when, position and habit, which are minor categories, are of almost the same nature and weight in relation to those actions to which they are attached as companions. For they are nothing but certain relations of lesser note and circumstances wholly extrinsic to the actions themselves. It does not therefore seem reasonable that we should be bound by the example of Christ and the Apostles to imitate them in position alone, while in the other three, the where, the when and the habit, we are not bound, even by the judgment of those who press this example. For they do not themselves think it necessary that the holy Eucharist be celebrated as to the where, in private houses and in the upper room of a house [ὑπερῴῳ]; or as to the when, on the first night and after supper; or as to the habit, that the minister be clothed in a seamless tunic. Yet it is clear from sacred history that all these things were observed at the first supper, and this has not been denied by them. Since then they both take this liberty for themselves and grant it to others, so that one may depart from the practice of Christ and the Apostles in all these matters with a clear conscience, I should gladly be taught by these new masters what is so singular about that category of position that it alone deserves to be held in such regard above or below its fellows, and that one may not depart from that primitive example in this one respect without great sacrilege. It is surely only fair that either these four: where, when, position and habit, should walk on equal terms, or some just reason should be assigned why they may not; which, so far as I know, has not hitherto been done by them, let alone attempted.

units.la: XIX. Observate tertiò, quum debeat omne factum exemplare ita esse certum ut non possit negari: quod ab illis assumitur, (& ego lubens concedo.) Christum & Apostolos non genibus flexis sed alio aliquo gestu celebrasse primam illam cœnam, id non ita liquidò constare ex aliquo Scripturæ textu, ut si pernegetur possit probari. At illud ἀνακεῖσθαι[?], quod est in Evangeliis, annon innuit saltem gestum tricliniarem, illis temporibus & regionibus familiarem? Imò omnino nego ex solo usu istius vocabuli posse probari certam aliquam Speciem situs. Ab ea situs specie, quæ in triclinii olim adhibita est, utriusque vocis origo fuit: Græcæ ἀνακεῖσθαι, & quæ huic respondet Latinæ Discumbere. Sed vocabulorum vim & pondus improbo examini subjiciet, quisquis ea, post quam multo usu adoleverint & se latius extenderint & dilataverint, ad prima quasi incunabula reocare, & antiquis finibus includere velit. Signicant ergo illæ dictiones ex communi usu loquendi [?]um illum quo nos destinato applicamus alicui oco idoneo cibi capiendi causâ ; quocunque de[?]um situ vel positura corporis id fiat, statu, cessione, ingeniculatione, discubitu proprie dicto, vel quolibet alio.
units.tr: XIX. Third, observe that, since every fact to be imitated must be so certain that it cannot be denied (which they assume, and I gladly grant): that Christ and the Apostles did not celebrate that first supper kneeling but in some other posture, is not so clearly established by any text of Scripture that it could be proved if it were denied. But does not that word ἀνακεῖσθαι in the Gospels at least hint at a reclining posture, familiar in those times and regions? Indeed I altogether deny that any definite species of posture can be proved from the mere use of that word. The origin of both words lay in that species of posture once employed at the dining couch: the Greek ἀνακεῖσθαι, and the Latin discumbere, which answers to it. But whoever wishes to call back the force and weight of these words, after they have grown up through long use and spread and extended themselves more widely, to their first cradle, and to confine them within their ancient limits, will be submitting their meaning to a bad test. Those expressions therefore signify, from common usage of speech, that act by which we apply ourselves, for the purpose of taking food, to some suitable place; whether this is done in any posture or bodily position whatever: standing, leaning, kneeling, reclining properly so called, or any other.

units.la: XX. Sed quia, licèt non ex vi vocis ἀνακλισιν[?], aliunde tamen (ex quibusdam scil. historiæ circumstantiis) colligi videtur admodum probabiliter, Christum & Apostolos in primâ illâ cœna gestu usos tricliniari : observate quarto, novos hosce Dictatores nostros legi illi, quam ita severè imponunt fratrum suorum conscientiis, ipsosmet interim non parere. Si enim Christus in sacra cœna instituenda gestu usus sit tricliniari ; expor-rectis sc. in substrato lectulo pedibus & tota corporis parte inferiore, superiore in cubitum reclinata : cur isti ipsi, qui hoc argumentandi genere tam operosè utuntur, hoc Christi exemplum, (quod est certe imitabile,) non imitantur ? Cur non sibi lectulos parant & triclinia, ut sic ab omni necessaria in eam rem supellectili instructi, eodem quo Christus & Apostoli gestu sacræ mensæ participes fiant ? A quo gestu tam discedere certum est eos qui stant aut sedent, (quorum alterutrum & ipsi faciunt & aliis faciendum suadent,) quàm qui in genua procidunt. Si dicant, & quidem dicunt, exolevisse jam olim gestum illum tricliniarem in hoc occidentali orbe, & proinde nos non jam teneri ad eundem situm in specie : teneri tamen vi primitivi illius exempli ad eundem situm in genere, hoc est ut utamur saltem gestu (ut vocant) mensario, qui sit illi tricliniari analogus & succedaneus pro more nostræ gentis, quemadmodum illi tunc eo gestu usi sunt, qui ex passim recepto illorum temporum & locorum more ad menjam à convivis solebat adhiberi. Ad populum phaleras ! Adeone homines ex affectuum prajudicio, & contradicendi libidine quadam, ab omni sana mente excidisse, ut hæc tam futilia pro solidis orbi obtrudant, aut sperent istiusmodi offuciis cuiquam cordato viro imponi posse? Quæ quàm sint inania & abs re, ut breviter & liquidò ostendam; exorandi mihi sunt qui sic disputant, ut paucis his interrogatiunculis directè & sine aliquâ tergiversatione respondeant.
units.tr: XX. But because, although it is not from the force of the word ἀνακλισιν[?], it nevertheless seems quite probably to be gathered from elsewhere (namely from certain circumstances of the history) that Christ and the Apostles used a reclining posture at that first supper, observe, fourth, that these new dictators of ours read out to others the law which they impose so severely on the consciences of their brethren, while they themselves do not obey it. For if Christ, in instituting the holy supper, used a reclining posture, namely with his feet stretched out upon a couch laid down, and the whole lower part of the body, with the upper part propped on the elbow: why do these very men, who use this kind of argument so laboriously, not imitate this example of Christ (which is certainly imitable)? Why do they not prepare couches and dining couches for themselves, so that, equipped with all the furniture needful for that purpose, they may partake of the sacred table in the same posture as Christ and the Apostles? It is certain that those who stand or sit (which of the two they themselves do and urge others to do) depart from that posture as far as those who fall on their knees do. If they say, and indeed they do say, that the reclining posture has long since fallen out of use in this western world, and that therefore we are no longer bound to the same posture in species: yet we are bound by the force of that primitive example to the same posture in genus, that is, to use at least the table posture (as they call it), which is analogous and a substitute for that reclining posture according to the custom of our nation, just as they then used that posture which, according to the custom of those times and places commonly received, was wont to be adopted by guests at table. To the people with their trappings! Are men so utterly bereft of all sound sense by the prejudice of their passions and a certain lust for contradiction, that they press these trifles upon the world as solid matter, or hope that such deceptions can be palmed off on any sensible man? That these things are so empty and beside the point, I shall show briefly and plainly; those who argue thus must be urged to answer these few little questions directly and without any evasion.

units.la: XXI. Quæro ab illis primò, quum tam certum sit Christum, si usus est gestu triclinïari, nec sedentem comedisse, nec stantem, quàm certum est eum, si eo gestu usus est, non comedisse genibus subnixum: cur non vi illius exempli tam obligemur à sedendo vel stando abstinere in ipso communicandi actu & articulo, quàm ab ingeniculando? Ex ista enim suppositione, sequitur, è tribus illis corporis posituris nullam esse, quæ non exemplo Christi æquè destituatur ac reliquæ duæ. Equam proinde esse, quod de quatuor ultimis prædicamentis paulò ante dictum est, ut pari jure fruantur singulæ: pariterque universæ vel ut reæ damnentur, vel ut inculpatæ absolvantur. Si dicant, quod est ipsorum solenne diverticulum, successisse gestui triclinïari ex more gentis sessionem vel stationem, non successisse ingeniculationem:
units.tr: XXI. I ask them, first: since it is so certain that Christ, if he used a reclining posture, did not eat sitting nor standing, just as it is certain that, if he used that posture, he did not eat kneeling: why are we not bound by that example to abstain from sitting or standing in the very act and moment of communion, just as much as from kneeling? For from that supposition it follows that of those three bodily postures there is none which is not equally deprived of the example of Christ as the other two. It is therefore fair, as was said a little before of the last four categories, that each should enjoy the same right; and likewise that all of them should either be condemned as guilty or absolved as blameless. If they say, which is their customary sidestep, that sitting or standing succeeded to the reclining posture by the custom of the nation, but kneeling did not succeed:

units.la: Quæro secundo, unde fiat ut alicujus gentis (puta Anglicanæ) tacita consuetudo sufficiat ad hoc, ut gestui triclinïari succedat sessio vel statio ad mensam communem: Lex autem positiva ejusdem gentis non sufficiat ad hoc, ut eidem gestui succedat ingeniculatio ad mensam sacram? Poteritne sensim & sine publicâ authoritate immutata consuetudo id efficere, ut non ultrà deceat vel liceat quod olim nec indecens habitum est nec illicitum? non poterit publicâ authoritate sancita Lex, populi etiam expresso consensu stabilita, usúque diuturno & moribus comprobata id efficere, ut saltem licitum deinceps habeatur, quod nulla legitima ratione constat fuisse unquam illicitum. Ubi revera pugnant inter se duæ res, Lex & Consuetudo (quod hic tamen vix fit) æquam esse fatebitur quisquis incolumi capite est, ut cedat Legi Consuetudo, non Consuetudini Lex. Quæro abs illis tertiò, existiménte serió, an non existiment, continuò peccare eum qui ad mensam communem fixis genibus cibum caperet. Si peccare dicant; quum fit omne peccatum divinæ legis transgressio, cedò ejus legis præceptum aliquod, contra quod sic faciendo peccetur; si fateantur sine peccato id fieri posse; annon animadvertunt eâ confessione sua se vineta cædere, & argumentationis suæ vim omnem evertere? Quarto, supposito quòd exolevisset jam olim gestus ille triclinaris, eique successisset statio vel sessio ante primam illam cœnam, ita ut oportuerit Christum & Apostolos aut stantes comedisse aut sedentes; quum utrumque simul fieri non potuerit: quæro, num si illi stantes comedissent, nobis etiam ita stare necessarium esset, ut sedendo peccaremus, & è contrà; vel liberi essemus ad utrumlibet? Si dicant nos liberos esse ad utrumlibet; omninò jacet argumentum ab exemplo Christi dućtum: quia supponitur illum alterutrum tantùm fecisse, non utrumque. Si dicant, nos præcisè teneri ad illam Speciem quâ supponitur Christum fuisse usum; cur ergo ipsi tam severi dićtatores libertate cujusque Ecclesiæ permittunt standi vel sedendi optionem? Quæro quintò, si nos obliget exemplum Christi ad sui imitationem; cur determinetur hæc obligatio præcisè in gestu mensario, quæ est species subalterna, & non vel citeriùs stet in genere aliquo superiori, vel ulteriùs protendatur ad speciem aliquam inferiorem? Hoc est quærere, Quum sint tria hæc Gestus ut genus su-[?]perius, Gestus mensarius ut species ei subalterna, Gestus triclinaris ut species infima; Christus au-tem & gestus usus fuerit, & gestu mensario, & gestu triclinaris: cur gestu mensarius, quæ est intermedia species, censeri debeat ad rectam Christi imitationem & necessaria & sufficiens: & non vel gestus aliquis in genere sufficiens? vel gestus triclinaris in specie necessarius? Quæro denique fueritne gestus triclinaris à Christo & Apostolis in primâ cœnâ adhibitus imitabilis, vel non? l. imitabilem fuisse (sat scio) non negabunt, imo ne possunt quidem negare, qui inde præcipuum causæ suæ firmamentum petunt: sic enim proponunt Christi exemplum nobis de necessitate imitandum: non omne simpliciter, sed omne quod est imitabile. Quod igitur illi ultrò largiuntur, libens accipio: & Propositionem scilicet, Omne Christi exemplum imitabile, obligare Christianos ad sui imitationem; & Assumptionem pariter, sc. gestum illum in specie (sive fuerit ille triclinaris, quod admodum probabile est, & nunc saltem supponimus, sive quis alius) quo Christus in prima illa cœna usus est, esse imitabilem. Ex his præmissis sic colligo, Ergo vi istius exempli obligabantur proximi post Christum seculi Christiani ad eundem gestum in specie quo usus est Christus; ergo similiter obsignabantur & secundi seculi, itemque tertii, & sic deinceps usque ad hæc tempora. Ergo & præsentem Ecclesiam ad gestum triclinarem in specie obligari fatendum est, si Christus eo gestu usus est: aut saltem ostendendum est, quo tempore, qua ratione, quo authore, quo jure & authoritate sublata sit illa obligatio.
units.tr: I ask, secondly, how it comes about that the tacit custom of some nation (say the English) is sufficient for sitting or standing at the common table to succeed to the reclining posture, while the positive law of the same nation is not sufficient for kneeling at the sacred table to succeed to the same posture? Can a custom changed gradually and without public authority bring it about that what was once held neither unseemly nor unlawful is no longer fitting or permitted? Can a law sanctioned by public authority, and confirmed by the express consent of the people, approved by long use and by custom, not bring it about that at least what is shown by no lawful reason to have ever been unlawful is henceforth held to be lawful? Where two things truly conflict, Law and Custom (though this hardly happens here), whoever is sound in mind will admit that it is fair for custom to yield to law, not law to custom. I ask them thirdly, whether they seriously think, or do not think, that he who took food at the common table with knees bent would be sinning continually. If they say he sins: since every sin is a transgression of the divine law, then tell me some precept of that law against which one sins by so doing; if they confess that it can be done without sin: do they not notice that by that admission they cut their own throat and overthrow all the force of their argument? Fourthly, supposing that the reclining posture had long since fallen out of use, and that standing or sitting had succeeded to it before that first supper, so that Christ and the Apostles must have eaten either standing or sitting, since both could not be done at once: I ask, if they had eaten standing, would it also be necessary for us to stand so that we would sin by sitting, and conversely; or would we be free to do either? If they say we are free to do either: the argument drawn from the example of Christ wholly collapses, because it is supposed that he did one or the other only, not both. If they say that we are bound precisely to that species which is supposed to have been used by Christ: why, then, do these severe dictators themselves leave to the liberty of each congregation the option of standing or sitting? I ask, fifthly, if the example of Christ binds us to imitate it: why is this obligation determined precisely in the table posture, which is a subordinate species, and not either stopped at some higher genus or extended further to some lower species? This is to ask: since these three are posture as the higher genus, table posture as the species subordinate to it, and reclining posture as the lowest species; and since Christ used posture in general, and the table posture, and the reclining posture: why should the table posture, which is the intermediate species, be judged both necessary and sufficient for right imitation of Christ, and not either some posture in general as sufficient, or the reclining posture in particular as necessary? Lastly, I ask whether the reclining posture used by Christ and the Apostles at the first supper was imitable or not. That it was imitable they will not deny (I know well enough), nor indeed can they deny it, those who seek from this the principal support of their cause: for thus they put forward the example of Christ as something we must of necessity imitate: not every example simply, but every example which is imitable. What they therefore concede freely, I accept gladly: namely that the major premise, every example of Christ that is imitable, binds Christians to imitate it; and likewise the minor premise, namely that that posture in particular (whether it was the reclining posture, which is very probable and which we now at least suppose, or some other) in which Christ used at that first supper, is imitable. From these premises I draw this conclusion: Therefore by force of that example the Christians of the ages immediately after Christ were bound to the same posture in particular that Christ used; and therefore likewise those of the second and third ages, and so on down to these times. Therefore it must be admitted that the present Church is bound to the reclining posture in particular, if Christ used that posture; or at least it must be shown at what time, for what reason, by whose authority, by what right and power that obligation was removed.

units.la: XXII. Ex his quæ dicta sunt liquet, Argumenti illius, quod tanta cum pompa ab illis instruitur, vim omnem eo tandem recidere, ut non possit rectiùs[?] & in rem suam accommodatius proponi, quàm sub hac forma. Exemplum Christi & Apostolorum in tantum obligat, quantum nobis visum est expedire ut obliget; sed nobis expedire visum est ut obliget ad non ingeniculandum[?], ulterius verò non obliget: ergo eatenus tantùm obligat, & non ulterius. Piget ista fateor: non est aut hujus loci, aut istius ætatis, aut moris nostri, risum captare in re seriâ. Sed quid facias istis hominibus? Nimirum indiget istiusmodi patrocinio causa non bona: nec fieri potest, ut non multa inania, & si penitius examinentur perabsurda, sibique parum consentanea, dicere sæpenumerò cogantur, qui partium magis studio duci se patiuntur quàm veritatis. Equidem ex animo loquor, & quod res est: Etsi multa passim in eorum scriptis occurrant parum solidè disputata, utinam non quædam etiam parùm sincerè; non memini tamen usquam me observasse tanto cum conatu & molimine meras nugas agi, ut ex tanta montium parturitione tam miserè ridiculum prodire fœrum, quàm cum nuda piorum exempla è Sacris literis adducta, aut ad excusandum ea facta quæ videntur lege aliquâ divinâ prohiberi, aut ad inducendum obligationem in conscientia in his quæ non videntur lege aliquâ divinâ præcipi, importunè urgentur. Sed unde digressus sum, si tamen digressus sum, redeo, & pergo ad
units.tr: XXII. From what has been said it is clear that the whole force of that argument, which they set out with such pomp, comes down in the end to this: it cannot be put more correctly or more suitably to their own purpose than in the following form. The example of Christ and the Apostles binds us only so far as we judge it expedient for it to bind us. But we judge it expedient that it bind us to not kneeling, and no further. Therefore it binds us only so far, and no further. I admit that these things are tedious. It is neither the place, nor the age, nor our custom to seek laughter in a serious matter. But what can one do with such men? A bad cause certainly needs such advocacy, and it cannot be avoided that those who allow themselves to be led more by partisan zeal than by love of truth are often forced to say many empty things, and, if examined more closely, utterly absurd things that scarcely agree with themselves. For my part I speak from my heart and as the matter stands. Although many poorly argued points occur throughout their writings, and I wish some were not also poorly sincere, I do not remember ever observing anywhere such a great effort and struggle over mere trifles. Out of such a mountain of labour, a mouse so pitifully ridiculous is born: when bare examples of the godly taken from Holy Scripture are pressed importunately, either to excuse deeds that seem forbidden by some divine law, or to bring in an obligation on the conscience in matters that do not seem to be commanded by any divine law. But I return, if indeed I have digressed, to where I was leaving off, and proceed to

units.la: XXIII. Argumentum Quartum , ab Exemplo- rum fine & usu proprio.
units.tr: XXIII. Fourth Argument, from the proper end and use of examples.

units.la: Habere enim Exempla suum usum, eumque ad morum institutionem, vitæque[?] emendationem permagnum, omninò fatendum est. Alioquin nec tàm multa in sacris literis perscripta essent, (quæcunque enim præscripta sunt, εἰς τὴν διδασκαλίαν ἡμῶν. Rom. 15. 4. εἰς τὴν νουθεσίαν ἡμῶν[?]. I Cor. 10. 11. ad nos erudiendos aut commonefaciendos perscripta sunt,) nec tam constanter ab Apostolis ubique inculcarentur. Sumite, fratres mei, pro exemplari patientiae prophetas. Audivistis patientiam Iob. Elias oravit. ——— Omnia haec Jac. 5, 10, 11, 17. imitatores mei estote, sicut ego Christi, 1 Cor. 11. 1. Quae audivistis, & vidistis in me, haec agite, Phil. 4. 9. Eos considerate, qui sic ambulant, ut habetis nos pro exemplari, Phil. 3. 17. & similia passim: At non est is usus aut finis Exemplorum, ut sint nobis pro regula vivendi: sed ut sint subsidia quaedam & adminicula, & quasi stimuli ad excitandam ignaviam nostram & torporem excutiendum, cum segniores sumus & tardiores in officio faciendo, quàm par est. Solet enim fragilitas humana, objecta praesertim gravi tentatione, accedente etiam Satanae & mundi impulsu, de severitate legis Dei & obediendi difficultate multa apud se submurmurare, imò & aperte quandoque conqueri: in via qua eundum est grassari leones; undique struì pedibus suis laqueos, insidias, scandala; perferendas injurias, contumelias, calumnias, bonorum rapinam; charos parentes, chariora pignora, uxorem, amicos, possessiones, patriam, vitam ipsam relinquendo, imò & odio habendam. Quàm duri sunt hi sermones! quàm non ferendum jugum! Quoties subeunt mentes nostras ejusmodi cogitationes, ita ut jam penè {1}despondeamus animum, & omnem officii curam velut rei impossibilis & in quam inanis sit omnis opera nostra & irriti conatus, tantùm non abjicere incipiamus: excitantur aliquantulum languentes spiritus, & ad contemnendas omnes difficultates, superandas tentationes, perferendas contumelias, paulatim erigitur animus {2}opportunâ Exemplorum authoritate. Cum feriò cogitamus viros, pios quidem & Sanctos, sed ὁμοιοπαθεῖς ἡμῖν iisdem quibus nos perturbationibus, cupiditatibus, tentationibus obnoxios, gratiâ
units.tr: It must be wholly admitted that examples have their use, and a very great one, for the formation of manners and the amendment of life. Otherwise so many things would not have been written down in Holy Scripture (for whatever has been written has been written to instruct and admonish us [εἰς τὴν διδασκαλίαν ἡμῶν; Rom. 15. 4; εἰς τὴν νουθεσίαν ἡμῶν; 1 Cor. 10. 11]), nor would the Apostles so constantly press them everywhere. "Take, my brethren, the prophets for an example of patience. You have heard of the patience of Job. Elijah prayed." (Jam. 5. 10, 11, 17.) "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ" (1 Cor. 11. 1). "Those things which you have heard and seen in me, do these" (Phil. 4. 9). "Mark those who walk so, as you have us for an example" (Phil. 3. 17), and similar passages everywhere. But the use and purpose of examples is not that they should be for us a rule of living. Rather, they are aids and supports, as it were spurs to rouse our sloth and shake off our torpor, when we are more lazy and slower in doing our duty than we ought to be. For human frailty, especially when pressed by a grave temptation, with the added push of Satan and the world, is wont to murmur to itself a great deal about the severity of God's law and the difficulty of obedience, and sometimes even to complain openly. Lions roam on the road we must travel; snares, plots and stumbling-blocks are laid under our feet; injuries, insults, slanders and the plundering of goods must be endured; dear parents, still dearer children, wife, friends, possessions, country and life itself must be left behind, and even hated. How hard these words are! How unbearable this yoke! As often as thoughts of this kind enter our minds, so that we almost despair and begin to cast away all care of duty as a thing impossible, and as if all our effort were vain and our attempts fruitless, our languid spirits are somewhat roused, and the mind is gradually lifted up to despise all difficulties, overcome temptations and bear insults, by the fitting authority of examples. When we seriously consider men who were pious and holy, yet of like passions with us, liable to the same disturbances, desires and temptations, by the grace

units.la: {1} Turpiter desperatur quicquid fieri potest. Quintil. 1. Institut. 10.
units.tr: {1} It is shameful to despair of whatever can be done. Quintilian, Institutes, book 10.

units.la: {2} Cum quid difficile videtur, difficultas aliis obeundi tollitur, si eorum exempla reverenter [?]. Tert. 1. ad uxor. 6. Dei (quæ nec nobis defutura est, si ab eo tori pendeamus[?], & conatus simul nostros fideliter adjungamus, adjutos, ea omnia & perfecisse & perfulisse[?], quæ nobis aut facienda aut ferenda Deo sic dispensante incumbunt: redire mox animi, incalescere pia æmulatione peftora, & {1}inter meditandum exardescere ignem; dum erumpant tandem è plenitudine cordis hæ aut persimiles voces, En me paratum, Domine, obire quod jubes, Jubire quod imponis. {2}Nubes illa testium, quæ nos quacunque circumspectamus cingit undique, suadet ut omni abjecto ægri animi tumore & gravedine, peccatíque, quæ ut nos arctè compleEtitur, ita per Dei gratiam, si strenuè conemur, non ægrè comprimitur importunitate, propositum nobis stadium fortiter & constanter & patienter decurra-mus.
units.tr: {2} When something seems difficult, the difficulty of others in doing it is removed, if their examples are considered reverently. Tertullian, To His Wife, book 1, chapter 6. of God (which will not fail us either, if we depend on him and faithfully join our own efforts, having been helped to accomplish and carry through all those things which, as God so ordains, lie upon us either to do or to bear), our spirits soon return, our hearts grow warm with pious emulation, and {1} "while I meditated, the fire burned"; until at last from the fullness of the heart there break forth these or similar words: "Behold me ready, Lord, to do what you command; to bear what you lay upon me." {2} That cloud of witnesses, which surrounds us on every side wherever we look, urges us that, with all swelling and heaviness of a sick spirit cast off, and with sin, which so closely clings to us, being restrained without difficulty by God's grace if we strive strenuously, we should run the race set before us with courage, constancy and patience.

units.la: XXIV. Hortatur Jacobus Apostolus, cap. 5. ad exhortationis instantiam, exemplo Eliæ, qui importunis suis precibus (προσευχῇ προσηύξατο[?]) cœli ostia quasi pro arbitrio obieravit & reseravit. Quod nequis existimaret Eliæ meritis & sanctitati debeti potius, quàm Divinæ Promissioni fidelium precibus ex fœdere gratiæ factæ; præripit hanc suspicionem Apostolus in ipso narrationis exordio, Elias, inquit, homo erat, ὁμοιοπαθὴς ἡμῖν[?] — verf. 17. Homo erat: non Deus, aut Angelus: nec de meliore lato, sed ex eadem qua cæteri homines masså effictus. Hic est ergo usus Exemplorum proprius & perutilis: ast meminisse interim oportet, Exempla non esse regulam ipsam, nec regulæ pondus & instar habere: imò esse & ipsa, siqua dubitandi ratio appareat rectène an recus facta sint, ad regulam diligenter exigenda. ὑπόδειγμα λάβετε τῆς κακοπαθείας[?], inquit Jacobus, Jac 5. 10. Ubi nescio an illud ὑπόδειγμα specialem habeat ἐνέργειαν & vim: Mihi certè innuere videtur Sanctorum prophetarum actus non esse [?παράδειγμα], Exemplar illud Principale quod est praecipuè nobis intuendum ; sed quasi illius [?ἀπόγραφον] & Secundarium Exemplar, quod non est ex se & propter se authenticae authoritatis, sed eatenus fidem habet & authoritatem, quatenus concordat cum Originali. Ex hactenus di-ctis ergo conficitur, non sufficere ad bonitatem actus humani, quòd fit alicujus viri Sancti exemplo conformis : nec proinde posse cujusquam conscientiam in ejusmodi conformitate, nisi sit & ipsum exemplum regulae conforme, secure & tuto acquiescere.
units.tr: XXIV. The Apostle James, in chapter 5, urges by the example of Elijah the urgency of exhortation, since Elijah by his importunate prayers [προσευχῇ προσηύξατο] shut and opened the doors of heaven, as it were at will. Lest anyone suppose that this was owed to Elijah's merits and holiness rather than to the Divine promise made to the prayers of the faithful under the covenant of grace, the Apostle forestalls this suspicion at the very beginning of the narrative: "Elijah," he says, "was a man [ὁμοιοπαθὴς ἡμῖν], of like passions with us" (ver. 17). He was a man: not God, nor an angel, nor made of a better clay, but formed from the same mass as other men. This, then, is the proper and most useful use of examples. But one must remember meanwhile that examples are not the rule itself, nor do they have the weight and standing of a rule. Indeed they themselves must be carefully tested against the rule, should there be any ground for doubt whether they were done rightly or wrongly. "Take the prophets as an example [ὑπόδειγμα] of suffering," says James (Jam. 5. 10). Here I do not know whether the word ὑπόδειγμα has a special force and meaning. It seems to me at least to indicate that the acts of the holy prophets are not the [παράδειγμα] principal pattern, which chiefly is to be regarded by us, but rather a copy [ἀπόγραφον] of it and a secondary example, which has no authentic authority of itself and for its own sake, but has faith and authority only so far as it agrees with the original. From what has been said so far it follows that it is not enough for the goodness of a human act that it is conformed to the example of some holy man. Nor, therefore, can anyone's conscience securely and safely rest in such conformity, unless the example itself is also conformed to the rule.

units.la: XXV. Porrò, ut ad alteram propositi nostri partem tandem accedamus, eadem fermè ratio est Judicii alieni, quae & Exempli ; idque ob easdem fere causas : ita ut hac in re non sit opus multis. Percurram itaque breviter. Primò, sunt omnes homines, quantumvis docti & pii, non minus Erroribus quam Peccatis obnoxii, imò fortasse vel multò magis quò acutiore mentis indagine opus est, ad internoscendum veri & falsi discrimen, quàm boni & mali. Ex Ignorantia illa naturali quâ mentes nostrae velut caligine quadam obductae sunt ; ex Educatione, quae animos nostros adhuc teneros fingit & efformat, & notionibus quibusdam instruit & imbuit, quas non facile est eradicare ; ex longo usu & Consuetudine, quae velut altera natura est ; ex pravis affectibus, qui judicio offundunt nebulas, & rectum ejus usum impediunt ; ex aliis ejusmodi causis permultis, adeò proclive est homini errare, labi, decipi, ut jam olim in proverbium abierit Humanum esse errare.
units.tr: XXV. Next, to come at last to the other part of our proposition, the reasoning about the judgement of others is almost the same as that about examples, and for almost the same causes, so that in this matter there is no need for many words. I shall run through it briefly. First, all men, however learned and pious, are liable to errors no less than to sins, and indeed perhaps far more, since a sharper penetration of mind is needed to distinguish true from false than good from evil. From that natural ignorance by which our minds are, as it were, overspread with a certain darkness; from education, which shapes and forms our still tender minds and instils and imbues them with certain notions that are not easily eradicated; from long use and custom, which is as a second nature; from evil affections, which cast clouds over judgement and hinder its right use; from many other causes of this kind, it is so easy for a man to err, slip and be deceived, that long ago the saying passed into a proverb: "To err is human."

units.la: XXVI. Adde huc Secundò, quod nec ipsi femper de eorum pietate & prudentiâ, quorum judicia sequi volumus, sincere judicamus. Quin
units.tr: XXVI. Add to this, secondly, that people do not always judge sincerely about the piety and prudence of those whose judgments they choose to follow. Indeed,

units.la: {1.} Cicero. Philip. 12. solenne est iis qui se permittunt alieno arbitratu duci; eos sibi duces diligere, quos jam ante sciunt duƥuros se in ea via, qua ipsi jam ante constituerant proficisci. Sic homines incautos Satanas quasi circulo inclusos tenet. Si quæras, cur hoc putent esse verum & rectum, respondent quia ita nos docuit hic vel ille vir pius & prudens: Si quæras iterum qui sciant doctorem illum suum esse virum pium & prudentem? respondent, vel responderent saltem si ex animo loqui vellent, quia nobiscum sentit.——— {1}Et Sapit, & mecum facit, & Jove judicat æquo. Metiuntur nimirum plerique mortalium pietatem alienam, non ex praxi officiorum vitæ Christianæ, & ex operibus justitiæ, misericordiæ, charitatis, & devotionis; sed ex studio earum partium quibus se addixerunt, & earum odio quibus se inimicos profitentur,——— Κατὰ τὰς ὁμοιό-μιας τὰς ἰδίας ἑαυτῶν ἐπισωρεύοντες διδασκάλους inquit Apostolus, 2 Tim. 4. 3. Coarcervantes sibimetipsis doctores secundum proprias concupiscen-tias: Κνηθόμενοι τὴν ἀκοήν, ut ibidem sequitur aptissimâ metaphorâ. Cum iis aures pruriunt, quærunt sc. qui eas scabant, atque ita accidit eis quod veteri proverbio dici solet, Muli se mutuo scabunt.
units.tr: {1} Cicero, Philippics 12. It is customary for those who allow themselves to be led by another's judgment to choose as their leaders those whom they already know will lead them along the very road they had already resolved to take. In this way Satan holds unwary men as if enclosed in a circle. If you ask why they think this is true and right, they answer: because this or that man who is pious and prudent taught us so. If you ask again how they know that their teacher is a pious and prudent man, they answer (or would answer, at least, if they were willing to speak from the heart) that he agrees with us. ——— {1} "He is wise, and agrees with me, and judges as Jove would." Indeed most mortals measure the piety of others not by the practice of the duties of the Christian life, nor by works of justice, mercy, charity and devotion, but by their zeal for the parties to which they have devoted themselves and their hatred of those whom they declare to be their enemies. ——— The Apostle says, "heaping up for themselves teachers according to their own lusts" [κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας ἑαυτῶν ἐπιθυμίας ἐπισωρεύοντες διδασκάλους], 2 Tim. 4. 3: heaping up teachers for themselves according to their own desires; and, as the same passage goes on with a most apt metaphor, "having itching ears" [Κνηθόμενοι τὴν ἀκοήν]. Their ears itch, and they seek out those who will scratch them; and so it happens to them as the old proverb says: "mules scratch one another."

units.la: XXVII, Tertiò, diserte nos prohibet sacra Scripptura, aut alterius cujuslibet judicio conscientias nostras subjicere, aut in alterius conscientiam dominium exercere. Ne vocemini Rabbi, unus est enim vester ὁ καθηγητής, magister, præceptor, doctor, ductor Christus, Matth. 23. 10. Ne multi estote magistri, fratres mei, Jac. 3. 1. Pascite qui in vobis est gregem Dei, ὡς ποίμνιον, ut sacem ei præferentes, verae fidei doctrinam & piæ exemplum, sed non ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων, 1 Pet. 5. 1. Non quasi exercentes dominatum
units.tr: XXVII. Thirdly, Holy Scripture plainly forbids us either to subject our consciences to the judgment of anyone else, or to exercise dominion over another's conscience. "Be not called Rabbi; for one is your Master [ὁ καθηγητής], even Christ," Matt. 23. 10. "Be not many masters, my brethren," Jas. 3. 1. "Feed the flock of God which is among you, [ποίμνιον] not as lords over God's heritage [ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων], but being examples to the flock," 1 Pet. 5. 1, setting before them the doctrine of the true faith and the pattern of godly living.

units.la: {1} Horat. 2. Epist. 1. dominatum & imperium merum in Clerum & Populum Dei. Empti estis pretio: nolite fieri servi hominum, 1 Cor. 7. 23. Ut Conscientias vestras cujusquam hominis authoritati ex ipsius arbitrio & imperio regendas permittatis.
units.tr: {1} Horace, Epistles 2. 1. Dominion and absolute rule over the clergy and the people of God. "You were bought with a price; do not become servants of men," 1 Cor. 7. 23, so that you should not allow your consciences to be governed by the authority and command of any human being according to his will.

units.la: XXVIII. Hinc ergo illud imprimis sequitur, (ut ex iis quæ à nobis hactenus posita sunt & probata, corollaria nonnulla inferam, sed pauca, & paucis) merito exosam esse debere cuilibet Christiano Romani Pontificis conjunctam cum summo fastu, non ferendam tyrannidem: qui dum sibi suæque Cathedræ arrogat judicium infallibile, exercet eo nomine, quasi jus suum, dominatum in conscientias hominum: eousque, ut si dicat virtutes esse vitia, & vitia virtutes, teneantur sub mortali peccato omnes Christiani ipsius judicio sine ulla hæsitatione semet subjicere. Et proinde agnoscendam esse cum omni grati animi significatione summam & singularem Dei Opt. Max. in nos bonitatem & misericordiam, qui nos patresque nostros & Ecclesiam Anglicanam tam iniqua tyrannide dudum exemerit, & justæ libertati quasi postliminio restituerit.
units.tr: XXVIII. Hence, therefore, there follows above all else (I will draw a few corollaries from what we have so far set out and proved, but few, and briefly) that the intolerable tyranny of the Roman Pontiff, joined with the greatest arrogance, must be hated by every Christian. While he claims for himself and for his chair an infallible judgment, he exercises under that name, as if it were his own right, dominion over the consciences of men, to such an extent that if he should say that virtues are vices and vices are virtues, all Christians are bound under mortal sin to submit themselves to his judgment without any hesitation. And accordingly we must acknowledge, with every sign of a grateful mind, the great and singular goodness and mercy of God Most Good and Most Great toward us, who long ago freed us, our fathers and the English Church from so unjust a tyranny, and restored us to just liberty as if by right of return.

units.la: XXIX. Atqui Secundo, cavendum nobis & universis & singulis, ne illa tyrannide liberati, novo jugo colla subdamus; nec tam excussisse jugum quam permutasse deprehendamur.
units.tr: XXIX. But secondly, we must take care, both all of us and each of us, that, having been freed from that tyranny, we do not bend our necks to a new yoke; and that we are not found to have merely exchanged the yoke rather than thrown it off.

units.la: {*} ——— Qua bellua ruptis / Quum semel effugit, reddit se prava catenis ?
units.tr: {*} "The beast, once it has broken its chains, does it not return, wicked, to them?"

units.la: Interest profecto nostrâ, si aut internæ Conscientiæ, aut externæ Reipublicæ & Ecclesiæ pacifico confultum velimus, omnino curare, ne ut olim in Ecclesiâ Corinthiacâ Ego sum Pauli, ego Apol[?] Apollo, ego Cephæ, sic apud nos istiusmodi voces audiantur, ego sum Lutheri, ego Calvini, ego Arminii, ego Socini. Quin esto {1} omnis homo mendax, & verax solus Deus. Non est dignus qui sit Christi, qui non est unius Christi discipulus. Actum est de fidei Christianæ simplicitate & sinceritate, postquam itum est in partes: Neque ulla spes est ante restitutum iri pristino vigori & virori Religionem Christi, quàm diducta tot fracturis & scissuris vulnera, fraternæ condescensionis oleo velut malægmate delinita, in eandem Fidei & Charitatis unitatem coëant & coalescant.
units.tr: Certainly it is in our interest, if we desire a peaceful inner conscience and a peaceful outward commonwealth and Church, to take care that, as once in the Church of Corinth, "I am of Paul, I of Apollos, I of Cephas," so such words are not heard among us: "I am of Luther, I of Calvin, I of Arminius, I of Socinus." Indeed, let "every man be a liar, and God alone true" [Rom. 3. 4]. He is not worthy to be called Christ's who is not a disciple of Christ alone. The simplicity and sincerity of the Christian faith is undone once men have split into parties; and there is no hope that the religion of Christ will be restored to its former vigour and strength until the wounds torn open by so many fractures and schisms, soothed as with a salve by the oil of brotherly condescension, come together and grow again into the same unity of faith and charity.

units.la: XXX. Cavendum porrò Tertiò, ne pravis affectibus indulgentes, ita nos abduci patiamur in cujusquam personæ admirationem, ut ex ipsius authoritate toti pendeamus, {2}Θαυμάζοντες ὠφελείας χάριν[?]. Quibus verbis intendit digitum Apostolus ad ipsissimum totius mali fontem. Nempe non aliunde emanavit omnis illa omnium[?] perversa admiratio quam ex perdita illa & nimia sua admiratione. Dum quisque propriæ utilitati studet, inservit honori, gloriæ velificatur; alios omnes æstimat ex suo commodo: & corrupto jam hisce affectibus judicio, eos protinus admiratur maximè, quos utilitati, honori, gloriæ, aliisque suis cupiditatibus minimè adversaturos arbitratur.
units.tr: XXX. Next, thirdly, we must take care that, indulging depraved affections, we do not allow ourselves to be drawn into such admiration of any person that we hang entirely upon his authority, {2} "admiring people for the sake of advantage" [Θαυμάζοντες ὠφελείας χάριν]. With these words the Apostle points his finger at the very source of the whole evil. Indeed, that entire perverse admiration of everyone springs from nothing else than from that ruinous and excessive admiration of oneself. While each man pursues his own advantage, serves his honour and sails toward glory, he judges all others by his own convenience; and with his judgment now corrupted by these affections, he forthwith admires most of all those whom he thinks will least oppose his advantage, honour, glory and his other desires.

units.la: Quod ipsum alter etiam Apostolus, quem ante citavimus clare significat, ubi notat homines sibi {3}κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας praeceptores de-ligere.
units.tr: The other Apostle too, whom we cited before, clearly indicates this when he notes that men choose teachers for themselves {3} "according to their own desires" [κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας].

units.la: XXXI. Cæterùm ut, non obstantibus quæ à me dicta sunt, sua constet interim & Ecclesiæ Catholicæ, & unicuique viro docto & pio, justa authoritas: Admonendi estis primò, judicio & piæ Universalis Ecclesiæ, in sacrarum literarum interpretatione, & in dijudicandis fidei & mo-
units.tr: XXXI. But so that, notwithstanding what I have said, the just authority both of the Catholic Church and of every learned and pious man may for the present stand firm, you must be reminded, first, that great deference is due to the judgment and piety of the Universal Church in the interpretation of the sacred writings, and in deciding the controversies of faith and
{2} Jude v. 16.

units.la: {3} 2 Tim. 4.3. rum controversiis plurimum deferri oportere: Secundò, & viri docti judicio & authoritati nonnihil tribuendum, ad eximendum ex animis hominum scrupulos minus necessarios, atque etiam ad dirigendum conscientias in rebus dubiis, de quibus non potest aliter haberi ulla certitudo. Sed de horum utroque, erit fortasse posthac commodior dicendi locus.
units.tr: {3} 2 Tim. 4. 3. morals; secondly, that some weight must be given to the judgment and authority of a learned man, both for removing from men's minds the less necessary scruples, and also for guiding consciences in doubtful matters, in which no certainty can otherwise be had. But of both these points there will perhaps be a more convenient place for discussion hereafter.

units.la: PRÆLECTIO QUARTA,
units.tr: CHAPTER FOUR,

units.la: In quâ Quæ sit Adæquata Conscientiæ Regula disquiritur & statuitur.
units.tr: In which it is inquired into and established what is the adequate rule of conscience.
JAMES 4. 12.

units.la: Unus enim est Legislator, qui potest servare & perdere.
units.tr: There is one Lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy.

units.la: QUàm parùm sit unicuique præsidii, ad Conscientiæ suæ sive fructum, ad excusandum ea quæ hactenus fecerit, sive securitatem ad ἀφόβως aggrediendum quæ porrò facturus est, si ea aut sola boni finis intentione, aut aliena tantùm exempli vel judicii authoritate nituntur: satis à me superque proximis duabus prælectionibus demonstratum est. Eo nimirum consilio, ut sublatis è medio his velut obicibus, expeditior mihi & complanatior esset via, ad ea quæ de Conscientiæ obligatione dicere instituera m. Quæ Obligatio cùm sit duplex: Activa scilicet, per quam alterius obligationi subest: postulat ordinis ratio, ut à passiva ordiamur. Tunc enim de re mensurata securius pronunciare poterimus, postquam constituerit mensuram ipsam esse iustam. Quod ergo nunc agitur hoc est, ut inquiramus quid sit id quod proprie obligat Consci-entiam: sive, quod idem est, quae sit propria & adæquata Conscientiæ Regula, cui se (ut recta sit) conformare teneatur. Quæ inquisitio ut certius & commodius instituatur, paucis quibusdam velut explicandi gratia præmissis, rem ipsam tandem quibusdam Conclusionibus completar.
units.tr: How little help there is for anyone, either for the benefit of his conscience, to excuse what he has done hitherto, or for the security to act without fear in what he is going to do in future, if these things rest either on the good intention of the end alone, or only on the authority of another's example or judgement, I have shown sufficiently and more than sufficiently in the two previous lectures. My purpose was that, with these obstacles removed, my way might be clearer and smoother for what I have undertaken to say about the obligation of conscience. This obligation is twofold: the active kind, by which one thing is bound to another's obligation, and the passive kind. The order of the argument requires that we begin with the passive. For then we can speak more securely about the thing measured, once we have established that the measure itself is just. What we now take up, therefore, is this: to inquire what it is that properly binds conscience, or, what is the same, what is the proper and adequate rule of conscience, to which conscience must conform itself in order to be right. So that this inquiry may be conducted more certainly and conveniently, I shall first set out a few preliminaries, as it were by way of explanation, and then complete the matter with certain Conclusions.

units.la: II. Sciendum itaque Primo, Conscientiæ ut munus suum debite exequatur, necessariam esse aliquam Regulam, cui subesse debeat: Ubicunque enim est Virtus aliqua Activa, quæ non est de natura sua determinata ad unum in agendo, sed est in potentia ad utrumlibet, ita ut possit recte agere vel secus; sive ea virtus sit habitus de prima, sive potentia naturalis de secunda specie Qualitatis: oportet ut sit Lex aliqua vel Regula, (νόμῳ sive κανών) quæ eam in agendo dirigat. Quotiescunque enim aliquid se ut faciendum offert phantasia, sive à sensu externo repræsentatum; sive ex interna quadam animi suggestione; quia Voluntas, quæ est proximum agendi principium, est (ut dici solet) potentia cæca, nec potest ex se malum à bono discernere, ut ita sit ipsa sibi Regula: ratio inquisitiva mox ad Conscientiam recurrit, ut ejus dictamen audiat. Cujus munus est rem propositam statim examini subjicere; examine facto, sitne persequenda vel fugienda, facienda vel omittenda judicare; & prout judicaverit, ita voluntati stare: hoc est, rem eam libero arbitrio ut eligendam vel non eligendam proponere. Ad quod examinandi, judicandi, distandi munus, ne temere id præster & ὡς ἔτυχεν, & cæcam voluntatem ipsa non minus cæca in transversum ducat: Opus est ut certa aliqua sit norma, ad quam fiat examen.
units.tr: II. First, then, we should understand that, for conscience to discharge its office rightly, some Rule is necessary to which it must be subject. For wherever there is some active power which is not by its nature determined to one in acting, but is in potency to either, so that it can act rightly or otherwise (whether that power is a habit of the first kind, or a natural faculty of the second kind of quality), there must be some law or rule (νόμος or κανών) to direct it in acting. For whenever an appearance presents something to us as to be done, whether represented by the external senses or by some inner prompting of the mind, the will, which is the proximate principle of acting, is (as it is commonly said) a blind power. It cannot of itself distinguish evil from good, so as to be its own rule. Therefore inquiring reason at once has recourse to conscience, to hear its verdict. Its office is to submit the matter proposed to examination at once; having made the examination, to judge whether it is to be pursued or avoided, done or left undone; and, as it has judged, so to stand by the will, that is, to propose the matter to the free choice as something to be chosen or not chosen. And lest it carry out this office of examining, judging and distinguishing rashly and at random (ὡς ἔτυχεν), and lest the blind will, itself no less blind, lead it astray, there must be some fixed norm by which the examination is made.

units.la: III. Sciendum Secundò, esse in Regulis, sicut & in Causis. subordinationem quandam : & sicut in Causis, invicem ordinatis, posteriores quæque si ad priores comparentur habent rationem Effectuum[?] sic in regulis & mensuris invicem ordinatis, posteriorem quamque respectu superioris haberi rationem regulati sive mensurati. Regula igitur Conscientiæ cùm sit duplex ; altera proxima & immediata, prima & remotior altera : regula illa proxima, sicut habet rationem Regulæ, respectu ipsius Conscientiæ, quam dirigere debet, sic habet rationem regulati, respectu regulæ primæ, à quâ & ipsa dirigenda est.
units.tr: III. Second, we should understand that there is a certain subordination among rules, as also among causes. And just as, among causes ordered one under another, each later cause, when compared with the earlier ones, has the character of an effect, so among rules and measures ordered one under another, each later one, with respect to the higher, has the character of the thing ruled or measured. Since the rule of conscience is therefore twofold, one proximate and immediate, the other first and more remote, that proximate rule, just as it has the character of a rule with respect to the conscience it must direct, so has the character of a thing ruled with respect to the first rule, by which it too must be directed.

units.la: IV. Sciendum Tertiò, quùm consistat cujusque rei rectitudo in conformitate ipsius ad suam regulam: sicut est duplex, ut jam diximus, Conscientiæ Regula, proxima & remota ; ita duplex est etiam Conscientiæ rectitudo, duplici illi regulæ respondens. Potest enim Conscientia recta dici, vel ἁπλῶς[?], simpliciter, absolutè & ut quaque quaque recta[?] : ex in- voluntas, est (ut alum à ratio ut ejus ropoli- fine ittenda rati di- eligen- uod ex- nere id fa non s est ut Scienvel χ[?] τὶ, secundum aliquid & quadantenus reßa. Hoc modo recta est, si sit conformis Regulæ suæ proximæ & immediatæ: quemadmodum is dicitur de aliqua propria passione habere scientiam certam & veram, qui potest ipsam de suo Subjecto per proximam sui causam demonstrare, etsi nequeat ulterius ascendere. At illo modo tum demum recta est Conscientia, cum & ipsa regulæ suæ proximæ conformis est, & illa insuper regula regulæ primæ: quemadmodum is dicitur habere rei alicujus certam, (id est, perfectam) scientiam, qui omnes ejus causas novit usque ad primas. Tunc enim unamquamque rem scire dicimur, (inquit Philosophus initio Lib. 1. Phys.) cum omnes ejus causas, principia, & elementa cognoscimus usque ad prima. Proinde ut certitudo scientia, etsi oriatur immediatè ex cognitione causæ proximæ, resolvitur ramen ultimatè in cognitionem causæ primæ : Sicut Eitudo Conscientiæ, etsi attendatur immediatè penes conformitatem ad regulam suam proximam, resolvitur tamen ultimatè in regulam suam primam & supremam.
units.tr: IV. Third, we should understand that, since the rectitude of anything consists in its conformity to its own rule, just as the rule of conscience is twofold, as we have said, proximate and remote, so the rectitude of conscience is also twofold, corresponding to that twofold rule. For conscience may be called right either absolutely (ἁπλῶς), simply, unconditionally, and in every respect right; or in some respect (κατά τι), in a certain way and right to a degree. It is right in the second way if it conforms to its proximate and immediate rule. In the same way, a person is said to have certain and true knowledge of some proper attribute if he can demonstrate it of its subject through its proximate cause, even though he cannot ascend any further. But conscience is right in the first way only when it both conforms to its proximate rule, and that rule in turn conforms to the first rule. In the same way, a person is said to have certain (that is, perfect) knowledge of a thing if he knows all its causes up to the first. For, as the Philosopher says at the beginning of the Physics, Book 1: We say that we know each thing when we know all its causes, principles and elements, up to the first. Accordingly, although the certainty of knowledge, even if it arises immediately from knowledge of the proximate cause, is nevertheless ultimately resolved into knowledge of the first cause, so the certainty of conscience, even if it is judged immediately by its conformity to its proximate rule, is nevertheless ultimately resolved into its first and supreme rule.

units.la: V. Sciendum Quarto, cum de Obligatione Conscientiæ loquimur, Obligationem illam non significare conditionem aliquam (Conscientia enim proprie loquendo) non magis cogi potest, quam ipsum Liberum arbitrium; sed imperium potius & pote-statem urgendi eam (cum authoritate tamen cui ipsa obedire tenetur) ad faciendum quod sui est officii: eodem omnino modo, quo Princeps qui habet potestatem νομοθετικὴν[?], ferendo leges obligat subditos ad ipsarum observationem. Sicut ergo in foro externo subditos ad obediendum obligat proprie & formaliter, non Lex ipsa, sed potestas Legislatoris; verè tamen dicitur & Lex ipsa obligare, etsi improprie & quasi materialiter, sive terminative, quia per eam & ad eam fit obligatio; sicut dicitur Lex etiam judicare [Num lex nostra judicat quenquam? Joh. 7. 51.] etsi ipsa non judicet, sed Prætor, quia Prætor debet secundum legem judicare: Sic & in foro interno Conscientiam proprie obligat, non Regula sive Lex ei imposita, sed potestas & authoritas imponentis: ita tamen ut ex consequenti verè & non incommodè, licet minus proprie, dici possit regulam ipsam obligare. Cum ergo quæritur, quid sit illud quod obligat Conscientiam ad faciendum officium suum; utrumque hoc quæritur: Primo & principaliter, quis sit Dominus Conscientiæ, qui jus habeat & potestatem imponendi ei Legem seu Regulam cui se debeat conformare; deinde secundario & consequenter, quæ sit Regula Conscientiæ, ceu Lex ab illo domino suo imposita, cui ex ejus imperio conformare se teneatur?
units.tr: V. Fourth, we should understand that when we speak of the obligation of conscience, that obligation does not signify some condition (for conscience, properly speaking, cannot be compelled any more than the free will itself can).
