It signifies rather a command and the power of urging conscience (yet with the authority to which it is itself bound to obey) to do what belongs to its office; in exactly the same way as a Prince, who has legislative power (νομοθετικήν), obliges his subjects to observe the laws by enacting them. Just as, therefore, in the external court it is not the Law itself but the power of the Lawgiver that properly and formally obliges subjects to obey, yet the Law itself is truly said to oblige as well, though improperly and as it were materially or terminatively, because the obligation is made through it and toward it; so the Law is also said to judge [Does our law judge any man? John 7. 51.], although it does not itself judge, but the Praetor does, because the Praetor ought to judge according to the law*. So also in the internal court, what properly obliges conscience is not the rule or law imposed on it, but the power and authority of the one imposing it. Yet in consequence it can truly, and not inappropriately, though less properly, be said that the rule itself obliges. Therefore, when we ask what it is that obliges conscience to perform its duty, two things are asked: first and principally, who is the Lord of conscience, who has the right and power to impose on it the Law or Rule to which it ought to conform itself; and then secondarily and consequently, what is the Rule of conscience, as the law imposed on it by that Lord, to which by his command it is bound to conform itself?

units.la: VI. Scien
units.tr: VI. Scien

units.la: VI. Sciendum quintò, cum quicquid alteri attribuitur attribuatur vel per se, vel non per se ; idque iterùm dupliciter, vel non per se, i. e. per aliud, vel non per se, i. e. per accidens : res illas proinde, quibus vis obligandi Conscientiam quovis modo attribui posse videtur, esse in triplici discrimi-ne. Vel enim primò obligant Conscientiam per se simpliciter ; hoc est, directè ex se & vi propriâ obligant, non solùm ut τὸ per se opponitur τῷ per accidens, sed etiam ut opponitur τῷ per aliud. Vel secundò obligant per se respectivè, prout τὸ per se opponitur τῷ per accidens, sed non prout opponitur τῷ per aliud ; hoc est, obligant non ex vi suâ propriâ, sed virtute alicujus alterius vim obligandi habentis : Vel tertiò obligant per accidens tantum, & neutro modo per se. Quin & in illis quae secundo modo obligant, discrimen aliquod observandum est, pro diversâ ratione illius causae ex quâ oritur Obligatio. Aliter enim se res habet, cum ex alienâ authoritate necessariò inducitur obligatio : aliter, cum ex propriâ voluntate sponte contrahitur. Ex quibus omnibus efficitur, ut sint eorum quae obligant Conscientiam gradus omninò quatuor. Exempli gratiâ (ut & ea quae dicta sunt rectiùs intelligatis & eorum quae dicenda forent rudem quandam ἀναγεγραμμένως[?] ὡς ἐν τύπῳ habeatis ;) Obligat primò, per se & vi propriâ, expressum Dei mandatum : Obligant secundò, nullâ tamen vi suâ, sed virtute divina praecepti, Leges humanae & mandata Superiorum : Obligant tertiò, ex liberâ cujusque electione & facto proprio, cum ei integrum ante esset aliter fecisse, sponte suscepta Vota : quartò denique, & ex accidente, obligat Lex sive ratio Scandali.
units.tr: VI. It should be noted, fifthly, that whatever is attributed to another is attributed either per se or not per se, and that this again happens in two ways: either not per se, that is through another, or not per se, that is by accident. So the things to which the power of binding the conscience may seem to be attributed in any way fall into a threefold distinction. For they either bind the conscience primarily, per se simpliciter; that is, they bind directly, of themselves and by their own power, not only as τὸ per se is opposed to τῷ per accidens, but also as it is opposed to τῷ per aliud. Or they bind secondarily per se respectively, in so far as τὸ per se is opposed to τῷ per accidens, but not in so far as it is opposed to τῷ per aliud; that is, they bind not by their own power but by the virtue of some other thing that has the power of binding. Or they bind thirdly by accident only, and in neither way per se. Moreover, among those which bind in the second way, a distinction must be observed according to the different nature of the cause from which the obligation arises. For the case is one thing when an obligation is necessarily induced by another's authority, and another when it is freely contracted by one's own will. From all of this it follows that there are altogether four degrees of things that bind the conscience. For example (so that you may understand what has been said more correctly, and have a rough outline, as it were in a sketch [ἀναγεγραμμένως ὡς ἐν τύπῳ], of what is yet to be said): the express command of God binds first, per se and by its own power; human laws and the commands of superiors bind secondly, not by any power of their own but by the virtue of the divine precept; vows, freely undertaken, bind thirdly, from each person's free choice and own deed, since it was previously open to him to have acted otherwise; and fourthly, and by accident, the law or reason of scandal binds.

units.la: VII. Sciendum ultimò, Obligationem illam duntaxat quae est in primo gradu esse absolutam & universalem ; reliquas tres relativas & particulares.
units.tr: VII. It should be noted, lastly, that only that obligation which is in the first degree is absolute and universal; the remaining three are relative and particular.

units.la: Illa absoluta est, qui directè obligat, & semper, & universos: & est ejus vinculum planè insolubile. Reliquæ relativæ dici possunt, tam quia non ex se & vi propria obligant, sed per relationem ad præceptum aliquod aut institutum Dei ; tùm quia non semper, ubique, & in omni casu obligant, sed quando rationes illæ, quas respicere debent, exigere videntur. Præjudicat ergo primi gradus Obligatio cuivis obligationi in aliis quibuscunque gradibus : ita ut ipsa reliquas irritas faciat, non autem ipsam illæ. Imò universim Obligatio in Superiore quoquo gradu validior est, cæteris paribus, obligatione in gradu quocunque inferiore, atque ei præjudicat : vel tollendo jam contractam, ut plerumque : vel saltem, idque perpetuò, impediendo contrahendam. Cedant ergo oportet quantum ad obligandi vim leges humanæ divinis, privatæ pactiones & promissiones Constitutionibus publicis, hiface demum omnibus Scandali Lex.
units.tr: The absolute obligation is that which binds directly, and always, and all people; and its bond is wholly insoluble. The others may be called relative, both because they do not bind of themselves and by their own power, but through a relation to some precept or institution of God, and because they do not bind always, everywhere, and in every case, but when those reasons which they ought to regard seem to require it. The obligation of the first degree therefore takes precedence over any obligation in any of the other degrees, so that it makes the others void, and they do not make it void. Indeed, in general, an obligation in a superior degree is, other things being equal, stronger than an obligation in any inferior degree, and takes precedence over it: either by removing an obligation already contracted, as is usually the case, or at least, and perpetually, by preventing one from being contracted. Human laws must therefore yield to divine laws in their power to bind, private agreements and promises to public constitutions, and, finally, all of these to the law of scandal.

units.la: VIII. His ita præmissis, ut certa nobis constet vivendi Lex, ea quæ de Conscientiæ Regulâ & ejus Obligatione passivâ sunt maximè scitu necessaria, quibusdam Conclusionibus, prout pollicitus sum, complectar. CONCLUSIO PRIMA. Deus solus merum & directum habet imperium in Conscientias hominum. Ita ut extra Deum potestatem habeat legem imponendi Conscientiæ cujusquam hominis, cui ut per se obligatoriæ subjicere sese debeat. Dico per se, quia obligamur omnes in conscientiis justas leges humanas observare, fidem Deo vel hominibus datam præstare, ne simus aliis scandalo cavere : sed ad ista omnia non aliunde obligamur, nisi in quantum ad Dei voluntatem ista omnia imperantis revocantur ; ut de singulis suo loco videbitur.
units.tr: VIII. With these things thus set out, so that we may have a certain rule of living, I shall, as I promised, deal with the matters most necessary to know concerning the rule of conscience and its passive obligation under certain conclusions. FIRST CONCLUSION: God alone has pure and direct authority over the consciences of men. So that outside God no one has the power to impose a law on the conscience of any man to which that conscience must submit itself as binding in itself. I say in itself, because we are all obliged to observe in our consciences just human laws, to keep faith given to God or to men, and to avoid giving scandal to others; but we are not bound to all these things from any other source, except insofar as they are referred to the will of God who commands all of them; as will be seen in its place for each of them.

units.la: IX. Probatur hæc Conclusio : Primò, ex verbis illis Apostoli jam propositis, Unus enim est legislator, qui potest seruare & perdere. Ubi duo se offerunt in rem nostram argumenta. Primo enim Deum asserit esse unum Legislatorem: non unum è multis, vel præ cæteris unum; sed exclusive unum, hoc est, unicum. Alias argumento usus esset Apostolus ad probandum quod volebat parum efficaci. Reprehendit nimirum eos, qui de personis aut factis alienis temerè ferebant judicium, ut juris alieni invasores. Quis tu, inquit, qui alium judicas? Quasi diceret, Noris te qui sis, & quas res agas. Non est tuum falcem tuam in alienam messem immittere; multò autem minùs in omnipotentis Dei solium temet audacter ingerere. Si nescis, illius unius est de conscientiis hominum judicium ferre, cujus unius est ipsorum conscientiis Leges imponere, is autem præter unum Deum nullus est. εἷς ἔζιν ὁ νομοθέτης[?] Deinde soli Deo potestatem asserit servandi & perdendi: Unde secundum extruitur argumentum. Is solus jus habet conscientiis aliquid imperandi aut prohibendi, qui potestatem habet conscientiam imperata facientem gratuitis præmiis, detrectantem justis suppliciis afficere: At penes unum legislatorem Deum est hominibus præmia & pœnas pro conscientiæ cujusque qualitate retribuere: Ipsi ergo soli jus est in hominum conscientias.
units.tr: IX. This conclusion is proved: first, from those words of the Apostle already cited, For there is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. Here two arguments present themselves for our purpose. For first he asserts that God is one Lawgiver: not one among many, or one above the rest, but exclusively one, that is, unique. Otherwise the Apostle would have used an argument of little force for what he wished to prove. He rebukes, of course, those who rashly passed judgment on the persons or deeds of others, like invaders of another's right. Who are you, he says, who judge another? As if he were saying: know who you are and what business you are about. It is not yours to thrust your sickle into another's harvest; still less should you boldly intrude yourself into the throne of almighty God. If you do not know it, the judgment of men's consciences belongs to that one alone whose alone it is to impose laws upon their consciences; and he is no one but the one God. There is one lawgiver [εἷς ἔστιν ὁ νομοθέτης]. Secondly, he asserts that the power of saving and destroying belongs to God alone; hence the second argument is built. He alone has the right to command or forbid anything to consciences, who has the power to reward with free rewards those who obey what is commanded, and to punish with just penalties those who refuse. But it is in the power of the one lawgiver, God, to repay men with rewards and punishments according to the quality of each one's conscience. Therefore the right over men's consciences belongs to him alone.

units.la: X. Probatur Secundo. Qui solus novit internos Conscientiæ motus, solus potestatem habet Legem illis præstituendi; quia Lex de ignotis nec statuit nec judicat: at soli Deo καρδιογνώστῃ[?] cogniti sunt interni cordium & conscientiarum motus; ergo penes ipsum solum potestas est Legem Conscientiis imponendi, quæ ipsas obliget. Hinc est quòd Leges humanæ externos tantùm corporum motus obligant ad externam conformitatem; à quorum imperio & cognitione interna interim cogitationes,omnésque mentium & conscientiarum motus prorsus immunes sunt. Adeò ut non tantùm viri Sancti & veri Dei cognitione imbuti quales fuere tresviri illi apud Babylonios captivi, Dan. 3. & Maccabæi fratres septem ; sed & Ethnicorum sapientes plurimi tyrannorum minas & tormenta riserint, ut qui non ipsos, sed in ipsorum ψυχὰς[?] tantùm & [illegible, ~7 letters] sævierint. Quin audiamus quid Servator noster Christus hac in re & ipse senserit, & suis præceperit, Nolite, inquit, timere eos, qui cùm interemerint corpus, non habent quod amplius faciant : sed metuite eum, qui potestatem habet ubi occiderit, & in infernum conjiciendi, Luc. 12. 3, 4.
units.tr: X. It is proved secondly. He who alone knows the inward motions of conscience alone has the power to prescribe a law for them; for law neither decrees nor judges concerning things unknown. But the inward motions of hearts and consciences are known to God alone, the searcher of hearts [καρδιογνώστης]; therefore the power of imposing on consciences a law that binds them rests with him alone. Hence it is that human laws bind only the outward motions of bodies to outward conformity; from whose command and knowledge inward thoughts, and all the motions of minds and consciences, are wholly exempt. So that not only holy men imbued with the knowledge of the true God, such as those three men held captive among the Babylonians, Dan. 3., and the seven brothers of the Maccabees, but also many of the wise men of the Gentiles have laughed at the threats and tortures of tyrants, since the tyrants have raged not against them but only against their souls [ψυχάς] and [illegible]. Indeed, let us hear what our Saviour Christ himself thought in this matter and commanded his own: Do not fear those who, when they have killed the body, have nothing more that they can do; but fear him who has power, after he has killed, to cast into hell, Luke 12. 3, 4.

units.la: Quasi dixisset, Habent tyranni ex permissione Dei in corpora potestatem : at in Animas hominum & Conscientias nullam habent ἐξουσίαν[?], jus nullum. Non possunt aut Leges rogare, aut irrogare pœnas, quæ ad interiorem hominem pertineat. In totum hominem Dei unius jus est : qui potest negle&i officii non à Corpore solùm, sed & ab Animâ pœnas sumere, & totum hominem æternis suppliciis addicere.
units.tr: As if he had said: tyrants have by God's permission power over bodies; but over the souls of men and their consciences they have no authority [ἐξουσία] and no right. They cannot either make laws or inflict penalties that pertain to the inner man. The right over the whole man belongs to God alone, who can exact punishment for neglect of duty not only from the body but also from the soul, and consign the whole man to eternal punishments.

units.la: XI. Probatur tertiò, ex conditione ipsius Conscientiæ, & naturali ejus statu : quam jam ante diximus ita medio quodam inter Deum & hominis voluntatem intervallo positam ; ut quod de Regibus & Imperatoribus verè dici solitum est, de singulorum hominum Conscientiis non minùs vere dici possit, Solo Deo minores esse, nec aliquem interris Superiorem agnoscere. Memorabile est Maximiliani primi Imperatoris quod legimus dictum illud, Conscientiis dominari velle est arcem cæli invadere. Prædator est gloriæ Dei, & potestatis ei debitæ nefarius invasor, quisquis in conscientias hominum aut sibi jus arrogat, aut dominatum exercet. Viderint Romani Pontifices, quique illis aut Canoniste parasitantur, aut supparasitantur Jesuitæ, cæterique, ut se hujus tàm immanis sacrilegii crimine liberent. Quin & illos quoque, qui Conjcientias suas quæ soli Deo absolute subesse debent, ullius creaturæ potestati ita subjiciunt, ut ex illius arbitrio toti pendeant, cautos velim, ne dum servitutis honorem, qui Deo soli jure debetur, in creaturam conferunt, è creatura (quod interpretative saltem idolatria est) Deum faciant. Ex hac primâ Conclusione quam hactenus firmavimus, sequitur hoc mó-[illegible, ~4 letters], Regulam Conscientiæ propriam eam esse, quam ipsi Deus Supremus Legislator præstituerit, nec extra eam aliam admitti oportere.
units.tr: XI. It is proved thirdly, from the nature of conscience itself and its natural state: which we have already said is placed, as a kind of interval between God and the human will, in such a way that what is truly said of kings and emperors can be said no less truly of the consciences of individual men, namely that they are subject to God alone and acknowledge no superior on earth. Memorable is the saying of the Emperor Maximilian I, which we read: to wish to rule over consciences is to invade the citadel of heaven. Whoever either claims for himself a right over men's consciences, or exercises dominion over them, is a plunderer of the glory of God and a wicked invader of the power due to him. Let the Roman Pontiffs see to it, and those who either play the parasite to them as canonists, or the Jesuits who play the under-parasite, and the rest, that they may free themselves from the guilt of so monstrous a sacrilege. Indeed, I would have those also be cautious who so subject their consciences, which ought to be subject to God alone absolutely, to the power of any creature, that they wholly depend on its will; lest, while they transfer to a creature the honour of servitude, which is due to God alone by right, they make a god of the creature (which, at least by interpretation, is idolatry). From this first conclusion, which we have so far established, it follows that the rule of conscience is that which God the Supreme Lawgiver himself has prescribed, and that no other should be admitted beside it [illegible].

units.la: XII. Sequitur Conclusio Secunda. Conscientiæ Regula proxima & immediata (etsi nec adæquata, nec summa,) est Lumen mentis pro tempore præsens: Id quod alii Lumen rationis, alii Legem mentis, Scholastici ferè post Philosophos rectam Rationem appellare solent. Probatur hæc primò ex S. Scripturæ locis aliquot, Luc. 12. 57. Quare non ex vobismetipsis judicatis quod justum est? Inquit Servator Christus. Quasi diceret, est vobis internum lumen, à vera illa luce mentibus vestris inditum, quæ illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum; cujus ope, nisi vobis ipsis deesse velitis, poteritis Rectum dignoscere curvo, & iniquo secernere justum. Est & notissimus locus, Rom. 2. 14, 15. Cum gentes quæ Legem (Scriptam &c.) non habent, naturâ ea quæ sunt legis faciunt (i. e. exercent actus prudentiæ, justitiæ, fortitudinis, temperantiæ, & reliquarum virtutum,) ipsi legem non habentes sibi ipsis sunt Lex: Qui ostendunt opus Legis Scriptum in cordibus suis, testimonium perhibente conscientia suâ, & invicem se cogitationibus accusantibus vel etiam defendentibus. Ex quibus verbis manifestum est Conscientiam in illis suis actibus (Testificandi, Accusandi, Defendendi,) quos exercet circa jam facta, de illis omnibus ex impresso mentis Rationis lumine judicare. Unde consequitur, cum fit de præteritis & futuris eadem judicandi regula, Conscientia & in illis suis actibus qui circa facienda versantur, (Examinandi, Judicandi, Dijudandi, &c.) eodem illo lumine, ut eorundem actuum regulâ & mensurâ, uti. Illud Psal. 4. 6. quod à plerisque Latinorum Patrum, posterioris præsertim ævi, & à Scholasticis passim affertur in firmamentum hujus Conclusionis [Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine,] prudens omitto, cum nitatur illa verborum interpretatio versione non probâ, nec videatur ad mentem & scopum Prophetæ multùm pertinere.
units.tr: XII. It follows that the second conclusion is: the proximate and immediate rule of conscience (though not its adequate or highest rule) is the light of the mind present at the time. Some call this the light of reason, others the law of the mind, and the Schoolmen, following the Philosophers, usually call it right reason. This is proved first from several passages of Holy Scripture. Luke 12:57: "Why do you not judge of yourselves what is right?" says the Saviour Christ. It is as if he said: you have an inner light, placed in your minds by that true light which enlightens every man coming into this world. By its help, unless you wish to fail yourselves, you will be able to distinguish the right from the crooked and to separate the just from the unjust. There is also the well-known passage, Rom. 2:14, 15: "When the Gentiles, who do not have the Law" (written, etc.) "do by nature the things of the Law" (that is, they exercise the acts of prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, and the other virtues), "they, not having the Law, are a law to themselves; they show the work of the Law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness" and their thoughts accusing or even defending one another. From these words it is plain that conscience, in those acts of its own (of witnessing, accusing, defending) which it exercises on things already done, judges all those things by the light of reason impressed on the mind. From this it follows that, since past and future actions are judged by the same rule, conscience also, in those acts of its own which concern things to be done (of examining, judging, deciding, etc.), uses that same light as the rule and measure of those acts. I deliberately pass over the text Psalm 4:6, which most of the Latin Fathers, especially those of a later age, and the Schoolmen everywhere cite in support of this conclusion: "The light of your countenance is signed upon us, O Lord." That interpretation of the words rests on an unsound version, and it does not seem to have much to do with the mind and purpose of the Prophet.

units.la: XIII. Probatur secundò, ex communi more loquendi.
units.tr: XIII. It is proved secondly from common usage of speech.

units.la: Solemus enim dicere, eum qui secundum lumen mentis suæ operatus est, bonâ usum Conscientiâ; etsi fortassis id fecerit vel omiserit, quod non fuit ab eo faciendum vel omittendum: eum è contra, qui dictamini mentis suæ non auscultaverit, sed contra fecerit, malâ conscientiâ rem egisse. Paulus Apostolus. Act. 23. 1. profitetur se omni bonâ Conscientiâ Deo servijsse usque ad illum diem. Quæ verba, si & ad anteriorem vitæ partem, cum nondum factus esset Christianus, extendenda sint, (quod multis placuisse video, & mihi quidem videtur valdè probabile:) Statuendum est eum, etsi Christiano nomini & fidei infensissimum hostem. &, ut ipse fatetur, persecutorem adhuc & blasphemum, dici tamen potuisse etiam tum omni bonâ conscientiâ quod omni illo tempore nihil fecerit, nisi quod Conscientiâ ipsius pro mensurâ luminis quod tunc habuit, faciendum sibi dictaverat. Revera enim existimabat, ut ipse, in alterâ suâ apud Regem Agrippam apologiâ palam & sincerè profitetur [ἐδόκουν ἐμαυτῷ] oportere se adversus nomen Jesu Nazareni multa contraria facere, Act. 26. 9. Sed quicquid de Paulo ejusque tunc temporis Conscientiâ statuendum sit, illud interim certum
units.tr: For we are accustomed to say that a person who has acted according to the light of his mind has used a good conscience, even if he has perhaps done or omitted something that he ought not to have done or omitted. On the contrary, we say that someone who has not listened to the dictate of his mind but has acted against it has acted with an evil conscience. The Apostle Paul, in Acts 23:1, professes that he has served God in all good conscience until that day. If these words are to be extended also to the earlier part of his life, when he was not yet a Christian (which I see has pleased many, and which seems to me highly probable), we must hold that, although he was then a most bitter enemy of the Christian name and of the faith, and, as he himself confesses, still a persecutor and a blasphemer, he could nevertheless be said even then to have acted in all good conscience, because throughout that whole time he did nothing except what his conscience, according to the measure of light he then had, had dictated to him as needing to be done. For, as he himself openly and sincerely declares in his other defence before King Agrippa, he thought [ἐδόκουν ἐμαυτῷ] that he ought to do many things contrary to the name of Jesus of Nazareth (Acts 26:9). But whatever should be decided about Paul and his conscience at that time, this much is certain:

units.la: ΠΡΟΛΙΠΟΝΤΕΣ ... (Greek marginal note, as printed) certum est, Deum ipsum testimonium perhibuisse {1}Abimeleco, quæ Abrahæ uxorem ignarus rei in contubernium suum accersiverat, id ab eo in integritate cordis sui, (id est, bonâ conscientiâ) factum fuisse: non alia sanè ratione, quàm eâ quâ se excusabat {2}Abimelecus, quòd scilicet si eam scisset fuisse maritam, non eam effet in ædes suas deducturus. Potest ergo Conscientia, ex ignorantiâ non culpabili, (fortean & aliunde) erronea, vel Deo judice dici (non quidem simpliciter & absolute, sed tamen quadantenùs & secundum quid) bona & recta, propter conformitatem quam habet cum lumine mentis suæ, ut regula sua proxima & immediata. Sed ut ὁλοχληρως[?] & usquequaque Recta dicatur, huic Conformitati accedat oportet altera & ulterior, ut nimirum conformis sit Regulæ suæ primæ & supremæ. Quænam autem sit illa, aliquantò propiùs inquirendum est.
units.tr: certain is it that God himself bore witness to Abimelech, who had unknowingly taken Abraham's wife into his household, that he had done this in the integrity of his heart (that is, with a good conscience). This was surely for no other reason than the one on which Abimelech himself excused himself, namely that, had he known she was a married woman, he would not have brought her into his house. Conscience, therefore, arising from inculpable ignorance (and perhaps also from some other source), can be called erroneous, yet before God as judge it can be called (not indeed simply and absolutely, but still in some measure and in a certain respect) good and right, on account of the conformity it has with the light of its mind, as its proximate and immediate rule. But for it to be called wholly and in every respect right, another and further conformity must be added, namely that it be conformed to its first and supreme rule. What that rule is, however, must be inquired into somewhat more closely.

units.la: XIV. Esto itaque hæc Conclusio tertia. Sacra Scriptura, sive verbum Dei Scriptum, non est Conscientiæ Regula adæquata. Probatur primo, Extra cujuscunque rei regulam adæquatam, non est necessarium ut sit ejusdem rei regula aliqua alia: adæquatio enim excludit necessitatem alicujus supplementi: Sed extra sacram Scripturam necesse est ut sit alia Conscientiæ Regula. Alias Gentes quæ non habent Scripturam, nullam haberent conscientiæ suæ regulam: quod rationi, experientiæ, & Apostoli {3}loco paulò ante citato, aperto testimonio vel maximè adversatur. Inesse omnibus hominibus conscientiam, eámque alicui legi subesse, quæ ipsam ut norma dirigat, res ipsa clamat. Unde enim illæ quarum meminit Apostolus, extantque in historiis & in vitâ communi plurima passim exempla, graves illæ conscientiæ accusationes: eásque consecutæ animorum ægritudines, flagella, cruciatus, tormenta, illæ Tragicorum Furiæ & Ἐρινύες[?]: nisi ex violatâ Conscientiæ lege? Quæ si nulla essent eò feliciores barbarissimi quique populi, quantò ab Evangelii voce & sonitu remotiores; utpote quibus nulla posset justè imputari peccati culpa. Ubi enim non est Lex, nec transgressio esse potest, Rom. 14. 15. quum sit Peccatum nihil aliud quàm Legis transgressio, ἡ γὰρ ἁμαρτία ἡ ἀνομία [?], 1 Joh. 3. 4. Magnam esse Conscientiæ vim in utramque partem, ut & nihil metuat, qui nullius sibi culpæ conscius est, & nihil non metuat, quem exagitant scelerum suorum conscientia; Veterum Ethnicorum non Scholæ tantùm personant, sed & Rostra & Theatra: qui tamen nihil de Mose, nihil de Christo, nihil de Lege & Prophetis, nihil de Evangelio & Apostolis, unquam inaudiverant. Ergo non nisi Scriptura sola & adæquata Conscientiæ Regula.
units.tr: XIV. Let this therefore be the third conclusion: Holy Scripture, or the written Word of God, is not the adequate rule of conscience. It is proved first: where there is an adequate rule of any matter, there is no necessity that there be some other rule of the same matter, for adequacy excludes the need of any supplement. But outside Holy Scripture there must necessarily be another rule of conscience. Otherwise the Gentiles, who do not have Scripture, would have no rule for their conscience, which is directly opposed to reason, to experience, and to the clear testimony of the Apostle in the passage cited a little above. That all men have conscience, and that it is subject to some law which directs it as its norm, the thing itself cries out. For whence come those grave accusations of conscience of which the Apostle speaks, and of which there are very many examples everywhere in histories and in ordinary life, and the sicknesses of soul, scourges, torments, and tortures that follow them, and those Furies of the tragic poets [Ἐρινύες]? Unless they come from a violated law of conscience? If there were no such law, the most barbarous peoples would be the happiest, the further they are from the voice and sound of the Gospel, since no guilt of sin could justly be imputed to them. For where there is no law, there can be no transgression (Rom. 4:15), since sin is nothing other than the transgression of the law [ἡ γὰρ ἁμαρτία ἡ ἀνομία], 1 John 3:4. That conscience has great power in both directions, so that he who is conscious of no guilt fears nothing, and he whom the consciousness of his own crimes torments fears everything, is proclaimed not only by the schools of the ancient Heathens, but also by their rostra and theatres; yet these men had never heard anything about Moses, nothing about Christ, nothing about the Law and the Prophets, nothing about the Gospel and the Apostles. Therefore Scripture alone is not the adequate rule of conscience.

units.la: XV. Probatur secundò, à proprio Sacræ Scripturæ fine, qui est σοφίσαι εἰς σωτηρίαν [?], 2 Tim. 3. 15. Sapientes nos reddere ad salutem æternam per fidem quæ est in Christo Jesu. Cùm enim non posset lumen naturalis Rationis ad ea quæ nos perducant ad finem supernaturalem sufficienter pertinere, cùm propter obscuratum nimis ex Adæ lapsu naturale illud lumen, tùm etiam quia ad finem supernaturalem, opus est mediis supernaturalibus: placuit Deo, imbecillitatis nostræ habitâ ratione, voluntatem suam pro eâ quâ ipsi visum est mensuram hominibus in verbo suo patefacere. Gratioso admodùm, & nobis salutari consilio; ut non solùm quæ propriè sunt fidei, nec possunt lumine naturali cognosci, nobis nota fierent per revelationem divinam; sed & in iis quæ natura nobis cognita sunt perfectiùs & salutariùs instrueremur: qui nimirum ea ipsa opera, quæ natura dictat esse utcunque facienda, ex nobiliori principio orta Dei amore, & ad nobiliores fines ordinata Dei gloriam & animarum nostrarum salutem, è mortalibus Spiritualibus sierent, Deóque per Christum grata & accepta. Est ergo Scriptura, quoad supernaturaliter credenda, sola & adæquata Fidei Regula: éstque eadem quoad agenda etiam, quatenus sunt Spiritualia & ad finem supernaturalem ordinata, sola & adæquata Morum Regula; atque ita ex consequenti, agendorum Regula principalis, & ut ita dicam, Architectonica. Sed cum ad Conscientiam spectat circa res agendas inquirere, non eâ duntaxat ratione quâ sunt Spirituales, an fiant ex charitate, & in finem supernaturalem dirigantur; sed eâ etiam quâ Morales sunt, suntne bona vel mala, licita vel illicita, libera vel necessaria: ut de his rebus rite judicetur, non ex sola Scriptura, sed & aliunde etiam petenda sunt opportuna adjumenta.
units.tr: XV. It is proved secondly from the proper end of Holy Scripture, which is to make us wise unto salvation [σοφίσαι εἰς σωτηρίαν], 2 Tim. 3:15, that is, to make us wise unto eternal salvation through the faith that is in Christ Jesus. For since the light of natural reason could not sufficiently lead us to the supernatural end, partly because that natural light had been too greatly obscured by Adam's fall, and partly because the supernatural end requires supernatural means, God, having regard to our weakness, was pleased to reveal his will to men in his word, to the measure that seemed good to him. This was a most gracious counsel, and salutary for us, so that not only those things that are strictly of faith, and cannot be known by natural light, might be made known to us by divine revelation, but we might also be more perfectly and more profitably instructed in those things that are known to us by nature: namely, that those very works which nature dictates ought in some way to be done might, arising from a nobler principle (the love of God) and ordered to nobler ends (the glory of God and the salvation of our souls), become spiritual works rather than merely mortal ones, and be acceptable and pleasing to God through Christ. Scripture is therefore, as regards what is to be believed supernaturally, the sole and adequate rule of faith; and it is the same, as regards what is to be done too, insofar as those things are spiritual and ordered to the supernatural end, the sole and adequate rule of morals; and so, by consequence, the principal rule of things to be done, and, so to speak, architectonic. But since it belongs to conscience, with regard to things to be done, to inquire not only in the respect in which they are spiritual (whether they are done out of charity and directed to the supernatural end), but also in the respect in which they are moral (whether they are good or evil, lawful or unlawful, free or necessary), then, in order that such matters may be rightly judged, appropriate aids must be sought not from Scripture alone, but also from elsewhere.

units.la: XVI. Probatur tertiò, ex ipsius Scripturæ formâ, charactere, temperamento. Quæ cum pluima continet non unius generis praecepta, quarum alia ad Mores pertinent, alia ad Ritus; alia omnibus ex æquo communia, alia certo alicui populo, ordini aut personæ peculiaria; quædam ad tempus aliquod duratura, alia perpetuæ obligationis; quædam ἢ γνωμικῶν vel κατὰ συγγνωμικὸν [?], & quasi per modum consilii de rebus aut plerunque expedientibus, aut pro certo rerum statu & conditione temporum, quædam κατ' ἐπιταγὴν, & quasi per modum mandati, de rebus simpliciter & ubique necessariis: si non esset alia aliqua regula extra Scripturam discernendi moralia præcepta à ritualibus, temporaria à perpetuis, singularia à communibus, omninò in incerto hæreret sæpissimè Conscientia, quo se verteret nescia; præsertim cum diversi generis præcepta eodem quasi halitu prolata, eodem sermonis tenore, & verborum continuo nexu, immediatè invicem se consequuntur. Exempli gratia, Levit. 19. 18. præceptum est de diligendo proximo sicut seipsum; Versibus immediatè sequentibus præcipitur ne duorum generum jumenta coire sinantur, ne ager diversi generis feminibus feratur, ne vestis è lini lanaque textura conficiatur. Quorum illud morale & universale præceptum esse, ista (sive Ceremonialia sive Judicialia) uni Judaico populo peculiaria, nemo est qui dubitat. Sed cum hæc leguntur in Ecclesiis, quòd sit inter ea aliquod ejusmodi discrimen, non potest ex aliquo ipsius textus indicio constare. Ejusdem etiam capitis vers. 3c. Sabbati (sanctificatio, & Sanctuarii reverentia, continuâ verborum serie pariformiter præcipiuntur, idque eadem solenni juris Sanctione, Ego Jehovah: esse tamen non dubito qui putent, altero præcepto Conscientias hominum etiamnum teneri, altero non teneri. Cur tamen sic putent, cum sit in ipso Textu ubi omnia sunt pa-ria tam lati discriminis nec vola nec vestigium, non aliunde certè est, quam ex rationis & prudentia judicio: quo seclusò non possunt obligatoria præcepta à non obligatoriis sic dignosci, ut non fluctuet sæpenumerò Conscientia, nec certò sciat quid sibi faciendum sit, quid non faciendum, judicare.
units.tr: XVI. A third proof comes from the very form, character and temperament of Scripture. It contains very many precepts of different kinds. Some concern morals, others rites. Some are common to all alike, others peculiar to a certain people, order or person. Some are to last for a certain time, others are of perpetual obligation. Some are gnomic [γνωμικῶν] or given by way of indulgence [κατὰ συγγνωμικόν], offered as it were as counsel, about things that are for the most part expedient or suited to a certain state of affairs and the conditions of the times. Others are given by injunction [κατ' ἐπιταγήν], as it were by way of command, about things that are simply and everywhere necessary. If there were no other rule outside Scripture for distinguishing moral precepts from ritual ones, temporary from perpetual, and particular from common, conscience would very often hang in uncertainty and not know where to turn. This is especially so since precepts of different kinds, uttered as it were with one breath, in one tenor of speech and in an unbroken connection of words, immediately follow one another. For example, Lev. 19.18 commands that one love one's neighbour as oneself. In the verses immediately following, it is ordered that animals of two kinds not be allowed to mate, that a field not be sown with seeds of different kinds, and that a garment not be made of a weave of linen and wool. That the first is a moral and universal precept, and these others (whether ceremonial or judicial) peculiar to the Jewish people alone, no one doubts. But when these are read in the churches, it cannot be established from any indication in the text itself that there is any such distinction among them. Likewise in the same chapter, verse 3, the keeping of the Sabbath and reverence for the sanctuary are commanded in the same way, in a continuous series of words, and with the same solemn sanction of law, "I am Jehovah." Yet I do not doubt that there are some who think that men's consciences are still bound by the one precept but not by the other. But why they think so, when in the text itself, where all things are alike, there is no sign or trace of so great a distinction, is certainly from nowhere else than the judgment of reason and prudence. Apart from that, binding precepts cannot be distinguished from non-binding ones in such a way that conscience does not waver very often and never surely know what it is to do or not to do.

units.la: XVII. Probatur quartò, ex incommodis diversæ sententiæ; nimirum gravissimis illis malis, quibus Ecclesiam Christianam jamdiu exercuerunt, potius quam ex malè intellectâ de Sacra Scriptura perse-ctione doctrinâ, obtinuit apud aliquot magni no-minis viros periculosissimus error, nihil licitè fieri posse nedum præcipi, quod non esset à Deo in Scriptura aut præceptum, aut laudabili saltem exemplo comprobatum. Hoc semel jacto fundamento, coepere mox præfervidi ingenii viri non pauci, Zelo Dei (ut ex charitatis judicio credere par est) sed non secundum scientiam abrepti de ritibus Ecclesiasticis rixas & turbas ciere non necessarias. Scilicet eliminandas ex Ecclesiis Christi & abigendas procul Ceremonias in sacris literis non præscriptas; Leges de rebus Adiaphoris ab hominibus latas refigendas; reformandas per orbem Ecclesias; & ad Evangelicam puritatem & simplicitatem omnia revocanda. Stetit hîc aliquandiu, sed non diu hîc stetit effrænis hominum temeritas: sed, ut fieri amat, ἔρις δ᾽ [?]ἔτ᾽ ἄλλα συμβαίνει. Hoc fonte derivata audacia, effluxit tandem in apertam rabiem, & exivit jamdiu in furorem Anabaptisticum. Et quamvis quò porrò progrediatur vix habeat; usque tamen progreditur indies, & novas quotidie parturit opinionum monstra: ut nisi ex sacrosancto Dei verbo didicissemus firmum stare fundamentum Dei, neque adversus Ecclesiam Christi prævalituras unquam ex toto inferorum portas; omninò metuendum foret, ne universa Christi Ecclesia Atheismi velut diluvio obruta, toto orbe funditus periret.
units.tr: XVII. A fourth proof comes from the inconveniences of the opposing view, namely those most grievous evils with which they have long afflicted the Christian Church. Rather than from a badly understood doctrine of the perfection of Holy Scripture, a most dangerous error has prevailed among some men of great name: that nothing may lawfully be done, let alone commanded, unless it has been either commanded by God in Scripture or at least approved by a praiseworthy example. Once this foundation was laid, not a few men of over-heated wit, carried away by zeal for God (as charity must believe) but not according to knowledge, began to stir up quarrels and unnecessary tumults about ecclesiastical rites. Namely, they began to demand that ceremonies not prescribed in the sacred letters be removed and driven far from the churches of Christ; that laws concerning things indifferent, enacted by men, be torn up; that the churches throughout the world be reformed; and that everything be recalled to evangelical purity and simplicity. Here they stood for a while, but unbridled human rashness did not stand here for long; rather, as it loves to happen, "strife brings forth other things" [ἔρις δ᾽ ἔτ᾽ ἄλλα συμβαίνει]. Audacity derived from this source at last flowed out into open frenzy and has long since gone out into Anabaptist fury. And although it hardly has any limit to how far it will proceed, it proceeds day by day and gives birth every day to new monsters of opinion. Had we not learned from the most holy word of God that the firm foundation of God stands, and that the gates of hell will never prevail against the Church of Christ, it would have to be feared without any doubt that the whole Church of Christ, overwhelmed as by a flood of atheism, would perish utterly throughout the world.

units.la: XVIII. Neque verò existimet quis, ista me declamatorio more invidiosius conqueri, quàm pro rei ipsius merito. Id enim mihi persuasissimum est, qui hunc errorem penitus imbiberit, importunis Anabaptistarum, Socinianorum, aliorúmque quos nominare non libet apud nos Sectariorum argumentis, in plerisque earum quæ nunc dierum agitantur controversiis, nullo modo posse satisfacere. Nam, ut certam Ecclesiastici regiminis formam prætæam[?], quam heri nati Politico-Theologi nostri non aliunde quàm ex hoc ipsissimo fundamento quòd eam è Scripturis nusquam constare putent, aut penitus sublatam volunt, aut (quod parum abest) ad civilem Magistratum delatam ; Diei Dominicæ observationem, Ministrorum Evangelii missionem, Baptismum Infantium, aquæ in baptismo pro totius corporis immersione inspersionem, Sacramentalem gratiam, aliaque permulta quæ depromptus è Socini pharetra telis strenuè oppugnant moderni Sectarii ; aut ex Ecclesiâ unâ cum ritibus & legibus Ecclesiasticis exterminanda esse, ex suo illo principio concedant necesse est ; aut mutata in melius sententiâ, unâ cum illis & ista etiam sine peccato retineri posse fateantur.
units.tr: XVIII. Let no one think that I complain of these things in a declamatory manner, more bitterly than the real merit of the matter deserves. For I am thoroughly persuaded that whoever has been steeped in this error will in no way be able to satisfy, in most of the controversies now being debated, the importunate arguments of the Anabaptists, the Socinians, and the other sectaries among us whom it does not please me to name. For, as to a fixed form of ecclesiastical government, which our newly hatched Politico-Theologians, thinking it is nowhere established from the Scriptures, want either wholly abolished or (which is little short of that) transferred to the civil magistrate; as to the observance of the Lord's Day, the sending of ministers of the Gospel, infant baptism, the sprinkling of water in baptism instead of the immersion of the whole body, sacramental grace, and very many other things which the modern sectaries, drawing their weapons from the quiver of Socinus, vigorously assail: they must concede, from that principle of theirs, that either these must be banished from the Church together with ecclesiastical rites and laws, or, if they change their opinion for the better, they must admit that these too may be retained without sin together with those others.

units.la: XIX. Atqui hoc est, inquietis, Scripturæ persectioni (quam libenter agnoscunt omnes Reformatorum Ecclesiarum Theologi) derogare, Pontificiorum Traditionibus januam aperire, & argumentis à Scripturâ negativè ductis, quibus usi frequenter & prisca Ecclesiæ Patres, & utuntur etiam horum temporum doctissimi quique Theologi, vim omnem adimere.
units.tr: XIX. But this, you say, is to detract from the perfection of Scripture (which all theologians of the Reformed Churches gladly acknowledge), to open the door to the traditions of the Papists, and to take away all force from arguments drawn negatively from Scripture, which the ancient Fathers of the Church frequently used, and which the most learned theologians of our own time also use.

units.la: Respondeo, Pontificios perfectioni Scripturæ in eo derogare, quòd in Fidei dogmatibus, & rebus ad salutem necessariis Traditiones obtrudant non Scriptas, cum scripto Dei verbo pari veneratione recipiendas : qualis non ex se valeret [?]ἀρκεῖ εἰς σωτηρίαν, & conferre Filiis Dei paternam hæreditatem Christi Testamentum, sine affixis humanarum Traditionum codicillis. Eos autem qui à Scripturis negativè disputant, de rebus ad salutem necessariò credendis aut agendis intelligendos esse, siquidem uti debent, eo utantur argumento.
units.tr: I answer: the Papists detract from the perfection of Scripture in that they thrust upon us, in the doctrines of faith and in matters necessary to salvation, unwritten traditions to be received with the same reverence as the written word of God. Such a thing would not of itself be sufficient for salvation [ἀρκεῖ εἰς σωτηρίαν], nor could it convey to the sons of God the paternal inheritance of Christ's Testament without the appended codicils of human traditions. But those who argue negatively from Scripture must be understood to speak of things necessary to be believed or done for salvation; and if they must use an argument, let them use this one.

units.la: Cæterum nunc non de Fidei regulâ quæritur, sed Conscientiæ : nec de ejus Regulâ præcipuâ, sed adæquata : nec quid homini Christiano sit necessarium credendum vel agendum ad consequendam animæ salutem, sed quid à viro pio & prudente licitè fieri possit vel non pro hic & nunc. Summa est, Scripturam sacram esse fidei & supernaturaliter credendorum, actionum item moralium, quâ ex parte Spirituales sunt & ad finem supernaturalem ordinantur, adæquatam regulam ; esse etiam Conscientiæ legem & agendorum moralium regulam præcipuam & supremam, ita ut ubi Scriptura de re quavis aliquid in universum statuit præcipiendo prohibendove, non fas sit alteri cuicunque Legi ex adverso inter-cedere :
units.tr: Moreover, what is now sought is not the rule of faith but of conscience; and not its principal rule but its adequate rule; and not what a Christian man must believe or do in order to obtain the salvation of his soul, but what may lawfully be done, or not, by a pious and prudent man here and now. The sum is this: that Holy Scripture is the adequate rule of what is to be believed by faith and supernaturally, and likewise of moral actions, insofar as these are spiritual and ordered to a supernatural end; and that it is also the principal and supreme law of conscience and rule of moral actions, so that wherever Scripture lays down anything about any matter whatever, by commanding or forbidding, it is not right for any other law to interpose against it.

units.la: † cedere : non esse tamen ita Conscientiæ Legem unicam, ut quod non est ibi præceptum continuò illicitum sit, quia non est præceptum. Et hactenus de tertia Conclusione.
units.tr: It does not follow, however, that Scripture is the sole law of conscience, so that whatever is not commanded there is at once unlawful merely because it is not commanded. And so far concerning the third conclusion.

units.la: XX. Sequitur Quarta, Propria & adæquata Conscientiæ Regula Dei voluntas est, qualitercunque hominibus revelata. Hanc alii Legem Dei, alii Legem æternam dicunt; vocabulis pro suo cujusque arbitrio, sed eodem sensu. Hujus Conclusionis singulæ particulæ expendendæ sunt. Dico primò, Voluntas Dei. Cujus Voluntatis, notissima est illa distinctio, (quam tamen à Scriptoribus aliquoties animadverti aut non rectè explicari, aut non ritè applicari,) in Voluntatem Beneplaciti, & Voluntatem Signi. Prior illa, quam Beneplaciti vocant, ea est, quâ Deus ab æterno apud se constituit quid ipse velit facere: Altera quam Signi appellant, ea est, quâ Deus ab æterno apud se constituit quid velit à nobis fieri. Quarum illa propriè & univocè Voluntas Dei est; hæc improprie & ἀναλόγως [?], sic dicta. Voluntas illa Beneplaciti est ipsi quidem Deo (si de tantâ Majestate κατ' ἄνθρωπον [?] loqui fas sit,) quodammodo agendi Lex; semper enim ille facit quod ipsi complacitum est: sed non est à Deo nobis in Legem data, ut sit Conscientiæ nostræ Regula, saltem quod ad res agendas attinet. Pertinet illa quidem aliquo modo ad Conscientiam respectu perpessionum: à posteriori scilicet, & hoc sensu, quòd obligamur in Conscientiâ quodcunque contigerit, id omne {1}æquo animo ferre, postquam nobis ex eventu constiterit id Deum voluisse; quia hoc dictat rectâ ratio, non debere nobis divinæ providentiæ ordinem displicere, qui nil velle potest nisi quod est rectissimum. Reliquum est ergo, ut sit Conscientiæ nostræ regula Voluntas illa quæ Signi dicitur. Cum enim Deus præcipiendo & prohibendo, quid à nobis fieri velit & non fieri, sig-
units.tr: XX. There follows the fourth conclusion: The proper and adequate rule of conscience is the will of God, however it has been revealed to men. Some call this the Law of God, others the eternal Law; the words differ according to each one's choice, but the sense is the same. Each part of this conclusion must be weighed. I say first, the will of God. Of this will the well-known distinction is familiar, (which, however, I have observed writers to have sometimes either not explained correctly or not applied properly,) into the will of good pleasure and the will of sign. The former, which they call the will of good pleasure, is that by which God from eternity determined within himself what he himself wills to do. The other, which they call the will of sign, is that by which God from eternity determined within himself what he wills to be done by us. Of these, the former is properly and univocally the will of God; the latter is so called improperly and analogously [ἀναλόγως]. The will of good pleasure is, for God himself (if it is lawful to speak of such a Majesty after the manner of men [κατ' ἄνθρωπον]), in some sense the law of his acting, for he always does what is pleasing to himself. But it is not given by God to us as a law, to be the rule of our conscience, at least as far as things to be done are concerned. It does indeed pertain in some way to conscience with respect to things suffered: namely a posteriori, and in this sense, that we are bound in conscience to bear calmly whatever happens, once it has become clear from the event that God willed it. For right reason dictates that the order of divine providence should not displease us, since he can will nothing but what is most right. It remains, therefore, that the rule of our conscience should be that will which is called the will of sign. For when God, by commanding and forbidding, signifies what he wills to be done or not done by us, it is our duty simply to conform our wills to his will itself.{1}

units.la: {1} Id, Epist. 71. nificaverit ; nostri est officii ipsius Voluntati voluntates nostras simpliciter conformare. Multa apud Scholasticos disputantur inutili subtilitate, an & quatenus teneatur voluntas creaturæ rationalis conformare fe voluntati creatoris, in re volita ? quum possit, quod instituto nostro & ad vitæ usum fit fatis, res tota aperte & breviter uno verbo confici ; nimirum, teneri nos semper id velle, quod Deus vult nos velle. Ut cum præcepisset Abrahamo Deus, ut filium Ifaacum ipsi offerret in holocauftum, etsi D[?]us voluntate beneplaciti (uti mox ex eventu patuit) vel tum cum ei hoc faciendum præcepit, id fieri noluerit : tenebatur tamen Abrahamus id ipsum velle, quia Deus præcipiendo significaverat se velle ut Abrahamus id vellet.
units.tr: Id, Epist. 71. It is for us, as a matter of duty, simply to conform our wills to his will. The Schoolmen dispute at great length, with useless subtlety, whether and how far a rational creature is bound to conform its will to the will of the Creator in the thing willed. But since this does not concern our purpose or the practical use of life, the whole matter can be settled plainly and briefly in one phrase: we are always bound to will what God wills us to will. So when God commanded Abraham to offer his son Isaac as a burnt offering, even though God, by his will of good pleasure (as the outcome later showed), did not want this to be done, even at the time he gave the command, Abraham was nonetheless bound to will the same thing, because by commanding, God had signified that he wished Abraham to will it.

units.la: XXI. Dico fecundo, voluntas Dei hominibus revelata ; quia revelatio est formalis ratio obligandi : Voluntas enim Dei non obligat eos, quibus non est revelata. Unde Gentes quibus Evangelium non est prædicatum, non obligantur credere Evangelio, ut ad fidem in Christum. Nemo enim tenetur ad impossibile : impossibile est autem ei cui Evangelium non fuerit prædicatum, nec qui de Christo quicquam inaudiverit, credere Evangelio & Christo, cum lumen rationis non possit eò pertingere; juxta illud Apostoli, Rom. 10. 15. Quomodo credent ei de quo non audierint ? & quomodo audient absque prædicante ? Nec idem Apostolus æquum esse censet, ut per Legem judicentur alii quàm qui in Lege peccaverunt, Rom. 2. 12. Imò verò nec illud per se sufficit ad inducendam obligationem in conscientia, Voluntatem Dei esse alicui revelatam, nisi insuper ei revelata sit voluntas Dei quoad ipsum. Adeo ut si quis ex Gentibus ἀλλόφυλος incidisset forte in libros Mosis atque ex eorum lectione percepisset mandata Hebraeo populo inibi data ; non mox obligatus esset ad ea præstanda licet essent ei revelata, quia quia pulo omn data X revel fe, & habe de e ptum Id e nobi pro, Dei q fit m note aćtu ligan que tatem sed Dei ée D Quod jus fc est Deus Pergi xum ftræ hit ad excita scienti nimir hæc e ligatio quia ad ipsum non pertinebant, sed erant illi populo peculiaria; & scitum est Legem non obligare omnes quibus cognita est, sed omnes & solos quibus data est.
units.tr: XXI. I say secondly: the will of God is revealed to men. For revelation is the formal reason for obligation. The will of God does not bind those to whom it has not been revealed. Hence the Gentiles to whom the gospel has not been preached are not bound to believe the gospel so as to have faith in Christ, since no one is bound to the impossible. But it is impossible for one to whom the gospel has not been preached, and who has heard nothing of Christ, to believe the gospel and Christ, since the light of reason cannot reach that far. This accords with the saying of the Apostle, Rom. 10. 15: "How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher?" Nor does the same Apostle think it right that others should be judged by the Law except those who have sinned under the Law, Rom. 2. 12. Indeed, it is not enough in itself to create an obligation in the conscience that the will of God has been revealed to someone, unless the will of God has also been revealed to him as it concerns himself. So if someone from the Gentiles, a stranger to the people of Israel, had happened upon the books of Moses and from reading them had learned the commandments given there to the Hebrew people, he would not at once be bound to perform them, even though they had been revealed to him, because they did not pertain to him but were peculiar to that people. And it is settled that the Law does not bind all who know of it, but all and only those to whom it has been given.

units.la: XXII. Dico tertiò, Voluntas Dei qualitercunque revelata: quia authoritatem habet Voluntas Dei ex se, & non ex modo revelandi. Ita ut non opus habeant Pontificii, in Controversia de Traditionibus, de eo laborare ut probent Verbum Dei non Scriptum paris esse authoritatis cum Verbo Dei Scripto. Id enim nos ultrò largimur: modò, ut de Scripto nobis constat, constare posset pariter de non Scripto, quòd sit indubiè Verbum Dei. Ergo Voluntas Dei quocunque demum modo revelata, dummodo sit menti ita sufficienter revelata, ut ei aut actu innotescat, aut (nisi obstet negligentia culpabilis) actu innotescere possit, est regula Conscientiæ; obligans eam ad agnoscendam Dei voluntatem, eamque voluntati propriæ proponendam ut Dei voluntatem cui se conformare teneatur, nec id solùm, sed & potentiis executivis imperare ut ad eam Dei voluntatem adimplendam se accingant. Recte Damascenus, τοῦτο ἀγαθὸν ὅ τῷ ὁ Θεὸς βούλεται[?]. Quod vult Deus id bonum esse necesse est; cujus scil. Voluntas boni mensura est. Lex autem Dei est ἡ τοῦτο διδασκόμενον ἐντολή, mandatum illud quo Deus nos docet suam illam bonam voluntatem. Pergit δικαιῶν ὁ τῷ Θεῷ νόμος τῷ νῷ ἡμῶν, ἐφελ- κυόμενος πρὸς ἑαυτόν[?].
units.tr: XXII. I say thirdly: the will of God, however it is revealed, is binding. For the will of God has authority in itself, and not from the mode of revelation. So the Papists, in the controversy about Traditions, need not labour to prove that the unwritten Word of God has equal authority with the written Word of God. We freely grant this: provided that, as we are certain of the written word, we could be equally certain of the unwritten word, that it is beyond doubt the Word of God. Therefore the will of God, revealed in whatever manner, provided it is revealed to the mind sufficiently, so that it either is actually known to it or (unless culpable negligence stands in the way) can actually become known, is the rule of conscience. It binds conscience to acknowledge the will of God, and to set that will before one's own will as the will of God to which it is bound to conform; and not only this, but also to command the executive powers to gird themselves to carry out that will of God. Damascene rightly says: "What God wills is necessarily good" [τοῦτο ἀγαθὸν ὅ τῷ ὁ Θεὸς βούλεται], for the will of God is the measure of good. The law of God is the commandment teaching this [ἡ τοῦτο διδασκόμενον ἐντολή], that is, the command by which God teaches us his good will. He goes on: the law of God, when it touches our mind, draws it to itself [δικαιῶν ὁ τῷ Θεῷ νόμος τῷ νῷ ἡμῶν, ἐφελκυόμενος πρὸς ἑαυτόν].

units.la: Accedens autem menti nostræ Dei Lex, ubi semel eam occupaverit, attrahit ad se ἡ γνώμη τῆς ἡμετέρας συνειδήσεως[?], hoc est, excitat, pungit, subjectis quasi stimulis, urget conscientiam nostram, ut officium suum faciat, dictando nimirum voluntati nostræ Voluntatem Dei. Atque hæc est ipsissima illa quam diximus Conscientiæ obligatio.
units.tr: When the law of God touches our mind, once it has taken hold of it, it draws to itself the judgment of our conscience [ἡ γνώμη τῆς ἡμετέρας συνειδήσεως]. That is, it stirs and pricks it, as if with goads placed beneath, and urges our conscience to do its duty, by dictating to our will the will of God. And this is precisely that obligation of conscience of which we spoke.

units.la: XXIII. Cujus Obligationis vim & effectum va-rie exprimit Beatus Paulus. Nunc se debitorem fatetur, Græcis & Barbaris debitor sum, Rom. 1. 14. quasi diceret, cum me sciam Voluntate Dei sepositum ad prædicandum Evangelium Gentibus, sive ii Græci sint sive Barbari indiscriminatim, agnosco me utrisque hac ex parte debitorem, 2. Cor. 1. 14. ait se σωνέχεσθαι [?], ut solent vinculis ligati constringi & coarctari ad officium faciendum, 1 Cor. 9 16. ἀνάγκη μοί ἐπίκειται, fidei meæ, inquit, concredita est Evangelii prædicatio, ita ut non sit mihi liberum otiari & curare cutem: sed gravis mihi incumbit necessitas Evangelizandi, quam væ mihi si neglexero. Qualem sibi etiam impositam necessitatem, ita ut non possent eam excutere, senserunt ante eum & palam professi sunt, duo summi Apostoli & longo tempore individui comites Petrus & Johannes, Act. 4. 20. οὐ δυνάμεθα μὴ λαλεῖν. Iussit nos Deus παρρησία loqui; vos tacere jubetis: utris parendum sit potius, Vosmet judicate. A vestro imperio liberi esse possumus, imo & sumus; quibus jus nullum est in Conscientias nostras: sed arctat nos Dei imperium, & ita constrictos tenet, ut nobis non sit liberum, ne perire velimus, aliter facere, quàm ipse jusserit.
units.tr: XXIII. Blessed Paul expresses the force and effect of this obligation in various ways. Now he confesses himself a debtor: "I am a debtor to the Greeks and to the barbarians," Rom. 1. 14, as if to say: since I know that by the will of God I am set apart to preach the gospel to the Gentiles, whether they are Greeks or barbarians without distinction, I acknowledge that I am a debtor to both in this respect. In 2 Cor. 5. 14 he says that he is "constrained" [συνέχεσθαι], as men bound with chains are usually held in and compelled to do their duty. In 1 Cor. 9. 16: "necessity is laid upon me" [ἀνάγκη μοι ἐπίκειται]. The preaching of the gospel, he says, is entrusted to my faith, so that it is not free for me to be idle and take care of my own skin; rather a heavy necessity is laid on me to preach the gospel, and "woe to me if I neglect it." The two chief Apostles, Peter and John, who were companions for a long time, felt such a necessity laid on them before him, and openly professed it, and it was such that they could not throw it off: Acts 4. 20, "We cannot but speak" [οὐ δυνάμεθα μὴ λαλεῖν]. God has commanded us to speak with boldness; you order us to be silent. Judge for yourselves which of the two should rather be obeyed. We can be free of your command, and indeed we are; you have no right over our consciences. But the command of God constrains us, and holds us so bound that we are not free, if we do not wish to perish, to act otherwise than he has commanded.

units.la: XXIV.
units.tr: XXIV.

units.la: Porrò cum dictum sit, Conscientiæ Regulam proximam & immediatam esse Lumen mentis, primariam & Supremam Verbum Dei Scriptum propriam & adæquatam Voluntatem Dei qualitercunque revelatam, sive (quod idem est) Legem a Deo rationali creaturæ impositam: ut ista plenius intelligantur, sciendum est, triplex esse Lumen Mentis prout Deus creaturæ rationali voluntatem suam triplicibus modis patefacit; Lumen sc. innatum, Lumen illatum, & Lumen acquisitum; sive Lucem Naturæ, Scripturæ, Doctrinæ. Primum illud Lumen quod innatum [Right printed page, left-hand column, cut off at the scan edge; only word-ends and line beginnings are visible:] Innat… Deu… tis &… nant… & ej… prop… [Dea… mini… ratio… limi… divi… crea… pelle… est, verb… aute… sxv… men… ad q… matu… esse… stra… bona… prop… men, sum… unde… quib… duè… Deo… evas… volu… pract… voca… scite… cend… vini… innatum dixi, è lege Naturæ oritur. Indidit enim Deus in primâ mundi creatione, ut creaturis brutis & inanimatis instinctum naturalem, quo inclinantur ad ea facienda quæ sunt congrua naturæ suæ & ejus conservativa : quæ est ipsis instar Legis, propterea que & Davidi Lex dicitur, Psalm 148. 6. [Dedit illis legem, quæ non præteribit : ] Ita & Homini Legem quandam Naturalem, naturæ suæ ut rationalis creatura est proportionatam ; h. e. sublimiorem multò, & nobiliorem, & (si fas dicere) diviniorem, quàm quæ aliis inferioris hujus orbis creaturis, data est ; quæ ipsum ad ea agenda impellat quæ sunt naturæ suæ congrua quatenus homo est, animal nempe ratione præditum ; hoc est, ut verbo dicam, ad vivendum secundum rationem. Est autem hæc Lex naturalis impressio quædam, & quasi ἀντίτυπον Legis illius archetypa & æternæ quæ est in mente divinâ ; ëstque pars illius divinæ imaginis ad quam dicitur homo primùm conditus & efformatus Gen. 1. per quam certò cognoscentes aliqua esse ex Dei creatoris voluntate rationali naturæ nostræ congruentia, alia autem secùs ; statuimus illa bona esse & à nobis fieri oportere, ista mala & propterea non oportere. Ex hac lege ortum lumen, in gravi illâ naturæ humanæ ruinâ, quæ lapsum Adæ insecuta est, admodum obscuratam est : unde crassæ illæ erroris & ignorantiæ tenebræ, in quibus dum hic vivimus omnes ejus posteri assiduè versamur. Ita tamen sapientissimè providente Deo ut ex communi naufragio illæsius aliquantò evaserint quàm aliæ pleræque facultates. Nempe voluit Deus quasdam propositiones & principia practica, quas [?]κοινὰς ἐννοίας ʼ{1} [?]σπερματικοὺς λόγους φυσικὰς [?] vocant Philosophi, [?]ἐγκεκρυμμένον ἡμῖν ἀπὸ Θεοῦ[?] scite Basilius, quasi conservatam ex tanto incendio inter medios cineres & favillas ignis divini {2}Scintillulam, in nobis remanere : ut habeat beret in intimis pectoribus nostris voluntatis suæ præcones. Sunt hæ ἄγραφοι [?] ἔγγραφοι [?] Lex illa Dei quam Apostolus, Rom. 2. Scriptum ait in cordibus hominum; prorsus ut Leges civitatum aut Principis tabulis æneis inscribi solitæ sunt. Habent enim rationem Legis sive regulæ nobis à Deo impositæ; sicut Voluntas Legislatoris publico instrumento significata & populo proposita, Legis nomine censetur.
units.tr: Since it has been said that the nearest and immediate rule of conscience is the light of the mind, and the primary and supreme rule is the written Word of God, the proper and adequate will of God, however revealed, or (which is the same thing) the law imposed by God on the rational creature, these points may be understood more fully if we note that the light of the mind is threefold, according to the threefold ways in which God makes his will known to the rational creature: namely the innate light, the infused light, and the acquired light; or the light of Nature, Scripture, and Doctrine. The first of these, which I have called innate, arises from the law of Nature. For in the first creation of the world God implanted in the brute and inanimate creatures a natural instinct, by which they are inclined to do those things which are congruous to their nature and preserve it. This instinct serves them in place of a law, and therefore even David calls it a law, Psalm 148.6: [He has given them a law which shall not pass away]. So too he gave to man a certain natural law, suited to his nature as a rational creature; that is, far more sublime and noble, and (if I may say so) more divine, than that given to the other creatures of this lower world. It impels him to do those things which are congruous to his nature insofar as he is a man, that is, an animal endowed with reason; in a word, to live according to reason. This natural law is a kind of impression, and as it were an antitype of that archetypal and eternal law which is in the divine mind. It is part of that divine image in which man was first created and formed, Gen. 1. Through it, knowing with certainty that some things, by the will of the Creator God, are congruous to our rational nature and others are not, we judge that the former are good and ought to be done by us, and the latter evil and therefore not to be done. The light arising from this law was greatly obscured in that grievous ruin of human nature which followed the fall of Adam. Hence those thick shadows of error and ignorance in which all his posterity constantly dwell while we live here. Yet God, providing most wisely, has ensured that from this common shipwreck it has escaped somewhat more unharmed than most of our other faculties. For God willed that certain propositions and practical principles should remain in us, which the philosophers call common notions [κοινὰς ἐννοίας] or seminal reasons [σπερματικοὺς λόγους], and which Basil wisely calls a spark hidden in us by God [ἐγκεκρυμμένον ἡμῖν ἀπὸ Θεοῦ], preserved, as it were, from so great a fire among the middle ashes and embers of the divine fire, a little spark, so that they might be heralds of his will in our inmost hearts. These are the unwritten [ἄγραφοι] and yet written [ἔγγραφοι] law of God, which the Apostle, Rom. 2, says is written in the hearts of men; just as the laws of cities or of a prince are wont to be inscribed on bronze tablets. For they have the character of a law, or rule imposed on us by God; just as the will of the lawgiver, made known by a public instrument and set before the people, is reckoned under the name of law.

units.la: XXV. Constet autem hæc Lex naturalis ex variis Principiis practicis: quæ tamen ad unam primam & universalem Legem quæ reliquas complectatur revocantur, videlicet hanc bipartitam; Bonum esse faciendum, Malum fugiendum: Sicut omnia præcepta decalogi ad unam Legem universalem, eamque bipartitam, reducuntur, illam sc. quæ est de Dilectione Dei & Proximi. Huic universali legi in Synteresi conservatæ subjiciuntur aliæ; ceu Leges particulares, ex eâ derivatæ, ut conclusiones ex præmissis: quarum aliæ sunt de primo (ut loquuntur) naturæ dictamine, & principali illi legi proximè conjunctæ, aliæ quæ remotius ei appendent, nec nisi secundario, & virtute illarum propinquiorum. Quæ sunt de primo naturæ dictamine, simulac menti nostræ & cogitationibus offeruntur, fidem nostram statim imperant, coguntque nos eis assentiri, propter summam earum evidentiam. Neque enim fas est alicui de ipsarum veritate dubitare, neque possibile est quenquam, cui satis perspecta sit ipsarum vocum significatio, circa eas errare. Audito Deum esse colendum, Injuriam nemini faciendum; acquiescit statim animus, & sine ambage præbet assensum. At in posterioribus illis, propter discrepantiam quæ potest oriri ex circumstantiis, & dubitare sæpissimè contingit, & errare: & quò remotius à primis illis principiis recedítur, eò proclivius est in errorem labi. Prima enim & atis sua illa Dei cordibus Princint enim positæ; umento ne cenex vaam priomplen ; Boomnia lem, equæ est ali legi eu Lnes ex quunproxindent, inquiofimuir, fios eis Neubitaperas eremini e amillis, rcumrare: litur, m & falia Universalia tantò certiora sunt posterioribus & particularibus, quantò sunt minùs circumstantiata. Nam [illegible, ~14 letters] (ut dici solet) & descendendo contingit errare. Ejus generis præcepta sunt, Honorandos esse parentes, Liberos alendos, Conservandam proximi vitam, Depositum reddendum. Quæ utut communiter & ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ[?] observanda sunt, non tamen simpliciter & absolutè, si res & locus (quod fieri potest) aliud postulent. Nam & parentum jussa præ Dei amore spernenda sunt; & justa potest esse causa abdicandi liberos, & vitam proximo adimendi; nec est gladius furioso restituendus. Affinis huic distinctioni est illa {1}Ci- ceronis, à Stoicis accepta, Officiorum distributio. Aliud enim est ipsis Rectum & perfectum Officium, quod Græci κατόρθωμα, aliud Medium & Commune, quod καθῆκον vocant. Quare ut Conscientia de rebus propositis, quantum ad hanc Regulæ partem attinet, quæ sit Dei voluntas rectius & certius judicare posset; opportunum erit ea ad universalissima, quàm fieri potest, præcepta & ad prima illa & αὐτόματα axiomata revocare atque exigere. Sed de hac Naturæ Lege, quia ad alia properandum est, quum non liceat plura dicere; accipite quæso illa Ciceronis, quæ ex amissis ejus de Rep. Libris affert Lactantius 6. Instit. 8. “ Est quidem vero Lex recta ratio, naturæ congruens, diffusa in omnes, constans, sempiterna, quæ vocet ad officium jubendo, vetando à fraude deterreat. — Huic Legi nec abrogari fas est, nec derogari ex hac aliquid licet, neque tota abrogari potest. Nec vero aut per Senatum aut per populum solvi hac lege possumus. Nec est quærendus explanator, aut interpres ejus alius: Nec erit alia lex Romæ, alia Athenis: alia nunc, alia posthac: sed & omnes gentes & omni tempore, una lex & sempiterna & immortalis continebit. Unusque erit communis “ quasi Magister & imperator omnium Deus ille Legis hujus inventor, disceptator, lator, cui qui non pare-bit, ipse se fugiet, ac naturam hominis aspernabitur, atque hoc ipso luet maximas poenas, etiamsi caeteras supplicia, quae putantur effugerit. Insignis sanè locus & qui hujus Innati luminis naturam & vim luculentissimè explicat, adeò ut nihil opus sit plura in hanc rem adjicere.
units.tr: XXV. Now this natural law consists of various practical principles, which nevertheless are all referred back to one first and universal law which embraces the rest, namely this twofold one: Good is to be done, evil is to be avoided. Just as all the precepts of the Decalogue are reduced to one universal law, itself twofold, namely that concerning the love of God and neighbour. Other laws are subordinate to this universal law, which is preserved in synteresis, as particular laws derived from it, as conclusions are drawn from premises. Some of these concern what is called the first dictate of nature and are closely joined to that principal law; others hang more remotely from it and are only secondary, having their force through those nearer ones. Those which concern the first dictate of nature, as soon as they are presented to our mind and thoughts, at once command our belief and compel us to assent to them, on account of their supreme evidence. For it is not right for anyone to doubt their truth, nor possible for anyone, to whom the meaning of the words is sufficiently clear, to err about them. When it is heard that God is to be worshipped, and no one is to be wronged, the mind at once acquiesces and gives its assent without hesitation. But with the latter principles, because of the discrepancy which can arise from circumstances, it very often happens that one doubts, and errs; and the further one recedes from those first principles, the more prone one is to slip into error. For the most universal principles are more certain than the later and particular ones, in proportion as they are less circumstantiated. For [...] error also occurs when one comes down by descent, as is commonly said. Precepts of this kind are: Parents are to be honoured, children are to be nourished, the life of the neighbour is to be preserved, a deposit is to be returned. Although these are to be observed commonly and for the most part, they are not to be observed simply and absolutely, if the matter and the place (which can happen) require otherwise. For the commands of parents are to be spurned for the love of God; and there can be a just cause for disinheriting children and for taking life from a neighbour; nor is a sword to be returned to a madman. Akin to this distinction is that division of duties which Cicero took from the Stoics. For one kind of duty is right and perfect, which the Greeks call katorthōma, and another is middle and common, which they call kathēkon. Therefore, so that conscience may judge more rightly and certainly what the will of God is in the matters proposed, as far as this part of the rule is concerned, it will be opportune to refer and reduce them to the most universal precepts possible, and to those first and self-evident axioms. But concerning this law of Nature, since we must hasten on to other things and it is not permitted to say more, please accept that passage of Cicero which Lactantius cites from the lost books of his On the Republic, Lactantius 6. Instit. 8: "There is indeed a true law, right reason, agreeing with nature, diffused among all, constant, everlasting, which calls to duty by commanding, and by forbidding deters from fraud. This law can neither be abrogated, nor is it lawful to derogate anything from it, nor can it be wholly abrogated. Nor can we be released from this law either by the Senate or by the people. Nor is there need to seek any expounder or other interpreter of it: nor will there be one law at Rome and another at Athens, one now and another hereafter; but one law, everlasting and immortal, will hold all nations at all times. And there will be one common master and emperor of all, that God who is the author, judge, and proposer of this law; whoever does not obey him will flee from himself and despise the nature of man, and by this very thing will suffer the greatest penalties, even if he escapes those punishments which are thought to be penalties." A remarkable passage indeed, which explains most brilliantly the nature and power of this innate light, so that there is no need to add more on the subject.

units.la: XXVI. Secundum Lumen, quod menti illatum diximus, ei ab extrà advenit oritúrque à Revelatione divinà : nempe ab illà luce, quam Deus nobis subministravit in Sacrà Scripturà, in quà voluntatem suam humano genere uberiùs adhuc patefecit ; nequid ei deesset adminiculi, quod ad mores regendos & beatitatem consequendam esset necessarium ; quùm ad ista non sufficeret lumen internum naturale, ut jam ante ostendimus. Differt autem hoc Lumen à Naturali, non origine solùm, sed & perfectione : Primò, quia voluntatem Dei manifestat in his, ad quæ non potest lumen naturale pertingere. Secundo, quia actus morales à naturali Lumine dictatos ad finem sublimiorem ordinat. Tertiò, quia cùm Lex mentibus insculpta à Deo tanquam authore Naturæ instituta sit, Lex ista in verbo revela-ta est ab eo instituta tanquam authore Gratiæ & Salutis. Ergo ubi aut deficit, aut debile est Naturæ Lumen (deficit autem in his quæ sunt extra orbem suum, cujusmodi sunt mysteria fidei ; debile verò est, in his quæ ab universalissimis præceptis sunt aliquantò remotiora : } ad Lumen Verbi recurrendum est, sicut ad lucernam in loco caliginoso fulgentem , 2 Pet. 1. 19. Ad Legem & ad Testimonium : si non loquantur secundum hoc verbum, non est eis Lux, Isa. 8. 20. Lucerna pedibus meis verbum tuum, & lumen gressibus meis, Psal. 119. 105. De hujus Legis perfectione & utilitate, si sermonem instituerem, nullus esset dicendi finis. Videte sodes in hanc rem Davidis Psalmum decimum nonum, ubi multa paucis & contractius; ac Psalmum etiam centesimum[?] decimum nonum, ubi eadem pluribus & diffusius exposita reperietis.
units.tr: XXVI. The second light, which we said is poured into the mind, comes to it from outside and arises from divine Revelation: namely from that light which God has supplied to us in Holy Scripture, in which he has revealed his will to the human race still more fully. Nothing was to be lacking of the help needed for governing manners and attaining blessedness, since the inner natural light is not sufficient for these things, as we have already shown. This Light differs from the natural light not only in origin but also in perfection. First, because it makes known the will of God in those matters which the natural light cannot reach. Second, because it orders the moral acts dictated by the natural Light to a higher end. Third, because although the Law inscribed on the minds was instituted by God as author of Nature, that Law revealed in the Word was instituted by him as author of Grace and Salvation. Therefore where the light of Nature either fails or is weak (it fails in matters outside its own sphere, such as the mysteries of faith; it is weak in those things which lie somewhat further from the most universal precepts), we must have recourse to the Light of the Word, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, 2 Pet. 1.19. To the Law and to the Testimony: if they do not speak according to this word, there is no light in them, Isa. 8.20. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path, Psal. 119.105. If I were to set out on the perfection and usefulness of this Law, there would be no end of speaking.
