Please look at David's nineteenth Psalm on this matter, where many things are said in few words and more compactly; and you will also find the same things set out at greater length and more fully in the hundred and nineteenth Psalm.

units.la: XXVII. Porrò hujus Legis duæ partes sunt: Lex proprie dicta, & Evangelium. Legem vero & Evangelium non hîc intelligo in sensu, quo plerumque à Theologis sumuntur, pro binis Dei initis cum humano genere fœderibus; Operum sc. & Gratiæ: sed popularius, pro Scripturæ Libris Veteris & Novi Instrumenti. Patres, ad nostrum saltem institutum non incommodè, Legem Veterem & Novam dixerunt. Utramque Legem, & Veterem illam Mosis in universum, & novam Christi quantum ad illam partem quâ Moralia continet, ut inutilem prorsus, & Christiani hominis curâ studiòve (postquam adultæ in Christo ætatis fuerit, & unctione Spiritus perfusus) indignam exagitant; nec nisi fidei legem & Spiritus distamen admittunt, nostri sæculi Antinomi, Anabaptistæ, Enthusiastæ, & reliqua id genus prodigiosa nomina. Quos non est nunc refutandi locus, alia agentibus: neque est id profecto multùm necessarium; quùm in istiusmodi errorum monstra ita gladium jam olim strinxerit Jacobus Apostolus, ut videri possit spiritu quodam prophetico eorum refutationem datâ operâ suscepisse.
units.tr: XXVII. Furthermore, this Law has two parts: the Law properly so called, and the Gospel. I do not here understand Law and Gospel in the sense in which the Theologians commonly take them, as the two covenants of God with mankind, that of works and that of grace; but more popularly, as the books of the Old and New Testament. The Fathers, at least for our present purpose not inappropriately, called them the Old Law and the New. Both laws, the old one of Moses in general and the new one of Christ so far as it contains moral precepts, the Antinomians, Anabaptists and Enthusiasts of our age, and that tribe of monstrous names, assail as wholly useless and unworthy of the care and zeal of a Christian (once he has reached adult age in Christ and been bathed in the anointing of the Spirit); they admit only the law of faith and the distinction of the Spirit. These I need not refute now, since others are engaged in that task; nor is it indeed very necessary, since James the Apostle long ago drew the sword so vigorously against monsters of this kind that he might seem, by a certain prophetic spirit, to have undertaken their refutation on purpose.

units.la: XXVIII. Legis veteris, quæ & Mosaica dici solet, notissima & illa distributio, quâ in tres partes distinguitur; Moralium sc. Cerimoniarum, & Judiciorum. De quibus singulis multa à multis variè disputantur. Quibus præteremissis, quid de earum obligatione mihi sentiendum videtur, salvo tamen suo cuique judicio, breviter proponam. Dico igitur Primò, nullam omninò latam à Mose Legem obligare Christianorum Conscientiam directè, formaliter & per se; quatenus sc. est à Mose lata aut tradita,
units.tr: XXVIII. Of the Old Law, which is also commonly called Mosaic, the division into three parts is well known: moral, ceremonial and judicial. Many have disputed about each of these in various ways. Passing these by, I will briefly set out what seems to me to be the case about their obligation, saving however each person's own judgment. I say, therefore, First, that no law given by Moses binds the conscience of Christians directly, formally and in itself, insofar as it has been given or delivered by Moses,

units.la: tradita, dita. Ratio est, quia omnis Lex Mofaica, quatalis, fuit positiva : & Lex positiva non nisi eos obligat quibus posita est. Cum ergo Lex à Mose tradita, uni tantùm genti Hebræorum posita fit, ut vel ex ipso statim exordio [Audi Israël] & toto insequentis sermonis charactere facilè quisquis animum adverterit intelliget ; non poterit ad eos qui extra illius gentis censum sunt ita pertinere, ut eo nomine quòd fit à Mose tradita, eos obliget. Quod fiqua pars illius Legis nunc obliget Christianos, (ut certè obligant præcepta Decalogi ; ) ex accidente id fit, & ratione Materiæ : non quia sic Moses præceperit, sed quia id quod ab eo sic præceptum est, aut est Legi-Naturæ consentaneum, aut à Christo est in Lege nova confirmatum.
units.tr: delivered. The reason is that every Mosaic law, as such, was positive, and a positive law binds only those to whom it has been given. Since therefore the Law delivered by Moses was given to one people only, the Hebrews, as anyone who attends to it can easily understand from the very beginning [Hear, O Israel] and from the whole character of the discourse that follows, it cannot pertain to those outside that nation's register so as to bind them by the fact that it was delivered by Moses. If some part of that Law now binds Christians (as the precepts of the Decalogue certainly do), this happens by accident and by reason of the matter: not because Moses so commanded, but because what he so commanded either accords with the Law of Nature, or has been confirmed by Christ in the New Law.

units.la: XXIX. Dico Secundò, Legem Mosis Ceremonialem obligaffe quidem Judæos in Conscientiâ ante prædicatum ipsis Evangelium Jesu Christi : non item alios, nisi qui proselyti fierent Cultus & Religionis Judaicæ : qui cùm effent duorum generum, (Proselyti fcil. Portæ, & Proselyti Justitiæ, Judæis difti,) obligabantur ad præcepta ritualia observanda : pauciora quædam illi prioris generis, pofterioris generis hi, pariter ac ipsi Judæi univerfi[?]. A Christi autem morte & resurrectione, ex quo tempore cœpit Judæis solis primùm, dein post paulò & Gentibus, prædicari Evangelium, usque ad eversionem Templi Hierofolymitani & politiæ Judaicæ, fuisse hanc Legem ; ut post Augustinum loqui amant Mortuam, sed non mortiferam ; hoc est, amisisse quidem vim obligandi ; non tamen fuisse ritus à Mose traditos prorsus illicitos, sed liberæ observationis ; ita ut fas effet homini cuivis, prout res postulàret, (habità interim prudentiâ & charitatis justâ ratione, ) ipsis pro arbitrio vel uti vel non uti. Quam fuisse B. Pauli mentem, ex ipsius constanti tum doctrina tum praxi manifestius est quàm ut probari debeat. Post euersionem Templi senique à plerisque dici solere, non mortuam solum esse hanc legis Mosaicæ partem, sed & mortiferam. Quod subvereor ne ingeniosius dictum deprehendatur quàm solidius: nisi dextrè explicetur & cum adhibita distinctione. Non enim sunt omnia Ceremonialia pari loco habenda: sed illa quæ sunt Ordinis, & decentiæ, ab illis quæ futurum Christum figurabant, prudenter separanda. Ceremonias illas figurativas, quæ à Deo institutæ sunt, ut essent typi Christi redemptoris in carne venturi cujusmodi fuere Circumcisio, Sacrificia, & alia nonnulla similia, certum est ex quo Christus omnia illis ceremoniis typicè figurata reipsà adimpleverit, & omnia ritè esse adimpleta universo orbi per Evangelii sui præcones sufficienter annunciaverit, nullum jam ultrà usum habere posse; proinde non solùm ut emortuas & putidas è medio tollendas esse, sed & pestiferas & exitiosas ab omni verè Christiano summopere fugiendas. Illud præsertim studiosissimè cavendum ne cum aliquâ necessitatis opinione observentur: juxta illud, Gal. 5.
units.tr: XXIX. I say Secondly, that the Ceremonial Law of Moses did indeed bind the Jews in conscience before the Gospel of Jesus Christ was preached to them; but not others, unless they became proselytes to the Jewish worship and religion. Since these were of two kinds (proselytes of the gate and proselytes of righteousness, as the Jews called them), they were bound to observe the ritual precepts: fewer of these for the former kind, and for the latter the same as for the Jews themselves in general. From the death and resurrection of Christ, from which time the Gospel began to be preached, first to the Jews alone and soon after also to the Gentiles, until the overthrow of the Temple of Jerusalem and the Jewish polity, this Law was (as after Augustine they like to put it) dead, but not deadly. That is, it had indeed lost its force of obligation; yet the rites delivered by Moses were not utterly unlawful, but of free observance, so that it was lawful for any man, as circumstances required (with prudence and charity duly observed), to use them or not use them at his own discretion. That this was the mind of St Paul is more evident from his constant teaching and practice than it needs to be proved. After the overthrow of the Temple, many say that this part of the Mosaic law is not only dead but also deadly. I fear this saying may be found more clever than solid, unless it is explained skilfully and with due distinction. For not all ceremonial things are to be held in the same place: those which belong to order and decency must be prudently separated from those which foreshadowed the Christ to come. As for those figurative ceremonies, instituted by God to be types of Christ the Redeemer coming in the flesh (of which kind were circumcision, sacrifices, and some other similar things), it is certain that since Christ has in reality fulfilled all the things typically figured by those ceremonies, and has sufficiently announced to the whole world through the heralds of his Gospel that all has been duly fulfilled, they can no longer have any use. Therefore they must be removed from the midst not only as dead and foul, but must also be shunned by every truly Christian person as pestilential and deadly. Above all it must be most carefully guarded against that they be observed with any notion of necessity, according to that saying in Gal. 5.

units.la: 2. Ego Paulus dico vobis, Si circumcidamini, Christum vobis nihil profuturum esse. Ast illæ Ceremonia quæ ad externum tantùm decorem & cultus divini solemnitatem quandam pertinebant, etsi præstare fortasse non usurpari, ubi saltem lubesse potest justus Scandali metus; non sunt tamen simpliciter damnandæ, ut illicita, hoc solo nomine quòd pædagogiæ Mosaicæ pars fuerint.
units.tr: 2. "Behold, I Paul say unto you, that if ye be circumcised, Christ shall profit you nothing." But those ceremonies which pertained only to external decency and a certain solemnity of divine worship, although perhaps it is better not to use them where at least a just fear of scandal can be present, are nevertheless not to be condemned simply as unlawful on the single ground that they were part of the Mosaic pedagogy.

units.la: XXX. Dico Tertiò, utut nonnulli distinguant inter Leges Mosis Politicas eas quæ erant Juris Communis, quarum etiam notas quasdam assignant & κειμένα[?], & eas quæ erant Juris Particularis; non esse necessarium ista sic distingui: imò rotundè affirmari posse, ex iis Legibus Mosis quæ Politica aut Judiciales dicuntur, nullam omninò obligare Christianos Magistratus in utramvis partem : quin ut iplis liceat, pro arbitratu suo, & prout incolumitati & utilitati Reipublicæ videbitur expedire, eandem apud subditos suos sancire, vel non sancire.
units.tr: XXX. I say Thirdly, that although some distinguish between the Political Laws of Moses, those which were of common law (for which they also assign certain marks and [κείμενα]), and those which were of particular law, it is not necessary to distinguish them thus. Indeed it may be affirmed bluntly that of those Laws of Moses which are called political or judicial, none at all binds Christian magistrates to either side. Rather, it is lawful for them, at their own discretion, and as they judge it expedient for the safety and advantage of the commonwealth, to enact the same among their subjects, or not to enact it.

units.la: XXXI. Dico Quarto, Legem Moralem, à Mose traditam, hoc est, Præcepta Decalogi, obligare omnes Christianos, pariter ac Judæos, ad eam observandam. Et hoc quidem omnes, quod sciam, Protestantes uno ore confitentur : quod majorem nobis injuriam facit Bellarminus, qui nos fingit in eponere Christianam libertatem, ut nulli legi subjecti simus in Conscientia, Moses autem cum suo Decalogo nihil ad nos pertineat. Viderit quomodo se calumnia liberet ; suosque (si nos in hac culpa) eodem crimine. Agitatur enim haec controversia inter suos Scholasticos, teneanturne Christiani Præceptis Decalogi, quatenus sunt declarativa Legis Naturæ tantum, an etiam quatenus sunt Mosi à Deo, Deíque jussu à Mose populo Dei tradita, & in sacros Codices relata : aliis utrumque affirmantibus, aliis è duobus alterum negantibus. Est & in nostris Ecclesiis eandem reperire hac de re sententiarum, (si tamen sententiarum, & non verborum potius) diversitatem. Cæterum cum illi inter se, & nos cum illis in eo quod rei caput est, haftenus consentiamus ; habere moralem legem earn, quæ à Mose tradita est in præcepti Decalogi continetur, vim obligandi nostras Christianorum conscientias : fortasse non est operæ pretium, unde illam obligandi vim obtineat, multum litigare. Consultius tamen mihi loqui videtur qui dicunt Legem illam Mosis non obligare Christianos formaliter & qua talis, hoc est quatenus à Mose tradita est ; sed tantum ratione materiæ, quatenus declarativa est legis Naturalis: proinde vim suam obligandi omnem non ab authoritate[?] thor[?] rivar[?] Deu[?] tion[?] etian[?] gt vo[?] X[?] gelius[?] sub[?] tuita[?] ftica[?] dico[?] gelitu[?] quib[?] nec tr[?] fertir[?] appar[?] fit iis[?] 22. [?] haber[?] igar[?] obed[?] omn[?] Chrif[?] tori p[?] leñi[?] XX[?] Chril[?] bi pr[?] Minif[?] tùm[?] iis on[?] juxta[?] non l[?] cui c[?] immi[?] crorg[?] thoritate Mosis eam sive ferentis sive tradentis derivare, sed ab ipso naturalis legis dictamine, quam Deus mentibus nostris & insevit in prima creatione, & ut voluntatis suæ monitorem in iisdem etiam post lapsum voluit permanere. Hæc de Legi[?] vetere, & Mosaicâ.
units.tr: XXXI. I affirm, fourthly, that the moral law delivered by Moses, that is, the precepts of the Decalogue, binds all Christians as much as Jews to observe it. So far as I know, all Protestants confess this with one voice. Bellarmine does us a greater wrong when he pretends that we explain away Christian liberty, so that we are subject to no law in conscience, and that Moses with his Decalogue has nothing to do with us. Let him see how he clears himself of calumny, and whether his own people are not guilty of the same charge. For this controversy is debated among their own Scholastics: whether Christians are bound by the precepts of the Decalogue insofar as they are only declarations of the law of nature, or also insofar as they were given by God through Moses, and handed down by Moses to the people of God by God's command, and recorded in the sacred books. Some affirm both, others deny one of the two. Among our own churches there is also a diversity of opinion on this matter (if it is a diversity of opinions and not rather of words). Still, since they agree among themselves, and we agree with them, on the main point, namely that the moral law contained in the precepts of the Decalogue, which was delivered by Moses, has the force of binding the consciences of Christians, it is perhaps not worth much dispute from where it obtains that binding force. Yet it seems to me more prudent to say that the law of Moses does not bind Christians formally and as such, that is, insofar as it was delivered by Moses, but only by reason of its matter, insofar as it declares the natural law. Accordingly, it derives all its binding force not from the authority of Moses, whether of the one who enacted it or of the one who handed it down, but from the very dictate of the natural law, which God implanted in our minds at the first creation, and willed to remain in the same minds after the fall as the monitor of his will. So much concerning the old law, and the Mosaic.

units.la: XXXII. Lex nova sive Christi, hoc est, Evangelium, tria ista continet: Mysteria fidei credenda, sub quo capite completor & Promissiones Dei gratuitas; Instituta Sacra Cæremonialia & Ecclesiastica; & Præcepta demum Moralia. De quibus dico, & Primum de omnibus universim, Evangelium non obligare nisi vocatos, id est, eos solos quibus annunciatum est. Quia ubi Lex non est, nec transgressio esse potest: moraliter autem præsertim in supernaturalibus idem est non esse, & non apparere, sive non ita sufficienter proponi, ut possit iis innotescere. Diserte Servator ipse, Joh. 15. 22. Si non venissem, & locutus essem eis, peccatum non haberent: i. e. non rei essent Spreti Evangelii. Obligare tamen omnes quibus prædicatum est, ad obedientiam tum fidei tum vitæ, ita ut teneantur omnes quibus Evangelium annunciatum est, & in Christum credere ut redemptorem, & ipsi ut Legislatori parere: quod utrumque ni fecerint, in neglecti officii supplicium, pœnas æternas luent.
units.tr: XXXII. The new law, or the law of Christ, that is, the Gospel, contains three things: the mysteries of faith to be believed, under which heading come the promises of God freely given; the sacred and ceremonial ordinances of the Church; and lastly the moral precepts. Concerning these I say, first of all in general, that the Gospel binds only those who are called, that is, those alone to whom it has been announced. For where there is no law, there can be no transgression; and morally, especially in supernatural matters, not to exist and not to appear, or not to be proposed sufficiently for it to become known to them, are the same thing. The Saviour himself says plainly, John 15.22: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; that is, they would not be guilty of rejecting the Gospel. Nevertheless, the Gospel obliges all to whom it is preached to obedience both of faith and of life, so that all to whom the Gospel has been announced are bound both to believe in Christ as Redeemer and to obey him as Lawgiver; if they fail in either, they will pay the punishment of eternal penalties for the neglected duty.

units.la: XXXIII. Dico Secundò, obligari Ecclesiam Christianam ad Instituta Sacra, (hoc est, ad Verbi prædicationem, Sacramentorum administrationem, Ministrorum Evangelii ordinationem, & Clavium tum scientiæ, tum Potestatis, Exercitium,) in iis omnibus quæ ad ipsorum essentiam pertinent, juxta institutionem Christi & Apostolorum: ita ut non liceat ei, multò vero minùs particulari alicui cœtui aut personæ, inde quicquam sponte vel imminuere vel immutare. Cæterum externas Sacrorum Institutorum circumstantias ita esse liberas, ut possit Ecclesia quævis particularis, pro ratione locorum & temporum, prout ex usu fuerit populi Dei, & ut ædificationi videbitur expedire, ita de eis statuere.
units.tr: XXXIII. I affirm, secondly, that the Christian Church is bound to the sacred institutions (that is, to the preaching of the Word, the administration of the Sacraments, the ordination of the ministers of the Gospel, and the exercise both of the knowledge and of the power of the keys), in all those matters which pertain to their essence, according to the institution of Christ and the Apostles. So it is not permitted to the Church, and much less to any particular assembly or person, to diminish or change anything of these at will. But the external circumstances of the sacred institutions are so free that any particular Church may decide about them according to the circumstances of places and times, as the practice of the people of God shall require and as shall seem expedient for edification.

units.la: XXXIV. Dico Tertiò, Novi Testamenti Moralia Præcepta, eadem esse quoad substantiam cum Moralibus Veteris Testamenti: & utraque ad Legem Naturalem, quæ in decem præceptis Decalogi continetur, esse revocanda; sicut omnia entia realia revocantur ad decem Prædicamenta. Esse tamen præcepta Christi in Lege nova, ut Sancti Ecclesiæ Patres ubique testantur, præceptis Mosi in veteri Lege, quoad aliqua multò præstantiora. Non eo solùm respectu, quòd plenius, clariùs & explicatiùs proponuntur: sed quatenus etiam altius assurgunt, & ad eminentiorem perfectionis gradum Christianos provocant; idque efficacissimis utrinque [illegible, ~9 letters], propositò scilicet eis ex unâ parte Exemplo Christi præterito, ex alterâ amplissimo regni cœlestis futuro præmio. Ut in duobus illis magnis vitæ Christianæ officiis vel maximè patet, de diligendis inimicis, & tollendâ cruce, in lege novâ imperatis. Neque enim sunt illa, sicut aliqui somniarunt, eo duntaxat loco habenda, acsi Consilia tantùm essent vitæ perfectioris; quæ sint omnibus propositæ quidem sub conditione præmii amplioris, neminem tamen obligent sub peccato, nisi fiqui se voto ad ea observanda obstrinxerint. Quinimo verè Præcepta sunt, eaque proprie dicta, & universaliter obligatoria: ad quorum observationem, sub gravissimi peccati culpâ (abnegati scil. Christi,) & æternæ damnationis (ni resipiscant) pœnâ obligan-tur, quotcunque Christi fidem nomenque profitentur. Et hæc de secundo mentis lumine dicta sunt.
units.tr: XXXIV. I affirm, thirdly, that the moral precepts of the New Testament are the same in substance as the moral precepts of the Old Testament, and that both must be traced back to the natural law contained in the ten precepts of the Decalogue, just as all real beings are traced back to the ten categories. Nevertheless, the precepts of Christ in the new law are, as the holy Fathers of the Church bear witness everywhere, far more excellent in some respects than the precepts of Moses in the old law. This is not only because they are set forth more fully, more clearly and more explicitly, but also insofar as they rise higher and call Christians to a more eminent degree of perfection; and this is done by most effective means on both sides, namely by setting before them, on the one hand, the example of Christ in the past, and on the other, the most ample reward of the future kingdom of heaven. This is most clearly seen in the two great duties of the Christian life enjoined in the new law, the love of enemies and the bearing of the cross. For these are not, as some have dreamed, to be regarded merely as counsels of a more perfect life, which are proposed to all under the condition of a greater reward, but which bind no one under sin unless they have bound themselves by vow to observe them. Rather, they are truly precepts, and precepts properly so called, and universally binding: all who profess the faith and name of Christ are bound to observe them, under the guilt of the most grievous sin (namely, denying Christ) and the penalty of eternal damnation (unless they repent). These things have been said concerning the second light of the mind.

units.la: XXXV. Tertium restat, quod Lumen Acquisitum diximus. Quod sanè nihil aliud est, quam [illegible, ~5 letters] Αὔξησιν[?] quoddam & incrementum illius luminis (sive Naturæ, sive Revelationis) quod ante menti inerat, quoad aliquem claritatis gradum: Cum sc. Voluntas Dei, cujus cognitio mentibus nostris hactenus illuxit, (sive interne impressa in lege Naturæ, sive externe in verbo revelata,) aut propria meditatione, aut aliena institutione, clarius adhuc nobis innotescit. Cujus media præcipua sunt; Discursus Rationis, & Authoritas, (hoc est, judicium & praxis) Ecclesiæ: de quibus nec patitur tempus, ut multa dicam; nec ut multa dicantur, res ipsa postulat. E Lege Naturæ deducuntur per discursum Rationis ad usum conscientiæ, multæ particulares de quibus agendis Propositiones; velut Conclusiones ex suis Principiis. Quà in re, nisi à primo ad ultimum rite procedatur, proclive est errare; ut ante dictum est. Quare diligenter videndum, ut in singulis partibus discursus legitimus fiat progressus; utque posteriora quæque à prioribus aptè pendeant, & ex eis necessariò consequantur: ut Conscientia in errorem prolapsa voluntati aliud aliterve, quàm oportuit, dictet. Periculum itidem est, ne in applicandà sacrà Scriptura ad usum Conscientiæ similiter erretur; nisi & Rationis justa ratio habeatur, & Authoritati sua constet authoritas. Pontificii, dum in illam partem omnia studia sua conferunt, ut nequid Ecclesiæ suæ authoritati decedat, parum deferunt Rationi: Sociniani ex adverso, dum rejectâ omni Authoritate fidem solà ratione metiuntur, id tandem agunt ut cum ratione insaniant. Unus utrisque Error; sed variis illudit partibus. Vitabitur uterque scopulus non aliter commodius, quàm si cum ratione Authoritas, cum authoritate Ratio, scitè & prudenter conjungantur.
units.tr: XXXV. There remains the third, which we called the acquired light. This is nothing other than a certain increase [αὔξησιν] and growth of that light (whether of nature or of revelation) which was already in the mind, to some degree of clarity: namely, when the will of God, whose knowledge has hitherto shone upon our minds (whether inwardly impressed in the law of nature or outwardly revealed in the Word), becomes clearer still to us, either by our own meditation or by another's instruction. Its principal means are the discourse of reason and the authority (that is, the judgment and practice) of the Church. Of these, time does not permit me to say much, nor does the matter itself require that much be said. From the law of nature, through the discourse of reason, are deduced for the use of conscience many particular propositions concerning what is to be done, as conclusions from their principles. In this matter, unless one proceeds rightly from the first to the last, it is easy to go astray, as has been said before. Therefore one must take care that in each part the reasoning makes a legitimate progress, and that each later point depends aptly on the earlier and follows necessarily from them, lest the conscience, having slipped into error, dictate to the will something other or otherwise than it ought. There is likewise a danger that one may go wrong in the same way in applying Holy Scripture to the use of conscience, unless both due account is taken of reason and it is evident that authority has its own authority. The Papists, while they direct all their efforts to that side, so that nothing may be lost to the authority of their Church, pay too little regard to reason. The Socinians, on the other hand, while they reject all authority and measure faith by reason alone, bring it about in the end that they go mad with reason. The error is one and the same for both, but it mocks them in different parts. Each rock will be avoided in no better way than by authority being joined with reason, and reason with authority, wisely and prudently.

units.la: XXXVI. Utraque quatenus in sacra Scriptura dextrè explicandâ, ritéque applicandâ, locum habere debeat; non est præsentis aut temporis aut instituti plenè differere. Agendum paucis. Rationi circa Scripturam duplex potissimum est usus: Collativus sc. & Illativus. Collativus; ut nempe diuerfa Scripturæ loca, ea præsertim quæ insignem aliquam invicem aut cognationem aut repugnantiam habere videntur, diligenter conferamus: Illativus ut eruta è verborum proprietate, contextu & scopo, documenta debitè & artificiosè inferamus. Mores interim, humanæ rationi in rebus agendis tantò plus tribuendum esse, quàm in credendis quantò plus naturalis ingenii captum superant fidei mysteria, quàm officia vitæ.
units.tr: XXXVI. How far each of these should have its place in rightly explaining and rightly applying Holy Scripture is not something to be fully worked out at this time or in this lecture. I must deal with it briefly. Reason has two main uses in relation to Scripture: the comparative and the inferential. The comparative use is that we carefully compare different passages of Scripture, especially those that seem to have some striking kinship or conflict with one another. The inferential use is that we properly and skilfully draw out the teachings that are gathered from the precise meaning of the words, from the context and from the purpose. Meanwhile, human reason must be given much more weight in matters of conduct than in matters of belief, by as much as the mysteries of faith surpass the natural grasp of the mind more than the duties of life do.

units.la: XXXVII. Authoritatis autem præcipuus usus est, ad retundendam Hæreticorum & Impostorum audaciam, qui clarissimis Scripturæ testimoniis tenebras offundunt, earumque vim distinctiunculis & subtilitatibus suis eludunt. Quibus non opportuniùs os obturabitis, aut saltem vosmet ipsos aliosque ab ipsorum contagione illæsos efficaciùs conservabitis, quàm si judicium & praxin, non unius aut paucorum hominum, non unius anguli aut seculi Ecclesiæ, sed Catholicæ (hoc est, diffusæ per totum orbem) omnium locorum & temporum Ecclesiæ, ipsorum strophis & sophismatis opponatis. Sic olim prisci illi fidei Christianæ advocati Irenæus, Tertullianus, Vincentius, reliqui, præscriptionis jure cum adversariis agendum judicarunt: quod quantum orbi Christiano profuerit, eventus docuit. Sed ista omnia, pleniore tractatione digna memor temporis meique & vestri, omittere cogor & quæ de Legum humanarum obligatione proximè senda[?] sunt in aliud tempus remittere.
units.tr: XXXVII. The chief use of authority, however, is to blunt the boldness of heretics and impostors, who cast darkness over the clearest testimonies of Scripture and evade their force with their petty distinctions and subtleties. You will not silence them more opportunely, or at least keep yourselves and others unharmed by their contagion more effectively, than by setting against their twists and sophisms the judgment and practice not of one or a few men, nor of one corner or age of the Church, but of the Catholic Church (that is, spread throughout the whole world), the Church of all places and times. Thus of old those early advocates of the Christian faith, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Vincent and the rest, judged that the case must be conducted against adversaries by the right of prescription; how much this benefited the Christian world the outcome has shown. But all these matters, which deserve a fuller treatment, I am compelled, mindful of the time and of myself and of you, to omit, and what must be said next about the obligation of human laws I must defer to another occasion.

units.la: PRÆLECTIO QUINTA. IN QUA, DE Le- gum Humanarum Obligatione in ge- nere, Quæstio pertractatur.
units.tr: PRÆLECTIO QUINTA. Lecture Five, in which the question of the obligation of human laws in general is treated.

units.la: ROM. XIII. 5.
units.tr: ROM. XIII. 5.

units.la: Quare Subjici necesse est, non solum propter Iram, sed etiam propter Conscientiam.
units.tr: Wherefore you must be subject, not only because of wrath, but also for conscience' sake.

units.la: DE Obligatione Conscientiæ Passivâ tractationem exorsus superiori Termino, hactenus progressus sum, ut retectis ante rejectisque illis latibulis in quibus inesse aliquid præsidii ad Conscientiæ suæ sive fructum quoad jam facta, sive securitatem quoad faciendā[?], frustra sibi blandiuntur vulgus hominum (boni sc. finis Intentione, & alieni Exempli judiciive authoritate,) propriam illam & adæquatam Conscientiæ regulam, cui se absolutè & simpliciter conformare teneatur, Investigarem. Ubi ostendi Primò Deum solum in Conscientias hominum merum & directum imperium habere: Secundò, Conscientiæ Regulam proximam & immediatam esse Lumen mentis pro tempore præsens, sive (quod idem est,){'} ultimum judicium intellectus practici. Tertiò, Verbum Dei Scriptum esse quidem supremam & primariam, non tamen adæquatam Conscientiæ Regulam. Quartò, propriam & adæquatam Conscientiæ Regulam esse Voluntatem Dei qualitercunque revelatam, sive (quod etiam idem est) Legem à Deo rationali creaturæ impositam. Dixi insuper, ut quænam effet illa Dei voluntas plenius & distinctius intelligeretur, Deum Opt. Max. Voluntatem suam humano generi triplici medio, velut Lumine patefecisse. Lege sc. Naturæ, quæ constat ex quibusdam Principiis practicis per se notis quæ & Lex Dei Scripta in cordibus nostris dicitur, Rom. 2. 15. velut Lumine Interno & mentibus innato: Verbo Dei Scripto, quod in sacris utriusque Instrumenti voluminibus continetur, velut Lumine Externo supernaturaliter revelato, & mentibus illato: Scientiâ denique ex utroque priore, aut propria meditatione, aut aliena institutione eruta, velut Lumine acquisito; cujus iterum Media præcipua sunt, discursus Rationis, & Authoritas (i.e. Judicium & Praxis) universalis Eccle-siæ.
units.tr: Having begun the treatment of the passive obligation of conscience from the earlier term, I have so far proceeded that, after first uncovering and rejecting those hiding-places, in which the common sort of men vainly flatter themselves that there is some help, either for the fruit of their conscience regarding deeds already done, or for its security regarding deeds still to be done (namely through the intention of a good end and the authority of another's example or judgment), I have sought out that proper and adequate rule of conscience to which a person is bound to conform absolutely and simply. Here I showed, first, that God alone has pure and direct authority over men's consciences. Second, that the proximate and immediate rule of conscience is the light of the mind present for the time being, or (which is the same thing) the final judgment of the practical intellect. Third, that the written Word of God is indeed the supreme and primary rule, but not the adequate rule of conscience. Fourth, that the proper and adequate rule of conscience is the will of God, however revealed, or (which is also the same) the Law imposed by God upon the rational creature. I further said that, so that what that will of God is might be understood more fully and distinctly, God Most Good and Great has made his will known to the human race by three means, as it were three lights. First, by the Law of Nature, which consists of certain practical principles known in themselves, and which is also called the Law of God written in our hearts (Rom. 2. 15.), as an inner light and innate to the minds. Second, by the written Word of God, which is contained in the sacred books of both Testaments, as an outer light supernaturally revealed and brought into the minds. Third, by knowledge drawn from either of the former, either by one's own meditation or by another's teaching, as an acquired light*; the chief means of which again are the reasoning of reason and the authority (that is, the judgment and practice) of the universal Church.

units.la: II. Quin & illud submonui, (quò futuræ translationi viam saltem aliquam præstruerem) præter Dei Legem, quæ per se absolutè & vi propria omnium hominum conscientias obligat, idque in summo gradu; esse & alia nonnulla, quæ gradum quendam obligandi obtinent, sed summo illo inferiorem: ut quæ non primariò & per se, sed secundariò & ex consequenti; non absolutè, sed relativè; non vi propria, sed virtute divini alicujus præcepti sive instituti in quo fundantur, obligant conscientias. Quæ tamen in eo conveniant omnia, quòd quamcunque habent obligandi vim, eam ex toto divinæ Legi acceptam debeant; (Primum enim in unoquoque genere est causa reliquorum; nec esset divina Lex adæquata Conscientiæ Regula, quod jam antè positum est, si extra ipsam aliquid obligaret, quod non ipsius virtute obligaret :) differunt tamen inter se singula: quemadmodum Specie, propter diversitatem Materia; sic & Gradu, quantum ad obligandi vim. Sunt autem illa in triplici potissimum discrimine. Quædam enim constanter obligant, quorum rursus sunt duo genera: unum eorum quorum obligatio oritur ex potestate alterius, ut Leges humanæ, mandata Parentum, Dominorum, &c. Alterum eorum quorum obligatio oritur ex libera propriæ Voluntatis electione, ut Vota, Juramenta, Pacta, Promissa, & his similia: quædam verò ex accidenti tantùm obligant & velut ambulatoriè, pro hic & nunc, secundùm exigentiam circumstantiarum; ut Lex sive Ratio Scandali.
units.tr: II. Moreover, I also gave this warning (at least to pave some way for the translation to come): besides the Law of God, which of itself binds the consciences of all men absolutely and by its own power, and that to the highest degree, there are also some other things which hold a certain degree of binding, but one lower than that highest one. These bind consciences not primarily and of themselves but secondarily and by consequence; not absolutely but relatively; not by their own power but by the power of some divine precept or institution on which they are founded. All these agree in this, that whatever binding force they have, they must receive it wholly from the divine Law. (For the first thing in each kind is the cause of the rest; nor would the divine Law be the adequate rule of conscience, as has already been said above, if anything bound outside of it that did not bind by its power.) Nevertheless the individual items differ among themselves, as they differ in kind because of the diversity of their matter, so also in degree as regards the force of binding. These differences fall mainly under a threefold distinction. Some things bind constantly, and of these there are again two kinds: one kind is those whose obligation arises from the power of another, such as human laws, the commands of parents, masters, and so on; the other kind is those whose obligation arises from the free choice of one's own will, such as vows, oaths, pacts, promises, and similar things. Other things bind only by accident and, as it were, in a wandering manner, for here and now, according to the demands of circumstances, such as the law or reason of scandal.

units.la: III. Postulat ordinis ratio, ut à primo illo genere ordinamur, in quo familiam ducunt Leges Humanæ. De quarum obligatione quæ à nobis dicendi erunt, ad duas hasce quæstiones revocari possint universa. An sc. obligent conscientias Leges humanæ? & Quatenus obligent? Casuum plerorumque particularium determinatio ad posteriorem quæstionem magis pertinet; de quâ (si Deus annuerit) instituentur futuræ aliquot prælectiones: priorem solam hoc tempore attingemus, hanc sc. An Leges humanæ obligent Conscientias: Subjectum quæstionis non indiget multa explicatione. Lex, sive primò à {1}legendo, i. e. eligendo dicto electivè, ut Ciceroni placuit, quòd Legislatores ea quæ Reipublicæ magis utilia fore judicabant eligerent: sive quod alii malunt, secundò, à legendo item, sed in alia significatione, eâque passivè acceptâ, quod oporteret Leges, mox ubi latæ essent, æneis tabulis incisas, autalias perscriptas & columnis appensas proponi in publico, ut à populo legeretur; sive denique ex aliorum mente tertiò, à {2}ligando, quòd subditos ad eos observandum obligarent. In genere nihil aliud est quàm regula agendi subdito à superiore potestatem habente impositæ. Dicuntur autem Humanæ Leges per oppositionem ad Divinas. Sicut enim Divinæ appellantur eæ Leges, quæ Dei ipsius authoritate immediatè constitutæ sunt, sive eæ Naturales sint, sive Positivæ: sic Humanæ dicuntur eæ Leges, quæ, etiamsi per authoritatem ipsis à Deo derivatam, ab hominibus tamen immediatè imperatæ & subditis impositæ sunt.
units.tr: III. The order of the argument requires that we deal first with that first kind, in which human laws take the lead. All that we shall have to say about their obligation can be reduced to two questions: whether, that is, human laws bind consciences? and how far they bind? The determination of most particular cases pertains more to the latter question, and concerning that some lectures will be given in future, if God grants it. At this time we shall touch only on the former, namely, whether human laws bind consciences. The subject of the question needs little explanation. The word lex (law) is derived, first, from legere, that is, to choose (taken actively), as Cicero thought, because lawgivers chose those things which they judged would be more useful to the commonwealth. Or, as others prefer, second, from legere too, but in another sense, taken passively, because it was necessary that laws, as soon as they were enacted, be set forth in public, engraved on bronze tablets, or otherwise written out and hung on columns, so that they might be read by the people. Or finally, according to the mind of others, third, from ligare (to bind), because they bound subjects to observe them. In general a law is nothing other than a rule of action imposed on a subject by a superior who has power. Now human laws are so called by contrast with divine ones. For just as those laws are called divine which are established immediately by the authority of God himself, whether they are natural or positive, so those laws are called human which, although by an authority derived to them from God, are nevertheless commanded immediately by men and imposed on subjects.

units.la: IV. Definitur porro Lex Humana ab Aquinate, ¹ Rationis ordinatio ad bonum commune, ab eo qui curam communitatis habet promulgata : ab aliis alter; quoad verba, sed ferè in eundem sensum.
units.tr: IV. Furthermore, human law is defined by Aquinas¹ as an ordinance of reason for the common good, promulgated by him who has charge of the community; others define it differently in words, but almost to the same sense.

units.la: Et quidem rectè : siquidem convenit ista definitio Legi publicæ, quæ est notissima & usitatissima ejus vocabuli acceptio ; & Analogum per se positum (ut dici solet) pro famosiore significato stare præsumitur. Sed in præsenti quæstione, & quod nostrum instituum attinet, sub nomine Legum Humanarum intelligendæ veniunt, non tantùm Leges publicæ Communitatum, (licet eæ potissimùm & primariò,) sed & mandata particularia parentum, dominorum, aliorumve quorumcunque prælatorum sive superiorum, filiis, servis aliisve subditis suis imperata. In hoc enim uno inter Legem propriè di-ctam & Mandatum discrimen præcipuè cernitur, quum utrumque fit Præcepti species ; quòd Mandatum sive Jussum fit personæ privatæ privatam authoritatem habentis Præceptum, Lex autem Præceptum communiter personæ publicæ potestate præditæ : Cætera fere sunt paria. Certè ad obligandi vim & effectum quod attinet, qua de re nunc agitur, quum ex hujus Capitis versu 1. constet, omnem omninò legitimam potestatem, quæcunque demum illa fuerit, non publicam modò, (de qua tamen sola fateor inibi ex instituto loqui Apostolum,) sed & privatam, à Deo constitutam esse ; & hinc mandatum mandatum patris filio, non minus quàm lex principis subdito, agendi regula: quæ de obligatione Legum Humanarum à me dicenda erunt, ita intelli- gi par est, (quod semel præmonuisse sufficiet) ut [?]una cum publicis legibus privatorum etiam mandata cum politicæ constitutionibus œconomicæ quoque [?]iura, aliaque id genus similia (quatenus saltem [?]ratio analogiæ ratio) complectantur. Et hæc de Subjecto Quæstionis.
units.tr: And rightly so: for that definition fits public law, which is the best known and most common sense of that word; and an analogous term, when set down on its own (as is commonly said), is presumed to stand for its more famous meaning. But in the present question, and as far as our purpose is concerned, under the name of human laws are to be understood not only the public laws of communities (although these chiefly and primarily), but also the particular commands of parents, masters, or of any other superiors or prelates whatever, imposed on their sons, servants, or other subjects. For the chief difference between a law properly so called and a command lies in this alone: that both are kinds of precept, but a command or order is a precept of a private person who has private authority, whereas a law is a precept of a person generally invested with public power. In other respects they are nearly alike. Certainly, as regards the force and effect of binding, which is the matter now under discussion, since it is clear from verse 1 of this chapter that every lawful power, of whatever kind it may be, is established by God, not only public power (although I grant that the Apostle is speaking there specifically of public power) but also private power, it follows that a father's command to his son is a rule of action no less than a prince's law to a subject. What I shall say about the obligation of human laws should be understood (it will suffice to have warned of this once) so as to embrace, along with public laws, also the commands of private persons, and along with political constitutions* the economic rights of households, and other things of that sort, at least insofar as the reason of analogy extends. And so much for the subject of the question.

units.la: V. Prædicatum est, Conscientiæ obligatio. Quid sit Conscientia, quid item in genere Obligatio, fuit à me dudum fusè satis explicatum; nec opus est repetitu: Legem autem obligare cum dicimus, nil aliud volumus, quàm quòd Lex imponit subdito necessitatem parendi ipsámque observandi. Scindum est enim Legem ex sui naturâ, & quatenus lex est, duplicem habere vim, sive effectum necessarium: vim sc. dirigendi, unde & κανὼν[?] dicitur seu Regula, quatenus notificat subdito voluntatem superioris, & ostendit quid superior ab eo fieri velit; & vim obligandi (per quam differt à Consilio & Monitu,) quatenus imperat ut voluntati suæ à subdito mos geratur, & ipsum ita ad imperata facienda obstringit, ut si non pareat peccet.
units.tr: V. The predicate is the obligation of conscience. What conscience is, and likewise what obligation is in general, has been explained by me at length some time ago, and there is no need to repeat it. When we say that a law obliges, we mean nothing other than that the law imposes on the subject a necessity of obeying and of observing it. For it must be noted that a law, from its own nature and insofar as it is a law, has a twofold force or necessary effect: first, the force of directing, whence it is also called a canon [κανὼν] or rule, insofar as it makes known to the subject the will of the superior and shows what the superior wishes to be done by him; and second, the force of binding (by which it differs from counsel and admonition), insofar as it commands* that its will be obeyed by the subject, and so binds him to perform what is commanded, that if he does not obey, he sins.

units.la: Siquidem nihil aliud est Peccatum, quàm aberratio, sive recessus à regulâ illâ sive Lege quam sequi debemus, (ἡ ἁμαρτία ἢ ἀνομία[?]) licut monstra, propter recessum ab ordinaria Naturæ Lege dicuntur Peccata Naturæ. Sciendum tamen secundo, Legis hunc effectum, vim sc. obligativam, fundari in Voluntate & Potestate Legislatoris: ita ut proprie loquendo, non tàm Lex ipsa, quàm Voluntas & Potestas Legislatoris, obliget effectivè; causando scil. vel inducendo obligationem per modum Causæ efficientis. Dici tamen potest & solet Lex obligare terminativè, sc. ut terminus obligationis, & per modum Causæ exemplaris: quia est id ad quod obligatur quis, qui ex ejus præscripto operetur; sicut artifex in operando dirigitur ab exemplari sibi proposito. Sciendum tertio, quòd obligare Conscientiam, est ita astringere aliquem ad obediendum sub mortali (ut loqui amant Scholæ Magistri) hoc est, sub culpâ mortali; ut si non pareat, non solum pœnæ temporali, aut legibus constitutæ, aut ex arbitrio superioris inferendæ, obnoxius sit, sed & à propria Conscientia velut negligenti officii, contraæque inde offensionis Dei reus, merito redarguatur.
units.tr: For sin is nothing other than a straying or departure from that rule or law which we ought to follow [ἡ ἁμαρτία ἢ ἀνομία], just as monsters are called sins of nature because they depart from the ordinary law of nature. It must be noted, secondly, that this effect of the law, namely its obligating force, is founded in the will and power of the lawgiver. So, properly speaking, it is not so much the law itself as the will and power of the lawgiver that obliges effectively, causing or inducing obligation by way of an efficient cause. Yet a law can be said, and is customarily said, to oblige terminatively, that is, as the terminus of the obligation, and by way of an exemplary cause: because it is that to which a person is bound, and by whose prescription he acts, just as the craftsman in his work is guided by the pattern set before him. It must be noted, thirdly, that to bind the conscience is so to bind a person to obey under mortal sin (as the Schoolmen like to put it), that is, under mortal guilt; so that if he does not obey, he is liable not only to temporal punishment, whether fixed by law or to be inflicted at the discretion of the superior, but is also rightly reproached by his own conscience as negligent of duty, and guilty of offence against God.

units.la: VI. Sensus itaque Quæstionis est, An Leges Humanæ habeant vim obligandi Conscientias eorum quibus feruntur, eo quo jam expositum est modo? Negant è Protestantibus Calvinus, (ut ipsi saltem {1}objicit Bellarminus) Beza, & alii nonnulli: è Pontificiis Gerson (fatente etiam Bellarmino,) Almain, & (ut aliqui volunt) Navarrus. Affirmant è Protestantibus Musculus, Ursinus, & alii: & è Pontificiis, Jesuitarum & Scholasticorum plurima turba. Sunt qui distinguunt; ut {2}David Pareus, & alii. Et sanè fatendum est, si non ἐριδολογίας [?] & nimio contradicendi studio utrinque peccatum esset, jamdudum è medio tolli potuisset istam controversiam. In istiusmodi disputationibus subinde mihi veniunt in mentem, quæ apud Aristotelem adolescentem me legisse memini, ἀλλ' ὡς μὲν δεῖ, πῶς δ' ἐ [?]. Ubi disputat An Priora sint contraria? An detur infinitum? &c. Et sanè ταῦτα δεῖ [?] (liquidem est illa vera illius loci lectio, Phys.) arbitrio nimirum potius opus est, qui utramque sententiam (specie magis pugnantem quàm re) in unum conciliet; quàm Judices, qui dum statuunt alteram partem, alteram damnent. Quod fortassis in non paucis earum controversiarum, quæ in orbe Christiano magnâ cum animorum contentione & stylique acrimonia jamdiu inter partes agitantur, obtineret ; si tam studio pacis & charitatis, quam odio partium agerentur, qui Theologica tractant. Equidem in præsenti quæstione, quantum ex paucorum eorum lectione, quos mihi & alias occupato, & parum firmæ valetudinis, in hac temporis angustia consulere licuit, judicare possum, demptis utrinque quæ expressit contentionis æstus, neutri mihi pessimè[?] sentire videntur. Existimo tamen eos qui affirmative definiunt, (ut aperte quid de tota re sentiam eloquar) & commodius ad vitæ institutionem, & cautius utriusque ad vitandum errandi periculum, & ad formam sanorum verborum propius locutos, quam qui negative. Cæterum, ut quid hac in re (ut mea fert sententia) statuendum sit, distinctius vobis ab oculis ponam; rem universam quam potero breviter & dilucide quibusdam Conclusionibus complectar; sententiam meam, ubi opus est, aliquot rationibus confirmabo, & quæ afferri solent ex adversa parte objectiones diluam.
units.tr: VI. The sense of the question, therefore, is: Do human laws have the power to bind the consciences of those to whom they are given, in the manner just explained? Among Protestants, Calvin (as Bellarmine at least objects to him), Beza, and some others deny it; among the Papists, Gerson (Bellarmine too admits this), Almain, and (as some hold) Navarrus. Among Protestants, Musculus, Ursinus and others affirm it, and among the Papists a very great crowd of Jesuits and Scholastics. Some distinguish, as David Pareus and others do. And indeed it must be admitted that, if it were not for [ἐριδολογίας] wrangling and an excessive zeal for contradiction on both sides, this controversy could have been removed long ago. In disputations of this kind there often come to my mind things which I remember reading as a young man in Aristotle, where he argues whether contraries are prior, whether the infinite exists, and so on, in the passage beginning [ἀλλ' ὡς μὲν δεῖ, πῶς δ' ἐ]. And indeed [ταῦτα δεῖ] (for that is the true reading of that passage in the Physics) what is needed is a judgement that would reconcile both opinions, more opposed in appearance than in reality, into one, rather than judges who, while they decide for one party, condemn the other. This would perhaps prevail in not a few of those controversies which have long been contested among the parties in the Christian world with great heat of spirit and bitterness of style, if those who treat theological matters acted as much from zeal for peace and charity as from hatred of parties. For my part, in the present question, as far as I can judge from reading a few of those authors (since I have had little time, being occupied with other matters and of rather weak health, in this present scarcity of time), with the heat of contention removed on both sides, neither side seems to me to be altogether wrong. Yet I think those who define affirmatively (to state plainly what I think of the whole matter) have spoken more suitably to the conduct of life, more cautiously to avoid the danger of error on either side, and closer to the form of sound words, than those who define negatively. But, to set before your eyes more clearly what must be determined in this matter, as my opinion holds, I will embrace the whole thing as briefly and clearly as I can in certain Conclusions; I will confirm my view, where necessary, by several reasons, and I will dissolve the objections usually brought from the other side.

units.la: VII. Conclusio Prima. Leges humanæ injustæ non obligant ad obediendum. Manifesta res, modò verba rectè intelligantur. Nequis tamen ea secus quàm par est interpretetur, animadvertendum est, posse Legem aliquam injustam dici ; vel ratione Finis, Modi, aut Circumstantiæ alicujus Legi ipsi extrinsecæ, vel ratione Materiæ sive Objecti ipsius Legis: Distat enim, imperetúrne quod manifestè injustum est ; an quod alias fortasse non sit injustum, injustè tamen imperetur. Tollit obligationem id injustitiæ genus, quod Legi ipsi per se adhæret respectu rei imperatæ : non tollit id genus, quod extrinsecus ei advenit & ex accidenti, vitio sc. imperantis. Esto enim Princeps lege latâ juberet aliquid fieri quod non esset ex se factu illicitum ; vel fieri prohiberet quod non esset simpliciter necessarium ; nulla tamen justa subesset causa cur aut illud juberet. aut hoc prohiberet, sed aut turpis lucri; cupiditate, aut exercendae tyrannidis mera libidine, aut pravo alio quocunque animi affectu adductus: injusta quidem esset Lex ex parte imperantis; subditus tamen ad parendum, nihilominus obligaretur. Ratio est, quia injustitia illa tenet se ex parte imperantis tantum, non autem ex parte rei imperatae. Adeo ut, quamvis non posset Princeps sine peccato ejusmodi legem ferre, poterit tamen subditus quod ea lege imperatum est sine peccato facere. Et quicquid potest ab ipso sine peccato fieri, id omne subditus, si postuletur ex obedientiae debito, tenetur praestare. Qua intentione quove consilio Princeps legem tulerit, ipse viderit: id mea qui subditus sim nihil interest, nec siquid ille ea in re peccaverit, mihi imputabitur: Imputabitur, modo nihil imperetur nisi quod a me licite fieri poterit, si officio meo defuero, nec paruero.
units.tr: VII. First Conclusion. Unjust human laws do not bind to obedience. This is a plain matter, provided the words are rightly understood. Lest anyone interpret them otherwise than they should, it must be noted that a law may be called unjust either by reason of its end, mode, or circumstance, which are extrinsic to the law itself, or by reason of the matter or object of the law itself. For there is a difference between whether what is manifestly unjust is commanded, and whether what perhaps is not unjust in itself is commanded unjustly. That kind of injustice which adheres to the law itself per se, with respect to the thing commanded, removes the obligation; that kind which comes to it from outside and by accident, namely through the fault of the commander, does not. For suppose a prince, having issued a law, should command something to be done which is not in itself unlawful, or forbid what is not simply necessary; yet there is no just cause why he commands this or forbids that, but he is moved by a desire for base gain, or by the sheer lust of exercising tyranny, or by some other wicked passion of mind. The law would indeed be unjust on the part of the commander; yet the subject would nonetheless be bound to obey. The reason is that this injustice pertains only to the part of the commander, not to the part of the thing commanded. So that, although the prince could not enact such a law without sin, the subject can do without sin what is commanded by that law. And whatever can be done by him without sin, the subject, if it is demanded by the debt of obedience, is bound to render. With what intention or purpose the prince passed the law, he himself will see; it matters nothing to me, who am the subject, nor will any fault he has committed in this be imputed to me. It will be imputed to me only if nothing is commanded except what can lawfully be done by me, and if I fail in my duty and do not obey.

units.la: VIII. Quin & illud insuper adjicio, si Lex ipsa etiam ratione Materiae sive Objecti sit forte injusta & subditum gravet; ut exempli gratia, si imperet pensiorem gravioris tributi quam res postulat, non tamen propterea continuo solvi obligationem.
units.tr: VIII. Moreover I add this too: if the law itself, even by reason of its matter or object, is perhaps unjust and burdens the subject, for example, if it commands a heavier tax than the thing requires, the obligation is nonetheless not dissolved straightaway.

units.la: Sed hic iterum opus est distinctione. Potest enim aliquid esse injustum, vel eo solum nomine quod sit perpessu iniquum, vel eo quod sit etiam factu illicitum. Illo modo si injustum est, quod Lege imperatur, hoc est, si iniquum sit tantum & non inhonestum, & tamen fiat, unius imperantis culpa est: tamen abest a culpa qui obsequitur imperio, ut omnino peccaret si non obsequeretur. At posteriori modo siquid imperetur injustum, hoc est, si quod postulatur sit non solum grave perpessu, sed etiam factu turpe, & tamen a subdito fiat; utrinque peccatur: a praelato, quod rem iniquam postulaverit; a subdito quod rem illicitam effecerit. Sensus ergo Conclusionis est, ubicunque Lex imperando aliquid prohibet fieri quod est ita necessarium ut non possit à subdito omitti sine peccato, vel imperando jubet aliquid fieri quod est ita illicitum ut non possit ab eodem sine peccato fieri, Legem illam non obligare in Conscientia.
units.tr: But here again a distinction is needed. For something may be unjust either merely on the ground that it is grievous to suffer, or on the ground that it is also unlawful to do. In the former sense, if what is commanded by law is unjust, that is, if it is merely unfair and not dishonourable, and yet it is done, the fault lies with the commander alone; the one who obeys is free from blame, since he would have sinned altogether had he not obeyed. But in the latter sense, if something unjust is commanded, that is, if what is demanded is not only grievous to suffer but also base to do, and yet it is done by the subject, sin is committed on both sides: by the superior, because he has demanded an unfair thing; by the subject, because he has done an unlawful thing. The sense of the Conclusion, therefore, is this: wherever the law, by forbidding, prohibits something from being done which is so necessary that it cannot be omitted by the subject without sin, or, by commanding, orders something to be done which is so unlawful that it cannot be done by the same subject without sin, that law does not bind in conscience.

units.la: IX. Ratio Prima, quia rei illicitæ (ut {1}alias fuse ostendimus) nulla potest esse obligatio. Secunda; quia (ut ibi etiam dictum est) Obligatio prior præjudicat posteriori, ita ut ei non possit superinduci Obligatio nova contraria: At Lex jubens rem illicitam, ut Homicidium, Perjurium, Sacrilegium, &c. aut prohibens officium necessarium, ut Cultum veri Dei, Debitum Principibus & parentibus obsequium, &c. id exigit quod contrarium est obligationi priori, quâ virtute præcepti divini subditus jam ante constrictus tenebatur. Proinde Lex humana istiusmodi non potest inducere subdito obligationem. Tertia, quia nemo potest simul obligari ad contradictoria. Sed si Lex ejusmodi esset obligatoria, obligaret ad id faciendum, ad quod non faciendum Lex Dei eodem tempore obligaret: facere autem & non facere sunt contradictoria.
units.tr: IX. First reason: because for an unlawful thing (as we have shown at length elsewhere) there can be no obligation. Second: because (as was also said there) a prior obligation prejudices a later one, so that a new and contrary obligation cannot be superinduced upon it. But a law commanding an unlawful thing, such as murder, perjury, sacrilege, and so on, or forbidding a necessary duty, such as the worship of the true God or the due obedience owed to princes and parents, and so on, demands what is contrary to the prior obligation, by virtue of which the subject was already bound by the precept of God. Therefore a human law of this kind cannot induce an obligation on the subject. Third: because no one can be bound to contradictories at the same time. But if such a law were binding, it would oblige a person to do what the law of God at the same time obliges him not to do; and to do and not to do are contradictories.

units.la: Quarta ; ab exemplis piorum, qui ex fidei suæ principiis sic instituti semper fuerunt, ut Imperatorum jussa, (tametsi gravia, si non inhonesta,) alacri animo capesserent, obirent, exequerentur: at si quid abs eis vel Lege lata exigeretur, quod esset contra fidem aut bonos mores, vel cum honesto quomodolibet pugnaret, palam & constanti animo imperium detrectarent, & præ Dei timore Leges & instituta quævis humana contemnerent. Lege lata Babylonica ut audito musico concentu aureum grande simulachrum quod erexerat potentissimus Monarcha, singuli adorarent, idque severissima propositâ si quis secus facerent pœna, non se passi sunt ea Lege obligari tres Hebræi adolescentes, Dan. 3. Quia scilicet jubebatur ut illicita, cita, cultus Idoli. Lege itidem Persica lata, nequis per aliquot dies à quoquam Deo vel homine præterquam uno Persarum Rege quicquam peteret, non paruit Daniel, sed eo ipso quo solitus est more, statis temporibus Deum precatus est. Dan. 6. Et prohibiti Petrus & Johannes ne ultra loquerentur in nomine Jesu, Act. 4. non solùm non paruerunt imperato, sed & fidenter responderunt, Utrum justum sit coram Deo vobis potius obaudire quam Deo, ipsi judicate. Nimirum quia utrobique quæ prohibebantur erant res necessariæ, illic cultus veri Dei, hic concredita ipsis Evangelii prædicatio.
units.tr: Fourth: the examples of pious people, who have always been formed by the principles of their faith to obey the commands of emperors, even when they were burdensome, if not dishonourable, with a ready mind, carrying them out and executing them. But if anything was demanded of them, whether by a law passed or otherwise, that was against the faith or good morals, or in any way conflicted with what is honourable, they openly and steadfastly refused the command, and out of fear of God they despised all laws and human institutions whatever. When the Babylonian law was passed, that at the sound of the music everyone should worship the great golden image that the most powerful monarch had set up, under the most severe penalty for anyone who acted otherwise, the three young Hebrews did not allow themselves to be bound by that law, Dan. 3. Clearly because it was commanded as unlawful: the worship of an idol. Likewise, when the Persian law was passed, that for some days no one should ask anything of any god or man except the one King of the Persians, Daniel did not obey, but at the set times, in the very manner he was accustomed to, he prayed to God, Dan. 6. And when Peter and John were forbidden to speak any more in the name of Jesus, Acts 4, they not only did not obey the order, but also answered boldly: Whether it is right in the sight of God to obey you rather than God, you judge. Indeed, because in both cases what was forbidden was a necessary thing: there the worship of the true God, here the preaching of the Gospel entrusted to them.

units.la: X. Conclusio Secunda. Lex Humana prohibens rem simpliciter malam, ut furtum, adulterium, sacrilegium; aut jubens rem bonam & necessariam, ut cultum Dei, solutionem debiti, honorem parentum; inducit novam obligationem in Conscientia. Ratio prima; quia, posita Causa propria, sequitur effectus ejus necessarius, nisi aliunde impediatur. Obligatio autem est Legis effectus ita neceffarius, ut aliqui exiftimârint ab hoc ligandi effectu ipsum Legis nomen (sicut ante dictum est) originem suam traxisse; nec videtur hic aliquid assignari posse, quod istius effectus consecutionem impediat. Ratio secunda, à minore ad majus. Obligat omnium confessione Lex prohibens rem alias licitam, aut jubens rem alias liberam: ergo multò etiam magis prohibens rem illicitam: vel jubens rem necessariam. Est tamen quod utrique huic rationi ex adverso opponi posse videtur: Scilicet, Non esse multiplicanda entia sine necessitate; obligari jam ante unumquemque vi Legis Divinæ ad faciendum quicquid est necessarium, & ad non faciendum quicquid est illicitum, quæ obligatio excludit eam quam ex Humana Lege consequi supponimus, ut superfluam, sicut præexistens in vase pleno liquor impedit infusionem novi liquoris : Nec videntur admitti posse duæ obligationes ad eandem rem in eadem Conscientia magis quàm duo accidentia ejusdem speciei in eodem subjecto. Sed respondeo, dici quidem solere & quidem verè Obligationem priorem præjudicare posteriori, (quo argumento & ipsi paulò ante usi sumus in firmamentum superioris Conclusionis ;) sed hoc dictum in iis tantùm Obligationem locum habere, quæ sunt invicem destructivæ, & quarum effectus tantum habent inter se contrarietatem & repugnantiam, ut posita alterutra necessariò tollatur reliqua : hoc tamen non impedire quin obligationi priori accedere possit altera, quæ sit ejusdem rationis, & possit cum ea consistere. Neque est simile quod de liquore affertur in vase pleno : quia impedimentum ne vas plenum novum liquorem admittat, non fit ex parte liquoris, sed provenit ex incapacitate vasis & natura Loci, qui non potest simul recipere plura corpora. Et accidentia nihil prohibet esse in eodem subjecto ejusdem speciei plura, modò sint relativa, non absoluta : ut in Socrate, supposito quòd decem haberet filios, decem essent quoque paternitates : Quia relationes multiplicantur ad multiplicationem suorum terminorum : & modò iximus[?] Legem obligare ad modum termini. Ergo quot sunt Leges, (quum sit omnis Lex, ex natura sua & quatenus Lex est, inductiva obligationis,) totidem etiam erunt Obligationes, illis ut suis terminis correspondentes. Neque verò hoc est multiplicare entia sine necessitate : quia multiplicatis causis, necesse est multiplicari effectus illarum causarum. Immo hoc ipsum, ne cui incredibile videatur, aut quod huic persimile est, quotidie contingere videmus, & in Naturalibus & in Moralibus. Nam & sensui evidens est, posse aliquem ad columnam duobus vel tribus vinculis alligari : ut Petrus, Act. 12. 6. Cubavit [illegible, ~9 letters] ἁλύσει[?] δυσί. Nec potest cuiquam esse dubium, quin possit aliquis ad id officium quod ipsi ex Lege Divina praestandum incumbit, non obstante illa obligatione, denuo se obligare Voto, vel Juramento, vel Promissione. Quemadmodum vovit Jacobus Patriarcha, unicum sibi Deum fore Jehovam, Gen. 28[?]. 21. Et David juravit justa se Dei judicia custoditurum. Psal. 119. 106[?]. Et quotquot fumus Christiani, cum sacro fonte tingeremur, novo nomine baptismali obstrinximus ad fidem in Christum, ad abrenunciandum Satanae, Seculo, Carni; ad observanda Dei mandata: ad quae tamen omnia praestanda nos ante Obligatos fuisse certissimum est.
units.tr: X. Second Conclusion. A human law forbidding a thing that is simply evil, such as theft, adultery, sacrilege, or commanding a thing that is good and necessary, such as the worship of God, the payment of a debt, honour to parents, induces a new obligation in conscience. First reason: because, once the proper cause is posited, its necessary effect follows, unless it is hindered from elsewhere. Now obligation is the effect of law so necessary that some have thought the very name law (as was said before) derived its origin from this effect of binding; nor does it seem that anything can be pointed out here which would prevent the following of this effect. Second reason, from the less to the greater: a law forbidding a thing otherwise lawful, or commanding a thing otherwise free, obliges, as everyone admits; therefore much more does a law forbidding a thing unlawful, or commanding a thing necessary, oblige. There is, however, something which seems to be able to be opposed to both these reasons: namely, that entities are not to be multiplied without necessity; that each person is already bound, by the force of Divine Law, to do whatever is necessary and to refrain from whatever is unlawful; and this obligation excludes the one which we suppose follows from human law, as superfluous, just as the liquid already present in a full vessel prevents the pouring in of new liquid. Nor does it seem admissible that two obligations to the same thing can exist in the same conscience, any more than two accidents of the same kind in the same subject. But I answer: it is indeed commonly said, and truly, that a prior obligation prejudices a later one (by which argument we ourselves a little earlier used to support the above conclusion); but this saying holds only for those obligations which are mutually destructive, and whose effects have such contrariety and repugnance between them that, once one is posited, the other is necessarily removed. This, however, does not prevent another obligation from being added to the prior obligation, one of the same kind, which can exist together with it. Nor is the comparison made about the liquid in the full vessel apt: for the hindrance to a full vessel admitting new liquid does not lie on the side of the liquid, but arises from the incapacity of the vessel and the nature of the place, which cannot receive several bodies at once. And nothing prevents several accidents of the same species from being in the same subject, provided they are relative and not absolute: as in Socrates, supposing he had ten sons, there would also be ten fatherhoods; for relations are multiplied according to the multiplication of their terms; and I have just said that law obliges according to the mode of a term. Therefore, as many laws as there are (since every law, by its nature and insofar as it is law, induces obligation), so many obligations will there also be, corresponding to them as their terms. Nor indeed is this multiplying entities without necessity: for when causes are multiplied, it is necessary that the effects of those causes be multiplied too. Indeed, lest this seem incredible to anyone, or something similar to it, we see it happening every day, both in natural and in moral matters. For it is evident even to the senses that someone can be fastened to a pillar by two or three chains, as Peter, Acts 12. 6: sleeping [between two soldiers], bound with two chains [ἁλύσει δυσί]. Nor can anyone doubt that a person may, despite that obligation, bind himself again by a Vow, an Oath, or a Promise to the duty which is incumbent on him to perform by Divine Law. Thus Jacob the Patriarch vowed that Jehovah alone would be his God, Gen. 28. 21; and David swore that he would keep the just judgements of God, Psal. 119. 106. And all of us Christians, when we were washed in the sacred font, bound ourselves with a new baptismal name to faith in Christ, to renouncing Satan, the world and the flesh, and to observing the commandments of God; yet it is most certain that we were already bound to perform all these things before.

units.la: XI. Conclusio Tertia. Leges Humanae, (sive illicita imperentur, sive necessaria, sive adiaphora, lata à persona vel communitate non habente legislatoriam potestatem, non obligant in Conscientia. Ut si Praetor Urbanus Leges ferret huic Academiae; ut vicinus paterfamilias servum meum juberet boves meos jungere, segetes suas occare, &c. Aut collecta hominum seditiosorum manus in aliqua Angliae Comitatu, (quod in agro Norfolciensi, Eduardo sexto regnante sub Ketto duce, alibique aliquoties factum est) incolis certam pecuniae summam, aut operarum servitutem sibi indebitam publicatis edictis imperaret, eósque vi & armis ad imperata facienda cogerent: utut eis forte liceret (posito quòd resistendo pares non essent) imperata facere; ejusmodi tamen jussu neminem censeri ad ea observanda obligarent in Conscientia. Tum quia ejusmodi Leges, nomine tenus duntaxat, aequivocè Leges sunt, re autem vera Violentia magis quàm Leges: Et causa aequivoca non infert effectum; sicut non obligat partes lata à Judice sententia. Tum quia vis obligandi ([?] etiam modò dictum est) non causatur effectivè ab ipsa Lege, sed à conjunctâ cum potestate Legislatoris voluntate. Ergo ubi deficit Potestas, deficit & Causa propriè efficiens istius obligationis: & causâ propriâ deficiente, effectum ejus deficere necesse est. Quod ipsum ex hoc ipso Apostoli loco colligere licet, qui necessitatem τῆς ὑποταγῆς [?], debitum sc. Obedientiæ ex parte subditi, deducit ἀπὸ τῆς ἐξουσίας [?], à Potestate Jurisdictionis in prælato: unde efficitur non teneri quenquam ad parendum ei, qui non habet jus imperandi.
units.tr: XI. Third Conclusion. Human laws, (whether they command unlawful things, or necessary things, or indifferent things), issued by a person or community not having legislative power, do not bind in conscience. For example, if the City Praetor should pass laws for this Academy; or if a neighbouring head of household should order my servant to yoke my oxen, to harrow his crops, and so on; or if a gathered band of seditious men in some English county (as happened in Norfolk under Edward VI, under the leader Ket, and elsewhere several times) should, by published edicts, demand from the inhabitants a certain sum of money, or unjust servitude of labour, and should compel them by force and arms to do what was ordered: although perhaps it would be lawful for them (supposing they were not equal to resisting) to do what was ordered, nevertheless such a command does not oblige anyone in conscience to observe those things. First, because such laws are laws only in name, equivocally, but in truth are violence rather than laws; and an equivocal cause does not produce an effect, just as a sentence pronounced by a judge does not bind the parties. Second, because the power of binding (as was just said also) is not caused effectively by the law itself, but by the will joined with the power of the Legislator. Therefore, where Power is lacking, the Cause strictly efficient of that obligation is also lacking; and when the proper cause is lacking, its effect must necessarily be lacking. This can be gathered from this very passage of the Apostle, who derives the necessity of subjection [τῆς ὑποταγῆς], that is, the due obedience on the part of the subject, from authority [ἀπὸ τῆς ἐξουσίας], from the power of jurisdiction in the superior; whence it follows that no one is bound to obey one who does not have the right to command.

units.la: XII. Si dicas, colluviem ejusmodi qualem jam dixi hominum satis factiosorum habere imperandi potestatem, quia possunt eos in quos imperium exercent ad faciendum imperata cogere: Respondeo, Potestatem de qua loquimur, & à qua pendet Obligatio, non esse potestatem illam quam Græci δύναμιν [?] vocant, hoc est, potestatem, (seu potentiam potius, quâ voce libentius in ea notione plerique utuntur) physicam, sive de facto, per quam quis potens est id quod intendit ita effectui dare, ut finaliter non impediatur: sed eam potestatem quam ἐξουσίαν vocant, hoc est, potestatem legitimam sive de jure, quæ sc. ei competit jure aliquo Naturæ, Gentium, aut Civili, ratione personæ quam gerit, & per respectum ad eos qui ipsi quoquo modo subsunt. Hanc ἐξουσίαν in præsenti argumento ita premit Apostolus, ut eam trium commatum spatio quinquies nominaverit: de δυνάμει [?] interim ne quidem.
units.tr: XII. If you say that a rabble of men of the sort I have just described, being sufficiently factious, has power to command, because they can compel those over whom they exercise command to do what is commanded: I answer that the power of which we speak, and on which obligation depends, is not that power which the Greeks call [δύναμιν], that is, power (or rather might, a word which most people use more readily in that sense) which is physical, or de facto, by which someone is able to bring about what he intends in effect, so that it is not finally hindered; but it is that power which they call [ἐξουσίαν], that is, legitimate power, or de jure, which belongs to a person by some right of Nature, of Nations, or of the Civil law, by reason of the person he bears, and in relation to those who in any way are subject to him. This [ἐξουσίαν] the Apostle so emphasises in the present argument that within the space of three verses he names it five times: but of [δύναμει] he does not so much as mention it.

units.la: XIII. At certum est, inquies, eos qui Romæ principatum gerebant illo Apostolorum ævo, nec hereditario jure, nec liberis populi suffragiis, nec legitima aliàs vocatione ad imperii culmen conscendisse, sed aut vi aut dolo aut militari tumultu imperium usurpâsse: quibus tamen & ἐξουσίαν ut legitimis magistratibus, difertim tribuit Apostolus; & subditis parendi necessitatem [ἀνάγκην τάξεως] [?] imponit, idque non supplicii metu tam tùm sed & propter conscientiam. Primos illos post eversam Remp. Imperatores Romanos sanè fatendum est non optimo jure imperium adeptos; habuisse tamen jus gladii & legitimam [illegible, ~8 letters] , sive jurisdictionem, cui subesse deberent quotquot Romanae ditionis essent homines, fatendum est pariter. Neque enim quisquam erat singularium hominum qui eam potestatem; ut ubi potiore jure debitam vindicare posset; & Senatus populusque Romanus penes quem novissimè & ab aliquot retrò seculis summa fuisset potestas, quà metu quà obsequio, juri suo utcunque cesserant, eósque qui imperium malis artibus quaesivissent, pro suis tamen legitimis principibus agnoverant. Hoc dato, quod mihi certè omninò concedendum videtur, de obediendi necessitate nulla potest reliqua esse dubitatio. At in casu dubio, quod sit Christiani hominis officium, an & quatenus obligetur in foro Conscientiae tempori cedere, praesentibus moribus se accommodare; legibus, edictis, aliisque jussis ejus qui de facto, nullo tamen jure (suo saltem judicio) summae rerum praeest, obtemperare: non peraeque facile est dijudicare; nec prudentis est in re tam gravi, tam ardua, quicquam temerè definire.
units.tr: XIII. But it is certain, you will say, that those who held power at Rome in the age of the Apostles had reached the summit of empire neither by hereditary right, nor by the votes of the people, nor by any other lawful call, but had seized the empire either by force, or by fraud, or by military uproar. Yet to these men too the Apostle plainly grants authority, as to lawful magistrates, and he lays upon subjects the necessity of obedience [ἀνάγκην τάξεως], and that not only through fear of punishment at the time but for conscience' sake. We must certainly admit that the first Roman emperors after the commonwealth was overthrown did not obtain the empire by the best right; yet it must equally be admitted that they had the right of the sword and lawful jurisdiction, to which all who were within the Roman dominion ought to be subject. For there was no private individual who could claim that power by a better right; and the Senate and Roman people, in whom supreme power had last resided and for some centuries past, had yielded their right in some measure, partly from fear and partly from compliance, and had acknowledged as their lawful princes those who had sought the empire by evil arts. Granting this, which seems to me to be certainly to be wholly conceded, no doubt at all can remain about the necessity of obedience.
