But in a doubtful case, what is the duty of a Christian man: whether and how far he is bound in the forum of conscience to yield to the times and accommodate himself to present customs, and to obey the laws, edicts and other commands of one who de facto, but with no right (at least in his own judgment), presides over the highest affairs: this is not equally easy to decide, nor is it the mark of a prudent man to define rashly anything in a matter so grave and so difficult.

units.la: XIV. Nihil itaque statuo. Ne tamen aut officio meo, aut vestrae saltem expectationi defuisse existimer, si quam in medium produxeram quaestionem intactam prorsus relinquerem; quid mihi de tota hac re serio cogitanti visum est rectae rationi maximè consentaneum (nisi si forte, ut in istiusmodi deliberationibus ferè contingit, aliud suadeant [illegible, ~6 letters]) paucis exponam. Dico igitur Primò, Eum qui de facto summum in civitate imperium obtinet, etsi malis artibus potestatem illam sibi quaesiverit, civi tamen pro legitimo principe habendum esse, eique ut legitimo principi ex Conscientiæ Obligatione esse obtemperandum, modò nulla subsit in contrarium justa dubitandi ratio. Videtur autem ea sola esse in hoc casu justa & idonea dubitandi ratio, cum civi aut certò constet, aut saltem valde sit probabile, aliam esse aliquam personam cui summa potestas meliori jure debeatur. Hoc ni fuerit, non poterit civis bonâ conscientiâ possidentis imperium detrectare. Neque enim ad civem pertinet (ordinariè) quo jure possideat, qui possidet, curiosius inquirere: sufficit ei ad conscientiæ securitatem quòd de facto possideat, nec sit alius quispiam (saltem quod ipsi cognitum fit,) qui de jure possidere debeat. Huc facit, præter jam dicta de Romanis Imperatoribus oppressâ Rep. rerum potitis, universa penè Israeliticorum Regum historia. Quorum plerique nullo juris prætextu nixi, sed vi injustâ, & nefario scelere, regnum consecuti, simulac (extincta funditus regia antecessorum fobole, nequis superesset qui in jura paterna aut avitâ succederet) thronum conscendissent, Regnum deinceps quasi pleno & proprio jure administrarunt: præstitáque est eis à populo, haud secùs ac optimo jure imperium obtinerent, obedientia. Neque vero id ipsis vitio versum uspiam legimus: quin potius suadebat recta ratio sic fieri oportere. Interest nimirum salutis publicæ, ut esset qui ad Reipublicæ gubernacula sederet: nec civium rerumque[?] suarum incolumitati satis aliàs prospectum fuisset, si cujus jure (possidentis utique) nullum esset potius, ejus non haberetur jus potissimum. Et ex jure gentium, quæ nullius sunt transeunt in jus occupantium.
units.tr: XIV. I therefore lay down nothing. Yet, lest I should seem to have failed in my duty, or at least in your expectation, if I left untouched the question I had put forward, I will briefly set out what seems to me, thinking seriously about the whole matter, most consonant with right reason (unless perhaps, as usually happens in deliberations of this kind, other considerations suggest otherwise). I say, then, first: one who de facto holds supreme power in the state, even if he has sought that power by evil arts, is nevertheless to be regarded by a citizen as a lawful prince, and is to be obeyed as a lawful prince from the obligation of conscience, provided that no just ground for doubt stands against it. Now the only just and suitable ground for doubt in this case seems to be when it is either certain to the citizen, or at least very probable, that some other person has a better right to supreme power. Unless this is so, a citizen cannot with a good conscience refuse to obey one who possesses the empire. For it does not (ordinarily) belong to the citizen to inquire too closely by what right he who possesses, possesses; it is enough for the security of his conscience that he holds it de facto, and that there is no other person (at least so far as is known to him) who ought to hold it de jure. To this point, besides what has already been said of the Roman emperors who seized control of the ruined commonwealth, almost the whole history of the Israelite kings bears witness. Most of them, relying on no pretext of right but by unjust force and wicked crime, obtained the kingdom; and as soon as they had mounted the throne (the royal offspring of their predecessors having been utterly destroyed, lest any should survive to succeed to the paternal or ancestral right), they administered the kingdom thereafter as if by full and their own right; and obedience was rendered to them by the people just as if they held the empire by the best right. Nor do we read anywhere that this was counted against them as a fault; rather, right reason suggested that it should be so. For it is indeed in the interest of public safety that there should be someone to sit at the helm of the commonwealth; nor would the safety of citizens and of their property have been sufficiently provided for otherwise, if the one whose right (of possession at least) is unopposed were not regarded as having the strongest right. And by the law of nations, things that belong to no one pass into the right of the one who takes possession of them.

units.la: XV. Dico Secundò, In regno hæreditario, ubi inter duos aut plures petitores jus dubium est; lite adhuc pendente, & interim dum res aut amicâ tractatione aut bello cernatur, bohi[?] civis officium esse, ei qui in imperii possessione fit, ut legitimo Principi parere. Cujus casus occurrunt passim in hiftoriis plurima exempla. Inter illustriora quæ contigerunt inter competitores Regni Lusitaniæ complures post mortem Sebaftiani Regis; & Regni Scotiæ etiam (sex ad minimum post mortem Regis Alexandri de Regno lites; & inter nobilifsimas familias Eboracenfem & Lancaftrenfem de fuccessione Anglicani Regni acris admodum & diuturna contentio. Omnium toto Orbe populorum consensu, Jura ubique favisse certum est possidenti: & in istiusmodi casibus obtinuit semper celebre illud Jurisconsultorum pronunciatum, In rebus dubiis melior est conditio possidentis.
units.tr: XV. I say secondly: in a hereditary kingdom, where between two or more claimants the right is doubtful, while the suit is still pending, and in the meantime, while the matter is being decided either by amicable negotiation or by war, it is the duty of a good citizen to obey, as lawful prince, him who is in possession of the throne. Cases of this kind occur everywhere in histories, with very many examples. Among the more notable that have occurred are: several disputes among the competitors for the kingdom of Portugal after the death of King Sebastian; and in the kingdom of Scotland too (at least six lawsuits over the kingdom after the death of King Alexander); and between the most noble families, York and Lancaster, there was a very sharp and long-lasting contention over the succession to the English kingdom. By the consent of the peoples of the whole world, it is certain that the laws everywhere favoured the possessor; and in such cases that famous saying of the jurists has always prevailed: In doubtful matters the condition of the possessor is better.

units.la: XVI. Cæterum, ubi quis pulso vi & armis legitimo principe regníque hærede, vel ita oppresso ut ju[?]s suum persequi non possit, eo tamen adhuc superstite, imperii habenas arripit, & fe pro Rege gerit, quum sit verius Regni invasor quàm Rex; ita ut jam non sit ultrà jus dubium, sed aperta injuria: quæris quid in hoc casu bono civi faciendum sit? censeam, qui fidelitatem legitimo principi fortiter juravit; aut si non juravit, non minus tamen debet, quàm si juratus esset: Dico Tertiò, mihi videri non solum licere bono civi, legibus ab eo quasi summum imperium de facto, sed non de jure possidenti latis parere, aliàque ab eo Imperata (modò non sint factu turpe aut injustum quod imperatur) facere: verùm etiam, postulante humanarum rerum conditione, eò necessitatis deveniri posse, adeóque sæpissimè deveniri, ut ni sic fecerit, defuisse officio suo existimandus sit. Atqui dictum est modò, Leges à non habente legitimam potestatem latæ non obligare in conscientia. Dictum sanè, & quidem verè dictum: nec, ut opinor, ista pugnant. Obligetur licèt subditus ad faciendum quod legi cavetur, non tamen Legi obligatur, sed sibi Patri Patriæ. Legi, quæ verè Lex est, de se & quatenus Lex est, annexa est Obligatio, eámque sequitur necessariò, ut effectus suam causam. At legem à jus non habentem latam diximus non esse verè sed æquivocè legem: proinde nec obligandi vim habere. Quæcunque ergo subdito hac in re incumbit obligatio, aliunde exurgit, & non ab ipsa Lege: cui extrinsecus advenit ut obliget, & merè per accidens; ut si musicus ædificet.
units.tr: XVI. Furthermore, when someone, having by force and arms driven out the lawful prince and heir of the kingdom, or having so oppressed him that he cannot pursue his right, yet while he is still alive, seizes the reins of government and calls himself king, since he is more truly an invader of the kingdom than its king; so that the matter is no longer a doubtful right but a plain wrong: you ask what a good citizen should do in this case? I think of one who has firmly sworn fidelity to the lawful prince; or if he has not sworn, he owes no less than if he had sworn. I say thirdly: it seems to me that not only may a good citizen obey laws enacted by one who holds supreme power de facto but not de jure, and do other things commanded by him (provided that what is commanded is not shameful or unjust in itself); but also that, when the condition of human affairs demands it, a necessity can arise, and indeed very often does arise, so that if he does not act so, he must be judged to have failed in his duty. And yet it has just been said that laws enacted by one who does not have lawful power do not bind in conscience. Certainly it was said, and truly said; nor, I think, do these statements conflict. A subject may be bound to do what the law prescribes, yet he is not bound to the law, but to himself and to the Father of his country. To the law, which is truly law, insofar as it is law, obligation is attached, and it follows it necessarily, as an effect follows its cause. But we have said that a law enacted by one who has no right is not truly law but law only in name, and therefore has no power to bind. Whatever obligation therefore lies upon the subject in this matter arises from elsewhere, and not from the law itself: to which it comes from outside to bind, and only by accident; as when a musician builds a house.

units.la: XVII. Quæres : Si non ex Lege, unde tandem oritur ista subditi obligatio ? Respondeo, Cum sit pii & prudentis viri, non solùm quid liceat attendere, sed & quid ipsum deceat videre, & quid aliis expediat: posse bonum civem obligari ad id faciendum in sui & concivium suorum commodum, ad quod faciendum alias & de jure non tenetur. Oritur ergo ista obligatio ex duplici illa parte officii, quâ sibi quisque debitor est, & quâ Patriæ. Sed quod attinet imprimis, viri & prudentis est, sibi rebusque suis in futurum prospicere; & honesti, quâ sit præsenti conditione cogitare. Dandam esse unicuique operam (omnibus viis & modis licitis & honestis) se vitámque suam tueri, atque ita se gerere ut possit tutò & in pace vivere, agros, ædes, possessiones suas sibi habere, eorumque qui ipsi & vitam & facultates cum libuerit eripere possunt, offensionem devitare, nemo est (nimirum Natura id dictante,) qui non fateatur. Et hinc prima parendi necessitas, quam propterea non tàm urget noster Apostolus quàm supponit, velut cujus uniquique à natura insitus est sensus, ἀ μόνον διὰ[?] [illegible, ~12 letters]. Quasi hominis esset parum sanæ mentis, ejus qui gladii potestatem habet iram temerè provocare, & ejus offensam contumacia sua, nulla postulante necessitate, incurrere. Ipsius igitur interest, in salutis suæ compendium, iniqua nonnulla pati, legibus obtemperare, & quod sine peccato fieri potest) [illegible, ~12 letters] Sicque jugum, quod excutere non potest, bene ferendo levius aliquantò, mitius & tolerabilius efficere.
units.tr: XVII. You will ask: if not from the law, whence at last does this obligation of the subject arise? I answer: since it belongs to a pious and prudent man not only to consider what is lawful, but also to see what is becoming to himself, and what is expedient for others, a good citizen can be bound to do, for his own and his fellow citizens' advantage, what otherwise he is not bound by right to do. This obligation therefore arises from that twofold part of duty, by which each is a debtor to himself and by which he is a debtor to his country. But, as regards the first, it is the part of a wise and honourable man to provide for himself and his affairs in future, and to think about his present condition. That each one should take pains (by all lawful and honourable means) to protect himself and his life, and so conduct himself that he may live in peace and safely, keep his fields, houses and possessions for himself, and avoid offence to those who can at will take away both life and goods, no one denies (since nature so dictates). And hence arises the first necessity of obeying, which our Apostle therefore does not so much urge as presuppose, as a sense implanted by nature in everyone, not only because of wrath [οὐ μόνον διὰ τὴν ὀργήν]. It would be like a man of little sound mind, one who has the power of the sword, to rashly provoke his anger, and to incur his displeasure by his own obstinacy when no necessity demands it. It is therefore in his own interest, for the advantage of his own safety, to suffer some unjust things, to obey the laws, and (what can be done without sin) to yield. Thus the yoke, which he cannot shake off, he makes somewhat lighter, milder and more tolerable by bearing it well.

units.la: XVIII. Sed & altera insuper, eáque fortiore, quæque ad Conscientiam propius pertingit, Obligatione, ad hoc idem faciendum semet obstrictum sentiet, quisquis quæ ex politico regimine civibus proveniunt bona attentè cum animo suo cogitaverit. Et ita sanè Chrysostomus illa Apostoli verba διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν hoc loco interpretatur, ut ad illius protectionis beneficium quam præstat subditis civilis dominatio, potissimum respexisse putet Apostolum. Quasi diceret, Conscius cùm sit quilibet civis, quàm multis beneficiis fruatur sub principatu politico, sciat se, in tot & tantorum beneficiorum compensationem, ad deferendam vicissim ei qui principatum tenet debitam obedientiam, quadam quasi gratitudinis legi teneri: ἵνα μὴ ἀγωνῶν [illegible, ~10 letters] ut ibi loquitur Chrysostomus, a mente Apostoli alieno, (ut mox videbimus,) ast sensu alias haud multum incommodo.
units.tr: XVIII. But there is also a second obligation, and a stronger one, which comes closer to conscience itself. Anyone who carefully considers the benefits that citizens derive from political government will feel bound to do the same. This is how Chrysostom interprets the Apostle's words "for conscience' sake" [διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν] in this place: he thinks the Apostle had chiefly in mind the protection that civil rule gives its subjects. As if he were saying: since every citizen is conscious of how many benefits he enjoys under political rule, he should know that, in return for so many and great benefits, he is bound by a kind of law of gratitude to render in turn the obedience owed to the one who holds power. [ἵνα μὴ ἀγωνῶν] as Chrysostom there puts it, this is alien to the Apostle's mind (as we shall soon see), but otherwise it is not much amiss in sense.

units.la: Fateor equidem, (quod est à Tacito observatum) raro fieri, ut quis imperium flagitio quæsitum bonis artibus exerceat: pleraque enim quibus artibus parantur iisdem & confervanda esse videntur, & celere tuendum est scelus. Posse tamen id fieri, Hieronis Siculi, Edgari Anglorum Regis, & aliorum nonnullorum exempla, qui principatum non optimè acquisitum modestè tamen administrarunt, satis testantur. Sed utcunque rem gerat qui principatum tenet, non poterit unquam sic abuti sua potestate, ut non interim sit θεοῦ διάκονός [?] εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν, ut loquitur Apostolus istius capitis commate quarto. Nec enim ulla tam mera tyrannis esse potest, quæ non speciem aliquam justæ dominationis retineat, & non, aliquâ saltem ex parte, subsidium ad tuendam hominum societatem, ut etiam redè [?] ad hunc locum admonuit Calvinus. Cum itaque, quod rerum nostrarum Domini sumus, quò tuti à cædibus & rapinâ vivimus, imò & id ipsum quòd vivimus, summis potestatibus debeamus ; (absque quibus esset, nullum nobis adversus sceleratorum hominum libidines, furores, injurias, aut præsidium esset aut remedium ;) æquissima res est, ut pro tot tantisque beneficiis aliquid saltem ipsis vicissim rependamus. Exigit hoc à nobis (optima æqui boni Lex) vetus illa commutationum formula, Δὸς τι, χ̀ λάβε τι [?]. Et profectò perversissimæ mentis est, sub illius dominationis patrocinio velle vivere, cui parere nolis : & cujus protectione gaudeas, ejus imperium detrectare.
units.tr: I admit, indeed (as Tacitus has observed), that it rarely happens that a man who has gained power by crime exercises it by good arts, for most of the means by which power is obtained seem also needed to keep it, and "crime must be defended swiftly." Yet that this can happen is sufficiently attested by the examples of Hiero of Sicily, Edgar, King of the English, and some others, who administered a power not well won with moderation. But however the holder of power conducts himself, he can never so abuse his authority that he is not, for the time being, "God's minister for good" [θεοῦ διάκονός εἰς τὸ ἀγαθόν], as the Apostle says in verse four of this chapter. For no tyranny can be so sheer that it retains no semblance of just rule and does not, at least in some part, serve as a support for preserving human society, as Calvin also rightly reminded us on this passage. Since, then, we owe it to the highest powers that we are masters of our own affairs, that we live safe from murder and plunder, and indeed that we live at all (without them there would be no defence or remedy against the lusts, rages and injuries of wicked men), it is most just that we should repay them at least something in return for so many and great benefits. The ancient formula of exchange requires this of us, the best law of fairness: "Give something, and take something" [Δὸς τι, χ̀ λάβε τι]. And truly it is the mind of one most perverse to wish to live under the patronage of a rule which you do not want to obey, and to enjoy its protection while refusing its authority.

units.la: XIX. Porrò cùm nemo sibi solùm natus sit, sed humano generi & publicæ utilitati : hinc oritur tertia parendi necessitas præsenti potestati, quocunque jure ipsam adepti sunt qui rerum potiuntur. Unde etiam aliquo modo constare poterit, quis modus sit statuendus, & qui fines, illi obedientiæ, quæ imperium injustè possidenti, ex Conscientiæ debito, à cive præstanda est. Quicquid enim finis alicujus gratiâ faciendum est, eatenus fieri oportet, in quantum eo fini consequendo necessarium vel utile videbitur. Civilis autem regiminis, ejusque quæ ipsi debita est obedientiæ, finis est, humanæ societatis salus & tranquillitas. In quantum igitur illius societatis, cujus ipse membrum & pars est, salus & tranquillitas exigit, eatenus civis unusquisque imperiis ejus, qui de facto in illa societate summæ rerum præest, obtemperare tenetur. Sunt autem conservandis humanis societatibus tria hæc imprimis necessaria : I. Defensio patriæ, adversus externam vim & hostium conatus. II. Administratio Juris, ut sua bona civibus præmia, improbis supplicia, prout legibus constituta sunt, reddantur ; quod Justitiæ distributivæ munus est. III. Quod ad Justitiam commutativam spectat, Commercii cura & mercaturæ ; de rebus emendis, vendundis, permutandis, & omne genus contractibus. His tribus rebus ita continetur incolumitas humani generis, ut nisi ista adsint, fieri non potest, quin protinus pessum eant universa ; omnia rapinis, cædibus, fraudibus, injuriis repleantur ; innocentissimorum civium vitæ, conjuges, fortunæ, potentiorum libidini prædæ sint & ludibrio. Quibus malis ut obviam eatur, malorumque petulantia maturè coerceatur ; unicum remedium erit, si boni cives suum esse meminerint, eorum legibus & imperiis, quorum gladii & authoritate à sceleratorum injuriis defenduntur, in omnibus quæ ad publicam salutem faciunt obtemperare.
units.tr: XIX. Moreover, since no one is born for himself alone, but for the human race and the common good, a third necessity of obeying the present power arises from this, whatever right those who hold power have obtained it by. Hence it can also be established in some measure what limit, and what bounds, must be set to that obedience which a citizen owes out of the obligation of conscience to one who unjustly possesses power. Whatever is to be done for the sake of some end must be done so far as it appears necessary or useful for attaining that end. Now the end of civil government, and of the obedience owed to it, is the safety and tranquillity of human society. Therefore, so far as the safety and tranquillity of that society, of which he is himself a member and part, requires, each citizen is bound to obey the commands of him who in fact presides over the highest affairs in that society. Moreover, three things are chiefly necessary for preserving human societies: first, the defence of the country against external force and the attempts of enemies; second, the administration of justice, so that good citizens receive their rewards and wicked men their punishments, as the laws have established; this is the office of distributive justice; third, as far as commutative justice is concerned, the care of commerce and trade, concerning the buying, selling and exchanging of goods, and every kind of contract. The safety of the human race is so bound up with these three things that, unless they are present, it cannot but be that all things quickly perish; everything is filled with plunder, murder, fraud and injury, and the lives, wives and fortunes of the most innocent citizens become the prey and plaything of the lust of the powerful. To meet these evils and check promptly the wantonness of the wicked, there will be one remedy: if good citizens remember that they belong to the obedience owed in all matters that serve the public safety to those laws and commands by whose swords and authority they are defended from the injuries of the wicked.

units.la: XX. Sed hactenus obtemperare, (ne quis ista quæ dicta sunt secùs quàm par est interpretetur) ut simul meminerint, ad hanc obedientiam præstandam se non ultrà teneri, quàm aut gratitudinis ratio aut publicæ rei salus postulat : & observandas esse Leges potestatem injuste possidentis, non quasi ullo imperantis jure obligatorias, sed (ut recte {1} Aquinas) ad vitandum scandalum vel turbationem Reipublicæ. In quo casu (inquit ille) debet quis jure suo cedere : quod & probat ex illis Christi verbis, Mat. 5. 40. 41. Ei qui vult tecum litigare, & tunicam tuam capere, demitte & pallium : Et qui te angariabit ad miliare unum, abi cum eo duo. Potest ergo quis, & (prout res exigit) debet, etiam privatæ pacis, sed multò ergo magis publicæ tranquillitatis causâ, jure suo cedere ; & ei, qui imperandi jus non habet, parere. Sed & hic iterum cauto opus est, idque vel maximè : ut scilicet ita jure suo cedat, ne quid eo facto juri decedat alieno. Id juste & prudenter cavit Abraham, Gen. 14.
units.tr: XX. But obedience only so far (lest anyone interpret what has been said otherwise than it should be) so that at the same time they remember that they are bound to render this obedience no further than either the reason of gratitude or the safety of the commonwealth requires; and that the laws of one who unjustly possesses power are to be observed, not as binding by any right of the commander, but (as Aquinas rightly says) to avoid scandal or disturbance of the commonwealth. In such a case (he says) a man ought to yield his right; and he proves this from those words of Christ, Matt. 5. 40, 41: "If anyone wants to sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak also. And whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two." Therefore one can, and (as the matter demands) ought, to yield one's right even for the sake of private peace, but much more for the sake of public tranquillity, and to obey one who has no right to command. But here again caution is needed, and very much so: namely, that one yields one's right in such a way that by that act nothing of another's right is lost. Abraham prudently and justly took care of this, Gen. 14.

units.la: Prælectio Quinta.
units.tr: Lecture Five.

units.la: Dum Regi Sodomorum sic gratiam fecit partis suæ [?]rothiniorum[?], quæ sibi ex deviæctis quinque regibus Belli in prædam cesserant, ut- & sacerdoti sua decima, & tribus belli sociis ad suas portiones jus integrum remaneret. Proinde regni invasori sic præstandum est obsequium, ut fidelitas legitimo heredi debita nullatenus violetur, nec aliquid fiat juris sui præjudicium.
units.tr: When he thus granted to the king of Sodom the part of the goods of Rothiniorum[?], which had fallen to his own men as booty from the five kings of Bela, while the priest kept his tithe and the three allies of the war kept their full shares, he acted rightly. So too obedience must be rendered to the invader of a kingdom in such a way that the fidelity owed to the lawful heir is in no way violated, and nothing is done to the prejudice of his right.

units.la: XXI. At quî hoc fieri potest ? inquies. Quod regni invasori gratum est, non potest legitimo principi non esse ingratissimum. {1}Nemo potest duo[?]us dominis servire, tam adversa spectantibus; quoum omnia vota, studia, consilia, pronis in mutuam perniciem affectibus, in contrarias partes feruntur. Respondeo, rite subductis rationibus, non [?]e cur putemus, legitimo principi, sed extorri, ingratum omninò fore, injusto imperii possessori restitutum à cive, eo quo dictum est modo, & indictos fines, obsequium: quin potius ipso consentiente sic fieri oportuisse præsumendum est. Si-
units.tr: XXI. But how can this be done? you will ask. What is pleasing to the invader of the kingdom cannot fail to be most unwelcome to the lawful prince. {1}No one can serve two masters, when they look for such opposite things, since all their wishes, efforts and counsels, inclined by mutual and ruinous passions, are directed toward opposing ends. I answer: when the accounts are rightly reckoned, we have no reason to think that the obedience rendered by a citizen to the unjust possessor of power, in the manner described and within the limits set, will be wholly unwelcome to the lawful prince, who is in exile. Indeed, it must rather be presumed that it ought to have been done with his consent. If

units.la: idem ejusmodi obsequio, non tam injustè domiinti, quàm toti communitati, hoc est, Reipublicæ rviiffe existimandus est: quam salvam esse, justi eredis nihilominùs interest, quàm illius qui de [?]o in eâ dominatur. Fortassean & multo etiam magis, quò sincerius patriam diligere censendus [?], & ei bona omnia velle,qui genuinus patriæ pa[?]est, quàm qui eo excluso in ipsius ædes se inessit, & in familiam ipsius jus & imperium exeret; & quò puriores & vehementiores in liberos [?]atris affectus sunt, quàm novercæ. Ut in celebri lâ {2}duarum muliercularum coram Rege Solo[?]ne altercatione, quæ verè mater erat puerulum [?]em suum esse sciret, salvum utcunque cupiit, [?]aluitque alterius esse, imò adversariæ, quàm pere: Sic civium salutem, quos etsi subalieno jugo, tamen interim agnoscit, & sibi olim utiles fore
units.tr: the same kind of obedience is rendered, not so much to the unjust ruler as to the whole community, that is, to the commonwealth, it must be judged to have been rendered to that. The safety of the commonwealth is in the interest of the rightful heir no less than of the one who unjustly rules over it. Perhaps it is even much more so, since one is to be thought to love his country more sincerely and to wish it every good, if he is its genuine father, than one who, with him excluded, has insinuated himself into its house and claims right and rule over its family; and since the affections of a true mother toward her children are purer and more vehement than those of a stepmother. Thus in the famous quarrel of two women before King Solomon, she who was truly the mother, knowing her little son to be her own, wished him saved by any means and preferred that he be the other's, even the adversary's, rather than that he perish. So too the safety of the citizens, whom, though they are under a foreign yoke, he nonetheless acknowledges and who will one day be useful to him,

units.la: {2} Reg 3. 26. confidit, legitimo hæredi majori esse curæ & verisimile est & merito præsumitur, quàm ei, qui quum imperium injustè usurpaverit, de stabilienda recens quæsita dominatione suâ quàm de salute civium procuranda, par est esse magis solicitum; adeòque malle ipsum, ut præsentibus rebus, quò salvi sint, se quâ licet modestè accommodent, quàm ut potentiori in certam suam perniciem semet intempestivè opponant. Atque ita habetis meam de gravissima hac & ardua admodum quæstione sententiam; nihil interim temere statuentis, sed eam, ubi quis certiora docuerit, mutare parati, & in ipsius castra transfire.
units.tr: {2} Reg 3. 26. The lawful heir is both likely, and rightly presumed, to be more concerned for the safety of the citizens than the one who, having usurped power unjustly, ought to be more anxious to secure his newly won domination than to procure the safety of the citizens. Therefore he would rather they accommodate themselves to present circumstances, as modestly as may be, so that they may be safe, than that they rashly set themselves against the more powerful to their certain ruin. And so you have my opinion on this most grave and very difficult question. I determine nothing rashly in the meantime, but I am ready to change it, and to pass over into the camp of whoever teaches me more certain things.

units.la: XXII. Haftenus hæc : sequitur CONCLUSIO QVARTA. Leges humanæ de rebus non illicitis Conscientias obligant per se & directè in generali. Quod est dicere, Hoc præceptum generale, ut subditi obtemperent legibus humanis rectè constitutis, est per se & directè obligatorium. Id quod ipsam etiam Calvinus, qui non solet humanis constitutionibus nimium tribuere, agnoscit: qui 4. Instit. 10. Sect. 5. ita distinguendum esse monet inter genus & speciem, ut licet negandum sit leges in speciali obligare conscientias, concedendum tamen sit eas obligare in generali. Ratio perspicua: quia hoc præceptum generale ad ipsam æternam legem divinam pertinet; cujus omnis pars est per se & directè, & non ex consequenti solum, obligatoria conscientiarum. Pertinet autem ad divinam legem duplici nomine. Tum, quia rationalis ratio dictat, non posse pacem & ordinem, quæ anima est Rerumpublicæ, & omnis humanæ societatis, conservari, nisi legibus rite constitutis obediatur. Tum, quia in sacra Scriptura Deus præcepit, ut his, qui nobis in eo ordine quem Deus præstituit præsunt, subjiciamur; [illegible, ~12 letters] pareamus, nec iis resistamus, hujus capitis vers. 1. & nec ec[?] eorum jugo colla nostra subducamus, eo scicet prætextu[?], quod meri homines sint, & creatæ, sicut & nos, {1}κτίας ἀνθρωπίνη[?], filii Adæ, mortale genus, iisdem omnino affectibus, perturbationibus, infirmitatibus, casibus, quibus & nos obnoxii. Quin potiùs memores, Deum Opt. Max. eos nobis cum delegatâ potestate velut suos in terris Vicarios præfecisse, ipsosque propterea tanto honore dignatum esse, ut eis & nomen suum quasi visibilibus & mortalibus quibusdam Diis, communicaverit {2}[Ego dixi, Dii estis] par est ut eos summa cum reverentia colamus, honoremus, obsequamur. Etsi non ipsorum gratia; qui, ut homines sunt, pari nobiscum conditione sunt, nec de meliore luto effecti; at Divinæ tamen ordinationis intuitu, qui eos quâ principes sunt, sublimiore loco esse voluit quàm reliquos homines, & suæ potestatis aliquatenus participavit. Διὰ τὴν ἐξουσίαν[?], ut alibi Petrus; & ex consequenti διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν[?], ut hic loquitur Apostolus Paulus.
units.tr: XXII. So far these things. There follows the FOURTH CONCLUSION: Human laws concerning things not unlawful bind consciences per se and directly in general. That is to say, this general precept, that subjects obey human laws rightly enacted, is binding per se and directly. Calvin himself acknowledges this, though he is not accustomed to attribute too much to human constitutions. He advises, in Institutes 4.10.5, that a distinction must be drawn between genus and species, so that although it must be denied that laws in particular bind consciences, it must be conceded that they bind in general. The reason is plain: this general precept belongs to the eternal divine law itself, every part of which binds consciences per se and directly, and not merely by consequence. It belongs to the divine law on two counts. First, because right reason dictates that peace and order, which are the soul of a commonwealth and of all human society, cannot be preserved unless laws rightly enacted are obeyed. Second, because in Holy Scripture God commanded that we be subject to those who preside over us in the order which God has appointed, [illegible] obey them, and not resist them, as in verse 1 of this chapter; nor should we withdraw our necks from their yoke on the pretext that they are mere men, created like us, [κτίσις ἀνθρωπίνη], sons of Adam, a mortal race subject to the same passions, disturbances, infirmities and chances to which we are liable. Rather, we should remember that God, Best and Greatest, has set them over us with delegated power, as his own vicars on earth, and has therefore deigned to honour them so highly that he has communicated his own name to them, as to certain visible and mortal gods, {2}[I have said, You are gods]. It is fitting that we honour, reverence and obey them with the greatest respect. Not indeed for their own sake, since as men they stand in the same condition as we and were not made of better clay, but out of regard for the divine ordination, which, insofar as they are princes, willed them to stand in a higher place than other men and imparted to them some share of his power. [διὰ τὴν ἐξουσίαν], as Peter says elsewhere; and consequently [διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν], as the Apostle Paul speaks here.

units.la: XXIII. CONCLUSIO QUINTA. Leges humanæ rite constitutæ, etiam in particulari, etsi non directè & per se, ex consequenti tamen & virtute generalis præcepti Divini, obligant (subditorum conscientias. Dico primo, Leges rite constitutas. Id est, & ratione Causæ efficientis: ab eo, qui legitimâ potestate præditus est, latas: & ratione Materiæ; nil illicitum, inhonestum, turpe, aut officio hominis Christiani quomodolibet contrarium, imperantes. Jam enim diximus eas Leges, quæ utrovis nomine peccant, non obligare. Dico secundo, In particulari: id est, quantum ad determinationem particularem in rebus mediis aliquæ. Ut quale & quantum tributum sit solvendum; quæ merces liceat aut non liceat è regione exportare; In Academia qui habitus quibus gradibus competant; Quæ Statuta sint difpenfabilia, quæ[?] non, &c. Dico Tertio, Leges ejusmodi non obligant per se & directè. Probatur primo, quia Deus unus est Legislator, qui in conscientias hominum merum & directum imperium habet. Unus est Legislator, qui servare potest & perdere, Jac. 4. 12. Deum autem supponimus de rebus ejusmodi mediis & adiaphoris, quæ ferè sunt materia Legum humanarum; nullam legem tulisse in particulari, sed ea omnia eorum arbitrio, qui ipsius in terris[?] vices gerunt permisisse. Probatur secundo, qui illa tantum obligant directè & per se, quæ obligant ratione Materiæ velut internæ causæ, citra respectum ad causas externas, Efficientem sc. & Finem i. e. quæ obligarent, etsi ab hominibus mandat[?] non essent. At res mediæ & adiaphoræ lege humanæ positiva & particulari determinatæ, quum sint ita natura sua comparatæ, ut ante illam determinationem liberè possent à quoquam fieri vel non fieri, non obligant ratione materiæ; ergo nec per se. Dico tertio, ejusmodi leges obligare tamen in particulari ex consequenti, & virtute præcepti divini generalis. Et quia in hoc ultimo dicto totius controversiæ quasi cardo vertitur, propono Conclusionem, jam statim pluribus confirmandam, aliquanto explicatiùs, sic; Leges humanæ positivæ rite & legitimè constitutæ, quæ continent particulares determinationes circa res medias, in se adiaphoras, & antequam sic determinarentur, liberas ad utrumvis libet, virtute illius præcepti divini, quo tenemur iis parere qui nobis à Deo præpositi sunt, ita obligant subditorum conscientias ad præstandam eis obedientiam, ut sub peccato mortali & metu offensionis Dei teneantur ejusmodi legibus obtemperare; & ni sic fecerint, accusantis conscientiæ murmura & ictus perferre.
units.tr: XXIII. FIFTH CONCLUSION: Human laws rightly enacted, even in particular, though not directly and per se, nevertheless by consequence and by virtue of the general divine precept, bind the consciences of subjects. I say first, rightly enacted: that is, both with respect to the efficient cause, being enacted by one endowed with legitimate power, and with respect to the matter, commanding nothing unlawful, dishonourable, base, or in any way contrary to the duty of a Christian. For we have already said that laws which sin in either respect do not bind. I say second, in particular: that is, as regards the particular determination of some indifferent matters, such as what kind and amount of tribute is to be paid; what merchandise it is or is not lawful to export from the region; which academic degrees are to be conferred for which courses; which statutes may be dispensed with and which not, and so on. I say third: such laws do not bind per se and directly. This is proved first, because God alone is the Legislator, who has sole and direct authority over the consciences of men: "There is one Lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy," James 4. 12. We suppose that God, concerning such means and indifferent things, which for the most part are the matter of human laws, enacted no law in particular, but left all these things to the judgment of those who act in his place on earth. It is proved second: only those laws bind directly and per se which bind by reason of their matter as an internal cause, without regard to external causes, the efficient and the final; that is, laws which would bind even if they had not been commanded by men. But things that are indifferent and intermediate, once determined by positive and particular human law, since by their nature they are so constituted that before that determination anyone could freely do them or not do them, do not bind by reason of their matter; therefore they do not bind per se either. I say third, that such laws nevertheless bind in particular by consequence, and by virtue of the general divine precept. And because the whole controversy turns, as it were, on this last point, I propose the conclusion, to be confirmed presently by many arguments, somewhat more explicitly as follows: positive human laws, rightly and legitimately enacted, which contain particular determinations concerning indifferent things, and which before being so determined were free to be done either way, bind the consciences of subjects, by virtue of that divine precept by which we are obliged to obey those set over us by God, so as to render them obedience. Subjects are bound under mortal sin and fear of offending God to obey such laws; and if they do not, they must bear the murmurs and blows of an accusing conscience.

units.la: XXIV. Firmatur hæc Conclusio multis rationibus: quarum prima ex præsenti Textu desumitur, Quare subjici necesse est, non solum propter iram, sed & propter conscientiam. Verba sunt satis perspicua. Urserat [?] nempe Apostolus superioribus versibus aliquanto fusius Christianæ subjectionis necessitatem, duobus potissimum argumentis: altero ab instituto & ordinatione Dei, duobus versibus primis; totidem sequentibus, ab humani supplicii metu, altero. Utrinque argumentum ὡς ἐν ἀναλαμβάνεως ἔπῳ [?] breviter recolligit & repetit quinto hoc versu: idque (qui fere mos est sacræ Scripturæ,) ordine inverso, repetitionem exorsus à membro posteriore, & proximiore. Quasi dicat, Utrinque vobis incumbit gravis paremdi necessitas [?]; sive vos pœnæ metus tangat, sive pulsat officii Conscientia. Si quod malum est feceritis, spretâ nimirum potestatum, & legum authoritate: cogitate eum qui vobis præest Magistratum Dei ministrum esse, ἔκδικον εἰς ὀργὴν, neglecti officii vindicem; gladium sibi à Deo concreditum stringere paratum, ad infligendum legum suarum contemptoribus debitam pœnam corporalem. Sin vos ista parum moveant, quod spretis fieri posse, ut ipsius brachium aliquâ evadatis: Ast sperate Deum memorem fandi atque nefandi; hunc timete justum judicem: veremini Conscientias vestras, severos accusatores, testes veraces, importunos tortores. Hos nullis potestis aut latebris effugere, aut artibus eludere. Ex hujus ergo loci scopo sic struitur argumentum. Quæ violata conscientiam ledunt, ea conscientiam obligant, quia omnem conscientiæ læsionem sive gravamen ex alicujus obligationis sensu oriri necesse est, sicut omnes alii essectus consequuntur suas causas. At violatæ leges humanæ lædunt conscientiam. Id enim sibi volunt ista verba, Necesse est subjici propter Conscientiam,
units.tr: XXIV. This Conclusion is confirmed by many arguments. The first is drawn from the present text: Therefore it is necessary to be subject, not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience. The words are quite plain. The Apostle had argued at some length in the preceding verses for the necessity of Christian subjection, on two chief grounds: the first from the institution and ordinance of God, in the first two verses; the second, in the two verses that follow, from the fear of human punishment. In the fifth verse he briefly sums up and repeats both arguments, as in a summary [ὡς ἐν ἀναλαμβάνεως ἔπῳ]. He does this in reverse order, which is nearly the usual practice of Holy Scripture, beginning the repetition with the later and nearer member. It is as if he said: on either ground there lies upon you a grave necessity of obeying, whether the fear of punishment touches you or the conscience of duty strikes you. If you do wrong, namely by despising the authority of the powers and the laws, consider that the magistrate is God's minister, an avenger for wrath [ἔκδικον εἰς ὀργὴν], the punisher of neglected duty, who holds the sword entrusted to him by God, ready to inflict the bodily penalty due to the contemners of his laws. But if these things move you little, on the ground that you may escape his arm by despising them, yet hope that God remembers right and wrong; fear him as the just judge. Revere your consciences as severe accusers, true witnesses, and relentless tormentors. You cannot escape them by any hiding-place, nor elude them by any tricks. From the aim of this passage, then, the argument is built thus: whatever wounds the conscience when violated, that also binds the conscience, because every injury or burden to the conscience must arise from a sense of some obligation, just as all other effects follow from their causes. But violated human laws wound the conscience. For these words mean this: It is necessary to be subject for the sake of conscience,

units.la: i. c.
units.tr: that is,

units.la: i. e. Non potestis conscientiam integram & illæfam confervare nili[?] subjiciamini. Ergo Leges humanæ obligant Conscientiam.
units.tr: i.e. you cannot keep your conscience whole and unharmed unless you submit. Therefore human laws bind the conscience.

units.la: XXV. Ad hujus argumenti vim enervandam, sunt qui Conscientiam hoc in loco aliter interpretantur, & Chryfoftomi authoritate fe præcipuè tuentur; acsi non alia hic Conscientia intelligenda veniret, quàm illa Beneficiorum, quæ subditis obveniunt à regimine politico ; sensu à nobis prius allato ; pio quidem illo (fateor, & nos ante laudavimus,) sed, ut arbitror, parùm genuino. Contrà enim, Primò, singularis penè est inter veteres in eâ interpretatione Chryfoftomus, quem secuti è tot interpretibus vix unus & alter extra Oecumenium & Theophylactum, qui in recensendis teftimoniis nullo numero habendi sunt; quia Chryfoftomi vestigiis ita semper insistunt, ut universi tres unum tantum faciant testem. Secundò, nec potest afferri locus aliquis, in quo D. Paulus, aut alius quis sacrorum scriptorum Conscientia vocabulo in eo sensu usus fit, quem hic sibi fingit Chryfoftomus. Tertiò, adducere voluit Apostolus, ut res ipsa clamat, aliquid quod effet gravius, & ad excitandum hominum animos efficacius, supplicio temporali: cui rei aptius certe fuerat eos injecto offensionis Divinæ metu perterrefacere, quàm accepti ab hominibus beneficii admonuisse. Quarto denique, concludere hinc voluit Apostolus, brevi repetitione earum rationum quas jam antè adduxerat, suam de Christiana subjeCtione differtationem : adduxerat autem duobus primis versibus hujus capitis rationem, non à Beneficiis, sed ab Officii Conscientiâ desumptam.
units.tr: XXV. To weaken the force of this argument, some interpret conscience differently in this place, and rely chiefly on the authority of Chrysostom, as if the conscience here were to be understood as nothing other than that sense of the benefits which subjects receive from political government, in the sense I gave earlier. That sense is pious (I admit it, and I too praised it before), but, as I judge, scarcely genuine. For, first, that interpretation is almost peculiar to Chrysostom among the ancients; those who followed him, scarcely one or two of the many interpreters besides Oecumenius and Theophylact, are to be counted as no witnesses at all, since they always so closely follow Chrysostom's footsteps that all three together make only one witness. Second, no passage can be cited in which Saint Paul, or any other of the sacred writers, used the word conscience in the sense that Chrysostom here imagines. Third, the Apostle wished to bring forward, as the matter itself cries out, something weightier and more effective for stirring men's minds, namely temporal punishment. For this purpose it would certainly have been more suitable to terrify them by striking in the fear of divine offence than to remind them of a benefit received from men. Fourth and finally, the Apostle meant to conclude from this, by a brief repetition of the reasons he had already advanced, his own discourse on Christian subjection. Now in the first two verses of this chapter he had advanced a reason taken not from benefits, but from the conscience of duty.

units.la: XXVI. Sequitur Ratio Secunda ; ab usu & fine Legum. Quas condi, conditàsque observari, ad societates humanas in pace & publicâ tranquillitate confervandas, pernecessarium est : aliàs nulla effet certa contractuum, regulae, nulla fidei & justitiae civilis mensurae, quae sunt civitatum & societatum firmissima vincula. Lex enim Dei & Naturalis & scripta, licet sit in suo genere utraque vel seorsim perfectissima, completaturque conjuncta tum quae sunt fidei supernaturalis singula, tum etiam rerum agendarum principia generalia ad omnes vitae partes regendas accommoda: Neutra tamen ad omnia ea particularia descendit, quae ad conservandam in civitatibus & politiis pacem & ordinem possunt esse, & plerunque sunt necessaria. Exempli gratia. Lex Rationis, quae naturae Lex est, dictat, & Scriptura etiam hujus capitis versu proximo docet, ad alendos principes, ad bellorum sumptus, ad alios usus publicos, Tributa est pendenda. Sed nisi Lege lata definiatur quantum sit solvendum, & quota proportione, & a quibus, & quo temporis spatio, & id genus alia: aut nihil omnino pendetur, aut non tempestive satis, aut quod non satis sit ad usus Reipublicae. Si dicat, hoc argumento probari quidem Legum necessitatem, at non item statui obligationem: posse enim poenis propositis adigi subditos ad officium: Fatendum id quidem esset, si hic staretur; sed si illud insuper cogitetur, dum praeceps fertur {1}ad vetitum nefas, quam sit audax omnia perpeti gens humana, quamque officii infidelis custos sit metus, ni adsit etiam Religionis sensus aliquis qui homines in officio contineat: facile constabit quam provide a sapientissimo rerum moderatore Deo Opt. Max. consultum sit rebus humanis, quod indiderit Conscientiis hominum, quae cum ipso rationis usu simul adolesceret, religionem quandam, Legum Reverentiam. Unde factum ut apud Ethnicos veri Dei ignaros, vix repertus fuerit e prisicis Legumlatoribus, qui quas condebat Leges, non eas ab aliquo Numine sibi traditas mentiretur. De Numa, Zaleuco, Lycurgo, caeteris, quæ in hanc rem tradunt Historiæ, non pus est ut recenseam, quum sint omnibus notissima.
units.tr: XXVI. There follows the Second Reason, from the use and end of laws. It is most necessary that laws be made, and once made be observed, for preserving human societies in peace and public tranquillity. Otherwise there would be no fixed rules of contracts, no measure of faith and civil justice, which are the firmest bonds of states and societies. For the law of God, both natural and written, although each in its own kind is most perfect, whether taken separately or together, and although it contains both the individual matters of supernatural faith and the general principles of things to be done, suited to governing all parts of life, yet neither descends to all those particular matters which may be, and for the most part are, necessary for preserving peace and order in commonwealths and polities. For example, the law of reason, which is the law of nature, dictates, and Scripture too teaches in the verse next to this chapter's, that tribute must be paid for maintaining princes, for the expenses of wars, and for other public uses. But unless by a law passed it is determined how much is to be paid, in what proportion, by whom, and within what space of time, and other such matters, either nothing at all will be paid, or not in good time, or not enough for the needs of the commonwealth. If someone says that this argument proves the necessity of laws, but not likewise the obligation of the state, since subjects may be driven to their duty by penalties set before them: it must be admitted that this would hold if we stopped here. But if we also consider how headlong the human race is toward forbidden wickedness, how bold it is to endure everything, and how unfaithful a guardian of duty fear is, unless there is also some sense of religion to keep men in their duty, it will easily be plain how wisely the most wise Governor of all things, God Most Good and Most Great, provided for human affairs, in implanting in the consciences of men, which grow up together with the very use of reason, a certain religion, a reverence for laws. Hence it came about that among the heathen, ignorant of the true God, hardly any of the ancient lawgivers was found who did not pretend that the laws he made had been delivered to him by some divine power. I need not recount the stories of Numa, Zaleucus, Lycurgus, and the others which history records on this matter, since they are known to everyone.

units.la: XXVII. Ratio Tertia. Quod faciendum propter Dominum, ad id faciendum obligamur Conscientiâ. Sed Legibus Humanis rite constitutis, i. e. à suprema potestate, vel his qui ab eâ ad id delegati sunt, latis, subesse tenemur propter Dominum, 1. Pet. 2. 13. Subditi estote omni humanæ creaturæ propter Dominum, sive Regi, ὡς ὑπερέχοντι[?] (quod satis explicat quid sit Paulo [illegible, ~12 letters] istius capitis versu primo) sive præfectis ab eo missis, &c. Ubi illud [illegible, ~10 letters] propter Dominum, Conscientiæ obligationem significare, constat, primò, ex usu similium alibi locutionum, ut Eph. 6. 1. de officio liberorum erga parentes, Liberi, obedite parentibus vestris ἐν κυρίῳ in Domino; Et de servorum officio erga Domino ibid. verf. 7. Cum benevolentiâ δουλεύοντες τῷ κυρίῳ, Domino servientes, & non hominibus, quod Col. 3. 23. ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ, ut Domino & non hominibus: quasi dicat, propter Conscientiam, & non propter iram, vel ex timore Dei magis quam ob metum hominis. Constat id ipsum secundo ex verbis sequentibus in illo Petri loco verf. 15. οὕτως [?] τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ, quia sic est voluntas Dei: uti Paulus etiam jam laudato ad Ephesios capite verf. 6. de servorum officio locutus, hortatur ut Dominis suis obsequantur in simplicitate cordis ὡς τῷ Χριστῷ, ποιοῦντες τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐκ ψυχῆς, facientes voluntatem Dei a corde. Est autem Voluntas Dei ipsissima illa, quam adæquatam diximus, Conscientiæ regula.
units.tr: XXVII. Third Reason. We are bound by conscience to do that which must be done for the Lord's sake. But we are bound to be subject to human laws duly constituted, that is, enacted by the supreme power or by those delegated by it for that purpose, for the Lord's sake (1 Pet. 2. 13): Be subject to every human creature for the Lord's sake, whether to the king, as supreme [ὡς ὑπερέχοντι], (which sufficiently explains what Paul meant in the first verse of this chapter), or to governors sent by him, etc. That the phrase for the Lord's sake [illegible] signifies an obligation of conscience is clear, first, from the usage of similar expressions elsewhere: as in Eph. 6. 1, concerning the duty of children towards parents, Children, obey your parents in the Lord [ἐν κυρίῳ]; and concerning the duty of servants towards masters, in the same place, verse 7, serving the Lord with goodwill [δουλεύοντες τῷ κυρίῳ], serving the Lord and not men, which is in Col. 3. 23 as to the Lord and not to men [ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ]: as if he said, for conscience' sake, and not for wrath's sake, or out of fear of God rather than from fear of man. It is clear, secondly, from the words that follow in that passage of Peter, verse 15, for so is the will of God [οὕτως ἐστὶν τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ]: just as Paul also, in the Ephesian passage already cited, speaking of the duty of servants, exhorts them to obey their masters in singleness of heart, as to Christ [ὡς τῷ Χριστῷ], doing the will of God from the heart [ποιοῦντες τὸ θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐκ ψυχῆς]. Now the will of God is that very rule of conscience, which we have said is adequate.

units.la: XXVIII. Ratio Quarta. Quod Naturalis Ratio ita dictat esse faciendum, ut si non fiat, culpa & reatus contrahatur, ad id faciendum proculdubio obligamur in Conscientiâ. Quum enim ad Con[?]cientiam pertineat sensus peccati, & exinde natus supplicii metus; quicquid recte mens judicat culpam inducere, & poenae reatum, id omne & Conscientiam obligare censendum est. Naturalis autem ratio (cujus judicium non potest esse non rectum) legibus humanis parendum esse sic dictat; ut si non fiat, quod imperatum est, ipsi mox conscii nobis simus, mera id nostra culpa contingere quod non fiat.
units.tr: XXVIII. Fourth Reason. We are undoubtedly bound in conscience to do that which natural reason so dictates must be done, that if it is not done, guilt and liability are incurred. For since the sense of sin, and the fear of punishment born from it, belong to conscience, whatever the mind rightly judges to induce guilt and liability to penalty, all this must be held to bind the conscience. Now natural reason (whose judgment cannot but be right) dictates that human laws are to be obeyed in such a way that, if what has been commanded is not done, we ourselves will straightway be aware that it is entirely our own fault that it is not done.

units.la: XXIX. Ratio Quinta. Cujus violatio Legis Dei violationem necessario secum trahit, id obligat Conscientiam: quandoquidem nemo potest illaesa conscientia violare Legem Dei, quae est Regula Conscientiae. Violatio autem Legis cujuscunque particularis ab hominibus rite constitutae necessario secum trahit violationem Legis Dei: illius nempe praecepti generalis, quo Deus praecipit obedientiam praelatis. Ergo, &c.
units.tr: XXIX. Fifth Argument. Whatever violation necessarily carries with it a violation of the Law of God binds the conscience, since no one can violate the Law of God, which is the Rule of Conscience, and keep his conscience unharmed. But the violation of any particular law rightly made by men necessarily carries with it a violation of the Law of God, namely of that general precept by which God commands obedience to superiors. Therefore, etc.

units.la: XXX. Ratio Sexta. Obligamur in Conscientia ad non faciendum id, quod si fiat perinde est ac si Deo resisteretur. Obligamur enim subjici Deo, & proinde ei non resistere, quum sint Subjectio & Resistentia sibi invicem contraria, nec possit aliquis eidem personae simul & ὑποτάσσεσθαι[?] & ἀντιτάσσεσθαι[?]. At legibus humanis rite constitutis non obtemperare, est (interpretative) Deo resistere. Qui enim Legibus non obtemperat, potestati Magistratus Legislativae obsistit: quod qui facit, quum sit illa potestas a Deo ordinata, Dei ordinationi se opponit, adeoque consequenter, & interpretative ipsi Deo; quod est ipsius Pauli postulatum vers. 2. hujus capitis, ex quo legitime concludit subjectionis necessitatem διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν[?] in hoc versu.
units.tr: XXX. Sixth Argument. We are bound in conscience not to do what, if it were done, would be just the same as resisting God. For we are bound to be subject to God, and therefore not to resist him, since subjection and resistance are opposed to each other, and no one can at the same time both be subject [ὑποτάσσεσθαι] and set himself against [ἀντιτάσσεσθαι] the same person. But not to obey human laws rightly made is (by implication) to resist God. For he who does not obey the laws sets himself against the power of the legislative magistrate; and since that power is ordained by God, whoever does this opposes himself to God's ordinance, and so consequently, and by implication, to God himself. This is the very demand of Paul in verse 2 of this chapter, from which he rightly concludes the necessity of subjection for conscience's sake [διὰ τὴν συνείδησιν] in this verse.

units.la: XXXI. Ex his quae dicta sunt, non erit difficile quae ex adverso adduci solent argumenta dissolvere. Quorum primum & praecipuum est illud quod à Christiana libertate petitur : cui confirmando, pleraque Scripturæ loca quæ ad astruendam illam libertatem spectant, magna cum pompa[?] in medium afferuntur, & objectiones indè varie[?] efformantur. Scriptum est, inquiunt, à Paulo 1 Cor. 7. Pretio empti estis, nolite fieri servi hominum. Gal. 5. 1. State in libertate in quam vos asseruit Christus, nec rursus jugo servitutis implicamini. Col. 2. 16. Ne quis vos judicet in cibo vel potu, &c. his similia. Disputant etiam non esse verisimile, Christum ita nos demum liberasse à Dei ipsius legibus positivis, quæ fuerunt certè justissimæ, ut tamen nos Legum humanarum vinculo obstrictos relinqueret.
units.tr: XXXI. From what has been said, it will not be difficult to dissolve the arguments commonly brought against us. The first and chief of these is the one drawn from Christian liberty. To confirm this, many passages of Scripture that bear on establishing that liberty are brought forward with great display, and objections are variously framed from them. It is written, they say, by Paul: 1 Cor. 7. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men. Gal. 5. 1. Stand fast in the liberty with which Christ has made you free, and do not be entangled again in the yoke of bondage. Col. 2. 16. Let no one judge you in food or drink, and similar passages. They also argue that it is not likely that Christ freed us from God's own positive laws, which were certainly most just, only to leave us bound by the chain of human laws.

units.la: XXXII. Ad singula loca respondeo. Sed vos ante præmonitos velim, quum sint multa Christianæ Libertatis capita, cavendum esse diligenter ne ea temerè confundantur, neve illa Scripturæ loca quæ ad unum aliquod libertatis genus pertinent, ad aliud genus quò non spectant imperitè trahantur. Quæ μεταβάσις εἰς ἄλλο γένος[?], non Antinomis solùm & Anabaptistis, sed & aliis plerisque istius ævi Reformatoribus perpetuum & solenne vitium est : ut alias sæpissimè, ita vel maximè, ubi de ritibus Ecclesiasticis instituitur disputatio. Quod admonuisse sufficiat : nunc propius ad rem. In illo ad Corinthios loco hortatur Apostolus fideles, ut quisque quo ipsum loco Deus constituerit quibusque donis ornaverit, contentus statione suâ intra debitos fines se modestè contineat, & donis ac vocatione Dei se metiatur, vitamque & actiones ad illa accommodè instituat, sive servus sit, sive liber : nec ita se conscientiámque suam cujusquam hominis aut Judicio aut Imperio manciper, ut ab ejus Opinione aut Voluntate totus pendeat; Sed memor se Dei & Domini Jesu Christi servum esse, sic hominibus placere studeat, & ipsorum affectibus aut imperiis inservire, ut nihil indignum faciat eo homine, qui se servum Dei & Christi profiteatur. Quæ cum sit Apostoli in tota illa perioche certissima mens, rectissimè hinc concludi poterit, non debere nos dominorum, parentum, principum, aliorumque quorumcunque mortalium hominum placitis morem gerere, siquid a nobis fieri postulent quod impium illicitumve sit: quia hoc esset pro Dei servo servum se hominum præstare. At qui justis, honestis & utilibus hominum constitutionibus ex Conscientiâ obtemperat, tantum abest ut propterea servus hominum censendus sit, ut a duobus summis Apostolis differtè dicatur Domino Deo servire, & non hominibus. Ephef. 6. 7. Coloss. 3. 23. & 1 Pet. 2. 16. id est, (particula negandi, ut fieri amat, comparative sumpta,) Deo potius quam hominibus: quia Deo propter se, hominibus propter Deum. Hominibus servit quidem, quatenus quod imperatum est facit: Deo autem servit, quatenus ex officii conscientia id facit.
units.tr: XXXII. I answer to the individual passages. But I would have you first forewarned that, since there are many heads of Christian Liberty, care must be taken that they are not rashly confused, and that those passages of Scripture which pertain to one kind of liberty are not carelessly dragged into another kind to which they do not refer. This transition into another genus [μεταβάσις εἰς ἄλλο γένος] is a constant and customary fault not only of the Antinomians and Anabaptists, but also of many other Reformers of that age: as often elsewhere, so especially where a dispute is conducted about ecclesiastical rites. It is enough to have warned of this; now to the matter itself. In that passage to the Corinthians the Apostle exhorts the faithful that each should keep himself modestly within due bounds, content with the station in which God has placed him and with the gifts with which he has adorned him. Each should measure himself by his gifts and God's calling, and arrange his life and actions accordingly, whether he be a slave or free. Nor should anyone so surrender himself and his conscience to another man's judgment or command that he hangs wholly on that man's opinion or will. Rather, mindful that he is a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, he should strive to please men, and serve their feelings or commands, in such a way that he does nothing unworthy of one who professes himself a servant of God and Christ. Since this is the Apostle's most certain mind throughout that whole passage, it may rightly be concluded from it that we ought not to comply with the wishes of masters, parents, princes, or of any other mortal men, if they demand of us anything that is impious or unlawful, because this would be to make ourselves servants of men in place of servants of God. But he who obeys just, honest and useful human constitutions from conscience is so far from being thereby counted a servant of men that the two chief Apostles expressly say he serves the Lord God and not men: Eph. 6. 7; Col. 3. 23; and 1 Pet. 2. 16. That is, the negative particle, as it likes to be, is taken comparatively: rather to God than to men, because to God for his own sake, to men for God's sake. He serves men indeed, in so far as he does what is commanded; but he serves God in so far as he does it from a sense of duty.

units.la: XXXIII. Locus ille alter ad Galatas, ex totius Epistolæ scopo optimè intelligitur. E Judæis aut Judaizantibus Christianis Pseudo-Apostoli quidam in Ecclesiis Galatiæ, Gentiles ad fidem conversos, contra quàm Apostoli in Concilio Hierosolymitano [?] constituerant, non baptizari modò sed & circumcidi debere contendebant, multòsque (ut solent impostores obtentu pietatis, & improba diligentia apud credulum vulgum mirum quantum proficere) in eum errorem induxerant, ut nisi se circumcidi paterentur, existimarent æternam se salutem consequi non posse. Pessimam hanc & prosperam imposturam non ferens B. Pauli spiritus, crassum illum errorem, ne ultra serperet, majore quàm solet indignatione tota ferè Epistola infestatur [?]. Atque inter alia argumenta admonet Galatas ejus libertatis, qua Christus Ecclesiam ab inutili jam post ipsius adventum, Mosaicarum Ceremoniarum, onere & jugo liberaverat ; hortatúrque ut partam Christi morte libertatem constanter tueantur, nec jugo servitutis colla denuò subdant : quod omninò facerent, si emortuae jam Legis Rituum observationem sibi ducerent esset necessariam. Quod quàm incongruè ad Leges Humanas utiles & Reipublicae necessarias accommodetur, à quibus nullibi Scripturae docent nos Christum liberasse, cœcus sit oportet, qui non videat.
units.tr: XXXIII. That other passage to the Galatians is best understood from the scope of the whole Epistle. Certain pseudo-apostles from among the Jews or Judaizing Christians, in the churches of Galatia, were contending that Gentiles converted to the faith ought to be not only baptized but also circumcised, contrary to what the Apostles had decided at the Council of Jerusalem. They had led many into that error (as impostors are wont, under the pretext of piety and by a wonderfully great diligence, to make much progress among the credulous crowd), so that, unless they allowed themselves to be circumcised, they thought they could not obtain eternal salvation. Not bearing this wicked and successful imposture, the spirit of the blessed Paul, lest that gross error should creep further, attacks almost the whole Epistle with greater indignation than usual. And among other arguments he reminds the Galatians of that liberty by which Christ, after his coming, had freed the Church from the now useless burden and yoke of the Mosaic ceremonies. He urges them to keep constantly the liberty won by Christ's death and not to submit their necks again to the yoke of bondage; which they would certainly do if they regarded the observance of the now dead law of rites as necessary for themselves. How incongruously this is applied to human laws, which are useful and necessary to the commonwealth, and from which the Scriptures nowhere teach that Christ has freed us, anyone must be blind not to see.

units.la: XXXIV. Tertius item locus ex Epistola ad Coloffenses non ad Leges Humanas de rebus mediis ritè constitutas pertinet : sed ad Doctrinas Impostorum, qui populo Dei aliqua dogmaticè proponebant ut necessaria quae Deus non praeceperat ; qui fuit mos Pharisaeorum Traditionarium, quos eo nomine reprehendit Christus, Mat. 15. Quòd docerent doctrinas mandata hominum ; vel è contra aliqua dogmaticè prohibebant ut illicita, quae Deus nusquam vetuerat, dicentes non licere hoc vel illud, tangere, gustare, attrectare. Monet Apostolus, caveant sibi à dogmatixantibus [?] hisce doctoribus Colossenses, nec Conscientiis suis laqueum injici sinant ab eorum imposturis. Non ergo peccant Magistratus politici, qui in rebus mediis aliqua subditis praecipiunt aut prohibent, utilitatis, ordinis, aut honestatis & decori gratiâ ; citra tamen opinionem necessitatis ex utravis parte, quod ad rem ipsam praeceptam vel prohibitam spectant. Peccant potiùs Ministelli illi (Magistellos rectiùs dixerim, ita Magistraliter omnia pronunciantes) qui innoxias Magistratuum Leges importunè solicitant, dictaturam in Conscientias populi exercent, & quod non sapit ipsorum palato, id omne aut impietatis damnant extemplò, aut saltem superstitionis [?].
units.tr: XXXIV. The third passage, likewise from the Epistle to the Colossians, pertains not to human laws duly made about things indifferent, but to the doctrines of impostors, who dogmatically proposed to the people of God, as necessary, things that God had not commanded. This was the custom of the Pharisaic traditionists, whom Christ rebuked on this account, Matt. 15., because they taught doctrines that were the commandments of men. Or, on the contrary, they dogmatically forbade, as unlawful, things that God had nowhere forbidden, saying it was not lawful to do this or that: to touch, to taste, to handle. The Apostle warns the Colossians to beware of these dogmatizing teachers, and not to let a snare be laid on their consciences by their impostures. Therefore political magistrates do not sin when, in things indifferent, they command or forbid certain things to their subjects for the sake of utility, order, or honesty and decency, provided there is no opinion of necessity on either side, so far as the matter itself commanded or forbidden is concerned. Rather, those little ministers sin (I would more correctly call them little magistrates, since they pronounce everything in a magisterial manner) who importunately harass the harmless laws of the magistrates, exercise dictatorship over the consciences of the people, and who at once condemn as impious, or at least as superstitious, whatever does not suit their own palate.

units.la: XXXV. Quod quarto loco ex eo urgent, quòd nos Christus liberavit à legibus Dei positivis; ergo multò etiam magis à Legibus Humanis · non uno modo peccat. Imprimis non illud verè dicitur, Christum nos liberasse à Legibus Dei positivis, quibus scilicet nunquam tenebamur. Leges enim positivæ, sive Dei, sive Hominum, non obligant nisi eos duntaxat quibus posita sint. Dei autem Leges illæ, quas positivas vocant, & à quibus nos per Christi mortem liberatos volunt, sive Rituum, sive Judiciorum, Judæis tantùm positæ sunt; nobis, hoc est, populo Christiano, non item. Deinde, ubi quid Deus fieri velit satis constat, non est nostrum ex collatione comparatorum importuniùs statuere, quid fieri debuit. Constat autem utrumque Deum voluisse: & ut Leges ipsius positivæ Hebræo populo à Mose traditæ non obligarent Christianos: & ut Leges Humanæ à Magistratibus ritè institutæ subditos obligarent. Non animadvertunt denique qui ista objiciunt eo argumento, si quidem valeret, tolli Legum Humanarum non obligationem solum, sed & omnem penitus usum. Non enim aliter nos Christus liberavit à Legum Mosaicarum obligatione, quàm earum usum ita tollendo ut non amplius essent nobis pro Legibus habendæ. Si igitur eodem modo voluerit nos liberos esse ab obligatione Legum Humanarum, voluisse eum quoque necesse est, ut nullæ extarent amplius Humanæ Leges. Quod est Anabaptistarum & fanaticorum hominum delirium, nec ab ipsis admittitur, qui ista objiciunt.
units.tr: XXXV. As to what they press in the fourth place, namely that Christ freed us from God's positive laws, and therefore much more from human laws: this argument goes wrong in more ways than one. First, it is not truly said that Christ freed us from God's positive laws, by which we were of course never bound. For positive laws, whether of God or of men, do not bind except those alone to whom they are given. But those laws of God which they call positive, and from which they want us to have been freed by Christ's death, whether ritual or judicial, were given to the Jews only, not to us, that is, the Christian people. Next, where it is quite clear what God wishes to be done, it is not for us to decide too presumptuously, from a comparison of things compared, what ought to have been done. Now it is certain that God willed both: that his positive laws, given to the Hebrew people through Moses, should not bind Christians; and that human laws duly instituted by magistrates should bind their subjects. Lastly, those who raise these objections do not notice that, if their argument held good, not only the obligation of human laws but all their use would be wholly abolished. For Christ did not free us from the obligation of the Mosaic laws otherwise than by abolishing their use, so that they were no longer to be held as laws for us. If therefore he willed in the same way that we should be free from the obligation of human laws, he must also have willed that no human laws should any longer exist. This is the delirium of the Anabaptists and fanatical men, and it is not admitted even by those who raise these objections.

units.la: XXXVI. Objiciunt & illud Jacobi Apostoli, Unus est Legislator, &c. Jac. 4. Deus sc. & Christus, qui solus Dominus est Conscientiarum. Juris igitur Christi invasor est, & se in Dei Thronum ingerit, quisquis sibi potestatem assumit obligandi aliorum conscientias. Respondeo, Legislatorem unum esse tantum Supremum, qui merum & directum Imperium habet in Conscientias hominum, ut eas obligare possit per fe & virtute ac authoritate propria; Deum nempe & Christum : quod voluit Apostolus. Quod tamen non impedit, quo minus sint & alii Legislatores inferioris ordinis & gradus, qui per concessam sibi & derivatam à summo illo Legiflatore potestatem, jus habeant & ipsi Leges condendi, quae ex consequenti conscientias obligent. Prorsus ut Rex, qui solus habet in Regno suo Potestatem Legislativam αὐτοκρατευτικῶ [?], potest tamen per chartam suam alicui Communitati vel Collegio jus dare condendi Leges, quae obligent omnia illius corporis membra ; non Virtute propria, sed vi donationis Regiae & ex potestate sibi à Rege concessa. Gaudent hoc privilegio, ut omnes nostris, Academiae nostrae, ut possint in legitima Convocatione Leges (quae Statuta dicimus) rogare ; poenas delinquentibus irrogare ; eadem Statuta, fi sic expedire videbitur, abrogare & refigere. Cujus potestatis exercitium nemo tamen sanae mentis existimaverit Juri Regis νομοθετικῷ ullatenus derogare, vel ei fraudi esse posse aut praejudicio, nisi ultra definitos in charta donationis limites protendatur. Quin potius eximium est & singulare Regiae αὐτονομίας [?] indicium, quod Legislativam potestatem non tantum ipse habeat, sed & aliis etiam (salvo tamen suo jure) infra certos limites habendam utendam concedere possit.
units.tr: XXXVI. They also object that saying of the Apostle James, There is one Lawgiver, etc. Jas. 4. That is, God, and Christ, who alone is Lord of Consciences. Therefore whoever claims for himself the power of binding the consciences of others is an invader of Christ's right and thrusts himself onto God's Throne. I answer that there is only one supreme Legislator, who has mere and direct dominion over the consciences of men, so that he can bind them of himself, by his own virtue and authority: namely God and Christ, as the Apostle meant. Yet this does not prevent there being other Legislators of an inferior order and rank, who, through power granted to them and derived from that supreme Legislator, have the right themselves to make laws, which by consequence bind consciences. Just as the King, who alone has legislative power in his kingdom in its own right [αὐτοκρατευτικῶ], can nevertheless by his charter give some community or college the right of making laws, which bind all the members of that body; not by its own virtue but by the force of the royal grant and from the power conceded to it by the King. All our colleges in our University enjoy this privilege, so that in a lawful assembly they may propose laws (which we call statutes), impose penalties on offenders, and, if it seems fit, repeal and revise the same statutes. Yet no one of sound mind would think the exercise of this power in any way derogates from the royal legislative right [νομοθετικῷ], or could be to its harm or prejudice, unless it is extended beyond the limits defined in the charter of grant. Indeed it is an outstanding and singular sign of royal autonomy [αὐτονομίας], that the King not only has legislative power himself but can also grant it to others to hold and exercise within certain limits, his own right being preserved.

units.la: XXXVII Reliquae Objectiones, quum uno eodemque fere nitantur fundamento, una proinde eademque opera solvuntur. Attingam ergo breviter.
units.tr: XXXVII. The remaining objections, since they rest on almost one and the same foundation, are therefore answered by one and the same work. I shall therefore touch on them briefly.

units.la: Objiciunt Tertio potestatem civilem esse mere temporalem ; non ergo pertingere ad Conscientiam quae res est quaedam spiritualis. Quarto, finem Legum Humanarum esse pacem Reipublicae externam, non internam Conscientiae : ergo & Leges ipsas exterorem hominem tantum obligare, non item, quae intus est & latet, Conscientiam. Quinto, Magistratum scientias Judicare non potè, ergo nec Leges eis ferre: cum fit ejusdem potestatis Leges dare & fecundum Leges Judicare. Sextò, Magistratum Legem farendo non habere intentionem obligandi Conscientias subditorum, sed tantùm obligandi ad id præftandum quod Lex imperat; quod fi præstetur, perinde esse ad utilitatem Reipublicæ five id ex officii Conscientiâ fiat, five non: & effectus actionum sat esse fi commensurentur intentioni agentium, nec ultra extendi debere.
units.tr: They object, thirdly, that civil power is purely temporal and so does not reach to conscience, which is a certain spiritual thing. Fourthly, that the end of human laws is the external peace of the commonwealth, not the internal peace of conscience: therefore the laws themselves bind only the outward man, not also the conscience, which is within and hidden. Fifthly, that the magistrate cannot judge hearts, and therefore cannot give laws to them, since it is the same power that gives laws and judges according to them. Sixthly, that in making a law the magistrate does not have the intention of binding the consciences of subjects, but only of binding them to do what the law commands; and if that is done, it makes no difference to the good of the commonwealth whether it is done from a sense of duty of conscience or not; and the effects of actions are enough if they are measured by the intention of the agents, and ought not to be extended further.

units.la: XXXVIII. Respondeo: & primùm universim. His omnibus argumentis id tantùm effici, Leges humanas non obligare directè & per fe, aut vi propriâ; quod nos ultro largimur: qui Obligationem non aliam afferimus, quàm quæ ipsis obvenit ex consequenti, & virtute generalis præcepti Divini de præstanda sublimioribus potestatibus obedientiâ. Deinde ex hoc fundamento ad singulas Objectiones respondeo. Ad Tertiam dico, Potestatem Civilem, cùm fit merè Temporalis, habere non posse ex fe, & respectu Objecti circa quod proprie & immediate versatur, effectum spiritualem: proinde nec inducere ex fe obligationem spiritualem: posse tamen habere effectum spiritualem ex consequenti, per derivationem à potestate superioris alicujus causæ in cujus virtute operatur. Operatur autem Magistratus, quoties concessam sibi divinitùs Poteftatem Legislativam ritè & debito modo exercet in Virtute Dei ipsius, & ex ejus ordinatione: qui & ipse Spiritus est, & ut spirituum Dominus & pater, imperium habet in spiritus hominum.
units.tr: XXXVIII. I answer: first, in general. All these arguments achieve only this, that human laws do not bind directly and of themselves, or by their own force; which we freely grant, since we assert no other obligation than that which comes to them by consequence, and by virtue of the general divine precept to render obedience to the higher powers. Next, from this foundation I answer each objection.
