To the third I say: civil power, since it is purely temporal, cannot of itself, and with respect to the object with which it is properly and immediately concerned, have a spiritual effect; therefore nor can it of itself induce a spiritual obligation. Yet it can have a spiritual effect by consequence, through derivation from the power of some higher cause in whose virtue it works. The magistrate works in this way whenever he rightly and in due manner exercises the legislative power granted him by God, in the virtue of God himself and by his ordinance: God, who is himself Spirit, and as Lord and Father of spirits has dominion over the spirits of men.

units.la: XXXIX. Ad Quartam dico; Etsi pax communitatis sit res externa, internam tamen conscientiam obligari ad eam omnibus modis licitis & honeftis pro virili procurandam & confervandam: Eò quòd præcepit nobis Deus, Conscientiæ Dominus, ut pacem, cum privatam, tum multò adhuc magis publicam diligamus & sectemur. Nec inconveniens conscientiam, etsi sit internum quid, obligari ad rem externam: siquidem consurgit obligatio Conscientiae, non ex Natura vel aliquâ conditione rei sive objecti in quod fertur, sed ex voluntate ejus qui habet jus obligandi, i. e. unius Dei.
units.tr: XXXIX. To the fourth I say: although the peace of the community is an external thing, the internal conscience is nevertheless bound to procure and preserve it by all lawful and honest means, as far as it can. For God, the Lord of conscience, has commanded us to love and pursue peace, both private and, much more, public. Nor is it inconsistent that conscience, though it is something internal, should be bound to an external thing; for the obligation of conscience arises not from the nature or some condition of the thing or object to which it is directed, but from the will of him who has the right of binding, that is, of God alone.

units.la: XL. Ad Quintam dico, Potestatem νομοθετικὴν & κατακριτικὴν [?], Legislativam sc. & Judiciariam eidem personae competere originaliter; nempe τῷ ἔχοντι [?], ei qui supremam habet in subditos jurisdictionem: posse tamen dispensative, ex voluntate supremi Magistratus, ab aliis personis administrari, vel utramvis vel etiam utramque, prout ipsi collubitum est. Deus ergo, etsi solus habeat in Conscientias creaturae potestatem αὐτονομητικὴν [?], tum Leges ferendi, tum judicandi, jure originali, proprio & absoluto: dispensationem tamen utriusque potestatis potest ipse aut alteri delegare, aut sibi reservare, pro beneplacito suo. Proinde non esset hac ex parte absurdum, siquis concederet Deum Magistratui potestatem obligandi conscientias quadantenus delegasse, judiciariam vero in eas potestatem sibi integram reservasse. Sed nulla nos cogit necessitas, ut hoc concedamus, aut locutione utamur, quae sit leni interpretatione juvanda. Neque enim illud dicimus, Deum dedisse Magistratui potestatem obligandi legibus suis subditorum Conscientias; sed hoc potius (quod est aliquanto cautius & commodius loquendi genus,) Deum dedisse Magistratui potestatem leges ferendi, quae (ex sola tamen authoritate ipsius Dei) obligent subditorum conscientias. Non enim, proprie loquendo, Magistratus obligat conscientiam ad parendum Legi, sed Deus obligat conscientiam ad parendum Magistratui.
units.tr: XL. To the fifth I say: legislative and judicial power [νομοθετικὴν & κατακριτικὴν], that is, power to make laws and to judge, belongs originally to the same person, namely to him [τῷ ἔχοντι] who holds supreme jurisdiction over the subjects. Yet by the will of the supreme Magistrate it can be administered dispensatively by other persons, either one of the two or both, as he pleases. God, therefore, although alone he has over the consciences of creatures a power [αὐτονομητικὴν] of making laws and of judging, by original, proper and absolute right, can nevertheless either delegate the dispensation of either power to another, or reserve it to himself, at his good pleasure. Hence it would not be absurd, in this respect, if someone granted that God had in some measure delegated to the Magistrate the power of binding consciences, but had reserved to himself the judicial power over them entire. But no necessity compels us to concede this, or to use an expression that needs a lenient interpretation to help it. For we do not say that God has given the Magistrate the power of binding the consciences of subjects by his laws; rather (which is a somewhat more cautious and suitable way of speaking) we say that God has given the Magistrate the power of making laws which, by the sole authority of God himself, bind the consciences of subjects. For, properly speaking, the Magistrate does not bind conscience to obey the Law; God binds conscience to obey the Magistrate.

units.la: XLI. Et per hoc patet responsio ad ultimam [?]jectionem. Concedo quidem effectus actionum non debere extendi ultra intentionem agentium. Ubi ta-men sunt plura agentia subordinata, nihil impedit effectum actionis extendi ultra intentionem inferioris agentis, dummodo non excedat intentionem agentis principalis. Sicut in generatione monstri, (ut ex Aristotele pueri didicimus) effectus qui est productio monstri, est praeter intentionem secundae causae, sive naturae naturatae (ut loquuntur:) hoc est, gerantis: sed non est praeter intentionem primae causae, sive Naturae naturantis; hoc est, Omnipotentis Dei.
units.tr: XLI. By this the answer to the last objection is also made plain. I grant indeed that effects of actions ought not to be extended beyond the intention of the agents. Yet where there are several subordinate agents, nothing prevents the effect of an action from being extended beyond the intention of the inferior agent, provided it does not exceed the intention of the principal agent. As in the generation of a monster (as we learned as boys from Aristotle), the effect which is the production of the monster lies beyond the intention of the secondary cause, or nature natured (as they say), that is, of the acting thing; but it does not lie beyond the intention of the primary cause, or nature naturing, that is, of almighty God.

units.la: Licet ergo Magistratus ferendo Legem nullam habeat explicitam intentionem obligandi conscientias; tamen instituendo Legem instituit id, quod ex intentione & ordinatione Dei habet implicitam & sibi necessariò conjunctam vim obligandi. Atque hæc dicta sunto de obligatione Legum Humanarum in generali. Ad quæstiones, sive Casus dubios particulares progrediar, (si Deus permiserit & per ambiguam valetudinem licuerit,) sextâ feriâ proximâ.
units.tr: Therefore, although the magistrate, in making a law, has no explicit intention of binding consciences, yet in instituting a law he institutes that which, by the intention and ordinance of God, has implicitly and necessarily joined to it the power of binding. And let these things be said about the obligation of human laws in general. I shall proceed to particular questions, or doubtful cases, next Friday, if God permits and my uncertain health allows.

units.la: PRÆLECTIO SEXTA.
units.tr: LECTURE VI.

units.la: De Obligatione Legum Humanarum ex parte Causæ Materialis.
units.tr: On the Obligation of Human Laws from the Side of the Material Cause.

units.la: PROV. VIII. 15.
units.tr: PROV. VIII. 15.

units.la: Per me Reges regnant, & Legum conditores justa decernunt.
units.tr: By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just.

units.la: I. QUÆ de Legum Humanarum obligatione dicenda proposui, ad duas quæstiones generales, velut capita, revocavi. Alteram, An Leges Humanæ obligent subditorum Conscientias? de quâ quid mihi fentiendum videbatur, superiore prælectione exposui: Alteram Quatenus obligent? Quò pertinere dixi plerorumque Casuum & Dubiorum quæ in hac materiâ occurrunt, decisionem. Quæ, quoniam nec pauca sunt, nec unius generis; ad vitandam rerum confusionem, & ut vobis aliquis qualiscunque dicendorum ordo & ratio constet: non ab re fore judico, totius institutæ tractationis rudem quendam ὑπογραφὴν[?] & διαγραφὴν, ὡς ἐν τύπῳ vobis ob oculos proponere. Quod autem in prioribus illis meis de Juramenti obligatione exercitationibus factum plerique vestrum meministis, idem mihi nunc denuò imprimis censeo faciendum: ut sc.
units.tr: I. I have reduced what I proposed to say about the obligation of human laws to two general questions, as to heads. The first is Whether human laws bind the consciences of subjects? On this, I set out in the previous lecture what seemed to me the right view. The second is How far they bind? I said that the decision of most of the cases and doubts that arise in this matter belongs to this question. Since these are neither few nor of one kind, I judge it not out of place, to avoid confusion and so that you may have some kind of order and plan of what is to be said, to set before your eyes a rough outline [ὑπογραφὴν] and sketch [διαγραφὴν] of the whole treatment undertaken, as it were in a picture [ὡς ἐν τύπῳ]. As most of you remember was done in my earlier exercises on the obligation of an oath, I now think the same should above all be done again, namely that

units.la: [The margin fragments at the right edge are cut off and not transcribed here.] quæ[?] ad quatuor causarum genera commodè referri posse existimem, eò reducantur singula. Sed quoniam restare video adhuc nonnulla, quæ istis finibus non possunt ita facilè concludi : sunt & illis suæ quoque classes assignandæ. Æque potissimum duæ: de Personis quæ istiusmodi Legum obligationi subjacent, altera ; altera de collatione virtutis obligatoriæ quæ Legibus humanis inest cum ea quæ oritur ex Conscientiæ Judicio, ex Voto, Juramento, Promissione, vel Contractu, ex Scandali lege, aut siquid aliud sit aliunde obligatorium, quoties repugnare videntur invicem istæ obligationes, utra scilicet utri cedere debeat. Tertia enim classis ut addatur, propter Legum species quasdam, quæ videntur continere in se aliquid singulare, (quales sunt Leges Ecclesiasticæ, Leges quæ Pœnales dicuntur, Collegiorum & minorum Societatum localia Statuta, Privilegia, &c.) non erit, fortasse admodum necessarium : cum possint ista feré ab aliquo è quatuor Causarum generibus aliquo modo reduci ; si non ita oppositè, ut istarum rerum curiosis satisfiat, at quantum sufficit instituto nostro, qui dum quid rerum agitur auditores intelligant, de methodo non ultrà laborandum semper existimavimus. Agendum itaque (si Deus ad ea quæ proposui perficienda vitam , valetudinem , opportunitatem concesserit) primo loco de Legum obligatione quoad 4 Causarum genera ; proximo, de personis quæ ad Leges observandas obligantur ; novissimo, de obligationum invicem pugnantium comparatione : Præmissis tantùm unâ & alterâ distinctione, quæ in toto hoc negotio permagni erunt usus.
units.tr: [The fragments in the margin at the right edge are cut off and not transcribed here.] those points which I think can conveniently be referred to the four kinds of causes should each be reduced there. But since I see that some matters still remain which cannot so easily be concluded within those limits, they too must be assigned their own classes. There are chiefly two of these: one concerning the persons who are subject to the obligation of such laws; the other concerning the comparison of the binding virtue that is in human laws with that which arises from the judgment of conscience, from a vow, an oath, a promise, or a contract, from the law of scandal, or from anything else that is binding from elsewhere, whenever these obligations seem to conflict with one another, that is, which ought to yield to which. A third class need not perhaps be added, because of certain kinds of laws which seem to contain something singular in themselves (such as ecclesiastical laws, laws called penal, the local statutes of colleges and smaller societies, privileges, and so on). These can for the most part be reduced in some way to one of the four kinds of causes, if not so directly as to satisfy the curious about such matters, yet enough for our purpose. We have always thought that, provided the hearers understand what is being dealt with, we should not labour further over method. So, if God grants me life, health and opportunity to complete what I have proposed, I shall deal first with the obligation of laws as regards the four kinds of causes; next, with the persons who are bound to observe the laws; last, with the comparison of obligations that conflict with one another. I shall premise only one or two distinctions, which will be of great use throughout this whole business.

units.la: II. Sciendum ergo primò, quum sit ad ordinis politici finem in iis quæ præsunt duplex potestas necessaria ; Directiva sc. ut subditi quæ sibi facienda sint intelligant, & Coercitiva (sic enim potius dicendum ex Analogiæ ratione quàm Coerciva) sive Coactiva, Coactiva, ut ad imperata facienda, si ultrò nolint, compellantur: (quarum utraque in Legibus ita continetur, ut illa in praeceptionibus maximè, haec in poenarum sanctione cernatur; exurgere ex duplici illa praelati potestate, duplex etiam, quod utrique potestati respondeat, subditi debitum; ὑποταχὴ [?] &c. & ὑπακοὴ [?]. Debitum Obedientiae, respectu potentiae directivae, & debitum Subjectionis, respectu potentiae coercitivae. Subjectionem hic intelligo proprie dictam; nempe generis appellatione, ut alias saepe fit, ad unam certam speciem restricta: Nam & Obedientia species est Subjectionis, late sumptae. Utrumque hoc debitum simul complexus est Apostolus, Heb. 13. 17. & duabus illis vocibus significavit, πείθεσθε [?] καὶ ὑπείκετε [?]. Obtemperate praepositis vestris, & subditi estote. Quarum illa [πείθεσθε [?]] ad debitum pertinet Obedientiae, five faciendi quod a legitimo superiore praecipitur: haec [ὑπείκετε [?]] ad debitum Subjectionis, sive patiendi quod ab illo infligitur. Porrò ut ex duplici potestate duplex oritur debitum: sic ex duplici debito duplex oritur obligatio. Nam & omne debitum transit obligationem: & omnis obligatio supponit debitum. Est ergo obligationis humanae legis genus unum, quo tenentur subditi parere praeceptioni ipsius Legis; alterum, quo subesse tenentur potestati ipsius Legislatoris. Illa obligatio ad ἀκολουθ[?] est, hoc est, ad obedientiam activam: ista ad ὑποταγὴν [?], five ad obedientiam quam vocant passivam: nos subjectionem dicere maluimus.
units.tr: III. Now if it is asked: In what respects do human laws bind the consciences of subjects? I answer: first, that all laws enacted by one who has lawful power bind in some way to [ὑποταγή], to subjection, so that it is not lawful for a subject to resist the supreme power by force and arms, whether it commands just or unjust things. This has been the constant mind and practice of Christians, especially in the first ages of the Church, living under the most severe tyranny of the enemies of the Christian name; and this, to pass over for the moment the guidance of nature and the light of right reason, follows from the most plain teaching of both chief Apostles. Thus Peter, the Apostle of the circumcision, diligently instructed the Jews, and Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, his Gentiles. The former, in 1 Pet. 2., where he commands servants of households to be [ὑποτασσόμενοι] to their masters, not only to the good and gentle but also to the harsher ones, who would inflict blows on them though they had deserved nothing of the kind. The latter, in Rom. 13., where he presses the necessity of subjection at length, but grants to no one the liberty of resisting, in any case, under any pretext. Secondly, I say: subjection, however simply necessary, does not discharge the duty unless the command of the law is also obeyed, wherever this can be done without sin; and therefore the subject is bound in conscience to [ὑπακοή] in all things that are lawful and honest. Hence the Apostle so often and expressly urges that [ὑπακούετε], Eph. 6., Col. 3., and elsewhere. Thirdly, I say: where the precept of the law cannot be observed without sin, the subject, if he has patiently submitted himself to the power of the lawgiver, has done enough for his duty and obligation, and is not bound in conscience to do what the law commands; indeed he is bound not to do it, since there can be no obligation to unlawful things. Therefore it is always necessary to submit, [ἀνάγκῃ ὑποτάσσεσθαι], but it is not always necessary to obey.

units.la: III. Jam si quaeratur. Quatenus Legts Humana obligent conscientias subditorum? Dicendum primo, Leges omnes ab habente legitimam potestatem latas obligare utcunque ad ὑποταγὴν, ad subjectionem: ita ut subdito non liceat supremae potestati vi & armis resistere, sive is justa praeceperit sive injusta. Perpetua haec fuit mens & praxis Christianorum in primis Ecclesiæ seculis, sub gravissimâ hostium Christiani nominis tyrannide degentium : idque (ut Naturæ ductum interim taceam & rectæ rationis lumen,) ex apertissimâ utriusque summi Apostoli doctrinâ. Sic Petrus circumcisionis Apostolus Judæos, sic Gentium doctor Paulus suos Gentiles, sedulò instituit. Ille 1 Pet. 2. Ubi servis familiâs præcipit dominis suis ὑποτασσόμενοι[?] non solùm bonis & æquis, sed & severioribus illis, qui plagas ipsis nihil tale commeritis inferrent. Hic Rom. 13. Ubi subjectionis necessitatem pluribus urget, resistendi verò licentiam, quocunque in casu, quocunque sub prætextu, nemini concedit. Dicendum secundò; subjectione, utut simpliciter necessaria, non tamen satisfieri officio, nisi & obediatur legis imperio, ubi id sine peccato fieri poterit : & proinde subditum & ad ὑπακοήν[?] obligari in conscientia in rebus omnibus licitis & honestis. Hinc toties ab Apostolo disertim inculcatur illud ὑπακούετε[?], Eph. 6. Colos. 3. & alibi. Dicendum tertiò, ubi observari non potest Legis præceptio sine peccato, subditum, si patienter se subjecerit potestati Legislatoris, officio suo & debito fecisse satis ; nec obligari in conscientia ad faciendum quod Lex præcipit : imò obligari ad non faciendum, quum ad illicita nulla possit esse obligatio. Semper igitur necesse est subjici, [ἀνάγκῃ ὑποτάσσεσθαι[?]] non semper necesse est obedire.
units.tr: III. Now if it is asked, how far do human laws bind the consciences of subjects? I say, first, that all laws enacted by one who has lawful power bind, in whatever way, to submission [ὑποταγὴν], to subjection, so that it is not lawful for a subject to resist the supreme power by force and arms, whether it commands what is just or what is unjust. This has been the constant mind and practice of Christians, especially in the first ages of the Church, when they lived under the most grievous tyranny of enemies of the Christian name; and this (to pass over for the moment the guidance of nature and the light of right reason) rests on the very plain teaching of both chief Apostles. Thus Peter, the apostle of the circumcision, carefully instructed the Jews, and Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, instructed his Gentiles. Peter, in 1 Pet. 2., where he commands household servants to be submissive [ὑποτασσόμενοι] to their masters, not only to the good and gentle but also to the harsh, who might inflict blows on them though they had deserved nothing of the kind. Paul, in Rom. 13., where he presses the necessity of submission at length, but grants the liberty of resistance to no one, in any case, under any pretext. I say, secondly, that submission, however simply necessary, does not satisfy the duty unless one also obeys the command of the law, where this can be done without sin. Therefore the subject is also bound in conscience to obedience [ὑπακοήν] in all things that are lawful and honourable. Hence the Apostle so often and expressly urges that word [ὑπακούετε], obey, in Eph. 6. and Col. 3. and elsewhere. I say, thirdly, that where the command of the law cannot be observed without sin, the subject, if he has patiently submitted to the power of the lawgiver, has done enough for his duty and obligation; and he is not bound in conscience to do what the law commands. Rather, he is bound not to do it, since there can be no obligation to what is unlawful. So one must always submit of necessity [ἀνάγκῃ ὑποτάσσεσθαι], but one is not always bound to obey.

units.la: IV. Porrò, quum utrumque certum sit, tum Conscientias hominum liberas & esse, & esse debere, libertati nulla potestas humana præjudicare aut{4} possit, aut debeat ; tum etiam obligationem quoddam vinculum esse, & necessitatem aliquam inducere, quæ videtur cum justâ libertate pugnare, (neque enim aut omninò liber est, qui vinctus est ; aut ad utrumlibet liber, qui ad alterutrum necessitate aliquâ arctatur :) ut liquidò constet consistere posse cum justa Conscientiarum libertate hanc de qua nunc agimus Conscientiarum obligationem, necessario nobis adhibenda est altera adhuc distinctio : Scilicet praeceptionem Legis humanae posse sumi dupliciter: vel formaliter, pro ipso actu praecipiendi ; vel materialiter pro re praecepta. Legislator ergo, si intenderet obligationem sive parendi necessitatem, quam subdito imponit, a praeceptione suae legis materialiter accepta deducere ; hoc est, a necessitate ipsius rei praeceptae, quae tamen in rei veritate ante legem illam latam non esset necessaria : Vim sane faceret ipso facto Conscientiae subditi, quae ipsius libertati adversaretur. Quod si obligationem eam non aliunde ducat, quam a praeceptione suae legis formaliter accepta, hoc est, a sua praecipientis legitima authoritate, (rei ipsius praecepta morali ἀδιαφορίᾳ[?] in medio interim relicta, & in eodem statu quo ante legem latam fuerat permanente ; ) etsi obligatio sequatur, quae parendi necessitatem conscientiae imponat, illaesa tamen & integra manet interna Conscientiae libertas.
units.tr: IV. Furthermore, since both things are certain, namely that men's consciences are and ought to be free, and that no human power can or should prejudice liberty; and also that obligation is a kind of bond and induces some necessity which seems to conflict with true liberty (for one who is bound is not wholly free, nor is one who is pressed by some necessity toward one of two alternatives free to choose either): then, so that it may be clear that this obligation of conscience of which we now speak can consist with the just liberty of conscience, we must necessarily apply one more distinction. That is, the command of a human law can be taken in two ways: either formally, for the very act of commanding; or materially, for the thing commanded. Accordingly, if the lawgiver intended to derive the obligation, or the necessity of obeying, which he imposes on the subject, from the command of his law taken materially, that is, from the necessity of the thing commanded itself, which in the truth of the matter was not necessary before that law was enacted, he would indeed do violence to the very conscience of the subject, and this would be contrary to its liberty. But if he derives that obligation from nothing other than the command of his law taken formally, that is, from his own lawful authority as one who commands (the thing itself commanded being left in the meantime in moral indifference [ἀδιαφορίᾳ] and remaining in the same state it was in before the law was enacted), then, although an obligation follows which imposes on conscience the necessity of obeying, the inner liberty of conscience remains unharmed and whole.

units.la: V. Exemplo res, si cui obscura videatur, clarior evadet. Lege civili lata ; nequis carnes totâ Quadragesimâ comederet : si Legislator in proœmio vel corpore ipsius Legis alicubi significaret, hoc se propterea subditis imperare, quòd impium sit aut illicitum eo tempore carnibus vesci ; esset hoc quidem subditorum conscientiis laqueum injicere, earumque libertatem, quantum in ipso esset, labefactare. Quod si expresse significaret Legislator, se de re aliàs & in se liberâ, ad Reipublicae aliquam commoditatem sic statuisse, aut ut inde populus Christianus ad veteris Ecclesiae exemplum occasionem caperet ascetica disciplinae utcunque exercendae ; vel si ex verbis Legis aut alicunde constare posset, Legislatorem eâ lege non intendisse aliquam necessitatis opinionem rei ipsi imperatae affigere : nulla subditorum Conscientiæ, ejúsve libertati, hoc pacto fieret injuria. Longè enim alia res est, cum quid propterea à Magistratu præcipitur, quòd putetur esse necessarium; aut prohibetur, quia putatur esse illicitum: alia, cum quid tum demum incipit haberi necessarium, postquam est à Magistratu præceptum; aut illicitum, quia est ab eo prohibitum. Prior illa necessitas, quæ se habet antecedenter ad Legem, & ab ea supponitur, ut ejus causa aliqua conscientiæ libertati repugnat: at posterior ista, quæ consequenter se habet ad legem, & ab ea oritur ut effectus ejus, non repugnat. Cujus discriminis ratio est; quòd necessitas illa antecedens quam lex supponit, necessario requirit assensum aliquem judicii practici: ad necessitatem autem consequentem quæ ex lege oritur sufficit consensus voluntatis ad faciendum id opus extremum quod lege præcipitur. Actus autem voluntatis non potest libertati conscientiæ præjudicare, sicut præjudicat actus judicii: quia voluntatis actus sequitur conscientiæ dictamen, ut effectus sequitur suam causam; actus vero judicii præcedit illud dictamen, ut causa præcedit suum effectum.
units.tr: V. An example will make the matter clearer, should it seem obscure to anyone. Suppose a civil law is passed: that no one shall eat meat during the whole of Lent. If the Legislator, in the preamble or somewhere in the body of the Law itself, were to indicate that he imposes this on his subjects because it is impious or unlawful to eat meat at that time, this would indeed be to cast a noose over the subjects' consciences and to undermine their liberty, so far as lay in him. But if the Legislator expressly stated that he had decreed this about a matter otherwise free in itself, for some advantage of the commonwealth, or so that the Christian people might take from it an occasion, after the example of the ancient Church, of practising ascetic discipline in whatever way; or if it could be established from the words of the Law, or from elsewhere, that the Legislator did not intend by that law to attach any opinion of necessity to the thing commanded: then no injury would be done in this way to the subjects' conscience or to its liberty. For it is quite another matter when something is commanded by the Magistrate because it is thought to be necessary, or forbidden because it is thought to be unlawful; and another when something only begins to be held necessary after it has been commanded by the Magistrate, or unlawful because it has been forbidden by him. That former necessity, which stands antecedently to the Law and is presupposed by it as its cause, does conflict with liberty of conscience. But the latter, which stands consequently to the law and arises from it as its effect, does not conflict. The reason for this distinction is that the antecedent necessity which the law presupposes necessarily requires some assent of practical judgment; whereas for the consequent necessity which arises from the law, the consent of the will suffices to perform that external act which the law commands. But an act of the will cannot prejudice the liberty of conscience as an act of judgment does, because an act of the will follows the dictate of conscience as an effect follows its cause, whereas an act of judgment precedes that dictate as a cause precedes its effect.

units.la: VI. His distinctionibus præmissis, ad Dubia pergo: ubi primo loco illa occurrunt, quæ ad Materialem causam pertinent, hoc tempore sola discutienda. Dubium itaque primum esto de materia impossibili. De qua dico primò, Legem de re prorsus impossibili ferri non debere: si feratur; tyrannicam esse, & de jure nullam, nec quenquam obligare in conscientia. Ratio prima: quia leges feruntur de actibus ut ab homine agendis, qui est liberum agens: libertas autem dicit potestatem ad utrumlibet: sed in rebus Impossibilibus non est libera potestas ad utrumlibet, ut per se patet. Ratio secunda. Nemo potest jure obligari ad id faciendum, cujus omissio non potest ei imputari ad culpam, nec debet ei imputari ad pœnam ; (omni enim obligatio aut ad culpam est, aut ad pœnam, ve[?] etiam utramque :) sed rei impossibilis omissio non[?] potest alicui imputari ad culpam, nec debet alicu[?] imputari ad pœnam : ergo, &c. Sed quòd rei im-possibilis nulla possit esse obligatio, (five ea sit e[?] natura rei, five ex circumstantiis, five alio quocu[?] que modo impossibilis) est à me jamdudum ex ho[?] loco satis confirmatum, cum de {1}Juramenti obliga- tione disserui : nec opus est repetitu.
units.tr: VI. With these distinctions premised, I proceed to the Doubts. Where the first of them arise, they concern the material cause, and these alone are to be discussed at this time. Let the first doubt, then, concern an impossible matter. On this I say, first, that a Law should not be given about a thing altogether impossible. If it is given, it is tyrannical and null in right, and binds no one in conscience. First reason: laws are given about actions to be performed by a man, who is a free agent; liberty, however, means power to either alternative; but in impossible things there is no free power to either, as is plain in itself. Second reason: no one can rightly be obliged to do that whose omission cannot be imputed to him as a fault, nor ought to be imputed to him as a punishment (for every obligation is either to fault or to punishment, or even to both). But the omission of an impossible thing cannot be imputed to anyone as a fault, nor ought it to be imputed to anyone as a punishment. Therefore, etc. That there can be no obligation to an impossible thing (whether it is impossible by the nature of the thing, or by its circumstances, or in any other way) I have already sufficiently confirmed in this place, when I discussed the {1}obligation of an oath; nor is there need to repeat it.

units.la: VII. Dico secundò, Legem de re plerisque possi-bili, sed quæ videtur multis, aut paucis aut uni[?] forte alterive impossibilis futura, posse quidem si si[?] ex usu Reipublicæ licitè ferri ; non tamen nisi ad-modum gravis subsit causa, & postulet manifest[?] necessitas : latam verò, omnes eos obligare qui eam[?] servare possunt, reliquos autem non obligare. Ut[?] si tributum grande in necessarios Reipublicæ usu[?] imperetur, cui solvendo aliqui subditorum non sin[?] pares : qui pauperiores sunt quàm ut solvere pol-sint summam lege imperatam, non obligari in[?] conscientia ad id faciendum quod ab ipsis fie[?] non potest, ex jam dicta hypothesi certum est. Ob-ligantur tamen apud eos qui præsunt, tenuitatem suam aperte, sed sincere id & sine mendacio, prosi-teri : & nisi possint ab iis aut omnimodam à lege exemptionem, aut aliquotæ saltem summæ imperata partis remissionem mereri, quantum possunt con-ferre in publicum. Quia qui non potest quod debet, {2}debet tamen quod potest.
units.tr: VII. I say secondly, that a Law may indeed be lawfully given about a thing possible for most people, but which seems likely to be impossible for many, or for a few, or perhaps for one or another, provided it is for the use of the commonwealth. Yet this is only so if a very grave cause underlies it and a manifest necessity demands it. Once such a law has been given, it obliges all those who are able to keep it, but does not oblige the rest. For example, if a heavy tax is imposed for the necessary uses of the commonwealth, which some of the subjects are not equal to paying: it is certain, from the hypothesis just stated, that those who are too poor to be able to pay the sum imposed by law are not bound in conscience to do what cannot be done by them. Yet they are bound to make their poverty known openly, but sincerely and without lying, to those who preside over them; and unless they can obtain from them either a complete exemption from the law or at least a remission of some part of the sum imposed, they should contribute to the public as much as they can. For he who cannot do what he ought nevertheless ought to do what he can.

units.la: VIII. Dubium secundum. De re lege imperata, non impossibili, sed valdè tamen gravi & onerosa, & quam subditus præstare non potest sine summ[?] suo incommodo, damno, vitæ discrimine, vel to-tius rei familiaris ruina. Dico primò, Legislatorem si prævideat hoc futurum, debere aliqua cautionem in ipsa lege ferenda, quàm commode fieri potest, providere huic malo aliquod remedium. Id, si non possit ita commodè fieri in ipsa Legis formula, (ne variis hominibus, in ejusmodi occasiones plus satis attentis, aperiatur isto pacto rimula aliqua quâ evadant, & vim legis eludant :) illud saltem, quantum in ipso est, procurare debere, ut in legeexequenda aliquis modus adhibeatur, ne lex alias utilis & necessaria honesto cuiquam civi fraudi vel lucrumento fit. Dico secundo, subditum eo quo jam supponimus modo aggravatum, teneri in conscientia legi obedire, etiam cum ruina totius rei familiaris, si boni publici ratio aliqua evidens & necessaria id postulet. Ut, si lex feratur, exercitu hostili regnum invadente, ut in agris legetes omnes per aliquot milliarium à littore spatium devastentur; omne frumentum in horreis & apothecis, quod non possit alió deportari, exuratur; ædes suburbanæ diruantur; prata immissis fluminibus submergantur: obligatur omnino unusquisque civium ei legi parere, atque imperata libenter & alacriter facere, ut cum jactura rei privata redimat salutem publicam. Idque non ea solùm ratione, quod certum sit, prodita hostibus (intempestiva frugalitate) patria, calamitatem in privatos quosque cives propediem emanaturam: sed ex officii quoque conscientia vel maximè, quod sit omni viro bono bonum publicum privato anteferendum. Dico tertio, subditum, nisi insignis aliqua appareat necessitas, vel publici periculi metus, ordinariè non teneri valde onerosa legi parere, cum certa rei domesticæ ruina, aut capitis periculo: Teneri tamen, ut antè generatim dictum, (quod & in omnibus ferè casibus observandam moneo, ne sit necesse id ipsum multoties repetere,) quicquid sibi injuriæ vel contumeliæ à sublimioribus potestatibus illarum suerit, id æquo animo perpeti, nec eis ullatenus resistere.
units.tr: VIII. Second doubt. Concerning a thing commanded by law which is not impossible, but is very grave and onerous, and which a subject cannot perform without great inconvenience, loss, danger to life, or the ruin of his whole household property. I say, first, that the Legislator, if he foresees that this will happen, ought, when framing the law itself, to provide some remedy for this evil, with as much caution as can conveniently be done. If this cannot conveniently be done in the very wording of the law (lest through it some little crack be opened for various men, who are only too alert on such occasions, by which they may escape and evade the force of the law), he ought at least to arrange, so far as lies in him, that some method be adopted in executing the law, so that the law, otherwise useful and necessary, does not become a cause of loss or of gain to any honest citizen. I say, secondly, that a subject, burdened in the manner we have now supposed, is bound in conscience to obey the law, even with the ruin of his whole household property, if some evident and necessary reason of the public good demands it. For example, if a law were passed, when a hostile army is invading the kingdom, that in the fields all the crops for some miles from the shore be laid waste; that every grain in barns and storehouses which cannot be carried elsewhere be burnt; that suburban buildings be pulled down; that meadows be submerged by letting in the rivers: then every one of the citizens is wholly bound to obey that law and to do what is commanded willingly and eagerly, so that by the loss of private property he may redeem the public safety. And this is so not only for the reason that it is certain that the homeland, betrayed to the enemy by untimely thrift, will soon bring calamity upon every private citizen; but chiefly from the very conscience of duty, because every good man ought to prefer the public good to his private good. I say, thirdly, that a subject, unless some notable necessity appears or there is fear of public danger, is ordinarily not bound to obey a law that is very burdensome when his household is certain to be ruined or his life endangered. Yet he is bound, as I said above in general terms (which I advise to be observed in nearly all cases too, so that it need not be repeated again and again), to bear with equanimity whatever injury or insult he has received from the higher powers, and in no way to resist them.

units.la: IX. Dubium
units.tr: IX. Doubt

units.la: IX. Dubium Tertium, de re Necessaria. Si Lex Humana aliquid præcipiat, quod fuit ante necessarium & Lege Dei præceptum ; aut prohibeat, quod fuit ante illicitum, & lege Dei prohibitum : quæ sit Obligatio ? Respondeo breviter, subditum illâ lege simpliciter obligari. Nam primò, obligatio, quæ præfuit vi Legis Dei, non impedit effectum Legis Humanæ, excludendo obligationem novam: quum possit quis ad idem officium pluribus vinculis obligari, ut superiore lectione satis ostendimus. Cui rationi & illa adjicienda est secundò, Legem humanam addere plerunque aliquid Legi Divinæ : determinando sc. actum (quoad substantiam suam, Lege Dei imperatum, proinde & necessarium,) quoad modum, quantitatem, aut aliam sui circumstantiam, quæ fuit ante libera ; vel etiam adjiciendo Legi Divinæ prohibenti rem illicitam determinationem aliquam, quoad gradum criminis, vel pœnæ genus, ejusve mensuram, aliaque ejusmodi. Exempli gratia, Cætus publicos ad officia sacri cultus peragenda haberi, Divini juris est : at quibus horis, quo loco, populo fit conveniendum ; qua verborum forma, quo situ corporis in singulis sacrorum officiorum partibus sit utendum, cæterasque similia, constitutionibus humanis definienda restant. Sic ne furtum fiat, Lex Divina prohibet : sed quod furti genus quo supplicii genere sit puniendum, a Lege Humana est. Habet utique ex hac determinatum rei generalis & Lege Dei indeterminatæ Lex Humana, quod subditi conscientiæ inducere possit novam obligationem, ab illa priore obligatione non modò numero diversam & ratione termini, in quantum aliunde pendet, sed specie quoque diversam, & ratione materiæ, quæ versatur circa aliud objectum. Prior enim illa obligatio, quæ a Lege Dei oritur, est ad rem ipsam quoad substantiam ; hæc posterior, quam superinducunt Leges Humanæ, ad rei tei [?] modum est, aut aliquam ejus circumstantiam.
units.tr: IX. Third Doubt, concerning a necessary matter. If human law commands something that was earlier necessary and commanded by the law of God, or forbids something that was earlier unlawful and forbidden by the law of God, what obligation results? I answer briefly that the subject is simply bound by that law. For first, the obligation that already existed by the force of the law of God does not hinder the effect of the human law by excluding a new obligation, since a person can be bound to the same duty by several bonds, as we have sufficiently shown in the previous lecture. To this reason should be added, secondly, that human law generally adds something to the law of God, namely by determining the act: as to its substance it was commanded by the law of God and so is necessary, but as to its manner, quantity, or some other circumstance, which was earlier free. Or again, by attaching to the divine law that forbids an unlawful thing some determination as to the degree of the crime, or the kind or measure of punishment, and other things of this sort. For example, that public assemblies be held for the duties of sacred worship is of divine right; but at what hours, in what place, the people must gather; in what form of words, and in what posture of the body, each part of the sacred offices is to be performed, and other similar matters, remain to be settled by human constitutions. So the law of God forbids that theft be committed; but what kind of theft and with what kind of punishment it is to be punished belongs to the human law. Thus human law, by determining the matter of a general thing left undetermined by the law of God, is able to induce in the conscience of the subjects a new obligation, which differs from that earlier obligation not only in number and in relation to its end, insofar as it depends on something else, but also differs in kind and in relation to its matter, which concerns another object. For that earlier obligation, which arises from the law of God, bears on the thing itself as to its substance; this later one, which human laws superimpose, concerns the mode of the thing or some circumstance of it.

units.la: X. Dubium Quartum, de re turpi & illicita, quod est sanè magni momenti dubium, & multos casus continet: quia omnes ferè conditiones, quæ ad legem rectè constituendam requiruntur, ad unam {1}Justitiam reducuntur. Non ob eam dunttaxat rationem, quod universalis Justitia {2}[illegible, ~12 letters] ἀρετὴ δίκη, & universas virtutes suo ambitu complectatur: sed ob id etiam præsertim, quòd Justitia particularis, & speciatim illa quæ Græcis Justitia dici solet, præ reliquis virtutibus omnibus, præcipuum sit & quasi unicum Rerum-publicarum & omnium humanarum societatum columen. Circa hoc dubium quæritur primò, An propter utilitatem publicam ferri debeat lex injusta? Dicitur in ea fuisse sententia Nic. Machiavellus, ut diceret Legum debitam materiam esse eam, sive justam sive injustam, quæ statui politico confervando augendóque esset commodissima. Quum enim potestatis civilis (ex ipsius sententia) finis sit sui conservatio, & imperii amplitudo; nec possit ea potestas strenuè conservari, multò autem minùs proferri imperium, si leges omnes, omnia Principum consilia, ad exactam justitiæ & honesti normam essent exigenda: eorum qui præsunt interesse videtur, ita inflecti nonnunquam in alteram partem honesti regulam, ut utilitati publicæ possit inservire. Finem enim in omni re, optimam esse mensuram mediorum. Utut sit de Machiavello, fuit illa certè sententia magni nominis olim apud Lacones viri, qui palàm id esse honestum pronunciavit quod esset Spartis utile. Affertur firmandæ huic sententiæ dictum illud Horatianum. Ipsa utilitas justi prope mater & æqui: Exemplum etiam Turcarum, quòd quàm ipsis salutare fuerit res ipsa comprobavit, atque eventus; qui hoc nixi principio Imperii sui sines longè lateque per Asiam, Africam,
units.tr: X. Fourth Doubt, concerning a base and unlawful thing, which is a doubt of great importance and covers many cases, because nearly all the conditions required for rightly constituting a law are reduced to one thing, Justice. This is not only because universal Justice {1}[illegible, ~12 letters] virtue of righteousness [ἀρετὴ δίκη], and embraces all the virtues within its compass; but chiefly also because particular Justice, and especially that which the Greeks are accustomed to call Justice, is, above all the other virtues, the chief and, as it were, the sole pillar of commonwealths and of all human societies. On this doubt the first question is: Ought an unjust law to be enacted for the sake of public advantage? Niccolò Machiavelli is said to have held this opinion, so that he declared the proper subject matter of laws to be whatever, whether just or unjust, is most advantageous for preserving and increasing the political state. For since the end of civil power (in his view) is its own preservation and the extension of empire, and that power cannot vigorously be preserved, much less enlarged, if all laws and all the counsels of princes were to be directed by the exact standard of justice and honesty, it seems to those who govern to be in their interest sometimes to bend the rule of honesty to the other side, so that it may serve public utility. For in every matter the best measure of means is the end. Whatever may be true of Machiavelli, that opinion was certainly once held by a man of great name among the Spartans, who openly declared that whatever is useful to Sparta is honourable. To confirm this opinion is cited that saying of Horace: Utility itself is almost the mother of the just and the right. There is also the example of the Turks, whose success, and the event itself, has shown how wholesome it was for them; for relying on this principle they have extended the bounds of their empire far and wide through Asia, Africa,

units.la: {1} Πάντα τὰ νόμιμα δι' ἀρετὴν [?] ... πῶς δίκαια. Aristot. 5. Ethic. 3.
units.tr: {1} All lawful things through virtue [?] ... just things. Aristotle, Ethics 5, ch. 3.

units.la: {2} [?]συλλήβδην [illegible, ~12 letters] ἀρετὴ δίκη. Theognis.
units.tr: {2} In short [?] ... virtue is justice. Theognis.

units.la: {3} Satyr. 3 eam, Europam, felicissimè produxerunt. Quæ pessimo principio nisi reipsâ niterentur qui tamen se profitentur maximè (penè dixeram solos Christianos) & purioris Religionis instauratores audire gestiunt; sub tot sacrilegiis, perjuriis, seditionibus, bellis, tumultibus, tyrannide, non ingemiscerent hodie passim orbis Christianus.
units.tr: {3} Satire 3. Europe, most happily. Yet who would not, in these times, groan across the Christian world at so many sacrileges, perjuries, seditions, wars, tumults and tyrannies, if these things did not rest in fact upon that worst principle; though those who profess themselves most (I was about to say only the Christians) and eagerly claim to be restorers of the purer Religion.

units.la: XI. Sed contrà. Non debent principes terræ uti eâ potestate quam à Deo acceperunt contrà ipsius voluntatem, aut aliorsum quam ipse intendit. Neque enim tam data est illis ea potestas ut Dominis, quam à Deo credita ut administris: [λειτουργοὶ θεοῦ & διάκονοι, Rom. 13. 4. 6.] Credita autem eo fine, ut justitiam colerent, non ut tyrannidem exercerent & injustè dominarentur. Quod vel ex propositò textu manifestum est: Per me Reges regnant, & Principes justa decernunt: acsi id demum esset regnare, & verè principem agere, quod justum sit, hoc tantùm decernere. Quin & Prophetæ passim severam Dei iram & vindictam proclamant adversum Reges & Principes, qui iniqua decreta statuerant, & meditati erant iniquitatem sicut Legem. Neque verò est, quem hujus mundi Politici dicunt, potestatis civilis finis, Imperii dilatatio: sed conservatio populi in pace & tranquillitate, cum omni pietate & honestate, 1 Tim. 2. 2. Est autem Justitia publicæ pacis, siqua alia, conservatrix optima. Ut enim justitia fidei pacem conscientiæ internam, ita justitia legalis pacem Reipublicæ externam & parit & conservat. Erit fructus justitiæ pax, inquit Propheta: imò & Thebanus Vates, [illegible, ~20 letters] Neque Horatiani dicti ea mens est, quasi censuisset mera utilitate metiendum esse honestum, qui longe aliud spectavit eo versu; nimirum utilitatis publicæ & communis boni intuitu adductos initio homines rudes adhuc & vagos, ut in unum coirent, societates colerent, justis legibus & pœnis, vim, scelera, injurias coercerent. Quæ denique à Turcis ducuntur (quos videtur Deus eo potissimum fine excitasse, ut eo quasi flagello summam Christianorum perfidiam aliàque peccata corrigeret,) aut alias à prospero rerum successu trahuntur in malâ causâ præsidium argumenta, Alcoranum magis sapiunt spurci nebulonis, quàm puritatem Evangelii Servatoris Christi.
units.tr: XI. But on the contrary: the princes of the earth ought not to use that power which they have received from God against his will, or for any purpose other than the one he intends. For that power was given to them not so much as to lords as it was entrusted to them by God as to servants [λειτουργοὶ θεοῦ & διάκονοι, Rom. 13. 4, 6]. It was entrusted, moreover, for this end, that they might cultivate justice, not that they might exercise tyranny and rule unjustly. This is plain even from the text cited: By me kings reign, and princes decree justice; as if this were indeed to reign and truly to act as prince, to decree only what is just. Indeed, the prophets everywhere proclaim the severe wrath and vengeance of God against kings and princes who have enacted iniquitous decrees and have devised iniquity as if it were law. Nor is the end of civil power, as the politicians of this world say, the extension of empire, but the preservation of the people in peace and tranquillity, with all godliness and honesty, 1 Tim. 2. 2. Moreover, justice is the best preserver of public peace, as of anything else. For as the justice of faith produces and preserves inner peace of conscience, so legal justice produces and preserves outward peace in the commonwealth. The fruit of justice will be peace, says the prophet; indeed, the Theban seer also says so, [illegible, ~20 letters]. Nor was Horace's meaning in that line such as to suppose that the honourable must be measured by mere utility, since he had something quite different in view in that verse: namely, that men, at first rude and wandering, were led by regard for public advantage and the common good to gather into one place, to cultivate societies, and by just laws and penalties to restrain violence, crimes and injuries. As for those arguments which are drawn from the Turks (whom God seems to have raised up chiefly for this purpose, that by such a kind of scourge he might correct the great perfidy of Christians and their other sins), or which are drawn from prosperous success to support a bad cause, they savour more of the Alcoran of some foul rogue than of the purity of the Gospel of Christ the Saviour.

units.la: XII. Quæstio secunda, Lex injusta, etsi fieri non debuit, si tamen lata fuerit, an Obliget Conscientiam subditi, ita ut eam teneatur observare? Multa enim quæ fieri non debent, facta tamen valent; & fieri potest, ut quod non potuit sine peccato præcipi, possit tamen sine peccato præstari, ut in præcedentibus lectionibus abunde confirmavimus. Ratio dubitandi est, quia vera obedientia non est disputatrix. In hoc enim proprie consistit obedientiæ ratio, ut se quis alterius voluntati sine aliqua disceptatione subjiciat. Nimis delicata est obedientia, ut scitè Bernardus, qua transit in genus causæ deliberativum. Respondendum tamen breviter, subditi conscientiam ejusmodi lege non teneri: quæ fuit superioris Prælectionis Conclusio prima, & ibi etiam pluribus confirmata. Et potest etiam, si quis adhuc plura desideret, inde ulterius probari, quòd nulla potestas inferior potest obligare contra voluntatem superioris potestatis; ergo quum sit Dei potestas omni humanâ potestate superior, non potest ulla cujuscunque hominis potestas obligare contra voluntatem Dei, qui lege suâ prohibuit omnia prava & turpia. Unde Augustinus, Legem non videri, ait, quæ justa non fuerit. Et per hanc rationem solvitur argumentum à ratione obedientiæ ductum, concedendo subditum debere se voluntati superioris sine disceptatione subjicere; Superioris nempe supremi, in cujus voluntatem ultimatè resolvitur obedientia : non tamen superioris subordinati, si voluntatem ipsius voluntati supremi illius constet adversari. Et autem Deus {1}absolutè summus Imperator : cujus utique nuda voluntatis significatio sufficit ad inducendam parendi obligationem ; praesertim cum sit certissimum voluntatem ipsius non posse esse injustam. Paruit itaque Abra-hamus Deo ea mandanti, quae nisi praecepisset ipse Deus, videri potuissent non dura solum & iniqua, sed & impia scelerisque plena. Scilicet ut patre, patriâ, cognatione relictis, in terram longinquam pariter & incertam, pauper, exul, hospes prosi-ciceretur : imo ut filii unigeniti, in quo uno reposita essent non omnia modo solatia subsidiáque senectutis suae, sed & spes omnis promissionum Dei, propria manu jugulum solveret, eúmque aris impositum victimam offerret tam saeva imperantiDeo. Recte ille quidem, & ut virum decuit, qui dici mereretur fidelium pater, & esset universo orbi inconcussae fidei probatissimum exemplar ; qui se Dei dicto sine haesitatione audientem praebuit. Ast hominis cujuscunque imperata, quum fit erroris & peccato obnoxius omnis homo, possitque ejus voluntas esse prava, fas est, imo & ubi justa subest suspicandi causa, opus est, examini subjicere. Monitum illud Apostoli, 1 Theff. 5. 21. Omnia probate ; quod bonum est retinete, ad superiorum jussa non minus idoneè, quàm ad placita doctorum, de quibus tamen peculiaris ibi sermo est, accommodare jure optimo poterit. Apage ergo [illegible, ~14 letters] illa. Sic volo, sic jubeo. Apage illam Papicolarum, cùm turpem adulationem, qui nefas ducunt cuivis homini Jovis Jui Laterani effata quovis praetextu solicitare : tum caecam illam obedientiam, quâ voto sese obstringunt Religionem ingressi, superioribus sui ordinis in omnibus & singulis, sine discretione (sic enim loquuntur) obedire.
units.tr: XII. Second question: an unjust law, though it ought not to have been made, if nevertheless it has been enacted, does it bind the conscience of the subject, so that he is bound to observe it? For many things which ought not to be done, once done, are nevertheless valid; and it can happen that what could not be commanded without sin can nevertheless be performed without sin, as we have amply confirmed in the preceding lectures. The reason for doubt is that true obedience does not dispute. For the very nature of obedience lies in this, that a person submits himself to another's will without any debate. Obedience is too delicate a thing, as Bernard wisely says, once it passes into the deliberative kind of cause. Yet I answer briefly that the subject's conscience is not bound by such a law: this was the first conclusion of the previous lecture, and was confirmed there at greater length. And if anyone still desires more, it can be further proved from this, that no inferior power can bind against the will of a superior power; therefore, since the power of God is superior to every human power, no power of any man can bind against the will of God, who by his law has forbidden all wicked and base things. Hence Augustine says that a law is not seen to be a law if it is not just. By this reasoning the argument drawn from the reason of obedience is also resolved: we concede that the subject ought to submit himself to the will of a superior without dispute, namely of the supreme superior, into whose will obedience is ultimately resolved; not, however, of a subordinate superior, if it is clear that his will is opposed to the will of that supreme one. And God is absolutely the highest Commander, whose mere declaration of will is sufficient to induce the obligation of obeying, especially since it is most certain that his will cannot be unjust. Thus Abraham obeyed God commanding those things which, were it not that God himself had commanded them, might have seemed not only harsh and iniquitous but also impious and full of crime: namely, that he should leave father, country and kindred, and set out for a distant and uncertain land, poor, an exile, a stranger; and indeed that, as to his only-begotten son, in whom were laid up not only all the consolations and supports of his old age but also every hope of God's promises, he should with his own hand cut his throat, and laying him on the altar offer him as a victim to so cruel a command. Rightly indeed did he do so, and as became a man who deserved to be called the father of the faithful, and who was to be the most approved pattern of unshaken faith to the whole world; for he showed himself ready to hear God's word without hesitation. But the commands of any man, since every man is liable to error and sin, and his will may be wicked, must be submitted to examination, and indeed must be examined wherever there is just ground for suspicion. The admonition of the Apostle, 1 Thess. 5. 21, Prove all things; hold fast that which is good, may most rightly be applied no less fittingly to the commands of superiors than to the opinions of teachers, although the Apostle there speaks specifically of the latter. Away, then, with [illegible, ~14 letters] those things. Thus I will, thus I command. Away with that flattery of the Papist sycophants, base as it is, who count it wicked to solicit from any man, under whatever pretext, the pronouncements of the Lateran Jove; and away with that blind obedience by which those who enter a religious order bind themselves by vow to obey their superiors of their order in all and each things, without discrimination (for so they speak).

units.la: XIII. Quæritur tertiò, Liceátne saltem subdito cedere jure suo hac ex parte, & quamvis non obliget, legi tamen istiusmodi sponte suâ parere ? Respondeo, ne hoc quidem {'}licere : quia Lex Dei simpliciter obligat ad non faciendum aliquod turpe, vel illicitum. Injusta ergo Lex, (injustam intellige eo sensu, in quo nunc loquimur, injustam ex parte Materiæ) non potest licitè servari : quia non potest Deus licitè offendi. Quicquid enim Lege Dei, aut Naturæ Lumine notæ & cordibus inscriptæ, aut in verbo scripto revelatæ, adversatur, non est ob quodcunque vel detrimentum proprium, vel proximi scandalum, vel prælati sive gratiam promerendam , sive declinandum odium , viro Christiano admittendum. Da veniam, Imperator : tu carcerem, ille gehennam : Sic olim veteres illi Christiani. Sic ante eos Domini Jesu Christi Apostoli, {2}Oportetne vobis magis obaudire quàm Deo, ipsi judicate : & ante eos etiam Hebræi adolescentes, {3}Notum sit tibi Rex, quòd nolumus adorare imaginem auream quam tu erexisti.
units.tr: XIII. The third question is whether a subject may at least give up his right in this matter and, although the law does not bind him, obey such a law of his own accord. I answer that not even this is lawful, because the law of God simply obliges us not to do anything base or unlawful. An unjust law (understood as unjust in the sense we are now discussing, that is, unjust on the side of the matter) therefore cannot be lawfully kept, because God cannot lawfully be offended. Whatever is opposed to the law of God, whether known by the light of nature and written on the heart or revealed in the written word, must not be admitted by a Christian, whether for any loss to himself, or scandal to his neighbour, or to earn the favour of a superior, or to avoid his hatred. "Pardon us, Emperor: you threaten prison, he threatens hell." So the old Christians answered. Before them, the Apostles of the Lord Jesus Christ said: "Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye." And before them the young Hebrews said: "Be it known unto thee, O King, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up." {2} {3}

units.la: XIV. Quæritur quartò, Quæ Lex ita injusta censenda sit, ut non solùm non obliget, sed & ei parere non liceat ? Respondeo, Legem posse esse injustam ex multiplici causa. Primò, ex parte causæ Efficientis : Si feratur à non habente legitimam potestatem. Et ista est injusta, ob defectum justitiæ commutativæ : quia plus sibi assumit lator, quàm debet, aut ei ex æquo convenit. Propterea nec subditum obligat ad obediendum : potest tamen subditus, si ipsi videbitur expedire, nec aliunde impediatur, cedere jure suo, & legi obedire. Secundò, ex parte causæ finalis : Si non tendat in bonum publicum, nec conservet jura communitati debita. Ista est injusta, ob defectum Justitiæ quam Legalem vocant, quæ semper intendit bonum commune, & ne quid Respublica detrimenti capiat. Sed enim injusta ut sit, obligat tamen subditum; quia subditus non est legitimus & idoneus judex Justitiæ Legalis. Et si ex ipsius obedientia sequatur aliquid quod sit Reipublicæ incommodum vel noxium, non est id {1} ei imputandum, qui quod suarum erat partium rite obivit; sed prælato, cui ex officio incumbit boni publici procuratio. Tertiò, ex parte causæ Formalis: Si Lex onera, favores, præmia & pœnas iniquâ proportione, & non pro civium merito dispenset. Ista est injusta, ob desectum Justitiæ distributivæ: quæ omnia jubet ex æquo singulis, prout quisque commeritus est, tribuere. Est ista etiam quantumvis injusta, obligat tamen; pariter ut illa quam proximè dixi: idque ob eandem rationem. Quia sc. istarum rerum dispensatio ad subditi officium non spectat, sed prælati.
units.tr: XIV. The fourth question is: which law is to be judged so unjust that it not only does not bind, but it is not lawful to obey it? I answer that a law can be unjust for many reasons. First, on the side of the efficient cause: if it is enacted by one who does not have lawful power. Such a law is unjust through a lack of commutative justice, because the lawgiver claims more for himself than he ought, or than is fairly due to him. For this reason it does not bind the subject to obey; yet the subject may, if it seems expedient to him and he is not otherwise hindered, yield his right and obey the law. Second, on the side of the final cause: if it does not aim at the common good nor preserve the rights owed to the community. Such a law is unjust through a lack of the justice which they call legal, which always aims at the common good and that the commonwealth suffer no harm. But although it is unjust, it still binds the subject, because the subject is not a lawful and competent judge of legal justice. And if from his obedience something follows that is harmful or hurtful to the commonwealth, this is not to be imputed to him who has duly performed what belonged to his part, but to the superior, on whom the care of the public good rests by virtue of his office. Third, on the side of the formal cause: if the law distributes burdens, favours, rewards and punishments in unfair proportion, and not according to the merit of the citizens. Such a law is unjust through a lack of distributive justice, which requires that each thing be given to each in due proportion to what he has deserved. Even such a law, however unjust, still binds, just as the one I have just mentioned does, and for the same reason: because the distribution of these things does not belong to the duty of the subject, but to the superior.

units.la: Quartò, Ex parte causæ Materialis, de quâ nunc agimus: si lex jubeat rem turpem, inhonestam, vel quovismodo illicitam. Ista injusta est ob defectum Justitiæ quæ dicitur universalis, quæ debitam rectitudinem in omni actione requirit. Hæc sola tam non obligat subditum ad obediendum, ut omninò obliget ad non obediendum.
units.tr: Fourth, on the side of the material cause, which is what we are now treating: if the law commands a base, dishonourable, or in any way unlawful thing. Such a law is unjust through a lack of that justice which is called universal, which requires due rectitude in every action. This alone does not so much fail to bind the subject to obey, as it wholly binds him not to obey.

units.la: XV. Quæritur quinto, Quænam justitia requiratur, vel quanta sufficiat, ad hoc, ut Lex aliqua dicatur justa, & censeri debeat obligatoria? Pro responsione dico, Primò, non necessariò requiri, ut id quod lege imperatur sit justum positive, quod Philosophi honestum dicunt; hoc est, ut sit actus alicujus virtutis: sed sufficere si sit justum negative; id est, non injustum vel turpe, quales sunt actus omnium vitiorum. Alias non possent ferri leges de rebus mediis & adiaphoris: quæ tamen, ut mox patebit, sunt materia legum aptissima. Dico secundo, dato quòd Lex aliqua sit injusta ex parte causæ vel efficientis, vel finalis, vel formalis, aliquo eorum quo jam novissimè dictum est modorum: um : si tamen nullus fit justitiæ defectus ex parte Causæ Materialis, id est, si Actus ex vi & imperio Legis à subdito exercendus talis sit, ut possit ab eo præstari sine aliquo suo peccato ; sufficere istiusmodi justitiam ad inducendam obligatio-nem.
units.tr: XV. The fifth question is: what justice is required, or how much is sufficient, for a law to be called just and to be considered binding? In answer I say: first, it is not necessary that what is commanded by the law be just in a positive sense, which the philosophers call honourable, that is, that it be an act of some virtue; but it is sufficient that it be just in a negative sense, that is, not unjust or base, such as are the acts of all vices. Otherwise laws could not be made concerning things indifferent and adiaphora, which nevertheless, as will shortly become plain, are a most fitting matter for laws. I say second: granted that some law is unjust on the side of its efficient, final, or formal cause, by any of the modes just now mentioned last; if, nevertheless, there is no defect of justice on the side of the material cause, that is, if the act to be performed by the subject under the force and command of the law is such that he can perform it without any sin of his own, such justice is sufficient to induce obligation.

units.la: XVI. Cæterum ne subditus, quò se licentiùs vinculo Legis subduceret, mobedientiæ suæ scrupulum aliquem prætexeret, (quo paralogismo mirum quantum se facilè patiuntur decipi plurima hominun[?]urba :) videri sibi nimirum Legem iniquam, & cui bonâ cum conscientiâ obedire non possit, ac proinde nec debeat. (Hoc enim esset, inquiunt, dubitante conscientiâ obedire : quod autem fit dubitante conscientiâ sine peccato fieri nequit, docente Apostolo, Rom. 14. 23. Omne quod non ex fide est peccatum esse :) necesse est ut ulterius quæratur : & Sextò, Quæ continuò quòd Lex aliqua sit injusta, requiratur ad hoc, ut Jubditus possit esse securus in conscientia, se eâ lege non teneri. Pro responsione dico Primo, si Lex manifestè & notoriè injusta, certum esse posse subditum, se eâ lege non obligari. Quod idem dicendum est, si equiliqua Pro ut quod [?]tus egasunt erri en, ico arte alidom: vel morali certitudine, (post adhibitam in veritate disquirendâ debitam diligentiam,) judicet eam esse simpliciter injustam. Dico Secundò, si ex errore aliquo judicii obfirmato[?], & quem non sit facile deponere, existimet legem esse injustam, cùm non sit; obligationem tamen legis manere, errore illo mentis non obstante, ita ut peccati non sit immunis, si non obediat; graviùs tamen peccaturum, si errore illo nondum deposito obediret. De quo Casu, cum ad collationem utriusque obligationis deventum erit, (si Deo permittente eò perveniatur,) opportunior erit disputandi locus. Dico Tertiò, si ex levi aliquo injecto scrupulo aut objectiunculâ suspicetur tantùm legem fortè esse in-justam; justam ; contemnendum esse ejusmodi scrupulu[?] & omninò Legi parendum : à quâ parendi necessitate frustrà fuerit, quisquis se tenerâ conscientiâ obtentu satis excusatum iri existimaverit.
units.tr: XVI. Furthermore, lest the subject, in order to free himself more freely from the bond of the law, should put forward some scruple about his obedience (by which fallacy very many men allow themselves to be deceived, to a remarkable extent), namely that the law seems to him unjust, and one with which he cannot obey with a good conscience, and therefore ought not to obey: (for, they say, this would be to obey with a doubting conscience; but what is done with a doubting conscience cannot be done without sin, as the Apostle teaches, Rom. 14. 23: Whatever is not of faith is sin), it is necessary to inquire further. And sixth, what is required so that the subject may be secure in conscience that he is not bound by the law, once it is granted that some law is unjust? In answer I say: first, if the law is manifestly and notoriously unjust, the subject can be certain that he is not bound by that law. The same is to be said if, after applying due diligence in searching for the truth, he judges with moral certainty that the law is simply unjust. I say second: if, from some error of judgement that has become fixed and is not easily put aside, he thinks the law is unjust when it is not, the obligation of the law nevertheless remains despite that error of mind, so that he is not free from sin if he does not obey; yet he will sin more gravely if he obeys while that error is not yet laid aside. About this case, when we come to compare the two obligations (if God permits us to reach that point), there will be a more suitable place for discussion. I say third: if, from some slight scruple or little objection, he merely suspects that the law may perhaps be unjust, such a scruple is to be despised and the law is wholly to be obeyed. Whoever thinks he will be sufficiently excused by the pretext of a tender conscience from the necessity of obeying will be disappointed.

units.la: XVIII. Dico [illegible, ~6 letters], (quod utinam satis atten[?] derent, quibus crassam suam inobedientiam tenerâ conscientiæ prætextu tueri mos est,) si, ob appa[?] rentes utrinque rationes probabiles nesciat subditu[?] nec facilè apud se statuere possit, justáne sit Lex an secus, ita ut mens quasi in æquilibrio pendula hæreat, incerta utrò se potius inclinare d[?]ebeat obligare in eo casu subditum ad actualiter obediendum, ita ut peccet, si non obediat; si obediat, non peccet. Ratio prima : Quia ex regulâ juris In dubiis potior est conditio possidentis. Ergo ubi de jure lis est inter Legislatorem & Civem ; nisi occurrat ratio aliqua idonea in contrarium, semper præsumendum est pro Legislatore, ut qui est in possessione juris, contra civem : ut autem sit aliqua satis idonea ratio in contrarium, fieri non potest in casu proposito, quia esset contra hypothesin: supponimus enim, alias æquo inter eos jure contendi-
units.tr: XVIII. I say (would that those who are accustomed to defend their gross disobedience under the pretext of a tender conscience would pay sufficient heed to this) that if the subject, because of probable reasons appearing on both sides, does not know, and cannot easily decide for himself, whether the law is just or not, so that his mind hangs as if poised in equilibrium, uncertain to which side it ought rather to incline, then in that case the law obliges the subject to obey in act, so that he sins if he does not obey, and does not sin if he obeys. First reason: because by the rule of law, in doubtful matters the condition of the possessor is stronger. Therefore, where there is a legal dispute between the lawgiver and the citizen, unless some suitable reason to the contrary occurs, it must always be presumed in favour of the lawgiver, as the one who is in possession of the right against the citizen. But that there should be some sufficiently weighty reason to the contrary cannot happen in the case proposed, because it would be against the hypothesis: for we suppose, otherwise, that the parties contend on equal terms of right, contend-

units.la: Ratio secunda, ex aliâ itidem juris regulâ, Quia in re dubiâ tutior pars est eligenda. Et omninò tutius est dubitante conscientiâ obedire, quàm dubitante conscientiâ non obedire: quia tutius est in honore superioribus exhibenda excedere quem debeas modum quàm ab eo deficere. Ratio Tertia, ex eadem etiam regulâ, quia generaliter tutius est, ut quise obligatum judicet qui liber est, quàm ut liberum se credat, cum sit revera obligatus. Cùm enim ex innata cordis humani pravitate, à nimiâ audaciâ sæpiùs quàm à nimio metu peccetur; atque ad carnis licentiam procliviores quàm par est, & ad ferendum jugum minus patientes simus omnes: nam firmo animi proposito nobis ante steterit, legibus quæ non sunt evidenter injustæ parendum esse, suggeret nobis subinde prudentia carnis, accedente etiam serpentis astu, eas excusationes, quæ nos ab officio hac in parte præstando sæpissime impediant. Et hæc de dubio quarto.
units.tr: Second reason, from another rule of law: In a doubtful matter the safer part is to be chosen. It is altogether safer for a conscience in doubt to obey than for a conscience in doubt not to obey, because it is safer to exceed the measure one owes in showing honour to superiors than to fall short of it. Third reason, from the same rule: it is generally safer that one who is free should judge himself obliged, than that one who is really obliged should believe himself free. For since, from the innate wickedness of the human heart, men sin more often through excessive boldness than through excessive fear, and since we are all more inclined than is right to the licence of the flesh and less patient in bearing the yoke, then although we may have firmly resolved beforehand to obey laws that are not evidently unjust, the prudence of the flesh will from time to time suggest to us, with the cunning of the serpent also at work, those excuses which most often keep us from performing this duty. And this is what I have to say on the fourth doubt.

units.la: XVIII. Sequitur Quintum, de Lege Permissiva mali: An sit licita, & quatenus? Et an & quatenus obligatoria? Ubi imprimis observandum est, Lege permitti posse rem malam tripliciter: privative, scilicet, negative & positive. Privative permitti, idem est quo a Legislatore prætermitti, sic omnia illa permittuntur, de quibus vel prohibendis vel puniendis jura nihil statuunt. Negative permittitur id, cujus exercitium jura certis limitibus definiunt, intra quos qui se continuerint extra noxam sunt, qui vero eos excesserint sunt lege puniendi: Sic usuram exerceri permittunt plerarumque nationum jura. Positive id permittitur, cujus, sub certa tributi cujusdam pensione, exercitium toleratur. Sic Romæ permittuntur meretricum prostibula.
units.tr: XVIII. There follows the fifth question, concerning the permissive law of evil: whether it is lawful, and how far; and whether, and how far, it is binding. Here, first of all, it must be observed that a law may permit an evil thing in three ways: privatively, that is, negatively and positively. To be permitted privatively is the same as being passed over by the lawgiver; thus all those things are permitted about which the laws decree nothing, whether by forbidding or by punishing. Something is permitted negatively when the laws define the limits within which its exercise is allowed: those who keep within them are free from fault, but those who exceed them are to be punished by law. Thus the laws of most nations permit the practice of usury. Something is permitted positively when its exercise is tolerated in return for the payment of a certain tax. Thus at Rome the brothels of prostitutes are permitted.

units.la: XIX. Hac distinctione præmissâ. Dico Primò, Privative multa mala in omnibus Rebuspublicis necessariò tolerari: Impossibile enim est ut ad omnes species actuum vitiosorum jura se extendant, aut ut omne peccati genus legibus humanis coerceatur. Habet hoc Dei Lex peculiare & eximium, ut ea sola omnia facienda præcipiat, omnia fugienda prohibeat. Sed in istiusmodi permissione nullum esse obligationi locum; quia oriri necesse est omnem obligationem ex aliquo actu, non autem ex actus privatione sive non-actu. Dico secundò, Permissionem mali negativam posse esse licitam. Si enim malum aliquod non posset sine gravi incommodo publico penitus tolli: ad prudentiam politicam pertinet, ipsius usum ita moderari, & certis finibus circumscribere, ut possit utilitati publicæ inservire. Idque Dei ipsius exemplo, qui populo Israelitico permisit uxorum repudia : eo consilio, uti exponit optimus Legis interpres Christus, ne ex {1}duritiâ cordis humani & effræni maritorum in conjuges asperitate & sævitiâ graviora pullulárent incommoda. Dico tertiò, ejusmodi tamen lege neminem {2}obligari ad faciendum id quod Lex permittit : Finis enim permissionis est, non ut id fiat quod lege permittitur, sed ne ultra id quod leges permittunt fiat. Proinde, sicut permissio ipsa negativa tantùm est, ita obligationem inducit non nisi negativam : hoc est, obligatur subditus, si ipsi libuerit facere quod Lex permittit, præstitutos sibi à lege fines non excedere. Dico quartò, permissionem mali positivam, si plura aut graviora sint mala quæ ex ejusmodi permissione consequuntur, quàm sunt ea in quorum remedium adhiberi prætenditur, ut plerumque fit, non esse licitam : præsertim si permissioni rei turpis accedat, ex impolito tributo, turpis etiam lucri suspicio. Dico quintò, neminem obligari tali lege ad faciendum id quòd permittitur ; imò aliunde obligari unumquemque, non obstante legis permissione, ad id non faciendum.
units.tr: XIX. With this distinction laid down, I say, first, that many evils are necessarily tolerated privatively in every commonwealth. For it is impossible for the laws to extend to every kind of sinful act, or for every species of sin to be restrained by human laws. The law of God has this peculiar and distinguished feature: it alone commands all things to be done and forbids all things to be avoided. But in such a permission there is no place for obligation, since every obligation must arise from some act, not from the privation of an act or a non-act. I say, second, that a negative permission of evil can be lawful. For if some evil could not be wholly removed without grave public inconvenience, it belongs to political prudence to regulate its use in such a way, and to confine it within certain limits, that it may serve the public good. And God himself gave the example, when he permitted the Israelite people the divorce of wives, with the purpose, as Christ, the best interpreter of the Law, explains, that greater evils might not spring up from the hardness of the human heart* and from the unbridled harshness and cruelty of husbands towards their wives. I say, third, that nobody is however obliged to do what the law permits by such a law. For the purpose of a permission is not that what the law permits should be done, but that nothing should be done beyond what the laws permit. Therefore, just as the permission itself is only negative, so it induces only a negative obligation: that is, a subject is obliged, if it pleases him to do what the law permits, not to exceed the limits set for him by the law. I say, fourth, that a positive permission of evil is not lawful if the evils that follow from such a permission are more numerous or graver than those for whose remedy it is said to be granted, as usually happens; especially if, to the permission of a base thing, there is added, from an unseemly tax, a suspicion also of base gain. I say, fifth, that nobody is obliged by such a law to do what is permitted; indeed, on other grounds, every person is obliged, notwithstanding the law's permission, not to do it.

units.la: Ratio est ; Quoad priorem partem, quia est contra naturam permissionis, ut sit obligatoria : cùm permissio det libertatem, & omnis obligatio sit vinculum quoddam. Quoad posteriorem partem, quia supponimus id quod lege humanâ sic permittitur esse ex se malum ; & lege Dei obligamur ad non faciendum malum. Permissio itaque mali, quatenus nuda permissio est, neminem obligat ad faciendum ; quatenus autem mali permissio est, unumquemque obligat ad non faciendum id quod permittitur.
units.tr: The reason is this. As to the former part, it is contrary to the nature of a permission that it should be binding, since permission gives liberty, and every obligation is a kind of chain. As to the latter part, we assume that what is thus permitted by human law is in itself evil, and by the law of God we are bound not to do evil. Therefore the permission of evil, insofar as it is a bare permission, obliges no one to do it; but insofar as it is a permission of evil, it obliges each person not to do what is permitted.

units.la: XX. Atqui dictum est jam ante sæpius, omni Legi adesse vim obligativam, quæ eam ita individuè comitatur, ut posità Lege necesse sit sequi obligationem & obligatione sublatâ unà tolli & Legem. gm.[?] Ergo Legem Permissivam, aut negandum est esse Legem, aut fatendum est obligare. Huic objectioni ut occurratur, nulla nos cogit necessitas eò confugere, ut Legem permissivam negemus esse Legem; quàm non modò Legem, sed & legem proprie dictam esse fatemur.
