Certè Lex illa Mosaica de repudio, cujus, Matt. 16. mentio facta est, ut Permissionis nomine venit [Μωσῆς ἐπιτρέψεν[?]] illius capitis versu octavo, sic ejusdem capitis versu septimo mandatum dicitur sive praeceptio; [Μωσῆς ἐνετείλατο[?].] Quid quod ei Legis & Nomen passim tribuitur, & definitio illius nominis æquè congruit, ac legi vel præcipienti fieri aliquid vel vetanti : ut omninò concedendum sit Legem de his omnibus, ut suis speciebus, per modum generis & univocè prædicari. Ergo & illud concedendum erit, civem ejusmodi lege obligari? Omninò concedendum reor. Quod ut cum his quæ de lege permissiva haftenus dixi, quàm non malè cohæreat, rectiùs intelligatur :
units.tr: XX. But it has already been said more than once that every law carries an obligating force, which accompanies it so inseparably that, once the law is posited, obligation must follow, and with the removal of the obligation the law too is removed. Therefore a permissive law must either be denied to be a law, or be admitted to oblige. To meet this objection, we are under no necessity to take refuge in denying that a permissive law is a law; indeed we confess that it is not only a law but a law properly so called. Certainly that Mosaic law about divorce, mentioned in Matt. 16., is called by the name of permission in verse eight of that chapter [Μωσῆς ἐπιτρέψεν], and in verse seven of the same chapter it is called a command or precept [Μωσῆς ἐνετείλατο]. Moreover, the name of law is everywhere given to it, and the definition of that name fits it just as well as it fits a law commanding something to be done or forbidding it. So it must be fully conceded that law is predicated of all these, as species, by way of genus and univocally. Must it then also be conceded that a citizen is obliged by such a law? I think it must be conceded entirely. How well this coheres with what I have said so far about permissive law may be understood more rightly as follows.

units.la: XXI. Dico sextò, Legem omnem hujusmodi permissivam, quatenus Lex est, obligare subditum in conscientiâ ad sui observationem. Ratio manifesta : quia obligatio, ut sæpè dictum est, est Legis effectus necessarius, nec ab eâ separabilis. Quod ne pugnare videatur cum his quæ modò dicta sunt; duo ista sunt observanda, quæ propterea signanter sunt à me enunciata. Alterum, quòd dixerim Legem permissivam obligare ad sui observationem : aliud est autem obligari subditum ad observandam Legem, quod nunc assero ; aliud verò obligari subditum ad faciendum quod Lex permittit, quod & ante negavi, & jam adhuc nego. Alterum, quòd dixerim Legem permissivam obligare quatenus Lex est, quod verum est : non dixi obligare quatenus permissiva est, quod est falsum. Sciendum est enim legi permissivæ vim, quatenus Lex est, non consistere in ipsâ permissione, quæ cum legis differentiâ divisiva, necesse est ut sit lege posterior, sicut omnis differentia divisiva est natura posterior genere quod dividit, & ipsum supponit: sed in illa præceptione, quæ est Legis quasi constitutiva & formalis differentia, & in ipsis Legis verbis, utplurimum expresse, aut virtualiter saltem continetur. Hæc enim (præceptio inquam,) illud est, à quo primum oritur subditi obligatio, & ad quod ultimè terminatur ejus obedientia. Exemplo remostendo. Legislator ob mutandi necessitatem permittit usuram, moderatâ quadam proportione, inter cives exerceri: propositâ etiam pœnâ his qui modum fœnoris lege definitum excesserint. Sitne usura simpliciter & de toto genere illicita, necne, nihil hîc definio, nec ad præsens negotium quicquam interest: hoc interim certum est, utut vel maximè licita esset usura, neminem tamen illâ permissione ad eam exercendam obligari. Sed in istiusmodi lege, præter istam permissionem, quæ neminem obligat; duo sunt alia, quæ quum ad præceptionem Legis pertineant, habent proinde ex intentione Legislatoris vim obligandi omnes cives ad ea observanda. Quorum alterum formaliter & disertis verbis præcipitur, nequis sc. pecuniam ultra modum lege definitum pro fœnore exigat: alterum ex consequenti & virtualiter, nequis ob exercitam prout ea lege permittitur usuram puni[?]tur. Legis ergo permissivæ, ut verbo dicam, præceptio omnes cives obligat, permissio neminem.
units.tr: XXI. I say, sixth, that every law of this permissive kind, insofar as it is a law, obliges the subject in conscience to observe it. The reason is plain: obligation, as has often been said, is a necessary effect of law and cannot be separated from it. So that this may not seem to clash with what has just been said, two points must be noted, which for that reason I have stated with care. The first: when I said that a permissive law obliges to its observance, I meant that the subject is obliged to observe the law*, which I now assert; but it is another thing for the subject to be obliged to do what the law permits, which I both denied before and still deny now. The second: when I said that a permissive law obliges insofar as it is law, that is true; I did not say it obliges insofar as it is permissive, which would be false. For it must be understood that the force of a permissive law, insofar as it is law, does not consist in the permission itself. The permission, being the dividing difference of the law, must of necessity be posterior to the law, just as every dividing difference is by nature posterior to the genus which it divides and presupposes. The force is rather contained, mostly expressly or at least virtually, in that precept, which is the quasi-constitutive and formal difference of the law, and in the very words of the law. For this precept (I mean) is that from which the subject's obligation first arises, and to which his obedience finally tends. Let me show this by an example. A lawgiver, because of the need for lending, permits usury to be practised among citizens at a moderate rate, with a penalty proposed for those who exceed the rate of interest defined by law. Whether usury is simply and in its whole genus unlawful or not, I here define nothing, nor does it matter to the present business. This much is certain: however lawful usury might be, nobody is obliged by that permission to practise it. But in such a law, besides that permission, which obliges nobody, there are two other things which, since they pertain to the precept of the law, have by the lawgiver's intention the force of obliging all citizens to observe them. Of these, one is commanded formally and in express words: that no one should exact money for interest beyond the amount defined by law. The other is commanded by consequence and virtually: that no one should be punished for practising usury as that law permits. Thus, to put it in a word, the precept of a permissive law obliges all citizens; the permission obliges nobody.

units.la: XXII. Dubium Sextum, de rebus mediis & adia- phoris.
units.tr: XXII. Sixth Doubt, concerning means and adiaphora.

units.la: Res autem Media sive adiaphora sunt, quarum tota species nulla Divinâ Lege (naturali vel positivâ) aut præcipitur aut prohibetur. Quæ proinde sunt ex se & suâ naturâ, circa circumstantiarum considerationem, & licita observatio[?]is quatenus non prohibentur; & liberè tamen observationis, quatenus non præcipiuntur. Fuere qui existimarent, non debere Leges Humanas ferri de rebus adiaphoris, sed de his tantùm quæ sunt Juris Naturalis aut Divini; & proinde Leges Civiles dicerent non tam esse novi juris Constitutivas, quàm antiqui Declarativas, velut Divinæ voluntatis explicationes quasdam & evolutiones. Sed quid opus est refutare opinionem, tam ab omni sana ratione alienam, ut potiùs ex adverso rectè judicari debeant res ista adiaphora Legum Humanarum propriissima & maximè idonea Materia? Quandoquidem ad eorum, quæ Deus mandavit, observationem obligamur, vel tacentibus, imo etiam vel contradicentibus, quorumcunque hominum imperiis; ad ea verò quæ à Deo vetita sunt, non facienda obligamur, vel tacentibus vel etiam jubentibus hominum legibus. Restant ergo sola adiaphora, velut campus in quo se exerceat, exseratque vim illam suam inducendi obligationem ubi nulla præfuit potestas humana. Planè ut constet, posse magistratum civilem in rebus adiaphoris, & ante omnem ipsius actum liberis ad utrumlibet, statuere aliquid in utramlibet partem, (determinando illam ἀδιαφορίαν[?],) quod obliget conscientias subditorum ad obediendum.
units.tr: Now means or adiaphora are those things whose whole kind is neither commanded nor forbidden by any Divine Law (natural or positive). They are therefore, of themselves and by their own nature, things whose observance is lawful in so far as they are not forbidden, and which may be observed freely in so far as they are not commanded, given that circumstances are taken into account. Some have thought that Human Laws should not be enacted about adiaphora, but only about what belongs to Natural or Divine Law; and so they would say that Civil Laws are not so much constitutive of new law as declarative of old law, as certain explanations and unfoldings of the divine will. But why should we refute an opinion so alien to all sound reason? It is rather the case that these adiaphora are rightly judged to be the most proper and most suitable matter of Human Laws. For we are bound to observe what God has commanded, whether men's commands are silent or even contrary; and we are bound not to do what God has forbidden, whether men's laws are silent or even commanding it. There remain, then, only adiaphora, like a field in which that power may be exercised and put forth, of inducing obligation where no human authority has been present before. Clearly, then, the civil magistrate can, in things indifferent, and before any act of his own, when things are free either way, establish something to one side or the other (by determining that indifference [ἀδιαφορίαν]), so that it binds the consciences of his subjects to obey.

units.la: Sicut enim in cibo, potu & voluptatibus, in dando item & accipiendo, prudentia Ethica personæ privatæ, præstituendo sibi quandam Mediocritatem, sic evehit actus illos naturales & Indifferentes ultra statum suum & nativam conditionem, ut exinde incipiant esse actus virtutum, Temperantiæ scilicet & Liberalitatis: Sic personæ publicâ authoritate præditæ prudentia politica, præsumendo subditis suis certos circa res medias & liberas mediocritatis fines, sic evehit actus illos quos legibus præcipit ultra pristini sui status gradum, ut incipiant esse deinceps, actus virtutum, Obedientiæ sc. & Justitiæ Legalis.
units.tr: For just as a private person, by ethical prudence in food, drink and pleasures, and likewise in giving and receiving, sets for himself a certain mean, and so raises those natural and indifferent acts beyond their own state and native condition, so that they begin to be acts of the virtues, namely of temperance and liberality; so persons endowed with public authority, by political prudence, prescribing to their subjects certain limits of the mean in middle and free things, raise those acts which they command by law beyond the level of their former state, so that they begin henceforth to be acts of the virtues, namely of obedience and of legal justice.

units.la: XXIII. Res aperta nec habitura adversarium si non nostri seculi, imò & gentis, Reformatorum[?] quosdam rinxisset[?] tàm manifesta veritas: qui [illegible, ~6 letters] sibi ad illam, ad quam anhelabant, ἀναλύσεως[?] reformationem viam struerent; maluerunt communem hominum sensum ἀδιαφορίαν[?] omnem è rebus penitus sublatam iri, quàm ullam magistratui de ritibus statuendi potestatem concedere. Prorsus ut Macedo ille, qui Gordium difficilem nodum, quem nullà arte dissoluere potuit, gladio secuit. Veterum Stoicorum in hoc, ut & in aliis non paucis, genuini Discipuli; qui sapienti nihil docuerunt esse indifferens, cùm omnia, etiam minutula quæque, usque ad digiti exsertionem, ratione agat. Illi tamen ἀδιαφορίας è rebus sustulerunt verbis ut eam reipsâ, adversariorum rationibus adasti, tandem concederent; distinctiunculas quasdam commenti ἀφηγήσεως & ἀφηγήσεων, &c. quibus errorem suum, ne videretur errasse, honestius occultarent. At reperti sunt è nostris, qui hoc tàm putidum, & extritum jamdiu è scholis dogma γνώμη τῇ κεφαλῇ[?] publicis scriptis, idque rigidius multò quàm olim Stoici tueri ausi sint: Duo præsertim; alter, alicujus nominis apud suarum partium homines, Theologus; alter è Proceribus regni, Laicus: uterque ante annos quot annos mortuus. Quibuscum cùm interim simul putem illud suum dogma, nec facilè apud viros cordatos fidem, nedum patronum repertürum non existimo operæ foret pretium, ex refutando immorari.
units.tr: XXIII. This truth is so plain that it would have no opponent, were it not that some of our own age, and indeed of our own nation, Reformed, have, as it were, been stirred up by it. They wished to pave the way to the reformation for which they were longing, by an unravelling [ἀναλύσεως]; they preferred that all indifference [ἀδιαφορίαν] should be wholly removed from things, as common human sense holds, rather than concede to the magistrate any power of establishing rites. Just like that Macedonian who cut with his sword the difficult knot of Gordius, which he could not loosen by any art. They were genuine disciples of the ancient Stoics in this, as in not a few other matters; the Stoics taught that nothing is indifferent to the wise man, since he acts by reason in all things, even the smallest, down to the stretching out of a finger. Yet the Stoics, pressed by the arguments of their opponents, at last granted in fact what they denied in words, and invented certain little distinctions of narration [ἀφηγήσεως] and of narrations [ἀφηγήσεων], etc., by which they might more decently hide their error, lest it seem they had erred. But there have been found among our own people some who have dared to defend this dogma, so stale and long since worn out of the schools, in public writings, and that far more rigidly than the Stoics once did. Two in particular: one, a theologian of some name among men of his party; the other, a layman, one of the nobles of the kingdom. Both died some years ago. Since I think that their dogma would not easily find belief among sensible men, much less a defender, I do not think it worth the effort to linger over refuting it.

units.la: XXIV. Esse igitur & res & actiones indifferentes, ex naturâ suâ saltem & in specie (quod ἐπιστήμονικῶν[illegible, ~8 letters]) quenquam negaturum opinor) sac cipio pro confesso. De quibus, quod ad nostrum institutum attinet, illud proximè advertendum est. Actum suâ naturâ, (i. e. respectu materiæ sive subjecti [?]si,) indifferentem; si lege præcipiatur, è bono & licito fieri honestum & necessarium: si lege prohibeatur, è bono & licito, malum fieri & illicitum.
units.tr: XXIV. I therefore take it as granted that things and actions are indifferent, at least by their own nature and in kind (as to the scientific point, I think no one will deny it). Concerning these, as far as our purpose is concerned, the following is to be noted first. An act which is indifferent by its own nature (that is, with respect to its matter or subject): if it is commanded by law, it is made from good and lawful into honourable and necessary; if it is forbidden by law, it is made from good and lawful into evil and unlawful.

units.la: Quod non contingit ex aliqua immutatione circa rem ipsam facta, quæ seu jussa seu vetita, ut physicè, ita & ethicè, eadem permanet quæ ante fuit, (respectus enim non mutat naturam:) sed ex obligationis[?] illa obvenit, quam Lex inducit. Unde factum, ut quod ante fuit, sicut Natura & ex se, sic usu etiam, & quoad nos, liberum ad utrumlibet: Legis accedente authoritate evadat usu & quoad nos non liberum amplius, sed pro legis exigentia vel illicitum, vel necessarium.
units.tr: This does not happen through any change made in the thing itself, which remains, whether commanded or forbidden, physically and ethically the same as it was before (for a relation does not change a nature); but it comes about from that obligation which the Law introduces. Hence it happens that what was before, both by nature and in itself, and also in use and in relation to us, free either way, becomes, by the addition of the authority of the law, no longer free in use and in relation to us, but either unlawful or necessary, according to the demand of the law.

units.la: XXV. Si quæratur, cum videatur Lex parem habere vim in utramque partem, qui fiat, ut possit Lex vetando actum facere ex bono & licito malum & illicitum, non item possit Lex (id enim ante negavimus) jubendo actum reddere ex malo & illicito bonum & licitum? Respondeo, rationem discriminis esse manifestissimam ex notissimo illo axiomate, Bonum ex causa integra, Malum ex quolibet defectu. Actus ergo de sua specie & respectu objecti malus, necesse est ut semper sit malus, nec possit in aliquo sui exercitio, quibuscunque accedentibus circumstantiis fieri bonus: propter defectum bonitatis ex parte objecti, qui defectus sufficit ad totum actum vitiandum. At actus de sua specie bonus, aut saltem non malus, si vel una aliqua accesserit circumstantia minus recta, totus redditur vitiosus: propter defectum sc. debitæ rectitudinis in illa circumstantia. Unde consequitur aliud etiam discrimen inter legem humanam affirmativam & negativam, sive præcipientem & vetantem: quòd Lex affirmativa non dat actui quem præcipit bonitatem, si sit aliàs aliquà ex parte malus; sed Lex negativa dat actui quem prohibet: etsi sit aliàs ex omni parte bonus; malitiam. Præceptum ergo humanum affirmativum, quod invenit bonum; facit esse necessarium: negativum, quod invenit bonum, facit esse illicitum: utrumque quod invenit malum, malum etiam sicut invenit, relinquit. Utrumque tamen obligat, suo fc. modo, & quoad nos: illud ad faciendum, quod praecipiendo jam factum est necessarium; hoc ad non faciendum, quod vetando jam factum est illicitum.
units.tr: XXV. If it is asked: since the Law seems to have equal power in both directions, how is it that a law, by forbidding, can make an act from good and lawful into evil and unlawful, but cannot likewise (for I denied this above) by commanding make an act from evil and unlawful into good and lawful? I answer that the reason for the difference is most plain from that well-known axiom: good comes from a whole cause, evil from any single defect. An act which is evil in its kind and with respect to its object must therefore always be evil, and cannot in any exercise of it, however many circumstances are added, become good, because of the lack of goodness on the part of the object, which lack is enough to vitiate the whole act. But an act which is good in its kind, or at least not evil, becomes wholly faulty if even one circumstance is less than right, because of the lack of the due rectitude in that circumstance. From this there follows another difference between a human law that is affirmative and one that is negative, that is, one that commands and one that forbids: an affirmative law does not give goodness to the act it commands, if that act is otherwise in some respect evil; but a negative law gives evil to the act it forbids, even if that act is otherwise good in every respect. Therefore a human precept that is affirmative, when it finds the act good, makes it necessary; a negative one, when it finds it good, makes it unlawful*. Each, when it finds the act evil, leaves it as evil as it found it. Yet each binds, in its own way, and in relation to us: the one to do, since by commanding it what is already done becomes necessary; the other not to do, since by forbidding it what is already done becomes unlawful.

units.la: XXVI. Restat Dubium Septimum, de Legibus Ecclesiasticis in speciali: Leges autem Ecclesiasticas hic intelligo, non quae a personis Ecclesiasticis sine Magistratus civilis authoritate constitutae sunt (quae ichola non est hujus loci, sed ad alterius generis causam, Efficientem scilicet, pertinet:) sed quaecunque demum legitima potestate latae circa Ecclesiasticas versantur: de materiali enim causa solum ad praesens disputamus. Non mihi adhuc videre contigit, praeter duos illos antedictos, qui ἀδιαφορίαν[?] omnem negaret, aut qui Magistratui politico aliquam in rebus adiaphoris mere politici potestatem non concederet. At qui hominibus potestatem omnem adimant, ritus & ceremonias in publico Dei cultu instituendi, extra eas quae sunt a Christo & ejus Apostolis in Evangelio perscriptae, occurrit ubique magna Novatorum seges.
units.tr: XXVI. There remains the Seventh Doubt, concerning Ecclesiastical Laws in particular. By Ecclesiastical Laws I here mean not those which have been established by ecclesiastical persons without the authority of the civil magistrate (that question is not the subject of this place, but belongs to another kind of cause, namely the efficient cause), but whatever laws, enacted by lawful power, concern ecclesiastical matters. For we are disputing for the present only about the material cause. It has not yet been my lot to see anyone, apart from those two mentioned above, who would deny all indifference [ἀδιαφορίαν], or who would not concede to the political magistrate some power in adiaphora that is purely political. But those who would take away from men all power of instituting rites and ceremonies in the public worship of God, outside those which Christ and his Apostles have set down in the Gospel, find everywhere a great crop of Innovators.

units.la: Verum enimvero, (ut quod res est profitear,) dum, ut mihimetipsi aliisque hoc in negotio satisfaciam, multa a multis (noftratibus praesertim) in eam sententiam congesta volumina excutio; nusquam reperi, qui justam aut justae similem dijudicandi rationem in medium afferret, cur determinandi & statuendi circa res adiaphoras potestas, non in Ecclesiasticis obtineat, atque in Politicis. Quae enim a Scandalo, a Libertate Christiana, & aliis ejusmodi Locis communibus, opponi solent argumenta, adversus utriusque generis leges & constitutiones aequo Marte militant; & aut utrafque
units.tr: Indeed, to profess what is the case: while, in order to satisfy myself and others in this matter, I have been going through the many volumes written to this effect by many men (especially our own countrymen), I have nowhere found anyone who brought forward a just, or a just-seeming, rule of judgement as to why the power of determining and establishing concerning indifferent things should hold in ecclesiastical matters and not in political ones. For the arguments which are usually raised against these laws from scandal, from Christian liberty, and from other such commonplaces, fight with equal strength against the laws and constitutions of both kinds; and they either overthrow both equally, or neither. Those which are thought to have some peculiar force against the laws and rites of the Church are altogether four, and each of them (according to the scope of the time) must be briefly examined in its own order.

units.la: [Left page, cropped marginal notes, top to bottom:] trasque pariter evertunt, aut neutras. Quæ peculiarem aliquam vim adversus Leges & ritus Ecclesiasticos habere existimantur, quatuor omninò sunt, singula (pro temporis ratione) breviter & suo ordine examinanda : Christus Legislator, Perfectio Scripturæ, Natura sacri cultus, & veteris Ecclesiæ Exemplum.
units.tr: ...neither. Those arguments which are thought to have some peculiar force against the laws and rites of the Church are four in all. Each, as the time allows, must be examined briefly and in its turn: Christ the Lawgiver, the perfection of Scripture, the nature of sacred worship, and the example of the ancient Church.

units.la: XXVII. Objiciunt primò illud Apostoli, Jac. 4. 12. Unus est Legislator, qui potest servare & perdere. Hoc novatorum argumentum, ut totius caussæ suæ basin, regnante Elizabethâ, plurimi fecere qui nunc erant Disciplinariæ factionis Coryphæi. Christum nimirum unicum esse Ecclesiæ suæ, ut Primi[?]pem, ita & Legislatorem. Quas ille dedit Leges, Ecclesiam teneri in perpetuum observare; alias verò non admittere debere, nec alium Legislatorem agnoscere. Quicunque Leges Ecclesiæ ferre, præter eas quæ sunt à Christo latæ, præsumpserit, Antichristi partes agere, & se prodere Regii Christi muneris temerarium invasorem. Hunc Apostoli locum aliquoties ante, ut res postulabat, tractavimus: præsertim ubi probandum fuit Deum solum & ejus Christum in Conscientias hominum merum & directum imperium habere. Sed obtinere hoc in legibus Politicis, nihilo minùs quàm Ecclesiasticis, cæcus sit oportet qui non videat. Cur enim obligatio Legum Humanarum in rebus Civilibus, cum Legislativa unius Christi potestate consistere possit, non poterit consistere eadem in Ecclesiasticis; quis ullam discriminis vel tenuissimam umbram ex illo Textu eliciat tandem? Esto Ecclesiæ Christianæ Legislator Christus? Annon & Reipublicæ Christianæ pariter? Neque enim meminit Apostolus in toto illo commate Ecclesiæ; nec de rebus Ecclesiasticis omnino disputationem illam instituit: quinimò nec de politicis aut legibus aut juribus ibi agitur, sed de privatorum hominum censuris. Voluit[?] ille fideles admonitos, ut Christianæ Charitatis memores, à fratribus temerè judicandis abstinerent : Deum enim unicum esse Conscientiarum Judicem, qui solus Legem dedit, ex quâ in die ultimo judicandi essent singuli. Hic verus illius loci scopus ; hæc Apostoli mens. Quid hoc, quæso, ad Leges Humanas damnandas : aut si damnandas ; cur Ecclesiasticas magis quàm Politicas ? Quarum neutræ, saltem non unæ magis quàm alteræ, à nobis afferuntur per se & virtute suâ obligare Conscientias.
units.tr: XXVII. They object first that saying of the Apostle, Jas. 4. 12. There is one Lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy. The most of those who were then the leaders of the Disciplinarian faction, in the reign of Elizabeth, made much of this argument as the foundation of their whole cause. Namely, Christ alone is the sole Prince and also the Lawgiver of his Church. The Church is bound to observe the laws he has given, for ever; it ought not to admit others, nor acknowledge another Lawgiver. Whoever presumes to enact laws of the Church beyond those which Christ has enacted plays the part of Antichrist, betrays himself as a rash usurper of the office of Christ the King. We have treated this passage of the Apostle several times before, as the matter required, especially where it had to be proved that God alone and his Christ hold pure and direct authority over the consciences of men. But that this holds for political laws no less than for ecclesiastical, only one who is blind could fail to see. For why should the binding force of human laws in civil matters be able to exist alongside the legislative power of Christ alone, yet not be able to exist in ecclesiastical matters? Who, at last, can draw from that text even the faintest shadow of a distinction? Grant that Christ is the Lawgiver of the Christian Church*: is he not equally the Lawgiver of the Christian commonwealth? For the Apostle makes no mention of the Church in that whole verse, nor does he conduct that discussion about ecclesiastical matters at all. Indeed nothing is said there about political matters, nor about laws or rights, but about the judgments of private men. He wished the faithful, having been warned, to remember Christian charity and to refrain from rashly judging their brothers: for God alone is the Judge of consciences, who alone gave the Law by which each person will be judged on the last day. This is the true aim of that passage; this is the Apostle's meaning. What, I ask, does this have to do with condemning human laws; or, if they are to be condemned, why ecclesiastical rather than political? Neither kind, or at least not one more than the other, is put forward by us as binding consciences of itself and by its own power.

units.la: XXVIII. Objiciunt Secundo, Perfectionem Sacræ Scripturæ. Regulam hanc esse vitæ & morum ; Legem perfectam, & quæ sapientem reddere possit hominem Dei ad omne opus bonum ; cui quisquis de suo quicquam addiderit, insignem Deo injuriam fecerit, & sibi gravissimas accersiverit pœnas. Certissima omnia. Quòd si Scriptura sit regula vitæ & agendorum omnibus numeris absoluta ; idque (si novis his Stoicis fides) usque ad res quasque leviculas, ut nec festucam tollere liceat nisi ex verbi Dei præscripto : an non tam rebus civilibus regulandis sufficiet, quàm Ecclesiasticis ; aut qui magis derogabunt perfectioni Scripturæ Ecclesiæ Leges, quàm Reipublicæ ? Aut quis eum recte dixerit addidisse verbo Dei aliquid, qui Leges Ecclesiasticas condidit ordinis & honestatis causâ : quum nec ille Leges suas populo proponat ut Dei verbum ; & Deus in verbo suo præceperit, ut omnia in Ecclesiâ ordine & honestè fiant ?
units.tr: XXVIII. They object secondly, the perfection of Holy Scripture. This is the rule of life and of conduct; it is a perfect law, able to make the man of God wise for every good work. Whoever adds anything of his own to it does a great injury to God and brings the gravest punishments upon himself. All this is most certain. But if Scripture is the rule of life and of action, complete in every respect, and (if we are to believe these new Stoics) extends even to the smallest matters, so that it is not lawful to remove a straw except by the prescription of God's word: will it not be sufficient for regulating civil affairs as much as ecclesiastical? Or do laws of the Church detract more from the perfection of Scripture than laws of the commonwealth do? Or who could rightly say that he has added something to the word of God, who enacts ecclesiastical laws for the sake of order and decency, since he does not put forward his laws to the people as the word of God*, and God has commanded in his word that all things in the Church be done decently and in order?

units.la: XXIX. Objiciunt Tertiò, Naturam Cultus. Nempe Cultum Dei esse rem sacram : in eo cultu om-nia ex Dei præscripto esse peragenda : procul illinc abigendas, ut superstitiosas, imò plane idololatricas, quascunque humanas adinventiones, & ritus [?]ἐθελοθρησκίας[?]. Est profectò res sacra cultus Dei : nec fas est homini cultum aliquem instituere, præter eum quem ipse Deus praestituit. Sed quia latet in voce ambiguitas, distinguendum est de Cultu Dei: tripliciter enim accipitur ea vox. Imprimis Cultus Dei proprie dictus & praecipuus, est internus ille Animi Cultus, qui consistit in exercitio virtutum internarum, Fidei, Spei, Dilectionis, Invocationis, Fiduciae, &c. Secundo, Actus illi externi, quibus internus ille animi cultus, partim exprimitur, partim adjuvatur & fovetur; cujusmodi sunt Precationes publicae, Gratiarum actiones, Psalmodiae, Auditio verbi, participatio Sacramentorum, &c. suo quodam modo, i. e. reductivè & minus propriè, dici etiam possunt & solent Cultus Dei: in quantum sunt illius proprie dicti cultus externa sive testimonia, sive adminicula. Tertio, cùm sit impossibile actionem aliquam externam, praesertim sit solennis, sine circumstantiis quibusdam, (pluribus aut paucioribus,) locorum, temporum, gestuum, &c. praesentari; inde fit ut ipsae illae circumstantiae (quae, si aut legibus aut moribus stabilitae fuerint, Ritus etiam dicuntur,) interdum Cultus appellationem accipiant: sed id improprie admodum, & propter eam concomitantiam solum quam habent ad cultum illum externum, qui & ipse improprie quoque cultus dicitur. Dicendum ergo, internum[?] illum primarium & proprie dictum cultum, ita Deum solum authorem agnoscere, ut nulli homini fas sit, aut novum[?] cultum instituere, aut a Deo institutum alicui alteri praeterquam ipsi Deo exhibere. Externum quoque cultum, quoad substantialia, a Deo solo instituti. Ast circumstantiarum, quae sunt huic externo cultui accessoriae, & ipsum comitantur, (si quis eas quoque voluerit cultus nomine dignari,) longè aliam esse rationem. Quum enim non possit externus Dei cultus sine circumstantiis praestari, nec tamen Deus in Evangelio suo certas particulares circumstantias in sacris conventibus perpetuò observandas tradiderit, sed generatim duntaxat præceperit, ut ordini, honesti & ædificationi serviatur: necessario sequitur ejusmodi circumstantiarum determinationem, quæ sunt ipsi cultui accidentales, & pro locorum, temporum & occasionum ratione mutabiles, ad eos qui sub Christo regendarum Ecclesiarum jus potestatem habent, pertinere. Quas, & ab iis qui publica authoritate in singulis Ecclesiis præditi sunt præstitui, & præstitutas ab omnibus earundem Ecclesiarum membris religiose observari, sacri cultus non natura prohibet, sed exigit potius solennitas & decor. Quid quòd isti ipsi homines, qui in Canones & Constitutiones Ecclesiasticas tam severè & plenis buccis invehuntur, ritibus tamen in cultu Dei externo, à Christo aut ejus Apostolis nusquam præscriptis, quoties ipsis collibitum est, utuntur: ut manus levatione in juramento præstando, capitis denudatione in sacra synaxi, aliisque compluribus, quæ cum quotidie fieri videamus, non opus est recensere.
units.tr: XXIX. They object thirdly, the nature of worship. Namely, that the worship of God is a sacred thing: in that worship everything must be carried out according to God's prescription, and all human inventions and rites of will-worship [ἐθελοθρησκίας], whatever they are, must be driven far away from it as superstitious, indeed plainly idolatrous. Certainly the worship of God is a sacred thing, and it is not lawful for a man to institute any worship apart from that which God himself has appointed. But because there is an ambiguity in the word, we must distinguish concerning the worship of God, for the term is taken in three ways. First, the worship of God properly so called and principal is that inward worship of the mind, which consists in the exercise of inward virtues: faith, hope, love, invocation, trust, and so on. Second, those outward acts by which that inward worship of the mind is partly expressed and partly aided and fostered, such as public prayers, thanksgivings, psalm-singing, hearing the word, participation in the sacraments, and so on; in a certain manner, that is, by a reduced and less proper sense, these too can be and commonly are called the worship of God, in so far as they are the outward testimonies or aids of that worship properly so called. Third, since it is impossible for any outward action, especially a solemn one, to be presented without certain circumstances (more or fewer) of places, times, gestures, and so on, it follows that those very circumstances (which, if they have been established by laws or customs, are also called rites) sometimes take on the name of worship. But this is quite improper, and only because of the accompaniment they have with that outward worship, which is itself also improperly called worship. So we must say that the inward and primary worship, properly so called, acknowledges God alone as its author, so that it is not lawful for any man either to institute new worship or to offer to anyone other than God himself what God has instituted. The outward worship too, as regards its substantials, is instituted by God alone. But the case of circumstances, which are accessory to this outward worship and accompany it (if anyone wishes to give them the name of worship as well), is quite different. For since outward worship of God cannot be offered without circumstances, and yet God in his Gospel has not handed down certain particular circumstances to be perpetually observed in sacred assemblies, but has commanded only in general that order, decency and edification be served, it necessarily follows that the determining of such circumstances, which are accidental to the worship itself and are changeable according to the nature of places, times and occasions, belongs to those who have the right and power of governing the Churches under Christ. The nature of sacred worship does not forbid these to be prescribed by those who are invested with public authority in individual Churches, and that they be religiously observed by all members of those same Churches once prescribed; rather, solemnity and decorum demand it. Moreover, these very men who rail so severely and with full mouths against canons and ecclesiastical constitutions nevertheless use rites* in outward worship of God, which were nowhere prescribed by Christ or his Apostles, whenever it pleases them: such as the lifting of the hand in taking an oath, the uncovering of the head in the holy synaxis, and many others, which, since we see them done every day, there is no need to list.

units.la: XXX. Objiciunt Quarto, Veteris, (hoc est Judaica,) Ecclesiæ exemplum Mosen, datum à Deo Hebræo populo Legislatorem, non substantialia tantum cultus Judaici, sed (quà erat fidelitate) & minutissimas quasque circumstantias lege sua definivisse; & in construendo tabernaculo (qui futurus erat Ecclesiæ Christianæ typus) ad exemplaris sibi in monte propositi ideam omnia ad amussim perfecisse. Christum utique Novi Testamenti Legislatorem, nisi omnia & singula quæ in cultu Ecclesiastico peragenda sunt, usque ad minutissimas quasque circumstantias præscripsisset, merito credi posse (quod vel suspicari proximè à blasphemia abest,) minus fidelem in domo Dei fuisse quam fuerat Moses. Christo proinde insignem fieri injuriam pariter, & contumeliam; siqui novi ritus, quos ipse nusquam instituit, Authoritate Humana in Ecclesiam inferantur, [?]ut à plebe Christianâ recipiantur. Atqui imprimis cogitari debuerant, qui ista objiciunt, hoc argumento non minùs Leges humanas Politicas everti quàm Ecclesiasticas. Moses enim ex Dei mandato Hebræo populo legem dedit certam & definitam, non eorum rituum solùm quæ ad cultum Dei, sed & eorum judiciorum quæ ad civilis regiminis administrationem pertinebat.
units.tr: XXX. They object fourthly the example of the old (that is, the Jewish) Church: that God gave Moses to the Hebrew people as their Lawgiver, and that Moses defined by his law not only the substantials of Jewish worship but (as was fitting for faithfulness) even the smallest circumstances; and that in constructing the tabernacle (which was to be a type of the Christian Church) he carried out everything exactly according to the idea of the pattern shown to him on the mountain. Surely, unless Christ, the Lawgiver of the New Testament, had prescribed all and each of the things to be done in ecclesiastical worship, down to the smallest circumstances, it could fairly be believed (and even to suspect it comes close to blasphemy) that he was less faithful in God's house than Moses had been. Therefore a grave injury and insult is done to Christ alike, whenever new rites, which he himself nowhere instituted, are brought into the Church by human authority, so that they may be received by the Christian people. But those who put forward these objections ought first to have considered that by this argument human political laws are overthrown no less than ecclesiastical ones. For Moses, by God's command, gave the Hebrew people a law certain and defined, not only of those rites which pertain to the worship of God, but also of those judgments which pertained to the administration of civil government.

units.la: XXXI. Deinde & illud Secundò mirum est eos non animadvertisse, collatione ejus fidelitatis quæ fuit in utroque Legislatore, Mose & Christo, vix aliquid ab eis abduci potuisse importunius, quod causæ suæ majori esset nocumento, & quod sententiam nostram validius confirmaret. Sicut enim ex eo quòd Moses, & in ritualibus, & in judicialibus, populo Judaico Leges plurimas tulerit; rectè collegimus voluisse Deum populum Judaicum, sub illa pædagogia & disciplinâ Mosaicâ, quasi quodam servitutis jugo, sic in officio contineri, ut paucissimæ essent illis libera : Ita ex eo quòd Christus, paternæ voluntatis fidelissimus interpres, Ecclesiæ Christianæ paucissimas Leges tulerit Ceremoniarum, rectè colligimus Deum voluisse, ut Magistratus & populus Christianus in iiustiusmodi rebus libertati suæ permitteretur. Ita ut jam liberum sit & privato cuique hmini[?] sponte suâ (nullo interveniente superioris potestatis imperio vel interdicto,) quod sibi consultius visum fuerit facere : & singulis Ecclesiis earumque gubernatoribus ea præscribere & sancire, quæ sibi pro temporum & locorum conditione, ordini, honestati, ædificationi & paci maximè inservitura videbuntur.
units.tr: XXXI. Secondly, it is also remarkable that they did not notice how, when one compares the faithfulness of the two lawgivers, Moses and Christ, scarcely anything could have been brought forward more damaging to their cause, or more strongly confirming our view. For just as, from the fact that Moses gave the Jewish people very many laws, both ritual and judicial, we rightly infer that God wished the Jewish people, under that pedagogy and Mosaic discipline, to be held in obedience as if under a yoke of servitude, so that very few things would be free for them; so from the fact that Christ, the most faithful interpreter of the Father's will, gave the Christian Church very few laws of ceremonies, we rightly infer that God wished the magistrate and the Christian people to be left to their liberty in matters of this kind. So now it is free for each private person, of his own accord (with no command or prohibition of any superior power intervening), to do whatever seems more advisable to him; and for individual churches and their governors to prescribe and sanction those things which, according to the condition of times and places, seem most likely to serve order, decency, edification and peace.

units.la: XXXII. Quin & illud Tertiò cogitasse debuerant, qui hoc argumento utuntur, Ne ipsis quidem Judicibus, sub illâ Mosis pædagogiâ, ita omnem adempta fuisse rituum libertatem in rebus ad Dei cultum pertinentibus, ut non illis liceret propriâ authoritate propria authoritate & observare & instituere, quæ nullibi constat fuisse vel ab ipso Deo, vel à Mose Dei ministro præcepta. Accipite instantias è multis paucas. Primò, Paschatis Solennitatem ex Lege Mosis septiduo observandam, Speciali Lege Rex Hezekias (qui tamen singulare pietatis suæ testimonium à Deo ipso accipere meruit) ex populi consensu in alterum septiduum continuari decrevit. Cujus rei historia extat, 2 Paralip. 30. Secundò, festum Purim in memoriam ejus liberationis, quæ Judæorum genti sub Persarum Rege Assuero contigerat, annuatim celebrari instituerunt Ester & Mardochæi, Esth. 9. Tertiò, cùm Moses diem solennis jejunii annuatim unicum duntaxat, Septimo mense, observandum præcepisset; Reges & Magistratus illius populi (quibus de causis non satis constat, sed ut par est credere, in memoriam insignium aliquot judiciorum Dei) annua solemnia jejunia authoritate suâ instituerunt alia: ita ut temporibus ultimorum prophetarum quatuor observarentur annua jejunia: videlicet, præter illum Septimi mensis, tria alia; mensibus quarto, quinto & decimo; quorum omnium fit mentio, Zachar. 8. 19. Quartò, festum dedicationis Altarii, quod Encænia dicitur ab Assamoni[?] sine aliquo Dei mandato institutum, (cujus historia ex 1 Macc. 4. 59. petenda est,) Christus ipse non tantum comprobasse, sed & præsentiâ suâ cohonestasse, plurimorum eorúmque melioris notæ interpretum judicio exîstimatur, Joh. 10. 22. Quintò, ut in solennibus jejuniis & luctu pœnitentiali sacro se induerent, & cineres crinibus inspergerent, nullo Dei mandato præceptum legimus; apud Judæos tamen, longò per aliquot retrò secula usu ita moribus receptum est (consuetudine diuturnâ, ut fieri amat, vim legis obtinente,) ut Christus eo loquendi genere, tanquam ex recepto more gentis, sine aliquo affixo nigro Theta, aliquoties usus fuerit:
units.tr: XXXII. Indeed, thirdly, those who use this argument ought to have considered that not even the judges, under that pedagogy of Moses, were so deprived of all freedom of rites in matters pertaining to the worship of God that it was not lawful for them, by their own authority, both to observe and to institute things which nowhere are found to have been commanded either by God himself or by Moses, God's minister. Take a few instances out of many. First, the solemnity of the Passover, to be observed for seven days by the Law of Moses, King Hezekiah (who nevertheless deserved to receive a singular testimony of his piety from God himself), by a special decree and with the consent of the people, resolved should be continued for another seven days. The history of this matter is extant, 2 Paralip. 30. Secondly, the feast of Purim, in memory of that deliverance which had befallen the Jewish nation under the Persian king Ahasuerus, was instituted by Esther and Mordecai to be celebrated annually, Esth. 9. Thirdly, when Moses had commanded only one solemn fast to be observed annually, in the seventh month, the kings and magistrates of that people (for what reasons is not sufficiently clear, but as is right to believe, in memory of some notable judgments of God) by their own authority instituted other annual solemn fasts, so that in the times of the last four prophets annual fasts were observed: namely, besides that of the seventh month, three others, in the fourth, fifth and tenth months; all of which are mentioned in Zachar. 8. 19. Fourthly, the feast of the dedication of the altar, which is called Encaenia, instituted by the Hasmoneans without any command of God (the history of which is to be sought from 1 Macc. 4. 59.), Christ himself is judged by the opinion of many, and those of better repute, not merely to have approved but also to have honoured by his presence, Joh. 10. 22. Fifthly, we read of no command of God that in solemn fasts and penitential mourning they should clothe themselves in sacred sackcloth and sprinkle ashes on their hair; yet among the Jews, by long usage through some centuries past, it was so received into custom (by long-standing custom, as it likes to happen, holding the force of law) that Christ, speaking in that manner, as from the accepted custom of the nation, without any black Theta affixed, used it several times:

units.la: Prælestio Sexta.
units.tr: Lecture Six.

units.la: Matth. 11. 21. Sextò, è scriptis Rabbinorum constat, Judæis illud etiam in morem positum suisse, ut ante cœnam Paschalem pater-familiâs pedes eorum incurvatus lavaret: quod etsi nullâ Dei lege imperatum, à Christo tamen observatum liquet ex historia Evangelica, Joh. 13. Quid attinet Synagogas ad commoditatem sacrorum conventum per oppida & vicos ubique extructas; aliáque complura, quorum ingentem farraginem suppeditant Judæorum commentarii, enumerare? Ex quibus omnibus illud saltem efficitur: si Judæis sub illo severioris disciplinæ jugo tàm multa fuerint ad Dei cultum pertinentia, quæ nullo Spe- ervan- us po- ut par judi- te sua iorum iuma: alia; omni- m de- moneti hifto- s ipse à co- nota Quin- ntiali rent, d Ju- u ita ut o lo- ntis, erit: ut [?]nali Dei mandato niterentur: non posse ab illius populi exemplo, ad evertendas Leges Humanas Ecclesiasticas, idoneum peti argumentum.
units.tr: Matth. 11. 21. Sixthly, it is clear from the writings of the Rabbis that the Jews also had the custom that before the Paschal supper the head of the household would bend down and wash their feet. Although no law of God commanded this, it is plain from the Gospel history (John 13) that Christ observed it. What is the point of listing the synagogues built everywhere in towns and villages for the convenience of sacred assemblies, and the many other practices of which the Jewish commentaries offer a huge heap? From all of these this much at least follows: if the Jews, under that yoke of stricter discipline, had many observances pertaining to the worship of God that rested on no command of God, then no suitable argument for overturning human ecclesiastical laws can be drawn from that people's example.

units.la: PRÆLECTIO SEPTIMA. De Obligatione Legum Humanarum ex parte Causæ Efficientis.
units.tr: THE SEVENTH LECTURE. On the Obligation of Human Laws from the Side of the Efficient Cause.

units.la: PROV. VIII. 15.
units.tr: PROV. VIII. 15.

units.la: Per me Reges regnant, & Legum conditores justa decernunt.
units.tr: By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just.

units.la: I. DE Legum Humanarum Obligatione egimus superiore Termino: cum in genere, Quod nimirum Leges Humanæ rite constitutæ obligent subditorum conscientias ad obediendum: tum etiam in speciali, quoad illa dubia quæ ad Causam Materialem propius pertinere videbantur. Quatenus scilicet obligent latæ Leges, primò de rebus impossibilibus; secundò, de possibilibus sed multum onerosis; tertiò, de necessariis; quartò, de illicitis & inhonestis; quintò, de malis permittendis; sextò, de rebus mediis & adiaphoris in communi; septimò, de ritibus Ecclesiasticis in speciali. In quibus omnibus eorum quæ dicta sunt, (ne, dum singula repeto, molestus sim,) summa huc redit: obligari subditos ad parendum Legibus Justis, ad parendum injustis non obligari; juxta quod in Textu propositò exigit à Legum conditoribus Salomon, ut non nisi quæ justa sunt decernant. Pergendum porrò ad eorum reliqua quæ sunt antè à me proposita prosequenda: In quibus tractandis, utar quâ potero, & res feret, brevitate, ut rem universam, Item[?] quod ad Legum obligationem attinet, idoneo tempore absolvam.
units.tr: I. We treated the obligation of human laws in the previous lecture, both in general, namely that human laws duly enacted bind the consciences of subjects to obey, and in particular, with regard to those doubtful questions which seemed to belong more closely to the material cause. These concerned whether enacted laws bind: first, with regard to impossible things; second, with regard to possible but very burdensome things; third, with regard to necessary things; fourth, with regard to unlawful and dishonourable things; fifth, with regard to evils to be tolerated; sixth, with regard to things indifferent and adiaphora in general; seventh, with regard to ecclesiastical rites in particular. In all of these, so that I do not weary you by repeating each point, the sum of what has been said comes to this: subjects are bound to obey just laws, and are not bound to obey unjust ones. In accordance with this, Solomon in the text requires of lawgivers that they decree only what is just. We must now proceed to pursue the remaining points I proposed earlier. In treating them I shall use as much brevity as I can and the matter allows, so that I may complete the whole subject, including what concerns the obligation of laws, at a suitable time.

units.la: II. In Causarum ordine, pro observata mihi amethodi ratione, Materiam proximè sequitur Efficiens: excipit hanc Forma: ultimum agmen ducit & claudit Finis. De Legum causâ Efficiente, quum in Quinta Prælectionis Conclusione tertiò satis ostensum fuerit, Leges Humanas nisi à persona legitimam potestatem habente latas non obligare; illud nunc imprimis dispiciendum restat, penes quos sit ἐξουσία νομοθετικὴ, hoc est, justa & legitima Leges ferendi potestas; sive quinam sint Legum latores illi, quibus ex mente Salomonis justa decernendi jus competit. Huic Dubio primo & in hoc causæ genere longè præcipuo, ut plenè respondeatur, duo interim supponenda sunt. Suppono itaque primo, potestatem Legumlativam esse potestatem alicujus Superioris, sicut præcipere, (præceptionis appellatione prohibitionem etiam complector) qui est actus Legis proprius, est actus Superioris. Distare non parum hac ex parte animadvertere est tria hæc: Promissionem, Petitionem, Præceptionem. Commune est omnium indiscriminatim, Superiorum, Inferiorum, Æqualium, promittere. Potest enim promittere aliquid, & Pater filio, & Filius patri, & Frater Vicinusve fratri aut vicino. Petere autem proprie est Inferiorum, Parium etiam aliquatenus; ut petit sibi dari veniam, vel gratiam fieri, à patre filius, & à vicino vicinus: non item Superiorum, nisi impropriè admodum, & per quandam [illegible, ~9 letters] . At Superiorum, & in aliquâ [illegible, ~8 letters] vel dignitatis præeminentiâ constitutorum adeò peculiare est Præcipere, ut omninò ridiculus esset, quisquis superiori, vel etiam pari aliquid faciendum par aut inferior ferió præciperet. Actus enim omnis requirit principium sibi proportionatum: & par[?] in parem non habet potestatem.
units.tr: II. In the order of causes, following the method I have observed, the matter comes next after the efficient cause; the form follows this, and the end leads and closes the procession. Concerning the efficient cause of laws: since it was shown in the fifth conclusion of the lecture, in the third place, that human laws do not bind unless they are enacted by a person having lawful authority, what remains to be examined first is in whose hands lies the legislative power (ἐξουσία νομοθετική), that is, the just and lawful power of enacting laws; or, who those lawgivers are to whom, according to the mind of Solomon, the right of decreeing what is just belongs. To answer this first question fully, and it is by far the chief question in this kind of cause, two things must meanwhile be assumed. I assume, therefore, first, that the legislative power is the power of some superior; just as to command (under the term command I include also prohibition), which is the proper act of a law, is the act of a superior. It is worth noting, in this respect, that there is no small difference among these three: promising, requesting, and commanding. To promise is common to all without distinction, to superiors, inferiors, and equals alike. For a father can promise something to a son, a son to a father, and a brother or neighbour to a brother or neighbour. To request, however, properly belongs to inferiors, and to equals in some measure too: a son requests from his father that pardon be granted or favour shown to him, and a neighbour from a neighbour; but not so with superiors, except very improperly and by a certain figure of speech. But to command is so peculiar to superiors, and to those set in some degree of dignity or pre-eminence, that anyone who would command a superior, or even an equal, to do something, or an inferior at all, would be utterly ridiculous. For every act requires a principle proportionate to itself; and an equal has no power over an equal.

units.la: III. De Obligatione autem, quoad ista tria, sic statuendum. Qui abs alio petit quid, petendo neutrum obligat; nec se, nec eum à quo petit: quia Petitio est actus indigentiæ, non potestatis; cujus effectus cùm aliunde pendeat, & non procedat ab ipso agente, (petente sc.) non potest inducere aliquam obligationem. Qui autem alteri aliquid pollicetur; Promittendo se quidem obligat; eum verò cui facta est promissio non obligat. Quum enim promissio sit actus liberæ voluntatis: potest quivis homo in quantum est liberum agens & ἐξουσίαν ἔχει [?]περὶ τῶ ἰδίω θελήμα[?] (ut loquitur Apostolus, 1 Cor. 7. 37.) jus illud & potestatem quam habet in propriam voluntatem in semetipsum exercere; at non propterea & in alterum. Quia ex vi liberi arbitrii, homo est dominus voluntatis propriæ & actuum suorum tantùm, non item alienorum. E contrà verò qui alteri præcipit, si præcipiendi jus habet, eum cui præcipit præcipiendo obligat; seipsum non obligat. Eò quod præceptio est actus potestatis, authoritatis & juris in alterum: ëstque ex se aptus natus, nisi aliquid impediat, inducere obligationem. Si Pater filio, Dominus servo, Imperator militi, Rex populo, Deus homini, ut Superior, facienda præcipit cum authoritate; & præcipiendo ad imperata facienda obligat.
units.tr: III. Concerning obligation, however, in respect of these three things, the following must be laid down. One who requests something from another binds neither himself nor the one from whom he requests by requesting; because a request is an act of need, not of power, and since its effect depends on something else and does not proceed from the agent himself (that is, the one requesting), it cannot induce any obligation. One who promises something to another, indeed, binds himself by promising, but does not bind the one to whom the promise is made. For since a promise is an act of free will, any man, insofar as he is a free agent and has authority over his own will (as the Apostle puts it, 1 Cor. 7. 37), can exercise that right and power which he has over his own will upon himself, but not for that reason upon another. For by the force of free choice a man is master of his own will and of his own acts only, not of the acts of others. On the contrary, one who commands another, if he has the right to command, binds the one to whom he commands by commanding, but does not bind himself. This is because a command is an act of power, authority, and right over another; and it is of its own nature fit and apt, unless something hinders, to induce obligation. If a father to a son, a master to a servant, an emperor to a soldier, a king to a people, or God to a man, as superior, commands with authority that things be done, then by commanding he obliges them to do what is enjoined.

units.la: IV. Suppono Secundo, potestatem Legumlativam esse potestatem publicæ Jurisdictionis. Neque enim sufficit ad potestatem Leges ferendi, ut quis in alios jus qualecunque habeat & imperium, ut possit eis facienda præscribere: nisi & potestate sit prædictus externâ, ita ut possit eos ad imperata facienda cogere, & nolentes supplicio afficere. ‘Ὁ γὰρ νόμος ἀναγκαστικὸν ἔχει δύναμιν[?] inquit Aristoteles Ethic.
units.tr: IV. I assume, secondly, that the legislative power is the power of public jurisdiction. For it is not enough for the power of enacting laws that someone have any sort of right and dominion over others, so that he can prescribe to them what they are to do; unless he is also endowed with external power, so that he can compel them to do what he commands, and punish them with penalty if they are unwilling. "For law has coercive power" [ὁ γὰρ νόμος ἀναγκαστικὸν ἔχει δύναμιν], says Aristotle in the Ethics.

units.la: 1o Diftin-[?]
units.tr: 1. Distinction

units.la: Ic. Distinguunt igitur Scholastici ἐξουσίαν sive potestatem eam quam habet superior in inferiorem, in potestatem quam vocant Dominativam, & potestatem Jurisdictionis: Quarum illa minor est, privata magis, & externæ Jurisdictionis expers; hæc major, & ἀναγκαστικὴ[?]. Distant enim inter se non parum duæ istæ potestates? idque triplici potissimum discrimine. Primo, ratione Materiæ sive Objecti, quia potestas dominativa, versatur proprie circa communitatem imperfectiorem & privatam, ut Domum, Scholam, Familiam: potestas verò Jurisdictionis circa perfectiorem & magis publicam, ut Civitatem, Exercitum, Rempublicam. Secundo, ratione Finis, quia potestas dominativa per se & primariò ordinatur ad utilitatem personæ eam potestatem habentis, id est, Domini; in bonum verò communitatis secundariò tantùm & consequenter: quatenus nimirum utile est familiæ ut patcr[?]familias ditescat. Potestas autem publicæ Jurisdictionis ordinatur primariò in bonum publicum ipsius communitatis: in bonum verò personæ tali potestate præditæ, id est, ipsius Magistratus, non nisi secundariò & consequenter; quatenus nimirum utile est Principi, ut Respublica floreat. Tertiò, ratione efficacis administrationis: quæ in potestate Jurisdistionis Major est quàm in Dominativâ, propter Majorem vim coactivam. Exempli gratiâ, non potest tam efficaciter procurare pater-familias, ut iussa sua executioni mandentur à filiis aut servis suis, quos ei non licet nisi virgâ aut fuste corrigere ; quàm potest Magistratus Civilis à subditis suis, quos carcere & exilio punire, bona eorum fisco addicere, capitis etiam supplicio in ipsos animadvertere, pro iure suo potest, ἡ παιτικὴ σχέ-σις ἐκ ἔχει τὸ ἰσχυρὸν ὡς τὸ ἀναγκαῖον, inquit loco proximè laudato idem Aristoteles. Ergo ad Leges condendas non sufficit quaevis superioritas ; sed sed praeter Dominatiuam illam, requiritur etiam δύναμις ἀναγκαστική[?], siue potestas Iurisdictionis prius dictae: ita ut Leges ferri non possint, nisi persona habente Publicam Coactiuam Potestatem. Intelligitis ut opinor, ne sit necesse me vos admonere, quae sunt a me jam dicta ad Legum κυρίως[?] dictas absolutè pertinere; ad reliquas, nisi κατ᾽ ἀναλογίαν[?], suo quodam modo & proportione: prout earum unaquaeque; ad istarum perfectionem aut accedunt propius, aut ab ea longius absunt.
units.tr: I. The Schoolmen therefore distinguish the authority (ἐξουσία), or power, which a superior has over an inferior, into the power which they call dominative, and the power of jurisdiction. The former is lesser, more private, and lacks external jurisdiction; the latter is greater and coercive (ἀναγκαστική). For these two powers differ from each other not a little, and chiefly in three respects. First, in respect of matter or object: the dominative power is properly concerned with a more imperfect and private community, such as the household, the school, or the family; but the power of jurisdiction is concerned with a more perfect and more public community, such as the city, the army, or the commonwealth. Second, in respect of end: the dominative power is ordered primarily and in itself to the advantage of the person who holds that power, that is, the master; and to the good of the community only secondarily and by consequence, insofar as it is useful to the family for the father of the family to grow rich. But the power of public jurisdiction is ordered primarily to the public good of the community itself; and to the good of the person endowed with such power, that is, of the magistrate himself, only secondarily and by consequence, insofar as it is useful to the prince that the commonwealth should flourish. Third, in respect of the efficacy of administration: this is greater in the power of jurisdiction than in the dominative power, on account of its greater coercive force. For example, a father of a family cannot procure as effectively that his commands be carried out by his sons or servants, whom he may correct only with a rod or cudgel, as the civil magistrate can, by right, procure that his commands be carried out by his subjects, whom he may punish with prison and exile, whose goods he may hand over to the treasury, and against whom he may even inflict the penalty of death. "The paternal relation does not have force in the same way as the necessary" [ἡ πατρικὴ σχέσις οὐκ ἔχει τὸ ἰσχυρὸν ὡς τὸ ἀναγκαῖον], says the same Aristotle in the passage cited just above. Therefore, for enacting laws any kind of superiority is not sufficient; but, besides that dominative power, there is required also coercive power (δύναμις ἀναγκαστική), or the power of jurisdiction mentioned earlier, so that laws cannot be enacted except by a person holding public coercive power. You understand, I think, so that I need not remind you, that what I have already said pertains absolutely to laws properly so called; and to the rest, only by analogy (κατ᾽ ἀναλογίαν), in a certain manner and proportion: each of them approaches nearer to the perfection of the former, or falls further from it, accordingly.

units.la: V. His duabus Hypothesibus, quae quorsum tendant, ex his quae statim dicturus sum facile intelligetis, addo jam tertio loco Conclusionem responsivam; hanc scilicet: Potestatem νομοθετικὴν esse potestatem αὐτοκρατορικὴν[?]. Hoc est, jus ferendi Leges quae obligent totam communitatem esse penes eum solum (sive sit is singularis persona, ut in statu regiminis Monarchici, sive plures ut in aliis) qui cum summa potestate toti communitati praeest. Hanc Conclusionem explico primum, deinde confirmo. Pro ejus explicatione sciendum primo, ad societatem humanarum civilem felicitatem, & commodiorem Rerump. administrationem, ordinis authorem Deum Opt. Max. non regimen modo politicum instituisse, ut essent qui populo praeessent Magistratus; sed & in ipso regimine etiam politicum instituisse, ut vel inter ipsos Magistratus essent διαιρέσεις διακονιῶν[?], varii quidam cum Dignitatis, tum Potestatis gradus. Fortassis illud τεταγμέναι ἐξουσίαι[?], quo militari verbo usus est Apostolus, Rom. 15. 1. eo respicit, ut Magistratum a Deo non Ordinationem solum, sed & subordinationem (qualis in militari acie cernitur) innuere voluerit.
units.tr: V. From these two hypotheses, and where they tend you will easily understand from what I am about to say, I now add, in the third place, the responsive conclusion; namely this: that the legislative power is sovereign power (αὐτοκρατορική). That is, the right of enacting laws which bind the whole community belongs to that one alone (whether he is a single person, as in a monarchical form of government, or several, as in others) who presides over the whole community with supreme power. I shall explain this conclusion first, and then confirm it. For its explanation, it should be known, first, that God, Best and Greatest, the author of order, instituted for the civil happiness of human society and for a more convenient administration of commonwealths not only a political government, so that there should be magistrates to rule the people, but also, within the government itself, a political arrangement, so that among the magistrates themselves there would be distributions of services (διαιρέσεις διακονιῶν), various grades both of dignity and of power. Perhaps the Apostle, in using the military term "ordained powers" [τεταγμέναι ἐξουσίαι] at Rom. 15. 1., meant to indicate that magistrates are from God not only in their ordination but also in their subordination (such as is seen in a military line).

units.la: VI. Sciendum secundo, in rebus omnibus, inter quas est aliquis ordo, ne fiat, (quod natura horret) infinitum processus, necessario tandem perveniri aliquod in suo ordine primum & summum, in suo stetur. Magistratus ergo ejusdem communitatis cum sint alii aliis dignitate & potestate superiores; oportet ut sit inter eos aliquis ita reliquis sublimior, ut ab illo reliqui pendeant, ipse utem[?] a nullo: ut Caput in corpore, Gubernator in nave, in exercitu Imperator: Supremus scilicet Magistratus; solo Deo minor; quique in gubernando commisso sibi populo, nec superiorem habet nec parem: Quem Apostoli, Petrus ὑπερέχοντα[?], Paulus ὑπερέχουσι[?], & τὸν ἐν ὑπεροχῇ ὄντα[?] ap-ellant; & Scholastici fere Caput communitatis: Cujus est αὐτοκεφαλεία[?], & Imperii Majestas; & inferiores omnes Magistratus universam illam quâ apud populum pollent potestatem suam acceptam ferunt, ὡς δι᾽ αὐτῆς πεμπόμενοι[?], 1 Pet. 2. 13.
units.tr: VI. Secondly, it must be noted that among all things where there is some order, an infinite progression (which nature abhors) must be avoided, and so we must necessarily arrive at some first and highest thing in its own order, where things stop. Therefore, since the magistrates of the same commonwealth are superior to one another in dignity and power, there must be among them one who is so much more exalted than the rest that they depend on him while he depends on no one: as the head in the body, the helmsman in the ship, the commander in the army. This is the supreme magistrate, less than God alone, who in governing the people committed to him has neither a superior nor an equal. The Apostles call him Peter's "one who overtops" [ὑπερέχοντα], Paul's "higher powers" [ὑπερέχουσι], and "the one who is in eminence" [τὸν ἐν ὑπεροχῇ ὄντα]; and the Scholastics commonly call him the head of the commonwealth. To him belong self-headship [αὐτοκεφαλεία] and the majesty of the empire; and all the inferior magistrates trace to him the whole power they hold among the people, as those sent through him [ὡς δι᾽ αὐτῆς πεμπόμενοι], 1 Pet. 2. 13.

units.la: VII. Sciendum Tertiò, pro diversa Rerump. forma supremam hanc potestatem, quam Majestatem vel αὐτοκεφαλείαν dicimus, vel in una aliqua persona, vel in pluribus positam esse. In statu populari, quam Democratiam vocant, summa Imperii est fere penes Magistratus plures popularibus suffragiis annuatim, aut per alia certa temporum intervalla delectos: qui fuit olim status populi Romani, cum a Consulibus, Praetoribus, Tribunis plebis, Aedilibus, aliisque annuis Magistratibus regerentur. Unde frequentes occurrunt apud Ciceronem alios istiusmodi locutiones; Populi Romani Majestas, Laesa populi Majestas, Visum est Senatui Populoque Romano, &c. In statu Aristocratico eadem Majestas est penes Optimates quosdam, quos alibi Illustrissimos vocant, alibi regni Proceres, alibi aliis titulis & appellationibus pro more gentis insigniunt. Quorum, etsi unus aliquis fortassis (ut in Rep. Veneta) vel etiam plures, possunt habere præ reliquis aliquam dignitatis & loci præeminentiam, veluti quendam ordinis primatum, (qui fuit olim Romani Episcopi, & reliquorum Patriarcharum in Conciliis honos :) nemo tamen est ita reliquis potestate Superior, ut aut possit de eis singulis authoritate sua judicium ferre, aut non possit ab eis universis ipse judicari. Cujus regiminis effigiem qualemcunque Majores & Aldermanni in villis nostris ; Collegiorum Præfecti & Socii in Academiis, etsi leviter admodum, aliqua tamen tenus repræsentatam nobis exhibent. At in statu Monarchicō (ut vel ipsum nomen indicio est) unius Regis personæ inhæret summa potestas. Unde Petrus, optimus Pauli interpres, monet populum Christianum, ut Regi pareant ὡς ὑποτασσόμενοι [?]. Nemo quis ultra dubitare possit, quid sibi velit illud Paulinum τῆς ὑπεροχῆς ἐξουσίας [?], Rom. 13. 1, Samuel etiam, ut propheta Dei, ita Regiæ Potestatis plenitudinem populo cogitandam proponit, 1 Sam. 8. Ut si quis Rex in suo Regno Supremus, singula quæ ex illo capite sibi licere constat, nulla subeunte justa causa, sed mera dominandi libidine faceret, & se pro Rege tyrannum offenderet; etsi non esset ἀναμάρτητος [?], nec peccato careret apud Deum : esset tamen αὐτοκράτωρ [?], nec deberet à populo coerceri ; dicique propterea meriretur, abusus quidem ille potestate sua, sed tamen sua. Apud nos Anglos saltem qui potest aut certius constare aut liquidius, (nisi si qui in sole meridiano cœcutire malint, quàm uti oculis,) quàm ad unam serenissimam Majestatem Regiam supremam trium istorum Regnorum potestatem pertinere ? Quem & Majestatis titulo, non modo ex usu loquendi communi, sed & in solennibus Legum Sanctionibus, & in omnibus juris formulis & actionibus, insignire solemus ; & omnium personarum causarumque in suis regnis supremum, imo & solum supremum. [?]premum Moderatorem, solenni præstito juramento (tactis sacrosanctis Dei Evangeliis) agnovi-mus.
units.tr: VII. Thirdly, it must be noted that, according to the different form of the commonwealth, this supreme power, which we call majesty or self-headship, is placed either in one person or in several. In a popular state, which they call democracy, the sum of empire lies for the most part with several magistrates chosen by popular vote each year, or at some other fixed intervals. This was once the condition of the Roman people, when they were governed by consuls, praetors, tribunes of the plebs, aediles, and other annual magistrates. Hence such phrases as "the majesty of the Roman people", "the injured majesty of the people", "it seemed good to the Senate and Roman People", etc., frequently occur in Cicero. In an aristocratic state the same majesty lies with certain optimates, whom elsewhere they call most illustrious, elsewhere the nobles of the realm, and elsewhere they mark with other titles and appellations according to the custom of the nation. Although one of these (as in the Venetian republic), or even several, may have some precedence of dignity and place over the rest, a certain primacy of order (which was once the honour of the Roman bishop and of the other patriarchs in councils), yet no one is so superior to the rest in power that he can either pass judgment on each of them by his own authority, or cannot himself be judged by all of them together. Some likeness of this kind of government, however faint, is shown to us by the mayors and aldermen in our towns, and by the heads and fellows of colleges in our universities. But in a monarchical state (as the very name indicates) the supreme power inheres in the person of one king. Hence Peter, the best interpreter of Paul, urges the Christian people to obey the king as those who are subject [ὡς ὑποτασσόμενοι]. No one can further doubt what Paul means by "the higher power" [τῆς ὑπεροχῆς ἐξουσίας], Rom. 13. 1. Samuel too, as a prophet of God, sets before the people the fullness of royal power to be considered, 1 Sam. 8. So if any king, supreme in his own realm, were to do each of the things which by that headship he is known to be allowed, without any just cause but from sheer lust for domination, and so showed himself a tyrant instead of a king; then even if he were not sinless [ἀναμάρτητος], and were not free from sin before God, he would nevertheless be sovereign [αὐτοκράτωρ], and should not be coerced by the people; and he would rightly be said to have abused his power, but it would still be his own. Among us English, at least, what could be more certainly or clearly established (unless some prefer to go blind in the noonday sun rather than use their eyes) than that the supreme power of these three kingdoms belongs to the one most serene Royal Majesty? We are accustomed to honour him with the title of Majesty, not only in common speech but also in solemn statutes and in all legal forms and proceedings; and we acknowledge him, with a solemn oath sworn on the holy Gospels of God, as the supreme, indeed the sole supreme, governor of all persons and causes in his realms.

units.la: VIII. Sciendum quartò, Cùm dicimus penes [?]num Regnum esse jus condendarum Legum, non id [?]ta intelligendum, quasi vellemus quicquid Regi [?]ibuerit jubere id continuò Legis vim obtinere: nam & populi consensum aliquem, aliàque nonnulla ad Legem constituendam requiri mox ostendam. Quin hoc est quod volumus, quòd scilicet Plebiscita, Senatus-consulta, caeteraeque Procerum, Plebis, aliorumque quorumcunque rogationes, nisi Regiâ in-super authoritate muniantur, non obligent subditos, nec habeant vim Legis: quibus tamen maturè & ritè praeparatis, simul ac Regis accesserit consensus, Legis nomen, formam & authoritatem protinus accipiunt, incipiúntque statim ac promulgari fuerint, subditos obligare. Cum igitur illa sola censenda sit cujusque rei causa Efficiens principalis & sufficiens, quae per se & immediate producit, & in materiam praeparatam introducit eam formam, quae illi rei dat nomen & esse; etsi ad productionem ipsius effectus alia etiam concurrere oporteat, vel antecedere potiùs, ut praevias dispositiones quo materia ad recipiendam formam ab agente intentam aptior reddatur: omninò constat, quocunque demum ea sint quae ad Legem rectè constituendam antecedenter requiruntur, voluntatem tamen Principis (ex cujus unius arbitratu & jussione omnes Legum rogationes aut ratae habentur aut irritae,) esse solam & adaequatam publicam Legum efficientem causam.
units.tr: VIII. Fourthly, when we say that the right of enacting laws lies with the king in his realm, this is not to be understood as if we wished that whatever the king has commanded at once has the force of law. For I will show presently that some consent of the people, and certain other things, are also required for making a law. What we mean is this: that plebiscites, decrees of the Senate, and the other proposals of the nobles, the commons, or of anyone else, unless they are confirmed by the king's authority over and above, do not bind subjects and do not have the force of law. Yet once they have been duly and properly prepared, as soon as the royal consent has been added, they immediately receive the name, form and authority of law, and begin to bind subjects as soon as they are promulgated. Since, then, that alone is to be regarded as the principal and sufficient efficient cause of anything which of itself and immediately produces that form which gives the thing its name and being, and introduces it into prepared matter, then even though other things must also concur in producing the effect, or rather precede it, such as previous dispositions by which the matter is made more apt to receive the form intended by the agent, it is wholly clear that, whatever those things are which are antecedently required for rightly constituting a law, the will of the prince (by whose sole decision and command all proposals of laws are held either valid or void) is the sole and adequate public efficient cause of laws.

units.la: IX. His praemissis, confirmatur Conclusio multiplici argumento. Imprimis testimonio Sacrae Scripturae, 1 Gen. 49. 10. in celebri illo Jacobi Patriarchae jam morituri testamento, Non auferetur Sceptrum de Juda, & Legislator de femore ejus, vaticinium est de futurâ in illa tribu Regia dignitatis quam ἀειφεγεσιτικῶς[?] describit pius senex, adhibitis in eam rem potestatis regiæ & notissimo infigni, Sceptro [Σκηπτροῦχοι βασιλῆες[?]] & potiffimâ prærogativâ, Jure Legislativo, 2 Deut. 33. 4. 5. Moses eo nomine fuisse dicitur quasi Rex in Ifraele, quòd congregatis principibus populi & tribubus Legem eis præceperit; 3. Pfal. 60. 7. Judah Legistator meus, id est, Rex: sicque ibi vertit vulgatus interpres, Judah Rex meus. 4. In Textu demum proposito, Prov. 8. 15. Per me Reges regnant, & Legum conditores justa decernunt. Ubi (quod folenne est Salomoni in toto hoc Proverbiorum volumine, ut versus pars posterior prioris, aut exegesin contineat, aut antithesin,) iidem ipsi, qui in priore compositis parte, Reges, in posteriore ἐξηγητικὸς Legum conditores dicuntur. 5. In novo etiam Teftamento νόμως βασιλικὰς meminit Jacobus Apostolus, Jac. 2. 8.
units.tr: IX. With these things premised, the conclusion is confirmed by many arguments. First, by the testimony of Holy Scripture, Gen. 49. 10, in that famous testament of the patriarch Jacob, now about to die: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor the lawgiver from between his feet." It is a prophecy of the royal dignity that would be in that tribe, which the pious old man describes by means of the power of kingship and its most familiar ensign, the sceptre [σκηπτροῦχοι βασιλεῖς], and its chief prerogative, the legislative right. Second, Deut. 33. 4, 5: Moses is said to have been king in Israel for this reason, that when the princes of the people and the tribes were gathered together, he gave them the law. Third, Ps. 60. 7: "Judah is my lawgiver", that is, king; so the Vulgate translator renders it, "Judah my king." Fourth, in the text proposed, Prov. 8. 15: "By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just." Here (as is characteristic of Solomon throughout this whole book of Proverbs, that the latter half of a verse either explains the former or sets it in contrast) the same persons who are called kings in the first half are called lawgivers, by way of explanation, in the second. Fifth, in the New Testament too the Apostle James mentions the "royal law" [νόμον βασιλικόν], Jas. 2. 8.

units.la: Confirmatur Secundò, Philosophorum, Historicorum, & Juris cùm Civilis, tum nostri Anglorum municipalis Confultorum, quæ passim occurrunt frequentibus testimoniis: Nos paucissimis, ut re manifestâ, contenti erimus. Legem Principis opus esse afferunt Aristoteles, Plutarchus, aliique innumeri optimæ notæ authores. Sed imprimis celebre est illud Ulpiani, quod in Jure Romano habetur, Quod Principi placuit Legis habet vigorem. Quod, ne ἀ[illegible, ~5 letters] & perperam intellectum tyrannicæ dominationi viam struere videatur, sic olim explicuit Bractonus nostras: Quod Principi placuit; id est, non quicquid est à Rege temerè & ex animi perturbati impetu quodam & æstu præsumptum, sed quicquid ex Magnatum suorum consilio (Regio assensu authoritatem præstante) & habita super hoc deliberatione & tractatu (sic enim ille loquitur) rectè fuerit definitum.
