Quin & in Jure nostro, & in quotidianis processibus juridicis in foro contentioso, ex solenni formulâ Regiæ Leges dici solent [The Kings Lawes :] non aliam ob causam, ut nos docuerunt Juris nostri periti, quàm quod Leges Angliæ sint Fons Justitiæ & Legum : & Legibus ipsis (ipsis legibus id ipsum αὐτολεξεὶ profitentibus) ut pro Legibus habeantur vim omnem imponendi habeant concessam sibi à Deo ' αὐτοἐξουσιαστικὴν [?] potestatem. Ut nihil sit opus, in pluribus congerendis testimoniis operam collocare non necessariam.
units.tr: It is confirmed, secondly, by the frequent testimonies of philosophers, historians, and of the jurists both of the civil law and of our English municipal law, which occur everywhere. We will be content with very few, since the matter is manifest. Aristotle, Plutarch, and countless other authors of the highest repute say that the law of the prince is necessary. But above all famous is that saying of Ulpian, found in Roman law: "What has pleased the prince has the force of law." Lest this be misunderstood and seem to pave the way for tyrannical domination, our Bracton long ago explained it thus: "What has pleased the prince"; that is, not whatever has been rashly presumed by the king from a disturbed mind, in some impulse and heat, but whatever has been rightly determined by the counsel of his magnates (the royal assent giving it authority), and by deliberation and discussion held upon the matter (for so he speaks). Indeed, both in our law and in the daily legal proceedings of the courts of contentious business, the royal laws are customarily named by a solemn formula [The Kings Lawes]. This is for no other reason, as our legal experts have taught us, than that the laws of England are the fount of justice and of laws; and that the laws themselves, professing this very thing in so many words, have been given by God the power of imposing obligation, a self-authorizing power [αὐτοεξουσιαστικὴν], so that they may be held as laws. So there is no need to spend effort in gathering many testimonies that are not necessary.

units.la: XI. Sed enim & istis supersederi potuisset, si non tam claræ luci nebulas offundere conatus esset, putidissimo suo & ante hæc infelicia tempora inaudito figmento, de coordinatâ nescio quâ potestate, ἀναρχυμος [?] nescio quis tenebrio. Qui ut ὑπερεχόντων [?] quorundam nefariis consiliis & conatibus supparasitaretur, (quæ cùm omni Juris præsidio destituerentur, specioso tamen aliquo tibicine quantumvis tenui & infirmo, fuerant pro tempore suffulcienda :) edito libello id agit sedulò, ut populum dedoceat inanem illam philosophiam, quâ hastenus ei impositum est ab iis qui negant contradictoria posse simul esse vera. Regem scilicet & supremum esse, id est, non habere parem ; & habere parem, id est, non esse supremum. Fuisse tamen, qui hoc tam ridiculum commentum, ut cœlitus delapsum σοφὸν φάρμακον, (nimirum quòd ipsorum interesset hæc vulgò credi) avidè arriperent, & ambabus ulnis amplexarentur, non tam mirandum est ; quàm dolendum reperiri potuisse, qui tam crasso sophismate sibi persuaderi paterentur, ut turpissimo se interim perjurio alligarent. Quid enim perjurium dici mereatur, si hoc non sit manifestum perjurium ; quem solum esse supremum in suo regno moderatorem conceptis verbis juraveris, ei parem aliam in suo regno potestatem constituere & agnoscere ? Apage ergo cum suis portentosis strophis Coordinatorum nostrum, qui nobis hanc remoram injecit: & pergamus.
units.tr: XI. But these matters might have been passed over, had he not tried to cast clouds over so clear a light, with that most foul fiction of his own, unheard of before these unhappy times, concerning some co-ordinate power, a certain nobody, a shadowy figure. In order to play the parasite to certain superiors in their wicked schemes and endeavours, (which, since they were destitute of every support of law, had nevertheless to be propped up for the time being by some specious prop, however slight and weak,) he has zealously set about, by publishing a pamphlet, to teach the people that empty philosophy by which they have hitherto been imposed upon by those who deny that contradictories can be true at the same time: namely, that the king is both supreme, that is, has no equal, and has an equal, that is, is not supreme. That there were some who eagerly snatched up this ridiculous invention, as a wise remedy come down from heaven (of course because it was in their interest that this be believed by the public), and embraced it with both arms, is less to be wondered at than to be lamented: that men could be found who allowed themselves to be persuaded by so gross a sophism, and so bound themselves in the meantime to the most shameful perjury. For what should deserve to be called perjury, if this is not manifest perjury: to have sworn in express words that the king is the sole supreme governor in his kingdom, and yet to appoint and acknowledge another power in his kingdom equal to him? Away then with the monstrous contortions of our Co-ordinator, who has thrown this obstacle in our way: and let us proceed.

units.la: XII. Confirmatur dicta Conclusio, tertio, Ratione. Præcipuus actus gubernationis præcipuam requirit potestatem: Actus enim omnis, cum sit exercitium alicujus potentiæ, supponit in agente potentiam sibi proportionatam. Est autem νομοθεσία [?], sive Legumlatio actus gubernationis supremus & præcipuus. Non ergo potest exerceri nisi à persona habente aut saltem in virtute & ex authoritate habentis supremam potestatem & jurisdictionem in communitatem sibi subjectam. Cùm enim Jurisdictionis sive Potestatis politicæ duæ sunt nobilissimæ & præ reliquis præcipuæ sive species sive partes, νομοθετικὴ [?] & κριτικὴ [?], Potestas scilicet Legumlativa, & Potestas Judiciaria, harum utraque in jure dicundo consistit: unde & Jurisdictionis nomen. Sed cum hoc discrimine, quod Jurisdictio Judicis sit Juris tantum dati dictio; Jurisdictio vero Legislatoris sit Juris etiam dandi dictio: Unde sequitur multo angustiorem esse illam Judicis potestatem, angustiorem hanc Legislatoris. Illius est Jus populo dicere, & ex Lege jam lata sententiam ferre: hujus vel ipsi Judici Jus dicere, & quæ sit ipsi judicandi norma Legem de novo condere. Ille ex præscripto Juris Constituti pronunciare tenetur: hic ex plenitudine potestatis præscribit & constituit Jus, quod non minùs Judex ipse inferior, quàm reliquus populus, tenetur in posterum observare. Non est igitur inconveniens, potestatem Judiciariam; cùm sit inferioris generis potestas, ab inferiore etiam persona ordinariè exerceri: at suprema illa & architectonica Legis ferendi Potestas omninò expedit, ut, non nisi à persona cujus sit Suprema Potestas exer-
units.tr: XII. The aforesaid conclusion is confirmed, thirdly, by reason. The chief act of government requires the chief power: for every act, since it is the exercise of some power, presupposes in the agent a power proportionate to it. Now lawgiving, or the making of laws, is the supreme and chief act of government. It therefore cannot be exercised except by a person who has supreme power and jurisdiction over the community subject to him, or at least by one acting in virtue and by the authority of the one who has it. For since there are two most noble and, above the rest, chief kinds or parts of jurisdiction or political power, the legislative and the judicial, namely the power to make laws and the power to judge, and both of these consist in declaring law: whence also the name jurisdiction. But with this difference, that the jurisdiction of a judge is only the declaring of law already given, whereas the jurisdiction of the lawgiver is the declaring of law that is also to be given. Hence it follows that the judge's power is much narrower than the lawgiver's. It belongs to the judge to declare the law to the people and to pronounce sentence according to a law already passed; it belongs to the lawgiver to declare the law to the judge himself, and to establish anew the law which is to be the norm of his judging. The judge is bound to pronounce according to the prescription of the established law; the lawgiver, from the fullness of power, prescribes and establishes the law, which the inferior judge himself no less than the rest of the people is bound to observe in future. It is therefore not inappropriate that the judicial power, since it is a power of the inferior kind, should ordinarily be exercised even by an inferior person; but that supreme and architectonic power of making law should by all means be exercised only by the person whose supreme power it is.

units.la: XIII. Dubium Secundum est, An ad Legis Obligationem requiratur populi consensus? Ex jam dictis enim possit fortassis aliquis existimare potestatem ferendi Leges ad Principem ita pleno jure pertinere, ut ex nostrå sententia subditorum nullæ essent omninò hac in re partes, nec, siquid ille statuerit, populo quicquam superesse, aliud quàm jussa capessere & colla jugo subdere. Et sanè videtur pro dominantium libidine, illud, Sic volo sic jubeo, apud prisci sæculi Reges ita obtinuisse, dum mera Principum arbitria pro Legibus erant: ut ipsum Tyranni nomen innocens initio honestum, ex tam salutaris potentiæ fœdo abusu, in contumeliam jamdiu abierit, & horrendum aliquid auribus nostris, quoties auditur, inferre putetur. Atqui populi saltem consensum aliquem requiri, & ante prænmonui; & ab omnibus, quos mihi videre contigit, probatissimis scriptoribus conceditur. Adeò ut ipsi Jesuitæ, qui sunt Oecumenicæ & nullis conclusæ finibus Pontificis sui Omnipotentiæ assertores acerrimi, excusandos tamen ob non servatas Concilii Tridentini & Bullæ Cœnæ Leges, eo solo nomine putent in Germaniâ & alibi multos, quòd in iis gentibus nunquam fuerint illæ Leges usu receptæ. Dico igitur, & est communis sententia, institutas & propositas à capite communitatis seu Principe Leges ; non obligare subditos, nec vim Legis habere, nisi ab ipsa communitate recipiantur, & utentium vel suffragiis vel moribus comprobentur. Demosthenis Lex est πόλεως ξυνθήκη κοινή, Communis sponsio civitatis : cujus siquem minùs moveat hac in causâ authoritas, quòd in Atheniensium Republ. populari versaretur ; accedat Juliani Jurisconsulti authoritas, qui sub Romanis Imperatoribus vixit pleno jure imperantibus ; cujus verba sunt, l. 32. ff. de Legibus, Ipsæ Leges nullâ aliâ ex causâ[?] nos tenent, quàm quòd judicio populi recepta sunt.
units.tr: XIII. The Second Question is: is the consent of the people required for the obligation of the law? From what has been said, someone might perhaps suppose that the power of making laws belongs so fully to the Prince that, on our view, subjects have no part at all in this matter, and that, whatever he has decreed, the people have nothing left to do but to receive his commands and bow their necks to the yoke. Indeed, it seems that the saying "Thus I will, thus I command" held sway among the kings of the early age, when the mere will of rulers stood for law. So too the name tyrant, innocent and honourable at first, has long since come to mean an insult, through the foul abuse of such a beneficial power, and whenever it is heard it is thought to bring something dreadful to our ears. Yet I have already said that some consent of the people is required, and this is granted by all the most approved writers I have happened to read. So much so that the Jesuits themselves, who are the most fervent champions of their universal Pontiff's unbounded power, nonetheless think that many in Germany and elsewhere deserve pardon for not observing the laws of the Council of Trent and the Bull In Cena Domini, on the sole ground that those laws were never received into use in those nations. I therefore say, and this is the common opinion, that laws instituted and proposed by the head of the community or by the Prince do not bind subjects, nor have the force of law, unless they are received by the community itself and approved by those who use them, either by their votes or by their customs. The law of Demosthenes is "a common agreement of the city" [πόλεως ξυνθήκη κοινή], a common covenant of the state. If anyone is less moved by this authority, because it belonged to the popular republic of the Athenians, let him add the authority of the jurist Julian, who lived under the Roman emperors who ruled with full power. His words are in law 32 of the Digest On Laws: "Laws themselves bind us for no other reason than that they have been received by the judgement of the people."

units.la: XIV. Sed enim istius receptionis sive consensus necessitatem, etsi omnes agnoscant, non tamen ex eodem fonte omnes accersunt. Sunt qui putent, populi consensum in condendis Legibus propterea requiri quod Principes potestatem suam omnem à populo effluxam habeant, quâ si abusi fuerint (abuti autem potestate sua censendi sunt, si eam longius latiusve proferre extendere velint, quàm populo visum fuerit,) poterit populus pro jure suo potestatem quam ipsis ante concesserat denuò resumere. Periculoso admodum errore, & quem merito abominari debeant, quotquot non sunt humani generis & publicæ tranquillitatis hostes. Nititur enim tota hæc ratio duplici fundamento; debili utroque & ab omni sanâ ratione alieno: altero, Principes totam potestatem suam populo acceptam ferre; altero, potestatem quisquis alteri concesserit, posse eam cum ipsi libuerit revocare. O egregium Sophistam, si hæc ita essent. Samuelem magis, qui ut populum Στοχαστὴν[?] jamdiu pertæsum à perverso rerum novandarum studio absterreret, Regiæ Potestatis amplitudinem eis ob oculos proposuisse satis habuit? an magis fatuum popellum Israeliticum qui sui juris ignarus pati se potuit tam futili sophismate sic πρὸς ἀγχοῦ[?] ut plane obtumesceret? Adeóne omnes bardos & stupidos, nulliusque aut mentis aut animi, ut nec unus aliquis in tam magna populi corona reperiri potuerit, cui tantum inesset acuminis audaciæ ut ad ista omnia prompte responderet? cùm tam facile fuerit Samueli sic peroranti statim regessisse, “Pueris hæc minare & qui nihil sapiunt: nos, si sic dominari cœperit: “Rex noster, jure nostro utemur; auferemus ei mox eam quam ante dedimus potestatem.” Quàm brevi responsio totum negotium confecissent & os prophetæ in æternum obturassent, si superioribus illis sæculis tam credita fuissent hæc novorum Magistrorum figmenta, quàm sunt ab illis fidenter discipulis suis obtrusa, & à temerariâ plebe lubenter excepta.
units.tr: XIV. But although all acknowledge the necessity of this reception or consent, not all derive it from the same source. Some think that the consent of the people is required in enacting laws because Princes hold all their power flowing from the people, and that if they have abused it (and they are held to abuse their power if they wish to extend it further or wider than the people have approved), the people may, in exercise of their right, take back the power they had previously granted them. This is a most dangerous error, and one which all who are not enemies of the human race and of public peace ought rightly to abhor. For this whole argument rests on a double foundation, both parts weak and alien to all sound reason: first, that Princes bear all their power received from the people; second, that whoever has granted power to another may revoke it whenever he pleases. O splendid sophist, if these things were so! Did Samuel, who, when the people had long been weary of kingship and had to be restrained from a perverse desire for revolution, think it enough to set before their eyes the greatness of royal power? Or was the foolish Israelite rabble, ignorant of its own rights, so able to endure such a flimsy sophism that it was plainly struck dumb? Were they all so dull and stupid, lacking both wit and spirit, that not one man could be found in so great a crowd of people with enough sharpness and boldness to answer all this promptly? Yet it would have been easy for them, when Samuel made this speech, to reply at once: "Threaten these things to children and to those who know nothing. If he begins to rule in this way, we shall use our right as a king: we shall soon take back the power we gave him." How quickly would they have finished the whole business and silenced the prophet's mouth for ever, if those earlier centuries had believed these inventions of the new teachers as readily as they are confidently pressed upon their disciples by those men and eagerly accepted by a rash common people.

units.la: XV. Sed ut serio agamus, & ad rem ipsam accedamus propius: Dico primò, Præsidendi in Republ. potestatem, quocunque tandem modo ad eam perveniatur, ab {1}ipso Deo esse, solo & immediatè, nullatenus autem à populo. Apertissima sunt in hanc rem Sacræ Scripturæ testimonia. Per me reges regnant, Prov. 8. id est, meâ unius, non humanâ aliquâ authoritate. Quæ sunt, à Deo sunt (non à populo,) constitutæ potestates, Rom. 13. 1. Ipsi Magistratus qui populo præsunt, Dei sunt administri, θεοῦ λειτουργοί, θεοῦ διάκονοι, Ibid. vers. 4. 6. Dii propterea dicti, Psal. 82. 6. quòd ipsius Dei in terris {2}vices gerant, idque Deo ipsis conserente hanc potestatem, non populi suffragiis, Ego dixi, Dii estis. Poteritne populus aliquis sine turpis idololatriæ crimine sibi Deos constituere, cum sit ufcujufque hominis, ei qui ipsius vices gerat, potestatem vicariam suâ authoritate demandare, non alieno arbitratu? Audebitne quisquam mortalium id juris sibi arrogare, ut qui Dei in terris Minister & vice-Deus futurus sit, omnem illam suam Authoritatem & Potestatem ab ipso sibi collatam agnoscat? Utut fortassis poterint esse populi circa personam ut potestatis subjectum partes aliquæ (ut mox videbimus;) quemadmodum in generatione rerum naturalium, sunt aliquæ prævia alterationes, quæ præparent & disponant materiam ad recipiendam formam introducendam: collatio tamen Potestatis Regitivæ, sive applicatio ejus ad personam non est, populi opus, sed Dei ipsius immediatè; sicut productio formæ in subjectam materiam est immediatum opus agentis sive generantis. Scitum est illud Irenæi, {1}Cujus jussu homines nascuntur, hujus jussu & Reges constituuntur.
units.tr: XV. But to deal seriously, and to come closer to the matter itself: I say first that the power of presiding in the commonwealth, by whatever means it is reached, is from God himself, alone and immediately, and by no means from the people. The testimonies of Holy Scripture on this point are most clear. "By me kings reign," Prov. 8, that is, by my authority alone, not by any human authority. "The powers that be are ordained of God" (not of the people), Rom. 13. 1. "The magistrates who are over the people are God's ministers" [θεοῦ λειτουργοί], "God's servants" [θεοῦ διάκονοι], ibid. verses 4 and 6. They are called gods, Ps. 82. 6, because they bear the place of God himself on earth, and this because God, and not the votes of the people, bestows this power on them: "I have said, You are gods." Can any people, without the crime of gross idolatry, make gods for themselves? Since it belongs to each man to commit to another who bears his place a delegated power by his own authority, and not at another's pleasure, will any mortal dare to claim this right for himself, that one who is to be God's minister and vice-God on earth should acknowledge all that authority and power to have been conferred on him by the people? Although the people may perhaps have some part in the person as the subject of power (as we shall presently see), just as in the generation of natural things there are some preliminary alterations which prepare and dispose the matter to receive the form to be introduced, nevertheless the conferral of ruling power, or its application to the person, is not the work of the people but of God himself, immediately; just as the production of a form in the underlying matter is the immediate work of the agent or generator. That saying of Irenaeus is well put: "By whose command men are born, by his command also kings are appointed."

units.la: XVI. Dico Secundò, (ut digitum ad fontes intendam) dominationem politicam ab initio non nisi patriæ potestatis propaginem fuisse. Ipsa rerum primordia quibus otium est paulò diligentius rimari, gentes deprehendunt olim non ex mutua populorum consensione in Regna & Respub. coaluisse; sed inter Noachi posteros aliquandiu omne imperium intra paternæ authoritatis metas constitisse. Nondum Reges erant; sed nec Reguli quidem; nedum amplissimarum ditionum Monarchæ: multò autem minimè Aristocratici vel popularis status regimina; inaudita priscis sæculis toto orbe nomina, & in Græcia primùm, gente levi & cupidâ novitatis, [illegible, ~10 letters] quorundam libidine vel furore, introducta. Penes adhuc omnis dominatio, in quibus qui aut electione aliquâ, quodam quasi naturæ jure, & sacrorum & civilis administrationis antistes, & totius cognationis princeps habebatur. Qui pro suo arbitratu delinquentes moderatis primò poenis castigabat; mox excrescentibus in magnam multitudinem familiis, gravioribus supplicis nocentes coercuit: donec tandem, auctâ indies hominum multitudine, & succrescentibus unâ vitiis, irrogandi sceleribus capitalia supplicia accessit necessitas. Inde factum ut pater in liberos totámque familiam jus olim haberet vitæ & necis: cujus juris, etiam postea constitutos plerisque in gentibus Reges, manserunt tamen diu vestigia quædam. Hinc illa notata Aristoteli, (sed improbata) patriæ potestatis apud Persas nimia severitas: & vetus illa quæ apud A. Gellium Noct. Attic. l. 5. c. 19. extat arrogandi liberos solennis Romanorum formula, [UTI EI VITÆ. NECIS. QUE. IN. EO. POTESTAS. SIET.
units.tr: XVI. I say secondly (to point the finger at the sources): political dominion was at the beginning nothing but an offshoot of paternal power. The very beginnings of things, if one has leisure to examine them a little more carefully, show that nations did not in earlier times coalesce into kingdoms and commonwealths by the mutual consent of peoples; rather, among the descendants of Noah, all government for some time remained within the bounds of paternal authority. There were as yet no kings, not even petty kings, much less monarchs of vast dominions; and still less were there aristocratic or popular forms of government, names unheard of in the early centuries throughout the whole world, and first introduced in Greece, a light race eager for novelty, [illegible, about ten letters] by the whim or frenzy of certain men. All dominion was still in the hands of those who, by some election or by a kind of natural right, were regarded as both priest of the rites and civil administrator and chief of the whole kindred. Such a man, at his own discretion, first punished offenders with moderate penalties; then, as the families grew into a great multitude, he restrained the guilty with heavier punishments; until at last, as the number of men increased day by day and vices grew along with them, the necessity arose of capital punishments for the punishment of crimes. Hence it came about that the father once held the right of life and death over his children and his whole household; and although kings were later established among most nations, certain traces of this right long remained. Hence Aristotle's remark (though he disapproved of it) on the excessive severity of paternal power among the Persians, and that ancient solemn Roman formula, recorded by Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae 5.19, for adopting children: [THAT HE SHALL HAVE OVER HIM THE POWER OF LIFE AND DEATH, AS A FATHER HAS OVER A SON], [THAT HE SHALL HAVE OVER HIM THE POWER OF LIFE AND DEATH, AS A FATHER HAS OVER A SON]. From these beginnings, through the growth of families, kingdoms sprang up here and there across the lands, and those who ruled them were called kings, and within their dominions, which in those times were sometimes a single small town with a few neighbouring villages and hamlets, mere…

units.la: [UTI.[?] PATRI. ENDO. FILIO. EST.] Ab his ini-iis[?], per incrementa familiarum, pullularunt pau[?]im ubique terrarum Regna quibus qui prærant, & Reges dicti sunt, & in suis ditionibus, iguis illis quidem (unicà fortassis urbecula cum paucis adjacentibus pagis & vinculis) merum tamen imperium exercuerunt. {1}Principio rerum , genum nationumque imperia penes Reges erant: sic historiam suam orditur Justinus. Et ante eum Cicero, {2}Omnes, inquit, antiquae gentes regibus quondam fuerunt. Et utroque antiquior {3}Aristoteles eas civitates testatur quae suo tempore liberae habebantur (Graecas nimirum & earum exempla secuintelligit,) sub regio primitus imperio fuisse. Huus quam dixi Originis, inter alia plurima, hoc uoque argumentum est non leve, quòd tam artis finibus claudebantur olim Regum ditiones, ut in unâ Canaanitide, regione non magnâ, triginta & unum Reges ab Israelitarum Duce Josue debellatos habeamus, Jos. cap. 12. quibus tamen superstìtem reliquisse eum istiusmodi Regulorum numerum duplo ferè majorem, non improbabili conjecturâ vel ex eo mihi colligi posse videtur, quòd non multò post ipsius Josue excessum Adoni-bezekum in septuaginta Reges à se deviætos barbaro more sævise legimus, Jud. .. 7. Quid multa! Magnæ similiæ principem inter, & angusti territorii Regem, am exile discrimen est, ut nomine & {4}mole majis quàm re & potestate, distare inter se videantur: ut nemini posset esse dubium, siquidem rationes ritè subducere velit, patriam dominationem progredente tempore, paulatim & imperceptibili actu, regium nomen & imperium adolevisse ; necaliunde quàm ex hoc capite petendam esse summi imperii originem. Et hactenus sanè in conferendâ Regiâ potestate, nullas fuisse, nec quidem esse potuisse, populi partes, certo certius est.
units.tr: [As the father has power over the son.] From these beginnings, through the growth of families, kingdoms sprang up here and there throughout the world, and those who presided over them were called kings. In their domains, which were small (perhaps a single little town with a few neighbouring villages and hamlets), they nonetheless exercised full imperium. {1}In the beginning of things, the power of peoples and nations lay in the hands of kings: so Justinus begins his history. And before him Cicero says: {2}All ancient nations, he says, were once under kings. And Aristotle, older than both, {3}testifies that the cities which in his own time were considered free (he means the Greeks and those who followed their example) were at first under regal rule. Among many other proofs of this origin I have described, this is no slight argument: the dominions of kings were once so narrowly bounded that in the single region of Canaan, which was not large, Joshua, the leader of the Israelites, defeated thirty-one kings (Josh. 12). From this it seems to me we may reasonably conjecture, though not improbably, that the number of such petty rulers left alive was nearly double. For not long after Joshua's death we read that Adoni-bezek, in barbarous fashion, treated seventy kings whom he had subdued (Judg. 1.7). In short, between the prince of a great realm and the king of a narrow territory there is only a slight difference, so that they seem to differ more in name and {4}bulk than in power and authority. No one could doubt, if he were to reckon the matter properly, that as time went on paternal lordship grew by slow and imperceptible steps into the royal title and rule, and that the origin of supreme power is to be sought from no other source than this. And so, most certainly, in the establishment of royal power the people had no part, nor could they have had any.

units.la: XVII. Ex his, ut opinor, satis conficitur (ut illud obiter adnotem, quod dignum est obserua[?]tu,) illam regiminis formam, in quâ totius familiæ primogenitus in jura paterna succedit ut propinquior[?] hæres, merito cæteris præferendam esse; cùm ob alias plurimas nec contemnendas rationes, tùm vel hac unâ de causâ maximè, quòd originis suæ[?], ad quam homines natura ipsa quodammodo instituisse videtur, optimè respondeat. A quâ æquissimâ & naturæ congruentissimâ formâ firmul[?] abicessum est, (impotenti scilicet & effræni dominandi libidine alias sibi vias quibus ad imperii culmen ascenderetur moliente,) tyrannidi pariter & popularibus studiis opportuniora exinde facta sunt omnia. Qui enim aliâ quàm Legitimâ successione imperium obtinent, uno è tribus modis ad regna promoveri necesse est: aut apertâ vi, & militaribus armis; aut fraudibus & astu; aut liberâ demum electione. Qui vi & armis sibi quæsiverunt imperium, sive meræ usurpatione sine aliquo juris prætextu id factum fuerit, sive Bello justo hostibus à quibus injustè lacessiti sunt illato, (utrovis modo enim fieri contingit:) hos etiam certum est, authoritatem suam nihilo magis subditis suis debere, quàm qui Jure Hæreditario in regna avita succedunt. Quin multò etiam minùs: in quantum isti volentibus civibus & jugo assuetis, illi invitis & (si resistendo[?] pares essent) repugnare paratis dominantur. Ergo nec hactenus apparent in conferendâ summâ potestate, populi ullæ partes.
units.tr: XVII. From these things, I think, it is sufficiently established (I note this in passing, as it deserves attention) that that form of government in which the firstborn of the whole family succeeds to the paternal rights as the nearer heir is rightly to be preferred to the others. This is so for many other reasons that are not to be despised, but above all for this one: it best corresponds to its origin, to which nature herself seems in some way to have directed mankind. From this most equitable and most natural form men have departed, since they were devising other ways by which to climb to the summit of power, driven by an unbridled and headstrong lust to rule. Thus everything became equally favourable to tyranny and to popular arts. For those who obtain power by any means other than lawful succession must needs rise to kingship in one of three ways: by open force and military arms; by fraud and cunning; or finally by free election. Those who have sought power for themselves by violence and arms, whether this was done by mere usurpation without any pretext of right, or by a just war waged against enemies by whom they had been unjustly provoked (for it happens in either way), are certainly no more indebted to their subjects for their authority than those who succeed to ancestral kingdoms by hereditary right. Indeed much less so: for these rule over citizens who are willing and accustomed to the yoke, whereas those rule over the unwilling, who are ready to resist if they were a match for them. Thus, here too, no part of the people appears in the conferring of supreme power.

units.la: XVIII. At in stabiliendâ eorum potestate, qui tyrannidem per dolum occupant, negari non potest, populum suas habere partes, eâsque præcipuas. Solent enim qui tyrannidem affectant, animum imprimis ad favorem popularium conciliandum inten-dere; ciente. citur (u observas familia ropinquiu ; cùm rationes d origin ummodo quâ an à simul æni de imperii pariter fa&a fuccef odis ad vi, & ut lice æsive aliquo o Justo (utro m cer ubditii regnas : in suetis, epug us ap i ulla , qui otest, So im nten lere; dere ; potentiam ex vulgi adulatione quærentes, Affatim hujus rei exemplorum suppeditarunt [?]plurimarum gentium historiæ. Apud unum Trogi abbreviatorem, quibus artibus Pisistratus Atheniensium, Heracliensium Clearchus, Dionysius junior Siculorum, alii aliorum populorum turbam in suas partes pellexerint, reperire est. Invidiosis orationibus credulæ multitudinis animos adversus optimos quosque cives concitare: nonnulla publicè laudanda & quæ speciem habérent Clementiæ, Justitiæ, & in plebem benignitatis, facere; omne genus blanditiis ac delinimentis, quibus decipi amat & solet vulgus, in civium affectus se insinuare, velut publicæ libertatis unicos futuros assertores, vindices & patronos; simulatio officii, crebræ pollicitationes, injecta spes feliciorum temporum & mutandæ in melius publicarum rerum administrationis: hæ nimirum sunt egregiæ illæ artes, quibus qui ad imperium per fraudes assectant viam, incautum & leve vulgus solicitant, inflectunt, quà libet impellunt, [illegible, ~18 letters] Et quidem perraro hac alea fallit. Fit enim plerunque ut populi favore suffulti, ipsorumque ope & operâ adjuti, ad summum illud honoris & imperii culmen, quò jamdiu anhelabat eorum ambitio, tandem conscendant.
units.tr: XVIII. But in establishing the power of those who seize tyranny by deceit, it cannot be denied that the people have their parts to play, and those the chief ones. For those who aspire to tyranny usually bend their minds above all to winning the favour of the populace, seeking power from the flattery of the crowd. The histories of very many nations supply plenty of examples of this. In the abridgement of Trogus one may find by what arts Pisistratus among the Athenians, Clearchus among the Heracleots, and the younger Dionysius among the Sicilians, and others among other peoples, drew the crowd to their side: by inflammatory speeches to stir the minds of the credulous multitude against all the best citizens; by making public praises and acts that had the appearance of clemency, justice, and kindness towards the common people; by every kind of flattery and soothing by which the crowd loves and is wont to be deceived, insinuating themselves into the feelings of the citizens as the sole future champions, avengers and patrons of public liberty; by a pretence of dutifulness, frequent promises, and the hope of happier times and of a change for the better in the administration of public affairs. These, surely, are the excellent arts by which those who aim at power through deceit court and bend the incautious and fickle crowd, and drive it whichever way they please. And indeed such a gamble seldom fails. For it generally happens that, supported by the people's favour and aided by their help and labour, they at last climb to that highest summit of honour and power towards which their ambition had long been straining.

units.la: XIX. Verùm enimvero ista omnia quàm parum habeant momenti ad probandam legitimam populi in conferendo summo imperio potestatem, facilè providebit, quisquis cogitaverit; Imprimis à facto ad jus debile semper habitum esse argumenti genus. Deinde, quæ à populo hunc in monum facta legimus, non fuisse judicio facta sedatoque & sereno, sed concitato & perturbato assectibus animo. Quinetiam, ubi resederit paulum illa animorum tempestas, & astu deceptum se ac ludificatum populus tandem, sed foro nimis deprehenderit ; facti sui semet poenitere, pudere nimiae credulitatis ; temeritatem suam & imprudentiam damnare, qui avida amplificandae libertatis spe inducti, sua se opera in servitutem tyrannicae dominationis ultro tradiderint. Spirant haec omnia menam[?] impotentiam, & animorum infirmitatem : ita ut mirus artifex sit oporteat, qui se hinc aliquod sobrii juris aut legitimae potestatis argumentum elicere posse confidat.
units.tr: XIX. But how little all these things weigh in proving the people's lawful power in conferring supreme rule, anyone who reflects will readily see. First of all, an argument from fact to right has always been regarded as a weak kind. Next, what we read was done by the people in such a mutiny was not done with judgment, with a calm and serene mind, but with a mind stirred and disturbed by passions. Moreover, when that storm of minds has subsided a little, and the people, deceived and mocked by cunning, at last recognise it too plainly, they repent of what they have done and are ashamed of their excessive credulity, condemning their own rashness and imprudence, for they had been led on by the eager hope of enlarging their liberty and had of their own accord handed themselves over into the slavery of tyrannical domination. All of this breathes unruly weakness and the frailty of minds. So a remarkable craftsman must be the one who trusts that he can draw from these things any proof of sound right or of lawful power.

units.la: XX. Reliqua est igitur unica duntaxat Reipubl. species, in qua popularis in constituendo principe Juris aliqua saltem apparet imago : Regnum scil. Electivum, ubi in demortui Regis locum novus succedit Rex liberis populi suffragiis eligendus. Esse hic populo suas partes, easque legitimas & jure bono sibi competentes, prolixè fatemur : non tamen & illud ullatenus largiendum censemus, totam propterea sic electi Regis potestatem a populo pendere, aut populo acceptam ferri debere. Aliud enim est potestatem aliquam instituere ; aliud personam qui eam potestatem exerceat eligere : nec aliud solum, sed & (plerumque) alterius. Praetor urbanus istius villae ab oppidanis & comburgen-sibus suis quotannis eligitur : electus, Jurisdictionem quandam exercet, quam nisi sic electus fuisset non licuisset ei exercere, infra pomoeria istius urbis.
units.tr: XX. There remains, therefore, only one kind of commonwealth in which some image of popular right, in the constitution of a prince, at least appears: namely an elective kingdom, where a new king, to be chosen by the free votes of the people, succeeds in place of the dead king. We freely admit that here the people have their parts, and that these are lawful and rightly theirs. Yet we do not think it should in any way be conceded that the whole power of the king so chosen therefore depends on the people, or ought to be said to be received from the people. For it is one thing to institute some power, and another to choose the person who is to exercise that power; and not only a different thing, but (usually) that of another. The praetor of an urban town is chosen each year by his townsmen and fellow burgesses. Once chosen, he exercises a certain jurisdiction which, had he not been so chosen, he would not be permitted to exercise within the bounds of that town.

units.la: Penes Collegiorum etiam Socios, quoties praesecturam vacare contigerit, jus est eligendi Praefectum ; ad quem sic electum & virtute dictae electionis, spectat totius Collegii regimen. Eligentium utrobique jus universum in sola personae designatione versatur, quae potestatem muneri suo competentem non ab eligentibus derivatam, sed aliunde sibi concessam, exerceat. Neque enim Praetor, Jurisdictionem in urbe exercet, concivibus suis qui ipsum ad gerendum magistratum elegerunt, acceptam fert; sed Chartæ Regiæ, qui pro suo beneplacito indulsit urbi tale privilegium: nec Collegii præfectus quam obtinet in Collegio authoritatem accepit à sociis quorum suffragiis electus est, sed à fundatore ejusque statutis, qui istam ei authoritatem conceffit. In summâ, ubi Principis electio à populo aut legibus aut moribus recepta est, ibi populus personam regentis designat quidem, ast Deus unus confert regendi authoritatem.
units.tr: The fellows of colleges too, whenever the headship happens to fall vacant, have the right of electing the head, to whom, so elected and by virtue of that election, the government of the whole college belongs. The whole right of the electors lies solely in the designation of the person, who exercises a power suited to his office, not derived from the electors but granted to him from elsewhere. For the praetor does not exercise jurisdiction in the city as received from his fellow citizens who elected him to the magistracy, but from the royal charter, which at its pleasure granted the town such a privilege. Nor does the head of the college receive the authority he holds in the college from the fellows by whose votes he was elected, but from the founder and his statutes, who conferred that authority on him. In sum, where the election of a prince by the people is received by laws or customs, there the people indeed designate the person who rules, but God alone confers the authority to rule.

units.la: XXI. Sed donemus istis vulgi palponibus (ut eorum importunitati tantisper gratificemur) suam hanc hypothesin: nec hilum promoverit tamen, nisi & illud insuper largiamur, quod cùm solidè probare debuissent, sumere maluerunt; quisquis alteri contulerit potestatem, ei jus esse collatam potestatem, ubi ipsi visum fuerit opportunum, eidem adimere, & in manum suam resumere. Contra stat ratio, & omnia jura, omnia fora reclamant. Scilicet, Legitima pacta non esse rescindenda; Donationem absolutè nec interpositâ conditione factam non posse revocari, vel in totum vel ex parte; jus quod ante electionem plenum fuit in eligentibus, electione jam peractâ ipso facto transfire in personam electam: aliáque in eandem rem plurima naturæ sunt & rationis toto orbe receptissima [?]constata, & omnium gentium consensu, ut ex usu quotidiano satis constat, firmata & comprobata. [?]eptem Germaniae Principes eligendi Imperatorem [?]lenam habent potestatem ; electum autem impe- [?]io submovendi nullam. Singulorum Anglia Comitatuum & Burgorum communitas plebis, hoc est, [?]ncolæ & liberi homines (ut nostrates loquuntur) Quotquot sunt infra majoris nobilitatis gradum, [?]quites & Burgenses, communibus suffragiis eligen[?]jus habent, quos ad Comitia Parliamentaria velut [?]gatos suo nomine mittant cum fiduciariâ potestate publicis regni negotiis ipsorum vice tractandi : ast abrogandi impofterum jam electis demandata semel potestatem, etiamsi forte votis eligentium parûm responderint, nullum jus habent. Eadem ratio est eorum, penes quos Praetorem urbanum Collegii praefectum, aut alterius ejusmodi communitatis aut corporis civilis caput eligendi jus est: quae peracta electione, non habent ultra quod agant, jure[?] nimirum & authoritate praesidendi in personam electam translatis, cujus potestati deinceps subesse tenentur, & in electione quam ipsi fecerunt acquiefcere ; nec, fi electus indignum fe Magistratu praebuerit, aliis id quàm fibimetipfis imputare.
units.tr: XXI. But let us grant these pats on the back of the common people (to humour their importunity for a while) their hypothesis. It will still advance them nothing unless we also concede what they ought to have proved solidly but preferred to assume: whoever has conferred a power on another may take that power back again whenever it seems fitting to him, and resume it into his own hand. Reason stands against this, and all laws and all courts cry out against it. Namely: lawful pacts are not to be rescinded; a gift made absolutely, without any attached condition, cannot be revoked, either wholly or in part; a right which before the election was full in the electors, once the election is completed, passes by the very fact into the person elected. Many other points on this matter are most widely received by nature and reason throughout the world, and are confirmed and approved by the consent of all nations, as is sufficiently clear from daily practice. The seven Electors of Germany have the full power of electing an Emperor, but none of removing the one elected. The commonalty of the Counties and Boroughs of England, that is, the inhabitants and freemen (as our countrymen say), all who are below the rank of the greater nobility, knights and burgesses, have the right of choosing by common vote, and send them to the Parliament as their deputies on their behalf, with a trust-power to deal with the public affairs of the kingdom in their stead. But they have no right to revoke for the future the power once committed to those elected, even if perhaps they have answered little to the wishes of the electors. The same reasoning applies to those in whom lies the right of choosing the city Praetor, the head of a college, or the head of some other such community or civil body. Once the election is made, they have nothing further to do: the right and authority of presiding have been transferred to the person elected, whose power they are thenceforth bound to submit to, and to acquiesce in the election they themselves made. Nor, if the one elected shows himself unworthy of the magistracy, should they impute this to anyone but themselves.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: XXII. Potuerunt ista, fateor, longius porrigi & quidem dignum effet opera pretium, liberum excurrere in istam probationem, & tam noxiae in seditionem pullulantis radicis fibras omnes e animis hominum penitus evellere, nisi me temporis & instituti mei ratio, eò unde egressus sum revocaret. Nec fortassis multum opus est hac in re longiori excursu ; cum & ex his quae jam dicta sunt satis constare posse arbitror, quàm temere simul & periculosè haec tam vasta populo potius attribuatur ; & alii suppetant idoneae rationes, quae ut in ferendis legibus-populi etiam consensus accedat & approbatio, vehementer persuadeant. Primo, quia Lex debet esse{1} νοῦς ἄνευ ὀρέξεως, Mens cupiditatis expers: jussa autem Principum, in aulicorum & adulatorum gratiam temere & inconsultis subditis emissa, sunt fere νοῦ ἄνευ ὀρέξεως, pravis nempe impotentium affectuum cupiditatibus vitiata. Secundo, quia Leges illae, quae cum proponuntur subditis non probantur, moraliter loquendo praesumuntur esse aut injustae in se, aut subditis onerosae nimis aut saltem inutiles bono publico ; & proinde ejusmodi, ut expedit eas non sanciri, quum sit Reipublicae valdè incommodum, multiplicari Leges sine necessitate. Tertio, quia Leges jam legitimè constitutae
units.tr: XXII. I admit these points could have been pursued further, and indeed it would be worth the effort to range freely into this proof and tear out from men's minds all the fibres of this harmful root of sedition that is sprouting up. But the nature of my time and of my subject calls me back to where I had departed from. Nor, perhaps, is there much need for a longer digression on this matter, since I think it can already be sufficiently clear from what has been said how rashly and at the same time dangerously such a vast power is attributed to the people rather than to the prince. And other suitable reasons are at hand which strongly persuade that the consent and approval of the people should also join in the enacting of laws. First, because a Law ought to be mind without desire [νοῦς ἄνευ ὀρέξεως], a mind free of passion; but the commands of princes, issued rashly and without consultation of the subjects for the favour of courtiers and flatterers, are almost mind without desire [νοῦ ἄνευ ὀρέξεως], namely tainted by the depraved appetites of unrestrained passions. Second, because those Laws which are not approved when they are proposed to the subjects are, speaking morally, presumed either to be unjust in themselves, or too burdensome to the subjects, or at least useless to the public good; and therefore such laws ought not to be enacted, since it is very inconvenient for the commonwealth that laws be multiplied without necessity. Third, because it is established that laws already lawfully enacted

units.la: {1} Aristot. 3. Pol. 16. onstitutas ita abrogari posse constat per contrariam consuetudinem, ut ultrà obligare desinant: quæ consuetudo nihil aliud est quàm conjuncta populi sensio eam legem ut inutilem observare negligentis[?], & consensio principis observationem ejus non exigentis. Ergo quum sit ejusdem potestatis struere & destruere, videtur Legum vis ex approbatione & consensu populi non minimùm pendere. Quarto & præcipuè, quia hoc ipsum (scilicet ut ad Leges condendas concurrat unà cum Principis potestate[?] consensus etiam populi) & ad publicam totius orius Regni pacem, & ad salutem securitatémque rincipis in tantum conducit, ut nihil magis. Omnino enim verisimile est subditos universos, egibus qui ipsorum consensum expectaverint, & Legibus in quas ipsi consenserint, promptè & alacriter, nec gravatè parituros. Neque verò imminutum iri isthoc pacto supremam Principis νομοθε-[?] [?]ulu potestatem (quod unum objici ex adversâ parte solet) verendum est. Posse enim duo hæc, (populi nquam consensum, & supremam Principis in ferendis Legibus potestatem) simul & amicè satis consistere, præterea quod in rebus ipsis nulla videtur esse repugnantia,) vel inde constare potest quod Anglię nostræ Reges, quorum supremam potestatem, ante infelicissima hæc tempora omnes hujus Regni incolæ prolixissimè semper agnoverunt, nunquam tamen Legislativam suam Potestatem ita exercuerint, ut sine subditorum suorum consensu leges aliquas ipsis imposuerint.
units.tr: {1} Aristot. 3. Pol. 16. can be abrogated by contrary custom in such a way that they cease to bind any further. This custom is nothing other than the joined feeling of the people in negligently observing that law as useless, together with the consent of the prince in not exacting its observance. Therefore, since the power to build up and to tear down belongs to the same authority, it seems that the force of laws depends not a little on the approval and consent of the people. Fourth and chiefly, because this very thing (namely, that the consent of the people also concur together with the power of the prince in making laws) conduces so much to the public peace of the whole kingdom, and to the safety and security of the prince, that nothing could do more. For it is entirely likely that all the subjects will obey promptly and willingly, and not reluctantly, laws whose consent they have awaited, and laws to which they themselves have consented. Nor is it to be feared that by this arrangement the supreme lawgiving power of the prince would be diminished (which is the one objection usually raised from the other side). That these two things, namely the consent of the people and the supreme power of the prince in enacting laws, can consist together both amicably and sufficiently, and that there seems to be no contradiction in the things themselves, can be shown from this very fact: our Kings of England, whose supreme power all the inhabitants of this kingdom have always most fully acknowledged before these most unhappy times, have never yet so exercised their legislative power as to impose any laws upon them without the consent of their subjects.

units.la: XXIII. Concedendum ergo putamus, ad confirmandas Leges quæ subditos obligent in conscientià, requiri aliquem saltem populi consensum.{1}
units.tr: XXIII. We think it must therefore be conceded that, to confirm laws which bind subjects in conscience, at least some consent of the people is required.

units.la: sed[?] porrò dubitari potest non immeritò, estóque igitur hoc Dubium Tertium, qualis quantusque populi consensus requiratur ad hoc, ut Principis placitum habeat vigorem Legis. Respondeo considerari posse in isto de quo nunc agimus populi consensu duo hæc; Consentiendi scil. & Tempus, & Modum: & horum rursus utrumque bifariam. Vel enim consentitur in Legem, quoad Tempus; ante ejus promulgationem rogationemque, vel post: quoad Modum: consensu expresso, sive suffragiis; vel consensu tacito, sive moribus. Ex horum complexione, quatuor oriuntur populares consensus modi sive gradus.
units.tr: But it may still be doubted, and not without reason. Let this therefore be the Third Doubt: what kind and what amount of consent of the people is required so that the prince's decree may have the force of law? I answer that in the consent of the people with which we are now dealing, two things may be considered: the Time of consenting and the Mode; and each of these again in two ways. For the consent to a law is given either as to time, before its promulgation and proposal, or after it; and as to mode, either by express consent, that is by votes, or by tacit consent, that is by customs. From the combination of these, four kinds or degrees of popular consent arise.

units.la: XXIV. Primus, isque omnium minimus & infimus, gradus est, consensus tacitus ante rogationem Legis; cum scilicet populus aliquis se suaque omnia sic in victoris potestate posuit, aut longi parendi consuetudine ita in integrum permisit Principis arbitrio, ut quicquid is statuerit, id ipsis ratum esse debeat. Utrovis enim modo id contingat, tantundem est: siquidem ex Jure Gentium, justa est illa Principis potestas, quæ aut Justi Bello parta est, aut diuturnâ possessione, quasi quodam præscriptionis jure, confirmata. Et iste quidem gradus, etsi populo non multum sit profuturus, si Principi libuerit potestate sua in tyrannidem abuti: sufficit tamen ad hoc, ne quæri possit populus sibi factam injuriam, si Principem gravius aliquid in ipsos, (quod forte non sit injustum, sed quod ipsi tamen nollent,) statuere contigerit. Quemadmodum apud nos, importune (ut solent) & iniquè è Presbyterianorum grege nonnulli conqueruntur, pastorum parochialium electionem populo injustè ereptam; cum quos oporteret à parochianis ad id munus vocari, à privatâ aliquâ singulari persona, aut Collegio, sub patroni nomine fine ipsorum consensu præsententur. Illud interim parùm cogitantes, eligendi jus si quod populus olim habuerit, (quæ tamen incerta [?] res est, & quam si negetur nunquam probare po-terunt) ex justà certè aliquâ causâ ab initio, sed longi- temporis præscriptione jam ignoratâ, ad beneficiorum patronos quos vocant jamdudum transiisse, adeóque in factâ à Patronis electione involvi virtualiter & contineri Populi Consensum. Quod si homines dogmatum suorum nimiùm pertinaces non permoveat ; ast illud saltem submonendi sunt, quod vel importunissimo adversario faciat satis, Juris Patronatus & Ecclesiarum Advocationes Authoritate Parliamentariâ, hoc est, communi & pleno cotius populi consensu, dudum sancita esse ; & proinde quod à legitimo Patrono hoc in casu fit, populum ut id ei facere liceret con-sen[?]se.
units.tr: XXIV. The first degree, and the least and lowest of all, is tacit consent before the proposal of the law: when some people have so placed themselves and all their affairs in the power of a conqueror, or by long habit of obedience have so surrendered themselves entirely to the will of the prince, that whatever he decrees must be ratified by them. For it makes no difference which of these ways this happens; for by the Law of Nations that power of the prince is just which has been gained by a just war, or confirmed by long possession as by a kind of right of prescription. And this degree, although it will not greatly profit the people if the prince chooses to abuse his power into tyranny, is nevertheless enough so that the people cannot complain of an injury done to them if the prince happens to decree something more severe against them (which perhaps is not unjust, but which they would nevertheless not wish). Just so among us, some of the Presbyterians' flock complain, importunately (as they usually do) and unjustly, that the election of parish ministers has been wrongfully snatched from the people; whereas those who ought to be called to that office by the parishioners are presented, in the name of patron, by some private individual or College, without their consent. Thinking little of this in the meantime: if the people ever had a right of election (which, however, is an uncertain matter, and which, if it is denied, they will never be able to prove), it passed long ago, for some just cause at the beginning but now forgotten through long prescription, to the so-called patrons of benefices, and therefore in the election made by the Patrons the consent of the People is virtually included and contained. But if this does not move men who are too stubborn in their opinions, yet at least they must be reminded of this, which would satisfy even the most importunate adversary: the Right of Patronage and the Advocations of Churches were long ago sanctioned by Parliamentary authority, that is, by the common and full consent of the whole people; and therefore what is done in this case by the lawful Patron is something the people have consented to allow him to do.

units.la: XXV. Secundus gradus est, tacitus populi consensus in Legem, post ejus promulgationem. Cùm scilicet populus Legi à Principe latæ & promulgatæ non contradicit, sed eam potiùs moribus & factis comprobat ; conformando se voluntati Principis, & id observando, quod Lege imperatum est. Si enim qui vel tacet duntaxat, consentire videtur, multo magis consentire praesumitur qui & facit. De quo consentiendi gradu sic iterum Julianus, ubi supra; Quid interest, inquit, suffragio populus voluntatem suam declaret, an rebus & facto?
units.tr: XXV. The second degree is the tacit consent of the people to a law after its promulgation. This happens when the people do not contradict a law enacted and promulgated by the Prince, but rather approve it by their customs and actions, conforming themselves to the will of the Prince and observing what the law commands. For if one who merely keeps silent seems to consent, much more is he presumed to consent who also acts accordingly. On this degree of consent, Julian again, in the passage cited above, says: "What difference does it make," he says, "whether the people declare their will by vote, or by deeds and conduct?"

units.la: XXVI. Tertius gradus est, expressus populi consensus in Legem a Principe rogatam & sibi propositam post factam rogationem. Cum scil. Princeps Legis materiam domi ante praeparatam, & ex consilio virorum prudentium, si non perfecte expolitam, aliquatenus tamen exasciatam, & in concepta verba quaedam redactam, nequid quod palam esset absurdum aut incommodum contineret, subdiris suis ulterius examinandam & expendendam permittit: postulans, ut ipsi aut plerque ipsorum pars, eandem si futuram putent Reipublicæ salutarem, aut saltem bono publico nihil incommodaturam, suffragiis suis confirment, ut ipsis etiam consentientibus abeat in Legem. Qui fere fuit apud Romanos olim, stante abhuc Repub. rogandarum Legum mos: unde & Rogandi vox obtineat, cujus apud Romanarum rerum scriptores frequentissima mentio est.
units.tr: XXVI. The third degree is the express consent of the people to a law proposed to them by the Prince after the proposal has been made. This is when the Prince, having first prepared the matter of a law at home, with the advice of prudent men, and having drawn it up, if not perfectly polished, at least roughly shaped and set down in certain set words, so that it contains nothing manifestly absurd or inconvenient, allows his subjects to examine and weigh it further, asking that they, or at least most of them, if they think it will be salutary to the Commonwealth, or at least will do no harm to the public good, confirm it by their votes, so that it may become a law even with their consent. This was almost the custom among the Romans of old, while the Commonwealth still stood, of proposing laws; whence the term Rogandi came into use, which is very frequently mentioned by the writers of Roman affairs.

units.la: XXVII. Ultimus & supremus gradus, (quæ est ipsissima illa Populi Libertas, quâ tandiu sub optimis Regibus ad invidiam usque felices fuimus Britanni, & nihil stupide ingrati nimium nos indignos præstitissemus tantâ felicitate, adhuc facillimis[?] esse libuisset) est consensus & expressus interrogationem Legis. Cùm scilicet Legis Formulâ per-scripta, habità priùs inter ipsos justâ & de rebus & de verbis deliberatione, Procerum regni & delegatorum plebis conjunctis suffragiis comprobata, Regiæ tandem Majestati, (cui uni competit Legum ferendarum summa potestas,) exhibetur, ut ipsius calculo, si id ipsi commodum visum fuerit, confirmata, Legis exinde habeat vigorem, alias irrita sit penitus, nec pro Lege habeatur. Quæ Legum sanctissimarum[?] ratio, à Majoribus nostris prudentissimè excogitata, & ad nostra usque secula per tot Regum & annorum series traducta, omnium superiorum ætatum experientia usuque comperta est adeò Reipublicæ salutaris: ut si de movendis loco suo veteribus terminis non essent intempestivè fœtis[?] (nequid durius dicam) capi cœpta ccnsilia[?], floruissent adhuc fortassis, ut Dei olim beneficio, quæ nunc justissimo ipsius judicio perierunt, eúntque magis magisque indies Ecclesiæ, Academiæ, Rex, Populus, Respublica, Res cujusque privata. Quandoquidem non posse arbitror humano ingenio facilè excogitari, ad moderandam hinc Regum Potentiam, illinc
units.tr: XXVII. The last and highest step (this is that very liberty of the people, by which we Britons, under the best kings, have for so long been happy, even to the point of envy; we would have shown ourselves utterly ungrateful and unworthy of so great a happiness had we wished to be too easily led) is the express consent to the enactment of a law. When a form of the law has been drawn up in writing, and has first been fully debated among the members, both as to the matters and as to the wording, and has been approved by the joint votes of the nobles of the realm and the chosen representatives of the commons, it is then presented to the royal Majesty (to whom alone belongs the supreme power of making laws), so that it may be confirmed by his assent, if that seems fitting to him. Only then does the law have force; otherwise it is wholly void and is not regarded as law. This method of making laws, most wisely devised by our forefathers and handed down to our own age through so many reigns and years, has been found by the experience and practice of all earlier times to be so beneficial to the commonwealth that, had not designs been undertaken (to say nothing harsher) to move the old landmarks unseasonably, they would perhaps still have flourished, as they once did by God's blessing, and what has now perished by His most just judgment would have survived. The Church, the universities, the King, the people, the commonwealth, and each person's private affairs are all going from bad to worse day by day. For I do not think that any more suitable method of making laws can easily be devised by human wit, one which both restrains the power of kings on the one side and checks and curbs the license of the people on the other.

units.la: XXVIII. Sequitur Dubium Quartum De Legibus minorum Communitatum ; ut exempli gratiâ Civitatum, Academiarum, Collegiorum, Scholarum, aliarumque quas Corporatas vocant Societates : quæ præter Leges omnibus Regni subditis communes, suis etiam privatis gaudent Legibus, Iuribus & Statutis. Ad quas nimirum personas pertineat ejusmodi Legum ferendarum Potestas ? & latæ quos & quoad obligent ? Nec est difficilis responsio.
units.tr: XXVIII. There follows the fourth doubt, concerning the laws of smaller communities, such as cities, universities, colleges, schools, and the other bodies which they call corporate societies. Besides the laws common to all the subjects of the kingdom, these enjoy their own private laws, rights and statutes. To which persons, then, does the power of making such laws belong? And by whom, and to whom, are the laws so made binding? The answer is not difficult.

units.la: Dico ergo Primo, Quum omnes hujusmodi Sodalitates, corpora, sive collegia minora, magni sint corporis, (hoc est, Regni sive Reipublicæ,) membra, & in eo contineantur ut Cœlorum[?] orbes inferiores in superioribus, nec liceat cuiquam Collegio, societati, eorumve moderatoribus aut inspectoribus, Leges privatas sibi condere, quæ publicis totius Regni Legibus adversentur, aut ullo modo præjudicent.
units.tr: I say therefore, first, since all such fellowships, bodies, or smaller colleges are members of the greater body (that is, of the kingdom or commonwealth), and are contained in it as the lower spheres of the heavens are in the higher, it is not lawful for any college, society, or their governors or overseers to make for themselves private laws which oppose or in any way prejudice the public laws of the whole kingdom.

units.la: Dico Secundo, Quum ex concessione Principum, idque ex gratiâ speciali (ut loquuntur) corporentur istiusmodi Societates, nec aliis gaudeant juribus, privilegiis vel potestate, extra ea quæ vel ex diuturna temporis præscriptione, vel ex chartis diplomatibusque Regiis constare potest fuisse sibi concessa : Potestatem proinde quæ in ipsis est [illegible, ~9 letters] omnem derivatam esse potestatem, non autem primitivam, atque in supremam Regiam Potestatem, ut veram sui Originem, ultimatè resolvi ; & propterea non posse ejusmodi Societates earumque Magistratus pro arbitrio suo constituere, aut Potestatem aliquam in legibus ferendis actualiter exercere, nisi ad modum & mensuram indultæ sibi à Principe facultatis.
units.tr: I say secondly, that since such societies are incorporated by the grant of Princes, and that by special favour (as they say), and do not enjoy any other rights, privileges or power beyond those which can be shown to have been granted to them either by long prescription of time or by charters and royal diplomas, therefore the power which is in them [illegible, about nine letters] is wholly derived power, and not primitive, and is ultimately traced back, as to its true origin, to the supreme royal power. For this reason such societies and their magistrates cannot constitute themselves at their own discretion, nor actually exercise any power in enacting laws, except according to the measure and manner of the faculty granted to them by the Prince.

units.la: Dico Tertio, Leges à privatis Collegii & Societatibus Corporatis juxta tenorem facultatis sibi à Principe concessæ legitimè latas, obligare omnia membra earundem societatum, & quotquot earum jurisdictioni se regimini subduntur, eósque solos, per se, directè & vi suâ: ast virtute supremæ Majestatis Regiæ, cujus authoritate nituntur, & à quâ vim suam omnem & authoritatem accipiunt, obligare aliquotenus & indirectè universos & singulos totius Regni subditos. Sed utriusque obligationis nec eadem ratio est, nec gradus idem. Obligant enim hæ L-ges, suos, quidem, ut eas diligenter observent: riquo[?] vero hactenus tantum obligant, ne eas aliquo modo violent, imminuantve, aut earum observationem impediant.
units.tr: I say thirdly, that laws enacted by the private authorities of colleges and corporate societies, in accordance with the tenor of the faculty granted to them by the Prince, are lawfully enacted and bind all the members of those societies, and all who are subject to their jurisdiction and government, and these alone, directly, of themselves and by their own force; but by virtue of the supreme royal Majesty, on whose authority they rest and from which they receive all their force and authority, they bind all and each of the subjects of the whole kingdom, somewhat and indirectly. But the reason of the two obligations is neither the same nor of the same degree. For these laws oblige their own members to observe them diligently; whereas they oblige others, so far, only so that they do not violate them in any way, diminish them, or hinder their observance.

units.la: XXIX. Dubium Quintum, de Legibus Ecclesiast- icis in specie.
units.tr: XXIX. Fifth Doubt, concerning Ecclesiastical Laws in particular.

units.la: Posse de novo condi Leges de ritibus, rebus & personis Ecclesiasticis, omnibúsque sacri cultus externi circumstantiis ad ordinem, honestatem & ædificationem spectantibus, extra eas quæ sunt à Christo & ejus Apostolis in sacris literis traditæ; adeo manifesta res est, & rationi consentanea, ut perversi judicii obstinatique animi se suspicione ægrè liberaverit, qui siccus & sobrius negaverit. Sed cujus sit Ecclesiasticas Leges condere, ex quo in diversa studia abiere Theologi, parum inter partes convenit. Pontificii, qui clericos omni civilis Magistratus Jurisdictione exemptos volunt, (de quâ controversiâ non est hunc disputandi locus,) Episcopis solis, inque eis summo Pontifici maxime, quem Oecumenicum Episcopum prædicant, hoc juris asserunt, ut ipsis Leges condere liceat, quæ non Clericorum modò sed & Laicorum conscientias obligent; etiam sine consensu vel licentiâ Magistratus Politici. Papistæ hunc articulum, ut & alios non paucos, (manentes tantùm personâ, dogmate non mutato,) ampl[?] suntur[?] qui se tamen Papistæ acerrimos hostes profitentur, sed omnia interim novi interturbant Davi, Disciplinarii nostri Reformatores: qui omnem Potestatem, Authoritatem, Jurisdictionemque Ecclesiasticam Regibus ademptam, sibi unis suisque Classibus & Conventibus vendicant. Erastiani ex adverso, Reformatores quoque non minus & hi (Deus bone! sub specie Reformationis quot nominum & opinionum monstra, nisi quòd sunt deformia pariter, alias immane quantum invicem difformia, parturivit, peperit, aluit, fovit prodigiorum ferax novissimum hoc septennium!) Erastiani inquam, clericis omni Jurisdictioni Ecclesiasticæ penitus exutis, Externi Ecclesiæ regiminis jus universum Magistratui Civili ex asse & in solidum attribuunt.
units.tr: That new laws may be made concerning the rites, persons and matters of the Church, and concerning all the external circumstances of sacred worship that relate to order, decency and edification, beyond those laid down by Christ and his Apostles in the holy writings, is so plain and so consonant with reason that only a man of perverse judgement and obstinate mind, who denied it while sober and in his right senses, could hardly clear himself of suspicion. But since the theologians have gone off in different directions, the parties agree little on whose right it is to make ecclesiastical laws. The Papists, who want the clergy exempt from all jurisdiction of the civil magistrate (a controversy that is not the place to dispute here), claim this right for bishops alone, and above all for the supreme Pontiff, whom they proclaim the Ecumenical Bishop, so that they may make laws binding not only the consciences of the clergy but also of the laity, even without the consent or licence of the civil magistrate. The Papists hold this article, as well as not a few others, remaining only in name with their doctrine unchanged, [text garbled]; who nevertheless profess themselves the bitterest enemies of the Papists, yet in the meantime throw everything into confusion: our Davi and Disciplinarian Reformers, who claim for themselves alone, and for their Classes and Conventions, all the power, authority and ecclesiastical jurisdiction taken away from kings. On the opposite side are the Erastians, and the Reformers no less than these. (Good God! what a crop of monstrous names and opinions, deformed alike and yet hugely unlike one another, has this most recent seven years, so fruitful of prodigies, brought forth, borne, nursed and cherished under the pretext of Reformation!) The Erastians, I say, with the clergy wholly stripped of every ecclesiastical jurisdiction, assign the entire right of the external government of the Church wholly and entirely to the civil magistrate.

units.la: XXX. Non est mihi animus, sed nec otium, (nisi vobis plus æquo molestus esse vellem) cum utriusvis generis adversario manum conserere. Hic, ut aliis plerisque rebus usuvenit, verior esse videtur, & est certè tutior, quæ inter duas extremas media interjacet sententia: in quam vestris omnium pedibus eò lubentius itum iri confido, quòd & Doctrinæ Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ, & Regni insimul Legibus maximè sit consentanea. Nempe, Jus condendi Leges Ecclesiasticas esse penes Episcopos, Presbyteros, aliásque personas à totius Regni Clero ritè electas, & in legitima Synodo ritè congregatas. Ita tamen ut ejus juris sive potestatis exercitium in omni Repub. Christianâ, ex Authoritate Supremi Magistratûs Politici pendere debeat. Idque & à parte ante, (ut loqui solemus) & à parte post: Videlicet, ut nec eis statuendi Canones Ecclesiasticos causâ liceat convenire, nisi aut ipsius mandato & jussu ad id negotii convocatis, aut ejus saltem authoritate, ve[?]nià ab eo petità[?] pariter & obtentà[?], munitis: nec Canones, in quos illi sic con-senserint, rati sint, aut vim aliquam habeant obli-gandi, quoad Supremi Magistratus assensus acce-dat, cujus approbatione & publicâ authoritate ir-mulac[?] confirmati fuerint, illico pro Legibus haben-di sunt, & subditos obligant. Atque hæc de Causa Efficiente dicta sufficiant.
units.tr: XXX. I have no wish, nor indeed the leisure (unless I wished to be more troublesome to you than is fair), to engage with an adversary of either kind. Here, as happens in most other matters, the opinion that lies midway between the two extremes seems the truer, and is certainly the safer. I am confident that you will all the more gladly go over to it, since it agrees most closely both with the doctrine of the Church of England and with the laws of the realm alike. Namely, the right of making ecclesiastical laws belongs to bishops, presbyters, and other persons duly elected from the whole clergy of the realm and duly assembled in a lawful synod. Yet the exercise of this right or power, in every Christian commonwealth, ought to depend on the authority of the supreme civil magistrate. This holds both beforehand (as we are wont to say) and afterwards. That is, they may not lawfully meet to decree ecclesiastical canons unless either summoned to that business by his mandate and command, or at least furnished with his authority, having sought and obtained his permission. Nor are the canons to which they have so agreed to be considered valid, or to have any force of binding, until the assent of the supreme magistrate is added; once they are confirmed by his approval and public authority, they are at once to be held as laws and bind the subjects. Let these things said about the efficient cause suffice.

units.la: De Obligatione Legum Humanarum ex parte Causæ Formalis; Ubi, De Promulgatione Legum. Legibus Poenalibus.
units.tr: On the Obligation of Human Laws as regards the Formal Cause; where, On the Promulgation of Laws. On Penal Laws.

units.la: 7. Ita promulgarunt per Judah & Jerusalem omnibus filiis captivitatis, ut se congregarent Jerosolymis,
units.tr: 7. So they made a proclamation throughout Judah and Jerusalem to all the children of the captivity, that they should gather themselves together at Jerusalem,

units.la: 8. Et quisquis non veniret infra triduum— sub anathemate ut essent omnes facultates ejus.
units.tr: 8. And that whoever did not come within three days, under the ban, all his substance should be forfeited.

units.la: I. DE Legum Humanarum Obligatione quod ad earum Causas Materialem & Efficientem pertinet, in his quæ jam ante nobis tractata sunt, satis pro instituti nostri ratione vidimus. Dicendum proximè de his quæ ad Causæ genus Formale, (etsi fortassis non admodum proprie, siquis velit ista ad accuratam methodi normam exigere, haud tamen prorsus incommodè, ut mihi saltem videtur,) reduci pofsunt. Quæ omnia, ad duo omninò capita revocare licet: alterum de Legum Promulgatione; de adjunctâ eis pœna delinquentibus irrogandâ alterum. Quarum utraque ut in propositò Textu expressè continetur, Promulgatio versu septimo, Pœna versu octavo: ita est utriusque, & ex ipsâ Legis naturâ & ad effectum Legis consequendum, usus pernecessarius. Quum enim Lex, ex naturâ sui, & quatenus est regula quædam rerum agendarum, duplicem habere debeat vim; vim scil. dirigendi, ostendendo subditis quid sit faciendum vel non faciendum, & vim obligandi, ingerendo animis eorum parendi necessitatem: non poterit Lex duplicem hanc vim debitè & cum effectu exercere, nisi & subdito innotescat, quæ sit Principis voluntas, quod fit Promulgatione; & intelligat etiam ex appositâ pœnâ, quantum sibi refert eam præ-stare.
units.tr: I. On the Obligation of Human Laws, as far as it concerns their material and efficient causes, we have seen enough in what has already been treated before us, given the plan of our work. Next I turn to what belongs to the formal kind of cause. Strictly speaking, this may not be the most proper place for it, if anyone wished to hold these matters to the exact rule of method, but it is not wholly out of place, at least as it seems to me. All of these can be traced back to two main heads: one concerning the promulgation of laws, and the other concerning the penalty attached to them and imposed on offenders. Both are expressly contained in the text before us: promulgation in the seventh verse, and the penalty in the eighth. The use of each is absolutely necessary, both from the very nature of law and for achieving the effect of the law. For since a law, by its nature and insofar as it is a rule of things to be done, ought to have a twofold force, namely the force of directing, by showing subjects what is to be done or not done, and the force of obliging, by impressing on their minds the necessity of obeying, a law cannot exercise this twofold force properly and effectively unless it is made known to the subject what the prince's will is, and this is done by promulgation; and unless the subject also understands from the attached penalty how much it matters to him to fulfil the law.

units.la: II. De Promulgatione Legis, Dubium Primum est, An Promulgatio sit de ratione Legis? quod est quæ-rere, An ad hoc ut Lex habeat vim dirigendi & obligandi, ita necessariò requiratur ejus Promulgatio, ut ea vi careat nisi promulgata sit? Promulgationem autem in tota hac tractatione non intelligo quoad usum ejus vocabuli apud Ciceronem & alios Romanos Scriptores, sed juxta receptum morem loquendi Scholasticorum & Canonistarum posteriorum sæculorum. Illa enim veterum promulgatione, proponebatur publicè tribus nundinis Lex adhuc ferenda, ut populo probaretur: at hæc de quâ nunc loquimur promulgatio est ipsa publicatio Legis jam Latæ, ut populo innotescat. Ad dubium ergo propositum respondeo breviter, Promulgationem esse de ratione Legis, ut aliquo modo dici possit ejus Forma, adeoque apud plerosque authores ingrediatur ejus definitionem: & proinde simpliciter esse necessariam ad hoc, ut Lex exerceat Of-
units.tr: II. Concerning the promulgation of law, the first question is: Is promulgation part of the nature of law? That is to ask whether, in order that a law may have the force of directing and obliging, its promulgation is necessarily required, so that it lacks that force unless it has been promulgated. In this whole discussion I do not understand promulgation in the sense the word has in Cicero and the other Roman writers, but according to the accepted manner of speaking of the Schoolmen and the Canonists of later centuries. For that promulgation of the ancients was the public proposal, for three market-days, of a law still to be enacted, so that the people might approve it. But the promulgation of which we now speak is the very publication of a law already enacted, so that it may become known to the people. To the question proposed, then, I answer briefly: promulgation is part of the nature of law, in the sense that it can in some way be said to be its form, and so it enters into the definition of law in the view of most authors. Consequently it is simply necessary in order that a law may exercise its office,

units.la: reve. e ; de a alte- etu ej. Peru a Leg usus ra su, larum; rigeni, on si. is co- ex du- cere, volu- etiam i pra. m est, qu- ndi & mulg- mulg- elligo alios m le- orum pro c se- nunc jam pro n in possit s in- plici- t Of- cium ium[?] Legis, quod est, dirigere & obligare subdios ; quos ne dirigere quidem potest, multò autem minùs obligare, quantumcunque sit justa & optima authoritate lata, nisi sit illis cognita, & cognita esse non potest nisi promulgetur. Illud enim quod proprie inducit obligationem, est vo- luntas & authoritas præsidentis sive principis, non ut est persona singulis, sed quatenus sustinet personam publicam & est caput communitatis. Atqui nisi suam illam voluntatem publica aliqua ratione populo patefieri & proponi curaverit, non poterit de aliqua Lege (juris saltem interpretatione) certò constare, quòd sit ipsius voluntas, & ab ejus authoritate, prout publicam personam sustinet profecta. Hinc illud juris Canonici Leges constituuntur, cum promulgantur : itémque illud alterum juris civilis effatum, Leges quæ constringunt hominum vitas, intelligi ab omnibus debent. Quod quùm omnium Doctorum communi consensu ; ratione scilicet sic dictante, comprobetur : nihil opus est ei firmando aut Dei ipsius exemplum in medium adducere, Legem suam populo Hebræo de monte Sinai solenniter promulgantis ; aut florentissimarum toto orbe Rerumpub. & civitatum praxin, quæ Leges suas mox ut latæ fuerunt, tabulis æneis incifas, aut insculptas ligneis, in locis maximè publicis civibus inspiciendas proposuerunt.
