Notissimæ sunt illa vocabula quæ passim apud authores occurrunt & ad hanc classem pertinent, Atheniensium Νόμοι, κύρβεις, ἄξονες, XII. Tabulæ Romanorum, aliorumque populorum alia : de quibus consulant, queis vacat esse istarum rerum curiosis utriusque linguæ Lexicographos & Philologos. Nobis ad alia pergendum.
units.tr: which is to direct and oblige subjects. A law cannot even direct them, much less oblige them, however justly and excellently it has been enacted, unless it is known to them; and it cannot be known unless it is promulgated. For what properly induces obligation is the will and authority of the ruler or prince, not as he is a private person to individuals, but insofar as he sustains a public person and is the head of the community. Now unless he has taken care to make that will known and proposed to the people by some public means, it cannot be certain, at least by the interpretation of law, that a given law is his will and proceeds from his authority as he sustains a public person. Hence the saying of canon law, laws are constituted when they are promulgated, and the other saying of civil law, laws which bind the lives of men ought to be understood by all. Since this is approved by the common consent of all the learned, namely as reason itself dictates, there is no need to confirm it by bringing forward the example of God himself, who solemnly promulgated his law to the Hebrew people from Mount Sinai, or the practice of the most flourishing commonwealths and cities throughout the world, which, as soon as their laws were enacted, set them out, cut on bronze tablets or carved on wooden boards, in the most public places for citizens to inspect. The terms that occur everywhere in the authors and belong to this class are well known: the Nomoi of the Athenians, the kyrbeis, the axones, the Twelve Tables of the Romans, and other such things among other peoples. Those who are curious about these matters and have the leisure may consult the lexicographers and philologists of both languages. For our part, we must proceed to other things.

units.la: II. Positâ promulgandæ Legis Necessitate, exoritur dubium secundum, qualis debet esse promulgatio Legis, ut legitima censeatur, & inducat obligationem ? gationem ? Pro responsione dico primò, promulgadi legum modum & rationem, quoad particulares ritus & circumstantias, pro more cujusque gentis variari posse ; in eo tamen consentire omnes, ex communi usu requiri, ut Legislator voluntatem suam curet ita proponi & manifestari subditis externo aliquo signo, ut eis publicè innotescat, nec aliquis eorum qui tenentur legem observare, possit (materialiter loquendo) esse ignarus ejusmodi legem esse latam. Atque hoc propterea requiritur, quod dirigendi vis legi intrinseca est & essentialis : non autem possunt subditi actiones suas secundum Principis sui voluntatem dirigere, nisi cognoscant hanc esse ejus voluntatem ; nec id scire possunt, nisi ipsis externo aliquo signo (puta voce, scripto, scriptura, linguave alio) sufficienter proposita & manifesta.
units.tr: II. Having established the necessity of promulgating a law, a second question arises: what sort of promulgation must a law have to be deemed legitimate and to induce obligation? In answer I say, first, that the manner and method of promulgating laws, as regards particular rites and circumstances, may vary according to the custom of each nation. Yet all agree in this: that common usage requires the lawgiver to take care that his will is so proposed and made manifest to subjects by some external sign that it becomes publicly known, and that none of those bound to observe the law can (speaking materially) be ignorant that such a law has been enacted. This is required because the power of directing is intrinsic and essential to law. Subjects cannot direct their actions according to their prince's will unless they know that this is his will, nor can they know it unless it has been sufficiently set forth and made manifest to them by some external sign, such as voice, writing, script, or other language.

units.la: IV. Dico Secundò, ad promulgationem Legis ita ut obliget subditos non sufficere quòd Legislator voluntatem suam eis publicè significet ; sed ulterius etiam requiri, ut solenni aliquo adhibito ritu id fiat : aut saltem ita fiat (quod solennis ritus infra habet & tantundem valet) ut satis testatum sit subditis Legislatorem intendere, ut illa ipsius voluntas Legis vigorem habeat, & eos obliget. Cujus ratio est, quia non omnis Voluntas Superioris, etiì subdito cognita, continuò & ipso facto eum obligat ; nisi etiam constet superiorem intendisse ut obligaret. Omnis enim superior Legislativa potestate praeditus, quum duplicem sustineat personam ; unam privatam qua homo singularis, alteram publicam qua legitimus superior : potest idcirco duplicem subire considerationem live respectum. Peperit nobis haud ita pridem inter medias turbas inauspicata quorundam folertia novam distinctionem, de Regis nempe capacitate (sic enim loqui placuit) personali, & politica ; praesenti negotio (meo saltem judicio) quàm ei rei quæ tunc agebatur, aliquanto commodiorem. Nimirum sic est: Voluntas Principis, si consideretur princeps in capacitate suâ personali, hoc est, ut persona singularis & quasi privata, non habet rationem Legis nec obligat subditos ut secundùm eam dirigant actiones suas. Ergo ad obligandum subditos non satis est, ut Princeps quocunque modo eis significet hoc vel illud se velle: nisi etiam alicunde constare poterit, eum idipsum velle ut in capacitate suâ Politicâ; hoc est, quatenus Princeps est, & caput communitatis, & ut personam publicam sustinet cum Legislativâ potestate. Quod quum ex simplici voluntatis suæ significatione satis constare non potest, opus est ut aliquâ magis publicâ & solemni ceremoniâ iis quorum id scire interest testatum sit; nequis possit excusandæ suæ inobedientiæ putidum illud & vulgare Non putâram obtendere.
units.tr: IV. I say, secondly, that for a law to be promulgated so as to bind subjects, it is not enough that the lawgiver publicly signify his will to them. It must further be done with some solemn rite employed, or at least in such a way (which a solemn rite does, as below, and to the same effect) that it is sufficiently attested to subjects that the lawgiver intends his will to have the force of law and to bind them. The reason is that not every will of a superior, even when known to the subject, binds him continually and by the very fact, unless it is also established that the superior intended to bind. For every superior endowed with legislative power sustains a double person: one private, as an individual man, the other public, as lawful superior. He can therefore undergo a double consideration or respect. Not long ago, in the midst of the troubles, the ill-starred cleverness of certain men produced a new distinction, between the king's "personal" and "political" capacity (for so they chose to speak), which is somewhat more suited, in my judgement, to the present question than to the affair then in hand. The matter stands thus: the will of a prince, if he is considered in his personal capacity, that is, as a single and almost private person, does not have the character of law and does not oblige subjects to direct their actions by it. Therefore, to oblige subjects, it is not enough that the prince signify to them in any way that he wants this or that. It must also be clear from some source that he wills it precisely in his political capacity, that is, insofar as he is prince and head of the community, and as he sustains the public person with legislative power. Since this cannot sufficiently be established from the mere signification of his will, it is necessary that by some more public and solemn ceremony it be attested to those who have an interest in knowing it, lest anyone be able to plead in excuse of his disobedience that stale and common plea, "I did not think so."

units.la: V. Dico Tertiò, in amplioribus imperiis, quæ multas continent Provincias, utile saltem esse ut promulgatio novæ Legis fiat in singulis imperii Provinciis. Sunt quibus hoc videtur simpliciter necessarium, & requiri ex naturâ Legis, quæ non obligat nisi à populo acceptetur: & proinde si Lex in curiâ Principis, aut totius Regni Metropoli, aut primariis aliquot civitatibus solùm promulgetur, non sufficere ejusmodi promulgationem ad obligandum eos, qui in locis & provinciis remotioribus degunt. Sed utut non sit hoc simpliciter necessarium, nec videtur enim natura Legis id requirere, & ex alterâ parte stat cùm communis opinio Doctorum, tum communis plerarumque gentium praxis, utile tamen est id fieri, ut Lex, quâ singuli tenentur, ad singulorum, quoad fieri potest, notitiam perveniat. Quod quantò facilius nostro seculo, quam prioribus illis (nondum adinventâ arte Typographicâ) præstari potest, tantò inexcusabilius negligitur. Ne longè abeam ; quæ est apud nos usu recepta, non modò sufficiens, sed & facillima videtur esse Legis Promulgandæ & commodissima ratio : ut scilicet Leges in Comitiis Parliamentariis totius Regni Ordinum consensu à Rege sancitæ, finitis jam Comitiis mox typis mandentur, idque à Typographo Regio & noto charactere, ita ut nemo possit esse dubius, leges eas & legitimè latæ[?] esse, & sufficienter promulgatas.
units.tr: V. I say thirdly, that in larger empires, which contain many provinces, it is at least useful for the promulgation of a new law to be made in each of the provinces of the empire. Some think this simply necessary, and required by the nature of law, which binds only if it is accepted by the people. They hold that if a law is promulgated only in the prince's court, or in the capital of the whole kingdom, or in a few chief cities, such a promulgation is not sufficient to bind those who live in more distant places and provinces. But although this is not simply necessary (for the nature of law does not seem to require it, and on the other side stands both the common opinion of the learned and the common practice of most nations), it is nonetheless useful that it be done, so that the law by which individuals are held comes, as far as possible, to the knowledge of each individual. The more easily this can be done in our age than in those earlier times (before the art of printing was discovered), the more inexcusably it is neglected. Not to go far afield: the method in use among us seems not only sufficient but also the easiest and most convenient way of promulgating law. Namely, the laws enacted by the King in Parliamentary assemblies, with the consent of all the estates of the kingdom, are printed as soon as the assemblies have ended, by the King's printer and with a recognised mark, so that no one can doubt that those laws have been lawfully passed and sufficiently promulgated.

units.la: VI. Dubium Tertium. Supposito quod Lex fue-rit sufficienter promulgata, quando incipiat obligare subditos : an statim post promulgationem factam?
units.tr: VI. Third question. Granted that a law has been sufficiently promulgated, when does it begin to bind the subjects: immediately after the promulgation has been made,

units.la: An post aliquod temporis intervallum ? Pro responsione dico primò, quod & extra controversiam est, Leges illas, in quibus definitum est certum tempus obligationis, quamprimum illud tempus advenerit, statim obligare incipere, & obligare deinceps in omne tempus futurum, nisi aut terminus obligationis ipsis illis legibus definiatur, aut ipsæ leges vel novâ lege vel contrariâ consuetudine abrogentur. Unde ex communi juris civilis sententiâ Leges Imperatoriæ de novo constitutæ non obligant Imperii subditos, ni post duos menses à promulgatione factâ : quia id tempus Authentica quadam in Novellis, ut in omnibus legibus observandum, universaliter definitum est, idque eo consilio, quòd præsumitur facillimè posse duorum mensium spatio notitiam legis ad omnes subditos pervenire.
units.tr: or after some interval of time? In answer I say, first, which is also beyond controversy, that those laws in which a definite time of obligation is fixed begin to bind immediately once that time has arrived, and continue to bind for all future time, unless either the term of obligation is set by the laws themselves, or the laws are abrogated by a new law or by contrary custom. Hence, according to the common opinion of civil law, imperial laws newly enacted do not bind the subjects of the empire until two months after the promulgation has been made, because a certain Authentic in the Novels has universally fixed that time to be observed for all laws, and this with the intention that it is presumed the knowledge of the law can very easily reach all subjects within the space of two months.

units.la: Dico Secundò, in Regnis & Rebuspublicis, ubi nihil certi de tempore quo Leges de novo latæ incipiant obligare aut jure definitum est, aut moribus receptum, Leges in quibus non opponitur certum tempus obligationis, obligare in conscientiâ, quamprimùm sunt pro consueto regionis more promulgatæ, omnes illos ad quorum notitiam pervenerint, aut quibus per Legislatorem non steterit, quò minùs innotescere potuerint. Quum enim obligasio Legis ex voluntate Legislatoris pendeat, non ex scientia subditi: sequitur vigere obligationem Legis, quando Legislator voluntatem suam subditis externo signo sufficienter expresserit, sive id singulis subditis cognitum fuerit, sive contigerit ut aliqui forte idipsum ignorent. Posita siquidem Lege ponitur obligatio; quae convenit legi quatenus Lex est, & eam necessario sequitur, sicut omnis necessarius effectus sequitur propriam suam causam, ut a nobis saepe ante dictum est. Ergo quum Legi quamprimum legitime lata est & sufficienter promulgata, nihil ultra deest quod ad complendam ejus essentiam requiratur; omnino consequitur legem sic latam & promulgatam statim inducere obligationem. Neque inconvenit nasci posse in nobis obligationem per voluntatem & factum alterius solum, nobis etiam nescientibus; si obligatio illa habeat rationem debiti moralis, ut loquuntur; etsi in obligationibus & debitis quae oriuntur ex contractu, aliter se res habeat.
units.tr: I say secondly, that in kingdoms and commonwealths where nothing certain about the time at which newly enacted laws begin to bind has been fixed either by right or received by custom, laws in which no certain time of obligation is set bind in conscience as soon as they have been promulgated in the customary manner of the region, for all those to whose knowledge they have come, or whom the lawgiver has not prevented from learning of them. For since the obligation of a law depends on the will of the lawgiver, not on the knowledge of the subject, it follows that the obligation of the law is in force when the lawgiver has sufficiently expressed his will to the subjects by an external sign, whether or not this has come to the knowledge of each subject, or it happens that some perhaps are ignorant of it. For, granted the law, the obligation is granted; this belongs to the law as it is law, and necessarily follows it, just as every necessary effect follows its own cause, as we have often said before. Therefore, when a law has been lawfully enacted and sufficiently promulgated, nothing further is lacking that is required to complete its essence; it wholly follows that a law so enacted and promulgated induces obligation at once. Nor is it inconsistent that an obligation may arise in us through the will and act of another alone, even without our knowing it, if that obligation has the character of what they call a moral debt; although in obligations and debts that arise from contract the matter stands otherwise.

units.la: VII. Dubium Quartum ; quatenus Lex afficiat eos, quibus, postquam sufficienter promulgata est, aut post elapsum tempus lege constitutum, actu tamen non innotescit? Quod est quaerere, an cui Lex actu cognita non est, aut culpae reus sit, ita ut peccet si contra legem faciat, aut poenam propterea mereatur, quam Lex delinquentibus irrogat? Ratio dubitandi est, ex una parte, quia frustra est obligatio, vel potius nulla, quae nec ad culpam obligat, nec ad poenam. Ex altera parte, tum quia absurdum videtur, ut quis obligetur ad impossibile, at certe lege servare quam nescias, impossibile est: tum etiam quia e duobus Legis quae diximus officiis, necesse est dirigendi illam vim, ut natura priorem, alteram illam obligandi vim antecedere, ita ut Lex nequeat obligare nisi quem dirigit, dirigere autem non potest nisi sit cognita. Hoc imprimis suppositio, quod nullam admittit dubitationem, subditum cui Lex actu cognita est, obligari & ad culpam, & ad poenam: quod ad ignorantes legem attinet, pro responsione ad dubium propo-situm, Dico primo, qui legem ignorat ex crassa negligentia, quum id suo vitio & lata culpa contingat ut eam nesciat, nihilo aut saltem non multo minus, & peccati reum esse, & poenam mereri, quàm eum qui cognitam legem violat. Ignorantia enim crassa ejus quod quis scire debet & potest, neminem excusat: nec multum dissere videntur (juris interpretatione) dolus malus, & lata culpa.
units.tr: VII. Fourth question. How far does a law bind those to whom, after it has been sufficiently promulgated, or after the time fixed by the law has elapsed, it nevertheless does not actually become known? This is to ask whether one to whom the law is not actually known is liable for fault, so that he sins if he acts against the law, or therefore deserves the penalty which the law inflicts on offenders. The reason for doubt is, on the one hand, that an obligation is pointless, or rather is nothing, if it binds neither to fault nor to penalty. On the other hand, it seems absurd that anyone should be bound to the impossible, and certainly it is impossible to keep a law that you do not know. Moreover, of the two offices of law we have mentioned, the power of directing must by nature come before the power of obliging, so that a law cannot bind anyone unless it directs him, and it cannot direct unless it is known. Above all, the proposition, which admits no doubt, that a subject to whom the law is actually known is bound both to fault and to penalty. As for those ignorant of the law, in answer to the question proposed, I say first: one who is ignorant of the law through gross negligence, since through his own fault and by gross fault he comes not to know it, is in no way, or at least not much less, guilty of sin and deserving of penalty than one who violates a known law. For gross ignorance of what a man ought and is able to know excuses no one; and, by the interpretation of law, malicious deceit and gross fault seem not to differ much.

units.la: VIII. Dico secundo, eum qui Legem propterea ignorat, quia aliquanto incuriosior aut negligentior in eam partem fuerit, quàm in re tàm gravi oportuerat; etsi culpa, quam Jurisconsulti levem vel etiam levissimam dicunt; quia & culpa tamen, & sua id factum constat, non prorsus immunem esse à Legis Obligatione. Ratio est, quia istiusmodi ignorantia fuit vincibilis: si enim subditus tantam diligentiam adhibuisset, quantam & rei ipsius dignitas postulabat, & adhibere solent in gravioribus suis negotiis homines cauti, potuisset (id enim jam supponimus) certum fuisse de legis promulgatione. Vincibilis autem ignorantia ejus Juris, secundum quod tenetur quisque dirigere actiones suas, non potest non esse culpabilis: si vero culpabilis in quocunque demum gradu, eatenus etiam & inexcusabilis est. Quo tamen levior culpa est, eò & in utroque foro excusatior est ignorantia, & facilius apud æquos rerum æstimatores veniam meretur. At lege antea obligatum fuisse, licet eam ignoraret, vel exinde patet, quòd quamprimum ex testimonio viri alicujus fide digni intelligit legem promulgatam esse, se protinus ea lege obligatum judicat: at nulla oritur de novo ex illius viri testimonio obligatio, (neque aut testi ipsi, aut ipsius testi-
units.tr: VIII. I say secondly, that one who is ignorant of a law because he has been somewhat more careless or negligent in that matter than so weighty a matter required, is not wholly free from the obligation of the law, although his fault, which the jurists call slight or even very slight, is his own and is established as such. The reason is that such ignorance was conquerable: for if the subject had applied as much diligence as the dignity of the matter demanded, and as cautious men are wont to apply in their weightier affairs, he could (for we are now supposing this) have been certain of the promulgation of the law. But ignorance of that law by which each person is bound to direct his actions, if it is conquerable, cannot but be culpable; and if it is culpable to any degree whatever, it is to that extent also inexcusable. Yet the lighter the fault, the more excusable the ignorance is in either court, and the more readily it earns pardon from fair judges of things. That a man was bound by a law before, even though he was ignorant of it, is clear from this: as soon as, on the testimony of some trustworthy man, he learns that the law has been promulgated, he at once judges himself bound by that law; yet no new obligation arises from that man's testimony (nor is there any force of binding in the witness himself, or in his testimony),

units.la: nio, vis aliqua inest obligandi ;) ergo proculubio jam antea lege obligabatur, etsi nec Legis otitiam ante haberet, nec conscientiam Obliga-tionis.
units.tr: therefore, beyond doubt, he was already bound by the law before, even though he had neither knowledge of the law nor awareness of the obligation.

units.la: IX. Dico Tertiò, eum qui bonâ fide & invinciliter, ex casu aut impedimento aliquo fortuito, ullâ tamen suâ negligentiâ, culpáve, legem promulgatam ignorat, (ut siquis insaniâ, aut gravi & diuturno morbo laboraverit, aut nuperrimè ab exteris regionibus reversus fuerit, nec quicquam de lege premulgatâ aut inaudiverit, aut audire potuerit,) nec ad culpam nec ad pœnam proprie dictam a lege obligari : posse tamen ea lege quam invincibiliter ignorat eatenus affici, ut obligetur ad pœnam impropriè dictam, hoc est, ad damnum aliquod, sustinendum. Probatur hujus assertionis pars prior. Nemo aut culpam incurrit, aut pœnam meretur, qui non peccat : at qui legem non servat quam invincibiliter ignorat, non peccat : si enim peccaret, obligaretur ad impossibile : ergo nec meritò culpari potest, nec juste puniri. Quod tamen possit obligari ad damnum aliquod ex lege [?]sustinendum, quae fuit nostrae assertionis altera pars, exemplo adducto clarissimum evadet. Esto lex prohibens certum aliquod genus contractus, quia lege inter alia decernitur omnes ejusmodi contractus post unum mensem a legis promulgatione [?]irritos, irritos prorsus esse & nullos: si quis legis illius bona fide & invincibiliter ignarus mense jam elapso contractum ejusmodi forte inierit: immunis quidem erit a culpa, propter invincibilem ignorantiam; immunis etiam consequenter debet esse & a poena, quae nemini juste debetur nisi propter culpam: damnum tamen, si quod ex nullitate illius contractus emergere contigerit, non solum sustinebit, sed & sustinere tenetur, etiam secundum conscientiam; ex vi obedientiae legibus debitae, & ex intuitu publicæ utilitatis. Quod idem statuendum est, & in aliis quibusdam legibus quampluribus: verbi gratiâ, in eis quibus inhabilitantur personæ, quibus revocantur privilegia, quibus temporantur fœnora, quibus certa rerum venalium pretia constituuntur, & similibus; de quibus fusè tractant Canonistæ & Theologi. Nec debet hoc cuiquam videri iniquum: etsi enim damnum quandoque pœna dicatur, id tamen fit per Analogiam tantum, valde improprie. Nam aliàs pœna proprie dictæ, & damni longè diversa ratio est. Pœna si quis insons afficiatur, fit ei injuria: & damnum innocenti citra injuriam sæpissimè inferri contingit. Et hæc de Promulgatione legis, quantum nostro instituto sufficiat, dicta sunto.
units.tr: IX. I say thirdly, that one who, through good faith and invincibly, by chance or some accidental hindrance, and yet without any negligence or fault of his own, is ignorant of a promulgated law (as, for example, if someone has suffered from insanity or a grave and lasting illness, or has only lately returned from foreign regions and has neither heard nor been able to hear anything of the promulgated law) is not bound by the law to fault, nor to penalty properly so called. Yet he can be affected by a law that he is invincibly ignorant of, to the extent of being bound to what is called a penalty improperly, that is, to the bearing of some loss. The first part of this assertion is proved as follows. No one incurs fault or deserves penalty unless he sins; but one who does not keep a law that he invincibly ignores does not sin, for if he did sin he would be bound to the impossible; therefore he cannot rightly be blamed, nor justly punished. That he can nevertheless be bound to bear some loss by the law, which was the second part of our assertion, will become very clear from an example. Suppose a law forbids a certain kind of contract, and by the law it is decreed, among other things, that all such contracts made after one month from the promulgation of the law are void, altogether invalid and null. If someone, in good faith and invincibly ignorant of that law, happens to enter such a contract after the month has elapsed, he will indeed be free from fault, on account of invincible ignorance; and consequently he ought also to be free from penalty, which is justly due to no one except for fault. Yet any loss that happens to arise from the nullity of that contract he will not only bear but is also bound to bear, even according to conscience, by virtue of the obedience owed to laws and out of regard for public utility. The same must be held also in many other laws: for example, those by which persons are disabled, by which privileges are revoked, by which interest on loans is limited, by which fixed prices of saleable goods are set, and similar ones, which the Canonists and Theologians discuss at length. Nor should this seem unfair to anyone. For although a loss is sometimes called a penalty, this is done only by analogy, and very improperly. For otherwise the reason of a penalty properly so called and that of a loss are quite different. If someone innocent is made to suffer a penalty, an injury is done to him; and a loss can very often be inflicted on an innocent person without any injury. And let these things concerning the promulgation of law* be said, so far as is sufficient for our present purpose.

units.la: X. De Lege Pœnali proximè agendum. Ubi missis eorum plerisque, quæ solent à Casuistis multis & inutiliter disputari, quæque magis ad forum externum & litigiosum, (idque ferè ex jure Canonico & Pontificio, quod nostrà non multum interest.) quàm ad forum Conscientiæ internum pertinent: contenti erimus pauca quædam & præcipua delibasse, quæ propius ad conscientiæ regimen conducere judicamus. Occurrit in hoc genere Dubium primum, an ad Legis essentiam aliquo modo pertineat pœnæ constitutio? Respondeo, videri pertinere. Non quidem ut aliquid intrinsecè requisitum ad complendam legis essentiam, ita ut Lex, nisi appositâ pœnâ, non esset Lex: sed consultive tamen, ut aliquid necessarium ad hoc, ut Lex finem quem intendit efficaciter consequatur. Forma enim & essentia legis in præceptione consistit, (Præceptionem hic intelligite latiùs sumptam, ut prohibitionem simul complectatur: quomodo in Scripturis accipi solent voces [illegible, ~4 letters] & ἐντολὴ[?] & Theologis communiter tam negativa mandata quam affirmativa, Præcepta dicuntur) Et ab hac præceptione sola pendet utraque illa vis, quam Legi nelle diximus, dirigendi scilicet actiones & obligandi conscientias subditorum. Habet enim subditus sufficientem normam secundum quam dirigere debet actiones suas, & ad cujus observationem, nisi velit officio suo deesse, astringitur in Conscientiâ, simulac rescierit legitimum superiorem suum, hoc vel illud lege præcepisse, sive sit illi legi appositá aliqua pœnâ, sive non. Non ergo ex naturâ ipsius legis, quæ in mera præceptione consistit, exurgit hæc pœnam apponendi necessitas: sed, (ut legis præceptio quæ nuda non {'}sufficeret, suum cum vigore sortiatur effectum, ex duplici alia hypothesi: subjecti nempe, & finis. Expedit enim ut leges sanctissimæ observentur, quæ est hypothesis ex parte finis: suppositá tamen humani cordis innatâ pravitate (quæ est altera hypothesis ex parte subjecti) fieri vix ac ne vix potest, quin contemptui habeantur vel utilissimæ leges (quæ est plerorumque mortalium quâ negligentiâ, quâ pervivacia,) ni {2}metu saltem contineantur utcunque in officio, qui ludos faciunt Conscientiæ dictamen. Hinc factum, (ex duplici inquam hac hypothesi) ut Reipubl. salutare, & sibi necessarium semper judicarint prudentissimi quique Legislatores, sancire pœnis legum observantiam. Idque Dei ipsius exemplo, cui visus est eam quam primam dedit homini legem, non sine pœnæ interminatione edicere, Gen. 3. Aliquot forrassis boni cives, quorum parcissima ubique seges est, solâ officii conscientiâ, patriæque & virtutis amore adductí, etsi nulla esset propositá pœnâ, ultrò legibus obtemperarent; ast plurima turba solâ formidine pœnæ adiguntur ad officium faciendum. Patet igitur quæ sit in condendis legibus pœnarum constituendarum necessitas.
units.tr: X. We must next deal with the penal law. Here I shall set aside most of the matters that the casuists commonly and unprofitably dispute, which belong more to the external and litigious forum (and that largely from the Canon and Papal law, which does not greatly concern us) than to the internal forum of conscience. I shall be content to touch briefly on a few points, the principal ones, which I judge more conducive to the governing of conscience. The first question that arises in this kind is whether the imposition of a penalty belongs in some way to the essence of a law? I answer that it seems to belong. Not indeed as something intrinsically required to complete the essence of law, so that a law without an attached penalty would not be a law; but consultatively, as something necessary for the law to attain effectively the end it intends. For the form and essence of a law consists in precept (understand precept here in the wider sense, so as to include prohibition as well, as in Scripture the words are customarily taken, and as theologians commonly call both negative commands and affirmative ones precepts). And on this precept alone depend both those powers which we said belong to law, namely directing actions and binding the consciences of subjects. For the subject has a sufficient rule by which he ought to direct his actions, and to whose observance he is bound in conscience, unless he wishes to fail in his duty, as soon as he learns that his lawful superior has commanded this or that by law, whether or not any penalty is attached to that law. Therefore the necessity of attaching a penalty does not arise from the nature of the law itself, which consists in bare precept; but, so that a precept which by itself would not suffice may obtain its effect with force, it depends on two further hypotheses: that of the subject and that of the end. For it is expedient that the most holy laws be observed, which is the hypothesis on the part of the end; yet, given the innate wickedness of the human heart (which is the other hypothesis on the part of the subject), it can scarcely if ever happen that even the most useful laws are not held in contempt, owing to the negligence and perversity of most mortals, unless they are restrained in some measure in their duty by fear at least, those who make a mockery of the dictate of conscience. Hence it has come about (from this double hypothesis, I say) that the wisest legislators have always judged it both salutary for the commonwealth and necessary for themselves to sanction the observance of laws with penalties. And this they did by the example of God himself, who was pleased to decree, not without the threat of a penalty, the first law he gave to man (Gen. 3.). Perhaps a few good citizens, of whom the harvest is everywhere very scanty, moved by the sense of duty alone and by love of country and virtue, would obey the laws even if no penalty were proposed; but the greater crowd is driven to do its duty by fear of punishment alone. It is plain, then, what the necessity of establishing penalties is in enacting laws.

units.la: XI. Dubium
units.tr: XI. Question

units.la: XI. Dubium Secundum est, de Obligatione legis pœnalis, quoad extensionem: utrum scilicet Lex pœnalis obliget ad pœnam tantum, vel etiam ad culpam? Quod est quærere, an subditus legi & officio suo ita faciat satis, si paratus sit pœnam legi constitutam subire, ut non sit peccati reus etsi legis præceptionem non observet, aut annon etiam obligetur in conscientia ad præstandum illud quod lege præcipitur. Cui dubio ut distinctius & clarius respondeatur, quia magni momenti quæstio est, & cujus frequentissimus usus est in vitâ communi: explicandæ rei gratiâ non erit alienum, nonnulla quæ præcognosci utile est, præmittere. Sciendum igitur Primò, legem humanam positivam eam solam pœnalem dici, quæ ex arbitrio Legislatoris expresse statuit in transgressores pœnam aliquam temporalem: adeoque in tota hac tractatione, quoties occurrit pœnæ mentio, non aliam intelligi pœnam, nisi temporalem. Dupliciter autem sumitur Temporalis: aut ut Spirituali opponitur, aut ut Æternæ. Accipiuntur enim fere in communi sermone ut membra invicem contradistincta: nunc Spirituale & Temporale; nunc Æternum & Temporale. Quin ergo tria sunt omninò Pœnarum genera; sive quis species aut modos, aut gradus dicere malit. Quicquid enim Pœnæ nomine venit, aut est primò, Pœna Spiritualis; qualis est amissio sive carentia gratiæ & amicitiæ Dei, sive gaudii interni & consolationis quæ ex ejus gratiæ amicitiæque sensu oritur. Aut est secundò, Pœna Æterna, quæ consistit partim in æternâ carentiâ beatificæ visionis Dei & Christi, partim in æternis cruciatibus. Aut est tertiò, Pœna Temporalis, ab utraque priori distincta; quæ & pertinet ad statum præsentis vitæ, & circa corpus ac res externas tantùm versatur; nec tollit ex se & necessariò aut sensum gratiæ Dei, aut vitæ æternæ spem: cujufmodi sunt amissio pecuniæ, exilium, carcer, infamia, minutio capitis, flagella, & quæ sunt ejusmodi alia, ipsa denique mors corporalis. Ejusmodi pœnarum quæ præcipuæ habentur, & frequentioris sunt usus, ad 4 capita revocantur, Ezr. 7. 26. Mortem scilicet, Exilium, Amissionem bonorum, & Carcerem,
units.tr: XI. The second question concerns the obligation of a penal law as to its extent: namely, whether a penal law binds only to the penalty, or also to the fault? This is to ask whether a subject does enough for the law and for his duty if he is ready to undergo the penalty fixed by the law, so that he is not guilty of sin even though he does not observe the precept of the law; or whether he is not also bound in conscience to perform what the law commands. To answer this doubt more distinctly and clearly, since it is a question of great weight and of very frequent use in common life, it will not be out of place, for the sake of explaining the matter, to premise some points which it is useful to know beforehand. It must be known, therefore, first, that a human positive law is called penal only when, by the will of the Legislator, it expressly fixes some temporal penalty upon transgressors; and so throughout this whole treatment, wherever mention of a penalty occurs, no penalty is to be understood except a temporal one. Now temporal is taken in two ways: either as opposed to spiritual, or as opposed to eternal. For in ordinary speech they are taken as mutually distinct members: sometimes spiritual and temporal, sometimes eternal and temporal. Therefore there are altogether three kinds of penalties, or, if anyone prefers, three species, or modes, or degrees. For whatever comes under the name of penalty is either first a spiritual penalty, such as the loss or lack of the grace and friendship of God, or of inward joy and consolation which arises from the sense of his grace and friendship. Or it is second an eternal penalty, which consists partly in the eternal lack of the blessed vision of God and Christ, partly in eternal torments. Or it is third a temporal penalty, distinct from both the former; which both pertains to the state of the present life and concerns only the body and external goods, and which does not of itself and necessarily take away either the sense of God's grace or the hope of eternal life: such are the loss of money, exile, prison, infamy, loss of civil status, stripes, and other things of this kind, and finally bodily death itself. The penalties of this kind which are regarded as chief, and are of more frequent use, are reduced to four heads (Ezr. 7. 26.): namely death, exile, confiscation of goods, and imprisonment.

units.la: XII. Sciendum Secundò, Pœnam, ut culpæ oppositam, iterum duobus modis accipi. Aliquando enim latè & Materialiter accipitur, prout ei opponitur oppositione contrariâ; id est, ut species altera condividens idem genus. Et sic omne malum quod cuiquam obvenit, quod non est malum culpæ, Pœna dicitur, vel malum pœnæ; etiamsi non infligatur ei qui id ipsum patitur propter aliquam antecedentem culpam, sed aliunde (ut casu fortassis aut per injuriam) contingat. Sic morbus inopinus, pecunia furto ablata, vulnus à latrone illatum, naufragio aut incendio amissa bona, omne denique damnum aut nocumentum quod perpessu grave est, inter Pœnalia numeri solent; & sub Pœnæ appellatione venire.
units.tr: XII. It must be known secondly that penalty, as opposed to fault, is taken in two ways. For sometimes it is taken broadly and materially, as it is opposed to fault by contrary opposition; that is, as one species dividing the same genus. And in this sense every evil that befalls anyone which is not an evil of fault is called a penalty, or an evil of penalty; even if it is not inflicted on the person who suffers it on account of some preceding fault, but comes upon him from elsewhere (perhaps by chance or through injury). Thus an unexpected sickness, money stolen by theft, a wound inflicted by a robber, goods lost by shipwreck or fire, in short every loss or harm that is grievous to endure, are usually counted among penal things and come under the name of penalty.

units.la: Quandoque etiam restrictius accipitur Pœna vocabulum, & quasi formaliter, prout culpæ opponitur oppositione relativâ; id est, quatenus quis eâ afficitur propter præcedentem culpam : ut si quis ob rem alterius furto ablatam multetur quadruplo, aut exulare jubeatur propter seditionem. Et hæc est propria, prior illa impropria, vocis Pœnæ significatio : improprie[?] nim Pœnæ dicitur, quam non præcessit Culpa. Unde illa notissima Pœnæ definitio, quòd sit Supplicium, quo quis propter delictum afficitur. Secundum utramque vocis significationem loqui intendimus, in præsenti disputatione prout res postulabit. Sed posterior hæc præcipua est: quia pœnalis Lex dicitur,non tam respectu damni aut nocumenti, quod alicui potest occasione Legis, (idque fortassis juste, sine aliquâ tamen suâ culpâ) contingere; quàm respectu illius supplicii, quod ex Legis determinatione constitutum est eis qui eam transgrediuntur.
units.tr: Sometimes, however, the word penalty is taken more narrowly, and as it were formally, as it is opposed to fault by relative opposition; that is, insofar as someone is afflicted with it on account of a preceding fault: for example, if someone is fined fourfold for another's property stolen by theft, or is ordered to go into exile on account of sedition. This is the proper meaning of the word penalty, and the former is improper; for that is improperly called a penalty which was not preceded by fault. Hence that most familiar definition of penalty: that it is punishment, by which someone is afflicted on account of a crime. I intend to speak in the present disputation in accordance with both meanings of the word, as the matter shall require. But the latter is the principal one: because a law is called penal not so much with respect to the harm or loss which may happen to someone by occasion of the law (which may perhaps happen justly, and yet without any fault of his), as with respect to that punishment which has been fixed by the determination of the law for those who transgress it.

units.la: XIII. Sciendum Tertiò, Legem Pœnalem, aliam esse purè Pœnalem, aliam mixtam. Lex purè pœnalis est, quæ simplici ordinatione pœnam apponit tantum, nec tamen quicquam, expressè aut jubendo præcipit aut vetando: Exempli gratiâ, Lex fit quæ potestatem faciat popularibus alicujus urbis vel oppidi, eligendi quotannis unum aliquem ex honestioribus civibus in Prætorem, cum adjectâ hujusmodi clausulâ. “Qui civium electus prætor urbanam recusaverit, centum aureos in commune pendito.” Hæc Lex purè pœnalis est: quia pœnam constituit quidem recusantibus id munus suscipere; nulli tamen idipsum aut suscipere præcipit aut prohibet recusare. Lex Pœnalis mixta est, quæ aliquid fieri præcipit aut vetat, adjectâ insuper pœna transgressoribus irrogandâ. Exempli gratiâ ponamus Legem sub hac aut simili formâ promulgari, “Nemo merces domesticas extra regnum exportet, aut peregrinas merces advectas intra regnum divendito, nisi consuetum vectigal ante solverit, qui locus fecerit, mercium amissione luito.” Lex pœnalis est, quia appositam habet pœnam: non tamen purè pœnalis, sed mixtè; quia (sub illâ pœnâ) præcipit vectigalia solvi, vetat afferri aut distrahi merces vectigali insoluto. Sunt qui duabus hic tertiam Legi pœnalis speciem addendum putant: scilicet, quæ præceptionem simul contineat & pœnam neutram tamen positivè & specialiter, sed sub disjunctione ἀδιαφόρως alterutram. Exemplo sit Lex sub tali forma, “A popularibus electus, aut prætor urbanus, centum aureos in commune pendito.” Atqui nihil opus est ob hanc causam addi speciem novam. Nec enim multiplicandæ sunt rerum species sine necessitate. a) conquod et qui eam , aliam è pœnapponi aut jutia, Le us urbi uem e adjectas. præcommu uia pœnus fui præcipi st, qu iper pœ gratia promul pœrrato ium di lverit Le non ta à pœnâ distrah ibus hi t: sci pœnam sub di sit Le præt ilopu Nec e necessitate tate : & disjunctiva hæc forma proponendi legem ad purè pœnalem referri debet, quia præceptionem reipsa nullam continet. Si dicas, præcipi duarum rerum, etsi non definitè alteram, indefinitè tamen alterutram : facilè regeram, at præcipere indefinitè, & sub disjunctione, non magis præcipere est, (siquidem proprie loqui velimus,) quàm homo pictus est homo. Est ergo disjunctiva hæc Lex, purè (ut dixi) pœnalis : quod vel ex collatâ utriusque exempli forma manifestum est. Sive enim edixerit Legislator illo modo, Qui electus prætuiram recusaverit centum pendito ; sive hoc altero, Electus aut prætuiram gerito, aut centum pendito : tantundem est. Utrobique Jensus idem, eadem verborum vis, par obligatio.
units.tr: XIII. It must be known thirdly that a penal law is one thing purely penal, another mixed. A purely penal law is one which by simple ordinance attaches a penalty only, and yet expressly commands or forbids nothing, either by bidding or by forbidding. For example, let there be a law which gives the people of some city or town the power of choosing each year one of the more respectable citizens as praetor, with this clause added: "Whichever citizen chosen praetor refuses the city office shall pay a hundred gold pieces into the public treasury." This law is purely penal, because it fixes a penalty indeed for those who refuse to undertake that office; yet it does not command anyone to undertake it or forbid him to refuse it. A penal law is mixed which commands something to be done or forbids it, with a penalty to be imposed on transgressors added besides. For example, let us suppose a law promulgated in this or a similar form: "No one shall export domestic goods beyond the kingdom, or sell foreign goods brought within the kingdom, unless he has first paid the customary duty; whoever does so shall forfeit the goods." This law is penal, because it has an attached penalty; yet it is not purely penal but mixed, because (under that penalty) it commands duties to be paid, and forbids goods to be brought in or sold while the duty is unpaid. There are some who think that a third species of penal law should be added to these two: namely, one which contains a precept and yet attaches neither penalty positively and specifically, but either one of them by disjunction, indifferently. Let an example be a law in such a form: "Whoever is chosen by the people as praetor or city magistrate shall pay a hundred gold pieces into the public treasury." But there is no need for a new species to be added on this account. For species of things are not to be multiplied without necessity. Nor is this disjunctive form of proposing a law to be referred to the purely penal class, because in fact it contains no precept. If you say that one of two things is commanded, though not that one in particular, yet indefinitely one or the other, I will readily reply that to command indefinitely, and by disjunction, is no more to command (if we wish to speak properly) than a painted man is a man. This disjunctive law is therefore purely penal, as I said; and this is plain from comparing the form of each example. For whether the Legislator has decreed in the one way, "Whoever is chosen and refuses the praetorship shall pay a hundred," or in the other way, "Let the one chosen either hold the praetorship or pay a hundred": it amounts to the same thing. In both the sense is the same, the force of the words the same, and the obligation equal.

units.la: XIV. Sciendum Quarto, inter obligationem ad Culpam & obligationem ad pœnam temporalem, non esse necessariam connexionem ; aut certè non ita necessariam ut sit etiam reciproca. A pœnâ quidem temporali proprie dictâ ad culpam necessaria est consecutio: validum proinde est hoc argumentum, Petrus ex lege puniendus est, ergo culpam admisit.
units.tr: XIV. It must be noted, fourthly, that between obligation to fault and obligation to temporal punishment there is no necessary connection, or at least not one so necessary that it is also reciprocal. From temporal punishment properly so called to fault the inference is necessary. So this argument is valid: Peter is to be punished by law, therefore he has committed a fault.

units.la: Sed à pœnâ temporali minùs proprie dictâ, putà damno aut re simili, non necessariò infertur culpa : potest enim aliquis sine culpâ sua obligari ad damnum, ut aliquoties ante diximus. Neque etiam à culpâ ad pœnam temporalem reciproca est consecutio, quia fieri potest ut quis obligetur ad culpam ut interim non obligetur ad pœnam: pœnam nimirum temporalem ; nam spiritualis & æternæ pœnæ longè alia ratio est. Verbi gratiâ ; siquis culpam admiserit (puta si mendacium dixerit, si amici arcana consilia prodiderit, si proximi famam susurris læserit, aut aliud simile) cui lege humanâ nulla sit pœna constituta, non poterit sine injustitiâ ab homine neque verò necesse est eum à Deo affici pœnâ aliquâ temporali. Cæterum, ne quis sibi improbus nimis adblandiatur, peccétque ista licentiùs, quòd putet se exsortem fore pœnæ temporali: expedit ei subinde meminisse, obligatum se nihilominùs ad pœnam multò graviorem, spiritualem scilicet, & æternam. Quæ utraque pœna cum omni culpâ ita necessariò & reciprocè conjuncta est, ut Pœna semper supponat antecedentem Culpam, (Deus enim neminem punit immeritum; ) & culpam necessariò tandem consequatur (nisi scu[?]currat Dei clementia culpam remittentis in Christo, per fidem & pœnitentiam, ) commerita pœna.
units.tr: But from a temporal punishment taken less properly, such as a loss or something similar, fault does not necessarily follow. For a person can be obliged to a loss without his own fault, as we have said several times before. Nor again is the inference from fault to temporal punishment reciprocal, since a person may be obliged to fault while for the time being not being obliged to the penalty, namely the temporal penalty. The case of spiritual and eternal punishment is quite different. For example: if anyone has committed a fault (say he has told a lie, betrayed a friend's secret counsels, injured a neighbour's reputation by whispering, or something similar) for which no penalty is fixed by human law, he cannot be punished by a man without injustice, and it is by no means necessary that God should visit him with any temporal punishment. Yet, lest any wicked person flatter himself too much and sin more freely because he thinks he will be exempt from temporal punishment, it is useful for him to remember from time to time that he is nonetheless obliged to a far heavier penalty, namely spiritual and eternal punishment. Each of these penalties is so necessarily and reciprocally joined to every fault that the punishment always presupposes a preceding fault (for God punishes no one who does not deserve it), and the fault must in the end be followed by the punishment it has earned, unless the clemency of God, who remits the fault in Christ through faith and repentance, intervenes.

units.la: XV. His ita præmissis, ut dubio propositò respondeatur, pono aliquot conclusiones. C O N. C L U S I O P R I M A. Quatenus Lex pœnalis obliget subditum in Conscientia, ex mente & intentione Legislatoris, si de eâ certi aliquid constet, imprimis judicandum est. Hoc est, si certò constet Legislatorem intendisse obligare subditos ad culpam etiam & non solùm ad pœnam; certum est eos obligari ad observandum id quod lege præcipitur, nec satisfacere officio, si parati sint pœnam lege constitutam subire. Quod si manifestum sit eum non intendisse obligare nisi ad pœnam tantùm; subditos etiam certum est ultra pœnam non obligari. Ratio est, quia fundamentum obligationis Legum, (ut alias ostendimus,) est Legislatoris potestatem habentis voluntas sufficienter manifestata: Ergo ubi voluntas Legislatoris, quæ est adæquata mensura ejus obligationis quam Lex inducit, manifesta est; de obligationis mensurâ non est quòd ulterius ambigatur.
units.tr: XV. With these things thus premised, so that the question proposed may be answered, I lay down several conclusions. FIRST CONCLUSION. So far as a penal law binds a subject in conscience, this must be judged chiefly from the mind and intention of the lawgiver, if anything certain about it is known. That is, if it is certain that the lawgiver intended to oblige subjects to fault as well as to punishment, it is certain that they are bound to observe what the law commands, and that they do not discharge their duty merely by being ready to undergo the penalty laid down by the law. But if it is plain that he intended to oblige only to the penalty, it is also certain that subjects are not bound beyond the penalty. The reason is that the foundation of the obligation of laws (as we have shown elsewhere) is the sufficiently manifest will of the lawgiver who holds power. Therefore where the will of the lawgiver, which is the adequate measure of the obligation that the law creates, is manifest, there is no reason to doubt further about the measure of the obligation.

units.la: XVI. Quæres fortassè, quæ certitudo sufficiat ad hoc, ut subditus aliquis possit esse securus in Conscientiâ, sibi satis constare quæ fuerit mens & intentio Legislatoris? Respondeo, frustrà expectari in Moralibus, propter infinitam circumstantiarum varietatem & incertitudinem rerum humanarum, certitudinem quam vocant Mathematicam, quæ demonstratione constat, & cui impossibile est subesse falsum. Haberi tamen potest de Legislatoris intentione plerumque certitudo quædam Logica; quæ scilicet colligitur ex ipsis Legis verbis: è quibus ita perspicuè claret quandoque ipsius intentio, ut non sit opus ulteriore evidentiâ. Elucescit autem mens Legislatoris, partim ex formâ & modo praecipiendi; partim ex pœnæ appositæ gravitate: sed præcipuè ex proœmio ipsius Legis; in quo, ut acceptior sit populo Lex, solet Legislator consilii sui de eâ Lege ferendâ causas & rationes exponere, quàm sit Lex justa, quàm fuerit tollendis incommodis & abusibus necessaria, quàm futura sit Reipublicæ utilis.
units.tr: XVI. You may perhaps ask what certainty is enough for a subject to be secure in conscience, in being sufficiently assured of the mind and intention of the lawgiver? I answer that in moral matters one vainly looks for that certainty which they call mathematical, which rests on demonstration and to which falsehood cannot possibly attach, because of the infinite variety of circumstances and the uncertainty of human affairs. Yet about the lawgiver's intention one can usually have a certain logical certainty, namely that which is gathered from the very words of the law. From these the intention itself is sometimes so clearly evident that no further proof is needed. The mind of the lawgiver shines forth partly from the form and manner of commanding, partly from the severity of the penalty attached, but chiefly from the preface of the law itself. In that preface, so that the law may be more acceptable to the people, the lawgiver usually sets out his reasons for enacting it: how just the law is, how necessary it is for removing inconveniences and abuses, how useful to the commonwealth it will be.

units.la: Ex quibus omnibus debitè expensis, unà cum circumstantiarum etiam justâ collatione, non erit difficile, ut plurimum viro probo & prudenti intentionem Legislatoris perdiscere, & habere de eâ certitudinem sufficientem, id est, Moralem; (in moralibus enim sufficit certitudo moralis;) ita ut possit concludere Legislatorem hoc, vel diversum, indubiè intendisse. Quòd si subditus non sit tanti acuminis vel judicii, ut omnia possit rationum[?] ex utraque parte momenta rite expendere; aut si vereatur, (quum sit unusquisque in causa propria parum idoneus judex,) ne in sui ipsius gratiam, Legislatoris mentem favorabilius interpretetur quàm oporteret: consultissimum erit subdito in utroque casu, si negotium sit tanti, (hoc est, si futurum sit ei valde incommodum & onerosum, id observare quod Lege præceptum est) ad virum aliquem probatæ pietatis & peritiæ negotium deferre, ei rem totam nudè, simpliciter & sincerè aperire, & in ipsius demum judicio & sententiâ acquiescere.
units.tr: From all these things duly weighed, together with a fair comparison of the circumstances, it will not be difficult for a good and prudent man, in most cases, to learn the intention of the lawgiver and to have about it a sufficient certainty, that is, a moral one (for in moral matters moral certainty is enough), so that he can conclude without doubt that the lawgiver intended this or the contrary. But if the subject is not of such keenness or judgement that he can rightly weigh the considerations on both sides, or if he fears (since each man is a very poor judge in his own cause) that he may interpret the lawgiver's mind more favourably to himself than he ought, then in either case it will be wisest for the subject, if the matter is of such weight (that is, if it would be very inconvenient and burdensome for him to observe what the law commands), to refer the matter to some man of proven piety and skill, to lay the whole thing before him plainly, simply and sincerely, and in the end to rest in his judgement and opinion.

units.la: XVII. Sed quia fieri potest, nec rarò post adhibitam omnem diligentiam de [illegible, ~5 letters] gislatoris, ex ipsâ Lege, nulla habeatur certitudo aut non tanta ut in eâ tutò acquiescat viri boni conscientia : quærendum ulterius est, in tam dubio casu, utram interpretationem magis expediat sequi ; benigniorémne quod nonnullis visum, an vero alii suadent, strictiorem? Dicitur vir magnæ inter Canonistas authoritatis Martinus Navarrus in ea fuisse sententiâ, ut putaret nullam Legem pœnalem obligare ad culpam per se, sed tantùm ad pœnam. Alii è diverso docuerunt, omnem Legem pœnalem, nisi de Legislatoris mente constet in contrarium, obligare ad culpam. Fateor mihi semper [illegible, ~6 letters]stas fuisse extremas quasque sententias : & fieri potest, ut quemadmodum illi nimis laxè, sic illi nimium rigidè pronunciârint. Ut ergo in re tam dubiâ, certi aliquid quod sequamur habeamus: esto hæc CONCLUSIO SECUNDA. Lex pure pœnalis, per se & ordinariè, obligat tantùm ad pœnam, non item ad culpam. Dico primò, Lex pure pœnalis : sive ea categoricè enunciatur, sive disjunctivè. Dico secundò, Per se : quia per accidens, & ex suppositione prioris obligationis potest obligare & ad culpam. Cum scilicet Lex pœnalis eo fine lata est, ut metu pœnæ subditi cogantur ad officium, ad quod ante obligati erant aliquâ priore, Divinâ, Naturali, aut Humanâ. Sic istæ pœnales [“ Qui hominem occiderit, capite plectitor. Qui merces exportat, aut vectigal ante solvito, aut merces amittito,] obligant ad culpam: ita ut conscientiam non liberaverit siquis pœnam subierit, nisi & præceptioni Legis paruerit. Non tamen Per se virtute propriâ sic obligant, sed vi obligationis præcedaneæ ex anterioris alicujus legis præceptione enatæ. Obligatus enim erit subditus, dictis legibus ex hypothesi nostrâ nondum latis, & Lege Divina ne perpetraret Homicidium; & Lege Patria, ad vectigalia imperata folvendum. Dico tertio Ordinarie : quia fieri potest extraordinarie, rerum præsentium statu & conditione sic exigente, ut quod alias liberum esset potuisset omitti, evadat pro hic & nunc ita facto necessarium, ut peccet & officio suo desit qui idipsum non fecerit. Ordinarie tamen, & extra casus ejusmodi singulares ; qui paratus est pœnam legi appositam subire, lege illâ, si sit pure pœnalis, non ultra tenetur.
units.tr: XVII. But since it can happen, and not rarely, that after every diligence has been applied to the [illegible] of the lawgiver, no certainty is had from the law itself, or not so great a certainty that a good man's conscience can rest securely in it, we must further ask, in such a doubtful case, which interpretation it is more expedient to follow: the milder one, which has seemed right to some, or the stricter one, which others advise? A man of great authority among the Canonists, Martin Navarrus, is said to have held the view that no penal law binds to fault in itself, but only to the penalty. Others, on the contrary, have taught that every penal law, unless it is certain from the lawgiver's mind that the opposite is intended, does bind to fault. I confess that to me both extreme opinions have always seemed... and it may be that, as the former pronounced too loosely, so the latter pronounced too rigidly. So that in a matter so doubtful we may have something certain to follow, let this be the SECOND CONCLUSION: A purely penal law, in itself and ordinarily, binds only to the penalty, not likewise to fault. I say first, a purely penal law, whether it is stated categorically or disjunctively. I say second, in itself, because by accident, and on the supposition of a prior obligation, it can bind also to fault: namely when a penal law is passed with the aim that subjects, through fear of the penalty, may be compelled to the duty to which they were already bound by some prior law, divine, natural or human. Thus such penal laws as "Whoever kills a man shall be put to death" and "Whoever exports goods shall pay the duty beforehand, or lose the goods" do bind to fault, so that a person who has undergone the penalty has not cleared his conscience unless he has also obeyed the command of the law. Yet they do not bind in this way in themselves, by their own virtue, but by the force of a preceding obligation arising from the command of some earlier law. For the subject would already be bound, on our hypothesis, by those laws not yet enacted, and by the divine law not to commit homicide, and by the law of the country to pay the duties imposed. I say third, ordinarily: because it can happen extraordinarily, when the state and condition of present circumstances so require that what would otherwise have been optional may, for the here and now, become so necessary that whoever fails to do it sins and falls short of his duty. But ordinarily, and apart from such singular cases, a person who is ready to undergo the penalty laid down by the law is not further bound by that law, if it is purely penal.

units.la: XVIII. Ratio totius Conclusionis est, quia Legislator non obligat nisi præcipiendo: proinde simplex ordinatio, qui nihil præcipit, non magis ex se obligat, quàm amici consilium, aut viri gravis adhortatio. Ut enim qui dat alteri consilium, aut cum hortatur ut hoc vel illud faciat, declarat quid ab eo cupiat fieri, non tamen eum ut id faciat obligat, sed nec obligare intendit ; haud aliter Legislator ea lege, quâ nihil subdito præcipit, sed tantùm ostendit quid ab eo sub propositæ pœnæ conditione fieri velit, præsumendus est non habuisse voluntatem eum ulterius obligandi quàm ad propositam pœnam. Quia si intentionem habuisset obligandi & ad culpam, facillimum ei fuisset, addita duntaxat præceptione suam illam intentionem significare. Ergo cum nec simplex & nuda ordinatio ex se obliget ad culpam, nec possit additio pœnæ temporalis ex se obligare nisi ad pœnam temporalem subeundam ; manifestum est, Legem pure pœnalem, quæ præter ista duo (simplicem dico ordinationem, & adjectam pœnam temporalem) nihil in se continet, quorum neutrum est obligatorium ad culpam, non posse ex se ad culpam, sed ad pœnam tantùm obligare. Et est simile de Legibus quas vocant conventionalibus: quo exemplo libentius utor, quòd conclusionem nostram non confirmet modò, sed & egregiè illustret. Cui etiam addi posset Testatoris Voluntas; & alia nonnulla, quorum est (quod ad obligandi vim saltem attinet) ratio omninò consimilis. In colæ alicujus villæ, qui condendi Leges proprie dictas potestate carent, in curia Domini manerii (sic enim ex usu forensi loquendum est,) aut aliàs extra curiam, de rebus quibusdam ad pacem & justitiam inter vicinos conservandam conducentibus inter se pacijcuntur, multa enim pecuniaria nomine pœnæ iis constituta, qui sic inita pacta violaverint. Cujusmodi conventiones, nostratibus vernaculo sermone Byp=Lawes [?] dicuntur, hoc est, Incolarum Leges: Byp [?] etenim prisca Saxonum Lingua habitationem significare notant Antiquariæ rei peritiores viri docti: nos cum aliis, docendi causa, Leges Conventionales dicemus. Etsi enim Pacta sint solùm & Conventiones inter privatas personas, & non Leges (siquidem proprie loquimur) ob defectum publicæ authoritatis; Legu tamen dici solent propter ἀναλογίαν illam quam habent cum proprie dictis legibus, quantum ad duos illos sæpe dictos Legum effectus, dirigendi scilicet & obligandi. Nam sicut Leges subditos; sic istæ Conventiones personas consentientes & dirigunt in agendo, & obligant ad officium. Certum est autem in istiusmodi Conventionibus, personæ contrahentes non intendisse se mutuò obligare ad culpam, sed ad pœnam tantum: exempli gratia, "Pacijcuntur inter se incolæ alicujus villæ, singulos patrisfamilias mense Maio quotannis triduanam operam reficiendis viis publicis personaliter collocaturos: qui non fecerint (supponamus autem singulas diurnas operas decem denariis æstimari) viginti denariorum multa luitunt." Hæc Lege conventionali certum est personas contrahentes illud imprimis intendisse, ut viæ publicæ [?] quotannis
units.tr: XVIII. The reasoning behind the whole Conclusion is that a Lawgiver binds only by commanding. A bare ordinance that commands nothing therefore does not bind of itself, any more than a friend's advice or a grave man's exhortation does. When someone gives another advice, or urges him to do this or that, he declares what he wishes done but does not bind him to do it, and does not intend to. In the same way, a Lawgiver who, by a law that commands the subject nothing, merely shows what he wishes done under the condition of a proposed penalty, must be presumed to have had no will to bind him beyond the proposed penalty. For if he had intended to bind him also to guilt, it would have been very easy for him to signify that intention by simply adding a command. Therefore, since neither a simple, bare ordinance binds of itself to guilt, nor can the addition of a temporal penalty bind of itself except to undergo a temporal penalty, it is clear that a law purely penal, which contains nothing beyond these two (I mean the simple ordinance and the added temporal penalty), neither of which is binding to guilt, cannot bind of itself to guilt, but only to penalty. The same holds for the laws which they call conventional. I use this example more gladly because it not only confirms our conclusion but illustrates it admirably. To these one might add the will of a testator and some other things, whose reasoning (at least as far as the power of binding goes) is entirely similar. Some tenants of a village, who lack the power to make laws properly so called, agree among themselves, in the court of the lord of the manor (for so we must speak, by forensic usage), or otherwise outside court, about certain matters conducive to keeping peace and justice among neighbours; a sum of money is fixed in the name of a penalty for those who violate the agreements so made. Such conventions are called in our vernacular Byp-Lawes [?], that is, Laws of the inhabitants; learned men skilled in antiquities note that Byp [?] in the ancient Saxon tongue signifies dwelling. For the sake of teaching, we, with others, will call them Conventional Laws. For although they are only pacts and conventions between private persons, and not laws (strictly speaking), because they lack public authority, they are nonetheless customarily called laws on account of the analogy they bear to laws properly so called, in respect of the two often-mentioned effects of laws, namely directing and binding. For just as laws direct their subjects, so these conventions both direct the consenting persons in acting and bind them to their duty. It is certain, however, that in conventions of this kind the contracting persons did not intend to bind one another to guilt, but only to penalty. For example: "The inhabitants of a certain village agree among themselves that each householder shall personally give three days' labour every May to repairing the public roads; those who do not do so (let us suppose each day's labour is valued at ten pence) shall pay a fine of twenty pence." By this conventional law it is certain that the contracting persons especially intended that the public roads [?] be repaired every year

units.la: Camden. in Britan. i. p. 401. (marginal reference, left margin) quotannis reficerentur, quin & illud insuper voluisse, ut unusquisque pater-familias personalem operam in rem tam utilem conferrent: aliter enim dupli multam secùs facientibus non constituissent. Cæterùm non minùs ex altera parte certum est, eos non intendisse fe mutuò ulterius obligare quàm ad multam solvendam ; fi cui ipsorum aut per alia negotia non liceret, aut quacunque aliâ de causâ non liberet, personalem suam operam præstare. Sic in re testamentariâ (nam & {1}'Testamentum instar Legis est, Executorem & {2}Legatarios dirigendo pariter & obligando, ) "Caius vult ut Caia uxor, "quoad vidua remanserit, ædes cum fundo vicino "quas à Titio emit, retineat ; fi alteri nupserit, eas "amittat. Constat id voluisse Caium, ut uxor vidua remaneret, nec alteri nuberet, ea enim intentione conditionem illam apposuit, ut uxorem tanti damni metu à fecundis nuptiis arceret. Nec tamen apponendo talem conditionem intendit (imò ne potuit quidem intendere) uxorem obligare ad culpam, ita ut peccaret si alteri nuberet.
units.tr: Camden, Britannia, i. p. 401. be repaired every year; and moreover that each householder should contribute personal labour to so useful a work. Otherwise they would not have imposed a double fine on those who acted differently. On the other hand, it is equally certain that they did not intend to bind one another further than to paying the fine, in case either of them was not permitted by other business, or for any other reason did not wish, to render his personal labour. So too in a matter of a will (for a testament is also like a law, directing and binding the executor and the legatees alike): "Caius wishes that his wife, for as long as she remains a widow, retain the house with the neighbouring field which she bought from Titius; if she marries another, let her lose them." It is agreed that Caius wished his wife to remain a widow and not marry again, for with that intention he added this condition, to keep his wife from a second marriage through fear of so great a loss. Yet in attaching such a condition he did not intend (indeed he could not even intend) to bind his wife to guilt, so that she would sin if she married another.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: XIX. Ast, inquies, ad Culpam & Pœna obligant, & Testamenta obligant. Nam & is peccat, qui pactum conventum non servat : & peccat legatarius, si aliter fecerit quàm testamento cautum est. Respondeo, longe aliud esse, si quis conventa, testamentum, aut leges violet : aliud si quis contra ejus quicum contraxit, Testatoris aut Legislatoris voluntatem fecerit sub conditionem latam vel prolatam. Quid intersit, quæ ante adduximus exempla optimè docebunt. In legem illam conventionalem, de triduanâ operâ præstandâ sub multâ pecuniariâ ; non continuo peccat, qui operam non confert, nisi & multam solvere recuset : stat enim pœnis si alterutrum fecerit, idque secundum intentionem pacisccentium, qui intendebant ad illam operam præstandam se mutuò obligare quidem, non tamen simpliciter & absolutè sed sub conditione prædictâ. Sic & in lege illa Testamentaria, Caia, si Caio defuncto alteri nubat, non peccat nubendo, etsi certum sit maluisse Testatorem, proinde & voluisse (nam qui mavult vult) ne id fieret: peccaret tamen proculdubio, si alteri jam nupta, legatas testamento sub ea conditione ædes cum fundo sibi retineret nec hæredi restitueret. Ratio utriusque exempli eadem est; scil. quia obligatio utrobique non fuit pura, simplex & absoluta, sed conditionalis tantum obligatio: conditio autem semper & ex sui natura suspendit obligationem, ita ut conditione præstita, ipso facto, quasi jam soluto vinculo, cadat obligatio. In Legibus item pure pœnalibus eodem omnino modo se res habet, quantum, ad obligandi modum & mensuram: quod facile intelligent, quibus ista inter se conferre vacat & libet; ut non sit nobis opus his explicandis diutius immorari.
units.tr: XIX. But, you will say, men are bound to guilt as well as to penalty, and testaments bind too. For one who does not keep an agreed pact also sins, and a legatee sins if he acts otherwise than the testament provides. I reply that it is quite different if someone violates agreements, a testament, or laws, and different if someone acts against the will of him with whom he contracted, of the Testator, or of the Lawgiver, under a condition imposed or set forth. The examples we adduced above will teach very well what the difference is. In the conventional law concerning three days' labour under a monetary fine, a person does not sin at once if he does not contribute the labour, unless he also refuses to pay the fine. For he stands by the penalties if he has done one or the other, and this according to the intention of the contracting parties, who meant to bind themselves mutually to render that labour, but not simply and absolutely, rather under the aforesaid condition. So too in that testamentary law: if Caia, after Caius has died, marries another, she does not sin by marrying, although it is certain that the Testator preferred, and therefore willed (for he who prefers, wills), that this should not happen. Yet she would undoubtedly sin if, already married to another, she kept for herself the house and field left to her under that condition and did not restore them to the heir. The reason for both examples is the same: the obligation in each case was not pure, simple and absolute, but only a conditional obligation. A condition, however, always and by its nature suspends the obligation, so that once the condition is fulfilled the obligation falls, as it were with the bond already dissolved by the very fact. In laws purely penal the matter stands in exactly the same way, as far as the manner and measure of binding is concerned. Those who have the leisure and the inclination to compare these things with one another will readily understand this, so there is no need for us to dwell longer on explaining it.

units.la: XX. Sed instabit adhuc fortassis quispiam: primo, non quenquam obligari ad pœnam, quin obligetur etiam ad culpam: quia non potest juste aliqui pœna irrogari, nisi propter antecedentem culpam, juxta illud Augustini, 'Omnis pœna, si justa est, peccati pœna est. Secundò, de ratione legis esse, ut aliquid præcipiat: ergo legem illam, quam dicimus pure pœnalem, aut non habere rationem Legis, si nihil præcipiat; aut si contineat in se saltem implicitè aliquam præceptionem, obligare & ad culpam: cùm sit culpa nihil aliud, quàm justæ præceptionis transgressio sive violatio.
units.tr: XX. But perhaps someone will press further. First, that no one is bound to penalty without also being bound to guilt, since a penalty cannot justly be inflicted except on account of a preceding guilt, according to that saying of Augustine: 'Every penalty, if it is just, is the penalty of sin.' Second, it is of the nature of a law that it commands something. Therefore the law which we call purely penal* either lacks the character of a law, if it commands nothing; or, if it contains at least implicitly some command, it binds also to guilt, since guilt is nothing other than the transgression or violation of a just command.

units.la: XXI. Ad prius objectum variè responderi potest. Verè enim dici potest primò. Pœnam quidem æternam, in quantum perfectam habet pœnæ rationem, non potest aliter considerari nisi sub ratione pœnæ, propterea necessariò supponere culpam aliquàm antecedentem quæ eam promerita fit, & propter quam, sine ullo alio respectu, qui culpæ reus est, eâ pœnâ afficitur: at pœnæ spiritualis, tùm etiam multò magis pœnæ temporalis, non esse eandem per omnia rationem. Etsi enim supponat utraque, quatenus pœna est, antecedentem aliquam culpam tali pœna dignam (alias utique non esset justa:) quia tamen potest utraque aliter considerari quàm sub ratione pœnæ, per respectum scilicet ad finem à puniente intentam, hoc est, quatenus ordinatur non tam ad vindicandam culpam præteritam, quàm ad impediendam culpam futuram;) inde fit, ut nec Deus, cum hominem pœnâ, sive spirituali sive temporali affligit, nec homo, cum hominem pœna temporali afficit, semper eorum peccata aut culpas respiciant, sed habeant saepissimè propositos sibi alios fines. Quo pertinet responsum illud Domini nostri Jesu Christi Discipulis interrogantibus de homine cæco nato, suáne an paternâ culpâ id ei accidisset, ut cæcus nasceretur, Joh. 9. 3. Nec ipse peccavit, inquit, nec parentes ejus (scilicet ut cæcus nasceretur) sed ut opera Dei manifestentur in eo, hoc factum est. Ratio est, quia in moralibus, eorum quæ fiunt æstimatio, itémque & denominatio, à causâ finali potius sumi debet, quàm à causâ efficiente meritoriâ.
units.tr: XXI. The first objection can be answered in various ways. It can be said, first, that eternal punishment, insofar as it has the full character of penalty, cannot be considered otherwise than under the aspect of penalty, and so must necessarily presuppose some antecedent guilt that has merited it, and on account of which, without any other respect, the guilty person is afflicted with that penalty. But spiritual penalty, and still more temporal penalty, does not have the same character in every respect. For although both, insofar as they are penalty, presuppose some antecedent guilt worthy of such a penalty (otherwise indeed they would not be just), yet because each can be considered otherwise than under the aspect of penalty, namely with respect to the end intended by the one who punishes, that is, insofar as it is directed not so much to avenging past guilt as to preventing future guilt, it follows that neither God, when He afflicts a man with penalty, whether spiritual or temporal, nor man, when he afflicts a man with temporal penalty, always has regard to their sins or guilts, but very often has other ends set before him. To this pertains the answer of our Lord Jesus Christ to His disciples, who asked about the man born blind whether he or his parents had sinned, so that he was born blind: "Neither did this man sin," He said, "nor his parents (namely, that he should be born blind), but that the works of God should be made manifest in him" (Joh. 9. 3). The reason is that in moral matters the estimation, and likewise the naming, of what is done ought to be taken from the final cause rather than from the efficient meritorious cause.

units.la: XXII. Deinde, secundò, dici potest, pœnæ temporalis relationem ad culpam in eâ duntaxat pœnâ propriè spectari, quæ culpæ relativè opponitur; non item in eâ quæ culpæ contrariè tantùm opponitur, quæ est laxior ejus vocis significatio & minùs propria. Hanc distinctionem ante explicuimus in secundo hujus dubii præcognito; nec opus est multis repetere. Suffecerit meminisse poenam legi purè pœnali appositam, non strictè & propriè, sed improprie & latè pœnam dici, prout significat alterum mali genus à malo culpæ diversum. Quale genus pœna potest sine injustitia legali alicui inferri propter finem utilem, (ut, verbi gratiâ, ad vitandum aliquod incommodum publicum) citra peccatum personæ patientis. Sic enim accepta pœnæ appellatio, omnia Infortunia, Damna, Adversa, aut quicquid homini accidit quod mallet non evenisse, complexu suo continet.
units.tr: XXII. Secondly, it can be said that the relation of temporal punishment to fault is properly considered only in that punishment which is relatively opposed to fault, and not in that which is merely contrariwise opposed to it. That is a looser and less proper use of the word. We explained this distinction earlier, in the second preliminary point of this question, and there is no need to repeat much. It is enough to remember that a penalty attached to a purely penal law is called a punishment not strictly and properly but improperly and broadly, insofar as it signifies a kind of evil distinct from the evil of fault. Such a penalty can be inflicted on someone, without legal injustice, for a useful end (for example, to avert some public inconvenience), and without fault on the part of the one who suffers it. For so taken, the term "punishment" embraces all misfortunes, losses, adversities, or whatever happens to a man that he would rather had not happened.

units.la: XXIII, Ista si cui vestrum minus satisfecerint, (nec ego sanè multùm contendero,) ast illud saltem imprimis dignum est observatu, quod tertio loco nunc subjicio, quum & totam hanc exhaurit dubitationem, & alteri simul objectioni aptissimè occurrat. Nimirum legem pœnalem qualis nunc sub incude est, quam utrumque intendit, & obligare subditum scil. & tamen non nisi conditionaliter obligare; duplicitèr posse considerari, vel tripliciter potiùs. Primò, præcisè quantum ad id, ad quod sub tali conditione præstandum intendit obligare: Secundo, quantum ad conditionem illam præcisè sub quâ intendit obligare; quorum illud legis ordinationem, hæc appositam ei pœnam continet: Tertiò, quoad totum aggregatum, hoc est, legem ipsam totam, quæ ex utriusque complexione consistit, simul sumptam. Hàc posità distinctione, dico primò, legis partem illam quæ conditionem sive pœnam tantùm continet, per se non obligare ad culpam: nuda enim conditio nihil ponit in esse, ut omnes concedunt, & est ex se manifestum. Non ergo peccat, imò officio suo optimè defungitur, qui legis pœnam vitat, modò id quod Lex ordinat præstiterit.
