Dico Secundo, nec illam legis partem quæ ordinationem continet, per se obligare ad culpam. Quia nulla Lex obligat ultra intentionem Legislatoris: Legislatorem autem non intendisse eâ legis parte per se obligare subditum ad culpam certum est; non enim intendiffet diffet & pra nem ; patet præst in leg nalem & ad fit & parter nim a pend vera fit nif gem disjun Leger è duc utrum XX legis p ad le fit ter fcilic dilige tranf at, nec c lud ligare alias auten conti ad cu præce [illegible, ~3 letters] quod diffet eum simpliciter obligasse, quia illa pars per se & præcisè sumpta nullam continet in se conditionem; at ex addita in altera parte legis conditionem patet eum non intendisse simpliciter obligare ad id præstandum quod Lex ordinat, sed sub conditione in lege expressâ. Dico tamen Tertiò, Legem Pœnalem, integrè & conjunctim sumptam, obligare & ad culpam. Hoc sensu, ut nimirum culpæ reus sit & peccet contra legem, qui cum alterutram ejus partem præstare debeat, neutram præstat. Sicut enim apud Dialecticos veritas propositionis disjunctivæ pendet ex veritate unius alicujus partis; ita ut tota vera sit cujus altera pars est vera, falsa autem non sit nisi utraque pars sit falsa: sic in moralibus, legem disjunctivam (omnis autem Lex pure pœnalis disjunctiva est, aut formaliter, aut æquivalenter,) Legem, inquam, disjunctivam observat, qui facit è duobus propositis alterutrum; non violat nisi qui utrumque negligit.
units.tr: XXIII. If these points have not fully satisfied some of you (nor indeed will I contend much about them), yet this above all is worth observing, which I now put third, since it both exhausts the whole question and meets the other objection most aptly. A penal law, such as is now under discussion, which both intends to bind the subject and yet binds only conditionally, can be considered in two ways, or rather in three. First, precisely as to that which it intends the subject to perform under such a condition. Second, as to the condition itself under which it intends to bind; of these, the former contains the law's ordinance, the latter the penalty attached to it. Third, as to the whole aggregate, that is, the entire law taken together, consisting of the combination of both. With this distinction laid down, I say first that the part of the law which contains only the condition or penalty does not of itself bind to fault. For a bare condition posits nothing in being, as all concede, and this is evident of itself. Therefore he does not sin, but rather discharges his duty very well, who avoids the penalty of the law, provided he has done what the law ordains. I say second that neither does that part of the law which contains the ordinance bind of itself to fault. For no law binds beyond the intention of the lawgiver, and it is certain that the lawgiver did not intend, by that part of the law alone, to bind the subject to fault. For he would not have intended to bind him absolutely by that part, since that part, taken by itself and precisely, contains no condition in itself. But from the condition added in the other part of the law, it is clear that he did not intend to bind absolutely to what the law ordains, but under the condition expressed in the law [illegible]. I say, however, third, that the penal law, taken whole and conjointly, binds also to fault. This is in the sense that one is guilty of fault and sins against the law who, when he ought to perform one or the other part of it, performs neither. For just as among the dialecticians the truth of a disjunctive proposition depends on the truth of one of its parts, so that the whole is true if one part is true, and false only if both parts are false, so in moral matters: he who does one of the two alternatives of a disjunctive law observes the law; only he who neglects both violates it.

units.la: XXIV. His satis, ut opinor, explicatis, quæ de legis pure pœnalis obligatione dicenda videbantur, ad legem pœnalem mixtam transeamus. De quâ sit tertia nostra Conclusio; Lex pœnalis mista (quæ scilicet aperte aliquid præcipit, observari, & quò diligentius observetur quod præcipitur, pœnam transgressoribus constituit,) & ad culpam obligat, & ad pœnam: ita ut nec legi satisfaciat, nec conscientiæ suæ, qui pœnam sustinet, nisi & illud fecerit quod lege imperatur. Ad pœnam obligare ejusmodi legem nemini potest esse dubium: alias quis usus esse posset adjectâ pœnâ? Obligare autem & ad culpam inde patet quòd manifestam continet præceptionem; & omnis præceptio obligat ad culpam: siquidem nihil aliud est Culpa, quàm præcepti alicujus transgressio, ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶν ἡ ἀνομία[?], 1 Joh. 3. Nec potest probabiliter dici, quod tamen sensisse videtur Navarrus, Legislatorem apponendo pœnam voluisse significare, se nō habuisse intentionem obligandi nisi ad illam appositam pœnam tantum. Animadvertite quaeso, quàm perversum sit pœnæ constitutionem, quàm certum est eo fine appositam esse præceptioni, ut ipsa præceptio ejus pœnæ metu sanctius & diligentius observaretur, sic interpretari, ut præcepti obligationem invalidet & tollat? Infinitæ sunt per orbem terrarum, adjectis insuper pœnis, latæ in fures, latrones, homicidas, perjuros, aliósque nefarios & sceleratos cives, leges: tulit etiam legem Deus Creator protoplastis hominibus, quà eis esum ligni quod erat in medio paradisi interdixit, appositâ si comiderent mortis pœnâ, Gen. 2. 17. Adeóne reperiri quenquam sanæ mentis inopem, ut existimet obligatum lege hac divinâ, Adamum, obligatos legibus illis humanis, alios, ad pœnam tantum, non etiam ad culpam? Quis dixerit, (ut illas alteras omittam leges humanas) lege illâ divinâ Adamum non fuisse obligatum in Conscientiâ, ut à fructu vetito abstineret; sed ad hoc tantùm, ut si comederet paratus esset mortis sententiam subire? Rejectâ ergo Navarri sententia, (si ea fuerit ipsius indubiè sententia, quod de tanti nominis viro vix crediderim) quæ & periculosa est, & ab omnibus fere reprehenditur; dicendum est; Legem pœnalem mixtam, quum & pœnalis sit, & præceptiva, obligare & ad pœnam, & ad culpam: ad pœnam, quatenus pœnalis est, & ad culpam, quatenus præceptiva est.
units.tr: XXIV. These matters having, as I think, been sufficiently explained, which seemed to need saying about the obligation of a purely penal law, let us pass to the mixed penal law. Concerning it our third Conclusion is this: a mixed penal law (namely one which openly commands something to be observed, and which, so that what is commanded may be observed more diligently, sets a penalty for transgressors) binds both to fault and to penalty. So one who suffers the penalty satisfies neither the law nor his own conscience unless he has also done what the law commands. That such a law binds to penalty no one can doubt; otherwise what use would the added penalty be? That it also binds to fault is clear from the fact that it contains a plain precept, and every precept binds to fault, since fault is nothing other than the transgression of some precept: "sin is lawlessness," 1 John 3. Nor can it be reasonably said, though Navarrus seems to have thought so, that the lawgiver, by appending a penalty, meant to signify that he had no intention of binding except to that appended penalty alone. Consider, I beg you, how perverse it is to interpret the establishment of a penalty, which is certainly appended to a precept so that the precept itself may be observed more reverently and diligently through fear of the penalty, in such a way that it invalidates and removes the obligation of the precept! Throughout the world there are countless laws, with penalties added, passed against thieves, robbers, murderers, perjurers, and other wicked and criminal citizens. God the Creator also gave a law to the first human beings, forbidding them to eat of the tree that was in the midst of the garden, with the penalty of death appended should they disobey (Gen. 2. 17). Can anyone of sound mind be found so foolish as to think that Adam was bound by this divine law only to the penalty, and not to fault, while others are bound by human laws to fault as well? Who would say (to omit those other human laws) that Adam, by that divine law, was not bound in conscience to abstain from the forbidden fruit, but only to this: that if he ate, he would be ready to undergo the sentence of death? Therefore, the opinion of Navarrus being rejected (if indeed it was his sincere opinion, which I can hardly believe of a man of such great name), an opinion which is both dangerous and is censured by almost everyone, we must say: a mixed penal law, since it is both penal and preceptive, binds both to penalty and to fault. To penalty insofar as it is penal, and to fault insofar as it is preceptive.

units.la: XXV. Restat Dubium tertium. An & quatenus teneatur legis pœnalis transgressor, ad pœnam lege constitutam ipso facto subeundam? Festinato opus est; ideóque rem paucis absolvam. Dico igitur primò, si pœna lege constituta ejusmodi sit, ut non imponat transgressori aliquid ab ipso faciendum vel patiendum, sed consistat potiùs in quadam in-habilitate habilitate ad faciendum aliquid quod facere effet ipsi commodum, aut in incapacitate recipiendi ali-quid quod effet ipsi gratum vel utile ; teneri le-gis violatæ reum ipso facto pœnam subire. Multæ sunt Leges quæ prohibent transgressores hoc vel illud facere ; ut leges civiles propter certas causas impediunt translationem Dominii. Sunt etiam multæ leges, quæ delinquentes decernunt ad aliquod temporis spacium incapaces alicujus muneris vel dignitatis : ut si prohiberetur statuto Academiæ perturbator pacis, ne liceat ei, infra biennium post crimen admissum, in domo Congregationis gratiam suam proponere. In his aliisque similibus casibus, ubi pœna in solâ inhabilitate vel incapacitate[?] consistit ; quia ad ejusmodi pœnam sustinendam non requiritur aliqua personæ puniendæ co-operatio, sed operandi potiùs cessatio quædam : tenetur sine dubio qui legem violavit, eam pœnam, etiam non requisitus, ultrò sufferre. Dico secundò, si pœna lege constituta sit ejusmodi, ut ad legis executionem necessariò requiratur cooperatio aliqua personæ delinquentis ; hoc est, ut qui puniendus est ipse aliquid faciat : non teneri reum (ordinarie) ad ejusmodi pœnam ipso facto subeundam, ante latam à judice sententiam : sive, quod idem est, priusquam à persona legitimam authoritatem habente ea pœna ab ipso exigatur. Tenetur quidem reus pœnas dare ; sed si reposcantur : alias non tenetur. Dico tertiò, reum, post latam à judice sententiam, aut à persona legitimam authoritatem habente requisitum, ad pœnam sponte suscipiendam teneri, etiam cum aliqua sua coope-ratione ; si ejusmodi cooperatio non sit contra humanitatem, etsi alias fortasse[?] admodum gravis & onerosa. Exempli gratiâ, si jubeatur pœnæ nomine grandem pecuniæ summam dependere, regno exire, &c. tenetur reus vi legis id facere. Quòd si pœna imposita non grave sit tantum, sed aliquid etiam in se contineat quod sit inhumanum, ut si quis jubeatur se flagellare, dextram sibi praecidere, cicutam bibere, &c. Dico quarto, in ejusmodi casibus tenere[?] quidem reum, ad poenam eam, quam scivit lege constitutam, quamque culpa sua commeruit, pas-sive subeundam ; non item obligari ad activè cooperandum in eadem. Et haec de Legum promulgandarum necessitate, & de Legum Pænalium obligationem[?], quae ad legum causam formalem aliquo modo pertinere videntur, dicta sunto.
units.tr: XXV. There remains the third question: whether, and in what way, the transgressor of a penal law is bound to undergo the penalty established by law ipso facto. Haste is needed, so I shall settle the matter briefly. I say, then, first: if the penalty established by law is of such a kind that it does not impose on the transgressor anything to be done or suffered by him, but consists rather in a certain disability to do something that would be advantageous to him, or in incapacity to receive something pleasing or useful to him, then the transgressor of the violated law is bound to undergo the penalty ipso facto. There are many laws which forbid transgressors to do this or that; thus civil laws, for certain causes, forbid the transfer of ownership. There are also many laws which for a time declare offenders incapable of some office or dignity: for example, if a university statute should forbid a disturber of the peace to propose his suit in the house of Congregation within two years after the crime committed. In these and similar cases, where the penalty consists in disability or incapacity, because no cooperation of the person to be punished is required in undergoing such a penalty, but rather a certain cessation of action, the one who has violated the law is undoubtedly bound to undergo that penalty even unasked. I say second: if the penalty established by law is of such a kind that some cooperation of the offending person is necessarily required for the execution of the law, that is, that he who is to be punished must himself do something, then the offender is not (ordinarily) bound to undergo such a penalty ipso facto, before sentence has been pronounced by the judge; or, which is the same, before the penalty is demanded of him by a person having lawful authority. The offender is indeed bound to pay penalties when they are demanded, but otherwise he is not bound. I say third: the offender, after sentence has been pronounced by the judge, or when required by a person having lawful authority, is bound to undertake the penalty willingly, even with some cooperation of his own, provided such cooperation is not contrary to humanity, though perhaps otherwise very grave and onerous. For example, if he is ordered to pay a large sum of money by way of penalty, or to leave the kingdom, etc., the offender is bound by force of the law to do this. But if the penalty imposed is not merely grave but also contains something inhuman in itself, as if someone were ordered to flog himself, to cut off his own right hand, to drink hemlock, etc., I say fourth: in such cases the offender is indeed bound to undergo passively that penalty which he knew was established by law and which he has deserved by his fault, but he is not likewise bound to cooperate actively in it. And let these things be said about the necessity of promulgating laws, and about the obligation of penal laws, which seem in some way to pertain to the formal cause of laws.

units.la: PRÆLECTIO NONA.
units.tr: LECTURE NINE.

units.la: De Legum Humanarum Obligatione ex parte Causæ Finalis.
units.tr: On the Obligation of Human Laws as regards the Final Cause.

units.la: 1 Tim. II. 2.
units.tr: 1 Tim. II. 2.

units.la: —Pro Regibus, & pro omnibus qui in Sublimitate constituti sunt: ut quietam & tranquillam vitam agamus in omni pietate & honestate.
units.tr: —For kings, and for all who are set in high places: that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all godliness and honesty.

units.la: DE Legum Humanarum Obligatione quod ad Causam Materialem, Efficientem, Formalem attinet, prout res tulerat (susius alicubi fortassis, alibi contracius, quàm par erat,) egimus utcunque superioribus præleCtionibus: superest ut ad ea quæ ad Legum causam Finalem pertinent dubia pertractanda pergamus porrò. Sed antequam ad illa dubia diffolvenda perveniam, illud interim præmittendum est, & ut res indubia supponendum, Legum ultimum finem esse Bonum communitatis, five pacem & tranquillitatem publicam. Probatur hoc primò, ex ipsis istis Apostoli verbis, [ἵνα ἤρεμον καὶ ἤσυχον βίον διάγωμεν[?], ut vitam quietam & tranquillam agamus.] Hortatur nimirum hic Apostolus, ut fiant cùm privatim, tùm vel maximè in publicis cœtibus, (sic enim, cum optimis quibusque interpretibus, hunc locum intelligendum existimo,) obtestationes, preces, postulationes, & gratiarum actiones: ut pro omnibus in universum hominibus primò (ex intuitu Charitatis, & in ordine ad finem spiritualem, felicitatem scil. æternam in vita futura,) in quantum sunt omnes homines, aut actu, aut saltem potestate, membra Corporis Christi Mystici; ita pro Regibus aliisque supremâ potestate prædítis in specie (ex intuitu etiam Prudentiæ & in ordine ad finem Temporalem, felicitatem scil. externam in vita præsenti,) in quantum sunt præcipua membra Corporis Politici. A quorum potestate, Lativâ Legum & Executivâ, prout utraque rectè aut secus administraverint, plurimùm pendet reliquorum membrorum, adeóque totius corporis, vel felicitas summa, vel summa infelicitas. Proinde quum fit Legum-latio, ut jam ante diximus, Suprema Jurisdictionis Politica actus præcipua: qui est supremæ illius Jurisdictionis totiusque Politici Regiminis, idem est & Legum ferendarum supremus Finis; bonum scil. Communitatis. Probatur secundò, à natura Finis, quasi demonstratione priori. Is est rei cujusque Finis in suo ordine ultimus, ad quem omnes illius rei actus reducuntur, tanquam ad primum principium sui regulativum; & ad quem referuntur, tanquam ad id cujus gratiâ ultimatè fiunt: unde causa Finalis Aristoteli τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα[?] appellatur. Sed omnes {*} Legum actiones a Bono Communi regulantur tanquam a primo fine Principio & Canone; & ad Bonum Commune referuntur, tanquam ad ultimum id cujus gratiâ fiunt: ut patet discurrendo per singulos actus: ergo, &c. Quorsum enim res, aut bonæ præcipiuntur, aut malæ vetantur, aut permittuntur mediæ & neutræ. Aut quorsum hominibus, vel de Rep. bene me[?] tis præmia decernuntur, vel legum violatoribus constituta sunt supplicia, vel indiscriminatim utriflibet in judiciis jura dicuntur? quorum sunt illi, Legum actus primi, & per modum Formæ: isti remotiores, & per modum Effectus. Annon eo demum fine, ut Respublica in pace & tranquillitate floreat; & ut privati etiam cives publicæ felicitatis participipio, pro suo cujusque modulo & mensura, gaudeant & fruantur? hoc est uno verbo, ut communi utilitati inserviatur. Probatur denique tertio, à Posteriori, ex omnium hominum sensu consensuque. Nam & qui justa decernunt Legumlatores, revera videntur; & qui meditantur malum sicut Legem, videri tamen cupiunt, in ferendis legibus non tàm suam, quàm communem utilitatem respexisse. Εἴτε σαφρονῶν[?], εἴτε ἀληθείας[?], five id sincerè intendant, five subdole obtendant, qui Leges aliis dicunt; propositum fuisse sibi in ferendis Legibus Bonum Publicum, profitentur utcunque universi.
units.tr: CONCERNING the obligation of human laws, I have dealt in my earlier lectures, as the subject allowed, with the material, efficient and formal causes, some points perhaps more fully than they deserved and others more briefly than was fitting. What remains is to take up the doubts that concern the final cause of laws. Before I come to resolving those doubts, however, this must be laid down first and assumed as an undoubted matter: the ultimate end of laws is the good of the community, that is, public peace and tranquillity. This is proved first from the Apostle's own words, that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life [ἵνα ἤρεμον καὶ ἤσυχον βίον διάγωμεν]. The Apostle here urges that supplications, prayers, petitions and thanksgivings be made, both privately and especially in public assemblies (for so, with the best interpreters, I think this passage should be understood), for all men in general, first (from a regard to charity and in relation to the spiritual end, namely eternal happiness in the life to come) insofar as all men are, either in act or at least in potential, members of the Mystical Body of Christ*;* and then in particular for kings and others endowed with supreme power (from a regard also to prudence and in relation to the temporal end, namely external happiness in the present life), insofar as they are the chief members of the Political Body. On their power, both in the making of laws and in its execution, and on how well or badly each is administered, the welfare of the other members, and so of the whole body, depends very largely, either supreme happiness or supreme unhappiness. Therefore, since law-making, as we said before, is the chief act of supreme political jurisdiction, the end of that supreme jurisdiction and of the whole political government is also the supreme end of making laws: namely the good of the community. Secondly, it is proved from the nature of the end, by a kind of prior demonstration. The final end of anything is, in its own order, that to which all the actions of that thing are referred back, as to a first principle regulating them, and to which they are directed, as to that for whose sake they are ultimately done; whence Aristotle calls the final cause that "for the sake of which" [τὸ οὗ ἕνεκα]. But all the actions of laws are regulated by the common good as by the first principle and rule of the end, and are referred to the common good as to that for whose sake they are ultimately done: as is plain when one runs through the individual acts. For to what end are things either commanded as good, or forbidden as evil, or permitted as indifferent and neutral? Or to what end are rewards decreed for those who have done well by the commonwealth, or punishments set up for the violators of the laws, or rights pronounced without distinction between parties in judgments? Of these, the former are the primary acts of laws, and work by way of form*;* the latter are more remote, and work by way of effect. Is not the final end of all of them simply this: that the commonwealth may flourish in peace and tranquillity, and that private citizens too may share in and enjoy public happiness, each according to his own measure and capacity? In a word, that they may serve the common advantage. Lastly, it is proved thirdly, a posteriori, from the sense and consensus of all men. For both those who enact just laws are seen to be lawgivers in fact, and those who devise evil under the guise of law nonetheless wish to appear, in making laws, to have regarded not so much their own advantage as the common advantage. Whether wisely or truthfully [Εἴτε σωφρονῶν, εἴτε ἀληθείας], whether they mean it sincerely or put it forward craftily, all who lay down laws for others profess, in whatever way, that in making laws they have had the public good as their aim.

units.la: II. Hoc ita jacto disputationis fundamento, Legum finem esse Bonum Communitatis; ad Dubia pergo. Quorum esto primum, an sit Legum Humanarum usus aliquis, saltem necessarius? Cui nullus foret in hac (Dubiorum dico) classe concedendus locus, nisi hoc nobis facesseret negotium Anabaptistarum, aliorumque cum ipsis juxta sententiam, vesanus error. Ex quorum principiis, (quum negent licere viro Christiano Magistratum gerere, bello liteve contendere, jurare aut alteri juramentum deferre aliaque consimilia :) consequi videtur, omninò nullam esse Legum Humanarum necessitatem. Nec enim erit, sublatâ Jurisdictione, qui Leges ferat: nec sublatis Judiciis, qui reformidet. Quid testes quærimonia, si non supplicio culpa reciditur? Quid vana sine moribus
units.tr: II. With this foundation of the argument laid down, that the end of laws is the good of the community, I proceed to the doubts. The first of these is whether there is any use of human laws, at least a necessary one. In this class of doubts no place would be granted to this question, were it not that the mad error of the Anabaptists, and of others who agree with them, makes it necessary for us to deal with it. From their principles (since they deny that a Christian man may hold magistracy, wage war or lawsuits, swear or require an oath of another, and other such things), it seems to follow that there is absolutely no necessity for human laws. For with jurisdiction removed there will be no one to make laws, and with courts removed there will be no one to fear them. What use are witnesses to complain, if guilt is not cut off by punishment? What use are empty [laws] without morals

units.la: {3} Horat. 3. Ode 24. Leges proficiunt? Concidat necesse est Directiva, nisi ei accedat, quae ipsam tibicinis in morem suffulciat, Coactiva Legum vis. Ratio autem dubitandi est: quod sufficere videatur homini Generali Naturae Lex, quae dictat Peccata esse vitanda, Nulli injuriam faciendam, &c. Aut illa si forte deficit; sit tamen homini Christiano ad modum Lex altera sublimior & perfectior, Lex nempe {†}Dei, Justitiae, & Charitatis, ab eo quem Jacobus unicum agnoscit Judicem & Legislatorem, Christo servatore lata. Premit acriter, ut quidem mihi videtur, ist haec ratio Novatores nostros; è quorum puteis pleraque sua dogmata hauserunt Anabaptistae: dum ex illo Jacobi testimonio colligunt, extra unum Christum nulli hominum fas esse Leges Ecclesiasticas condere. Quum enim nullo modo constare possit, vel ex vi verborum, vel ex totius illius perioches ordine & scopo, Apostolum ibi de Ecclesiasticis rebus legibúsve magis locutum, quam de Civilibus: nisi videri malint praejudiciis agi, quam ratione duci, è duobus alterutrum faciant oportet; quorum penes ipsos optio esto. Scilicet, aut recta in Anabaptistarum castra concedant, tollantque è rebus humanis omnem omnino Legum etiam Civilium, ferendarum potestatem: aut praelatis concedant, ut par est, Legum etiam Ecclesiasticarum ferendarum potestatem.
units.tr: {3} Horat. 3. Ode 24. Laws avail nothing? The directive part must necessarily fall, unless the coercive force of law is added to it, to prop it up as a crutch does. The reason for the doubt is that the general law of nature seems sufficient for man, dictating that sins are to be avoided and that no one is to be wronged, and so on. Or if that law perhaps fails, there is nonetheless for the Christian man, in the same way, a law more sublime and more perfect, namely the law of God, of justice and of charity, given by Christ the Saviour, whom James acknowledges as the one Judge and Lawgiver. This argument, as it seems to me, presses hard on our innovators, from whose wells the Anabaptists have drawn most of their doctrines, since from that testimony of James they conclude that no one but the one Christ may make ecclesiastical laws. For since it cannot be established, either from the force of the words or from the order and scope of the whole passage, that the Apostle there speaks of ecclesiastical matters or laws rather than civil ones, they must, unless they prefer to be driven by prejudice rather than led by reason, take one of two courses, the choice being theirs. Either they must hand over the camp to the Anabaptists outright, and remove from human affairs every power of making laws, civil laws included; or they must grant to prelates, as is fitting, the power of making ecclesiastical laws as well.

units.la: III. Verum isti fratres nostri, ut abs Anabaptistarum telis se tuituri sint, nostra non multum interest: ipsi viderint. Nos facile respondemus, esse quidem Legem Naturae cordibus inscriptam; esse & Legem Christi in Evangelio revelatam; utramque in suo genere perfectissimam: ita tamen ut sua constet Legibus Humanis, non solùm utilitas permagna, sed & usus etiam necessarius. Quia Leges illae divinae generalia tantùm rerum agendarum principia continent: è quibus, ut ex suis principiis conclusiones, deducendæ sunt Regulæ magis speciales, ad publicarum societatum & singularium hominum mores rectè instituendos accommodæ. Neque verò omnino verendum est, ne Legis Divinæ perfectioni isto pacto quidquam derogetur: Non enim id agunt Legum Humanarum conditores, ut locupletissimo illi Divinæ Legis thesauro aliquid addant divitiarum: imo premunt inde potius eruuntque, quod sibi suisque judicant usui fore, & in commune utile. Ergo Leges Humanæ, si quidem justæ sunt, nihil aliud sunt quàm Legis Divinæ [illegible, ~9 letters] quædam & [illegible, ~10 letters]: hoc est Regularum Generalium, quas indeterminatas exhibent naturæ Lex, & Sacræ literæ, determinationes particulares, ad certorum populorum conditionem & utilitatem, pro locorum & temporum ratione prudenter accommodatæ. Exempli gratia; docet Lex Naturæ in genere, nulli faciendam esse injuriam: & qui alteri injuriam fecerit, ad eam compensandam teneri. At in specie, utrum is qui per vicinum agrum pecus plaustrúmve egerit, injuriam vicino fecerit, & quæ sit debita pro ea injuria compensatio; non utique ex Naturæ Lege, sed ex Civili Jure statuendum est. Et sceleratos esse à magistratu supplicio afficiendos aperte docet sacra Scriptura, Rom. 13.4. & alibi. Sed quæ tandem scelerum genera punire debeat Magistratus; & quo supplicii genere, quáve mensurâ; lege Dei nullibi definitum est: permissâ nempe Principibus & Legislatoribus à Deo potestate, ut pro sua prudentia quod Reip. commodum & salutare videbitur ipsi Legibus rite constitutis definiant. Sunt itaque Dei Legislatoris, & Judicis distinctæ, & sua cuique propria, jura sive munera, eaque optimo ordine sic disposita; ut præcepta, quæ Deus generalia mandavit & indeterminata, Legislator ad certas personarum & actionum species determinet & accommodet: Judex demum à Legislatore sic legibus determinata, ad singulares personarum & actionum casus cum essectu applicet. Ita ut, si Legislator Legem constituerit, quæ præceptis Dei non sit congrua, Legem iniquam tulisse; & si Judex in aliqua particulari causa sententiam protulerit, quæ constitutis à Principe legibus, non sit congrua, jus iniquum dixisse, censendus sit.
units.tr: III. But whether these brethren of ours will be able to protect themselves against the weapons of the Anabaptists is not much our concern: let them see to it themselves. We readily answer that there is indeed a law of nature written in men's hearts, and there is also the law of Christ revealed in the Gospel, both most perfect in their own kind; yet human laws have not only very great usefulness but also a necessary use. For those divine laws contain only the general principles of things to be done, and from these, as conclusions from their principles, there must be deduced more specific rules, suited to establishing rightly the morals of public societies and of individual men. Nor indeed need we fear that the perfection of the divine law is in any way diminished by this, for the makers of human laws do not aim to add anything of riches to that most abundant treasury of the divine law; rather they draw from it and bring out what they judge will be of use to themselves and their own, and for the common advantage. Therefore human laws, if indeed they are just, are nothing other than certain [illegible, ~9 letters] and [illegible, ~10 letters] of the divine law: that is, particular determinations of the general rules which the law of nature and the Holy Scriptures set forth in an indeterminate way, prudently adapted to the condition and advantage of particular peoples, according to the circumstances of places and times. For example, the law of nature teaches in general that no one is to be wronged, and that whoever has wronged another is bound to make amends for it. But in particular, whether a man who has driven a flock or a wagon across a neighbour's field has done his neighbour an injury, and what compensation is due for that injury, is to be decided not by the law of nature but by civil law. And that wicked men are to be punished by the magistrate Holy Scripture plainly teaches (Rom. 13. 4, and elsewhere). But what kinds of crimes the magistrate ought to punish, and with what kind of punishment, or in what measure, is nowhere defined by the law of God: since God has granted to princes and lawgivers the power to define, by their own prudence, whatever they see to be convenient and salutary for the commonwealth, in laws duly enacted. There are therefore distinct rights or offices of God as Lawgiver and of God as Judge, each proper to its own, and these are so arranged in the best order that the precepts which God commanded in general and indeterminately are determined and adapted by the Lawgiver to certain kinds of persons and actions; and finally the Judge, with the laws thus determined by the Lawgiver, applies them effectively to the individual cases of persons and actions. So that if the Lawgiver enacts a law that is not consonant with the precepts of God, he is considered to have made an unjust law; and if the Judge pronounces sentence in some particular case that is not consonant with the laws laid down by the Prince, he is considered to have given an unjust judgment.

units.la: IV. Dubium Secundum est, an Legislator teneatur, si possit, omnes omnium virtutum actus & officia præcipere, & omnia cujuscunque generis peccata prohibere? Aut si non possit omnia, an saltem teneatur quot possit utriusque generis præcipere, & prohibere? Ratio dubitandi est, quia ad proprium Legum finem, (quod est Bonum Commune,) nihil videtur esse conducibilius, quàm ut, quantum fieri potest, omnes Cives sint boni, nulli autem mali. Ergo Legislatoris est, qui hunc unum sibi finem propositum habere debet, Commune Bonum procurare quantum in se est, præcipiendo omnes omnium virtutum actus, ut omnes Cives sint Boni, & prohibendo omnia peccata, nequi sint Mali, Id quod postulare videntur à Magistratu Politico utrequc magnus Apostolus: Paulus, Rom. 13. 3, 4. Fac bonum, & habebis laudem: sin malum feceris, time; quia vindex in iram τῷ τὸ κακὸν πράσσοντι[?], ei qui malum fecerit, i. e. cuivis homini qui quodvis malum fecerit. Et Petrus, 1 Pet. 2. 14. εἰς ἐκδίκησιν μὲν κακοποιῶν[?], ἔπαινον δὲ ἀγαθοποιῶν[?], in vindictam male agentium, & laudem bene agentium, i. e. omnium male agentium, & omnium bene agentium. Utrobique enim indefinite enunciatum æquipollere universali, & Regulæ Dialecticorum consonum est, (in materia scil. necessaria) & voluntati Dei, qui magistratui σεμνο-[illegible, ~6 letters] interdixit. n & udex , ad esseitueinicauincixiffe, eneak ofs preltem pere, proune,) uanatem a sibi onum mnes Boni, Id nter3, 4. ceris, wyqui 14. abene nnifinite gulæ negouPro
units.tr: IV. The second doubt is whether the legislator is bound, if he can, to command all the acts and duties of every virtue and to forbid every sin of every kind; or, if he cannot do everything, whether he is at least bound to command and forbid as many things of each kind as he can. The reason for doubting is that nothing seems more conducive to the proper end of laws, which is the common good, than that, as far as possible, all citizens should be good and none bad. Therefore it is the legislator's task, since he ought to have this one end before him, to promote the common good as far as in him lies, by commanding all the acts of all the virtues so that all citizens may be good, and by forbidding all sins so that none may be bad. The great Apostle Paul seems to require this of the political magistrate, Rom. 13.3, 4: "Do good and you will have praise; but if you do evil, be afraid; for he is a avenger for wrath to him who does evil" [εἰς ὀργὴν τῷ τὸ κακὸν πράσσοντι], that is, to any man who does any evil. And Peter, 1 Pet. 2.14: "for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of well-doers" [εἰς ἐκδίκησιν μὲν κακοποιῶν, ἔπαινον δὲ ἀγαθοποιῶν], that is, of all evildoers and all well-doers. For in both places the indefinite statement is equivalent to a universal, as the rules of the logicians agree (in necessary matter, that is), and as the will of God agrees, who has forbidden the magistrate [words illegible in the scan].

units.la: V. Pro responsione dico primo & generaliter, legislatorem teneri pro virili sua parte procurare, ut omnes cives sint Boni, nulli autem Mali; & ut consequens præcipere omnes virtutum actus, & omnia peccata prohibere: quantum exigit ratio principii ex quo, & finis propter quem operatur; ulterius vero non teneri. Principium enim & Finis, in operationibus omnium sive naturaliter sive liberè agentium, adæquata sunt mensura actuum omnium intermediorum: in quantum actus illos conformes esse decet & proportionatos, cùm principio a quo procedunt, tum fini in quem tendunt. Actus igitur præcipiendi, prohibendi, cæterique, in quibus consistit Legumlativæ Jurisdictionis exercitium, proportionati sint oportet & principio suo, in cujus virtute fiunt; potestati scilicet [illegible, ~1 word] ἐξουσίας[?] à Deo concessæ; & fini suo, in cujus gratiam fiunt; bono scil. Communi. Debet proinde Legislator eatenus præcipere, prohibere, permittere, cæteráque qui sui sunt muneris præstare; quatenus convenit potestati sibi à Deo concessæ, & commissæ sibi à Deo communitati expedit.
units.tr: V. In answer I say, first and in general, that the legislator is bound to work, as far as in him lies, that all citizens should be good and none bad, and, as a consequence, to command all acts of virtue and to forbid all sins, so far as the nature of the principle from which he acts and of the end for which he acts requires; but he is not bound beyond that. For the principle and the end in the operations of all agents, whether acting by nature or freely, are the adequate measure of all the intermediate acts, since those acts ought to be in conformity with and proportioned both to the principle from which they proceed and to the end to which they tend. The acts of commanding, forbidding and the rest, in which the exercise of legislative jurisdiction consists, must therefore be proportioned both to their principle, in whose power they are performed, namely the authority granted by God, and to their end, for whose sake they are performed, namely the common good. The legislator ought therefore to command, forbid, permit and do the other things that belong to his office only so far as they accord with the authority granted him by God and are expedient for the community committed to him by God.

units.la: VI. Sed Generalia hæc sunt, & indefinita. Ut igitur dubio propósito satisfiat, addatur aliquid oportet[?] quod sit magis particulare, quod huic tamen generali velut fundamento nitatur. Dico itaque secundo, actus virtutum & vitiorum, quum sint alii interni; cujus generis sunt actus voluntatis eliciti Velle & Nolle,) motus affectuum (ut amare, odisse, gaudere, &c.) & quæ sint aliæ cognitiones & intentiones cordium & mentis: alii Externi, cujusmodi sunt omnes actus voluntatis imperati, & deliberati Affectuum motus, qui per organa corporea exercentur; ut videre, loqui, ferire, rapere, aliique innumeri: potestatem legislativam circa actus externos versari solum, non item internos. Potest ergo Legislator, præcipere solutionem debiti, reftitutionem furti, cultum Dei externum ; prohibere item furtum, adulterium, homicidium, blasphemiam, &c. At non potest praecipere dilectionem proximi, fiduciam in Deo, contemptum mundi; nec prohibere cupiditatem rei alienae, impudicas cogitationes, odium proximi, Atheismum cordis. Ratio est: quia statuere de actibus internis, nec principio ex quo, nec fini propter quem, operatur Legislator, proportionatum est. Deus enim Opt. Max. externi tantum hominis Regimen Magistratui permisit: internorum actuum cognitionem & judicium, cordiumque inspectionem & dominium, ubi sibi reservavit. Idem enim est Legislator & Judex, ut ex laudato nobis aliquoties Jacobi testimonio ante ostendimus: & omnino ineffcax effet ad intentum finem suum consequendum Legumlativa prae-eftas[?], fi directiva tantum effet, non item coactiva. Quum ergo non possit imprimis, forum externum de actibus internis cognoscere & judicare; & stultum[?] effet fecundo, id lege lata praecipere vel prohibere quod ubi peccatum fuerit, punire nequeas; & actuum denique bonorum externa operatio, malorum externa declinatio, sufficiat ad externam Reipublicae felicitatem: sequitur legumlatorem, nec prudenter posse, nec de jure debere, internos actus aut virtutum praecipere, aut vitiorum prohibere.
units.tr: VI. But these are general and indefinite points. So that the doubt proposed may be satisfied, something more particular must be added, which nevertheless rests upon this general principle as its foundation. I say, therefore, secondly, that acts of virtues and vices are of two kinds. Some are internal, of which kind are the acts of the will, to will and to nill, the motions of the affections (such as to love, to hate, to rejoice, and so on), and the other thoughts and intentions of the hearts and mind. Others are external, of which kind are all the acts of the will commanded and deliberate, and the motions of the affections, which are exercised through the bodily organs, such as to see, to speak, to strike, to seize, and countless others. The legislative power is concerned only with external acts, and not with internal ones. The legislator can therefore command the payment of a debt, the restitution of stolen goods, the external worship of God, and likewise forbid theft, adultery, murder, blasphemy, and so on. But he cannot command love of neighbour, trust in God, contempt of the world, nor forbid covetousness of another's property, impure thoughts, hatred of a neighbour, or atheism of the heart. The reason is that to legislate about internal acts is proportioned neither to the principle from which the legislator acts nor to the end for which he acts. For God, the best and greatest, has entrusted to the magistrate the governing of the external man only; the knowledge and judgement of internal acts, and the inspection and dominion of hearts, he has reserved to himself. For the legislator and the judge are the same, as we have shown before from the testimony of James, which we have quoted several times; and legislative authority would be wholly ineffective for attaining its intended end if it were only directive and not also coercive. Since, therefore, first, he cannot know and judge the external court concerning internal acts; and since, second, it would be foolish to command or forbid by law what, where a sin has been committed, you could not punish; and since, finally, the external performance of good acts and the external avoidance of bad acts suffice for the external happiness of the commonwealth, it follows that the lawgiver* can neither prudently nor rightfully be bound to command internal acts of virtue or to forbid vices.

units.la: Quo nomine, ut & aliis plurimis, infinities superat Leges Humanas vel praestantissimas Lex Dei & Christi; quae veritatem, puritatem & sinceritatem exigit in intimis praecordiis, & primos levissimósque pravae voluntaris inordinatos motus cohibet, prohibetque; & meditata scelera tam punit quam perpetrata. Ideo Davidi dicitur Dei Lex perfecta & immaculata, Pfal 9. & alibi non semel. Estque Lex ipsa Christi, qualis & ipse ejus latus describitur, Heb. 4. Sermo vivus & efficax, pentrantior omni gladio ancipiti, pertingens usque ad divisionem anima & spiritus compagum quoque & medullarum, & discretor cogitationum & intentionum cordis.
units.tr: For this reason, among many others, the law of God and of Christ infinitely surpasses even the most excellent human laws. It requires truth, purity and sincerity in the innermost heart, and restrains and forbids the first and slightest disordered motions of a wicked will; and it punishes premeditated crimes as much as those actually committed. Hence the law of God is called by David "perfect and undefiled," Ps. 19, and elsewhere more than once. And it is the very law of Christ, as Heb. 4 describes even his side: "The word of God is living and effective, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart."

units.la: VII. Dico tertiò, posse Leges Humanas de Jure præcipere omnes omnium virtutum actus externos, & externa omnia peccati opera prohibere; sed de facto non posse. Ratio prioris membri est, quia nullus est virtutis, viciive actus externus, de tota sua specie & natura ita comparatus, ut non possit quandoque ejus præceptio vel prohibitio esse, pro rerum & temporum conditione, ordinabilis in bonum publicum. Ergo non Justitiæ proprie dictæ solum, (quæ nonnullorum sententia est,) sed & cæterarum virtutum quarumcunque actus possunt esse debita legis materia sive objectum. Quod & Aristotelem alicubi observasse memini; & instantias etiam (si rectè memini) dare in actibus Fortitudinis & Temperantia. Ut si lege militari fanciatur, nequis militum audet in prælio fugere, aut arma abjicere: vel si lege sumptuaria cohibeatur convivium luxus: aut modus statuatur, quem nemini civium in vestitu, famulatu, supellectili excedere liceat. Ratio posterioris membri est: quia tanta varietas est, (etiam quoad ipsas species, multò etiam magis quoad gradus,) tum officiorum virtutis, tum operum peccati; ut si de singulis cavere legislatores curarent, ipsa legum multitudo gravamen esset Reipubl. non ferendum.
units.tr: VII. I say, thirdly, that human laws may rightly command all the external acts of all the virtues and forbid all the external works of sin, but in fact they cannot. The reason for the first part is that there is no external act of virtue or vice, considered in its whole kind and nature, such that its command or prohibition could not at some time, according to the condition of things and times, be arranged for the public good. Therefore not only the acts of justice properly so called (which is the opinion of some), but the acts of all the other virtues, can be the proper matter or object of law. I recall that Aristotle observed this somewhere, and, if I remember rightly, he gives examples in the acts of fortitude and temperance: for instance, if a military law decrees that none of the soldiers may dare to flee in battle or throw down his arms; or if a sumptuary law restrains luxurious feasting, or sets a limit that no citizen may exceed in dress, servants or household furniture. The reason for the second part is that there is so great a variety, both as to the very kinds and much more as to the degrees, of the duties of virtue and of the works of sin, that if legislators took care to provide for each one, the very multitude of laws would be a burden to the commonwealth that could not be borne.

units.la: VIII. Dico quartò, legislatorem ne ad illud quidem teneri, ut omnia quæ potest mala prohibeat vel bona præcipiat. Sufficit enim, utriusque generis graviora quæque legibus contineri: & quæ sunt cum insigni aliqua utilitate publica ita conjuncta, ut nisi de eis aliquid statueretur, sequi necesse esset grave aliquod malum, quod toti Communitati esset valdè incommodum. Neque enim inter cupiditates carnis, illecebras mundi, Satanæ præsti-gias, gias, ingenia hominum tam varia & omnigenum vitiorum feracia. Rempub. Platonicam vel Utopicam somniare f•s est. Praeclare nobiscum agi putandum est, si non haereamus in ultima (ut dici solet) face Romuli. Necesse est itaque in omni Rep. aliqua mala non prohiberi, sed tolerari; multa bona non praecipi sed cujusque arbitrio permitti; utriusque generis plurima legibus praeteriri, & in medio relinqui: ne ex unius mali succidendi intempestivo studio, succrescant fortasse alia mala plura aut majora.
units.tr: VIII. I say, fourthly, that the legislator is not bound even to this, that he should forbid all the evils he can or command all the goods. For it is enough that the more serious matters of each kind be contained in the laws, and those which are so joined with some notable public utility that, unless something were decreed about them, some grave evil would necessarily follow, which would be very harmful to the whole community. For among the lusts of the flesh, the allurements of the world, the deceits of Satan, and the so varied and every-kind-fruitful wits of men, it is a dream to imagine a Platonic or Utopian commonwealth. We should think ourselves very fortunate if we do not stick at the last "dregs of Romulus," as the saying goes. It is therefore necessary in every commonwealth that some evils are not forbidden but tolerated; many goods are not commanded but left to each one's choice; and very many matters of each kind are passed over in the laws and left undecided, lest, in an untimely zeal to cut out one evil, other evils, more numerous or greater, should perhaps spring up.

units.la: IX. Dubium tertium, de intentione Legislatoris: An & quatenus requiratur ad effectum obligandi? Quod est quaerere, si princeps nullo justitiae aut publici boni intuitu, sed odio aut gratia privata, sed ambitione & mera dominandi libidine, sed avaritia aliave prava impotentis animi cupiditate ductus, legem tulerit subditis; an illi ad parendum legi obligentur in conscientia? Facilis responsio, obligari; si non fit aliud impedimentum: id est, si qui legem tulit habuerit legitimam potestatem, & Lex ipsa fit alias justa, pro more gentis legitime rogata & sufficienter promulgata. Dico igitur primo, sicut in artificialibus non est semper idem finis operis & operantis; ut in domo aedificanda, finis operis (id est domus) est, ut sit commoda domino habitatio; finis operantis (id est Architecti) est, ut ipse ex labore lucrum percipiat; ita in Republica fieri posse, ut Legislator intendat commodum proprium, & ipsa tamen Lex tendat in bonum commune.
units.tr: IX. The third doubt, concerning the intention of the Lawgiver: does it matter for the binding force of a law, and if so how far, what the lawgiver intended? The question is this: if a prince, moved not by any regard for justice or the public good, but by hatred, private favour, ambition and mere lust for power, or by greed or some other depraved desire of an unrestrained mind, enacts a law for his subjects, are they nonetheless bound in conscience to obey that law? The answer is easy: they are bound, provided no other impediment arises; that is, provided the one who made the law has lawful authority, and the law itself is otherwise just, lawfully enacted according to the custom of the nation, and sufficiently promulgated. I say, therefore, first, that just as in artificial things the end of the work and the end of the worker are not always the same, so when a house is to be built, the end of the work (that is, the house) is that the dwelling be convenient for its owner, while the end of the worker (that is, of the architect) is that he himself gain profit from his labour; so in a commonwealth it can happen that the Lawgiver aims at his own advantage, and yet the Law itself aims at the common good.

units.la: X. Objicies fortasse, finem sive intentionem minus rectam semper vitiare opus: ergo & Legislatoris pravam intentionem vitiare legem, quod est ipsius opus. Ut huic objectioni occurratur, dico secundo, intentionem malam semper vitiare opus, prout opus dicit actionem operantis: non semper vitiare opus, prout opus dicitur effectum operationis. Differunt enim non parum duo ista inter se, etsi eodem operis nomine utrumque solet appellari, Actio, scil. ipsa, & actionis ἐνέργημα [?] prorsus ut ἐνέργεια [?] & ἐνέργημα [?], effectio & effectus. Architecti opus dicitur, & ipsa aedificatio domus, & ipsa domus aedificata; etsi sit illa actio transiens, haec autem res post finitam actionem permanens. Intentio ergo prava vitiat opus Legislatoris, id est, suam ipsius legem condentis actionem; quae ob defectum boni finis non caret peccato: non tamen vitiat opus Legislatoris, id est, legem ipsam ab eo conditam, si quod lege imperatur sit referribile in Bonum Commune. Sicut valida est, non obstante prava Judicis intentione, sententia ex gratia vel odio lata, modo sit ipsa sententia per se considerata non injusta. Potest enim, ut recte Augustinus, ex libidine imperantis sine libidine obtem-prori.[?]
units.tr: X. You may perhaps object that a bad or mistaken end or intention always vitiates the work, and therefore the depraved intention of the Lawgiver vitiates the law, which is his work. To meet this objection, I say secondly that a bad intention always vitiates the work insofar as "work" means the action of the agent, but does not always vitiate the work insofar as "work" means the effect of the operation. For these two things differ considerably, although both are commonly called by the same name of "work": the action itself, and the product of the action, just as ἐνέργεια and ἐνέργημα, effecting and effect. The work of the architect may refer both to the building of the house itself and to the house built; although the former is a transitive action, the latter is a thing remaining after the action is finished. A depraved intention therefore vitiates the work of the Lawgiver, that is, his action in framing his own law, which, because it lacks a good end, is not free from sin. It does not, however, vitiate the work of the Lawgiver, that is, the law itself enacted by him, provided that what the law commands can be referred to the common good. Just as a sentence passed out of favour or hatred is valid despite a depraved intention in the judge, provided the sentence itself, considered in itself, is not unjust. For, as Augustine rightly says, it is possible for obedience to arise from the lust of the one commanding without the lust of the one obeying.

units.la: XI. Dico tertiò, supposito quod Lex non malâ tantùm intentione lata, sed & publico inutilis, imò & aliquantulum noxia sit; obligari tamen subditum ad parendum legi justâ authoritate latæ, modò sit ipsa materia legis, sive res imperata, istiusmodi, ut possit sine peccato præstari. Ratio est, quia debet unusquisque quæ suarum sunt partium ea sedulò curare; in eis quæ alienarum sunt, non esse anxiè & religiosè solicitus. {1} Unusquisque enim suum portabit onus. Si Legislator officio suo defuerit, quid ad te? Tolle quod tuum est & vade. De intentione suâ, rectáne fuerit an secus, viderit ipse: qui omnium actionum, etiam & intentionum suarum redditurus est Domino suo rationem: tu videris, nisi parueris, ut sis eidem Domino inobedientiæ tuæ rationem redditurus.
units.tr: XI. I say thirdly: granted that the law was enacted not only with a bad intention but is also useless to the public, and even somewhat harmful, nonetheless the subject is bound to obey a law enacted by lawful authority, provided that the matter of the law, or the thing commanded, is of such a kind that it can be performed without sin. The reason is that each person ought to attend diligently to those things which belong to his own part, and need not be anxiously and scrupulously concerned with those things which belong to others. {1} For each shall bear his own burden. If the Lawgiver has failed in his duty, what is that to you? Take what is yours and go. As to his intention, whether it was right or otherwise, let him look to it himself: he who is to render an account to his Lord of all his actions, and even of his intentions. Look to yourself, lest, if you do not obey, you have to render an account to the same Lord for your disobedience.

units.la: XII. Dubium quartum, de legum mutatione, si videantur Reipubl. inutiles aut noxiae: An & quatenus earum mutatio fit vel à principe tentanda, vel à populo postulanda & urgenda? Ratio dubitandi est. Ex una parte, quia in corpore civili haud minus quàm in naturali, omnis {*}mutatio (præfertim si aut subita fit, aut magna) periculosa est: ex altera parte, quia Reipubl. interest ut leges sint moribus & temporibus accommodæ; hisce proinde mutatis, ut illæ mutentur. Pro responsione dico primò, certum esse leges mutari posse, interdum & debere. Nam & antehac immutatæ sunt cum magna utilitate publica: ergo & nunc immutari possunt, & posthac poterunt, si res postulet, & ex usu sit Reipub. id fieri. Quod enim olim licuit, cur non & olim licebit? Novi ad hæc subinde emergunt casus, nova succrescunt indies mala, nova incommoda; quibus nisi novis occurratur legibus, nullum erit remedium. Et quærunt omnes, inquit {†}Aristoteles, ἢ τὸ μὲν νέον[?], ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀγαθόν. Et si legem olim propterea ferri expedivit, quod tunc visa est Reipubl. utilis; postquam ex mutatâ temporum & morum conditione comperta est Reipubl. inutilis, cur non expediat eam nunc tolli.
units.tr: XII. The fourth question, concerning the alteration of laws, if they seem useless or harmful to the commonwealth: whether and how far their alteration is to be attempted by the prince, or demanded and pressed by the people? The reason for doubt is this. On the one hand, in the civil body, no less than in the natural, every alteration (especially if it is sudden or great) is dangerous. On the other hand, it is in the commonwealth's interest that its laws be suited to customs and times, and so, when these have changed, that the laws be changed too. In answer, I say first that it is certain that laws can, and sometimes must, be changed. For they have been altered before now with great public benefit. Therefore they can be altered now, and will be able to be altered hereafter, if the matter requires it and it is for the commonwealth's good. For what was once lawful, why should it not be lawful again? New cases keep arising, new evils grow daily, new inconveniences, and unless these are met with new laws there will be no remedy. "All men seek," says Aristotle, "not what is new but what is good" [ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀγαθόν]. And if a law was once rightly enacted because it then seemed useful to the commonwealth, but after the change in the condition of the times and customs it is found to be useless to the commonwealth, why should it not now be expedient to abolish it?

units.la: XIII. Dico secundò; Legum, etiam particularium, immutationem, non carere periculo: ideóque non esse nisi ex gravi admodum & evidenti necessitate tentandum. Varias rationes adducit Aristote-les, acutè & breviter, ut solet, 2 Polit. 8. (apud eum videte) in his, tres præcipuas hasce. Primò, ἀσθενῆ[?] τῶν νόμων ἐν τῇ ἀξίᾳ[?] τοῦ νομοθέτου. Derogant nimirum plurimum & Legum authoritati, & latoris, crebræ mutationes. Sicut levem & infirmi hominem judicii existimamus eum, qui nullâ solidâ & evidenti ratione permotus facilè mutat sententiam. – Se-cundò, τὸ ἐξ εὐχερῶς λύειν τὸν νόμον, φαῦλον, (Aristotelem
units.tr: XIII. I say secondly: the alteration of laws, even particular ones, is not free from danger, and therefore it is not to be attempted except from a very grave and evident necessity. Aristotle adduces various reasons for this, acutely and briefly as is his habit (see him in Politics 2, chapter 8), and among them these three chief ones. First, the laws are weakened in the authority of the lawgiver (ἀσθενῆ τῶν νόμων ἐν τῇ ἀξίᾳ τοῦ νομοθέτου). Frequent changes certainly detract much from the authority of the laws and of the one who proposes them, just as we judge a man of slight and weak judgment who changes his opinion easily, moved by no solid and evident reason. Secondly, to dissolve a law easily is bad (τὸ ἐξ εὐχερῶς λύειν τὸν νόμον, φαῦλον) (Aristotle

units.la: {†} Arist. 2. Poli. … (Aristotelem iterum auditis). Petacem facit populum, ne dicam petulantem, (res ipsa clamat, experti sumus nimirum jamdiu,) & cuncta moventem, si Legislatorem facilem hac ex parte, & ad vota libidinémque populi jure suo cedentem repererint. Reprehendit igitur jure merito & graviter, ibidem summus Philosophus Legem Hippo-damí cujusdam Milefii Legislatoris; [illegible, ~8 letters] illam quidem, primo aspectu speciosam satis, & plausibilem vulgo, ut qui aliquid utile civitati invenirent publico praemio afficerentur, sed si penitius intueare, nec prudentem omninò, nec falutarem. Quid enim ferè excogitari potest ad publicas res turbandas opportunius, quàm quòd proposito praemio invitentur homines factiosi, vafri & turbulenti ingenii, [illegible, ~8 letters] νόμων λύσιν ἢ πολιτείας, ὡς κοινὸν ἀγαθόν, ut sub specie boni publici, non eversionem modò legum inducere, sed & totius civilis administrationis formam, sub ineundem revocatam, & in novam ideam pro suo ubitu? refictam, civitati obtrudere studeant? Philosophume obsecro videmini vobis audire suis temporibus illustrem; an Vatem potiùs, eorum qui nunc sunt morum hominumque praescium ac praenuncium; Tertiò, quum Legum immutatio tollendi præsentis alicujus incommodi gratia instituatur; & fieri possit, ut ex istâ immutatione suboriantur, imò vix fieri possit ut non suboriantur,) & emergant tandem, utut fortassis occulta initio, plura & graviora incommoda: [illegible, ~10 letters], inquit idem gravissimus Philosophus. Omninò ducens aliqua incommoda, eáque non levia, in Rep. tolerare & perferre; (quod idem & de Ecclesiâ, quæ & ipsa Respublica quædam est, saluendum est:) quàm obtentu Reformationis sive Ecclesiasticæ sive Politicæ, vetera instituta solitare, leges refigere, τὰ ἄνω κάτω sursum vorsum omnia versare, & versando pervertere. Longe alia mens fuit prisci saeculi prudentium virorum, quorum haec & hujusmodi fuisse dicta accepimus. [illegible, ~4 words] Malum bene positum non movendum. Imperiti medici est, pejus malo remedium adhibere.
units.tr: {†} Arist. 2. Poli. … (hear Aristotle again). It makes the people grasping, not to say wanton (the thing itself cries out that we have long since learned this by experience), and ready to stir everything up, if they find the lawgiver pliant in this respect and yielding to the wishes and lusts of the people. So the supreme philosopher himself rightly and gravely censures, in the same place, the law of a certain Hippodamus of Miletus, a lawgiver. That law, at first sight quite attractive and popular with the crowd, rewarded with a public prize those who discovered something useful to the state; but if you look more closely, it is neither wholly prudent nor salutary. For what could be devised more suited to disturbing public affairs than that, with a prize offered, factious, crafty and turbulent men should be invited to seek the overthrow of laws or of the constitution, under the guise of the public good, and strive to thrust upon the state not merely the destruction of laws, but the whole form of civil administration, recalled from its foundations and remade at their own whim into a new idea? I beg you, philosopher, to consider whether you seem to yourself illustrious in your own times; or rather a prophet, foreseeing and foretelling the customs and men of the present age. Thirdly, since an alteration of laws is undertaken for the sake of removing some present inconvenience, and it may happen (indeed it can hardly fail to happen) that from this alteration there arise, and at last emerge, however hidden at first, more and graver inconveniences [illegible], says the same most weighty philosopher. He thinks it altogether right to endure and bear some inconveniences, and not slight ones, in the commonwealth (and the same must be said of the Church, which is itself a kind of commonwealth), rather than, under pretext of reformation, whether ecclesiastical or political, to disturb ancient institutions, rewrite laws, and turn all things upside down (τὰ ἄνω κάτω), and by turning them to pervert them. The mind of the wise men of the earlier age was far different, and we have received that these and similar sayings were theirs: [illegible] "An evil well placed is not to be moved." "It is the mark of an unskilled physician to apply a remedy worse than the disease."

units.la: XIV. Dico Tertiò, Legum immutationem, etiamsi ex gravi & evidente causâ videatur esse necessaria, non esse tamen à populo, invito Principe, tentandam, sed ab eo modestè petendam & patienter expectandam. Quod ut ex Capitis & Membrorum analogiâ colligi potest, (quàm enim & monstri simile esset, & toti corpori exitiale, si brachia, pectus, pedes, capitis sibi vel locum arriperent, vel officium?) Sic est in iis, quae de Causa Legum efficienti haud ita pridem disseruimus, cumulate satis demonstratum. Nimirum civilis jurisdictionis actum praecipuum non posse exerceri nisi ab eo qui totius communitatis caput & princeps est: Legum proinde constitutionem, abrogationem & quamcunque immutationem, quae sunt omnes summae Jurisdictionis actus è praecipuis, non posse ad populum pertinere, (nisi ubi populus Princeps est, ut in statu Democratico;) sed ad eum solum qui toti communitati cum summo imperio praeest; hoc est, in statu saltem Monarchico, ad unum Regem [illegible, ~1 word] & simpliciter [illegible, ~1 word]. In tam gravi negotio, hae sunt populi partes: justa gravamina sua (siqua sunt) aperte & sincere, sed cum omni debita reverentia Principi exhibere; quibus remediis praesentibus malis commodissime occurri posse censeant fideliter proponere; supplicesque rogare, ut votis subditorum, prout ipse ea Reipublicae salutaria & in commune utilia judicaverit, annuere dignetur, & eorum postulata grata ratâque habere; is denique si rogatus usque recusaverit, abstinere in id tempus a proposito, rebusque & legibus præsentibus contentos esse: idque sine omni-obmurmuratione, nedum vi; quoad is aut amicorum precibus & hortatibus permotus, aut rationum momentis perductus animi pertinaciam illam remiserit, & subditorum postulatis annuerit.
units.tr: XIV. I say thirdly that a change of laws, even if it appears necessary for a serious and evident cause, is not to be attempted by the people against the will of the Prince, but is to be sought from him modestly and awaited patiently. This can be gathered from the analogy of Head and Members (for how monstrous would it be, and how fatal to the whole body, if the arms, the breast, and the feet were to seize for themselves either the place or the office of the head?). So it is in those matters which we lately discussed concerning the efficient cause of laws, sufficiently demonstrated at length. Namely, the chief act of civil jurisdiction cannot be exercised except by one who is the head and prince of the whole community. Therefore the making of laws, their repeal, and any change whatever, which are all among the chief acts of supreme jurisdiction, cannot belong to the people (unless the people is itself the prince, as in a democratic state), but only to him who presides over the whole community with supreme power; that is, in a monarchical state at least, to the one King [illegible] and simply [illegible]. In so grave a matter, these are the duties of the people: to present their just grievances (if there are any) openly and sincerely, but with all due reverence to the Prince; to propose faithfully what remedies they think could most conveniently meet the present evils; and to ask him in supplication that he would deign to grant the wishes of his subjects, as he himself shall judge them salutary to the commonwealth and useful to the common good, and to hold their requests acceptable and approved. Finally, if he has refused them even when asked, they should refrain from their purpose for the time being and be content with the present state of affairs and laws; and this without any murmuring, let alone force, until he, moved either by the prayers and exhortations of friends or led by the weight of reasons, has laid aside his obstinacy and granted the requests of his subjects.

units.la: XV. Dubium quintum. Quandoquidem non Legum modò, sed & totius politici regiminis finis est bonum commune; an liceat, ex aliquo boni communis sive obtentu sive intuitu, præsentem regiminis formam immutare, aut ejusmodi immutationem attentare? & quatenus id liceat, & quibus; Exempli gratiâ, liceatne populo Regimen Monarchicum mutare in Aristocraticum, vel Democraticum; aut è contra? Dubium periculosæ plenum aleæ: his præsertim temporibus & moribus. Esto ergo hic suum cuique liberum judicium: Ego quid mihi sententia videtur sine fuco exponam; assentiendi nulli legem impono. Suppono tantum quod à plerisque conceditur, nec facilè negari potest, Monarchiam hæreditariam, sive Regnum successivum, inter omnes Rerumpublicarum formas esse ἀκρότατος[?] & absolutè præstantissimam, & duabus reliquis multis nominibus anteponendam. Hoc posito, Existimo primùm, posse populum (si ipsis visum fuerit) regimen Democraticum in Aristocraticum vel Monarchicum commutare. Imprimis, quia videtur esse commutatio in melius. Accedit quod in Democratiâ summa imperii est penes ipsum populum; ita ut possit populus de se prout sibi libitum est pro suo jure statuere, dummodo nulli fiat injuria. Injuriam denique à populo istiusmodi imperii immutatione nulli mortalium fieri, certissima res est: non alteri cuiquam, quia jus non habenti non fit injuria; nec ipsis sponte mutantibus, quia 'volenti non fit injuria. Existimo secundò, ob omnes easdem rationes, posse Optimates regimen Aristocraticum in Monarchiam commutare : nam & mutatio est in melius, & ipsi jus habent hoc faciendi, nec fit cuiquam eo facto injuria. An item ipsi liceat Aristocratiam in Democratiam convertere, non ita facile dixerim : quia licet & ipsi jus habeant faciendi, & res ipsa citra cujusquam injuriam fieri possit, non tamen videtur esse ista commutatio in melius. Existimo tertio, posse commutari Monarchiam Regni Electivi in aliam (fortasse quamlibet) regiminis formam, praesertim vero in Regnum hereditarium sive successivum : idque ob easdem [?]fere rationes : non tamen id fieri debere, primo, regno per mortem ultimo regnantis vacante, (alias enim praesenti Regi fieret injuria ;) nec secundo, nisi ex conjuncto consensu procerum Regni & Populi, earumque personarum quae jus habent eligendi. Existimo quarto, Monarchiam hereditariam, in Regnum Electivum, aut alterius Regiminis quamcunque formam, non posse legitime commutari : vel à sola plebe; vel ab universo populo subditorum, h. e. à plebe & proceribus junctim; vel etiam à toto populo in maximâ suâ latitudine, id est, à plebe, proceribus & Rege simul consentientibus : Nisi forte sicubi ita penitus defecerit Regalis prosapia, ut nemo supessit, qui regnum sibi iure hereditario debitum vendicare possit. Cujus sententiae rationes sunt, Primo, quia ex nostro suposito ista esset commutatio in deterius. Secundo, quia istiusmodi commutatione legitimo haeredi iniuria eret injuria. Tertio, quia videtur non ipsa commutatio tantum, sed & omne ejus desiderium & conatus, verbis illis Salomonis adversari, Prov. 24. 21. Fili mi, time Deum & Regem; nec sit tibi rei quiquam cum iis qui novis rebus student. Quod tamen ante dixi, nunc iterum repeto ; me non haec dicere ut affirmem, aut litem super hac re cuiquam moveam si aliter sentiat.
units.tr: XV. The fifth doubt. Since the end not only of laws but of the whole political government is the common good, may it be lawful, for the sake or with a view to some common good, to change the present form of government, or to attempt such a change? And if it is lawful, to what extent and for whom? For example, may the people change monarchical government into aristocratic or democratic, or the reverse? This is a doubt full of perilous hazard, especially in these times and manners. Let each person therefore have his own free judgment here: I shall set out plainly what my opinion seems to me; I impose no law of assent on anyone. I only assume what is granted by most and can hardly be denied: that hereditary monarchy, or a successive kingdom, is among all forms of commonwealth the most excellent [?] and absolutely the most outstanding, and is to be preferred to the other two in many respects. This being laid down, I hold, first, that the people (if it seems fit to them) may change democratic government into aristocratic or monarchical. Above all, because it seems to be a change for the better. Moreover, in a democracy the supreme power of rule lies with the people itself, so that the people may decide about itself as it pleases, by its own right, provided no one is wronged. Finally, it is most certain that no mortal is wronged by such a change of sovereignty made by the people: not any other person, because no injury is done to one who has no right; nor to those who change of their own accord, because no injury is done to one who is willing. Secondly, I hold that for all the same reasons the nobles may change aristocratic government into a monarchy: for the change is for the better, and they themselves have the right to do this, and no injury is done to anyone by the act. Whether it is likewise lawful for them to turn aristocracy into democracy I would not readily say: because although they too have the right to do it, and the thing could be done without injury to anyone, yet this change does not seem to be for the better. Thirdly, I hold that an elective monarchy may be changed into some other (perhaps any) form of government, and especially into a hereditary or successive kingdom, and for almost the same reasons; yet this ought not to be done, first, while the kingdom is vacant through the death of the last reigning king (otherwise an injury would be done to the present king), nor, secondly, except by the joint consent of the nobles of the kingdom and the people, and of those persons who have the right of electing. Fourthly, I hold that a hereditary monarchy cannot lawfully be changed into an elective kingdom or into any other form of government, either by the commons alone, or by the whole body of subjects, that is, by commons and nobles together, or even by the whole people in its greatest extent, that is, by commons, nobles and king consenting at once; unless perhaps in some place the royal line should so utterly fail that no one survives who could claim the kingdom due to him by hereditary right. The reasons for this opinion are these. First, because on our supposition such a change would be a change for the worse. Second, because by such a change an injury would be done to the lawful heir. Third, because it seems that not only the change itself but every desire for it and every attempt towards it is opposed to those words of Solomon, Prov. 24. 21: My son, fear God and the King; and have nothing to do with those who are eager for new things. Which thing I said before, and now repeat again: I do not say these things to assert them, nor do I stir up a quarrel over this matter with anyone who thinks otherwise.
