units.la: XVI. Dubium Sextum, quomodo fit intelligendum id quod dici solet, Salus Populi Suprema Lex? Ratio dubitandi ex eo oritur quod initio proposuimus & probavimus, Legum finem esse Bonum Publicum. Hinc sequi videtur, ex una parte, à Legum strictâ observantiâ pendere Reipublicæ salutem; ex altera parte, saluti Reipublicæ cedere debere omnium Legum observantiam. Hinc etiam fidenter satis, nec minùs perversè colligunt, qui intrà paucos hosce annos novam unà cum Theologiâ Politiam in Ecclesiam & Rempubl. invexerunt, Libertatem, hoc est, Jus Subditorum, (sic enim illi Populi salutem interpretantur,) & Regum prærogativis & Legum sanctionibus anteferendam esse; & proinde posthabendas præ illa omnem, & potestatem Regum, & Legum authoritatem. Pro solutione dubii, sciendum est, totam ferè hac in re deceptionem ex æquivocatione, quæ in terminis latet, ortam esse; præsertim in illo Populi vocabulo. Populus enim, quum sit corpus quoddam Metaphoricum, dupliciter accipi potest, sicut & ipsum corporis vocabulum: Collectivè scil. prout significat totam Rempublicam Communitatem, id est, Regem & Subditos simul; & Discretivè, prout significat Subditos præcisè, & seorsim à Rege, ut cum dicimus, Rex & Populus. Sicut Corporis vocabulo intelligenda veniunt aliquando reliqua membra simul cum capite, ut cum dicimus Animam & Corpus; aliquando membra reliqua præcisè & exclusò capite, ut cum dicimus Caput & Corpus.
units.tr: XVI. The sixth doubt: how is the saying commonly repeated, The Safety of the People is the Supreme Law, to be understood? The ground of the doubt arises from what we proposed and proved at the outset, that the end of Laws is the Public Good. From this it seems to follow, on the one hand, that the safety of the Commonwealth depends on the strict observance of the Laws; and on the other hand, that the observance of all Laws ought to yield to the safety of the Commonwealth. From this too, those who within these few years have introduced a new politics, joined with Theology, into the Church and the Commonwealth draw their conclusions quite confidently, and no less perversely: that Liberty, that is, the Right of Subjects (for so they interpret the safety of the people), is to be preferred to the prerogatives of Kings and the sanctions of Laws; and accordingly that, compared with it, both the power of Kings and the authority of Laws are to be set aside. To resolve the doubt, it must be known that almost the whole deception in this matter arises from an equivocation hidden in the terms, especially in the word people. For the people, since it is a certain metaphorical body, can be taken in two ways, just as the word body itself can: collectively, namely as it signifies the whole Commonwealth, the community, that is, King and subjects together; and distributively, as it signifies the subjects precisely, and apart from the King, as when we say King and People. Just as by the word body are sometimes understood the remaining members together with the head, as when we say soul and body; and sometimes the remaining members precisely, excluding the head, as when we say head and body.

units.la: XVII. Dico igitur Primo, malignè & pessimo consilio, detorqueri id, quod de populo in priore sensu dictum est, ut accommodetur populo in posteriore acceptione. Salutem populi, id est, totius Communitatis, ut ea vox Regem unà cum subditis complectitur, supremam Legem esse, nemo sanæ[?] mentis negaverit : ut salutem populi, id est, subditorum excluso Rege, supremam esse Legem quis dixerit, nisi aut Fatuus, aut Impostor ? Fatuus, fi ipsi sibi sic dicenti fidem habeat ; fi non habet, Impostor. Sed enim quisquis ipsius Aphorismi vi-ginem attentius inspexerit, lubentius concessurum arbitror, de salute Principis præcise intelligi debere, quàm de salute Subditorum præcise. Scilicet Romanis ad nos devenit celebre hoc dictum, illis tunc usurpatum, cùm maximè floreret Respublica sub statu populari. Non est autem quod quis mire[?]tur, fuisse illis salutem populi supremam Legem, quibus ipse Populus erat suprema Potestas. Erat ergo prudentium illorum veterum, qui Aphorismi hujus primi authores extiterunt, judicio, supremæ potestatis salus suprema Lex ; Populi nimirum in Democratiâ, aut in Monarchiâ Principis.
units.tr: XVII. I say, then, first, that what is said of the people in the former sense is twisted, with malicious and very bad intent, so that it is applied to the people in the latter sense. That the welfare of the people, that is, of the whole community (since that word embraces the king together with the subjects), is the supreme law, no one of sound mind would deny. But that the welfare of the people, that is, of the subjects with the king excluded, is the supreme law, who would say, unless a fool or an impostor? A fool, if he gives credence to himself while saying so; if he does not, an impostor. But whoever looks more closely at the very force of this maxim, I think will more willingly concede that it must be understood precisely of the welfare of the prince, rather than precisely of the welfare of the subjects. For this famous saying came down to us from the Romans, used by them when their commonwealth was flourishing most under a popular constitution. Nor is there cause for anyone to wonder that the welfare of the people was the supreme law for those to whom the people themselves were the supreme power. So, in the judgment of those wise men of old who were the first authors of this maxim, the welfare of the supreme power is the supreme law: namely of the people in a democracy, or of the prince in a monarchy.

units.la: XVIII. Dico fecundò ; dato non concesso, Aphorismum hunc de Populi, i. e. subditorum salute pròprie intelligi ; adhuc tamen, perversè detorquent in Regiæ dignitatis præjudicium, qui vel sic potestatem[?] ejus ampliorem reddit & illustriorem. Hoc sensu scilicet, Regem qui populo Leges & Jus dedit, non ita se voluisse Legum vinculis astringi, ut non liceret ipsi, ubi Reipublicæ salus palàm periclitaretur[?], regni populiqué sibi à Deo commissi saluti consulere, etiam contra verba Legis. Non quòd liceat subditis, tuendæ libertatis obtentu, Legum & omnia fidelitatis vincula abrumpere, & Regiam authoritatem intolerando fastu sub pedibus conculcare. Sed quòd Principi liceat, tuendæ subditorumque salutis causâ, strictam Legum observantiam ad tempus seponere, & arbitrario juri aliquantisper uti ; ne ex nimium superstitiosâ & intempestivâ Legum reverentiâ, sëque & subditum sibi populum, ipsasque etiam Leges, in hostium potestatem devenire patiatur.
units.tr: XVIII. I say second: granting, though not conceding, that this maxim is to be understood properly of the welfare of the people, that is, of the subjects, still they twist it perversely to the prejudice of royal dignity, those who by this very means make his power greater and more illustrious. In this sense, of course: that a king who gave laws and right to the people did not wish himself to be bound by the chains of the laws so that it would not be lawful for him, where the safety of the commonwealth was plainly in danger, to provide for the welfare of the kingdom and people committed to him by God, even against the words of the law. Not that it is lawful for subjects, under the pretext of defending their liberty, to break all the bonds of the laws and of fidelity, and to trample the royal authority under their feet with intolerable arrogance. But that it is lawful for the prince, for the sake of defending the welfare of his subjects and of the people, to set aside for a time the strict observance of the laws and to use an arbitrary right for a while; lest, through an excessively superstitious and untimely reverence for the laws, he suffer himself, his subjects, his people, and even the laws themselves, to fall into the power of enemies.

units.la: XIX. Dico tertiò, dato adhuc ulterius, nec concesso tamen, licentiam aliquam ipsis subditis eo Aphorismo concedi, ut posthabitis Legibus, ita postulante necessitate, saluti publicæ consulant: non tamen inde effici, quod nonnulli voluerunt. Non quasi subditis liceret, ubi libertatem suam in aliquâ re læsam aut sentiunt, aut sentire se vociferantur, mox omnia Legum & officii repagula disjicere, & inconsulto Principe arma rapere, tumultibúsque & seditionibus omnia complere. Sed quod pro salute Principis & suâ adversus externos hostes, aut perduelles domesticos tuendâ, (ubi tam gravis premit necessitas, ut vir pius & prudens non possit dubitare Legislatorem ipsum, si præsens esset, Legis sibi gratiam & relaxationem concessurum) liceat subditis, communis utilitatis, quæ Suprema Lex est, & omnium Legum Finis, rationem habere magis, quàm Legum particularium, quæ propterea latæ sunt, ut communi utilitati inserviant, non præjudicent.
units.tr: XIX. I say third: granting yet further, though not conceding, that some license is granted to the subjects themselves by that maxim, so that, with the laws set aside, they may provide for public safety when necessity demands it, still it does not follow from this what some have wished. Not as though subjects might, whenever they either feel, or loudly claim to feel, that their liberty has been injured in some matter, at once cast off all the restraints of law and duty, seize arms without consulting the prince, and fill everything with tumults and seditions. But that, for the sake of defending the safety of the prince and their own against foreign enemies or domestic traitors (where a necessity so grave presses that a pious and prudent man cannot doubt that the Lawgiver himself, if he were present, would grant relaxation and indulgence of the law), it is lawful for subjects to have regard to common utility, which is the supreme law and the end of all laws, rather than to the particular laws, which were therefore made so that they might serve common utility and not stand in its way.

units.la: XX. Summa est, Salutem Reipublicæ, hoc est, Principis & subditorum, Supremam esse Legem, cui inferiores Leges omnes ita inservire debent; ut postulante præsenti necessitate, Principi fas sit, ex potestatis suæ præ-rogativa, imò & subditis fas sit, ex rationabiliter præsumpto Principis consensu, à verbis Legum particularium quandoque recedere, ut periclitanti patriæ subveniant, ejusque Saluti, velut Supremæ Legi, consulant. Ita tamen, ut sub prætextu Publicæ Salutis libertatisve nisi ex voluntate & consensu Supremæ Potestatis, vel expresso, vel (ut dixi) rationabiliter præsumpto, non fit aliquid, quod leges non permittunt, attentandum.
units.tr: XX. The sum is this: the safety of the commonwealth, that is, of the prince and subjects, is the supreme law, to which all inferior laws ought so to be subservient that, when present necessity demands it, it is lawful for the prince, by virtue of the prerogative of his power, and indeed lawful for subjects, on the reasonably presumed consent of the prince, at times to depart from the words of particular laws, so as to come to the aid of the endangered fatherland and provide for its safety as for the supreme law. Yet this is to be so understood that, under the pretext of public safety or liberty, nothing that the laws do not permit is to be attempted, unless by the will and consent of the supreme power, either expressed or, as I said, reasonably presumed.

units.la: XXI. Restant adhuc Dubia non pauca, ad causam hanc Finalem quoquo modo pertinentia; ut de Privilegiis, de Dispensationibus, de Relaxatione Obligationis in periculo vitæ, aliisque ejusdem generis : quæ fortassis quibusdam videbuntur cum Fine legum Humanarum non usquequaque convenire. Quorum solutionem consultius duxi in aliud (longinquum licet) tempus rejicere ; quàm nimiâ prolixitate tam benevolos auditores fatigare.
units.tr: XXI. There remain not a few further doubts pertaining in some way to this final cause, such as concerning privileges, dispensations, the relaxation of obligation in danger of life, and other matters of the same kind; which perhaps will seem to some not wholly in agreement with the end of human laws. I judged it wiser to put off their solution to another time, though a distant one, than to weary such kindly hearers with excessive length.

units.la: I. Institueram ex hoc loco, si forte meministis, benevoli auditores, de utraque Consci-entiæ obligatione, passivâ, activâque justam tractationem. In priore illâ explicandâ, post excussam primo loco & Scholastico more conscientiæ definitionem; in prævestigandâ propriâ illâ & adæquatâ conscientiæ regulâ, cujus ex præscripto omnes & singulos suos tum dicendi [?] tum judicandi actus exercere debet, operam insumpsi. Ostensum ibi tunc esse quidem Scripturam Sacram ejus quam quærebamus Regulæ præcipuam partem: ait adæquatam esse voluntatem Dei, (quam signi vocant, ) cuivis homini qualitercunque patefictam[?]. Sive primum lumine innato: ex principiis practicis in Synteresi confervatis & per se notis: quas Philosophi συνειδήσεις[?], & ἀνελέγκτους[?], Apostolus Legem Dei in cordibus nostris scri-ptam dixerunt. Sive secundò, lumine illato; per externam revelationem: partim extraordinariam & privatam singularibus quibusdam personis per visiones, somnia, &c. πολυμερῶς ἢ πολυτρόπως: partim ordinariam & publicam universo generi humano in verbo scripto. Sive denique lumine acquisito; per conclusiones ex principiis illis practicis, aut è verbo Dei scripto, vel propriâ meditatione, vel institutione alienâ rite & legitimè erutas.
units.tr: I had undertaken, if you remember, most kind listeners, to deal fairly with both obligations of conscience, the passive and the active. In explaining the first, after first examining the definition of conscience in the Scholastic manner, I took pains to investigate the proper and adequate rule of conscience, by whose prescription each and every one of its acts, both of judging and of acting, ought to be carried out. I showed there that Holy Scripture is indeed the chief part of the rule we were seeking, but that the will of God (which they call the sign) is adequate, and is made known to any man in whatever way. This happens first by innate light, through practical principles kept in synteresis and known in themselves, which the philosophers called conscience [συνειδήσεις] and irrefutable principles [ἀνελέγκτους], and which the Apostle called the law of God written in our hearts. Or secondly, it happens by infused light, through external revelation: partly extraordinary and private, given to certain individuals through visions, dreams and so on, "in many portions and in many ways" [πολυμερῶς ἢ πολυτρόπως]; and partly ordinary and public, given to the whole human race in the written word. Or finally, it happens by acquired light, through conclusions rightly and lawfully drawn from those practical principles, or from the written Word of God, whether by one's own meditation or by another's teaching.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Ista omnia & singula Conscientias hominum obligare dixi; eáque solâ, absolutè, primariò, per se, & virtute propriâ: quia ea omnia & sola voluntatem Dei exhibent, cujus unius est in hominum Conscientias merum & directum imperium. Esse tamen admonui præter hæc, & alia nonnulla; quæ secundariò, relativè, & in virtute legis sive voluntatis Divinæ, in quâ fundantur, suo modo Conscientias obligant. Convenire insuper illa omnia in hoc, quòd quam habent obligandi vim, eam omnem Divinæ Legi acceptam debeant, (non esset aliàs Divina Lex adæquata Conscientiæ regula:) differre tamen inter se singula; cùm speciè, propter diversitatem materiæ: tùm etiam gradu, quantum ad vim obligandi. Esse porrò eorum quæ sic obligant gradus tres: Primum eorum, quorum obligatio oritur ex authoritate alterius jus habentis; in quorum numero sunt Leges Humanæ. Secundum eorum, quorum obligatio oritur ex actu libero propriæ voluntatis; qualia sunt vota, juramenta, promissiones, & pacta sponte inita. Tertium, eorum, quorum obligatio oritur ex intuitu fraternæ Charitatis [The right printed page is cut off at the scan edge. Visible fragments: Chari[?] / fcmd[?] / II / mihi[?] / pofi[?] / aut[?] / tidis[?] / dubi[?] / pulu[?] / solv[?] / sum[?] / gum[?] / haue[?] / præl[?] / rund[?] / Ubi / func[?] / Coms[?] / licit[?] / vitat[?] / quæ[?] / cessa[?] / colat[?] / præc[?] / & ö[?] / Quo[?] / gene[?] / gibu[?] / An[?] / quir[?] / publ[?] / latæ[?] / earui[?] / subd[?] / adeo[?] / ceat[?]. Each line is only partly visible; the words cannot be read in full.] Charitatis ; in qua classe consetur Lex sive ratio scandali.
units.tr: I said that all these things, each and every one, bind men's consciences, and that they bind them alone, absolutely, primarily, of themselves, and by their own power, because all of them, and they alone, express the will of God, to whom alone belongs the pure and direct authority over men's consciences. I warned, however, that besides these there are some others which bind consciences secondarily, relatively, and in the power of the law or will of God on which they rest, each in its own way. All of them agree in this, that whatever binding force they have, they must owe it entirely to the Divine Law (otherwise the Divine Law would not be the adequate rule of conscience), yet they differ from one another, each in kind, on account of the difference of their matter, and also in degree, as regards their binding force. There are, moreover, three grades of those things that bind in this way. The first is of those whose obligation arises from the authority of another who has the right to command; among these are human laws. The second is of those whose obligation arises from a free act of one's own will, such as vows, oaths, promises, and agreements freely entered into. The third is of those whose obligation arises from regard for fraternal charity, and in this class belongs the law, or rule, of scandal.

units.la: III. De Obligatione Legum Humanarum, multo mihi plura jam ante dicta sunt, quàm initio proposueram : multo tamen fortasse pauciora, quàm aut merebatur rei gravitas, cujus est in vita quotidiana usus longè frequentissimus, aut postularet dubiorum, quæ possent mentibus hominum scrupulum injicere, copia & varietas. In quibus dissolvendis, superioribus Terminis eò progressus sum, & post emensas eas difficultates, quæ ad Legum causas, Materialem, Efficientem & Formalem, haud incommodè revocari existimarem, ultima prælectione ad eas tractandas, quæ ad causam eorundem Finalem propiùs pertinerent, devenerim. Ubi jacto imprimis hoc totius disputationis velut fundamento, finem legum humanarum esse Bonum Communitatis, vel (quod idem est) pacem & felicitatem publicam : responsum est, quà licuit brevitate & perspicuitate, sex istis quæ sequuntur quæsitis. Primò, An sit in Rep. in ordine ad bonum commune, legum humanarum usus aliquis, saltem necessarius ? Secundò, quùm intersit Reip. ut virtus colatur, vitia coerceantur ; An Legislator possit praecipere omnes omnium virtutum actus & officia, & omnia cujuscunque generis peccata prohibere ? Quòd si non possit, An saltem teneatur, utriusque generis quotquot potest praecipere & prohibere legibus quæ obligent subditos in conscientia ? Tertiò, An & quatenus ad effectum obligandi subditos requiratur, ut intentio Legislatoris feratur in bonum publicum ? Quartò, si videbuntur leges jam antè latæ bono publico minùs utiles ; An & quatenus earum mutatio sit vel à principe tentanda, vel à subditis urgenda ? Quintò, quùm sit finis legum, adeòque ipsius regiminis, bonum commune, An liceat ob bonum commune ipsam totius regiminis formam immutare ? Vel ejus immutationem tentare ? Et quatenus ? ultimò, illud folenne dictum, Salus Populi Suprema Lex, quomodo fit rectè & sa-nè intelligendum ?
units.tr: III. Much more has already been said by me about the obligation of human laws than I had proposed at the beginning, yet perhaps much less than either the importance of the matter deserved (it is used most frequently in daily life) or the number and variety of the doubts that could put a scruple into men's minds would require. In resolving these, I advanced through the earlier lectures, and after I had gone through those difficulties which I thought could fairly be traced to the material, efficient and formal causes of laws, I came in the last lecture to treat those matters which belong more closely to the final cause of the same. There, having first laid down, as the foundation of the whole discussion, that the end of human laws is the common good, or (which is the same thing) public peace and happiness, I answered, as briefly and clearly as I could, the following six questions. First: is there in the commonwealth, with respect to the common good, some use of human laws, at least a necessary one? Second: since it concerns the commonwealth that virtue be cultivated and vices restrained, can the lawgiver command all the acts and duties of all virtues and forbid all sins of every kind? And if he cannot, is he at least bound to command and forbid, by laws that oblige subjects in conscience, as many of each kind as he can? Third: is it required, and how far, in order for a law to bind subjects, that the intention of the lawgiver be directed to the public good? Fourth: if laws already enacted seem less useful to the public good, is it, and how far, for the prince to attempt their change, or for the subjects to press for it? Fifth: since the end of laws, and therefore of government itself, is the common good, is it lawful, for the sake of the common good, to change the very form of the whole government, or to attempt such a change? And how far? Last: how is that well-known saying, "The welfare of the people is the supreme law," to be rightly and soundly understood?

units.la: IV. Hæc ego altiùs repetenda duxi, ut apud vos, post tam diuturnum Academicarum exercitationem justitium, totius instituti mei atque ordinis ratio meliùs constaret, & ut capita earum rerum, quas summâ cum humanitate jam olim auditas, tam longo temporis intervallo excidisse facilè credo, vobis in memoriam revocarem. Expectabitis opinor, nec immeritò, ut instítutum cursum currerem porrò, & ad ea quæ proximè reliqua sunt dubia dissolvenda rectà pergerem, de privilegiis scilicet, & dispensationibus, aliisque ad causæ genui[?] finale quomodolibet spectantibus. Fateor sanè, & mihi visum sic fieri oportere. Verùm interpellant amici: monent quorundam eorum qui nunc sunt hominum intolerandam pervicaciam postulare potiùs, ut quo illi (perversiùs haud facile dixerim, an fidentiùs,) abutuntur in publicam perniciem Aphorismo, eum etsi ultimâ superioris Termini prælectione novissimo loco explicuerim, sub incudem tamen revocarem denuò, & genuinum ejus sensum pleniùs aliquantò quàm est à me tunc factum, & explicatiùs aperirem; hoc est, me interprete, (addita duntaxat nonnullâ verborum pompâ) ut actum agerem, & coctam jam antè crambem recoctam vobis apponerem. Visa mihi parùm æqua postulatio: illi interim contrà, instare sedulo, prolixè rogare, ut facerem tamen. Veftræ erit humanitatis, donare hominis verecundiæ, quod rogantibus amicis concesserim: præsertim argumento usis[?] ad flectendum animum meum longè efficacissimo: & vestrum plerisque, hoc ipsum si facerem, gratum fore se non dubitare.
units.tr: IV. I thought it right to go back over these matters at some length, so that after so long an interruption of our academic exercises the reasoning of my whole undertaking and of its order might be clearer to you, and so that I might recall to your memory the heads of those things which you heard long ago with great courtesy, and which I readily believe have slipped from your minds over so long an interval. I suppose you will expect, and not unreasonably, that I should continue the course I began and proceed straight to resolve the doubts that remain, namely those concerning privileges and dispensations, and other matters that bear in any way on the final cause. I admit that I too think this is how it ought to be done. But friends interrupt me. They warn that the intolerable obstinacy of some men of our time demands rather that I should once more put on the anvil that maxim which they abuse (I could hardly say whether more perversely or more boldly) to the public ruin, and which I explained in the last lecture of the previous term, in the final place, and should set forth its genuine meaning more fully and more explicitly than I did then; that is, to repeat, with my own interpretation added and only a little verbal show, that I should be doing what is already done and serving up to you a cabbage already cooked and reheated. This request seemed to me not very fair. Yet they, on the other hand, pressed on, asking earnestly and at length that I do it nonetheless. It belongs to your kindness to pardon a man's modesty for having yielded to the entreaties of friends, especially since they used an argument that was by far the most effective in bending my mind; and I do not doubt that most of you will be glad if I do so.
