units.la: V. Quid ergo sibi velit pervulgatum illud axioma, Salus Populi Suprema Lex, & quomodo fit intelligendum expedire, praesentis est negotii. Excuderunt intra paucos annos homines non optimè feriati, & in Remp. etiam tandem, ut antè in Ecclesiam, invexerunt, novam unà cum Theologia Politicam. Qui, ut sub obtentu Libertatis Christianae (sive conscientiae,) totius regiminis Ecclesiastici; ita sub obtentu Libertatis Civilis (sive subditorum,) totius regiminis Politici, non modo vim omnem subnervare, sed ipsam quoque fabricam ab imis fundamentis revulsam labefactare, in hac tanta rerum perturbatione strenuè hactenus conati sunt; hodiéque pergunt, cum summo animorum ardore & terrore militari, conari. Hi, quoties conculcatae sub pedibus Regiae dignitatis, spretae sanctarum Legum authoritatis, perturbatae pacis publicae, ruptis omnibus jurium repagulis exercitae in concives effrænis & infandae tyrannidis, affectatae in Ecclesia, in Reip. (sublato omni natalium, honorum, statuum discrimine) paritatis, aliarumque ex Anabaptistarum puteis haustarum impietatum, postulantur: hoc unico, velut, clypeo, seque suósque mores tuentur, salute populi; hanc legibus, regibus, juribus, moribus, unam universis anteponendam scilicet.
units.tr: V. What the well-known axiom, "The welfare of the people is the supreme law," means, and how it is to be understood so as to be useful, is the business of the present matter. Within a few years, men not very well trained in the arts of peace hatched, and have at last introduced into the commonwealth, just as before they did into the Church, a new Political Theology along with it. Under the pretext of Christian liberty (or liberty of conscience), they have so far vigorously tried, in this great upheaval of affairs, to undermine not only all the force of the whole ecclesiastical government, but also to shake loose and weaken the very structure of the whole civil government from its lowest foundations; and today they still go on trying, with the utmost heat of spirit and military terror. Whenever they are challenged, these men, who trample underfoot royal dignity, despise the authority of the sacred laws, disturb public peace, break down every barrier of right and act with unbridled and monstrous tyranny against their fellow citizens, and who demand equality in the Church and in the commonwealth (with all distinction of birth, honour and rank abolished), along with other impieties drawn from the wells of the Anabaptists, they defend themselves and their own ways of life behind this one shield, the welfare of the people, which they set above all laws, kings, rights and customs alike.

units.la: VI. Ex hoc tam laxo & periculoso vulgaris dicti interpretamento, quum tumultibus, seditionibus, & omne genus licentiae popularî, non jam lata fenestra, sed decumana plane porta aperiatur; manifestum est, qui hoc clypeo nefaria sua scelera tuentur, non simplicem & genuinam ejus dicti sententiam amplecti, sed alienam ei affingere, quae pravis suis consiliis & causae non bonae praebeat, ex coacta interpretatione, speciem aliquam patrocinii. Quotus enim quisque est hominum, cui si (ut avaritiae, ambitioni, odio, iraeve suae inserviat) res novas moliri, & per fas nefasque latrociniis, rapinis, & concussionibus omnia complere libuerit: non proclive erit facinoribus suis & inceptis quibuscunque nefariis salutem populi praetexere? Excutite quaeso omnia quà patet orbis Annalium & Historiarum monimenta; sacrarum, prophanarum, veterum, recentiorum, exterarum, nostratium, invenietis hoc ipsum usque & usque factitasse, sub eodem libertatis & salutis popularis praetextu, omnium temporum, omnium locorum Catilinas & Cethegos: ut, {1} Pepenem cordis sui habere videatur (Tertulliani locutio est) qui sibi tam tenui fuco os sublini patiatur. Sed quo me, dum justae indignationi laxo habenas, incautum rapuit tempestas? Reprimo igitur me jam, ne videar [illegible, ~12 letters] & pro disputatore declamatorem agere; & ad rem ipsam accedo.
units.tr: VI. Since this so loose and dangerous interpretation of the common saying opens the way to tumults, seditions and every kind of popular license, and opens it not as a narrow window but as a plain great gate, it is clear that those who shelter their wicked crimes behind this shield do not embrace the simple and genuine sense of the saying. They attach to it a foreign meaning, and by forcing the interpretation they give some appearance of defence to their wicked designs and their bad cause. For how few people are there who, if it pleased them to stir up revolution, serving their greed, ambition, hatred or anger, and to fill everything with robbery, plunder and extortion by right or wrong, would find it hard to put forward the safety of the people as a pretext for their crimes and for whatever wicked undertakings they begin? Search, I beg you, all the monuments of annals and histories wherever the world extends: sacred, profane, ancient, recent, foreign, our own. You will find that the very same thing has been done again and again, under the same pretext of liberty and the safety of the people, by Catilines and Cethegi of every age and place, so that {1} he seems to have a pumpkin in his heart (Tertullian's phrase) who allows his face to be smeared with so thin a dye. But where does the storm carry me, as I give loose rein to my just indignation and lose my caution? I check myself now, lest I seem to play the declaimer rather than the disputant, and I come to the matter itself.

units.la: VII. Ubi illud imprimis expendendum est, quid in dicto axiomate salutis appellatione veniat intelligendum. Non enim, siquis aut dignitatem suam aut libertatem, in re aliqua levicula, vel etiam fortassis admodum gravi, laesam sentiat aut sentire se putet; illico salutis se jacturam fecisse, aut de salute periclitari, jure conqueri potent. Salutis enim alicujus rei aut personae, non laesio quaevis, aut incommodum, sed interitus opponitur; ut Graecis [illegible, ~6 letters]. Quinimo pariter omnino se res habet (servata utrinque debita analogia) in corpore Politico, & in Rep. sicut in corpore Humano persona singulari. Praeter contrariarum qualitatum in humano corpore pugnam, ex aliquo interni calidi aut humidi excessu vel defectu, & extrinsecus accidentium variâ immutatione, vix fieri potest ut quis tam integrâ valetudine usque perfruatur, quin aut saepiculè aliquâ saltem corporis parte, interna vel externa, id patiatur, quod ei molestiam afferat : fieri etiam potest ut ex po-dagrâ, odontalgiâ, calculo, aut alio partium mor-bo acutissimos sentiat dolores, vel etiam toto corpore affecto æger decumbat ; ut interim non sic opportunum, nedum necessarium, ut extrema quæque remedia,ut in aperto vitæ salutisque discrimine, confugere. Sic in Rep. non est mox aliquid attentandum contra Leges & Jura, non contrahenda vulgi collusies & tumultus excitandi, non ad arma, ad arma, continuò conclamandum, ut saluti populi consulatur scilicet ; quamprimum popularis aliquis tribunus, aut audaculus quispiam rhetoricator δημαγωγός[?], principem, proceres, magi-stratus, judices, eorumque ministros, aut eorum saltem aliquem, violati juris, illatæ injuriæ, aut neglecti quomodolibet officii, per calumniam (vel etiam si forte jure merito) reos apud plebem pro eminente peregerit. Fuerunt eruntque semper sub optimis Regibus & in optimè constitutis Rebuspublicis, ex abusu potestatis tenuiorum civium oppressiones : aliáque gravamina non pauca : quibus in integrum aut prævertendis aut medendis, nulla regentium cura & industria, nulla sufficere queat Legum severitas. Hujus generis si quoties unum aut alterum exemplum emerserit, licebit consestim factiosis civibus, obtentu salutis publicæ, legibus & jure contemptis, vi & armis rem gerere pro lubitu suo : à turbis & tumultibus nunquam tuta aut quieta erunt regna & Resp. Omninò praedixit Christus [illegible, ~30 letters] & mundo nobis exeundum esse monuit Apostolus ; vel quærendam Utopiam aliquam, aut Remp. Platonis, quæ nos salvos præstet ; si salutem populi sic interpretari velimus, ut nisi infimi quique cives ab omni injusta vi, & iniquâ potentiorum dominatione, sint prorsus securi, nulla sit reliqua publica salus. Tunc salus agitur Reipub. cùm ab externorum externorum hostium incursionibus, vel improborum Civium depraedationibus, manifestè in tam apertum discrimen res deductæ sunt, ut ni providè & maturè succurratur, patria fit indubiè peritura.
units.tr: VII. Here the first thing to weigh is what is to be understood by the word safety in the saying. For if anyone feels, or thinks he feels, that his dignity or liberty has been harmed in some trifling matter, or perhaps even in a very serious one, he cannot rightly complain at once that he has suffered a loss of safety, or that his safety is in danger. For the opposite of the safety of a thing or a person is not any injury or inconvenience whatever, but destruction; as the Greeks put it [illegible, ~6 letters]. Indeed, the case is entirely the same (with the proper analogy kept on both sides) in the political body and the commonwealth as in the human body of a single person. Apart from the clash of contrary qualities in the human body, arising from some excess or deficiency of the internal hot or moist, and from the varied change of external accidents, it can hardly happen that anyone enjoys such perfect health that he does not, at some time or other, suffer in some part of the body, internal or external, something that causes him discomfort. It may also happen that from gout, toothache, the stone, or some other disease of the parts he feels the most acute pains, or that, with the whole body affected, he lies sick in bed. Yet it is not so fitting, let alone necessary, to resort at once to the extreme remedies, as if in the open peril of life and safety. So in the commonwealth one must not at once attempt something against the laws and rights, nor enter into collusion with the crowd and stir up tumults, nor cry out at once to arms, to arms, in order, forsooth, that the safety of the people may be looked after, as soon as some popular tribune, or some bold rhetorician (a [δημαγωγός] demagogue), has brought before the common people, by calumny (or even, perhaps, with just cause), the prince, nobles, magistrates, judges, their ministers, or at least some one of them, as guilty of violating the law, inflicting injury, or neglecting their duty in any way. There have been and always will be, even under the best kings and in the best constituted commonwealths, oppressions of the lesser citizens arising from the abuse of power, and not a few other grievances, which no care and diligence of the rulers, and no severity of the laws, can wholly prevent or cure. If anyone of this kind comes to light once or twice, factious citizens may at once, under the cover of public safety, with laws and right despised, carry on affairs by force and arms as they please; and kingdoms and commonwealths will never be safe or quiet from tumults. Christ foretold this altogether, and the Apostle warned us that we must go out of the world; or else we must seek some Utopia or Plato's Republic which would keep us safe, if we wished to interpret the safety of the people in such a way that, unless the lowest citizens are completely secure from every unjust violence and the unjust domination of the more powerful, there is no public safety left at all. The safety of the commonwealth is at stake when affairs have been brought into such open peril, by the incursions of foreign enemies or the plundering of wicked citizens, that unless help is given wisely and promptly, the country will undoubtedly perish.

units.la: VIII. De salute vidimus. Videndum proximè, quàm rectè à novatoribus nostris accipiatur alterum illud populi vocabulum. Est autem populus, ut ex amissis de Republica Ciceronis libris definit {'}D. Augustinus, Coetus multitudinis hominum juris consensu & utilitatis communione sociatus. Quâ appellatione Romani olim omnes omnis ordinis & conditionis cives continebantur. Erat autem illi præter Monarchas (Reges primis, Imperatores ultimis sæculis,) in triplici gradu: Patricii scil. sive senatorii ordinis, Equites & Plebs. Sed quâ latitudine vox ea apud Romanos Scriptores, ubicunque occurrit, sit accipienda; ex adjunctis circumstantiis lectori colligendum est: id quod plerumque ex appositis oppositis terminis (si qui oppositi sint) optimè fieri potest, certissimo in eam rem argumento.{*} Accipi autem solet Populi vocabulum Romanis Scriptoribus, tribus hisce fere modis. Primò, & omnium modorum rarissimè, pro sola plebe, qui fuit totius Romani populi infimus ordo. Ut in illo
units.tr: VIII. We have seen concerning safety. Next we must consider how rightly our innovators understand the other word, people. Now populus, as St. Augustine defines it from the lost books of Cicero's On the Republic, is a gathering of a multitude of men bound together by agreement in law and by community of interest. Under this name the Romans once included all their citizens of every rank and condition. Apart from their monarchs (kings in the earliest ages, emperors in the last), they were in a threefold order: namely the Patricians, that is, of the senatorial order, the Knights and the Plebs. But in what breadth the word is to be taken wherever it occurs in Roman writers must be gathered by the reader from the attendant circumstances; and this can most often be done well from the opposed terms set beside it (if any are opposed), which is a most certain proof in this matter. The word populus, however, is usually taken by Roman writers in about three ways. First, and most rarely of all, for the plebs alone, which was the lowest order of the whole Roman people. As in that line of Martial:

units.la: Martialis :
units.tr: Martial:

units.la: Dat populus, dat gratus eques, dat thura Senatus.
units.tr: The people give, the grateful knights give, the Senate gives incense.

units.la: Ubi oppositus senatui & equitibus populus, non nisi plebem solam significare potest. Secundò, pro utroque inferiori ordine populi, plebe scil. & equestri ordine conjunctim, ordine supremo sive patricio tantum exclusò. Visum enim fuit patribus, initio constitutæ Reip. exactis jam regibus, aliquam honoris & dignitatis prærogativam supra alios cives apud se retinere, inque ejus rei significationem semet à reliquo populi cœtu nominis appellatione segregare. Unde illæ fluxerunt solennes formulæ, Senatus Populíque Romanus, vísum est Senatui Populoque Romano, &c. In quibus Populi nomen equites cum plebe, hoc est, excepto Senatu, reliquos cives omnes complectitur. Tertiò, pro omnibus omnium ordinum civibus indiscriminatim, patribus, equitibus, plebe: ex his enim tribus ordinibus, postquam desiissent esse Reges, necdum orti essent Imperatores, universa civitas constabat. Et in hoc sensu, siquidem toto illo spatio illius Reip, status erat popularis, intelligendi sunt Romanarum rerum Scriptores, quoties de salute, dignitate, majestate populi confervandâ loquuti sunt.
units.tr: Here populus, set against the Senate and the knights, can signify only the plebs alone. Second, for both lower orders of the people together, namely the plebs and the equestrian order, with only the highest or patrician order excluded. For it seemed good to the fathers, at the beginning of the constituted commonwealth, once the kings had been expelled, to keep for themselves some prerogative of honour and dignity above the other citizens, and as a sign of this to separate themselves by name from the rest of the body of the people. Hence arose those solemn formulas, The Senate and the Roman People; it has seemed good to the Senate and the Roman People, and so on. In these the name People embraces the knights with the plebs, that is, all the other citizens apart from the Senate. Third, for all the citizens of all orders indiscriminately, fathers, knights, plebs: for after the kings had ceased to be, and before the emperors had arisen, the whole state consisted of these three orders. And in this sense, since throughout that whole period the commonwealth was of a popular kind, the writers of Roman affairs are to be understood whenever they speak of preserving the safety, dignity or majesty of the people.

units.la: IX. Hæc ego diligentius paulò exposui; non solùm quia vocabulorum plerorumque hujus generis propriæ significationes ex ejus populi usu pendent, à quibus & voces ipsæ ad nos derivatæ sunt: sed etiam alia de causa duplici. Alterâ, ne ambi-gua vocis minùs commodâ interpretatione decipi nos & circumveniri patiamur: alterâ, ne in nudâ populi appellatione vis fiat, in præjudicium ejus qui princeps est communicatis, & populi caput. Quarum utraque quanti sit momenti ad rem præsentem, ex his quæ jam dicturus sum, statim intelligetis.
units.tr: IX. I have set out these things rather more carefully, not only because the proper meanings of most words of this kind depend on the usage of that people, from which the words themselves have come down to us, but also for another two-fold reason. The first is that we may not allow ourselves to be deceived and circumvented by the ambiguity of the word through a less fitting interpretation. The second is that violence may not be done to the bare word people, to the prejudice of him who is prince and the head of the people, as if they were merged together. How much each of these matters to the present question you will understand at once from what I am about to say.

units.la: X. Dico itaque primò, Populi vocabulum, (ut pleraque alia nomina multitudinem aggregatam significantia,) sumi posse dupliciter. Vel Collectivè, ut significet totam communitatem Reipublicæ; id est, principem & subditos simul: vel difcretivè, & præcisè, ut significet subditos tantùm & seorsim à Rege. Eodem omnino modo, quo corpus vel dicit reliqua membra simul cum capite; vel membra illa præcisè & seorsim à capite: Et Familiæ appellatio nunc omnes complectitur qui unaunarum sunt aedium, uxorem, liberos, famulos ipsamque etiam patrem-familias qui reliquis praeest; nunc eos tantum qui sub ipsius imperio sunt & quorum ipse curam gerit: Et Exercitus nomine alias continetur una cum militibus ipse etiam Imperator, alias non continetur. Quod idem & in Regni, Parlamenti, aliisque id genus vocibus, quae significant Collectionem quidem multorum, cum ordine tamen & ratione ad unum aliquod, veluti principium & caput, facile est cernere. Igitur, si non maxime maligne (ut suspicari liceat) at certè periculosissimo errore, factum est, ut quod de populo priore sensu dictum est, Collectivè scil. & ut ea vox complecticur inclusivè totam communitatem, i.e. una cum subditis principem, detorqueatur & accommodetur populo in posteriore acceptione, i.e. solis subditis exclusivè.
units.tr: X. I say, then, first, that the word populus (like many other nouns signifying an aggregated multitude) can be taken in two ways. Either collectively, so that it signifies the whole community of the commonwealth, that is, the prince and subjects together; or distinctively and precisely, so that it signifies the subjects only, and apart from the king. Exactly in the same way, the word body either denotes the remaining members together with the head, or those members precisely and apart from the head. And the name family sometimes embraces all who are under one roof, wife, children, servants, and the head of the household himself who is over the rest; sometimes only those who are under his authority and for whom he cares. And the name army sometimes includes the commander himself along with the soldiers, and sometimes does not. The same can easily be seen in the words kingdom, parliament, and other words of that kind, which signify a collection of many, yet with order and reference to some one thing, as to a beginning and head. So if it has happened, not out of the most malicious intent (though one may suspect it), but at least through a most dangerous error, that what has been said of the people in the former sense, namely collectively, and as that word includes inclusively the whole community, that is, the prince together with the subjects, is twisted and applied to the people in the latter sense, that is, to the subjects alone, exclusively.

units.la: XI. At qui constare poterit nobis, inquiet, Populi appellationem priore sensu & Collectivè in isto Axiomate intelligi debere potius, quàm posteriore & disjunctivè? Respondeo, ex communi usu loquendi, & analogia aliarum vocum ejusdem rationis & significationis abundè satis id constat. In quibus certissimus interpretandi Canon est; Voces collectivas collectivè semper sumi debere, nisi adjunctum ejus oppositum diversum postulet. Exempli gratiâ, ubi dicitur, Col. 1. 18. Christum esse caput corporis Ecclesiæ: manifestum est ex opposito adjecto; Capitis, scil. mentione, (cui Corpus ibi relativè opponitur;) Corporis vocabulum disjunctivè sumi, pro reliquis membris corporis præcisè & seorsim à capite. Sic etiam, si quis diceret Imperatorem Exercitum è castris eduxisse, aut in hyberna demisisse: vel patrem-familias inter dixisse, nequis domesticorum intempestâ nocte exiret ex aedibus; vel (quod de Davide scribitur) quidquid Rex fecisset, gratum id Populo fuisse: manifestum est, ex adjecto ubique opposito Imperatoris, Domini, Regis nomine, vocabula illa collectiva Exercitus, Familiæ, Populi, non esse tamen Collectivè intelligenda, sed Discretivè & exclusivè. Hoc est, Exercitus appellatione milites solùm contineri, Imperatorem non item; & Familiæ, domesticos solùm, non Dominum; & Populi, subditos solùm, non item Regem. Ratio est, quia adjectum in ipso orationis filo oppositum, quod est alterum correlatorum, necessariò innuit vocem collectivam, sibi ex adverso respondentem & ei relativè oppositam, continere suum correlatum præcisè: hoc est, multitudinem duntaxat, illi velut principio & capiti connexam & conjunctam, non autem totam communitatem ex utroque termino correlato quasi aggregatam.
units.tr: XI. But someone will ask: how can we establish that the word "people" in this axiom should be understood in the first sense and collectively, rather than in the second sense and disjunctively? I answer that this is sufficiently clear from common usage and from the analogy of other words of the same kind and meaning. There is a most certain rule of interpretation here: collective words must always be taken collectively, unless an opposite term added alongside demands otherwise. For example, where Col. 1. 18 says that Christ is the head of the body of the Church, it is plain from the opposed term added that body is taken disjunctively, for the remaining members of the body, separate and apart from the head, since the head is mentioned and the body is set over against it in relation. So too, if someone said that a general had led his army out of camp or moved it into winter quarters, or if a householder had ordered that none of his household should leave the house on a dark night, or (as is written of David) that whatever the king did was pleasing to the people: it is plain, from the term general, lord or king added in each case as an opposite, that the collective words army, household and people are not to be understood collectively but discretively and exclusively. That is, under the word army only the soldiers are included and not the general; under household, only the servants and not the master; under people, only the subjects and not the king. The reason is that the opposite term, added in the very course of the sentence, being the other of the correlatives, necessarily indicates that the collective word standing over against it in relation contains precisely its own correlate: that is, only the multitude joined and connected with that principle and head, and not the whole community gathered together out of both correlate terms.

units.la: XII. Cæterum ubi non est adjectum oppositum, quod ipsius significationem ad alteram tantùm relationis partem necessariò contrahat; ab omni sanè ratione alienum est, collectivam dictionem aliter quàm collectivè accipere, & in justa sua latitudine: ita scil. ut utrumque relationis terminum suo ambitu complectatur. Maximè, ubi in salutis, militaris, alterìúsque boni aut commodi quod sit utrique commune, ratione sermo versatur: Exempli gratiâ; Si statueretur cras movenda castra, ne Exercitui ab hoste opprimeretur; aut in Familiæ usum fruges colligendas: non esse incolumi capite vel Orestes juraret eum hominem, qui quæ de Exercitu & Familiâ dicta essent sic intelligeret, quasi militibus solùm & famulis prospectum esse vellent, nullâ interim Imperatoris qui exercitum, nullâ Patris-familiâs qui in familiam regit, habitâ ratione.
units.tr: XII. Moreover, where no opposite term is added which must narrow its meaning to only one side of the relation, it is certainly contrary to all reason to take a collective expression otherwise than collectively, and in its proper breadth, so that it embraces both terms of the relation within its compass. This holds most of all when the discourse concerns safety, military matters, or any other good or advantage common to both. For example: if it were decided that the camp should be moved tomorrow, so that the army might not be overwhelmed by the enemy, or that the crops should be gathered for the use of the household, then anyone who understood what was said of the army and household in such a way as to suppose that provision was made only for the soldiers and servants, taking no account of the general who commands the army or the father of the household who governs the family, would be a man whom even Orestes would swear was out of his mind.

units.la: Quod perinde est, ac si valetudinarius à medico admonitus, ut Corporis sui curam aliquantò diligentiorem in posterum haberet; pedes & crura & quæ post cervicem sunt membra inciperet exinde quàm diligentissimè fovere; quid interim Capiti fieret, supinè securus: eò quod medicus Corporis tantùm meminisset, non item Capitis.
units.tr: This is just as if an invalid, advised by his physician to take somewhat more careful thought for the care of his body in future, should begin to look after his feet and legs and whatever members lie behind the neck most diligently, while meanwhile he remained carelessly unconcerned about the head: because the physician had mentioned the body only, and not the head.

units.la: XIII. Accedo adhuc ad rem propiùs. Si gregariorum forte militum turba salutem Exercitus dicerent esse Supremam Legem militarem; suum autem imperatorem dura nimis nec ferenda militibus imperare, ita ut periculum fit ni maturè jugum collo excutiant, amissam brevi fore universam Exercitus libertatem: atque ex hoc principio de tuendâ vi & armis libertate, imperatis non faciendis, ipso etiam Imperatore tollendo, consilia inter se agitarent; Vel si servi domestici, (quod tamen vult Apostolus, 1 Pet. 2. 18. Heris, non bonis tantùm & aquis, sed duris quoque & morosis suiici,) factâ inter se conjuratione, herilia jussa ut iniqua recusarent, Herum ipsum ut asperiùs dominantem exturbarent ex aedibus, claves & loculos & universam supellestilem occuparent & omnem rem domesticam pro suâ libidine administrarent; hoc uno prætextu, quòd sit salus Familiae suprema Lex Oeconomica. Quis non fateretur scelera- ta illa & nefaria Consilia, ex istis Principiis, (quae sanè, sanè intellecta, & verissima sunt & utilissima,) non posse legitimâ ullâ consecutione deduci? Et tamen non est ovum ovo similius, quàm huic argumentandi generi eorum hominum ra- tiocinatio, qui seditionibus civilibus salutem populi obtendunt. Quasi vero non contineretur, idque eminenter, in salute Exercitus, & Imperatoris; in salute Familiae, & Patris-familias; in salute Populi, & Principis salus. Ut summatim dicam; salus Populi, id est, Regis & Subditorum simul, fatendum est esse Supremam Legem: at salutem Populi, id est, Subditorum secluso Rege non item.
units.tr: XIII. I come closer still to the matter. Suppose a crowd of common soldiers should say that the safety of the army is the supreme military law; and that their commander imposes harsh and intolerable commands on the soldiers, so that unless they quickly shake off the yoke from their necks, the whole liberty of the army will soon be lost; and suppose they then plotted among themselves, on this principle of defending liberty by force and arms, to refuse the commander's orders and even to remove the commander himself. Or suppose the household servants (though the Apostle requires otherwise: 1 Pet. 2. 18. Servants, be subject to your masters, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward) made a conspiracy among themselves, refused their master's orders as unjust, drove the master out of the house as too harsh a ruler, seized the keys and the strongboxes and all the household goods, and managed all the domestic affairs at their own pleasure, under the single pretext that the safety of the household is the supreme economic law. Who would not admit that such wicked and abominable plans cannot be derived by any lawful sequence from those principles (which, rightly understood, are indeed most true and most useful)? And yet the reasoning of those men who put forward the "safety of the people" as a pretext for civil sedition is exactly like this kind of argument, and nothing could be more alike. As if the safety of the army were not contained in that of the commander; the safety of the household in that of the householder; the safety of the people in that of the prince, and to a greater degree. To put it briefly: the safety of the people, that is, of king and subjects together, must be admitted to be the supreme law; but the safety of the people, that is, of the subjects with the king set aside, is not so.

units.la: IV. Dico Secundò, quiddam amplius. Etsi Populi vocabulo in hoc axiomate nec subditos sine Principe, nec sine subditis Principem, præcisè & solitariè intelligi debere, sed utrosque conjunctim, satis dilucidè à me confirmatum existimem: qui tamen aut dignitatem personarum, aut istius ipsius Aphorismi originem attentiùs consideraverit, libentius eum concessurum, de salute Principis præcisè intelligendum esse celebre id dictum, quàm de salute subditorum præcisè.
units.tr: IV. I say, secondly, something further. Although I think I have shown quite clearly that in this axiom the word people must be understood to include neither the subjects without the prince nor the prince without the subjects, but both together; yet whoever considers more attentively the dignity of the persons, or the origin of this very maxim, will more readily concede that the famous saying is to be understood chiefly of the safety of the prince, rather than chiefly of the safety of the subjects.

units.la: Imprimis, sacrosanctam esse Regum Majestatem, non veteres solum Patres Ecclesiastici (etiam tunc cum nulli adhuc essent Reges Christiani,) prolixissimè agnoverunt; qui eos ut homines à Deo secundos, & solo Deo minores coluerunt, pro eorum salute vota & preces Deo obtulerunt, ab eorum salute totius populi salutem & felicitatem pendere docuerunt; sed & ipse Deus Opt. Max. in sacris literis (ut fusè ostendi pofset, si opus effet) abunde testatum esse voluit.
units.tr: In the first place, the sacred majesty of kings was acknowledged most fully not only by the ancient Fathers of the Church (even when there were as yet no Christian kings), who honoured them as men second to God and less than God alone, offered vows and prayers to God for their safety, and taught that the safety and happiness of the whole people depend upon their safety; but God himself, the Best and Greatest, has been pleased to bear abundant witness to this in the sacred writings (as I could show at length, if there were need).

units.la: Unde factum, ut eâ semper mente fuerint pii omnes & bonæ indolis cives, ut ubi ex aleâ belli in extremum discrimen adductæ res essent, unius Regis salutem suæ omnium saluti anteponendam judicarent: Quod, uti bonos subditos decuit, aperte professi sunt Israelitæ illi, qui sub execrandâ conjuratione Absolonicâ, Davidi Regi debitam fidelitatem servaverant, 2 Sam. 18. 3. Nec illud voluere, qui Regem (non homini mortali in rem suam turpiter adblandientes, sed Spiritu Dei sancto dictante locuti) narium suarum Spiritum esse dixerunt. Sic enim pius, & ab utero sanctificatus propheta, Jeremias locutus est, Thren. 4. 20. Translatione usus aptissimâ: quum sit Spiritus ille qui per nares attrahitur & emittitur, {'}Spiritus ille vitalis, quo quasi vinculo connectitur anima corpori, & quo deficiente, exspirare protinus necesse est animal vivens, & interire. Cum exit Spiritus ejus ejus, revertitur homo in terram suam, Pfalm. 146. 4.
units.tr: Hence it has always been the mind of all pious and well-disposed citizens, when affairs have been brought to the utmost peril by the chance of war, to judge the safety of one king to be placed before the safety of them all. This the Israelites clearly professed, as became good subjects, who under the accursed conspiracy of Absalom had kept the fidelity due to King David: 2 Sam. 18. 3. Nor were those men unwilling to say the same, who, speaking not to flatter a mortal man for their own advantage but with the Holy Spirit of God dictating, called the king the breath of our nostrils. For so the pious prophet Jeremiah, sanctified from the womb, spoke: Thren. 4. 20, using a most apt metaphor. For it is that spirit which is drawn in and breathed out through the nostrils, that vital breath by which the soul is joined to the body as by a bond, and when which fails, the living creature must straightway expire and perish: When his breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth, Psalm 146. 4.

units.la: XV. Quin & illud obfervatu dignum est, à Romana gente ad nos devenisse illud de quo nunc agimus axioma: illis tunc usurpatum cum maximè floreret Roma sub statu populari. Non est utique quod quis miretur, illis salutem Populi fuisse pro Suprema Lege; quibus ipse Populus erat Suprema Potestas. Populi tunc erant Leges, Populi judicia, Populi universa jurisdictio, ipsa denique αὐτοκρατορεία Populi, & Majestas. Unde illa tam frequens, apud historicos omnes, apud Ciceronem, apud alios ejus aevi scriptores, de Majestate Populi Romani mentio; ut in statu Democratico: quae omnia in statu Monarchico, non populi sunt, sed Principis. Ergo quanti illis fuit Populi salus, apud quos Populi erat Majestas, quod quanti fuerit hoc ipso Aphorismo tori orbi testatum esse voluerunt: tanti nobis, si nos ejus Aphorismi authoritate tueri velimus, servata modò, ut par est, in tam differentibus utriusque Republicae formis Analogia, debet esse Regum Salus, qui non aliam quàm Regiam agnoscimus Majestatem.
units.tr: XV. Indeed it is also worth observing that this axiom which we are now discussing came down to us from the Roman people, who used it at the time when Rome flourished most under a popular constitution. There is certainly no cause for wonder that for them the safety of the people was the supreme law, for whom the people itself was the supreme power. Then the laws were the people's, the judgements were the people's, the whole jurisdiction was the people's, and finally the autocracy [αὐτοκρατορεία] and majesty were the people's. Hence the so frequent mention, among all the historians, among Cicero and the other writers of that age, of the majesty of the Roman people, as in a democratic state; whereas in a monarchical state all these things belong not to the people but to the prince. Therefore, as much as the safety of the people was worth to those for whom the majesty was the people's, and as much as they wished it to be attested to the whole world by this very maxim, so much, if we wish to defend ourselves by the authority of this maxim, must the safety of kings be worth to us, who acknowledge no majesty other than the royal majesty, provided only that the analogy is kept, as it should be, between two such different forms of commonwealth.

units.la: XVI. Ex his quae dicta sunt satis constare puto, nec in illa Salutis, nec in ista Populi appellatione eam inesse vim, ut inde possit sine summa perversitate pervulgatum hoc Axioma in Regiae dignitatis praejudicium distorqueri. Quod si reliqua illa, quae sola jam supersunt, verba rite pendantur, Suprema scil. Lex; agnoscent, uti spero, quibus aliquid reliquum est aut cordis aut frontis, isto Axiomate vix potuisse dici aliquid quod ad summam Regum Potestatem stabiliendum amplius esset & illustrius. Supponit enim ista locutio Suprema Lex, esse oportere necessariò alicubi in omni Rep. potestatem aliquam, quae fit[?] omni positivâ Lege Humanâ superior : ad quam prospicere pertineat, & authoritate suâ procurare, nequid ex Legum defectu, vel nimium superstitiosâ observatione, Respublica detrimenti capiat. Cujus rei ratio manifesta satis est : quia nec potest Legislator, vel prudentissimus, omnes circumstantias eventuum futurorum praevidere ; nec ut nihil contingat eorum quae insecutura suspicatur mala & incommoda, Legibus sufficienter praecavere. Quod nec Legum culpa fit, nec Legislatoris ; sed ( ut optimè observavit Aristoteles, ) ex ipsa natura earum rerum, quae Legibus definiendae sunt: quae cum sint & pro varietate sua indefinitae, & quia ex futuro pendent incertae, non possunt propterea certis aliquibus & definitis Regulis comprehendi. Satis igitur fecit officio suo Legislator, si legibus ea constituerit, quae sint plerumque justa, & utilia toti communitati : etsi fieri potest, saepissimeque fit, ut ex emergente aliqua inopinata occasione, deficiant illae Leges in casu aliquo particulari non praeviso. Quo in casu, nisi sit alicui personae vel personis exercendae Arbitrariae cujusdam Potestatis relictus locus: nullum erit reliquum remedium satis efficax, quo periclitanti Patriae subveniatur, & publicae saluti consulatur. Hoc est, quod viri prudentes semper statuerunt, & ratio etiam suadet, Æquitati cedere debere ubi exigit necessitas, Justitiam Legalem : quum sit Æquitas nihil aliud, (eodem Aristotele definitore,) quàm [illegible, ~6 letters] Emendatio scil. sive Correctio Justitiae Legalis, vel etiam ipsius Legis (ut ipse suam illam definitionem mox explicat) [illegible, ~20 letters], supplendo ejus defectum in casibus particularibus, in quibus ipsam aut à Justitia, aut ab utilitate publica, deficere contingit ob nimiam generalitatem. Leges enim necesse est constituti generaliter liter per respectum ad ea quae plerumque fieri solent; non autem ad omnia ea quae contingere possunt in particulari: quorum nonnullis si strictè & ex verborum praescripto accommodentur Legis, deficere eas necesse est etiam, aut à Justitia morali, aut ab Utilitate Communi, aut ab utraque.
units.tr: XVI. From what has been said I think it is sufficiently clear that neither the word Salus nor the word Populus carries such force that this widely repeated axioma could be twisted, without the greatest perversity, to the prejudice of royal dignity. If the remaining words, which alone are left, are weighed properly, namely Suprema Lex, then those who have some part of heart or brow left will acknowledge, I hope, that scarcely anything more full or more illustrious for establishing the supreme power of kings could have been said than this axioma. For the expression Suprema Lex presupposes that there must necessarily be somewhere in every commonwealth some power that is superior to every positive Human Law, and whose task is to watch over the state and, by its authority, see to it that the commonwealth suffers no harm either from a lack of laws or from an overly superstitious observance of them. The reason is plain enough: the lawgiver, however wise, cannot foresee all the circumstances of future events, nor can he sufficiently guard by laws against every evil and inconvenience that he suspects may follow. This is the fault neither of the laws nor of the lawgiver but, as Aristotle very well observed, arises from the nature of the matters that laws are meant to define. Since these are by their variety indefinite, and since they depend on the future they are uncertain, they cannot therefore be comprehended by any certain and definite rules. The lawgiver, then, does his duty well enough if he enacts laws that are for the most part just and useful to the whole community; although it can happen, and very often does happen, that some unforeseen emergency makes those laws fail in a particular case that was not foreseen. In such a case, unless room is left for some person or persons to exercise a certain arbitrary power, there will be no remaining remedy effective enough to help a country in danger and to provide for public safety. This is what wise men have always decided, and reason too suggests, that Equity must yield to legal Justice where necessity demands it; for equity is nothing other (to take Aristotle again as the definer) than the correction of legal justice, or even of the law itself (as he himself explains his definition shortly afterwards [...]), supplying its defect in particular cases in which it happens to fall short either of Justice or of public utility because of its excessive generality. For laws must necessarily be framed generally, with respect to what usually happens, and not with respect to all the things that can occur in particular. If some of these were strictly fitted to the wording of the law, the law would necessarily fall short either of moral Justice, or of the Common Good, or of both.

units.la: XVII. Hoc igitur posito, postulare Salutem Populi, hoc est, publicam utilitatem, ut sit in Rep. Authoritas aliqua Legibus superior, quae earum defectus suppleat: & illud etiam necessariò consequitur, quod idem Aristoteles in Politicis asserit, Supremam hanc Authoritatem non posse ad alium quempiam pertinere quàm ad ipsum {1}τὴν ἀρχ-ὴν[?], hoc est, eum qui toti communitati cum summo Imperio praeest.
units.tr: XVII. Given this, to demand the safety of the people, that is, public utility, is to demand that there be in the commonwealth some authority superior to the laws which supplies their defects. It also follows necessarily, as Aristotle asserts in the Politics, that this supreme authority cannot belong to anyone other than to the one who holds {1}τὴν ἀρχ-ὴν[?], that is, the one who presides over the whole community with supreme power.

units.la: Ὣς λαοί τ' [illegible, ~12 letters] [illegible, ~8 letters]
units.tr: Ὣς λαοί τ' [...] [...] — Thus the peoples [...] [...]

units.la: Sive is unus fit, ut in regimine Monarchico; sive plures, ut in aliis Rerump. formis. Ergóne licebit subditis, publicae Libertatis, vel etiam Salutis obtentu, Legum & omnia juris ac fidelitatis vincula abrumpere, Legúmque simul & Regum Authoritatem intolerando fastu sub pedibus conculcare? atque in tanti facinoris patrocinium, hoc uno Aphorismo turpiter abuti, quem crepare solent, ac sibi mutuò subinde succinere seditiosi cives Salus Populi Suprema Lex? Quî fit, ut contrà non intelligant, hoc ipso dicto agnosci Principis in ipsas Leges aliquod Imperium? Ita ut ipsi liceat ex plenitudine Potestatis, ubi cogit necessitas & res morâm non patitur, ut ab hostibus externis vel domesticis perduellibus suam subdirorumque salutem tueatur, strictam Legum observationem interim deponere, vel seponere saltem ad tempus: ne ex nimium superstitiosâ & intempestivâ Legum Reverentiâ, sequeque populumque suum, ipsas quoque demum Leges, in hostium potestatem devenire permittat.
units.tr: Whether it is one person, as in a monarchical government, or several, as in the other forms of commonwealth: will subjects then be permitted, under the pretext of public liberty or even of safety, to break all the bonds of law, of right and of fidelity, and to trample under foot in intolerable arrogance the authority of the laws and of kings alike? Will they shamefully abuse, in defence of so great a crime, this single axioma which seditious citizens are wont to bawl out and to echo back to one another, Salus Populi Suprema Lex? How does it happen that they do not see that this very saying acknowledges some power of the prince over the laws themselves? So that he may, by the fullness of his power, when necessity compels and the matter brooks no delay, set aside, or at least put aside for a time, the strict observance of the laws, in order to defend his own and his subjects' safety against foreign enemies or domestic traitors; lest, through an overly superstitious and untimely reverence for the laws, he allow himself and his people, and at last the laws themselves, to fall into the power of the enemy.

units.la: XVIII. Illi Quæstioni, An Princeps Legibus à se latis vel confirmatis, & populi consensu approbatis, usúque receptis, solutus fit? & quatenus eas (ordinariè) observare teneatur? erit fortasse (si Deus dabit) suus postea locus. Nunc illud tantùm quæritur, Nunquid ipsi liceat, extra ordinem & in casu necessitatis, pro salute publicâ tuendâ, præter vel etiam contra Leges aliquid facere? Sic facere licere, idque bonâ Conscientiâ, uti primò optimorum Regum, in omnium quâ patet orbis gentium historiis, exempla probant; & dictat secundò ipsa ratio, à Legum [illegible, ~6 letters] defectu, & eventuum particularium multiplicitate atque incertitudine modò adductâ; & tertiò satis firmant, quæ de Jure Regum sunt à Samuele disputata, nec possunt commodè (quod tamen est à multis tentatum) aliorsum trahi, 1 Sam. 8. Ita ne cui hac in re, ex præsente dicto pravè intellecto, aliquis aut superfit, aut oboriatur scrupulus; liceat mihi quaeso celebre hoc dictum ad primam suam Originem revocare denuò: Et ni id effecero ut fateamini, salutis publicæ procurationem posthabitis Legibus, idque ex sententia istius dicti, ex ipsius Principis voluntate solâ, nec omnino ex Populi Arbitrio, pendere; cæcutire in clarissima luce, & optimæ causæ non defensorem, sed proditorem & prævaricatorem hactenus fuisse me, exististimate.
units.tr: XVIII. As for the question, Whether the Prince is released from the laws enacted or confirmed by himself, approved by the consent of the people and received by use, and how far he is bound to observe them (ordinarily), that will perhaps have its own place later, if God grants it. For now only this is asked: whether it is lawful for him, outside the ordinary course and in a case of necessity, for the sake of protecting public safety, to do something beside or even against the laws. That it is lawful to do so, and with a good conscience, first the examples of the best kings, in the histories of all the nations of the world, prove; second, reason itself dictates it, from the defect of laws and from the multiplicity and uncertainty of particular events just adduced; and third, what Samuel disputed about the right of kings firmly confirms, and cannot conveniently be drawn elsewhere, though many have tried, 1 Sam. 8. So, lest any scruple remain or arise in anyone on this matter from the present saying, wrongly understood, allow me, I beg, to recall this celebrated saying once more to its first origin. And unless I shall have brought you to admit that the procuring of public safety, with the laws set aside, depends on the will of the prince alone according to the sense of that saying, and not at all on the judgment of the people, then judge that I have hitherto been blind in the clearest light, and have been not the defender of a good cause but its betrayer and prevaricator.

units.la: XIX. A Romana gente ad nos defluxisse hoc axioma paulò ante dixi: Illud nunc adjicio, in tertio Marci Ciceronis de Legibus libro, primò (quod sciam) id scriptum reperiri; haustum tamen ( ut ipse Cicero restatur ) ex veteribus ejus gentis Legibus, & ab eo ipsissimis Legum verbis descriptum. Is ergo, post descriptas & explicatas libro superiore Leges ad Religionem & Cultum Deorum pertinentes, Tertio demum Libro pergit ad eas recensendas quae ad Rempub. & Magistratus pertinent. Ubi, inter alia, haec habentur verba; (Attendite, obsecro;) "Regio imperio duo sunto: iisque[?] praeeundo, judicando, consulendo, Praetores, Judices, Consules appellantur. Militiae summum jus habento: Nemini parento: Ollis salus Populi Suprema Lex esto." Ollis, inquit, (sic enim prisci loquebantur) id est, Illis Salus Populi Suprema Lex esto. Sed quibus tandem illis? Illis nimirum, qui Regio Imperio praediti erant, qui Militiae Jus summum habebant, qui supra se potestatem aliquam, cui parere debebant, non agnoscebant. Hoc est, binis Consulibus; qui etsi ex Constitutione illius Reipublicae annuum tantum Magistratum gerebant, Urbi tamen & Orbi Romano cum summo Imperio pro tempore praerant. Adeste hic omnes, quotquot estis ubivis gentium, Popularis audaciae patroni aut asseclae: Legite, relegite totam hanc peridum[?]; singulas expendite sententias, clausulas, commata; excutite verbula, syllabas, minutissimos quosque apices. Ubi tandem reperietis, concessi[?] subditis (invito Principe) aut de salute Populi judicandi, aut aliquid Contra Leges facienda statuendive, potestatis, vel tenue aliquod vestigium? Annon aperte clamat tota haec apud Ciceronem rerum & verborum series, supremam illam authoritatem, quae sit omni lata Lege Superior, adeoque {1}Publicae Salutis curam universam, ad eum unum specare proprie, cui & Regium Imperium competit, & Militiae jus summum, & [illegible, ~7 letters] nullique subdita ἐξουσία[?]? Id od Aristoteles etiam ( ut præstantissimorum riusque Linguæ Scriptorum hac in re con-sultum habeatis,) his verbis expressit, 3. Polit. 2. Δεῖ τὸν ἄρχοντα, ἂν τι ᾖς, ἂν τι πλείονς [?] ἐ[illegible, ~6 letters] τέτων εἶναι κυρίως, ὥσπερ ἐξαδυνατὸν οὐ νόμοις λέγειν ἀκριβῶς· ἀλλὰ τὸ μὴ ῥᾴδιον εἶναι πόλιν σηλῶσαι [?] ἀ πάντων, id est, Penes eum qui præest Reipublicæ sive sit unus sive plures, is de rebus statuendi Arbitrium & Potestatem esse, de quibus Leges accuratè [id est, in particulari] loqui non possunt, propterea quòd non sit facile universa singula complecti.
units.tr: XIX. I said a little earlier that this axioma came down to us from the Roman people. Now I add that it is found written, so far as I know, first in the third book of Marcus Cicero's De Legibus; yet it was drawn, as Cicero himself declares, from the ancient laws of that people, and copied by him in their very words. He therefore, after setting out and explaining in the preceding book the laws pertaining to religion and the worship of the gods, in the third book at last proceeds to recite those that pertain to the commonwealth and the magistrates. There, among other things, these words occur (pay attention, I beg you): "Regio imperio duo sunto: iisque praeeundo, judicando, consulendo, Praetores, Judices, Consules appellantur. Militiae summum jus habento: Nemini parento: Ollis salus Populi Suprema Lex esto." "Ollis," he says (for so the ancients spoke), that is, "Illis Salus Populi Suprema Lex esto." But who, then, are those? Surely those who were endowed with regal imperium, who held the supreme right of war, and who recognised no power above themselves to which they must obey. That is, the two consuls; who, although under the constitution of that commonwealth they held office only for a year, nevertheless presided over the City and the Roman world with supreme power for the time being. Come here, all of you, wherever you are in the world, patrons or followers of popular audacity: read and reread this whole passage; weigh each sentence, clause and phrase; examine the little words, the syllables, the very smallest marks. Where at last will you find granted to subjects, against the will of the Prince, any power, or even a faint trace of power, to judge of the safety of the people or to decide or do anything against the laws? Does not this whole sequence of matter and words in Cicero plainly declare that the supreme authority, which is superior to every law enacted, and therefore the whole care of Publicae Salutis, belongs properly to that one alone to whom both regal imperium and the supreme right of war belong, and over whom no power is set? Aristotle too expressed this in these words, so that you may have the most distinguished writers of both languages consulted on the matter, Polit. 3. 2: Δεῖ τὸν ἄρχοντα, ἂν τι ᾖς, ἂν τι πλείονς [?] ἐ[...] τέτων εἶναι κυρίως, ὥσπερ ἐξαδυνατὸν οὐ νόμοις λέγειν ἀκριβῶς· ἀλλὰ τὸ μὴ ῥᾴδιον εἶναι πόλιν σηλῶσαι [?] ἀ πάντων — that is, "In the hands of him who presides over the commonwealth, whether he be one or more, is the power and authority of deciding on those matters about which the laws cannot speak accurately [that is, in particular], because it is not easy to embrace all single cases."

units.la: XX. Excipient hic fortasse nonnulli, pessimè [?]i cum genere humano, si ex unius hominis arbitrio sic penderet omnium salus, ut non liceret quiquam in casu summæ necessitatis, eo inconsulto, suæ publicæque saluti consulere. Quid si ex casu subito & inopino res non patiatur unius diei moram? Princeps interea aliquot dierum itinere abfuerit? Dum itur, consulitur, redditur, actum erit de Republicâ, si necesse sit in tantis temporum angustiis, & locorum spatiis, Principis consensum & veniam expectari. Respondeo, videri subditis aliquid in hoc genere licere, si gravis nec aliter evitanda postulet necessitas, idque inconsulto Principe, (Necessitas enim, quod dici solet ' Legem non habet :) Nego tamen id effici, quod inde aliqui effectum velint. Dico itaque primò, quicquid juris hac in re subditis competere potest, ut scil. Legibus posthabitis publica saluti consulant, id ipsis aliunde accrescere; præsentis autem Aphorismi authoritate, velut fundamento, niti nullo modo posse, qui curandam & procurandam populi salutem uni principi relinquit, non autem ipsi populo permittit. Deinde aliud esse, inconsulto Principe, aliud eo in-eito, vito, aliquid contra Leges attentare: fieri enim illud licere debitis conditionibus observatis; hoc nullâ conditione licere. Dico secundò, Subditi si quid attentare velint in ordine ad salutem publicam, duas præ cæteris conditiones sanctissimæ esse observandas: quarum alterutram qui neglexerint, nullâ necessitatis excusatione se tueri posse. Eas quàm sanctè observarint, qui funestissimorum in hoc regno motuum vel Authores extiterunt vel Fautores, dicere non est meum: ipsi viderint. Sunt autem duæ illæ conditiones, istæ: Altera, ut quid fiat, tentetúrve fieri in Principis præjudicium, cujus persona & dignitas interest salutis publicæ, ut sartæ tectæ conserventur. Altera, ne quid militer fiat, fierive tentetur contra Leges & jura, nisi ex Principis consensu; consensu nempe, vel expresso, ubi commodè haberi potest, vel (ubi longius abest, nec res patitur moram,) rationabiliter saltem præsumpto. Tunc autem abesse Principis consensus rationabiliter præsumitur; cùm tam magna tamque {1}evidens premit necessitas, ut nemo sanus & prudens possit dubitare, Principem ipsum, si ibi tum præsens esset, Legis gratiam & relaxationem subditis concessurum.
units.tr: XX. Some may object here, and with good reason, that it would be a wretched arrangement for the human race if the safety of all depended so entirely on the will of one man that, in a case of the greatest necessity, no one might look to his own and the public safety without that man's knowledge. What if, through a sudden and unforeseen event, the matter admits of no delay of even a single day, and the Prince is meanwhile away on a journey of several days? In the time it takes to travel, consult, and send back an answer, the Commonwealth would be lost, if in such a narrow span of time and distance one had to wait for the Prince's consent and permission. I reply that it may seem lawful for subjects to do something of this kind, if grave necessity demands it and cannot otherwise be avoided, and that this may be done without the knowledge of the Prince (for necessity has no law, as the saying goes). Yet I deny that the outcome which some wish to draw from this follows. I say, therefore, first, that whatever right in this matter may belong to subjects, namely to set aside the laws and look to the public safety, comes to them from some other source; it cannot rest, as on a foundation, on the authority of the present Aphorism, for whoever leaves the care and charge of the people's safety to a single prince, and does not permit it to the people itself, cannot claim that support. Next, it is one thing to act without the knowledge of the Prince, and another to act against his will, to attempt something contrary to the laws: the former may be lawful if the proper conditions are observed; the latter is lawful on no condition. I say secondly, that if subjects wish to attempt anything for the sake of the public safety, two conditions above all others must be most sacredly observed, and whoever neglects either of them cannot shelter himself behind any plea of necessity. How faithfully those observed them, who were either the authors or the abettors of the most disastrous disturbances in this kingdom, it is not for me to say; let them see to it themselves. These two conditions are as follows. The first is that nothing be done, or attempted to be done, to the prejudice of the Prince, whose person and dignity are bound up with the public safety, so that they may be preserved whole and entire. The second is that nothing be done, or attempted to be done, contrary to the laws and rights, unless with the Prince's consent; that is, either express consent, where it can conveniently be had, or (where he is too far away and the matter admits of no delay) at least consent reasonably presumed. Now the Prince's consent is reasonably presumed to be absent only when a necessity presses so great and so evident that no sane and prudent person could doubt that the Prince himself, if he were present there at the time, would grant the subjects relaxation and indulgence of the law.

units.la: XXI. Duabus hisce conditionibus observatis, nihil aliunde aboriatur (ex particularibus scil. circumstantiis,) impedimentum, {2}licere dico subditis pro tuendâ adversus externos hostes vel domesticos perduelles, Principis & Populi salute, ad communem utilitatem spectare magis, quæ Suprema Lex est, quàm ad voces & apices Legum particularium; quæ propterea latæ sunt, ut communi utilitati inserviant, non præjudicent. Ratio manifesta est: quia media sunt propter finem, non finis propter media: & proinde media fini inservire debent, non finis inservire mediis. Quum ergo salus publica habeat rationem Finis, Leges autem
units.tr: XXI. With these two conditions observed, and no other impediment arising from the particular circumstances, I say that subjects may lawfully, in defending the safety of the Prince and the People against foreign enemies or domestic traitors, look rather to the common good, which is the Supreme Law, than to the words and letters of particular laws; which were therefore enacted to serve the common good, not to harm it. The reason is plain: means exist for the sake of the end, not the end for the sake of the means; and therefore the means ought to serve the end, not the end serve the means. Since, then, the public safety has the character of the End, while the laws have that of the means,

units.la: {2} Certum est omnia licere propatria. Quintil. declamat. 369. diorum[?] ; & certum fit in agentis intentione finem esse priorem & potiorem mediis : utrumque sequitur & communem Patriæ utilitatem Legibus quibusque particularibus anteponendam esse ; & re-ste præsumi id ipsum sentire Principem, qui in ferendis Legibus est agens Principale ; adeoque in omnia illa se inconsulto gesta vel gerenda, tacitè consentire, quæ (salvâ ipsius dignitate & jure) pro communi salute geri fierive manifesta exigit necessitas.
units.tr: {2} It is certain that all things are lawful for one's country. Quintilian, Declamation 369. And it is certain that in the intention of the one acting the end is prior to and more important than the means. Both points follow: the common good of the country is to be placed before any particular laws; and it is rightly presumed that the Prince himself thinks so, since in enacting laws he is the principal agent; and therefore, in all those things done or to be done without his knowledge, he tacitly consents, which, saving his own dignity and right, the pressing necessity demands be done or carried out for the common safety.

units.la: XXII. Exempla Historiæ passim suppeditant: quæ, quum sit rei ipsius ratio tam in aperto, ut minus necessaria prætermitto. Unicum duntaxat, sed illustre illud, dignumque quod Annalibus hujus gentis in æternam hominis memoriam inferatur, quod nostro etiam ævo nostraque aliquorum memoriâ contigit, adducam: Vicecomitis scil. Wigorniensis memorabile factum. Singulis Angliæ Provinciis, (quas majores nostri Pagos, nos Comitatus dicere solemus) præest ad aliquos juris essectus annuus Magistratus, Vicecomes dictus, custodiendæ publicæ pacis causâ potissimum institutus.
units.tr: XXII. History supplies examples everywhere, but since the reasoning of the matter is so plain, I omit the less necessary ones. I will adduce only one, but a notable one, worthy of being recorded in the annals of this nation for the everlasting memory of mankind, which also happened in our own age and within the memory of some of us: the memorable deed of the Sheriff of Worcester. Each of the English shires (which our forefathers were accustomed to call pagi, and we counties) is presided over, for certain legal purposes, by an annual magistrate called the Sheriff, appointed chiefly for the sake of keeping the public peace.

units.la: Huic Magistratui, ad tam grave munus cum effectu obeundum, concessa est (ut par erat) Legibus hujus regni militem contrahendi potestas, & cum hominibus armatis quælibet Comitatus sui loca, quoties facto est opus, adeundi & perlustrandi: ita tamen, ut ei interim non liceat cum armata manu Comitatus sui fines & terminos excedere. Post proditam insperatò (summa & singulari Dei benignitate & providentiâ) execrandam in omne ævum proditionem pulveream; ejus conjurationis conscii nonnulli inque iis è principibus totius scenæ architectis unus & alter, in agrum Wigorniensem convenerant. Hos Vicecomes vir strenuus & prudens, collecta armatorum manu, dum hac illac fugitantes persequitur, ad extrema Comitatus fui loca simul perventum esset; veritus ne illi, si is metu Legum ibi subsisteret, incolumes evaderent, ausus est (Lege non obstante) in alienam Comitatum suo confinem, militem educere: quo perduelles insecutus, eos in potestatem suam redegit, eorumque primarios, cum reliquâ turbâ, captivos secum abduxit: Ratus nimirum (id quod res erat, si vellet boni Civis officio strenuè defungi, sic sibi omninò faciendum: in eo necessitatis articulo intempestivam fore Legum observantiam: Supremam Legi, hoc est, patriae saluti, parendum; utilitati publicae omnia postponenda. Consecto hunc in modum ex animi sententiâ negotio, ne eo exemplo (quod necessitati imputandum fuit) publicarum Legum vilesceret authoritas; quinetiam gnarus quàm gravi poenae obnoxii sint in ri-gore Juris istiusmodi Legum violatores: non satis existimaverit vir prudens, in solâ rectè facti conscientiâ acquiescere, nisi & suae in posterum securitati consuleret, & nequis ipsius exemplo ad audacius aliquid fortassis attentandum abuteretur, quantum in se esset caveret. Confestim itaque ad Regem advolat, (fuit is felicis memoriae serenissimus Rex Jacobus,) ad ejus genua provolutus, violatae Legis veniam supplex petit: & prout commeritus est, à Rege prudentissimo, non tam'pro-[?]ta Legis veniam, quam antehabitae publicae salutis laudem impetravit.
units.tr: To this magistrate, so that he may carry out so grave a charge effectively, the laws of this kingdom have granted (as was fitting) the power of raising soldiers, and of going with armed men through any places in his county as often as there is need, and of searching them; yet in such a way that he may not meanwhile go beyond the bounds and limits of his county with an armed force. After the unexpected discovery (by the highest and singular goodness and providence of God) of the execrable gunpowder treason, which is to be abhorred for all time, some of those who knew of that conspiracy, and among them one or two of the chief architects of the whole plot, had gathered in the territory of Worcester. The Sheriff, a vigorous and prudent man, with a band of armed men collected, pursued them as they fled hither and thither; and when they had arrived together at the outermost parts of his county, he feared that if they remained there, out of fear of the laws, they would escape unharmed. He ventured, (the law notwithstanding), to lead his soldiers into a neighbouring county that lay beside his own; there he followed the traitors and brought them into his power, and carried off their leaders as captives with the rest of the crowd. He judged, of course, (and the fact was so: if he wished to discharge the duty of a good citizen vigorously, he must act thus in every respect) that in that critical moment of necessity obedience to the laws would be untimely: the Supreme Law, that is, the safety of the country, must be obeyed, and everything must give way to the public good. When the business had been carried through in this manner according to his own judgement, he was not content merely to rest in the consciousness of having done right. Mindful lest the authority of the public laws be cheapened by that example (which had to be attributed to necessity), and aware how grave a penalty such violators of the laws incur under the strict rigour of the law, he took care, so far as lay in him, both for his own future safety, and that no one might abuse his example to attempt something perhaps bolder. Straightway, therefore, he flew to the King (it was the most serene King James of happy memory), and, throwing himself at his knees, sought as a suppliant pardon for the violated law; and, as he deserved, he obtained from the most prudent King not so much pardon for the law as praise for the public safety he had put first.

units.la: XXIII. Exposui jam vobis, Auditores, ut amicis quibusdam obsequerer, aliquantò fusius quam soleo, quid mihi videtur de isto Axiomate sententiandum, Salus Populi Suprema Lex: Simul ut os obturetur importunis hominibus, qui (ut cum Salmone loquar,) è naso nimium compresso eliciunt sanguinem: hoc est, qui ex sententiâ, piâ sanè (si & sanè intelligatur,) atque publico salutari, perversè interpretando sensum eliciunt impium, & rebus humanis perniciosum. Summa totius rei, ut in pauca contraham, huc redit. Non si lædantur, aut injuriâ afficiantur privatæ aliquot personæ; non si sua sint subditis, de quibus etiam merito conqueri possint, publica quædam gravamina; decurrendum est statim, quasi actum aliter esset de Salute populi ad remedia adhibenda extraordinaria, & quæ sint contra Leges. Quòd si justus sit metus ab externis hostibus aut seditiosis civibus oppressum iri Rempublicam, nisi aliquid fiat, quod Legibus non est permissum: Principi fas est, ex Potestatis suæ prærogativâ, imò & Subditis fas est, ex præsumptâ Principis voluntate, (modò nihil fiat in ipsius præjudicium,) præsente necessitate ita postulante, à verbis & sententiâ particularium Legum recedere, ut periclitanti Patriæ subveniatur, ejusque saluti, ut Supremæ Legi, inserviatur. Pergam propediem (si Deus permiserit & commodè potero) quæ reliqua sunt persequi. Gratia Domini nostri Jesu Christi, &c. pericolorum. Summa totius rei, ut in pace contrahatur, hoc redit. Non si [illegible, ~3 letters] iniuria afficiantur privatae aliquae personae; [illegible, ~12 letters] de quibus enim merito requiri potest, publica quaedam praescriptiones [?] consessum est statim [illegible, ~6 letters] quale aliter effet de hac pœnali ad remedia adhibenda extraordinaria, quæ sint contra Legem. Quod si sest situs sit merus [illegible, ~4 letters] in statuto [illegible, ~5 letters] si sest crimen [?], nihil aliud fiat, quod Legibus non est præscriptum: Principi ses est, ex Præfatio præscriptio, sed si subditi ses est, ex præscripto Principe sestuntur, (modo nihil sit in ipsis præjudicium) præcipue necessitate in posse-sione, à veris se sententia persuasioni Legem suadere, ut perspicuè Partes subseruntur, equus solus, ut supremæ legi infestantur. Ergo sic si [?] pœnæ sest imperio seu commodè pos[?] quæ reliqua sunt præstant. Gratia Domini nostri Jesu Christi, &c.
units.tr: XXIII. I have now set out for you, listeners, somewhat more fully than I usually do, in order to oblige some friends, what I think should be judged about that axiom, The safety of the People is the Supreme Law; at the same time that the mouths of troublesome men may be stopped, who (to speak with Salmon) draw blood from a nose squeezed too hard; that is, who, by twisting its meaning, draw from a sentiment certainly pious (if it is rightly understood) and conducive to public welfare an impious sense, ruinous to human affairs. The sum of the whole matter, to put it in a few words, comes to this. If some private persons are hurt or wronged, or if certain public grievances arise from the faults of subjects, of which they may justly complain, one must not at once run, as if the safety of the people had been otherwise undone, to extraordinary remedies that are against the laws. But if there is a just fear that the Commonwealth will be overwhelmed by foreign enemies or seditious citizens unless something is done which the laws do not permit, then it is lawful for the Prince, by the prerogative of his power, and indeed it is lawful for subjects, by the presumed will of the Prince (provided nothing is done to his prejudice), when present necessity so demands, to depart from the words and sense of particular laws, so that the endangered country may be aided and serve its safety, which is the Supreme Law. I shall proceed shortly (if the Lord permits and I can conveniently do so) to pursue what remains. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, etc. [The passage that follows in the scan is badly garbled: the sum of the whole matter, it seems, comes to this: if some private persons are wronged, the public complaints, of which they may justly complain, ought not at once to be met by extraordinary remedies contrary to the law; if there is a just fear of the commonwealth being oppressed, nothing that the laws do not prescribe should be done; the prince may act by his prerogative, and subjects by the presumed will of the prince, provided nothing is done to his prejudice, and the necessity of the case so demands; and the rest is to follow. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.]

units.la: HUcusque, postquam ventis vela dedissem subtristi licet cœli facie, incolumis tamen (Deo auspice) in instituto cursu processeram, jamque altum mare tenebam ; certus si per tempora liceret, quâ ire occœperim pergendi : cum coorta ante oculos sæva tempestas, & jam propiùs adventare visa, admonuit, parum tutam fore in posterum omnem in alto navigationem. Sensi itaque nova protinus mihi capienda esse consilia, nec nisi mallem ventis debere ludibrium, in undoso & periculoso mari moram trahendam longiùs. Vela ergo confestim retrorsum dedi, & navim maturè subduxi in portum. Namque & mihi paulò honestius visum est, gradu cedere, quàm depelli : & rebus meis longius salutarius, privatos inter lares in otio & in umbra vivere, quàm in Foro vel Theatro cum invidia & metu versari.
units.tr: Hitherto, after I had given my sails to the winds, I had made safe progress on the course I had set (God being my guide), though the sky was somewhat gloomy, and I was already holding the open sea, certain that I could keep on along the way I had begun for as long as the times allowed. Then a savage storm arose before my eyes and seemed to be drawing closer. It warned me that all voyaging on the deep would be little safe in future. I therefore felt that I must at once adopt new plans, and that unless I wished to be made a plaything of the winds, I must not prolong my stay on the stormy and dangerous sea any longer. So I immediately turned my sails back and brought my ship in good time into harbour. For it seemed to me somewhat more honourable to yield a step than to be driven from my place, and it is far more wholesome for my affairs to live in leisure and shade among private hearths than to be engaged in the Forum or the Theatre amid envy and fear.

units.la: Hinc eadem FINIS discriminis atque laboris.
units.tr: Hence the same END of danger and toil.
